A sample of "low-fat dairy whitener" manufactured by Nestle India, drawn from the premises of Hotel Lalit in Connaught Place in the national capital, has been found "unsafe and substandard," the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) said on Saturday (October 3, 2026).
In a post on social media, the food regulator said the sample was collected from the premises of Bharat Hotels Ltd (The Lalit), Connaught Place, New Delhi.
According to the FSSAI, the report of the food analyst’s laboratory declared the product “substandard” and “unsafe,” indicating non-compliance under the Food Safety and Standards (FSS) Act, 2006.
A copy of the laboratory analysis report was provided to the food business operator (FBO) for reference and necessary action, the regulator said. A notice has also been issued to Bharat Hotels Ltd over the non-compliant product.
The FBO was given an opportunity to appeal against the food analyst's report under the relevant section of the FSS Act, 2006, within the prescribed period. The FBO has also been directed to immediately stop the sale of the identified unsafe food product, the FSSAI added.

A rumor that female employees of Cornell University coined the term "sexual harassment" in the 1970s circulated online in October.
People on social media appeared to be surprised by the claim that the term was coined only about 50 years ago. The rumor spread as Cornell was in the national spotlight due to a lawsuit accusing a group of seven male students of drugging and raping a female student in 2024. (Snopes has previously reported on what we know about the lawsuit, as well as what we've learned about the seven accused men, often referred to as the "Cornell 7.)
The claim is true.
The term "sexual harassment" first entered the cultural lexicon in the 1970s and is widely credited to a journalist named Lin Farley, then director of the women's section of the human affairs program at Cornell University and co-founder of Working Women United, a group formed to combat sexual harassment in the workplace in 1975.
According to History.com, Farley settled on the term along with her colleagues Susan Meyer and Karen Sauvigne, who also worked in Cornell's human affairs office.
The women were approached by a former Cornell secretary named Carmita Wood who had resigned after being sexually harassed by her supervisor, renowned nuclear physicist Boyce McDaniel. When she filed for unemployment benefits, Cornell declined.
As a result, Working Women United was formed and campaigned for Wood. In April 1975, Farley gave testimony before the Commission on Human Rights of New York City, a speech that was reported in an Aug. 19, 1975, New York Times article titled "Women Begin to Speak Out Against Sexual Harassment at Work."
The piece reported Farley as saying: "Sexual harassment of women in their place of employment is extremely widespread. It is literally epidemic."
The newspaper cited Farley's work at Cornell, including a survey in which "the results indicated that more than 70 percent of the 155 respondents had experienced some form of sexual harassment and that 92 percent of the group believed it was a serious problem."
The survey also reported that "more than 50 percent of the women who did complain, through channels, found that nothing was done."
In May 1975, the group organized an event called "Speak-Out on Sexual Harassment of Women at Work" with an introductory speech from Farley, who said, "My name is Lin Farley and I'd like to welcome you to the first Speak-Out ever, that I know of or anyone else knows of, on the issue of sexual harassment on the job."
In 1978, Farley published a book titled "Sexual Shakedown: The Sexual Harassment of Women on the Job," which discussed "the scope and extent of the phenomenon." She gave credit to Meyer, Sauvigne, and Wood for their contributions and activism, and noted in her preface that the human affairs program at Cornell closed in 1976, which prompted her to write the book.
In the book, Farley credited the 1975 New York Times article as the "first nationally syndicated article about male sexual harassment," writing that it resulted in women across the country joining the grassroots campaign by sharing their own experiences and ideas.
Farley published an opinion piece about the term for the Times in 2017, amid the "Me Too" movement, titled "I Coined the Term 'Sexual Harassment.' Corporations Stole It."
She wrote:
It wasn't until April 1975 that women had a word for talking about what their male bosses were doing to them.
It was that month that I first used the phrase "sexual harassment" in public, during a hearing on women in the workplace by the New York City Human Rights Commission, at which I was testifying as an instructor at Cornell University. The New York Times covered the hearing in an article that was reprinted across the country. And thus, a concept was born.
[…]
The decades since have been disappointing. The working women's revolution I once envisioned hasn't happened. But not only that, the term, which once held so much promise, has been co-opted, sanitized, stripped of its power to shock, disturb and galvanize. Today the term "sexual harassment" may be ubiquitous; the behavior, unfortunately, remains ubiquitous, too.
For further reading on the Cornell 7 case, Snopes previously wrote a breakdown of the lawsuit and investigated what has happened to the accused since the lawsuit was filed.

On any given day, Elon Musk is worth about a trillion dollars. This does not mean that he has a trillion dollar bills sitting in an old-timey vault in a dusty basement somewhere; his wealth is mostly tied up in shares of SpaceX and Tesla. But if he were to cash those out, sell Neuralink and the Boring Company, and scrounge together some extra change, his checking account would hit 13 digits.
“Trillionaire” is an easy enough word to say. It’s fun, even! Rolls off the tongue. But research has shown that the human brain has a very hard time comprehending the actual size and scope of large numbers. “Trillion” sounds like a short hop from “billion,” after all, even though it is in fact 1,000 times bigger. And even if you are somehow able to wrap your mind around that immense scale, it still feels abstract, no matter how many times you compare it to the area of Central Park or the weight of a fleet of trucks. Maybe a better way to visualize a trillion dollars, then, is through what you can actually buy with it.
WIRED has partnered with Neal Agarwal, the proprietor of the consistently delightful website Neal.fun, to do just that. Spend Elon Musk’s Money is a new visualization that lets you, well, spend Elon Musk’s money, on anything from Big Macs to aircraft carriers to the Las Vegas Sphere. It keeps a tally as you go, so you can actually see how far a trillion dollars gets you these days, and it shows the items you’ve bought in a physical space.
WIRED spoke with Agarwal about this new project, why it feels so relevant now, and the state of building things on the web. You can read that interview below, and waste a few hours on Spend Elon Musk’s money right here.
This interview has been lightly edited for clarity and length.
WIRED: I’ve known about Neal.fun for a long time, I’m a big fan. But describe it for someone who’s never been there.
Neal Agarwal: I never wanted to constrain the site to one thing, so it ended up being almost like a journal at this point. I’ve been running it since I was 19, and it’s kind of a catalog of everything I’m interested in: visualizations, science, weird game mechanics. For me, it’s mostly an exploration of what you can do with a website.
Why is that important to you, the idea of exploring what a website is and means? If there’s one thing I know about you it’s that you love the web.
Very much so. I grew up on the web; I was 8 years old on forums. I probably spent more time in Club Penguin than any real-world walls. I’m definitely a child of the web, and it’s interesting that I’m around the same age as it. It’s a privilege. Painters are working in a medium that’s a thousand years older, a million years older, so a lot of things have already been found out, been fleshed out. But on the web there’s so much that we haven’t figured out yet. I think there’s still a lot of new stuff to discover, and that’s really interesting to me.
I think every medium has distinct things you can do with it. You can turn a book into a movie but it’s not quite the same. There are some things a book is always going to be better at, and vice versa. I think that’s true of the web too. This visualization we’re working on, you can’t print it in a newspaper.
I suspect people might be familiar with some of your individual projects, if not your site itself. To list some off that are huge in my household: The Password Game, Space Elevator, The Deep Sea, Infinite Craft. When something goes viral, as so many of these have, what’s it like on your end? Is it almost boring now to see things blow up?
I think each project has been very different. The ones that excite me the most now are where a lot of people play it and start doing things with it that I did not expect or intend. Within a few days of Infinite Craft launching, people started crafting Japanese words within the game. And they crafted enough Japanese words that they could play the whole game in Japanese. I’ve never released a game before where they unlocked a language.
I had another one called Internet Road Trip; it’s like a simulated road trip but through Google Street View. A Discord formed around that, and people started backseat driving and arguing over which city to go to next, should they make a pit stop here so they can see this monument. People started birdwatching within that game. All these emergent things started happening, and I think the web is really good at that, too. It’s really good at forming communities out of the silliest things, which I find really exciting.
There’s also this contrast with a more closed-off app environment; you don’t really work in apps as a medium.
When I was a teenager I did make some apps, but I always really disliked that Apple and Google had to approve what I could put in them, and you have to wait a week for approval, and if they don’t like your app you have no recourse. So just the idea of having a homepage where it’s like, this is my homepage. Nobody can tell me what to do with it. I can put whatever I want.
We should talk about this visualization, Spend Elon Musk’s Money. It’s sort of a sequel to Spend Bill Gates’ Money, which was one of your first projects, right?
That actually launched with the website itself. I just wanted to showcase how much $100 billion was, which I guess now seems like a little amount of money compared to the trillion we’re working with.
It’s almost quaint, right? The premise is you’ve got a $100 billion counter and a bunch of things you can buy with prices attached to them: a Big Mac, flip-flops, a lobster dinner, a year of Netflix, all the way up to things like a diamond ring, a Ferrari, a McDonald’s franchise, and then up again to the Mona Lisa. And you just keep trying to add it up. What was the response to that game when it first launched?
It was one of the biggest things I’ve launched, and it was really nice to see that the point got across. People understood that this is a way to visualize wealth that isn’t just graphs and bar charts. The game kept finding a new audience over and over again; it was an idea that kept being interesting to people.
And then we come to 2026, and we have a trillionaire in the world, and it felt like maybe the right time to revisit.
Yeah, I think so. There’s a lot more you can do to visualize that, too. That’s why this one is 3D. I think one thing with Spend Bill Gates’ money is, yeah, you can buy 10,000 cars, but it’s still a number on a screen. With Spend Elon Musk’s Money, I want you to see the cars you’re buying on a screen. The amount of physical stuff you can buy—it is an empire.
One thing that I certainly have a hard time with, and I think most people do, is really wrapping your head around what a trillion is. There’s been research that humans are really bad at processing how big the jumps are even from 1 billion to 2 billion, much less getting up to a trillion. Our brains just break.
I think that’s one thing the web is actually really good at, is that you have infinite space. You can visualize these numbers in ways that you can’t do in the physical world. Even for my project The Deep Sea, it’s a 1:1 of the ocean. If you wanted to print that out on paper, it would be a mile long, but on the web you can just keep scrolling and scrolling. So it’s kind of fun to have this infinite scroll mechanic to visualize these huge numbers.
Some of the items carry over from Spend Bill Gates Money, some are different. How did you think about the best mix of options to give people?
This time I was going for more tangible things, so you can visualize it. It’s honestly hard to think of items; once you get to $100 million, there are only so many things out on the market that you can buy. So we have the Las Vegas Sphere in there, and aircraft carriers.
After a point it’s kind of interesting that you’re like, OK, I could buy 1,000 more tanks, what would that really get me? Part of the fun of this one is just the futility of it. At a certain point, what more could a person need?
For sure. I just bought 1,000 monster trucks, and I still have $999,650,000 left.
There were a few different ideas. One is if you had a trillion dollars and just had a stack of money, and as you spend it you see the trillion dollars go down, but it’s actually pretty hard to render a trillion dollars in bills on the page.
I had thoughts of more abstract things. Once you get to a trillion dollars you’re really buying power, so how many companies you could buy or how much influence you have. But for most people, that’s a harder way to visualize things than, like, oh, that is a million racehorses I just bought.
Did you run into any technical challenges building this?
Initially I wanted everything to be 3D models on the site. But if you try to get your laptop to render a million monster trucks, it’s just going to freeze. So I had to do a lot of trickery to get this 3D effect without actually using 3D models.
It doesn’t just tell us about Elon Musk, it tells us about the things we’re buying. I looked back at the original Spend Bill Gates’ Money, and the Big Mac was $2. It’s $6 now. For anything where there’s a direct parallel, you’ve captured a real price jump.
It’s very inflation-adjusted. Which is crazy, because it’s only been six or seven years. If anyone has any recommendations about other items we should add to this, just let me know.

At least one listing postponed, while bankers scramble for investors to keep other offerings on track, according to sources
3-MIN READ3-MIN
Exuberance among cornerstone investors in Hong Kong’s booming initial public offering (IPO) market seems to be fading, forcing some issuers that had hoped to list this month to postpone their offerings.
With more than 60 per cent of new listings in the third quarter now trading below their issue prices, cornerstone investors – who typically receive guaranteed allocations in exchange for holding shares for six months – are reconsidering whether to subscribe to coming deals, according to people familiar with the matter.
At least one IPO originally planned for October had to be delayed until next month at the earliest after some institutional investors pulled out of verbal agreements to be cornerstone backers, they said.

A partial building collapse in Istanbul traps at least 7 people, including a child
A seven-story building in Istanbul has partially collapsed, trapping at least seven people, including a 6-year-old
ISTANBUL -- A seven-story building in Istanbul partially collapsed on Thursday, trapping at least seven people inside, including a 6-year-old, officials said.
The reason for the collapse was not immediately known and an investigation was underway. Rescue teams were working to reach those trapped even as there were warnings of a further collapse of the building.
The building’s three lower floors, including a ground-floor shop, caved in before dawn in the district of Maltepe, on the Asian side of Istanbul, a city that is bisected by the Bosporus Strait.
Residents from the upper floors were safely evacuated while rescue teams pulled five more people from the rubble and were continuing with efforts to reach the seven others, said Davut Gul, the governor of Istanbul.
Gul said rescuers had made contact with a 6-year-old trapped in the rubble but were unable to get to the child from their current location and were now trying a different approach.
He warned that the building was at risk of further collapse, hampering the rescue efforts. Nearby buildings were also evacuated for safety, the governor said.
Istanbul and other parts of Turkey are undergoing an urban transformation program that aims to replace old and earthquake-risky buildings with safer housing.

Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.
An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.
If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.
The plans were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.
But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.
Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.
Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.
Why it became Guimaraes and not Anderson, Tonali or Scott
Bruno Guimaraes's £75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.
Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.
For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.
Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.
At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.
But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum £92m - made their signings difficult.
Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.
By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.
Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.
Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.
It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.
For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.
But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.
That said, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.
Konsa was first-choice defensive option
The signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.
Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.
Konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.
But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a £40m offer, which was duly rejected.
Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at £51m, with £4m in add-ons.
In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets – but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.
Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.
Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.
In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about £35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.
It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.
Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.
So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.
Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.
The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined £126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.
Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.
Arsenal miss out on marque attacker
While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.
Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.
At the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at £100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at £80m.
Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.
In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.
Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.
Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.
Anderson's move from Forest to City for £116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.
Villa increased their valuation to £120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for £117m.
Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their £80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.
Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.
Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a new contract at Real Madrid.
Berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.
While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.
Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.
Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a new long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.
There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.
The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.
But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.
Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.
Did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.
When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.
Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.
It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.
For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is currently second-choice striker.
This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.
Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.
It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.
Arsenal will move towards player trading model
Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.
Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.
Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.
Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.
There was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose £60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.
The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of £114m.
Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about £80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.
Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.
Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.
As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.
The minimum £15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.
Having spent nearly £450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.
Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear issues in the squad - certainly in attack.
The summer window has left many supporters feeling questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.
And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

Kamal Haasan has paid tribute to veteran actor Nana Patekar following his demise on Thursday, October 8. Remembering the late actor as both a remarkable performer and a person committed to helping others, Kamal shared a photograph with Nana Patekar on X and penned an emotional note.
Kamal Haasan mourns the demise of Nana Patekar; calls him “an extraordinary artist and an even greater human being”
Sharing the fond memory, Kamal Haasan wrote, “Heartbreaking news of Nana Patekar Ji’s passing. An extraordinary artist and an even greater human being. The man was a force of nature, and he uplifted the lives of those around him. Beyond the screen, his work helping farmers in Maharashtra and his volunteer service during the Kargil War spoke volumes about his deep sense of duty. My deepest condolences to his family and his legions of fans.”

Nana Patekar, a Padma Shri recipient and one of the most recognised actors of Hindi and Marathi cinema, passed away in the early hours of Thursday at the age of 75. According to the details shared following his demise, the veteran actor suffered a severe cardiac arrest at his residence in Dona Paula, Goa.
After being found unresponsive, Nana Patekar was rushed to Manipal Hospital, where medical personnel reportedly attempted cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) for around 45 minutes. He could not be revived and was declared dead at approximately 5:20 AM IST. His son, Malhar Patekar, confirmed the news shortly afterwards.
The actor’s mortal remains are being transferred from Goa to Pune, where his last rites are scheduled to take place at his farmhouse in Donje on the outskirts of the city.
The Maharashtra government has announced that Nana Patekar will be accorded a state funeral with full state honours. The honour recognises his contribution to Indian cinema as well as his social welfare efforts through the Naam Foundation.
As tributes continue to come in from across the film industry, Kamal Haasan’s message highlighted not only Nana Patekar’s legacy as an actor but also his work beyond cinema. His contribution to farmers in Maharashtra and his volunteer service during the Kargil War were among the aspects of his life remembered by the veteran actor.

As an Indian woman, I often feel myself oscillating between states of anxiety or anger. The anxiety is about doing the mental maths of how to stay safe – thinking about what I’m wearing, where I am going and how I’ll get there, and so on. The anger is at the sheer absurdity of this, and the stories of of sexual violence and harassment I read about every day. I am not the only one.
Last week, two particularly enraging incidents captured national attention. First, a video showing a group of men accused of harassing and molesting two teenagers at night in Bihar’s Jamui went viral. Then, a 17-year-old, out with a friend in Delhi, was allegedly gang-raped in a park by men posing as police. After, women in Bihar told Outlook how the incident in Jamui triggers greater controls and pressure on them. In Delhi, authorities curbed access to public parks and a premier women’s college, Lady Shri Ram College (LSR), briefly moved classes online.
I have noticed this pattern repeatedly: after incidents of sexual violence go viral on social media, the fallout further ensnares women. We are the ones who get told to avoid certain places, regulate our behaviour, dress modestly or be home earlier, thereby placing the burden of escaping this menace on us. Feminist activist Kavita Krishnan has described this phenomenon as “perhaps the most widespread form of gender-based violence in India”.
Instead of figuring out why sexual violence remains entrenched in our society, how patriarchal agency perpetuates such violence or what kind of social conditioning is needed for men, women are instead expected to take up less public space. (It is another matter that women might not be safe even inside their own homes.)
Regulating women is easy because “it does not require any institutional cost and, most of all, it sends the signal to concerned parents that the problem is being handled”, says Meena Kandasamy, a feminist author, whose latest novel, Fieldwork As a Sex Object, is about a woman’s life being upturned when a deepfake video using her face goes viral. “Their target audience is not the young women who feel unsafe but the rest of society.”
In my experience, this repression happens at three levels: first in the realm of family, then in broader society, and ultimately by the state. It begins at home, under the guise of protection, with arbitrary curfews or dress codes. It gets reinforced at a community level with institutions and social groups through moral policing, victim-blaming and the expectation that women should not put themselves in “unsafe” situations.
Then there is the response of the state. Restricting access to parks after sunset can surely reduce the number of people in those places, but it doesn’t address why women are unsafe there. Harassment and sexual violence are, unfortunately, not tied to timings or daylight. And further restricting women’s lives is not the solution to injustices foisted on them. All three, Kandasamy says, consider women as a “problem to be handled”.
“She’s not a citizen (for the state), a member (for the community), or an adult (for the family). She is treated like an inanimate but precious object – like a diamond that has to be locked up to prevent theft,” she said.
‘Moral policing’ of the wrong target
Women, however, are pushing back against this approach. In recent days, students from Delhi University have come out on the streets demanding safer public spaces including more street lighting, usable public toilets, more housing and scholarships for female students. Vedayana, 20, a student at Lady Shri Ram College (LSR), says locking up parks is not the solution: “If you are not putting up safety measures to make it accessible to women, then it is as good as saying that the park is only for men.”
The scale of the issue is devastatingly clear. A recently published survey of more than 4,000 women in New Delhi and Bengaluru, found that 65% of women in New Delhi and 29% in Bengaluru experienced harassment in public spaces in the past year.
Another 2024 study from India and Pakistan found that women’s overall mobility remains abysmally low, and what freedom they do have is almost entirely tied to education, employment or unpaid care work. Substantive mobility for leisure or pleasure is practically nonexistent.
Despite how widespread and urgent the problem is, the political response can further shake public confidence. A female minister from Bihar, commenting on the molestation video said: “Moral policing can be done in a more decent and elegant fashion.” Another minister from the state drew fire for describing it as an “isolated” incident”.
Minimising crimes against women reflects a political culture in which accountability becomes optional. Students such as Vedayana want this to change. Political parties, she tells me, should pledge to not give tickets or positions to anyone accused of sexual harassment. “We don’t want the leaders sitting at the top to perpetrate and preach rape culture,” she adds.
Parliament is not immune to accusations, either: the BJP politician Brij Bhushan Singh, who formerly headed the Wrestling Federation of India, was recently accused of sexual harassment by six female wrestlers – he denies the allegations, and was acquitted by a magistrate, in a case that is undergoing appeal. According to an analysis of 2024 parliamentarians by the Association for Democratic Reforms, 15 winning candidates declared cases related to crimes against women.
For Vedayana, changing the mentality has to begin early with families and the way boys are raised. “If you are in a position of authority, use it to influence people by speaking out against patriarchy and groom your sons first.”
What else we’re reading about
Golden girls | Indian women’s cricket team beat Sri Lanka by 147 runs to win gold at the Asian Games last week. Smriti Mandhana’s smashing 79 off 45 deliveries helped India reach a formidable 216 in 20 overs. Deepti Sharma’s three-wicket haul helped India end Sri Lanka’s hopes with just 69 runs on board. Sri Lanka settled for silver, while Pakistan claimed the bronze after beating Bangladesh.
Moma | A solo exhibition by one of south Asia’s most distinguished artists, Nilima Sheikh, opened at New York’s Museum of Modern Art at the weekend. Fractured Skies, presented in collaboration with the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art in Delhi, will run until next June.
EC under fire | An explosive Indian Express investigation has revealed how two of the top three election officials objected at least 14 times over a period of 10 months to changes made by the Election Commission over its controversial exercise that has struck 130 million people from the voter rolls.
Count it
A number worth knowing
105
An inquiry committee probing the theft of donations from Ayodhya’s Ram Temple has uncovered 105 instances of cash being removed or concealed. The thefts were caught on CCTV cameras.
According to a preliminary report, some of the accused allegedly hid the money on themselves during the process of counting donations and then walked out.
Vibe check
Tony Klor’s city vlogs from Indian towns are “hella dope,” to use his own words. The 32-year-old American has visited about 200 cities around the country, taking his Instagram followers to places that rarely feature on a travel itinerary.
It’s a treat to watch him having the time of his life. He marched with Anganwadi workers in Nashik chanting “pay my didis”, ribbed with middle-aged uncles sweating it out in a park, whom he christened “Nizamaddies”. Wandering through the mining town of Ballari, which he describes as “highkey vibey”, he films its temple, church and mosque.
“A lot of people who watch my videos are Indians and they have no idea about these magnificent places in India,” the tech professional-turned-content creator says. “India is like the easiest place to make a friend in the world. People invite me to their weddings on the street that I met five minutes before that. Hospitality is so, so next-level.”

Elaborate arrangements are being made as the Dasara celebrations at Sri Durga Malleswara Swamy Varla Devasthanam, Vijayawada Utsav and the National Saras Aajeevika Mela would be organised simultaneously in the city, NTR District Collector G. Lakshmisha has said.
The Collector, along with Society For Elimination of Rural Poverty (SERP) CEO Vakati Karuna, National Rural Livelihoods Mission(NRLM) Director Molishree and Joint Collector S. Ilakkiya, reviewed the arrangements being made at Punnami Ghat, the veue for the mela, on Thursday, October 8.
Addressing the media later, Mr. Lakshmisha said up to 600 stalls would be set up, showcasing a wide range of handicrafts, handloom products and other articles made by women of self-help groups from across the country during the mela, to be held from October 13 to 31.
He said the mela was being organised by the Union and State governments to provide a platform for women self-help groups and artisans to market their products and promote their livelihoods. The stalls would showcase the culture, traditions, traditional arts and rural lifestyles of different States, he said.
The Collector appealed to people from Vijayawada and NTR district, as well as visitors from other places, to visit the mela and encourage products made by women SHGs from different States.
President Droupadi Murmu and dignitaries from other States are expected to participate in the event.
Local public representatives and officials were working together to ensure the successful conduct of all three events, he added.

Japan was named the world’s most attractive country for the fourth consecutive year, according to survey results released Wednesday, extending a winning streak as record numbers of overseas visitors continue to flock to the country.
Japan took the top spot in the U.S edition of the magazine Conde Nast Traveler’s Readers’ Choice Awards for “Best Countries in the World.”
Italy ranked second, followed by Ireland, Cambodia and Spain.
The results demonstrate the country’s enduring appeal among international travelers as inbound tourism continues to surge. A record 42.7 million overseas visitors came to Japan in 2025, according to justice ministry figures.
Tokyo’s Haneda Airport was ranked the sixth best in the world, with Singapore’s Changi Airport taking the top place.
In a news release Wednesday, the Japan National Tourism Organization (JNTO) said Japan’s strong showing reflected not only the appeal of its tourism resources, but also qualities distinctive to Japan, such as its hospitality and safety.
“We hope that this continued international recognition will generate even greater interest in Japan and encourage more people to visit,” the organization wrote.
Conde Nast Traveler readers cast 798,867 votes in this year’s awards, the magazine’s 39th edition. The awards, held annually since 1988, rank destinations and travel experiences based on readers’ overall evaluations, with voting across categories including countries, hotels and cruises.
In the magazine’s U.K. edition of the rankings, Japan placed second behind Greece, with Italy, Turkey and Portugal completing the top five. The magazine highlighted the country’s restaurants, hot springs, cherry blossoms and high-speed rail network, as well as its mix of traditional culture, design and technological innovation.
“We will continue to showcase the unique attractions of regions across Japan, including their nature, culture, and cuisine, to audiences around the world, while encouraging travel to regional destinations and working toward sustainable tourism,” JNTO wrote.

Cummins not worried about potential Khawaja revelations
- Published
Pat Cummins has spoken to Usman Khawaja about his former team-mate's upcoming autobiography, but the Australia captain said he has no concerns about potential sandpapergate revelations.
On Friday, Australia will begin their first Test series in South Africa since the ball-tampering scandal erupted in Cape Town in 2018.
At the time, captain Steve Smith, vice-captain David Warner and batter Cameron Bancroft were banned for their part in the plot.
Since then, the four Australia bowlers who played in that match, including Cummins, have denied they had any prior knowledge of the plan to cheat.
The quartet, who released a joint statement about the episode in 2021, are once again set to be united in the first Test against South Africa in Durban.
Khawaja played in all four Tests in 2018 and retired from international cricket in January. His autobiography will be released in November.
"Uz gave me a buzz a few weeks back that he is releasing a book," said Cummins. "He didn't go into too much detail, just basically gave me the heads-up that he is doing a book and, as always, no worries.
"Tell your story. It's fine. It's obviously a long time ago and all the investigations, everything was done back then and we answered every question a million times.
"It was dealt with then and all I can say is that as a group, we have moved on and we are very happy with the last eight to nine years how we have been as a group and evolved and obviously my focus is on captaining the cricket team."
At the time of the ball-tampering controversy, Smith explained it was devised by the "leadership group" of the Australian team on the third day of the third Test in Cape Town. Bancroft was caught rubbing sandpaper on the ball the same day.
While Smith, Warner and Bancroft – all batters – were punished, there was never an explanation of how bowlers Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon did not notice a change in the state of the ball.
In a 2021 interview with the Guardian, Bancroft was asked if the bowlers knew and replied: "It's pretty probably self-explanatory."

Days after Bancroft's interview was published, Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood and Lyon released their statement which said: "We feel compelled to put the key facts on the record again.
"We did not know a foreign substance was taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball until we saw the images on the big screen at Newlands.
"And to those who, despite the absence of evidence, insist that 'we must have known' about the use of a foreign substance simply because we are bowlers, we say this: The umpires during that Test match, Nigel Llong and Richard Illingworth, both very respected and experienced umpires, inspected the ball after the images surfaced on the TV coverage and did not change it because there was no sign of damage.
"We respectfully request an end to the rumour-mongering and innuendo. It has gone on too long and it is time to move on."
Earlier this week, left-arm seamer Starc referenced the scandal when he said: "What's left to come out after eight years?"
And, speaking on Thursday, Cummins said the episode was "a long time ago".
"It's nothing new," the 33-year-old told ABC. "We've spoken about it a little bit. If the crowd gets rowdy or whatever, if someone needs an extra helping hand, we're around.
"To be honest, it's so long ago and we, as a group, move on from things pretty quickly. It hasn't taken up too much of our time."
The trip to South Africa is the first in a year of high-profile away series for Australia. After what appears to be a stern challenge against New Zealand in their home summer, Cummins' men then travel to India and defend the Ashes in England next year.
With all-rounder Cameron Green ruled out because of injury, the tourists are likely to choose between Cooper Connolly and Nic Maddinson for a place in the middle order.
On a Durban pitch expected to turn, South Africa have included two spinners – Keshav Maharaj and Simon Harmer - in their XI.

For a while, those hoping to avoid the difficulty and expense of dealing with Adobe’s Creative Suite have been able to use several free and/or open-source alternatives that replicate some or all of those capabilities. Now, one developer is using AI-powered reverse engineering to mimic the look, feel, and functionality of Adobe’s well-known software with what he hopes will soon be perfect fidelity.
Artcraft got its start last year as a “controllable AI for artists” that allows for precise post-generation editing of AI-crafted images and videos. Over the weekend, though, the brand debuted its pivot to a suite of seven open source apps recreating the user interface and tools found in Adobe’s Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, Lightroom, After Effects, InDesign, and Acrobat Pro.
In announcing those new apps on Reddit earlier this week, software developer Brandon Thomas said he used Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 to create “clean-room replacements” for Adobe’s closed source software in Rust (with WebAssembly versions available for use in a browser). And while commenters on Hacker News and elsewhere have taken pains to point out the new software’s many current shortcomings, Thomas make the grandiose promise that the current “super early alpha” state will soon lead to something just as functional as anything Adobe has ever put out.
“We’re going to reach 100% [feature] parity within a month,” Thomas stated on Reddit of his plans to quickly squash bugs and add features with the help of community reports. Days later, on Hacker News, he amended that position slightly to say that “99% parity will take a while, but I’m sure it’ll be measured in months and not years.”

At a promotional event in Times Square on Wednesday for the security company NordVPN, brand ambassador Shaquille O’Neal said he is eager to raise awareness among regular people about the importance of digital security and personal privacy.
“I have a video of me beating up Charles Barkley, and I wouldn't want the world to see that. That was a joke,” O'Neal says. “But everybody needs to have control of their own information.”
After being targeted by scammers who claimed that he was trying to buy a house and they were working on the transaction, O’Neal says, he realized he needed to learn more about cybersecurity and digital defense.
“I was hacked for the first time, not a bad hack, and I didn't know what to do,” he told reporters. “So I had to look into it. Once that happened, I really had to start paying more attention, because I would think nothing like that could ever happen to me, but it could happen to anybody.”
O'Neal, of course, is not just anybody. Still, the four-time NBA champion and media personality says that he doesn't have particularly sensitive data on his devices and tries to live a normal life as much as possible. When WIRED asked, though, whether he worries that he needs to take extra precautions to protect himself and loved ones as a result of his high profile, O'Neal said, “Yes, I think about it all the time, but I don't let it consume me, because if you let it consume you you can go crazy. But you have to be able to have great reactionary skills if something happens.”
A prolific tech investor who was early to AI, O'Neal emphasizes that the goal of his relationship with NordVPN is to inform the public and help people protect themselves. NordVPN is, well, known for its VPN. But the company has other offerings, including antivirus, threat detection, and scam-defense products that are geared toward accessibility for consumers. Marijus Briedis, the company's chief technology officer, says he was surprised by the findings of a recent NordVPN poll showing that 73 percent of Americans have an overconfidence in traditional antivirus and believe it can protect them against anything from identity theft to online tracking.
“The weakest link is between the computer and the chair, and I've been thinking so much about how to solve that problem,” Briedis told WIRED. “So the thing we are doing right now is focusing on education. It's a really interesting problem, how to do it in the best way. It's still haunting me in my dreams.”

Bengaluru-based quantum compute startup Quanfluence has raised $10 Mn (around ₹92 Cr) in a funding round led by Chiratae Ventures, with participation Rainmatter by Zerodha and existing backer Pi Ventures. Quanfluence plans to deploy the fresh capital to further develop its full-stack photonic quantum computing system, bringing together indigenously designed photonic chips, control electronics and software into a single architecture. The startup is targeting early processors by 2027, followed by larger and scalable quantum machines by 2029. Founded in 2021 by Sujoy Chakravarty, Ravi Mehta, Biman Chattopadhyay, Aditi Vaidya, Anil Prabhaka, and Sandeep Goyal, Quanfluence is building a universal photonic quantum computer and has deployed a quantum-inspired optical Ising machine. The IIT-Madras incubated startup’s core technology includes an optical Ising machine that uses light waves as computational units. The system can process hundreds of interconnected variables simultaneously, making it 100X faster than traditional optimisation methods. Chakravarty told Inc42 that Quanfluence has already commercialised its optical Ising machine, selling the physical systems to customers as well as offering remote access to the machines on a usage-based model. The startup has sold around three machines and currently runs paid pilots with 10-15 corporations. The approach could help Quanfluence generate commercial traction while it works on the significantly harder problem of building a scalable universal quantum computer. The startup's immediate challenge, however, is less about proving the underlying concept and more about integrating its components, scaling manufacturing and navigating long chip-production and hardware-delivery cycles. With a current team size of 25 employees, it is expecting to scale their workforce to 40-member team over the next year. Previously, Quanfluence raised $2 Mn (around ₹16.7 Cr) in a seed funding round in December 2024, to scale up its near-term products and accelerate development of its quantum computer. Since then, the startup has designed and fabricated multiple photonic integrated circuits (PICs) and electronic integrated circuits (EICs). It has also developed low-loss chip-to-fibre coupling designs and demonstrated the generation of quantum light states. The funding comes as investors increasingly look at exploring deeptech bets that are moving towards commercial and industrial applications. Quantum computing is still largely at the experimental stage, with the industry yet to achieve the scale required for widespread commercial workloads. Quanfluence is taking a photonics-led approach to this challenge, betting that its architecture can eventually scale from a prototype to systems with millions of qubits. The development also comes as India's National Quantum Mission is creating closer links between startups, researchers and government-backed quantum hubs. Quantum cybersecurity startup QNu Labs recently raised ₹200 Cr (around $21 Mn) in its Series A1 funding round co-led by the state-backed National Quantum Mission and Speciale Invest, in September.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi has urged global tech companies, financial institutions and telecom operators to collaborate and form a comprehensive framework to curb cyber fraud and deep fakes. “At a time when telecom and digital technology have become so important, it is equally important to make the security framework associated with it ironclad. It is our priority to secure mobile phones and networks… trust is very important for ordinary citizens communicating or making payments through the phone,” PM Modi said. Speaking at the India Mobile Congress 2026, the PM highlighted India’s successful endeavour to protect citizens from cyber attacks and frauds, noting that global cooperation is required to nip the issue in the bud, especially as most such operations are borderless. He urged the GSM Association (GSMA), which is a global advocacy group for the telecom industry, and global telecom operators, to create a global mechanism that can potentially prevent cyber fraud before it reaches the masses. He also offered India’s deep expertise in the area to global regulators, noting that authorities in the country have gained vast knowledge on fighting cyber crime. He further noted that the discussions held during the IMC’s tenth edition this year will create a map for how the next decade of telecom will look like, in India and globally. India’s Cyber Fraud Battle The country has grappled with rising cyber fraud over the past few years, with Indians losing ₹3,588.2 Cr in more than 5.83 Lakh digital payment fraud cases between FY22 and FY26. The government has consequently taken several steps to curb such frauds, including a dedicated portal to report suspected crime. The Sanchar Saathi portal has received 12.8 Lakh inputs on suspected fraud communications since launch in 2023. The Centre announced this week that suspected cyber-fraud losses of more than ₹5,000 Cr were prevented through the Financial Fraud Risk Indicator (FRI). Nevertheless, nearly 7.1% of the attempted digital consumer transactions in India were suspected fraud in 2025, almost double the equivalent rate globally (3.8%). To curb this, union home minister Amit Shah directed officials to improve the National Cybercrime Helpline using AI to ease the process of reporting cybercrimes. He also called for addressing the issues related to bank accounts being frozen as part of cyber fraud investigations. The RBI has also come up with a compensation mechanism to aid fraud victims, under which the Centre and bank operators shoulder parts of the unrecovered losses. Customers, losing up to ₹50,000 in cybercrime cases, would be eligible for compensation of up to 85% of the net loss amount or ₹25,000, whichever is lesser.

Srinagar, Oct 7: Several key leadership positions in Jammu and Kashmir’s power sector have remained vacant or are being managed through additional charge arrangements, raising concerns over decision-making and administrative efficiency, according to the Jammu & Kashmir Electrical Engineering Graduates Association (JKEEGA).
The association has sought the intervention of Chief Minister Omar Abdullah, who also holds the Power portfolio, for filling the vacant positions on a regular basis.
According to JKEEGA, the posts of Managing Director of JKPTCL and JKPCL remain vacant or are being managed through additional charge. The post of Joint Managing Director, Chenab Valley Power Projects Limited (CVPPL), is also vacant.
The association said all four Executive Director (Electrical) posts in KPDCL, JPDCL, JKPTCL and JKPDC have remained vacant since the unbundling of the erstwhile Power Development Department. Two Chief Engineer posts and the post of Secretary (Technical) are also vacant.
JKEEGA said vacancies have also persisted at the levels of Superintending Engineer, Executive Engineer, Assistant Executive Engineer and Assistant Engineer.
The association said prolonged vacancies at senior levels were placing additional responsibilities on serving officers and could delay administrative and technical decisions related to project execution, financial management, transmission and distribution reforms and loss reduction.
JKEEGA General Secretary ErPirzada Hidayatullah urged the Chief Minister to intervene and ensure early appointments to the key positions.
He said stable institutional leadership was essential for improving accountability and strengthening public service delivery in the power sector. Hidayatullah reiterated the association’s willingness to work with the government on measures aimed at strengthening the sector.

Hyderabad-based B2B edtech startup byteXL has raised $9 Mn (about ₹86.7 Cr) in a funding round led by Elevar Equity, with participation from existing investors Kalaari Capital and The Michael & Susan Dell Foundation. The startup will use the capital to expand its college network, strengthen its technology and AI learning platform, build its academic and delivery teams, and introduce industry-aligned skilling programmes. Over the next two years, byteXL plans to grow its network from 40 institutions to 120 and expand its reach from 2 Lakh students to 5 Lakh across 15 states. It also plans to strengthen its institutional partnership teams to support the expansion. The latest investment follows its $5.9 Mn Series A round in July 2024, led by Kalaari Capital, with participation from the Dell Foundation. Founded in 2019 by brothers Karun and Sricharan Tadepalli, byteXL works with engineering colleges, particularly in Tier II and III cities, to integrate industry-relevant technology and AI training into students’ regular coursework. Its B2B model combines curriculum, hands-on learning, technology platforms, and trained educators within the college system. The startup said 7,600 of its graduates secured IT and engineering jobs last year. byteXL operates in the broader skilling and employability segment alongside players such as Emversity, Seekho.ai, SmartBridge, iNurture, Board Infinity, and Imarticus Learning. The fundraise comes amid a prolonged funding slowdown and consolidation in India’s edtech sector. According to Inc42’s ‘Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, Q3 2026’, the sector recorded three acquisitions during the quarter, including upGrad’s $200–210 Mn acquisition of Unacademy and Imarticus Learning’s $84 Mn acquisition of BELLS. Meanwhile, IMARC estimates India’s edtech market to grow from $4.60 Bn in 2026 to $33.31 Bn by 2034, at a CAGR of 27.94% during 2026-2034

Burmese network behind large-scale areca nut smuggling via Mizoram: ED probe
As part of the probe, the agency said it has attached a hotel, residential land and other landed properties situated in and around Champhai in Mizoram.
The Enforcement Directorate’s (ED) investigation into large-scale smuggling of dry areca nuts from Myanmar into India via Mizoram has found that an organised network of Burmese suppliers moved the consignments through the Tiau River and border areas around Zokhawthar and Champhai, officials familiar with the details said.
The probe has revealed alleged smuggling of 3103MT of dry areca nuts worth ₹1,022.25 crore, with alleged loss of basic customs duty estimated at ₹408 crore, the officials added.
The federal financial crimes probe agency has attached 10 properties worth ₹8.12 crore, including a hotel in Champhai, in the case.
The money laundering probe stems from the Central Bureau of Investigation’s (CBI) 2025 First Information Report (FIR) that alleged large-scale smuggling of dry areca nuts from Myanmar into India through Mizoram by use of fraudulent e-way bills, forged documents and other means.
“Investigation has revealed that an organised network wherein Myanmar suppliers smuggled areca nuts into India through the Tiau River and border areas around Zokhawthar/Champhai. Local facilitators based in Mizoram procured the smuggled areca nuts, arranged their storage and transportation and facilitated their onward movement towards Assam and other destinations. Investigation also revealed alleged use of local persons as claimants or owners of intercepted consignments before Customs authorities and routing of substantial funds through bank accounts and money exchangers for settlement of payments with suppliers situated in Myanmar,” ED said in a statement on Wednesday.
“The investigation revealed alleged smuggling of 3103MT (approx.) of dry areca nuts, having an assessable value of about Rs. 1,022.25 Crore, resulting in alleged loss of Basic Customs Duty of Rs. 408.90 Crore,” it added.
The investigation under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, scrutiny of bank accounts and examination of material seized during searches revealed substantial financial transactions, cash deposits and withdrawals and acquisition of immovable properties out of proceeds generated from the smuggling activities, ED said.
As part of the probe, the agency said it has attached a hotel, residential land and other landed properties situated in and around Champhai in Mizoram.
