Sri Lanka's ex-first lady arrested over alleged misuse of children's hospital donations
- Published
Sri Lanka's former first lady Shiranthi Rajapaksa has been arrested over allegations that a charity she is linked to misused donations raised for a children's hospital.
Anti-corruption authorities arrested the 73-year-old wife of former President Mahinda Rajapaksa at their Colombo home on Wednesday.
They are questioning her over the 10 million rupees ($30,300; £22,800) of donations collected by the Siriliya Saviya charity, meant to be spent on a specialised scanner for Colombo's Lady Ridgeway Children's Hospital.
But officials say such a scanner had already been donated by the Chinese government.
Shiranthi Rajapaksa has denied any wrongdoing and says the money has not been appropriated.
She returned to Sri Lanka on Monday from Singapore, where she was receiving medical treatment. She had filed a court petition to try to prevent her arrest, but the hearing was set for 12 October.
Ex-President Mahinda Rajapaksa's spokesperson, Manoj Gamage, has said the money is safe in Siriliya's accounts and that no fraud has occurred.
Mahinda Rajapaksa served as president of Sri Lanka from 2005 to 2015 and for years, his family held a tight grip over the country's politics. He was hailed by many as a hero for bringing an end to nearly three decades of civil war when Tamil Tiger rebels were crushed in 2009, during his first term as president.
But in 2022, protests broke out across the country as inflation surged and Sri Lanka ran out of fuel, food and medicine.
Mahinda's brother Gotabaya Rajapaksa, who was serving as leader at that time, was eventually toppled.
Sri Lanka's current government, under President Anura Kumara Dissanayake, has since revived long-stalled corruption investigations involving various members of the Rajapaksa family.
Mahinda and Shiranthi's eldest son, Namal Rajapaksa, was arrested earlier this year over allegations linked to an aircraft procurement deal made during his father's presidency. He is currently held in remand.
His brother Yoshitha was also arrested earlier this year on corruption charges.

Japanese authorities have raided the country’s four biggest breweries over suspicions they colluded to set the price of beer and other beverages – a practice media reports said could have forced drinkers to pay over the odds.
Officials from the Fair Trade Commission this week searched the offices of Asahi Breweries, Kirin Brewery, Suntory Beer and Sapporo Breweries – which together control more than 90% of the domestic market. The quartet are suspected of violating the anti-monopoly law.
The commission’s secretary general, Hiroo Iwanari, confirmed an investigation had begun, but declined to give details. The companies said they would cooperate with authorities.
The commission is understood to have launched the investigation given the potential effect the alleged cartel has had on prices after wholesalers sell their products on to supermarkets, convenience stores, bars and restaurants, the Mainichi Shimbun said.
Japanese media quoted sources as saying that sales managers and other executives from the breweries were suspected of meeting secretly over a prolonged period to coordinate on the timing and scale of retail price increases, which ranged from several yen to several dozen yen a time.
Prices for beer and a low-malt version called happoshu have risen multiple times to reflect the rising cost of raw materials and logistics. The commission suspects the breweries bypassed proper pricing competition and collaborated to ensure they made a profit, the Mainichi said.
Alcohol consumption in Japan has declined in recent decades as a result of depopulation and changes in drinking habits among younger people. But sales still reached ¥3.8tn ($24.3bn) in 2024, with beer accounting for 30% of the total, followed by happoshu and third-category beer, which contains little or no malt, with a combined 11.9%
The four breweries have all raised their prices at the same time, most recently in April last year, citing the rising cost of materials and distribution. Prices also rose in October 2022 and October 2023.
Shares in Asahi, Kirin, Suntory and Sapporo fell after Wednesday’s raids – the first investigation of its kind involving the food and beverage industry.
Japanese media quoted sources as saying the commission had judged the case to be particularly serious given its potential impact on consumers, adding that the probe could result in a criminal complaint.
The probe comes three months after the commission raided six Japanese ice-cream makers over allegations of operating a cartel.

Bengaluru’s Freedom Park is set to host a CJP protest on Thursday, bringing together activists and public figures to raise concerns surrounding the ongoing electoral roll revision exercise. The protest comes just two days before the Cockroach Janata Party's (CJP) planned October 10 demonstration.
During a joint press conference on Wednesday, CJP co-convener Saurav Das urged people across the country to travel to Delhi and to come prepared for a prolonged agitation. “This fight is not going to be easy. I appeal to everyone across the country to join us, book train and flight tickets,” he said.
Even if Kumar resigns, the protesters will not step back because the electoral system needs to be cleaned up, Das said, alleging that the BJP's pushback reflects a “lust for eternal power”.
The protestors have been demanding the CEC's resignation at various demonstrations across the country.
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, actor-activist Prakash Raj and YouTuber Dhruv Rathee will participate in a “people's tribunal” on the SIR of electoral rolls in Bengaluru today.
The “victims of SIR” from across Karnataka are expected to attend. The 'people's tribunal' will be followed by a “chappal protest”.
Announcing his attendance, Prakash Raj said on Wednesday, “People's Tribunal by Cockroaches (Cockroach Janata Party)... Dipke... Ashutosh... Sourav and all the youth organisations and the civil society... the victims of SIR from across the state will be present.”
“Requesting all the citizens to participate in this fight to save our democracy. Come join us tomorrow, 8th October at Freedom Park... Bengaluru,” he said.
In a video, Raj said Dhruv Rathee, an influencer, would attend the event.
Rathee also uploaded a video on his ‘X’ account confirming his participation in the programme and said the fight was to save democracy.
CJP co-convener Ashutosh Ranka had also announced on ‘X’ on October 6 that after attending the people's tribunal on SIR, they would interact with Kannadigas who have allegedly been wrongfully removed from the voters’ list.
The KPCC will hold protests across the state on Thursday as part of the Congress's nationwide call to observe a “Black Day” for Indian democracy over the detention of the party leaders, including Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Vadra.
The protests will be held at the state, district and block/mandal levels, with the main demonstration scheduled at the Karnataka Pradesh Congress Committee (KPCC) office on Queen's Road here from 10.30 am.
Similar protests will be organised at District Congress Committee (DCC) and Block Congress Committee (BCC) offices across Karnataka.

'Lost control of its Frankenstein': India lambasts Pakistan's doublespeak on terrorism at UN
The first secretary also recalled the 9/11 terror attacks in New York, whose main perpetrator, Osama Bin Laden, was found in Pakistan's Abbottabad.
India on Wednesday exposed Pakistan's doublespeak at the United Nations, stating that Islamabad had lost control of the "Frankenstein" monster of terrorism created by the state.
Raghoo Puri, India's first Secretary in the Permanent Mission of India to the UN, stated that Pakistan has presented itself as a "victim" while financing and facilitating terrorism.
"Pakistan has presented itself as a frontline state in combating terrorism and as a victim, while masking the fact that the Frankenstein (monster) the Pakistani state has created and lost control over has moved from wreaking havoc in neighbouring countries to doing the same in Pakistan," said Puri.
Puri's remarks came as India exercised its right of reply in response to the Pakistan representative's statement in the Sixth Committee of the UN General Assembly on the Agenda Item: Measures to Eliminate International Terrorism.
'Have not forgotten 9/11, 26/11 and Pahalgam'
The first secretary also recalled the 9/11 terror attacks in New York, whose main perpetrator, Osama Bin Laden, was found in Pakistan's Abbottabad.
The Indian representative also brought up the 26/11 attacks in Mumbai and the recent Pahalgam attack, which resulted in a five-day military standoff between India and Pakistan.
"The victims in Pahalgam were not asked about their political orientation; they were asked about their religion. It is therefore deeply ironic that Pakistan speaks of combating religious hatred while allowing the conditions that enable it to persist and thrive, especially by fomenting cross-border terrorism," he said.
"Pakistan continues with its narrative building, misinformation, and disinformation. If bombed-out airfields and cratered runways look like victory to Pakistan, they are of course welcome to enjoy it," Puri said.
Puri also said that Islamabad "glosses over its state support for terrorism by announcing enhanced rewards for apprehending the UN-listed head of Jaish-e-Mohammed terrorist and mastermind of several attacks against my country, Masood Azhar."
Adding that the world is aware of Pakistan's financing for terrorism, Puri highlighted Pakistani media interviews with Azhar regarding the “success of Operation Sindoor”
“If the media can reach Azhar and get his confirmation on Operation Sindoor, the Pakistani State surely knows his whereabouts,” Puri added.
India highlights internal contradictions
While exposing the doublespeak, Puri also recalled a statement by Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, who is the daughter of former Pakistan prime minister Nawaz Sharif.
Last month, Sharif had remarked that the threats faced by the Punjab province are "less from the neighbouring countries and more from neighbouring provinces.
Furthermore, a Nawaz Sharif interview given to Dawn newspaper in 2018 was also highlighted, where the former Pakistani prime minister explicitly confessed to his country's culpability regarding the orchestration of the 26/11 terrorist attack on Mumbai.
"Militant organisations are active. Call them non-state actors; should we allow them to cross the border and kill 150 people in Mumbai?" he had stated.
While delivering the remarks, the first secretary did not name the two members of the Nawaz family.
Puri also slammed Pakistan's "circular economy" of narrative and words, stating that if Pakistan made efforts to counter terrorism rather than narrative building, "the world would have been a better place."
"But nothing more can be expected from a Form 47 government," he added, referring to a term used to describe allegations of rigging and manipulation in the 2024 general elections in Pakistan.

The European Union has backed the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) to diversify trade routes and make India-Europe connectivity more resilient, with Apostolos Tzitzikostas, European Commissioner for Sustainable Transport and Tourism, warning that global trade cannot depend on a single maritime route, port or chokepoint. Tzitzikostas made the remarks at the ‘Sagarmanthan: The Great Oceans Dialogue 2026’ event being held from 7 to 9 October in New Delhi, amid renewed concerns over disruptions to global shipping through the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran war. “We cannot afford to depend on a single route, a single port or maritime chokepoint,” Tzitzikostas said on the opening day of the forum on Wednesday. “When one is disrupted, the consequences extend to factories, energy markets, supply chains and eventually citizens and their everyday lives.” The IMEC is a planned multimodal connectivity project announced on 9 September 2023, during the G20 Summit in New Delhi. The crisis around the Strait of Hormuz amid the war in Iran has renewed attention to the IMEC, highlighting the need for alternative trade and transport routes linking India with Europe. Tzitzikostas, while addressing a session on the India-EU Green Shipping Corridor: Innovation, Action and Scale, said IMEC could help diversify connectivity between India and Europe by creating a network of interconnected transport, energy and distribution links. He emphasized that ports and maritime connections would be central to the corridor, while the EU's Global Gateway initiative could help turn the IMEC vision into sustainable and resilient infrastructure projects. Recent disruptions have shown how quickly conflict, piracy, organized crime and cyber threats at sea can affect global trade, Tzitzikostas said. “Europe and India are natural maritime partners. The ocean connects our economies and our societies. Our ports are gateways to trade, energy and industrial value chains,” he said. Tzitzikostas highlighted the potential for India and Europe to cooperate on sustainable maritime fuels. “Europe is creating a very strong demand for sustainable maritime fuels,” he said. He said that India has significant renewable-energy potential and could become a major producer of green hydrogen derivatives such as green ammonia and methanol. “Europe can provide India a growing market, technology and investment. This complementarity gives our partnership real potential,” he said. Tzitzikostas said green shipping corridors can turn climate ambitions into concrete investments by bringing together ports, fuel producers, shipping companies and customers, with government support. “The priority now is implementation: credible projects, sustainable fuel supply, bold infrastructure, and trusted standards and certifications,” he said. The EU official said sustainable shipping, resilient connectivity, maritime security and healthy oceans should form the four pillars of India-EU maritime cooperation. Tzitzikostas said recent disruptions have demonstrated the vulnerability of global maritime trade to security threats. “It makes absolute sense for us to deepen our cooperation on maritime security, including port and cyber security,” he said. He also stressed the importance of establishing a global framework for shipping decarbonization that is workable, enforceable and pragmatic, while providing investors with certainty and supporting zero- and near-zero-emission shipping. Tzitzikostas described India as one of the world's three major maritime nations and a major source of seafarers, saying India's voice would therefore be important in shaping global maritime rules. “Our task now is to turn political ambition into concrete results: cleaner seas, more sustainable ports, safer rules and stronger global rules for our oceans,” he added. Russian strike on buses kills 33, say officials, as deadly attacks on Ukraine surge

Thirty-three people have been killed in a Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in the frontline city of Kramatorsk, rescue officials say.
Another 18 people were wounded, said Donetsk regional head Vadym Filashkin, accusing Russia of targeting a bus carrying passengers to kill as many civilians as possible.
Images posted by local prosecutors showed the burning metal shell of the bus along with debris and some of the victims on the road.
Kramatorsk and neighbouring Slovyansk are part of a so-called fortress belt that Russia is trying to seize as part of Vladimir Putin's claim to the entire Ukrainian industrial region of Donbas.
However, Thursday's attack follows a dramatic surge in Russian attacks across the country and a heavy increase in civilian casualties.
Russia is now launching constant air raids against Ukraine, with sirens ringing throughout the day in the capital Kyiv. According to the UN, Ukraine saw more civilians killed by August this year than were killed in all of 2025.
In one single attack that destroyed a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky east of Kyiv early on Wednesday, 22 people were killed, including five children. Three of the children were only one year old.
Moscow is yet to comment on the latest attack, however rescue officials said the attack caused a fire on two buses that were both carrying passengers.
Filashkin appealed to anyone who was still in the Donetsk region to move to safer regions of Ukraine.
Given the sharp deterioration of security in the two neighbouring cities, he said all public transport had been ordered to stop. The safety of civilians was paramount, and "we have no right to risk the lives of passengers and drivers", he said.
Moscow has often cited the "liberation" and "protection" of the predominantly Russian-speaking Donbas as justification for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. It is made up of two regions - Luhansk and Donetsk - and with most of Luhansk under Russian control, the Kremlin is also aiming to capture remaining 20% of Donetsk territory still held by Ukraine.

Zelensky offered his condolences to families and loved ones affected by the latest attack and said Ukraine's partners needed to provide "concrete action through new defence packages for the protection of Ukraine".
Ahead of the Pryluky attack, the Ukrainian leader had warned this week of warned of intelligence suggesting plans for a major Russian onslaught, and in Kyiv families responded by heading to metro stations for shelter.
Such warnings are for now one of the best defences Ukrainians have.
Interceptor missiles are in short supply around the world, so Ukraine has little chance to stop incoming Russian ballistics.
Both Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes on each other in recent months, with Russian attacks targeting Ukrainian data centres and logistics warehouses.
For much of the war Kramatorsk acted as a logistics and supply hub for the Ukrainian military, however it has now come under almost daily Russian attack as its military moves closer to the east of the city.
Glide bombs in particular have been launched at Slovyansk and Kramatorsk. The bombs are fitted with winglets so they glide towards their target rather than simply fall. In late August as many as nine glide bombs were fired at Kramatorsk in one day.
Kramatorsk City Council described the strike as a "horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population".
"Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there are absolutely no military targets."

Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the new Wembley?
You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 – but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.
Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 – an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.
The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times – including those three on the trot.
And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to plan historic cup success.
Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.
It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler says he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.
His team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.
After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.
Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.
"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.
"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.
"Then the lads wanted to do it again."
And again.
Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.
"There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he says.
"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised."
Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.
After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.
"We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," says McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.
"When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other."
A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.
Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east – including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.
Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software company Sage and at Hillheads Park.
"He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches."
And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.
"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he says.
Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.
"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," says Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.
"But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league."
Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.
Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the big games in a way most amateur sides are not.
"One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," says Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.
"By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand."
Off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.
And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.
They would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.
"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," says one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.
She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".
"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.
"I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now."
Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for big cup games.
But even the best laid plans can go awry.
"We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," says McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley."
By hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.
"It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn says. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.
"One of the security guys showing me to our seats said, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point."
Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, said it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.
"The first year was crazy, everything was brand new," he says. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.
"The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row."
And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.
After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.
The opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.
The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.
In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.
After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.
"In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson says. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.
"In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!"
The 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.
"Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," says Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year."
Success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.
Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.
"I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he says.
"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening."
Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT company after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".
"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he says.
"People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!"
Like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.
But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.
"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.
"Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely."

Washington – The administration of U.S. President Donald Trump has begun direct talks with Myanmar’s military-installed government, according to U.S. officials and others familiar with the outreach, in a sharp reversal of Washington’s efforts to isolate the country’s generals following the 2021 coup.
The U.S. assistant secretary of state for intelligence and research, Michael Vance, played a leading role in the outreach, which has focused on shutting down scam centers that target Americans but could lead to broader engagement, including on Myanmar’s rare-earth mineral deposits, according to seven current and former officials and others familiar with the policy shift.
Vance joined talks with coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing in the capital Naypyitaw on Sept. 15-16. The meeting was aimed at securing the release of American businessman Adam Castillo but also provided an opening for further engagement, four of the people said.

Uproar escalated on Friday (October 2, 2026) after a video went viral showing a Dalit woman who was allegedly denied admission at the government hospital in Bhadohi district during labour pain and forced to deliver outside the hospital in public.
While the victim’s family and Opposition parties alleged untouchability, claiming feudal elements are running the government in Uttar Pradesh, the authorities said disciplinary action has been taken against personnel found guilty of partial negligence.
“The family categorically alleged that hospital staff failed to provide timely treatment and did not admit due to her caste affiliation, this is so sad and inhuman that even after 79 years of independence, untouchability and discrimination prevails in government system, forcing a Dalit woman to give birth on the roadside, outside a government hospital. The feudal elements within the administrative system are emboldened by the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government. The fight of the Samajwadi Party (SP) for justice, equality is against such tendencies,” said Sunil Singh Yadav ‘Sajan’, the SP spokesperson.
“The incident is a cruel, evil act, which is unacceptable in a civilised society,” said Ajay Kumar Lallu, a senior U.P. Congress leader.
In the matter, Rani Vanvasi, a 20-year-old pregnant woman gave birth on the roadside outside government district hospital in Bhadohi on September 29, after she was allegedly denied admission for delivery. The victim’s family also alleged that hospital staff failed to provide timely treatment and did not admit her.
Ms. Vanvasi eventually went into labour near the hospital gate while she and her family were leaving. Women accompanying her used saris or a sheet to provide privacy as she delivered the baby beside the road.

Currently, both the infant and mother are completely healthy and recovering at the district hospital. Disciplinary action has also been taken against personnel found guilty of partial negligence. As many doctors are moving ahead with the latest advances of modern medicine—from powerful obesity drugs to breakthrough cancer treatments—pediatricians are being forced to turn back, fighting to maintain advances in children’s health that were hard-won decades ago.
With anti-vaccine advocate Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) has spent a considerable amount of time and resources in the past year fiercely defending lifesaving vaccinations—safe, routine shots that have saved the lives of millions of children over decades and thwarted untold suffering and disability.
But just this week, The New York Times reported that Ken Paxton, the attorney general of Texas, has opened aggressive investigations against pediatricians simply because they vaccinated their patients. Paxton falsely claims vaccines are part of a “multi-level, multi-industry scheme.” But critics say his anti-vaccine campaign appears more aimed at currying favor with Kennedy, President Trump, and their supporters as Paxton runs for the US Senate.
Meanwhile, the AAP this week had to renew another decades-old stance for children’s health—one against unpasteurized dairy, aka raw milk. Since the early 20th century, dairy producers in the US have briefly heated milk to kill the array of dangerous pathogens that naturally dwell in and around cattle and can easily migrate into milk. The simple intervention of pasteurization contributed to a sharp, “remarkable” drop in infant deaths and illnesses.
But, much like vaccines, a flood of misinformation has eroded trust and understanding of this public health triumph. And again, Kennedy has been among the advocates working to reverse this health victory.
Regressive health
In recent years, state laws have been loosening on raw milk, despite a federal ban on interstate commerce. At least 27 states now allow raw milk sales. In turn, outbreaks from raw milk have increased over the past two decades, the AAP highlights. Nearly half the illnesses in these outbreaks are in children—who are particularly vulnerable to foodborne pathogens.

Mercedes drivers George Russell, Kimi Antonelli to split car packages at Singapore GP after Sepang struggles with updates
Mercedes to run with two different aero packages; George Russell expects second grid drop for another engine change before end of season; watch Practice at 9.30am followed by Sprint Qualifying at 1.30pm on Friday live on Sky Sports F1 as the Singapore GP weekend begins
Thursday 8 October 2026 15:49, UK
George Russell will race Mercedes' older-specification car, while Kimi Antonelli will run an upgraded package at the Singapore Grand Prix as the team bid to get to the bottom of why the updates introduced in Malaysia did not deliver the expected performance.
The world championship leaders brought their first big upgrade to their W17 cars since the end of May to last week's race but unexpectedly endured a challenging weekend on F1's return to Sepang, with Max Verstappen instead proving the dominant force and claiming Red Bull's first win of the season.
In an unusual move, Mercedes will now split their packages across their two drivers for the whole Sprint weekend in Singapore, with Russell - who will start at the back of Sunday's main race grid owing to an engine penalty, following his car's failure last Sunday - running the older aerodynamic package last raced in Baku and Antonelli the one that debuted with difficulty at Sepang.

Russell revealed he was the one who first floated such an idea, with the decision to do so ultimately becoming a "no-brainer" once they knew he was going to be starting last for the Grand Prix this weekend anyway.
"Well, actually, I instigated the conversation prior to the race on Sunday," revealed Russell, who slipped a season-high 84 points behind team-mate Antonelli after dropping out of third place with five laps to go at Sepang.
"So when the failure happened, it was kind of a no-brainer because we were kind of 50-50 about it pre-race.
"And I was more in favour to do it, even pre-race. Whereas now, it is a total no-brainer."
It means Russell will again race with the package he took to an impressive victory in Azerbaijan two races ago.
"It is back!" said Russell of the Baku-spec W17.
"Obviously, Malaysia was the worst weekend of the year for us as a team in terms of pace, qualifying result.
"Of course, we probably both would have been on the podium [had his power unit not failed], but it was a difficult one. And we don't know whether that was a Malaysia specific or whether that was anything to do with the upgrade.
"There's no major science telling us there's anything to do with the upgrade, but we don't measure performance in F1 on how much downforce a car produces, you measure it with a stopwatch, and the stopwatch wasn't great in Malaysia.
"So let's see this weekend. I'm very happy to be back on that package and do the compare. I'm not really in any sort of fight this weekend, or the championship for that regard, so it's the right place to do it."
Will front wing addition unlock new package's performance?
Russell also revealed that the newer package running on Antonelli's car will be boosted by the arrival of a front wing in Singapore that had originally been due to be part of the initial package at Sepang.
"I hope the upgrade that is on Kimi's side works as we expect, because as a team, we need that to be the case, and it would be slightly concerning for us if the new package we had in Malaysia is not working as we expected," he added.
"We have a front wing this weekend that Kimi's running that we didn't have in Malaysia. The package was meant to come with the front wing - maybe that was a reason why it wasn't working so well.
"There's nothing telling us it shouldn't work. But of course, the car I had in Baku, I won in Baku, Kimi won in Madrid. It's still a fast car, so hopefully we can have some good fun."
Asked about the new front wing, Antonelli said: "I hope [it makes the difference]! That's the question we will try to answer.
"George is going back on the old package, which we know works really well, especially on these kind of tracks. On my side we will try to find and answer for this package and hopefully we will understand it more and finally extract the potential of the package.
"Of course, we will have the front wing, even though it's just one front wing, but let's see. I think Sepang was overall a little bit of an outlier because of the tarmac, the temperatures, but hopefully this weekend we will be able to put the car in a better place and extract more from the package."
Antonelli said he was happy to be sticking with the updated W17.
"We really want to understand this new package and try to strike the maximum out of it because the team has done a tremendous job," added the Italian
"They've put in so much work on this new package and it would be just a shame to write it off so early.
"I feel like I'm quite comfortable on keeping it and, actually, I really want to help the team out to understand it more and to try to extract the potential."
Antonelli also confirmed that he was "committed to the new package for the whole weekend", with no option to revert to the older-spec during the Sprint event should the older parts on Russell's car be proving more competitive.
Russell expects second grid penalty before season is out
While Antonelli will hope to contend for victory in both the Sprint and main Grand Prix at Marina Bay, Russell's hopes of fighting at the front are set to be restricted to the shorter-form race on Saturday ahead of his engine-change penalty being applied to Sunday's grid.
Russell will be running a fresh power unit all weekend, but it will not feature the ADUO (Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities) upgrade Mercedes have been working on as that update is not in Singapore.
The ADUO upgrade will instead be introduced at a later race, with the United States GP next up in two weeks' time.
Mercedes had hoped to coincide the expected introduction on Russell's car of a penalty-triggering fifth engine of the season at the same race that the ADUO was deployed, but that will now not be possible.
Russell said: "We were waiting to take the engine penalty with the ADUO update but obviously unfortunately we've had to take it here.
"But with seven races remaining, that's longer than the engines are designed for. Unfortunately it means I'll be taking another penalty at some point between the next race and the end of the season.
"So, yeah, it feels a little bit one thing after another right now but that's just how the cookie crumbles."
Russell, who won last year in Singapore, has vowed to throw caution to the wind this weekend as he bids to salvage a strong result.
"Yeah, all-out attack, just trying to enjoy the weekend," he added..
"Obviously, if you could choose where to take the penalty in the season, this would be probably second bottom of the list after Monaco. But, unfortunately, we had no choice but to take it here.
"Singapore is a place I love and, yeah, I'll try and carve my way through the pack."

President Donald Trump resorted to ‘your mom’ jokes when he his rally speech in Texas was repeatedly interrupted by hecklers.
Trump appeared on stage at the Freeman Coliseum in San Antonio Wednesday evening to drum up support for Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton.
At least a dozen demonstrators interrupted the president during his address, with some led away by police.
“He’s going back home to mom,” Trump said as one of the hecklers left. “But what he doesn’t know is his mom voted for Trump.”
In footage from the event, Trump can be seen smiling as the crowd of his supporters boo the protesters.
“Now I’m telling you they pay them for this. But do we have a good time?” Trump said, before pursing his lips.
Interrupted again, Trump lashed out: “That guy’s got to lose a lot of weight.”
At one point, Trump appeared to become so frustrated he made a direct appeal to any further opponents in the crowd.
“If there are any more paid protesters, please raise your hand and get the hell out of here,” he said.
Footage recorded by USA Today showed one man shouting as he made his way through the crowd of Trump supporters, filming while being pursued by another wearing a MAGA hat.
Trump has thrown his weight behind Paxton’s campaign despite Texas usually being a reliable state for Republicans during elections.
However, Trump’s approval ratings, concerns over the cost of living and the war with Iran have allowed Democrat James Talarico’s campaign to gain considerable ground and have put the Democrats in play to win the Senate race.
Wednesday’s appearance marked Trump’s third trip to Texas in less than a month, and party officials have devoted more than $300 million to elections in the state so far.
At the rally, Trump appeared confident about his party’s chances in the looming midterm elections.
“With your support, 27 days from now, we’re going to crush ‘dumocrat’ communist James ‘Tala-freak-o’,” he declared, using a nickname he invented for the Democratic Party and for Talarico.
Trump spent most of his remarks focused on the Senate contest, describing Paxton as “perhaps the greatest attorney general in the United States of America.”
“He was tough and he was with us all the way,” Trump said of Paxton, whom he endorsed in the state’s GOP primary over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn. “He’s a fantastic man.”
Paxton appeared to make a slight blunder during his own speech as he asked the crowd to pray.
“Pray that we will be delivered from socialism and cap-...” he said, before pausing and correcting himself: “From communism.”

An industrial park in Irvine, California, may seem an odd spot to show off technology that wouldn’t be out of place in Dune, but that’s what’s happening on a sweltering September morning.
The temperature is already over 80 degrees Fahrenheit as the sun rises on a 20-foot-tall, metal-clad machine in the parking lot of Atoco, an Irvine, California-based startup. Engineers open panels to check systems and an iPad that shows a steadily ascending line that reveals the device’s purpose: harvesting water from thin air using special materials known as metal organic frameworks, or MOFs.
The materials won Omar Yaghi, the company’s founder, the Nobel Prize for chemistry in 2025, and Atoco has shown they work in prototypes capable of producing gallons of water per day. What’s unique about this iteration of Atoco’s technology is what it doesn’t require. No grid connection or even electricity is needed to grab water from the air at the microscopic level, nor is it required to in turn wring the water out of the materials in a form useful for humans.
Instead, all that’s needed is low-level industrial heat. That, Atoco says, makes them a perfect candidate to hook up with AI data centers, which throw off loads of waste heat as servers churn out everything from math proofs to virtual editors while also often requiring massive amounts of water.
“We were not really thinking of AI data centers,” four or five years ago, says Atoco CEO Samer Taha. But the massive buildout has created an opportunity for the startup that could allow it to get a step closer to its larger goal of ensuring people living in water-stressed regions have control over an increasingly precious resource.
When Yaghi was a PhD student, he says, creating something like MOFs was “every chemist’s dream.” Part of his Nobel-winning work over the past 20 years has been taking theoretical research into the real world, creating a stable molecular structure that links organic material with metal ions.
The structure of a MOF looks somewhat “like a jungle gym on a playground,” says Seth Cohen, the dean of the School of Physical Sciences at UC Irvine. MOFs are essentially “molecular sponges—they’re a solid material that’s very, very good at absorbing other molecules,” says Cohen, who is not involved with Atoco. Like a sponge, the materials can also be wrung out using methods including heat to release whatever they’re holding onto.
These jungle-gym-like frameworks create open spaces on the microscopic level that can hold an unbelievable amount of material, and small tweaks can yield even more interior space.
“The footage of a gram of MOF could cover two football fields,” Yaghi explains. “They can store hydrogen in there to make clean energy, or you could store CO2 in there to make clean air. Or, in this case, you can store water.”
Atoco has developed what Taha calls “precision materials” with a specific objective of being able to harvest water, release it, and then do it over again and again. He quips that, as vice president of R&D Benjie Limketkai puts it, the material has to like water but not love it. To succeed commercially, it also has to use as little energy as possible.
“The scientists reach a level of precision [where] we really know even the angle of the atom,” in a given material, Taha says.
In Atoco’s technology, air passes through the MOF, which has been specially tailored to attract water molecules. Those molecules adhere to the pores. But the material feels completely dry to the touch even when saturated, and squeezing it doesn’t release a single drop. (Taha was kind enough to let WIRED try our hand at it.) Instead, the company relies on heat to release the captured molecules.
There are other means of harvesting water. Cohen notes that silica, a popular desiccant, can also pull water out of air, but it doesn’t hold as much moisture and requires you to “heat the heck out of it to get the water back out,” he says.
The monolith in the parking lot of the company’s Irvine facility is the culmination of decades of precision development. Atoco’s materials and approach allow its off-grid system to work even when relative humidity is in the teens. The MOFs in the device can harvest and release water with heat as low as 100 degrees Fahrenheit, Taha says.
With no data center nearby, Atoco’s team simulated it by piping heat from a source that was around 150 degrees Fahrenheit. A solar panel powers various systems but not the water-harvesting operation itself, making the metal-clad machine eerily quiet. Cars pulling into the adjacent businesses create more of a sonic disruption, but Taha is ready to show the device has been working hard. It’s a little after 9 am, and the temperature is over 90 degrees Fahrenheit when he pushes a button on the side and turns a spigot. Out tumbles a clear stream of water that looks good enough to drink.
Unfortunately it’s not on offer for legal liability reasons, though Taha notes it’s the equivalent of distilled water, because Atoco’s MOFs aren’t built to gather air pollution. Tossing it in the bushes, Taha retreats to an air-conditioned conference room where he lays out the company’s vision for its new machine.
“Roughly 70 percent of the industrial waste heat is low-grade, unutilized, thrown into oceans or into the air,” he says. “If you convert that waste heat to clean water using our technology, you're talking about trillions of liters of clean water.”
Data centers are an increasingly big source of that waste heat, with a single facility capable of pumping out as much heat as tens of thousands of homes. Operators are forced to disperse that heat into the surrounding environment, creating heat islands, while also paying for various types of cooling systems.
Many of those cooling systems also rely on water, and some can consume millions of gallons per day. Atoco’s technology would thus address two of data centers’ biggest problems.
Data centers are investing a lot of money to get rid of waste heat, Taha says. “We actually want it; we need it. We give you back water, the same product that is causing the issue.”
He says the company also wants to help deliver water to rural communities, where utilities sometimes bring in water by the truckload because of a lack of infrastructure.
To do that, let alone serve data centers that require millions of gallons of water daily, will require a big leap in scale. The demo in the company’s parking lot can generate up to 300 liters of water per day. Atoco envisions data centers using multiple units in a grid system to generate water and is working on a commercial offering that could produce up to 1,000 liters of water per day. Its parking lot prototype runs off the equivalent heat provided by a 20-kilowatt data center. Hyperscale data centers, in comparison, are orders of magnitude bigger, which presents both an opportunity and a challenge.
Atoco has deployed five on-grid prototype trials with partners in the US and within the Gulf Cooperation Council. The company says that it hopes to begin taking orders for its first product by the end of this year. It says it’s already in conversation with major tech companies about deploying a pilot project at data centers, though it declined to name them or how much customers could expect to spend on a unit. But there are signs that there could be a market: Microsoft, Google, and Amazon Web Services have all committed to being water positive—that is, returning more water to communities than they use—by 2030.
Atoco’s product might work at data centers and other industrial sites, as well as locations where there are abundant natural heat sources, such as geothermal sites. But Cohen, who worked at the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency on MOF projects—including on a project spearheaded by Yaghi—cautions that while MOFs have incredible promise, they’re not a silver bullet for water access everywhere. Without an outside source of heat, even the most well-designed MOFs still require energy to squeeze water out. That could make rural deployment, in particular, a challenge. Atoco’s on-grid system might offer a solution, but distant locations are also frequently underserved by energy infrastructure.
Taha says the company can produce water at a levelized cost of $5 per metric ton, which makes it competitive with older desalination plants. But newer facilities are able to deliver water at a cost of $2 per ton or even less in some cases—a target he says Atoco is still three to five years away from hitting.
MOFs also remain a cutting-edge technology that’s untested at scale. While big tech companies are more likely to take risks than, say, staid utilities, it will take time to vet that Atoco’s technology can work and for the startup to scale up production of its commercial units to provide meaningful amounts of water.
Still, Atoco’s technology has already solved some incredible challenges. The use of MOFs brings the world much closer to a place where, as Yaghi puts it, everyone can control access to their own water. Yaghi describes how as a child, growing up as a Palestinian refugee in Jordan, he was responsible for filling as many containers as he could with water for his household to use when the delivery truck came every two weeks.
That experience “makes you appreciate scarcity,” he says. “Now, we’re talking about going from scarcity to abundance.”

'Every day there is killing': Gazans face Israeli strikes despite ceasefire as peace deal stalls
- Published
In her tent in central Gaza early one morning last month, 31-year-old Fida al-Toutah, a mother of five, was combing her daughter's hair when the sound of gunfire erupted.
"My mother shouted at us to get down," her son Ezz recalled, weeping as he spoke.
He only realised Fida had been hit when he saw the bloodied hands of his younger brother, who had been clinging onto his mother as the bullets came in.
"Our mother was so kind and generous. What did she do wrong?" Ezz said.
Fida died on 21 September from a gunshot wound to the head.
She is among more than 1,400 people in Gaza who have been killed in Israeli attacks since the start of the ceasefire on 10 October last year, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for all of the 48 remaining hostages held in Gaza, and an agreement to end the war - which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage.
On the ground in Gaza, it meant that Israel's large-scale bombardment stopped, which brought substantial relief and an increase in humanitarian aid and medical supplies entering the territory.
But even during the ceasefire, Israel has continued launching strikes in Gaza almost every day. In the past week alone more than 30 people have been killed, according to Gaza's health ministry.
Israel says it is targeting Hamas operatives, and accuses Hamas of continued violations of the ceasefire.
"It [the ceasefire] is all lies. Every day there's a shooting. Every day there is killing and death lurking around," said Ahed, Fida's husband.
In response to the BBC's questions about Fida's killing, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said they had no record of the incident.
The total death toll from Israeli attacks since the start of the war in Gaza three years ago now stands at more than 74,000, according to the Gaza health ministry.
Outside Fida's tent, her brother Ibrahim pointed to the holes he said were made by a volley of bullets fired by Israeli forces.
"This tent is just a piece of cloth. Imagine that a military vehicle came down here and fired a spray of bullets," he said. "There was also gunfire coming from the sky, from above, from quadcopters, and it was directed at unarmed civilians."
Fida is the fourth of Ibrahim's siblings to be killed since the start of the war. "We left our neighbourhood Zeitoun to survive, but death is following us," he said.
The family has moved seven times but safety has been out of reach. Most of Gaza's 2.1 million population has been displaced multiple times by the war, the UN says, with many forced to live in tented cities and unsafe structures.
On the same day that Fida was killed, 14-year-old Ismail al-Bardawil was also shot dead. He was killed in the al-Mawasi area of Rafah, in southern Gaza.
His family told the BBC that he was shot by Israeli forces while he and his brothers were fishing in the Mediterranean Sea, around 20m (66ft) from the shore. He is one of more than 300 children killed since the start of the ceasefire, according to Gaza's health ministry.
The IDF said it had no information about this incident either.
Over the past year, the IDF has released videos of its operations in Gaza targeted at Hamas and other groups. At least seven Israeli soldiers have been killed in Gaza since the start of the ceasefire.
Both Fida and Ismail lived close to the so-called Yellow Line that separates the areas occupied by the Israeli military in Gaza from areas controlled by Hamas in the west.
Areas around the line are considered the most dangerous because Israeli forces have frequently opened fire there. But there are few options to move because there is an extreme shortage of space.
The strip was densely populated even before the war began. Now, its population is squeezed into under 40% of its area, which is controlled by Hamas.
In those areas the group maintains a tight grip, clamping down on dissent and still recruiting fighters.
In May this year, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he had directed the IDF to increase the area of Gaza under Israel's control to 70%.
Architect Amal Alabadla, who lived in a comfortable flat prior to the war, now lives in a tent on the coastline.
"Every time the rains come, it gets flooded. I feel very scared when the wind is strong because our tent gets destroyed or damaged," she said.
Amal is forced to raise her two boys - Mohammed and Noah - on her own.
Her husband was not in Gaza when the war broke out, and in three years they have not been reunited. Amal's three brothers, who helped her care for the boys, were killed in separate attacks before the ceasefire began.
"During the winter, my son suffers from epilepsy seizures because of the cold. It's very hard sometimes to keep him dry and warm," she said.
"Before the war, I had a job, a house, an ordinary life, but then everything turned upside down. Now we have no hope, nothing. It's only about survival day by day, to keep my kids alive, clean, healthy and fed."
There are camps further inland in Gaza that have even been built below sea level, which are at greater risk of flooding.
The October 2025 peace deal was supposed to pave the way for the reconstruction in Gaza, but rebuilding has not yet begun - stuck in limbo because of an impasse over the second phase of the deal.
Israel strictly controls what materials and machinery are allowed into Gaza, acting, it says, for reasons of its own security.
Earlier this year, US President Donald Trump put forward a plan to disarm Hamas, but in August it was rejected by Netanyahu, who stated that no military pull-out would happen until Hamas was "genuinely" disarmed.
Hamas has said handing over its heavy weapons is contingent on Israel ending "all forms of aggression" and withdrawing its forces from Gaza.
Half a world away, Trump's Board of Peace has also proposed a recovery plan for Gaza worth $2.45bn (£1.85bn).
But, one year on from the ceasefire and three years on from the start of the war, many like Amal are deeply sceptical of things actually changing on the ground.
"We are struggling and not being allowed to rebuild," she said. "I don't think they are telling us the truth about allowing us to rebuild a safe future for our children."

Deported to Central African Republic, a transgender woman who lived openly in Miami is hiding again
Daniela Fuentes is a transgender woman from Cuba who's been deported to the Central African Republic as part of a U.S. immigration policy
DAKAR, Senegal -- In Miami, Daniela Fuentes styled hair for clients and performed in drag at a nightclub called Azúcar. She wore her blond wig in public and dressed as the woman she had known herself to be since adolescence in Cuba.
Now, more than 6,000 miles (10,000 kilometers) away in the Central African Republic, she wears men’s clothes, lowers her voice and tries not to draw attention to the breasts she developed after beginning hormone treatment as a teenager. As part of U.S. efforts to deport people to countries other than their own, authorities sent her Aug. 29 to a place where she has no ties and where advocacy groups have reported arbitrary detention, torture, and other rights violations of sexual and gender minorities.
“Everything is difficult here because I have to hide who I am," said Fuentes, a 32-year-old transgender woman living on a compound she rarely leaves, sharing a room with four Cuban men also deported from the U.S. “I don’t know this place, the people or the language, and I have no idea what will happen to me.”
The Central African Republic — one of the world's poorest countries, a place with a history of conflict that the U.S. State Department advises American travelers to avoid — is one of at least 12 African nations that signed agreements to accept “third-country” deportations, a policy the U.S. Supreme Court last month allowed to continue, at least temporarily.
In the Central African Republic — where transgender people have little to no legal protections and are marginalized in much of society — Fuentes dons her wig only in the privacy of her bathroom. She described disguising herself as protection, first in U.S. detention and now in a country she first heard of when she was already headed there on a deportation flight.
“My whole life, my whole identity, was taken away from me,” Fuentes said.
Public records say a judge ordered Fuentes to leave the U.S. but offer no other information. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials did not reply to emailed questions.
Fuentes' compound in the capital, Bangui, is an apartment complex where the government houses male deportees.
Fuentes said she can leave but that officials have advised her and others to avoid it — they have no identification, which could lead to issues with the police. It also means they can't work, she said, and she's waiting on travel documents that would allow her to leave the country. The International Organization for Migration, an agency associated with the United Nations, has provided food, and the migrants say they've crowdsourced for donations to buy groceries.
The U.S. — via agreements often not made public — has deported about 25,000 people to more than two dozen countries that aren't their own, the vast majority to Mexico, according to a tally by Third Country Deportation Watch, a partnership of Refugees International and Human Rights First. The U.S. has not released numbers or details.
From January 2025 to August 2026, more than 500 were sent to countries in Africa, according to a Human Rights Watch report published Thursday — including at least 12 people who identify as lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender and were deported to places that criminalize same-sex relations or public same-sex romantic conduct. Some advocates say the number is likely higher.
“These are not bureaucratic errors or isolated incidents," said Bridget Crawford, of the group Immigration Equality. “They are the predictable result of policies that purposefully abandon our legal and moral obligation to protect LGBTQ+ immigrants fleeing persecution.”
The U.S. government says the policy is lawful and that receiving governments provide assurances deportees won't be persecuted or tortured.
Fuentes grew up in La Lisa, on Havana's outskirts, and said she understood from childhood that she was different. She began living as a woman in adolescence and started taking hormones at 18.
She ran a salon from her home, coloring and cutting hair. She said she was harassed because of her gender identity and attacked at least twice, leaving scars on her arm and head. Police also questioned her about operating a private business, she said — though housefront businesses are common in the area.
In 2023, Fuentes sold her home and left amid a deepening economic crisis and a crackdown on dissent — even as Cuba, one of Latin America's most progressive countries for LGBTQ+ rights, adopted new inclusion laws. Making her way to the U.S., she said, she presented as a man traveling through Central America; she believed it was safer.
After seven months in Mexico, she said, she entered the U.S. through Texas via CBP One, a President Joe Biden-era online appointment system that allowed migrants to live in the country for two years on humanitarian grounds. Then she went to Miami.
There, she began living openly as a woman again. She found work styling hair and performed at Azúcar. Though she lacked permanent legal status, Fuentes said Miami offered something she'd rarely experienced: the freedom to move through daily life as herself.
That ended when officers encountered her outside a motel. Fuentes said they learned she had missed an immigration court hearing in Texas. She said she asked that the case be moved to Florida but received no response.
Fuentes said she was taken into custody and later placed in immigration detention with men. Officials confiscated her wig and gave her a male detainee’s uniform, she said.
Such treatment is in line with a January 2025 executive order directing officials to exclude transgender women from women’s prisons and detention centers.
“When I learned that they were going to put me with men, I almost fainted,” Fuentes said.
Fuentes was held at two detention facilities in Florida, then transferred to Texas. When armed officers arrived there, she said, she suspected she was facing deportation, but they didn't reveal she was being sent to Africa until about five hours into the flight.
Other deportees on the flight told AP they also weren't told the destination until they were on the plane. Dozens have been sent to the Central African Republic, including an Iranian woman facing persecution in her home country and an Afghan whose brothers worked with the U.S. military.
Fuentes said she does not understand why she was sent to Africa rather than Cuba. She told AP she has no lawyer.
The U.S. does repatriate Cuban citizens, as part of agreements to resume deportation flights in 2023, despite tensions in relations between the countries. Charter flights have arrived in Havana regularly.
Yasmany Moreno, another Cuban deportee in Bangui, said that upon arriving, the group had no visas or documents establishing their legal status in the country. Officials spoke of providing assistance for 90 days, he said, but the deportees didn't know what would happen afterward or where they would live.
Several told AP their longer-term status remained unclear and that U.S. authorities had taken their identity documents.
A policy officer at the Central African Republic’s Foreign Ministry said the deportees are in “good hands” and are being monitored by the International Organization for Migration. He spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to discuss the matter publicly.
The U.S. this year committed to $85 million in funding to IOM for Central African Republic operations including “assistance to migrants” and “community stabilization.”
IOM says migrants can seek asylum in the country, request assistance to return home or get help traveling to another place they're authorized to enter. It referred questions about the deportees' status and individual cases such as Fuentes' to Central African Republic officials. A government spokesperson didn't reply to phone calls and text messages seeking comment.
Human Rights Watch's report says some people deported to third countries face detention, abuse and the prospect of persecution. Eswatini has held deportees in a maximum-security prison without charges. Equatorial Guinea has held them against their will at a hotel owned by the president’s family.
“Several of these African governments are not only complicit in U.S. abuses but have violated the human rights of these deported people themselves,” Michael Garcia Bochenek, of Human Rights Watch, said in a statement.
Fuentes said the Cuban men in her room know she is a woman and look out for her. She rarely feels safe enough to leave. Once, at a supermarket, workers pointed at her breasts and initially refused to sell her fruit, she said. Other people in Bangui have mocked her and pointed at her.
“My personal appearance is awful,” she said. “I look like a different human being.”
Moreno described restrictions on the group’s movements, saying officers accompanied them to the market and on occasional outings but restricted them from going out at night.
Fuentes and Moreno said they have no passports or other identification and cannot work. Most days, Fuentes remains at the compound, looking at her phone and waiting for travel documents.
She said Cuba has agreed to accept her return — a Cuban embassy document shows she is authorized.
But Fuentes said she hopes to seek asylum elsewhere, possibly Canada.
“The harassment and economic hardship that caused me to flee still remain,” she said.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

The zardozi embroidery on a Dior dress, the T-strap leather sandals at a Prada show, the mirror-work technique used on a Fendi bag – for decades, the skill of Indian artisans has been an invisible force behind some of the world’s most coveted fashion.
Now, that work is beginning to claim its own place in the spotlight, and the Mumbai-based textile and embroidery atelier Chanakya International is at the forefront.
Chanakya marked its 40th anniversary this month, celebrating with three exhibitions that trace its journey from an embroidery powerhouse to a present-day craft and cultural institution. The person steering it is 49-year-old Karishma Swali, whose father set up the group’s operations in the 1980s.
“What we have as a country is unique,” she tells me of India’s rich textile and craft heritage. “It’s unparalleled in many ways, and it’s the only place where we continue to practise it.” During the Renaissance, she says, France and Italy had established and varied traditions. “But what we have in India today is [what] other parts of the world have lost.”
Chanakya has a network of 1,400 artisans, and says that some are 13th-generation craftspeople, skilled in hundreds of embroidery traditions and supplying almost every luxury label you can imagine. Among the techniques they have revived is the Mughal-era silver filigree lace, or chaand jaal, reintroduced in a lighter form that has since become a regular feature in couture collections.
In 2023, Dior held a show at Mumbai’s Gateway of India, showcasing its partnership with Chanakya, in a high-profile acknowledgment of Indian craftsmanship. The runway saw sari-inspired skirts, vibrant madras-checks sets and Nehru-collar jackets.
These collaborations are supported by expert craft knowledge passed down and refined over generations, and they need institutional support to survive. The Kalhath Institute, a craft-preservation centre in Lucknow, runs residencies that pair artists from across the world with local artisans.
Kalhath’s co-founder Mohammed Amine Dadda tells me that Indian craftsmanship’s defining quality is “intelligence of the hand” – a sensitive, slow and cumulative process underpinned by patience and dexterity. “Without this technical mastery, and the considerable time required to create the most demanding pieces, haute couture and contemporary luxury simply could not bring their most ambitious creative visions to life.”
This mastery is not limited to textiles. When it comes to jewellery, global luxury brands have long sought Jaipur-based the Gem Palace, established in 1852 by the Kasliwal family, who still run it today. Samarth Kasliwal, 33, says part of the appeal lies in the visual language of Indian artistry itself. “There is something about Indian artistry that is inspired by nature,” he tells me, pointing to the recurring use of floral patterns and animals across Indian art and design. These motifs are universal, and travel across the lines of culture and language.
One recent collaboration Kasliwal is particularly proud of is a collection for Dior featuring green onyx and rock crystals, with engravings of birds, animals and flowers. The combination, he says, is reminiscent of traditional Indian jewellery, while drawing on techniques that remain central to the atelier’s work today.
With increased visibility, the question of credit and appropriation has become harder to ignore. Last week, a Ralph Lauren gown from the designer’s spring 2027 collection attracted criticism after many Indians pointed out that the embroidery the brand described as “embellishments” looked a lot like Indian zardozi, but without any accompanying credit. (Ralph Lauren did not respond to my request for comment.)
Then, Fendi came under fire when people noticed that a baguette bag from its autumn/winter collection featured mirrorwork often seen in Gujarati crafts. In April, Fendi credited Chanakya artisans in a social media video showcasing the same embroidery. But the product description on its site failed to mention any Indian inspiration, and its final label read “Made in Italy”.
After I asked Fendi about the discrepancy, the brand cited its “creative partnership” with Chanakya of more than three decades, saying it “remains committed to supporting and recognizing India’s rich craft heritage”. The website descriptor now reads: “Made in Italy and India with Chanakya”.
A recent Financial Times report noted that under EU rules, garments embroidered in India can still end up with a European label – so long as the final construction and finishing take place in Europe.
Last year, Prada was accused of appropriating Indian culture with Kolhapuri-inspired sandals, a controversy that showed us these debates around recognition can sometimes produce a more structural response. “We acknowledge the sandals … are inspired by traditional Indian handcrafted footwear, with a centuries-old heritage,” Lorenzo Bertelli, the corporate social responsibility chief at the Italian fashion house, had written in a letter to the Maharashtra chamber of commerce at the time.
Prada subsequently partnered with state-backed organisations in Maharashtra and Karnataka to produce a limited-edition collection, Made in India, and committed to a three-year training programme for artisans specialising in the craft.
Might these collaborations, controversies and corrections represent a shift in India’s place in the fashion industry? Anthropologist Phyllida Jay, author of Inspired by India: How India Transformed Global Design, appears to think so, placing the debate in a longer arc. “The stories of the ateliers producing highly skilled Indian craft in the elevated realm of European luxury and high fashion is part of a broader paradigm shift,” she writes, “where over 70 years after the end of colonial rule, India is being looked at in a different way on the world stage.” It is, in a way, a reversal, moving from a colonial history of extraction toward one in which Indians themselves get a voice in how their craft is represented.
Swali is ensuring this visibility also lives on through the Chanakya School of Craft, which she set up in 2016. Its 18-month programme provides free embroidery training and a travel honorarium to dozens of women, some of whom have gone on to work at the main atelier. Others have set up their own independent studios.
I had a chance to visit the space – inside a high-rise in Lower Parel, where those as young as 18 learn intricate needlework alongside grandmothers in their 60s. “Craft in India has never been institutionalised,” Swali says of the ethos behind the initiative. “It’s intergenerational,” she says, adding that women have often been excluded.
India’s culture of craft has always been precious. Growing up, I loved having the choice to affordably create any type of clothing. At one point, I had a small army of tailors, each with a different specialisation, whom I’d go to for different needs. I’d buy ajrakh and mashru silks from Dastkar or Nalli, and hand it to the right Masterji to stitch, embroider and tweak to my size. So, to me, Indian craftsmanship is not just a part of luxury, but a luxury itself.

Ashneer Grover, co-founder and former CEO of fintech firm BharatPe slammed the move, describing it as “tax collection”.
