Most were picked up and detained in midnight raids, the report said, and family members accused the police of not producing warrants.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Fashion designer Payal Khandwala, whose spring-summer ’26 collection featured handwoven silks, cottons and brocades, recommends the perfect saree weave: “The delicate poetry of a Jamdani saree is definitely my favourite. A 2,000-year-old craft, typically woven in fine muslin and of Bengali origin, it’s somewhat an unsung hero. The weaving process itself is exceptionally intricate. Using a supplementary weft technique, thousands of markings are meticulously mapped on to the warp to recreate the pattern, interlaced by hand with a wooden shuttle and metallic needle to guide the motifs in silver and gold yarn, on fine mulberry silk and organza.”

The true measure of my love for my friends is in the number of memes I send them. One of the accounts I rely on is Bahaish Kapoor’s. The screenwriter-turned-meme evangelist pairs black-and-white Bollywood stills with contemporary gen Z sass, and lets incongruity do the rest. What makes an image meme-worthy? “I always look for people who are in a deep philosophical, romantic, dramatic action moment which I can repurpose to bring in a whole new meaning,” he tells me. “I try to mix and match and see what’s working.” His 340,000-plus followers include Sharon Stone and Hrithik Roshan.
“I just want to make people feel a little better,” says Kapoor, adding that he receives a lot of DMs from people about how his page helped them through a bad day. “People confessing that they are lighter because of this experience is all that I can hope for. I mean, that’s the endgame.”

Does it feel like people are perhaps a little grumpier or more on edge these days? It’s not like it’s without reason. There are wars. The climate is going haywire. Someone just died of plague. Scientific research is under attack. Machines keep stealing humans’ work. The media is a mess. And just when it all starts to feel a little overwhelming, Jaguar goes and unveils a new car.
The Type 01 is the first model to arrive from Jaguar’s rebirth. The British carmaker was an early entrant to the modern EV market with the 2017 I-Pace, which was fun to drive even if it was too small inside and perhaps completely unreliable. An all-electric sedan was supposed to be next, but a year from the showroom, it was abruptly canceled, leaving the automaker with nothing to sell as old models like the F-Pace ceased production.
Instead, Jaguar got to work on an all-new electric vehicle platform called JEA, which will underpin an all-electric product line. An elevated ownership experience and a starting price of about double the brand’s previous $60,000 entry point was the idea, Jaguar boss Rawdon Glover told me in 2024. Then last year the brand started teasing its relaunch, and everyone got upset. Things got even worse when the first images of the slab-sided and pastel-shaded Type 00 coupe concept leaked.
Today, we can see an iteration of that design, now a four-door GT called the Type 01. The previously brutalist shape is now adorned with the jewelry of reflectors that are required by the necessities of street legality, and of course there are now four doors rather than two. There is no rear window, but then there’s no rear window in a Polestar 4, and to be frank, barely a view out the back of a Corvette or even a Land Rover Defender when the spare tire is on the back. These days the technology for a central rear-view camera that replaces the mirror is proven and robust, happily.

Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro vs Amazon Fire HD 10: What's changed, and is the upgrade worth it?
Amazon's best tablet ever didn't have to work hard for the title, but a new nanomatte screen and Kindle mode sweeten the deal.
With a brand new series of tablets announced today, including the top-end Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro which usurps the Fire HD 10 at the top of the lineup, Amazon's hardware is better and bolder than before. That may sound like high praise, but the e-retailer's tablet lineup has always been aimed at the bargain bin rather than taking aim at the iPads and Galaxy Tabs of the world. This time around, the new hardware still doesn't reach those heights, but it flies cleanly in between and soars above its predecessor.
To hear Amazon tell it, the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is built around two things that could hardly be further apart: reading, and lots of AI. To that end, its marquee features include a "nanomatte" display to better imitate paper, along with a new processor to power Alexa+, the AI-powered version of Amazon's long-running voice assistant. Whether or not you're enthused about the presence of AI here (Amazon would certainly like you to be), it's hard to turn down better hardware.
Compared to the Fire HD 10 tablet, which has until now occupied the top slot in Amazon's mobile hardware lineup since the Fire Max 11 was quietly discontinued in the US, the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro appears to be a significant upgrade in all the ways that matter. Here's how Amazon is taking its new tablets up a notch.
Amazon's latest tablet is its best ever (but that's faint praise)
The previous flagship tablet in Amazon's lineup was the Fire HD 10, but to call it a flagship risks overstating its appeal. Its base model has just 32 gigabytes of storage and 4 gigabytes of RAM, which in combination with its practically ancient MediaTek Helios chip means it has roughly the performance of a cheap Chromebook. Slap a 10.1-inch WUXGA display on it, and you've got a device that's perfectly suited to watching videos or reading books, but which isn't a productivity machine. But at $155 for the base model, it's a clear bargain pick for those on short budgets or who don't need a lot of tablet to begin with.
The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is a massive upgrade in every regard. An aluminum build does away with the plastic elements of the Fire HD 10, and cradled inside is a 4-nanometer, 8-core MediaTek Dimensity 8400 CPU, which can be paired with up to 16 gigabytes of RAM. There are also two display options, a standard glossy display or a textured "nanomatte" one which should be better for reading. Both panels measure 12 inches with a pixel density of 280 pixels per-inch (with some quick math, roughly 2,880 by 1,920 is the closest standard resolution).
Software gets a big overhaul, too. Sure, there's a ton of Alexa+ integration — Amazon is the preeminent builder of data centers, after all — from the expected smart home controls to the ability to chat about what's on your screen or go hands-free in a live voice chat mode. But arguably the biggest change is the addition of the Google Play Store. We relayed last year that Amazon might be ditching its Fire OS software, and sure enough, we're seeing Android as the underlying software here. The new home screen seems to have ditched the storefront-like layout Fire tablet users are used to in favor of a more Alexa-focused experience.
Amazon goes back to its roots with a dedicated Kindle mode
One major reason to buy an Amazon tablet is as a Kindle alternative. If you read a lot of ebooks but want the ability to watch videos and run Android apps, Fire tablets have had your back. Of course, the Kindle app runs perfectly well on tablets from other brands, so Amazon is leaning hard into its first-party advantage with the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro. In fact, all the new Alexa tablets announced today will offer a new Kindle mode, designed to "preserve the sanctuary of reading," according to Amazon's Panos Panay.
The updated Kindle reading experience will be enhanced if you're using the tablet with the optional nanomatte display. Amazon designed it in partnership with Corning, the company behind Gorilla Glass, to create a texture that lines up with the pixel grid in the panel. The upshot of this is that it should reduce screen glare, making it easier to read text in bright conditions. We've seen other new devices with similar finishes, including Apple's foldable iPhone Duo.
While reading in the Kindle app, the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro will silence notifications, reduce blue light, and extend battery life (presumably by killing some background processes you don't need while stuck in the Kindle app). You can also pick from three display settings: warm, paper-like, or grayscale. We'll need to test this in order to know whether it's a better experience than, say, programming a Samsung tablet to enter do-not-disturb and turn on a blue light filter when you open the Kindle app. But if you're fully ensconced within the Kindle or Alexa ecosystems, this is one device to keep on your radar.
Pricing for the Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro starts at $500 for the standard display version with 128GB of storage and 8GB of RAM, or $550 for the nanomatte display version with the same storage and memory configuration. There is also a Pro Keyboard case accessory for $150 and a Tablet Pro Pen stylus for $90, both sold separately.

Jammu, Oct 8: The Crime Branch has filed a chargesheet against two siblings in an alleged visa fraud case involving a consultancy firm based in Janipur here, officials said on Thursday.
The case was registered after Jaspal Singh of Digiana alleged he paid the accused Rs 2.30 lakh by cheque to secure an Australian work visa for his son, according to officials.
Investigators found that the accused, Poonam Sharma, allegedly provided a fake job offer letter purportedly issued by "Drillfit Energy Queensland, Australia" to induce the complainant to pay the money.
The investigation by Deputy Superintendent of Police Vishal Sharma revealed alleged fraudulent activities by Futuristic Education Consultancy, run by the accused siblings, Poonam Sharma and Akash Sharma, both residents of Janipur.
Records obtained from the Deputy Labour Commissioner, Jammu, showed that the consultancy was registered only up to March 31, 2015, and allegedly operated thereafter without valid authorisation or renewal, they said.
The investigation further revealed that Akash operated the unauthorised consultancy as its proprietor, while Poonam allegedly acted as an agent, luring unemployed youth with promises of overseas employment, officials said.
The Crime Branch said it completed the investigation and submitted the chargesheet before the court of the 13th Financial Commissioner, Jammu.
The chargesheet relates to an FIR registered in 2026 under Sections 420 (cheating), 468 (forgery), 120-B (criminal conspiracy) and 201 of the RPC ( causing disappearance of evidence), as well as Sections 10 ( Prohibition on emigration of certain persons) and 24 (penalties) of the Emigration Act, 1983.

The 2026 Atlantic hurricane season has been mercifully dull, but that’s set to change this week. Tropical Storm Isaias is forecast to become the season’s first hurricane before making landfall somewhere between Mississippi and Florida by the weekend.
El Niño has turned the Atlantic basin into a graveyard by changing winds high in the atmosphere so that they rip apart storms. That’s helped depress tropical cyclone activity to near-record-low levels and resulted in zero hurricanes. That could change imminently, though.
Isaias is churning in the Gulf of Mexico with winds of 65 mph, according to the latest update from the US National Hurricane Center. That’s just a shade below hurricane strength. The storm is forecast to pass over a patch of abnormally warm water, providing fuel for it to blossom into a hurricane. It could peak as a Category 2 storm with winds of 110 mph as it lumbers to the northeast. The storm is expected to weaken due to those aforementioned gnarly winds shortly before it makes landfall somewhere along the Gulf Coast.
The NHC has issued hurricane watches for all the coastline in Mississippi and Alabama as well as parts of the Florida Panhandle. (Tropical storm watches extend into Louisiana as well.)
Folks in that region can expect rainfall totals of up to 7 inches, though some spots in the Panhandle could see as much as 10 inches and storm surge as high as 7 feet. Tornadoes aren’t out of the question either. In other words, it’s a storm to take seriously.
Isaias could make also (or at least tie) history as the latest first Atlantic hurricane to form on record. The current record was set in 1905, when the season’s first hurricane formed on October 8. There’s still one more update scheduled for Isaias on Wednesday, so it’s possible it could just miss out on tying that mark.
Record or not, Isaias is indicative of the hurricane season that wasn’t. This year’s Atlantic hurricane season was forecast to be below average. But it’s been even quieter than expected owing to an El Niño that’s been dubbed “super,” “Godzilla,” and “supersized.” The superlatives—which meteorologists will be quick to tell you are not official designations—are indicative of the strength of this year’s event. El Niño is measured by ocean temperatures in a part of the tropical Pacific, and this year’s iteration has seen record highs throughout the summer and first part of fall.
The intensity has had a heavy hand in rearranging the atmosphere around the world, including over the Atlantic. Saharan dust has also played a role in quieting things by making the air in one of the major areas where hurricanes develop too damn dry.
For a sense of how that has impacted the Atlantic hurricane season, we can look at some averages. From 1991 to 2020, the basin saw an average of 14 named storms, seven hurricanes, and three major hurricanes—that is, storms of Category 3 or greater—annually, according to NHC data. This year has seen eight tropical storms and one soon-to-be hurricane.
Another metric to measure the season is accumulated cyclone energy (ACE for short), which takes into account not just the number and intensity of storms but how long they stick around. The ACE to date for 2026 is 10.8 units. The average for this time of year? Nearly 102, according to data maintained by Colorado State University. Most of that energy typically accumulates from mid-August through late September.
None of this is to say there might not be another surprise storm in the coming weeks. But with El Niño continuing to intensify and the peak of the season well past, the odds of this season seeing a sudden spurt of activity are minimal at best.

The Supreme Court on October 5 said it had not approved any modification to the contents of Form 6, directly contradicting the Election Commission’s (EC) recent claim that it alterations made in the form were upheld by the court. Form 6 is the document used by citizens to apply for inclusion of their names in the electoral roll.
The apex court was hearing a bunch of petitions challenging the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process and seeking the suspension of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar who has come under intense scrutiny following an Indian Express report published on September 25. It showed that Kumar had overruled written objections from election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi at least on 14 occasions in 10 months. One of the points of contention was modifications to Form 6.
On September 26, the ECI issued a press note saying that the “declaration attached to Form 6 for SIR” had been upheld by the Supreme Court.
On Monday, while arguing in front of a Bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, senior advocates Menaka Guruswamy and Vikas Singh questioned the decision-making process followed by the three-member Election Commission. Guruswamy raised concerns over the use of a modified Form 6 during the SIR process.
“Let us see how the SIR was conducted in Delhi. Form 6 has two new conditions added. The modified Form 6 was circulated. The Schedule to the RPA contains Form 6. It cannot be modified in this manner,” she submitted.
In response, chief justice Surya Kant made the court’s position clear: “We have not approved Form 6. A modified Form 6 has not been approved by us. Let us be very clear.”

Guruswami also noted that the supposed ‘illegality’ of the SIR process had prevented the conduct of free and fair elections in India. “We have grown up with free and fair elections in this country. They do not exist today,” she said.
The court issued notices to the central election commission, the chief election commissioner and the two other commissioners, seeking their responses. The Bench further mentioned that if any decision taken by the Election Commission was found not to be in accordance with the law, it would be annulled.
The Controversy Regarding Form 6
Form 6 is a statutory form prescribed under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, framed under Section 28 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950. This means the ECI cannot simply change the form or add new requirements whenever it wants. Any change to the statutory format has to be made through the parliament, rather than through an internal decision of the poll panel.
In states where the SIR is currently ongoing, such as Delhi and Karnataka, the online Form 6 available on the Election Commission’s website contains an additional declaration section between Sections J and K. In this section, an applicant has to state whether their name appears in the electoral roll from the previous SIR, whether their parents’ or grandparents’ names appear in that roll, or whether neither their name nor their parents’ names appear in the previous SIR electoral roll.
Although this declaration is not marked as mandatory, applicants cannot submit the online Form 6 without filling it in.
However, in states where the SIR has already been completed or has not yet started, such as West Bengal, the Form 6 link on the ECI website does not show this additional declaration.
Interestingly, if the Form 6 PDF is downloaded from the same ECI website for offline submission, there is no section asking for any SIR-related information. This means that the additional declaration appears to be present only in the online version of Form 6 being used in states where the SIR is underway.
SC’s May 2026 Bihar SIR Judgement
In a May 27, 2026 judgment on the Bihar SIR, the Supreme Court had said that the EC had some power to decide what documents it could ask voters to provide during an SIR.
On October 5, the ECI cited this to seemingly claim that the declarations added to Form 6 had been upheld by the Supreme Court. However, the SIR declarations in question added to Form 6 are different from what the Supreme Court had examined in the Bihar case. During the Bihar SIR, the ECI used a separate document called Annexure D.
The new declaration started appearing on the ECI’s online voter-registration system from July 2026.
Reacting to the controversy, Calcutta high court advocate Samim Ahammed said, “Despite being the holder of a constitutional post, the chief election commissioner’s conduct over the past few years has been arbitrary, with the Commission acting in violation of the Constitution and the laws of the land. The Commission does not have the power to legislate or make changes to a statute. The rules have to be laid before Parliament before they can be enforced. But the way in which the Commission has tried to bypass this process is extremely unfortunate for the health of our democracy.”
Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi commented on X that the SC observation “established beyond doubt that Gyanesh Kumar changed Form 6 illegally and unilaterally.”

A 1-kg mass of hair was removed from the stomach and small intestine of a nine-year-old girl in a rare surgery at a private hospital in Thiruvananthapuram, Keralam, authorities said on Saturday.
The girl, who was diagnosed with Rapunzel syndrome, underwent the surgery at NIMS Medicity in nearby Neyyattinkara, they said.
She was admitted to the hospital with persistent abdominal pain and vomiting, according to a statement issued by the hospital. Ultrasound and CT scans revealed severe intestinal obstruction, and a subsequent endoscopy confirmed a large mass of hair accumulated in the stomach and small intestine.
The hairball was completely removed through a complex surgical procedure led by Dr Biju I G Nair, senior consultant in the Department of Paediatric Surgery at the hospital. The girl recovered well, resumed eating normally and was discharged, the doctor said.
Dr Nair said a trichobezoar, or hairball, forms when a person repeatedly pulls out and swallows hair. The swallowed hair cannot be digested and can gradually accumulate in the stomach, forming a hard mass that may cause intestinal obstruction over time, he said.
Rare condition
Rapunzel syndrome is an extremely rare condition in which a trichobezoar extends from the stomach into the small intestine. It is usually seen in adolescent girls, according to medical literature. Hospital authorities said fewer than 100 cases have been reported worldwide.

Mumbai, Oct 08: Benchmark indices Sensex and Nifty drifted lower in early trade on Thursday as growing prospect of tighter domestic and global monetary conditions persisting for longer, surging crude oil prices and foreign fund outflows dented sentiment.
The 30-share BSE Sensex declined 264.97 points to 72,408.15 in early trade. The 50-share NSE Nifty was down 87.50 points to 22,507.65.
Among the 30 Sensex firms, ITC, Adani Ports, Bharat Electronics, Bajaj Finance, Bajaj Finserv and InterGlobe Aviation were among the major laggards.
Tata Consultancy Services, HCL Tech, Tech Mahindra and Infosys were among the winners.
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, traded 2.02 per cent higher at USD 102.2 per barrel.
Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) offloaded equities worth Rs 6,121.37 crore on Wednesday, according to exchange data.
"The outlook for Indian equities remains cautious after the RBI raised its repo rate to 5.50 per cent, tightening domestic financial conditions at a time when global markets are already contending with elevated Treasury yields and geopolitical uncertainty. Tighter domestic financial conditions and a fragile global risk backdrop could keep investors defensive," Ponmudi R, CEO of Enrich Money, an online trading and wealth-tech firm, said.
The Reserve Bank of India raised its benchmark repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent on Wednesday, its first hike in nearly four years, while signalling that rate cuts are off the table in the near term and that further hikes could follow amid rising inflation, a weak rupee and high crude oil prices.
The six-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) of the RBI voted unanimously to raise the repo rate, and sprang a surprise with a shift in policy stance to "calibrated tightening" from "neutral".
In Asian markets, South Korea's Kospi, Japan's Nikkei 225 index, Shanghai's SSE Composite index and Hang Seng index quoted lower.
US markets ended lower on Wednesday.
"The key overhang is no longer the RBI’s rate increase alone, but the growing prospect of tighter domestic and global monetary conditions persisting for longer, potentially keeping pressure on risk appetite and foreign flows. The RBI’s shift to calibrated tightening, followed by Federal Reserve minutes indicating another US rate increase may be required this year, could limit risk appetite," Hariselvan Radhakrishnan, Founder & CEO of HST Wealth, a research analyst firm, said.
On Wednesday, the Sensex fell 429.11 points, or 0.59 per cent, to settle at 72,638.70. The Nifty declined 173.05 points, or 0.76 per cent, to end at 22,603.05.

The New South Wales police commissioner made a last-minute bid to hold hearings into Sydney’s anti-Herzog protest behind closed doors, delaying the inquiry, the police watchdog has revealed.
The Law Enforcement Conduct Commission (Lecc) has said that its inquiry into the February protest at Sydney’s town hall, launched after widespread allegations of police brutality, would go ahead this month with a mix of public and private examinations, saying the timing of issues raised by police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, was “regrettable”.
Lecc launched an investigation after the protest on 9 February, during which numerous protesters – and 10 officers – were injured, including demonstrators in their 70s and 80s. Viral video footage showed police punching multiple protesters, and grabbing Muslim worshippers while they undertook their sunset prayers.
Thirty people were charged in the months after the protest, but four have since had their charges dropped. More than 20 of those charged are due to face a joint hearing next July.
In a decision made public on Thursday, the Lecc chief commissioner, Peter Johnson SC, revealed that legal representatives for Lanyon had indicated for the “first time” on 9 September that he wished to be heard on the issue of public and private examinations. The bid was made less than two weeks before the public hearings between September and November were due to start. Some hearings were also expected to be heard in private.
“The timing of these issues being raised by the Commissioner of Police is more than regrettable given its impact on the orderly progress of the investigation, the preparation for examinations and the efficient and effective use of public resources by both the Commission and the NSWPF and the associated cost and disruption flowing from the delay,” Johnson said.
Johnson said the start date of public hearings, 21 September, was subsequently delayed to “a date to be fixed” to allow a private hearing for submissions on the issue.
Lawyers acting on behalf of Lanyon submitted that Lecc’s opening address and the examination of witnesses should occur in private and not be livestreamed. They argued that the Lecc Act does not have the power to hear “broad ranging open submissions” and said Lecc should not take the “unconventional approach of hearing opening submissions in public part way through an investigation that is already underway”. 
But Lecc argued that it does have the power to decide when public examinations are appropriate. The counsel assisting submitted that public examinations were necessary because “there was already significant information concerning the events of 9 February 2026 in the public domain, including footage of use of force by police” and that senior police officers had advanced in public an “official narrative of what took place”. 
“Public comments made by senior police increase the need for independent scrutiny,” the commissioner wrote.
The counsel assisting had pointed to specific features of the investigation as reason for why only private examinations were not appropriate. This included the “significant public concern” after the protest, including in parts of the Islamic community in Western Sydney.
On Thursday, the watchdog said its inquiry into the protest would begin with a public address by counsel assisting on 19 October, followed by five weeks of private hearings. Lecc expects senior officers will then appear at public examinations.
It said its Operation Makalu inquiry would analyse the use of OC spray, as well as the “improper use of arrest powers and the police use of force” at the protest. It will consider police planning ahead of the protest and “any opportunities for improvement in the policing of protests”.
In his decision, the commissioner determined that private examinations would be held on “issues of fact” while public examinations would be held to deal with systemic issues, but only after the private examinations have been held.
In September, Palestinian Australian Eyad Shadid launched a civil case in the NSW district court, alleging he was assaulted, battered and falsely imprisoned by police near Sydney’s town hall. He alleged in his statement of claim that NSW police committed misfeasance in public office and subjected him to a malicious prosecution.
In a statement, NSW Greens justice spokesperson, Sue Higginson, described the push to hold hearings in private as “an extraordinary attempt by the police to suppress the public examination of allegations of serious misconduct by uniformed police officers, and to prevent public scrutiny of the political decisions and command structures that led to police violence against protesters”.
At a NSW parliamentary inquiry in May, Johnson said police had become “overly defensive” in response to requests for information in its investigations, describing the relationship between the agencies as “difficult”. He said the Lecc had received a record number of complaints, more than 800, as part of its investigation into the Herzog protest.
In a statement following Johnson’s comments, NSW police said it “complied with the requirements of the LECC Act in a cooperative manner”.
NSW police said in a statement it acknowledged the decision to hold private hearings and awaited the findings.

Christa Pike now walking after failed US execution, lawyer tells BBC
- Published
Christa Pike is "up and walking" while in hospital after last week's botched attempt to execute her in the US state of Tennessee, a member of her legal team says.
Pike, 50, who was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995, survived two lethal injections on 30 September. Experts described it as unprecedented.
Speaking late on Wednesday to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, lawyer Stephen Ferrell said he had not spoken to Pike directly but that he had learned she was moving around her hospital room for the first time while still being mentally "foggy".
Earlier, a court ordered the state of Tennessee to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution.
That evidence could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.
The Pike case is now in uncharted territory, as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
The failed execution was branded a "mess" by the mother of Slemmer, who was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death.
Pike's boyfriend at the time of Slemmer's gruesome murder, Tadaryl Shipp, was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison.
Pike was 18 and Shipp was 17 when they beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for troubled teens.

In their updates on Pike's condition after the attempted execution, her team had previously said she was awake and speaking, and experiencing anger and confusion. She was said at that stage to be handcuffed to her bed.
In the latest updates, given to the BBC, Ferrell said Pike was continuing to experience the after-effects of the drug pentobarbital, which was injected into her body in two doses by prison staff during the scheduled execution on 30 September.
Once it became clear that Pike was not going to die, she was taken to hospital, where she was initially unconscious and declared to be in a critical condition.
As of late on Tuesday, though, she was "fairly well", Ferrell told the BBC.
"What's been described to me is that physically there's quite a bit going on, that her arms are very injured and she's not able to use them very much."
Of her physical movements, he added: "She is up and walking for the first time today, but just around the room, not very far."
Turning to her mental state, he said: "I think it's kind of good and bad. Good that she is fairly with it, but she's also somewhat foggy. She can lose her train of thought really easily and forgets where she's going."
Ferrell said much remained unknown about what happens next. "I assume [the situation for Pike] will keep improving, but there could be some permanent damage. We don't know that yet."
He added that the team wanted Pike to receive psychological support, since that "clearly is necessary now".
Ferrell and his colleagues - who highlighted ahead of the attempted execution that Pike had a condition that would make the injection method difficult - oppose any new attempt by state prison authorities to follow the same approach.
They are also calling on the state governor, Bill Lee, to downgrade Pike's punishment to the lesser sentence of life in prison without parole.
Meanwhile, Tennessee's proponents of capital punishment have suggested that a different method be used. Senator Marsha Blackburn, the Republican candidate for state governor in next month's election, said: "Bring back the electric chair."
Asked during a court hearing on Wednesday whether the state intended to reschedule Pike's execution, the state's attorney general said he did not know.
For now, Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered a pause on all executions in the state for the rest of the year, and has said he wants answers about what went wrong. The state's prisons chief is resigning after the failed execution.
Wednesday's court hearing related to the preservation of evidence following the first attempt.
The judge, I'Ashea Myles, ordered that "anything that was in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained," including IV lines and syringes, as well as waste, like packaging, inserts, and labels.
The judge also demanded documentation on Pike's psychological condition prior to, during and after the 30 September execution attempt.
She advised the state to take "special care" not to misplace or accidentally delete any information that may be pertinent to the case.

Russell to take further grid penalty this season
- Published
George Russell says he will be taking a further grid penalty this season in addition to the one he has been hit with for this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix.
The Briton will start Sunday's race from the back of the grid because he needs to fit a new engine which takes him beyond his permitted number for the season.
But he says that he will have to take another new engine, as soon as a planned upgrade is ready, to get him to the end of the season.
Russell said: "You get (a limit of) four engines a season, so six races on each, and we have seven races to the end. So I will be taking another penalty, so yeah it's pretty relentless at the moment."
Russell's engine failure in Malaysia scuppered Mercedes' previous plan for him to last out with his older engine until the upgrade was ready, most likely for the next race, the United States Grand Prix in Austin.

"I knew I was going to have penalty," Russell said. 'The plan was always to go in Austin, and obviously Singapore is the second hardest track to overtake on on the calendars. So you would never choose to do it (here).
"But we have no engines because of all of the various failures, so there was no engine I could have reverted to from earlier in the season. With the failure I had to take it.
"We don't have the (upgrade) this weekend, and because there are seven races remaining, you can either choose to roll the dice and hope it lasts for seven races, but also suffer a performance offset (as the engine degrades), or just accept I'll be taking another penalty."
Antonelli will also likely have another back-of-the-grid penalty when the upgraded engine is introduced, following his previous one at the Italian Grand Prix, which he won from 19th on the grid.
Russell will also be reverting to an older specification car in Singapore this weekend.
Mercedes introduced an aerodynamic upgrade in Malaysia last weekend, but it did not give the car the performance uplift expected.
So in an attempt to prove whether that was because of idiosyncrasies to do with the Sepang track or a problem with the upgrade itself, Mercedes is splitting the specification of their cars.
Russell will drive the specification with which he won in Azerbaijan, the week before Malaysia, while Antonelli will run the new spec.
Russell said: "I actually asked a question already on Friday in Sepang. At the end of the day it's the car I'm reverting to is a car that was on pole by 0.8secs and Kimi won the race before, so it's important to remember the context. It's not like reverting back to a launch car.
"Given the circumstances of the grid penalty as well, it just seemed like a no-brainer. For me, unfortunately we're not going to be fighting for a podium this weekend, it's exceptionally unlikely, so it's more important for us to try and understand, was Malaysia a one-off or was it the upgrade?"

A beautiful Himalayan bird is changing its voice due to human activity, research shows
- Published
A sharp increase in human activity is having an impact on the way a Himalayan bird lives and communicates, two studies by Indian researchers have found.
The monal, a pheasant native to Himalayan mountain forests, is deeply woven into the region's cultural, folklore and identity. The eye-catching monal - the male has distinctive green, blue and copper feathers - is the state bird of India's Uttarakhand state and the national bird of Nepal, reflecting its cultural significance across the Himalayas.
But studies show that infrastructure development and tourism are squeezing its habitat, while increasing noise is altering how it communicates with potential mates and rivals.
Researchers from Uttarakhand conducted two separate studies over five years which flagged key threats to the bird.
One study found that the birds are forced to move higher in the mountains as their natural habitat in the alpine meadows above the tree line get crowded. The other says the monal is changing its pitch to cut through human noise in a busy valley.
"These two studies give a useful warning for other more vulnerable species - if the monal is forced to change both its voice and its address, how are the more sensitive species responding?" says Vishal Singh, an environmental practitioner working on ecology and climate issues in the Himalayas.
Dr Rajeev Lochan, lead researcher of both studies, told the BBC that they chose to study the monal as the bird has a narrow habitat range - it moves seasonally between the lower montane zone - an ecological belt found on the lower slopes of the mountains - and high-elevation alpine zones. This, he says, makes it a key indicator of ecosystem health in the north-western Himalayas.
"If the species is facing issues on this particular landscape, there might be a chance that the ecological disturbances are affecting other birds too," said Lochan.
The monal, researchers say, can be seen as a stand-in for the health of a fragile Himalayan ecosystem pushed to a tipping point due to unregulated tourism and heavy urbanisation.
While the region has always drawn tourists, trekkers and researchers given its scenic landscape and biodiversity, rapid infrastructure expansion in the past decade has made more places accessible, increasing footfall and disrupting the wildlife. This, coupled with mounting human pressures, suggests that climate change is emerging as another major threat to the region's already vulnerable biodiversity.
"There are a lot of factors at play but at a broader level, the problem is that the economic development of the region is not aligned to its ecological integrity," Singh said.
According to the first study, climate change is projected to continue shrinking and destabilising the Himalayan monal's habitat across the Indian Himalayas through 2100 under multiple climate scenarios.
Currently, the birds are found in alpine meadows, located high in the mountains above the forests, which form some of the Himalayas' most important seasonal grazing and biodiversity-rich habitats.
The researchers modelled how climate change could shift the monal's suitable habitat across the Indian Himalayan region in the states of Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh. It was based on the kind of global climate models and emissions scenarios used for assessments by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the UN's climate science unit.
"These birds are now slowly moving upwards in the Himalayas as the snow is melting and vegetation is growing, making the area accessible to them. They are anyway being pushed upwards as their natural habitats in alpine meadows are being encroached upon by humans," Lochan said.
The model assumes that the bird needs the current climate set-up that exists in alpine meadows in the future too, a reasonable but not certain assumption.
The birds' seasonal migration may become increasingly difficult as changes in climate may force them to move to higher elevations on hills, to smaller and fragmented areas. Their population would be scattered in disconnected pockets, which reduces chances of breeding between groups and increases their risks of long-term decline or local extinction, which is already a threat, the study says.
The second study, also conducted by Lochan, Dinesh Kumar Sharma and Anand Kumar, who work at the Hemvati Nandan Bahuguna Garhwal University, focuses on the bird's behavioural changes. They conducted the study in two valleys in Kedarnath Musk Deer Sanctuary in Uttarakhand - at Chopta, a tourist spot with busy traffic and visitors, and the largely quiet Madmaheshwar.
They recorded more than 700 monal calls across both sites using microphones and passive recording devices and then measured pitch, call length and background noise levels for a year from April 2023.
Birds in noisy environments consistently produced calls with significantly higher peak frequencies compared with those in quieter habitats, the study said.
The researchers found subtle changes in the monal's pitch that could be picked up by recording devices but might go unnoticed by the human ear.
"This does not mean that the species has undergone a permanent or evolutionary change in its vocal frequency; rather, our findings suggest behavioural flexibility in response to different acoustic environments," Lochan said.
Compared with the birds in Madmaheshwar valley, the monal in Chopta also produced shorter call durations likely to cut through low-frequency human noise from traffic and tourist footfall.
Bird calls are one of the most sophisticated forms of sound-based communication in the natural world, and significant changes can interfere with, among other things, their mating success.
"When a species must raise its pitch to be heard over tourist traffic, or climb higher as meadows turn crowded, it reveals how human pressure is rewriting the rules of life in the Himalaya," says Anjal Prakash, a public policy professor at FLAME University and contributor to IPCC reports.
Lochan says he and his team consider this a preliminary study and hope to expand the scope and depth of it.
The research comes with the caveat that it is not conclusive on ecological consequences, and more research is needed. But together, the two studies signal broader ecological stress across the Himalayas.
"In listening to the monal, we hear the Himalayas asking for space, silence and care," says Prakash.

A Texas man was put to death Wednesday evening, becoming the 30th person executed in the US this year and the first since Tennessee’s failed attempt to administer a lethal injection to Christa Pike a week ago.
Jamaal Howard was pronounced dead at 8:03 pm after receiving a fatal dose of pentobarbital at the state prison in Huntsville, the Associated Press reported.
Jamaal Howard, 46, was convicted of killing Vickie Swartout, 42, in a 2000 store robbery. The store clerk’s killing was caught on surveillance video.
Howard, who was 20 at the time, took $114 and a carton of cigarettes from the store in Silsbee, a small, rural town about 100 miles (160 kilometers) northeast of Houston, according to court records cited by the report.
He was convicted of capital murder in the killing of Swartout, who was shot once in the chest during the robbery.
Evidence presented at trial included surveillance video showing Howard shooting Swartout.
Asked by the warden if he had a final statement, Howard apologised profusely to some members of his victim’s family, who watched through a window just feet from the death chamber.
“I wish that you accept my apology and I wish for your forgiveness,” he said, shortly before the injection got underway. “I’m sorry for what happened. I wish you can learn to forgive me one of these days.”
He also thanked his friends and family and said he loved them, adding he was “in a good state of mind to find peace and the Lord, so I thank y’all.” He concluded with: "Hey, enjoy life, and peace to y’all.”
Howard's execution came a week after 1995 murder accused Christa Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital on September 30 in Tennessee.
Her lawyers continue to seek more information about what went wrong during her execution. Her lawyers said she was unconscious at a hospital after the attempt but was awake and speaking by Tuesday.
Pike, believed to be the first person to survive after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution, stunningly woke up as plans were being made to remove her from life support, just six days after she was strapped to a gurney in the death chamber, said attorney Randy Spivey.
“But on Tuesday, to the shock of everyone ... Christa woke up and began talking,” Spivey said.
Pike, who was sentenced to death for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer, is aware of what happened to her, at least up to a point, Spivey said.
Many questions remain, though, about her prognosis for recovery and whether Tennessee will make another attempt to execute Pike, now age 50.

Here's what the $6,000 Surface RTX Spark Dev Box looks like
It's covered in 1,000 air vents, which makes it look a bit like an oversized Lego brick.
The Surface Laptop Ultra may have been the highlight of Microsoft's AI-focused Windows event, but the company also showed off another intriguing piece of high-end hardware. The $6,000 Surface RTX Spark Dev Box, a powerful desktop PC optimized for AI development.
Microsoft offered a glimpse of the device earlier this year, but we just got our first good look at it. The company has previously called it a "compact PC," but after looking at it in person I'm not sure that's how I would describe it.
It may be relatively compact for its power, but it's still a beast of a machine. It's covered in air vents, which makes it look a bit like an oversized Lego brick. The box itself is relatively thin, but it's long. And it sits on an elevated base, so it will take up a sizable footprint on most desks. It's also surprisingly heavy. Microsoft hasn't shared a weight but I had trouble grabbing it with one hand. It's at least 5 to 6 lbs, possibly a bit heavier, and the base makes it awkward to hold.
That said, I don't think this is really meant to be a portable machine. It seems more in line with Apple's vision for the Mac Studio, a similarly beefy desktop (albeit one with a smaller overall footprint). The Surface RTX Spark Dev Box has a 6,1444-core GPU, 128GB of memory and a 2TB SSD. We didn't get to see it powered on during Microsoft's event but I am curious how much heat this thing will put off with more intensive tasks. It's covered in 1,000 air vents, so clearly heat management was a priority.
It has a decent number of ports, though I suspect some may be disappointed there aren't more. On the back side are three USB-C ports, a headphone jack, an HDMI port, ethernet and USB-A port. That should be enough for a decent monitor and whatever peripherals you want to connect, though unlike the Mac Studio, there's no card slot.
The Surface RTX Spark Dev Box is available now for pre-order for $5,999.99.

A “stunning” debut novel described as “unambiguously and distinctively Queensland” has won the $30,000 top prize at the Queensland literary awards (QLAs).
Meriam and Wagedagam author Lenora Thaker won the Queensland premier’s award for a work of state significance for her historical novel The Pearl of Tagai Town, which was inspired by her ancestors’ lives in an unmapped shantytown known as Cairns-Malay Town. The town once housed Indigenous Australians, Chinese, Indian, Japanese, Malaysian and Sri Lankan residents who had been segregated from the white population; it existed from the late 1800s until the late 1950s.
The QLA judges praised Thaker’s “accessible and deeply enjoyable” book for its “vivid sense of place”.
“Warm, richly drawn characters and an innovative integration of Ailan languages come together in a rich, cohesive whole, bringing new insight and fresh imaginative life to a far north Queensland community. The Pearl of Tagai Town is a stunning debut novel,” the judges wrote in a joint statement.
The winners were announced at a ceremony on Thursday night at Brisbane Powerhouse, as part of Brisbane writers festival.
Claire Thomas won the $15,000 fiction category for On Not Climbing Mountains, which follows a woman on a trip in Switzerland, who distracts herself from grief with research on famous names who had connections to the country.
The $15,000 nonfiction prize went to Find Me at the Jaffa Gate: An Encyclopaedia of a Palestinian Family by Australian-Palestinian writer Micaela Sahhar, about how her family’s story was shaped by the Nakba, when more than 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled from their homes by Israel during the country’s founding in 1948. Sahhar won the same category at the Victorian premier’s literary awards in February.
The $15,000 children’s book category was won by Once I Was a Giant by Zeno Sworder, which has also won book of the year at the Australian Book Industry awards and the children’s category at the Victorian premier’s literary award. Illustrated and written by Sworder, the book tells the tale of a tree transformed into a pencil that then writes its own story.
Julianne Negri won the $15,000 young adult category for her book The Belly of a Wolf, Helena Pantsis won the $15,000 short story category for her collection Mother Salad, and Eunice Andrada won the $17,500 poetry category for her collection Kontra.
The $15,000 people’s choice category was won by Sita Walker’s debut In a Common Hour, a novel that takes place across a single hour at a state high school. Walker has been a teacher for more than 20 years, and currently teaches English at a high school in Brisbane’s south-east.
Founded in 1999, the QLAs were previously known as the Queensland premier’s literary awards until 2012, when they were abolished by then premier Campbell Newman. Queensland’s literary community intervened to keep the awards alive.
The QLAs were administered by the State Library of Queensland from 2014 until 2025, when the awards were embroiled in controversy over the arts minister John-Paul Langbroek’s intervention to stop the library awarding a $15,000 fellowship to First Nations author K A Ren Wyld, over a social media post about the dead Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar.
Wyld said she had posted the comment in an “emotional moment”, and that her winning manuscript had nothing to do with Gaza.
Twelve QLA judges resigned in protest of Wyld’s treatment, leading to last year’s awards being delayed. Langbroek eventually handed their management over to the Brisbane writers festival from this year.

Carlos Alcaraz says tennis schedule 'going in wrong direction', players 'pushed too much' as Jannik Sinner ends season early
World No 1 Jannik Sinner, who has not played since winning Wimbledon in July, will miss the rest of the 2026 season with a knee injury; Carlos Alcaraz believes relentless schedule is contributing to injuries; Alcaraz missed over four months of action this summer due to a wrist problem
Thursday 8 October 2026 13:54, UK
Carlos Alcaraz believes tennis' relentless schedule is "going in the wrong direction" and feels players are being "pushed" to feature in too many tournaments.
The world No 3, who will play his Shanghai Masters opener on Saturday, was speaking two days after successfully defending the Japan Open for his third title of an injury-hit year which saw him miss four and a half months between April and August with a wrist issue.
World No 1 Jannik Sinner announced this week that he has ended his season early due to a knee problem.

Alcaraz said: "One of the reasons we had to see the players who are getting injured, they [ATP officials] are pushing us too much out of the line sometimes to play a lot of tournaments, to play a lot of matches.
"It's getting in the wrong direction.
"I just wish Jannik the best for these months, just to be in good shape for the next season.
"Hopefully see him soon, but they have to see a little bit what's going on on the tour along with the players."
Djokovic: Sinner has to think long term

"It's important that you give yourself more years to your career, so you have more chances to accomplish all of your objectives.
"If you're away from the tour for so long and then make a comeback, you have to deal with more things than you normally have to deal with. You're evaluating with your team constantly.
"When you get the green light to be able to compete, then it's mental. You're on the court and you're thinking: 'Am I really completely healed and free to make this run?'
"For him if it's a knee, it's affecting everything, affecting every single movement."

Newcastle University is facing a backlash from conservationists over the appointment of the heir to an Indian oil and gas fortune who runs a controversial mega-zoo as a professor of sustainability.
The university announced that Anant Ambani had been given a professorship of practice for “his work in conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship” and “significant contributions to advancing a more sustainable future”.
Ambani is the son of India’s richest person, Mukesh Ambani, who made his fortune primarily in oil and gas, owns the world’s largest oil refinery and has close ties with the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Mukesh Ambani has enthusiastically praised BJP policies, and firms linked to his Reliance conglomerate have recently made significant donations to the party. The prime minister, Narendra Modi, attended Anant Ambani’s lavish 2024 wedding in Mumbai.
Anant Amabani, 31, who is leads on renewable energy on the Reliance Group’s executive board and is worth an estimated £90bn, has set up Vantara, a 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo near the family’s oil refining facilities in Gujarat, which reportedly has more than 150,000 animals including 200 lions, 250 leopards and 900 crocodiles, and where he hosted his opulent pre-wedding celebrations attended by celebrity guests and politicians.
Conservation groups have previously raised questions about how some of the animals were sourced, given many were endangered species. Vantara has never been found guilty of any wrongdoing.
The university’s announcement was met with incredulity and derision from academic staff and Indian and international conservationists and environmentalists.
Ramachandra Guha, a leading Indian public intellectual and the author of the book Speaking With Nature: The Origins of Indian Environmentalism, said: “I must say that it is a rather mystifying choice. As a scholar of Indian and global environmentalism, I can name at least 50 – perhaps 100 – individuals who are far better qualified to be thus honoured. They include soil scientists, energy scientists, water conservation experts, community forest workers, ecologists, pollution abatement experts etc who have made real and tangible contributions to a more sustainable future for India and Indians.
“I wonder on whose advice Newcastle University has acted, and whether it did due diligence on what has and has not been done in these fields. Its appointment of Mr Ambani is puzzling in the extreme, and is likely to adversely affect the university’s institutional credibility and intellectual standing.”
Bhuvan Mangalore, an Indian investigator into illegal wildlife trade who is completing a dissertation on Vantara at Anglia Ruskin University, asked: “Is this a joke?”
Prof Matt Perry, the chair of the University and College Union branch at Newcastle University, said staff members had objected to the appointment citing environmental concerns.
Prof Lyla Mehta, the head of the climate, environment and sustainability department at the University of Sussex’s Institute of Development Studies, shared concerns that “as public funding for universities falls, there is a real danger that billionaire and corporate money begins to shape academia”.
She said: “Universities are supposed to be places that question power and hold corporations to account, not give them academic legitimacy.”
In April, Anant Ambani launched Vantara University, billed as the world’s first global university dedicated to wildlife conservation and veterinary science.
Lorne Stockman, a research co-director at Oil Change International, said: “At a time when the climate crisis demands an urgent phaseout of oil and gas, we must demand our publicly funded institutions do better.”
In 2025, an investigation by the German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung found that many animals delivered to Vantara arrived through countries with opaque wildlife trading networks such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the United Arab Emirates, raising concerns that endangered species may have been illegally trafficked.
In August last year, an investigation by India’s supreme court, which lasted less than three weeks, cleared the zoo’s operators of any wrongdoing. A subsequent fact-finding mission into the zoo by Cites, the UN body that regulates the trade of endangered species, found that some of the permits used to bring animals to Vantara were probably forged.
Its report said: “There is a need for caution to ensure that imports of large numbers of animals by these facilities are not inadvertently creating a demand for illegally sourced animals.”
Cites recommended restrictions on India’s imports of endangered wild animals. However, it subsequently reversed its decision after objections from India, the US and Japan at a Cites meeting after they argued there was not enough proof of illegal imports.
In August, the zoo launched a “reset” in its operations by appointing a former Cites head to oversee its operations and said it would voluntarily pause all wildlife imports until June next year.
Vantara has declined to comment. The Ambani family and Vantara have previously denied the allegations of wildlife trafficking. They have said: “Our mission and focus continues to be the rescue, rehabilitation and care of animals.”
A Newcastle University spokesperson said: “The award of a professorship of practice recognises Mr Ambani’s contributions to conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship through his work with Vantara, a wildlife rescue and conservation initiative, and as the executive lead for the Reliance Group’s transition toward a green energy future.”

After pleading guilty, a 54-year-old North Carolina man, Michael Smith, was sentenced to 18 months in prison for using artificial intelligence to generate songs for a scheme that stole millions from music streaming platforms.
In a press release Tuesday, the US Department of Justice said that Smith is the first American criminally charged with AI-assisted streaming fraud.
First charged in 2024, Smith successfully ran the scheme for seven years without detection.
Starting in 2017, Smith began using fake email accounts and “fraudulently obtained debit cards” to create “thousands of fraudulent accounts” on services including Amazon Music, Apple Music, Spotify, and YouTube Music, the DOJ said. He then employed software that pushed the bots to continuously stream songs that he claimed to own, which the DOJ said were AI-generated.
By his arrest in 2024, he had created “hundreds of thousands of AI-generated songs,” then dispersed billions of automated streams among them so that the bots could avoid raising any red flags by all targeting the same song at once. All together, the fake songs generated substantially more streams than some of the most popular artists today, however. According to the DOJ, in a glaring example from April 2023, Smith’s fake songs were fraudulently streamed 80.9 million times during that month, while Taylor Swift’s entire catalog only got 9.3 million streams during the same time period.

It’s no surprise that NASA’s new tack toward foreign partnerships—good deals only, please—is challenging preconceived notions of international cooperation in space.
Without a massive budget hike, the US space agency’s emphasis on building a Moon Base and winning a competition for lunar real estate and resources with China will inevitably leave lesser priorities behind.
Gone is the Lunar Gateway, a space station that was to be assembled in orbit around the Moon. For the United States, Gateway was an unnecessary distraction and expense as NASA goes all-in on placing a surface station near the Moon’s south pole.
NASA canceled the Mars Sample Return mission after its budget ballooned beyond $10 billion. It would have cannibalized the agency’s budget for robotic science missions, a funding line already in jeopardy as the Trump administration directs NASA to focus on human spaceflight and a Moon Base.
Before their cancellation, each project involved extensive cooperation with NASA’s international partners, but NASA was the leader on both. It’s not surprising that a nation’s priorities will change with elections and external pressures, like the 21st-century space race taking shape with China.
Going forward, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said NASA’s international partners must be ready to make “meaningful contributions,” with greater urgency than before. That means they should offer something that NASA or US companies aren’t already doing and deliver the contribution when NASA needs it.
This is creating friction in some areas. It’s most apparent between NASA and the European Space Agency, which is struggling to find a place in NASA’s Moon Base program after the cancellation of Gateway. Isaacman dismissed an ESA proposal earlier this year to develop a European cargo lander to carry supplies for the Moon Base, a role NASA officials expect US-built landers to fill sooner.
So what does a good deal in international spaceflight look like in the Trump era? Isaacman cited a couple of examples: Japan’s commitment to provide a pressurized rover for astronauts on the Moon and Italy’s agreement to build what will likely be the first habitat for the Moon Base.
The idea for the LISA mission has been around for decades, but the concept was supercharged in 2015 with the first detection of gravitational waves by a ground-based observatory and the launch of LISA Pathfinder, seen here, a satellite to demonstrate that the technologies behind LISA would actually work.

The idea for the LISA mission has been around for decades, but the concept was supercharged in 2015 with the first detection of gravitational waves by a ground-based observatory and the launch of LISA Pathfinder, seen here, a satellite to demonstrate that the technologies behind LISA would actually work.
Credit:
ESA–P. Sebirot, 2015
Cosmic vibes
Here’s another one. Scientists are in the early stages of developing the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) mission, the world’s first space-based observatory for detecting and studying gravitational waves.
As currently envisioned, the LISA mission will be led by the European Space Agency, with significant contributions from the United States. The mission will use three spacecraft flying in a triangle formation in heliocentric orbit, positioned nearly 1.6 million miles (2.5 million kilometers) apart to pick up the faint signals of low-frequency gravitational waves. Launch is scheduled for around 2035.
Gravitational waves are a relatively new area of astronomy, using detectors spread across a wide area, like on a continent or in space, to identify ripples in the fabric of space-time generated by cataclysmic events in the distant cosmos. Beginning with the first detection with a ground-based observatory in 2015, astronomers have used gravitational waves rippling across the Universe to reveal the collisions of black holes and neutron stars in faraway galaxies.
LISA will unlock a new wave of gravitational wave science by spreading its detectors over greater distances. Each spacecraft will carry two free-floating gold-platinum cubes inside an internal Faraday cage that protects them from all external disturbances other than gravitation, canceling out thruster firings, spacecraft vibrations, and the almost imperceptible influences from solar radiation pressure and interplanetary dust.
The LISA spacecraft will literally fly themselves around the free-floating cubes inside them, while inter-satellite lasers will measure the exact distances between the test masses. The laser ranging instruments must be sensitive enough to detect a change in distance smaller than the size of an atom to confirm a gravitational wave detection.
Under its agreement with ESA, NASA is responsible for supplying the transmitters and telescopes for the lasers. NASA will also provide charge management devices to reduce the buildup of electric charge on the proof masses inside each spacecraft and support data analysis on the ground to find the sources of LISA’s gravitational wave detections. Europe will build the spacecraft, launch them, and operate them.
This is exactly the kind of international partnership NASA should hold onto, according to Ira Thorpe, a gravitational wave astronomer at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center and leader of the US science team for the LISA mission. NASA isn’t working on its own gravitational wave observatory for space, and the agency likely couldn’t afford it if it wanted to.
An artist’s impression of gravitational waves generated by binary neutron stars.
An artist’s impression of gravitational waves generated by binary neutron stars.
Credit:
R. Hurt/NASA/JPL-Caltech
“We are in the era of people interested in having good deals, and LISA is a very good deal for the US,” Thorpe said in a recent presentation at the National Academies’ Committee on Astronomy and Astrophysics.
“We are paying for roughly a third [of the mission],” Thorpe said. “We’re getting all of the science data, 100 percent of it. That is very good leverage. We are giving them (ESA) this flagship. If the US was to do LISA on its own, it would probably be a… $3 billion kind of number as an off-the-top-of-my-head guess. For a fraction of that cost, we are getting the same science.”
Thorpe’s $3 billion estimate isn’t far off the mark. ESA approved development of the LISA mission in 2024 with a budget of 1.75 billion euros ($2 billion), but that figure doesn’t include contributions from the United States or individual ESA member states. As it stands today, NASA’s work on the LISA mission is expected to cost around $1 billion, but the agency hasn’t yet established a firm budget commitment.
“I think this is the largest science mission that ESA has attempted to do. Full stop,” Thorpe said. The LISA mission has a long history, with the first concepts for a gravitational wave observatory dating to the 1970.
“It’s bounced back and forth, depending on how the political winds have shifted on both sides of the Atlantic over decades,” Thorpe said. “I think we’re in a very stable system where ESA is going to clearly lead. NASA is going to be the major partner, a critical partner, for the project.”
But the Trump administration injected doubt into LISA’s future last year when the White House proposed canceling NASA’s participation in the project, alongside dozens of other science missions. Congress rejected the cuts and restored funding for fiscal year 2026, but the Trump administration again proposed cancellation in its 2027 budget request released earlier this year.
“That caused some concern in Europe, which I think is understandable,” Thorpe said. “But at the same time, speaking from the project side, we continue to do our work. We try to just focus on making our deliverables. We’ve met every deliverable commitment to ESA so far. We have not missed.”
The full-scale Engineering Development Unit Telescope for the LISA mission, still in its shipping frame, is seen inside a clean room in 2024 at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland.
Credit:
NASA/Dennis Henry
The full-scale Engineering Development Unit Telescope for the LISA mission, still in its shipping frame, is seen inside a clean room in 2024 at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland.
Credit:
NASA/Dennis Henry
Powerful friends
Congress is expected to continue funding LISA, which has powerful patrons on Capitol Hill and was one of a handful of future NASA science missions with a specific funding line in Congress’s appropriations bill for 2026.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), whose constituency includes NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center leading the US contribution to LISA, is the top Democrat on the Senate subcommittee responsible for writing NASA’s budget. Van Hollen could take over as chairman if Democrats win control of the Senate in this year’s midterm elections. Across the Capitol, Rep. Glenn Ivey (D-Md.), whose district also includes Goddard, sits on the corresponding subcommittee in the House.
“I think we’re in very good shape going forward,” Thorpe said.
The NASA official overseeing all of the agency’s astrophysics missions is Shawn Domagal-Goldman. Despite the White House’s attempt to end NASA’s contribution to the LISA mission, the 2026 budget passed by Congress and subsequently signed into law by President Trump should signal to ESA that Washington supports the project.
“Something this complex is always challenging, but it’s why it’s important that we reaffirm our commitment with the funding that we have in the FY ’26 appropriations bill,” Domagal-Goldman said. “As long as we have a continuing resolution or anything at our current funding levels, we will maintain our commitment to the LISA mission.”
“I’m really happy for that because when LISA launches, it’s going to answer some of these other big questions that you can only do with a space-based gravitational wave observatory,” he said.
LISA’s scientific pursuits include investigating the origins of black holes and galaxy formation. It could potentially be sensitive enough to detect gravitational waves originating shortly after the Big Bang, allowing scientists to test the theories about the birth of our Universe, according to NASA.
“These are propagating disturbances in space-time,” Thorpe said of gravitational waves. “They can carry energy. They can carry momentum, and I think most interesting for astronomers, they can carry information about the systems that produce them, and we can use them to understand the Universe.”
Physicists will use detections from LISA to test Einstein’s general theory of relativity. Some of the most cataclysmic events in the cosmos, such as mergers of supermassive black holes, should produce a very specific gravitational wave signature, according to general relativity. LISA will be more sensitive to lower-frequency gravitational waves than ground-based observatories, like LIGO, corresponding to the kind of waves scientists expect to be generated by the most massive black holes.
“GR gives us an exact prediction for what this waveform would look like, so any small deviation would give you some hint as to what might be going on,” Thorpe said. “I like to think if GR is going to break—and I don’t generally like to bet against Einstein—but if it is going to break, these are the kinds of places where it may break down.”

Another joint science mission between NASA and ESA has, at least so far, survived the White House’s budget ax. NASA has long been on the hook to provide the launch for Europe’s Rosalind Franklin Mars rover, along with a science instrument and retrorockets for the craft that will deliver it to the Martian surface. The Trump administration sought to cancel NASA’s role in the mission, but funding approved by Congress last year was enough for NASA to finally book a launch for Europe’s first Mars roveron a SpaceX rocket in 2028. Notably, Rosalind Franklin is currently the only future Mars rover with any NASA involvement.
Questions remain about NASA’s role in other joint missions with ESA. The New Athena X-ray observatory, scheduled to launch in the late 2030s, is supposed to be the largest X-ray telescope ever built, a successor to NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory, still operational after launching in 1999. As with LISA, New Athena was conceived as a European-led mission with major support from NASA.
Domagal-Goldman said NASA is “fully engaged” with ESA on the New Athena mission and remains “fully committed” to the partnership. But New Athena didn’t get a specific funding callout in Congress’s 2026 budget for NASA.
The chances of a major US contribution to ESA’s next mission to Venus, named Envision, are less assured. NASA has its own Venus missions in the pipeline, and although the US space agency has not officially announced that it is pulling out of the Envision partnership, ESA is moving ahead with contracts to begin developing a European-made radar mapping instrument for the Envision orbiter, which was previously supposed to be built at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California.
As NASA’s support wavered, ESA was on the clock to decide on Envision’s radar because the mission is slated for launch in 2031. With Envision, at least, ESA is ready to strike out on its own.
Stephen Clark is a space reporter at Ars Technica, covering private space companies and the world’s space agencies. Stephen writes about the nexus of technology, science, policy, and business on and off the planet.

The Trump administration is suspending Microsoft and Adobe from a federal program that companies use to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residency, Vice President JD Vance said Thursday during a press conference.
Vance accused Microsoft of abusing the Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM. The program is an initial step that employers generally must complete before sponsoring a worker for an employment-based green card, requiring them to show that no qualified and available US workers could fill the role.
“If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” Vance said.
Business Insider has reached out to Microsoft and Adobe for comment.
The announcement is the latest escalation for the administration against companies that rely on highly skilled foreign workers, particularly through the H-1B visa system. Microsoft is one of the biggest employers of H-1B workers in the US.
It was not immediately clear how long the suspension would last or what it would mean for Microsoft employees whose permanent-residency cases are already pending.

'Rock, paper, scissors' decides London Marathon dates
- Published
A game of rock, paper, scissors was used to determine when the elite female and male races will take place during next year's unique two-day London Marathon.
After confirming they were playing for the right to race on the traditional Sunday, women's wheelchair world record holder Catherine Debrunner beat men's world record holder Sabastian Sawe - both 2026 London Marathon champions in their respective races - in the contest.
As a result, the elite men and men's wheelchair races are set for Saturday, 24 April, with the women's races the following day.
Hugh Brasher, chief executive of London Marathon Events, said: "Sabastian and Catherine's rock, paper, scissors battle was an entertaining way to decide which day would host each elite race.
"Splitting the elite races will allow us to shine an even brighter spotlight on the extraordinary athletes taking part."
Earlier this year, organisers of the event confirmed the London Marathon will be held across two days in what is said to be a momentous one-off edition of the event.
The decision was made to enable more people to take part, after a record 1.33 million people entered the ballot for next year.
In 2027 a record-breaking 100,000 participants will take part and it is estimated that more than £150m will be raised for charitable causes.
The women's championship categories will line-up behind the women's elite field for the first time in the London race.
"Our outstanding elite women's wheelchair field will begin the action just ahead of them, creating a true celebration of women's marathon racing," Brasher added.
The main events on both days will be a mixed field of male, female and non-binary participants.

Women account for 43% of the workforce in India’s Ayush services sector, with their representation crossing 50% in several organised segments, including hospitals, day-care centres, educational institutions and wellness establishments, according to a new assessment of the sector released by the Central government on Thursday (October 8, 2026).
The Ayush Services Sector Report, prepared by the Research and Information System for Developing Countries (RIS) and released on Ayurveda Day 2026, estimates that the sector supports 1.76 million livelihoods across healthcare, wellness, education and allied services.
Women’s representation is highest in spas and wellness resorts, where it exceeds 60%, followed by educational institutions at 58%, day-care centres at 57% and hospitals at 53%, says the report.
The findings come as the Ayush services economy expands beyond traditional clinical practice into wellness, education, preventive health and medical value travel.
16.91% growth
The sector, comprising Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa and Homoeopathy, was estimated at $36.92 billion in 2024-25. It has registered a compound annual growth rate of 16.91% since 2022-23.
Standalone clinics remain the largest segment, generating an estimated $16.21 billion, or 43.9% of the sector’s revenue. Day-care centres contribute another $10.13 billion. Together, the two segments account for more than 70% of the sector’s revenue.
“More than one million livelihoods are concentrated in local and standalone clinics, underlining the sector’s employment footprint across urban and rural areas,’’ says the report.
The wellness segment has recorded a 21.29% compound annual growth rate, while yoga centres registered about 75% growth in revenue over two years, according to the assessment.
Ayurveda remains the largest individual Ayush system, accounting for $17.73 billion, or about 48% of the total services revenue.
The sector is also gaining a foothold in medical value travel. Ayush-related medical value travel generated an estimated $1.77 billion in 2024-25. Although international patients account for only around 5% of patient volumes, they contribute an estimated 15-25% of hospital-segment revenue, with therapeutic programmes typically involving stays of five to 11 days.
The assessment projects that the Ayush services economy could expand to between $216 billion and $318 billion by 2047.
Job opportunities
Union Minister of State for Ayush Prataprao Jadhav said the sector’s expansion was creating employment opportunities across healthcare, wellness, education and allied services, while also opening avenues for entrepreneurship and women’s participation.
The report projects further employment opportunities in healthcare delivery, wellness, education, medical travel, research, digital health and allied services as the sector expands.
