Dramatic scenes in Delhi as police break up protest by opposition MPs
- Published
Delhi witnessed dramatic scenes on Tuesday night when police broke up a protest by opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and other MPs who were seeking the resignation of India's top election official over a controversial voter roll revision.
Videos showing police forcing Gandhi onto a bus and preventing him from climbing out of the bus window subsequently went viral on social media.
The protest marks a fresh escalation in the opposition's standoff with the Election Commission.
Opposition parties accuse Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar of revising electoral rolls to benefit India's governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Both the BJP and the commission have rejected the allegation.
Gandhi, his sister Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and other MPs sat in protest at a nearby building for the entire day after they were stopped during their march to the Election Commission's office.
The commission said it was willing to meet the opposition, but objected to their proposed 240-member delegation meeting at the parliament.
In a statement released on Tuesday night, it said that a party representative must request an appointment and that meetings are held at the commission.
Gandhi had said earlier in the day that the opposition simply wanted to meet the election commissioners and ask questions about the voter roll revision.
"We are all opposition MPs... and we just want to speak with them," he told reporters. "I do not know why the Election Commission does not want to talk to us."
News agency ANI, citing a statement from the police, reported that the protesters were removed "to maintain law and order and prevent the situation from escalating".
A police complaint has also been registered against the Gandhis for entering Akashvani Bhavan (or the Broadcasting House) without permission, PTI news agency reported.
Security was tightened around the Election Commission headquarters on Tuesday, with police barricading roads along the route between parliament and the commission's office.
Police officers, some carrying batons and wearing body cameras, reportedly outnumbered protesters along the route to the poll panel's office.
In the afternoon, they detained several MPs who tried to take alternative routes to reach the commission, police official Manjeet Sheoran told the BBC.
"They were picked up in buses and taken to different police stations," he said.
The Gandhi siblings were also detained and taken away in a police bus, but were released shortly afterwards. They then resumed their march before staging a sit-in at Akashvani Bhavan near the Election Commission headquarters.
Police did not say how many lawmakers were detained. The opposition said 237 MPs from several parties took part in the march.
Tuesday's protest came just four days after the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a Gen Z-backed online satirical movement, organised demonstrations in Mumbai and Delhi, also demanding the CEC's resignation. The group has described those demonstrations as the beginning of a nationwide campaign and has called for another round of protests on 10 October.
At the centre of the controversy is the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. The exercise began in the eastern state of Bihar in June 2025 before being expanded to other parts of the country.
The commission says the revision is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible voters from electoral rolls. More than 130 million names have so far been removed from draft voter lists nationwide.
Opposition parties and activists allege that many eligible voters have been excluded and accuse the poll panel of conducting the process improperly.
The campaign against Kumar gathered momentum after an investigation by the Indian Express newspaper reported that election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally objected at least 14 times over a 10-month period to decisions and orders they said had been issued in the commission's name without their knowledge.
According to the report, the objections related to issues including additions and deletions from voter rolls, access to the voter database and the security of electoral data.
The three-member commission, comprising the CEC and two election commissioners, defended its decision-making process, saying differing views were part of institutional functioning and that decisions had ultimately been taken unanimously.
The revelations nevertheless triggered a political backlash, with opposition leaders intensifying calls for Kumar's resignation.
Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge said they had three "non-negotiable" demands: Kumar's resignation, cancellation of the SIR exercise and a return to paper ballot voting.
Mocking the election chief, Rahul Gandhi, tweeted: "Gyanesh, it's done, bro. Time to resign."
The BJP condemned the protests.
BJP MP Sambit Patra described them as a "sponsored attempt" to bring about a change of power through "anarchy". He accused opposition parties of seeking to undermine constitutional institutions, including the Election Commission.
The controversy has also reached India's Supreme Court, which has asked both the federal government and the Election Commission to respond to a petition alleging that Kumar took key decisions without the approval of the two other election commissioners.

Ebola creates new hot spots in Congo as responders describe ‘chaotic’ response
The Ebola outbreak in Congo is spreading rapidly to new hot spots where patients have little or no support
The Ebola outbreak in Congo is creating new hot spots where there's little to no support for patients, responders and officials say, as health workers admit there could still be a long way to go in fighting the disease that has killed over 4,000 people.
More than 70% of new cases are still coming from outside of known contacts and at least 60% of deaths are outside of treatment centers, Africa CDC Director-General Dr. Jean Kaseya told The Associated Press. “There are so many other people who are becoming sick, who are not tested, treated, or listed,” said Kaseya on Tuesday.
The conflict-battered, remote North Kivu province, which has emerged as the new epicenter, now accounts for around 40% of all newly confirmed cases in Congo, compared with 24% at the end of August. But the response on the ground is “chaotic,” said Stephanie Hoffmann, a project coordinator with Doctors Without Borders (MSF). “There is a lack of coordination and organization, but there’s certainly a lack of actors present here,” Hoffmann told the AP.
Congo's deadliest Ebola outbreak — caused by the Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved vaccine or treatment — was declared in May under some of the most challenging conditions imaginable fueled by mass population movements, rebel violence, mistrust and poor welfare of front line workers.
Congo has recorded more than 8,500 cases in the outbreak, according to government data, making it the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record and the country’s deadliest. On Tuesday, Kenya reported its first Ebola case, a man who arrived from Congo and died while receiving treatment.
The biggest challenge to date is contact tracing, Dr. Kayesa said. Only 23% of expected contacts of Ebola patients have so far been traced. The disease is spreading in a region of Congo with intense population movements due to economic activities, conflict displacement and mining, and where there’s deep mistrust with the government and misinformation about the virus.
“I’m unable to tell you when we can stop this outbreak unless we implement the village-centered approach,” the Africa CDC chief said, calling for direct involvement of villages and local leaders in contact tracing, burials of deceased patients and isolation of cases.
Many Ebola treatment centers in North Kivu are struggling with shortages of health workers and supplies, contributing to more deaths among patients, the World Health Organization has said.
North Kivu’s case fatality rate of 58% is the highest among Congo’s seven affected provinces. The disease has spread to half of its 34 health zones. In nine of those 17 affected zones, more than half of patients with confirmed infections have died, according to Health Ministry data.
Desperate for care, patients in some parts of North Kivu have turned to regular health facilities, MSF said.
“Local healthcare workers are the ones feeling this the most because they have to make the decision between sending their community members home to potentially die by themselves or putting themselves at risk to help treat them in their health center,” said Hoffmann, coordinator of MSF’s Ebola treatment center in Butembo, North Kivu.
Nearly five months after the outbreak was declared, it has become harder to track in parts of North Kivu, where residents still have “a hard time believing the disease exists,” said Michel Ngimba of the National Institute of Biomedical Research in Butembo.
He described cases in which families were reluctant to report a death or allow a sample to be taken from someone who died with Ebola symptoms. In other cases, families “want to arrange the funeral quickly,” Ngimba said, potentially creating new chains of transmission because the bodies of people who die from Ebola are highly contagious.
“The situation has become more difficult to monitor (and) surveillance has to deal with situations that are highly fluid and sometimes difficult to document,” he said.

Video: Live rat in gulaab jamuns at Maharashtra shop triggers outrage, FDA action
After a video surfaced online, the Maharashtra FDA took cognisance, issued a notice to Harish Gulab Jamun shop, and initiated action over the reported food safety violation.
A deeply distressing food safety incident has surfaced in Maharashtra’s Bhiwandi after a live rat was found moving inside a large container filled with Gulab Jamuns at a local sweet shop. A video showing the rodent inside the container has gone viral on social media, triggering public outrage and raising serious questions over hygiene, food storage and safety standards at the establishment.
The footage shows the live rat roaming inside the container while the Gulab Jamuns are kept for sale.
The incident has sparked anger among citizens, with questions being raised over how the rodent managed to enter the container and whether adequate precautions were being taken to protect food from contamination.
The matter was brought to the attention of the Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) after the video surfaced online. Officials subsequently issued a notice to the shop, identified as Harish Gulab Jamun, and initiated action over the reported food safety lapse.
According to the information available, the FDA has also directed that operations and the sale of food items at the establishment be halted until further notice.
Further action is expected after the department examines the circumstances surrounding the incident and determines whether additional violations of food safety regulations have taken place.
WIDER MAHARASHTRA FDA CRACKDOWN
The Bhiwandi incident comes amid an intensified crackdown by the Maharashtra FDA on food safety and hygiene violations under Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe.
In recent weeks, the department has taken action against eateries over poor hygiene, improper storage, inadequate documentation and other safety lapses.
Licences of eight eateries in Mumbai were suspended, while the registration certificates of three others were cancelled or suspended during separate inspections.
The department has also carried out seizures involving chemically ripened bananas, banned gutkha and pan masala, adulterated milk and khoya among others.
In one major investigation in Pune district, the FDA uncovered suspected milk adulteration involving detergent and Nonylphenol Ethoxylate, while 16,730 litres of milk were destroyed during related action.
In Akola, around 1,900 kg of khoya was seized ahead of the festive season for examination of its quality and hygiene standards.
The Bhiwandi case is now likely to face further scrutiny as the FDA examines the shop's food handling and storage practices.
With the viral video intensifying public concern, further regulatory or legal action could follow depending on the findings of the ongoing proceedings.

"The race is too hard for women. They are simply not tough enough to do it."
Those are the words of Lazarus Lake, race director of the Barkley Marathons - one of the world's hardest ultramarathons which to date, of the approximate 1,000 people who have started, only 20 have ever completed.
Speaking in 2015 and daring for someone to prove him wrong, it took nine years until a British ultra-runner did just that.
Completing the extreme 100-mile course with just one minute 39 seconds to spare of the 60-hour cut-off, Jasmin Paris from Midlothian made history and cemented her name in the ultra-running history books.
But now, increasingly, she is not alone.
Last summer, there was a female one-two for the first time in the gruelling Montane Summer Spine Race from Derbyshire to Scotland. Rachel Entrekin set a new course record and became the first woman to win the Cocodona 250 in Arizona in May, while last month Sophie Woods smashed the overall record by six days to complete the Via Alpina.
It appears female runners are no longer just taking part in ultra-endurance events, they are competing with their male counterparts, breaking records and in some cases, winning races outright.
All of this has prompted suggestions that they are perhaps better suited to these kinds of challenges.
But is there any scientific proof? Do women really have any physiological or psychological advantages in endurance exercise (anything that takes more than six hours)? And if so, could we see more of these records fall in the future?
In running distances up to the marathon, there is on average a 10-12% performance gap between males and females.
Men are generally stronger and built with a bigger aerobic engine.
But as the distance increases, those physical advantages appear to become less relevant and the gap starts to narrow.
The "gender pace gap" diminishes to 0.25% in 100-mile races, according to a study of more than 20 years of amateur ultra-race data conducted by RunRepeat, in collaboration with the International Association of Ultrarunners,
Anything further than 195 miles and women have the potential to be faster.
So why might this be the case?
For Professor Andy Jones, an expert in endurance performance at the University of Exeter, there are three potential physiological explanations why women could perform better over longer distances or durations.
Fat metabolism – women have higher fat stores and burn it more efficiently, giving them a steady energy source for longer.
Muscles – women have more oxygen-efficient muscle fibres, known as "slow twitch", that are better suited for endurance activities.
Fatigue resistance – women retain more strength over hours of endurance exercise.
However, Jones, who played a key role in Eliud Kipchoge's sub two-hour marathon challenge in 2019, is keen to point out that the science in this area is "behind".
"There isn't as much hard evidence as there would be for shorter distances, which have been studied for a long time in quite some detail," he adds.
That is a view shared by Dr Richard Burden, co-lead of female athlete health and performance at the UK Sports Institute, who feels a lot more information needs to be gathered before conclusions can be made.
"At the moment we are speculating … there are definitely some physiological adaptations that you see more in women than men that are favourable for ultra-type events. But those need to be better established and more studies would need to be done."
Physiology, however, only gets you so far. The realities of ultra-endurance exercise - multi-day events, sleep deprivation, extreme terrain and conditions, to name but a few – mean the journey to the finish line is as much mental as it is physical.
And for Sophie Woods, this is where women have the edge.
"It's not necessarily about being the fastest person at the start," she says. "It is about preparation, it is about mental strength and being able to continue to persevere when things go wrong."
During the New Zealand runner's record-breaking run of the Via Alpina, she was forced to expect the unexpected – from disruption caused by wildfires that made her route longer and more dangerous to swarms of horseflies.
"I was so tired and there were so many of them and I wanted to have a complete meltdown and just cry, but I couldn't because if I stopped moving, they started biting me," she says.
"I think women are really good at adapting and continuing and just knowing that once we start something, you've just got to keep moving until you get to the finish."
That view is echoed by Yngvild Kaspersen, who last month became the first woman to win the prestigious Ultra-Trail Mont Blanc CCC race in the Alps twice. She credits her victory to the "mental game" she puts herself through in training.
The Norwegian, who balances life as a professional runner with her job as a GP, also believes female ultra-runners are so strong because camaraderie in the community is unrivalled.
"We're competitors but we're also motivating each other, inspiring each other, pushing each other to do better in the races," she says. "If you see the podiums for the women this year [at UTMB], how close we are and how we're running together out there - that's very special and I'm very proud to be a part of that community and that group of women."
So can we explain why women might be more resilient?
Sports dietitian Renee McGregor, who specialises in athlete nutrition and hormonal health, believes the answer comes from the female body itself.
"The moment women step into puberty, we are dealing with a fluctuating hormonal system," she says. "We never ever give ourselves credit for that, it's just an accepted part of being female. But actually, it is an endurance in itself and I think that's probably where a big part of our resilience comes from."
McGregor, an ultra-runner herself, points to research that suggests female runners display more disciplined and even pacing strategies than men in distance races, maximising on what she terms the female "brain bank".
"I don't think women go into these races without a lot of thought and contingency planning," McGregor adds.
"For example, if you've been through a pregnancy and you've dealt with nausea, if you've had a baby and dealt with the lack of sleep or if you've gone through fertility treatment, you have to go through so much discomfort, but you know you can get through it. And I think it's that knowledge of 'I can get through this, I can find a solution'."
One of the biggest reasons why we cannot talk with any certainty about the potential physiological and psychological advantages that women may have in this field is because participation numbers are low, with women making up roughly only 20% of those on ultramarathon start lines.
Research by SheRACES, a network set up by British ultra-runner Sophie Power to correct gender disparities in running, suggests the reasons for this range from societal perceptions around women's abilities, to concerns around the time needed for training, or access to the right support at the events themselves.
Slowly but surely, however, things are starting to change.
Earlier this year, a trail race in New Zealand became the first UTMB World Series event to achieve a 50:50 gender split, while a leading UK race provider has launched a new initiative to target gender parity at its events.
And now, according to Dr Burden, society is talking about the limits of human performance in a different way too.
"Historically, the majority of the time it [the limits of the human] will be established from male models or male sports," he says. "Now we're starting to break it up into the limits of male performance and the limits of female performance and that's a distinction that needs to be made … but to make better comparisons, we would need more women taking part in ultra events."

When it comes to participation, visibility is key.
Kaspersen describes Rachel Entrekin's historic victory at Cocodona 250, one of the most demanding ultramarathons in the world, as an "inspiration" among the elites to "dare to try".
And at the amateur level, there are those like Emily Fairs, a 22-year-old ultra-runner who documents the realities of her training and races on social media as part of her mission to get more women of all ages on start lines.
"When it comes to endurance training, there are so many components that come into it and that we are fearful of but by seeing another woman do it you think 'right, if she can do it, if she has the tools, she has the knowledge, she has the ability to do all these crazy difficult challenges, then so do I. I'm no different to her. She's no different to me'," says Fairs.
Fairs says she has received thousands of messages from women about how her content has encouraged them to lace up their trainers, and believes recent trends of female success in ultra-running are just the start.
"When the proportion is so low, we have no clue what women are capable of. We're starting to see more women get faster and enter the sport and push themselves and break records. So, who knows where we'll be 10-15 years later down the line?"

It's been more than four years since the launch of LIV Golf rocked the game.
A brash breakaway league, bankrolled by Saudi Arabian billions, luring top players with promises of big money.
Still it divides opinion in golf, and has split the loyalty of its champions.
But it could all come to an end soon.
After the League's Saudi backers pulled its funding - having spent more than $5bn (£3.6bn) - this week's abortive season finale could be the end.
That's unless a new deal is struck, soon.
BBC Sport visited the final event of 2026 at an exclusive golf club in Indianapolis, and found a strange atmosphere of surface-level optimism, but deep uncertainty.
Get ready for LIV 2.0... or the end?
LIV staff have learnt to put on a brave face. And that was no more necessary than this week at Chatham Hills Golf Club.
Despite endless questions about the future, they still had a tournament to host, and LIV Golf's white knight was in town - "the investor", as he was most frequently described.
The phrase "LIV 2.0" was used on countless occasions by the league's leadership - and that is the dream they are clinging to.
It stands for a new chapter, a second life for LIV.
There did appear to be genuine optimism that a deal could be struck.
LIV Golf chief executive officer Scott O'Neil believes he can pull off the near-impossible, and so do many of those closest to him.
But there was widespread acknowledgement that, if they do achieve it, the process to get there won't be easy.
One insider remarked "it's darkest before dawn". Another said "it will get worse before it gets better".
Work is said to be happening at "breakneck speed" behind the scenes, because of the pressure of players needing clarity on their futures, events needing to be organised, and sponsorships agreed.
However, there were players, caddies, staff and volunteers who shared a more pessimistic view with BBC Sport, with one describing it as the "last hurrah".
One senior figure within golf's media remarked: "We're at the hospice, not the funeral."
What would new era of LIV look like?
Much of the format is expected to stay the same in any new LIV - a shotgun start, team competition, music blaring from speakers and party holes.
But change will be felt in the boardrooms and in players' pockets.
The "free-spending" days are over.
If LIV does get a second chapter, it will need to be run in a more financially-disciplined way, given overall losses of this era of LIV are expected to have run into several billions of dollars.
BBC Sport has had it confirmed by multiple sources that the prospective investor behind plans for LIV 2.0 is Ted Goldthorpe, head of the credit division of international investment firm BC Partners.
Indeed, one insider referred to him simply as "TG", a nickname that suggests he has become a familiar face.
Goldthorpe attended LIV's most recent event in Bedminster, New York, and O'Neil said he was spending time "looking under the hood" of the league.
But in Indianapolis, Goldthorpe kept himself out of public view, even ushered out of a side door of the clubhouse to avoid media huddled by the front entrance.
He did, however, meet players as a group and set out his vision for the future - the primary aim being to make LIV sustainable, and ultimately profitable.
Selling franchises will certainly be part of the plan, and BBC Sport heard from one of the team's general managers about "significant interest" from investors.
O'Neil said the ambition was to set LIV up so it was "built to last".
There would be a reduced schedule of 10 events a year, across five continents.
The final location of those may well depend on which players stick around, with Australia's former Open champion Cameron Smith particularly popular in Adelaide, for example.
O'Neil said the schedule would be aimed at maximising LIV players' ability to be match-fit come the majors.
Players have been promised equity under a deal with a new investor, but quite what that equates to remains unknown.
They will also get key commercial rights back - called 'Name Image Likeness' rights - which means they can maximise their own endorsements.
Prize money was roughly half this week compared to previous events, and that is a sign of things to come.
Over on the American-based PGA Tour - which LIV players are banned from - prize money has increased in recent years, in large part because of LIV.
If the PGA Tour follows through on its plans to have a two-track system - with a Championship Series and a Challenger Series - it is likely that LIV prize money would sit somewhere between those, and higher than the European-based DP World Tour prize money.
'57 players with 57 different mindsets'
If there are no players, there is no LIV 2.0.
So the next few weeks will be critical in providing the specific details players say they're currently lacking to make decisions over their future.
When asked if there was a critical mass of players needed to sign up for the future before a transaction could be done, O'Neil said: "The entirety of our focus is to get to this transaction and get through it.
"Without the players, that becomes very difficult. I have a good level of confidence in my conversation that we'll have a critical mass of the right players to move this league forward."
Northern Ireland's Graeme McDowell, who joined LIV in 2022, told BBC Sport the mood among the players was "subdued".
"There are 57 players out here on LIV and there are 57 different mindsets," said the 2010 US Open champion.
"Some guys have some exemptions in other tours, some have nowhere to go [if LIV folds]."
He said he would be "taking a step back" to work out his future after the Indianapolis event.
"If LIV 2.0 goes ahead, we'll look at the schedule and how it all plays out, and see if that suits me and my lifestyle," McDowell added.
"I have an opportunity to go back to the European Tour and play there as well.
"Whether the two of those can happen simultaneously, whether I can only do one or the other, there are questions like that we don't know the answers to. Until I get that, it's very difficult to make any decisions."
When asked by BBC Sport about his future, Smith, who joined LIV just after winning The Open in 2022, said there would be a "little bit of time to think about that once the season is done".
Would he like to stick with LIV? "I really love LIV," he said. "It has done wonders for my family, for golf in Australia, my friends, the people that we've got to meet around the world. It would be a shame for it to be done, but we'll see what happens."
Other players did not feel comfortable speaking on the record.
One senior player said there is an "emotional" feeling among the group as they await clarity.
Another told BBC Sport "it's been great", before quickly adding "it is great".
It was made clear Jon Rahm - whose future is the source of considerable speculation - would not speak to media aside from his tournament obligations.
American Bryson DeChambeau declined an interview request from BBC Sport.
But after Thursday's first round, he said: "We definitely have a lot against us.
"If it works, it works, awesome. If it doesn't, we'll figure things out. Time will move on, and I would say that time heals things.
"I hope people can see that we actually bring value to the game of golf. My wish is that people give us one more shot and be open minded."
Signs of a strange week
Several people over the past few days privately told me this week had been "extraordinary". Here are some examples.
On Monday, Englishmen Lee Westwood and Tyrrell Hatton were sitting side-by-side in the front row of their flight from Dublin to Indianapolis when official confirmation finally came that their season would be ending early this week.
While the Saudi Public Investment Fund had said it would continue funding LIV until the end of the season, the decision to cancel the team event at the end of August in Michigan was necessary financially, and allowed LIV bosses to "focus on the next chapter".
In the press release about the schedule change came significant news regarding the Indianapolis event too - no live music sets on the weekend, which have been seen as a staple at LIV events over the past four years.
Later on Monday it was announced that routine player news conferences the following day wouldn't happen. It was felt, BBC Sport understands, that players would be left fielding questions they simply didn't know the answers to.
There were reports of vendors suing LIV over unpaid invoices, and of prize money being paid more slowly than normal - although BBC Sport understands that latter issue has been resolved.
Then, at 16:30 local time on Tuesday, the driving range emptied, as players headed for a meeting with "the investor". Fifty minutes later they emerged from the clubhouse, with most swerving awaiting media.
A few stopped to chat, but appeared careful about what they divulged. Martin Kaymer said it was "productive and positive".
Sergio Garcia agreed it had been "productive", but when pushed on his future walked away and said "we'll see".
American Brendan Steele was the only player BBC Sport spoke to in the week who has nailed his colours to the mast - he wants to remain a LIV player.
"It feels new life has been breathed into [LIV]. There was a lot of excitement and energy in the room.
"I'm committed to being here, this is where I want to be."
A critical month ahead
When asked by BBC Sport if he had doubts about LIV's existence beyond this week's event in Indianapolis, O'Neil said the "facts are good" and finished his answer by saying "I wouldn't bet against us".
So what's he basing his optimism on?
In terms of uptake of LIV worldwide, LIV said Adelaide attracted a record 115,000 fans - said to make it Australia's highest-attended golf event - and had a global broadcast audience of 5.5m.
Meanwhile, 100,000 fans attended the event in South Africa, and 50,000 went to the recent UK event, according to LIV.
LIV said 30% of its event-goers had never attended a professional golf event before.
O'Neil said that annual attendance in 2026 would surpass that of 2025, with two fewer events.
LIV Golf said revenue grew by more than100% from 2024 to 2025, and the first half of 2026 suggested this would increase again.
O'Neil also said sponsors were not "running for the hills" despite the uncertainty.
Growth is clearly promising. But there will be no doubt in the minds of Goldthorpe and the LIV hierarchy that turning this into a profitable organisation will take a serious shift in outlook, and of course in spending.
Once everyone packs up from Indianapolis on Sunday night, the focus will turn entirely to securing a transaction to give LIV 2.0 a chance of getting off the ground.
There are a few options available - filing for bankruptcy, pre-packaged insolvency, or someone comes in and pays the outstanding bills.
If all outstanding payments were settled, including on player contracts - such as Rahm, who is understood to be owed millions – then players wouldn't be able to break their contracts early.
O'Neil said there was a deadline for players to sign up to LIV 2.0, but wouldn't provide details of what that was.
The manoeuvrings of the PGA Tour and DP World Tour will be crucial.
There are undoubtedly difficult decisions ahead.
This is the end of an era for LIV.
What no one knows yet is whether it is the end full stop.

OriginOS 7 adds useful upgrades like a customizable Control Center, Pet Pals themes, custom stickers, Liquid Glass controls, and Vivo Office Kit for seamless file sharing, clipboard sync, and screen mirroring across Windows and Mac.
Chinese smartphone makers replicate their software to look like iOS, aiming to appeal to users who want something familiar with an iPhone-like design. Vivo is no different. Their newly announced OriginOS 6 is a slight departure from the older Funtouch OS, which mimics iOS.
Vivo recently unveiled Origin OS 7 based on Android 17. Once again, Vivo gets heavily inspired by iOS and brought some of the biggest changes, many of which are welcome, while some I wish they had never made. You can view the full changelog here.
I have been using Origin OS 7 on my Vivo V80 for the past several days. Here are the 5 best Origin OS 7 features I found genuinely useful.
Table of Contents
5 Best OriginOS 7 Features
Adjust Liquid Glass Design
With iOS 26, Apple introduced a Liquid Glass design that most people hated.
The new glossy design made text harder to read and requires more power to render. Many Android skins have quickly adopted the Liquid Glass design, whether users like it or not, and Vivo is no different.
Vivo OriginOS 7 has incorporated the Liquid Glass design throughout the system. Unlike Apple, which introduced Liquid Glass transparency control a year after launch, OriginOS 7 offers three modes out of the box. You can set it to Realistic, Neutral, and Soft. If you are not a fan of Liquid Glass design, you can set it to Tinted.
One big note: the new Liquid Glass design seems limited to high-end smartphones, and the Vivo V80 lacks the feature entirely. It runs on Snapdragon 7 Gen 4. The biggest reason might be that mid-range chips can’t handle the heavy rendering required by the new glass design. Believing this, Vivo might have restricted this feature on other older and mid-range devices too.
Customizable Control Center
Another feature that Vivo borrowed from iOS is the ability to customize Control Center. For years, Android Control Center has remained the same. But with OriginOS 7, Vivo has taken a similar approach to Apple, letting you fully customize the layout and individual tiles.
The biggest change is that you can no longer be forced to use the default layout. You can rearrange or resize tiles however you want. With this functionality, you can also change the connectivity cards and media player, and remove them completely from the Control Center.
You can also rearrange the volume and brightness sliders, and even the network and media player, similar to what Apple allowed in iOS 26. If you’re not a fan of this new approach, Vivo also lets you choose the older Control Center layout in Settings.
However, by default, it is set to the old controls, and to change the layout, follow the steps below. Plus, you can also resize app icons on the home screen. You can simply long-press and drag them to your preferred size.
Lock Screen Customization and Pet Pals
Customization is the biggest focus on OriginOS 7. Vivo has brought several new theme options. I particularly liked the Pet Pals themes, where cute little pets appear on your home and lock screen and perform different actions based on the time of day, such as while the screen is on, tilting your phone, tapping, while your phone is on low battery, and also while you are doing actions such as listening to music and charging, and much more.
Stickers
In addition to more themes and lock screen customization, Vivo also added the ability to add custom stickers to the Home or lock screens; you can even add them to the always-on display.
Like widgets, you can drag and drop these stickers anywhere on the screen and resize them as you like. But these stickers won’t have any functionality like widgets or let you tap them to open an app. They are purely there for looks. Vivo offers some built-in stickers to get you started. However, you can also create any sticker using AI or photos already on your phone. You can tap it, convert it, and add it to your stickers; once done, you can add it anywhere on supported screens. Vivo also designed dedicated themes for adding stickers.
Vivo Office Kit
Vivo introduced Vivo Office Kit with OriginOS 6, and while it isn’t particularly new in OriginOS 7, it still remains one of the favorite features if you want to create an ecosystem. It lets your Vivo connect to your computer and sync the clipboard, share files, remote control, mirror your screen, sync your notes, and much more, similar to what you can do if you have an iPhone or Mac with the Apple ecosystem.
The best part is that it also works on Mac and other Windows devices. So unlike Apple, you don’t need to own a Mac and iPhone combination to use it. Whether you use Windows or Mac, your Vivo phone can connect to either of them and get all those handy features.
Even if you have never been in the Apple ecosystem, you might find these features very useful. Especially since every company has tried hard to bring an ecosystem between Android and Windows, or Android and macOS, or vice versa, and failed.
But somehow, many Chinese brands have figured out how to break the Apple ecosystem and connect a Vivo phone to an Apple device. And not just Vivo; OnePlus did the same with O+ Connect. Similarly, OPPO devices can connect to any PC or Mac apps.
Final Thoughts
Those are the five best features I truly love about OriginOS 7. To sum it up, OriginOS 7 brought Liquid Glass design to the OS. If you don’t like it, Vivo does offer options to disable it.
Next, it offers plenty of customization options, including the ability to add stickers (which I found unique) and new Pet Pals themes, which are my favorite. Plus, it has plenty of AI features, some of which run locally on your device, that can help with tasks like formatting text, plus AI features in the Photos app to edit and remove unwanted backgrounds.
Finally, the Vivo Office Kit is a great way to connect the Vivo phone to any PC, including Windows or Mac, and it lets you easily sync your clipboard and share files. Finally, Android’s Control Center is also customizable, similar to iOS, where you can set different sizes for each tile and rearrange them to suit your preferences.
Another feature that is missing on my Vivo V80 is a workbench feature. It is designed for power users who multitask a lot. You can place apps side by side and switch between them easily, just like windows on a PC. The best part is that you can rearrange them the way you want with different layouts, which makes proper multitasking possible on a small screen.
Another feature I really like is the ability to connect your Apple Watch or AirPods directly to your Vivo phone. Previously, Apple Watch only worked with an iPhone. With OriginOS 7, you can pair your Apple Watch and sync your data with a Vivo phone; for AirPods, it also shows the battery level and total, just like on iPhones.
Vivo officially announced OriginOS 7 globally, but still hasn’t announced an official global supported device list. However, we keep track of all the latest OriginOS 7 updates in a separate timeline post. You can bookmark the post for the latest OriginOS 7 updates.

Microsoft's Surface RTX Spark Dev Box costs an eye-watering $6,000
The developer-focused desktop PC is available to preorder now, and it will start shipping in November.
Microsoft has opened up preorders for the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box and shared that the device will start shipping to customers in November. The company announced the desktop PC alongside the Surface Laptop Ultra in June, and like that computer we now know it'll come at a hefty premium: $6,000.
The Surface RTX Spark Dev Box is specifically designed for local AI workflows and the developers and engineers who run them, Microsoft says. The PC features an austere, anodized aluminum grille on the top, with a port selection that includes two USB-C, one USB-A, Ethernet, DisplayPort 2.1 and HDMI 2.1b on the back. Inside, the Dev Box uses NVIDIA's RTX Spark N1X chip and ships with 128GB of unified memory and 2TB of storage. Storage is removable, but based on the company's product page, nothing else on the Dev Box can be customized. Given the ample performance the company is promising — including the ability to run AI models "exceeding 120B parameters" — that likely won't matter.
As one of Microsoft's Project Zenith devices, the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box also ships with Windows 11 Pro and a selection of developer-focused apps and runtimes pre-installed, including Visual Studio Code, Git, GitHub CLI, GitHub Copilot and Python.
While Microsoft and NVIDIA believe AI working across the cloud and local hardware seamlessly is the future of computing, price will likely be a big obstacle for everyone other than enterprise customers. The Dev Box is a larger, more expensive version of NVIDIA's earlier DGX Spark AI computer, which launched at $3,999 but now sells for nearly $7,000 if you want a 128GB model. The shift doesn't bode well for anyone buying a Dev Box a year from now.

While thousands of Indian students head overseas annually for medical degrees, comprising a heavily monitored segment under the National Medical Commission (NMC) and the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS), parliamentary disclosures indicate that centralised tracking of specific discipline-wise student outflows remains complex.
But for many, the journey culminates in a grueling, high-stakes afternoon inside an Indian examination hall. When the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS) released the results for the Foreign Medical Graduate Examination (FMGE) June 2026, the pass rate had plummeted sharply to just 12.4%, triggering nationwide discussions, student protests, and scrutiny over what is locking foreign medical graduates out of medical practice.
(Sign up for THEdge, The Hindu’s weekly education newsletter.)
The panic after the paper
Dr. Chaynika Soni, a medical intern in a Government Hospital in Rajasthan who cleared the exam in her second attempt after graduating from Belarus in 2024, recalls, “Every single year after the exam, you’ll see the same thing. Students come out saying, ‘The paper was impossible.’ ‘It was too hard.’ ‘Nobody could solve it.’ Coaching centers will upload videos saying, ‘The paper was unexpected.’ Telegram groups will be filled with panic.”
This panic was visible during the June session, where candidates faced sudden structural shifts. Describing his experience with the exam pattern, Dr. Kshitij Anand said, “The questions were relatively long and time-consuming. I felt the questions were completely unrelated to what I studied. There were some questions I could get direct answers for, but it wasn’t much. They give you questions and options in a way that you take time to figure out answers but not enough time to think.”
He adds that the introduction of unfamiliar video modules caught aspirants off guard: “The Board gave us video questions which I agreed were manageable, but it was a new pattern. The FMGE conducted last January was way more image-based, and the options were comparatively easier to tap than this one. Also, the diagrams I have never seen before.”
Acknowledging these pressures, Professor Dr. Karan Juneja, National Convenor of IMA Junior Doctors’ Network, points out that “More video-based questions (this time), clinical-based questions will be tough for FMG’s [as they are] not exposed to Indian setting and less time make the exam tough.”
Inside the recall analysis
As the National Board of Examinations does not release official FMGE question papers, student-reconstructed “recall” papers serve as the baseline for preparation. A look at the high-weightage sections — Community Medicine (PSM), Internal Medicine, and Obstetrics and Gynaecology — reveals distinct hurdles.
Community Medicine heavily tests India-specific public health administration, including domestic health committees like the Bhore or Kartar Singh committees, local staffing norms at Primary Health Centres, and administrative schemes that foreign universities naturally omit. For a student trained overseas, this often translates to unfamiliar civic administration rather than core medicine.
Conversely, Internal Medicine acts as a control case focused on universal clinical reasoning, ranging from ABG analysis to emergency cardiac protocols. Meanwhile, Obstetrics and Gynaecology balances international diagnostic criteria with clinical application, though candidate performance frequently hinges on interpreting embedded clinical images, manoeuvres, or diagnostic scans.
Weighing these system dynamics, Dr. Samar Kumar, National FMG In-charge for the Federation of All India Medical Association (FAIMA), explains, “In departments such as Medicine, Surgery, and Obstetrics & Gynaecology, Indian hospitals generally see a very large number of patients. This gives doctors and students exposure to a wide variety of clinical presentations and allows them to learn how to manage patients even when resources are limited. I would particularly highlight Community Medicine... If an FMG studies Medicine, Surgery, Obstetrics & Gynaecology, and Community Medicine properly, focuses on clinical concepts, and practices clinical and image-based questions, they should find these areas much more manageable in the FMGE.”
Conceptual depth and the gap in coaching materials
Beyond traditional curriculum differences, candidates found that the depth of questioning defied standard coaching modules. Dr. Ruhi Kumari, who appeared in the June session, explains, “We weren’t trained that way. For example, there was a question on cholera; the answer was an increase in cAMP. I knew it was an increase in cAMP (cyclic Adenosine Monophosphate), but the options were given in biochemistry language. Like, you have to know what cAMP is in biochemistry; only then can you answer that. No coaching institute is teaching anyone like this. Only USMLE tutors do. Because USMLE has always asked in-depth questions. Many clinical questions expect you to have clinical experience. But that’s just unfair, because I will only get that experience after I visit the clinic.”
Dr. Kumari further notes the obsolescence of traditional prep material: “Marrow [an online platform) questions were considered the standard before this exam, but I can tell you they are not anymore. There were a lot of questions that weren’t even asked in many previous years' papers, that flustered everyone... Honestly, I am not sure which resource would give me the most apt training, because no institute is teaching you like that at present. Doing INICET papers is not going to help you, or even NEET-PG papers.”
Logistics, exam conditions, and the transparency debate
The academic difficulty was further compounded by severe logistical hurdles on test day. Dr. Samar Kumar outlines the physical toll: “The first issue was related to examination centres. Multiple centres had inadequate facilities. Some did not have coolers or fans, and in some cases, even drinking water was not adequately available. As you know, the FMG examination is five hours, and overall it takes eight hours. Maintaining concentration in such tough conditions, especially during extreme summer, is something beyond the capacity of many students and FMG doctors particularly when they are not provided with adequate facilities.”
He added regarding the sudden format changes, “The second and most important issue was the sudden introduction of video-based questions in the FMG June 2026 examination. FMGs opposed this later as well and conducted protests regarding this issue in Delhi, Gautam Nagar. The demand of the students was to provide compensation for the sudden introduction of video-based questions, but NBEMS denied the demand.”
Adding to student frustration is a perceived lack of institutional accountability. Dr. Kumar said, “Moreover, the FMG examination does not have any kind of transparency. The questions and answers have never been shown to FMGs. Thus, no one knows how they failed by just one mark, five marks, or ten marks... Then why does NBEMS say that they cannot show the questions and answers together? Why can’t the examination questions and their corresponding answers be disclosed?”
FMGE versus NEET-PG and the time crunch
Comparing the screening test to domestic evaluations, Professor Dr. Karan Juneja, National Convenor of IMA Junior Doctors’ Network, notes that “NEET PG exam standard is being given in FMGE exam as the board-making exam is the same NBE.”
While Indian MBBS graduates prepping for NEET-PG sit within a mature ecosystem of shared question banks and peer networks, foreign-trained graduates often experience thinner access to these informal pipelines.
Dr. Samar Kumar contrasts the two exams, “Recently, FMGE has also included video-based and lengthy clinically oriented questions, which adds another dimension to the examination... FMGE continues to have 300 questions, whereas NEET-PG has moved from the earlier 200-question format to 180 questions. Therefore, FMGE tests not only clinical knowledge and application but also a candidate’s ability to maintain concentration and consistency throughout a long examination. NEET-PG, on the other hand, has its own competitive dynamics, including negative marking and a highly competitive selection process. But if you remove these factors from NEET-PG, then it becomes easier than FMGE.”
This time crunch is intensified by structural scheduling. Dr. Anjali Ayappan from Kochi points out, “Two months is simply not enough preparation time for FMG students, especially considering the amount of syllabus and the situation most FMGs are already in. And bringing the next exam forward to October is especially bad for the June pass-outs. They barely get any time to prepare after the result, and then suddenly they’re expected to appear again in October.”
The long road to registration
Clearing the exam is only the first milestone; graduates face a complex administrative labyrinth before they can practice. Dr. Parvathy Sabu, who cleared the exam and works in a Government Hospital in Thiruvananthapuram, said, “Internship posts for FMGs are fewer across almost every State, and protests to increase seats are seen often... By the time you get PR [permanent registration], best-case scenario, approximately 8 years have gone by (including course duration) and a lot of money. Abroad MBBS is a very long-term investment that many don’t realise initially. I think the integration into Indian healthcare and internship issues are the biggest challenges faced by FMGs.”
Reflecting on these cumulative pressures, Dr. Madhavi Gurung, an FMG aspirant who studied in the U.K., concludes, “Many of my friends skipped FMGE and are now doing residency in the U.S., some are working non-training jobs in the U.K., and some are on track to settle in Australia. The struggle doesn’t end after NEET-UG. And with rising competition and reservation quotas, the system is tough. Every year wasted in endless NEET attempts can drain your mental health and confidence. I’m now planning to take AMC Part 1 by the end of this year and hopefully move abroad permanently.”

Dehradun-based medtech startup Sunfox Technologies has raised $7 Mn (around ₹67 Cr) in a Series A funding round led by Ashish Kacholia, Lashit Sanghvi, Alchemy Capital, and 3one4 Capital. The startup will use the fresh capital to expand its portable cardiac diagnostics platform Spandan across India, grow its team, and invest in R&D, clinical evidence, engineering, and new cardiac technologies. It will also build regulatory, distribution, and commercial capabilities across the US, Europe, and Africa, the startup said in a statement. Sunfox said it has regulatory approvals in India, Ghana, Kenya, Tanzania, and South Africa, and is pursuing clearances in the US and the European Union. The fundraise follows a ₹15 Cr (around $1.8 Mn) round led by Venture Catalysts in 2024. Founded in 2016 by Rajat Jain, Arpit Jain, Sabit Rawat, Nitin Chandola, and Saurabh Badola, Sunfox develops portable and AI-enabled cardiac diagnostic solutions for hospitals, clinics, telemedicine networks, public health programmes, and home-based monitoring. Its Spandan devices allow users and healthcare workers to record ECGs using a smartphone and share them with doctors for remote interpretation. According to the startup, the platform can flag cardiac patterns requiring urgent attention, helping healthcare teams identify patients who need further assessment or treatment. Its digital service platform, Spandan One, supports remote ECG reviews, case coordination, and tele-ECG network management. In public health settings, nurses or health workers can record ECGs at primary and community health centres and send them to doctors or cardiologists at district hubs for review. Sunfox claims around 60,000 Spandan devices have been deployed across India, reaching more than 20,000 villages. Its Spandan One platform is used to screen around 5 Mn patients annually, it added. The startup, which secured investment from all five participating investors on the first season of Shark Tank India, also claims a presence in more than 15 countries. Sunfox competes in the portable ECG segment with the likes of Agatsa, which offers SanketLife devices, and Cardiotrack, which provides handheld ECG devices and remote interpretation solutions.

A gold statue depicting Donald Trump fully naked and perched on the shoulders of a much smaller man has been unveiled in the European Parliament building in Strasbourg.
The eight-foot installation, titled The Orange Plague, is designed by Danish sculptor Jens Galschiøt and covered entirely in 23-karat gold leaf.
Trump is shown holding a golf club and a world-shaped ball in one hand and a set of scales in the other.
Inscribed on the base is a satirical pledge attributed to “The King of Injustice”. It reads: “I am sitting on the back of a man. He is sinking under my burden. I will do anything to help him. Except stepping down from his back.”
Galschiøt, who is known for his politically charged sculptures, has framed the installation as a “satirical outcry” against the volatility of America’s green and foreign policy.
“Trump represents one of the greatest threats to the rule-based world order, democratic values, and our common effort to solving the climate crisis,” he said in a statement.
“We must address this issue and stand together against such destructive influence.”
The sculpture reimagines the artist’s earlier work Survival of the Fattest that shows a starved boy carrying an overweight woman as a visual metaphor for global inequality.
Danish MEP Per Clausen commended the unveiling of the new statue, saying: “If someone is so thin-skinned that they cannot tolerate this sculpture being exhibited in the European Parliament, then they have no place on the world stage.”
But this is not the first nude effigie of Trump.
Ahead of the 2024 US presidential elections, a 43-foot tall sculpture of the Republican leader went on tour across different swing states including Nevada, Arizona, Wisconsin and Michigan.
Similarly, in the run-up to the 2016 elections, five life-size depictions of Trump were erected around the country, with accompanying plaques reading, “The Emperor Has No Balls.”
The latest portrayal of the American president is scheduled to remain in Strasbourg through to Thursday. It is expected to be seen again in November at the UN COP31 Climate Conference in Turkey, where Galschiøt will distribute 3D-printed miniature replicas to delegates.

On Tuesday (October 6, 2026), Kenya confirmed its first Ebola case after a Kenyan national who had returned from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) died in Nairobi. According to media reports that quoted Kenya’s Health Minister Aden Duale, he had lived in the DRC for years and had travelled back home by road before taking a flight to Nairobi.
After the DRC declared an Ebola outbreak in May, Uganda also reported cases and deaths from Ebola. However, after Uganda was declared free of the disease by the World Health Organisation (WHO), the cases have occurred only in the DRC. This is the first case in which an Ebola death has occurred in another country, raising significant concern regarding transmissibility for public health authorities.
What are the details of the case
According to Mr. Duale, the Kenyan national had been living in the DRC for several years and had fallen ill about a month ago. He had been treated in several hospitals in the DRC and died days after arriving in the capital, Nairobi.
He had travelled by road from DRC to Uganda and then boarded a flight to Nairobi, undergoing public screening with other passengers at the airport, but missed being picked up. He went home and was taken to hospital by a relative when he became sicker. He tested positive for the dangerous Bundibugyo strain, which has neither specialised treatment nor a vaccine until now. (Human trials for a vaccine were started in July, and three other candidates are in the pipeline.)
Eight of the patient’s family members and 21 healthcare workers have been quarantined. Screening at all airports. Another 23 passengers and four crew members who travelled on the flight he took from Uganda are also being traced. The traced individuals will remain in isolation for 21 days and will be allowed to leave if they do not show any symptoms.
Why is this fresh cause for concern?
The virus is highly infectious and spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids. This is the 17th outbreak in the DRC and is said to be its deadliest, having claimed over 4,000 lives since May this year. Over 8,300 cases have been confirmed across the country.
Meanwhile, the WHO has warned that the epidemic will surpass the regional 2014-2016 outbreak, which killed over 11,000 people, primarily in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
Despite an outbreak in the region, the global health body has not been in favour of imposing travel and trade restrictions on the affected regions. However, not all international travellers are required to fill out a self-declaration form specifying whether they have been in any of the Ebola-affected countries or if they have suffered any symptoms lately.
In Kenya, health authorities explained that the patient who died had managed to pass through the screening without raising any red flags because the medicines he was on probably masked the symptoms as he walked past.
The course ahead
Now that the virus has entered Kenya, the key task for health authorities in the country is firstly to stop the chain of transmission, beginning with the primary contacts already isolated. As per the outbreak protocol, this includes rapid contact tracing, immediate isolation of anyone who develops symptoms, and testing. Strict infection-control measures must be put in place in Kenya, and targeted information on prevention and control disseminated among communities.
Screening and surveillance have been intensified at airports in Kenya. However, at a time when it is impossible to stop global movement, it’s crucial to make sure that all nations maintain vigilance at their entry ports and pick up patients with detectable symptoms. Port authorities should also stress on the seriousness of honestly declaring travel history and symptoms.

A mysterious death of a woman in Russia following a lab accident has stoked fears about plague spreading. But the odds of that actually happening remain very low, with the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention saying on X Tuesday afternoon that the circumstances of the case remain unconfirmed and that there is “no indication of a broader threat to the United States” at this time.
“We are working across the US government to assess developments as additional information becomes available,” the agency said. “CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely.”
Last week, a young researcher died from severe pneumonia of “unknown” origin after reportedly breaking a test tube at her workplace, the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute in Siberia. The hospital that treated her before her death was placed under quarantine, and her coworkers at the lab were isolated, according to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty.
Christian Lindmeier, a spokesperson for the World Health Organization, told reporters in Geneva on Tuesday that the group has been in touch with Russian authorities. Based on currently available information, WHO says the public health risk to the general population is very low.
“I think that’s the correct assessment,” says Gigi Gronvall, an immunologist and senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. “We don’t know anything about anything right now.”
Russian authorities have said contact tracing hasn’t yielded any signs of dangerous pathogens spreading, according to the Associated Press. Infamous for causing millions of deaths in Europe during the Middle Ages, plague is rare today. It is caused by the bacteria Yersinia pestis, which is found in wild rodents and their fleas in many parts of the world. It’s spread to humans through the bite of an infected flea and occasionally through direct contact with an infected animal. Antibiotics can cure plague, but they must be started as soon as an infection is suspected.
Pneumonic plague occurs when a person inhales infectious droplets that contain the bacteria. In July 2025, an Arizona man died from pneumonic plague after exposure to infected cats. It can also spread from person to person through respiratory droplets during close contact. But human-to-human transmission is rare, with the last reported occurrence happening in 1924 in Los Angeles. The possibility, though, is why the CDC says it’s important to rapidly identify cases and treat them.
“Once you know that somebody has been exposed to it, and even if you have a doubt that somebody has been exposed to it, you can immediately start antibiotics to prevent the person getting afflicted with the disease and to avoid the continuous spread of the disease,” says Rutul Dalal, an infectious disease physician at Penn State Health St. Joseph Medical Center.
Dalal says if the Russian lab worker did die from plague, he is confident that the disease could easily be contained. “With Covid, that was a virus we had not dealt with in the past,” he says. That required novel interventions, while “here, we do have antibiotics to deal with this.”
The incident also occurred in a remote part of Russia, which could naturally limit its spread. “Siberia is not exactly Paris,” Gronvall says. “There’s not a lot of travel going back and forth.”
Whether plague is the culprit or not remains an open question. Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s federal public health and consumer protection agency, said “extensive” testing found “no microorganisms associated with the patient’s professional activities.” But the US has urged the country to share as much information as possible, while other nations that share borders or are near Russia, including Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan, have set up quarantine protocols.

The Democrats are surging as the U.S. midterms near. Here's the data that has Trump's Republicans spooked
Traditionally 'red' states are suddenly in play as president's popularity craters, various polls show
The upcoming midterm elections are a crucial test for U.S. President Donald Trump and the party he's dominated for the past decade — and early data points suggest it could be something of a bloodbath for the Republicans come November.
Poll after poll released in recent days suggests the Democrats are poised to make major gains among voters who, only two years ago, would have never given the party a chance.
Large swaths of the American electorate appear to be souring on Trump, who returned to power promising lower prices and no more foreign wars — but instead delivered higher prices and a war on Iran in the first two years of his second mandate.
Inflation is also running hotter than it was in January 2025, when Trump's second term began — which is significant because his predecessor, Joe Biden, also presided over an era of higher consumer prices.
Researchers say Trump's tariffs have only worsened affordability; without them, prices might have actually fallen slightly, affirming what many economists long predicted.
Oil and diesel costs have spiked partly because of the war on Iran and the ongoing Russia-Ukraine conflict, the latter of which he promised to solve within 24 hours of taking office but has since struggled to help end.
After some early victories — stopping the surge of migrants with his border policies, and brokering peace deals — Trump's popularity has plummeted.
One number-cruncher says Trump is now the most unpopular Republican president since Herbert Hoover, whom historians generally regard as a failure given how he governed during the Great Depression.
"These are historically low approval ratings, like below Richard Nixon at the height of Watergate, and that really doesn't augur well for Trump and his party," said Asa McKercher, the Hudson Chair in Canada-U.S. Relations at the Brian Mulroney Institute of Government.
"Not only is Trump unpopular but so are his policies, which have not borne out or bared any fruit."
That's why he is floating what McKercher calls "gimmicks" such as $5,000 cheques for every adult if the Republicans retain power in the midterms.
"There's a sense of desperation there," McKercher said.
Some Republicans distancing themselves
While Trump has repeatedly told his supporters to "pretend I'm on the ballot," thinking it will boost Republican fortunes in these congressional races, some of the party's candidates are distancing themselves given how toxic the president is in certain circles.
Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate candidate in Michigan, who closely aligned himself with Trump in the past, released a new campaign ad Wednesday denouncing the president's trade war with Canada.
Just this summer, Rogers said Canadians "have not been good partners," but that was before polling showed the vast majority of Americans are opposed to tariffs on their northern neighbour. Politico found only 26 per cent of Americans surveyed think the Canadian tariffs are the right thing to do.
Susan Collins, the Republican incumbent running in Maine's tight Senate race, has said something similar about tariffs, while strongly suggesting she doesn't want Trump to campaign in her state.
"I’m not exactly his favourite senator," she said in a debate Tuesday.
More Americans now identify as Democrat
Perhaps the most revealing recent data point is the dramatic swing in how voters identify themselves when Gallup pollsters ask them to pick between the two parties.
For much of the last four years, Republicans held a clear edge.
Now, the Democrats hold a double-digit lead as some voters reject a party they thought would deliver better economic results, temper inflation and bring about peace.
Mark Bednar, a former spokesperson for House Speaker Kevin McCarthy who now works as a Republican strategist, said all is not lost for the party — Trump is still hugely popular among the MAGA base and he's defied the odds before.
But he said the party needs to urgently address what he calls the "enthusiasm gap," in which Democrats are much more motivated to turn out and vote than their Republican counterparts this year.
Bednar said there's one big bright spot for the Republicans that can help get those people fired up and off to the polls: a massive fundraising advantage.
Trump alone sits on a roughly $400-million campaign war chest that he can deploy in the closing weeks of this campaign to blanket the airwaves with ads and help boost candidates in tight races.
"The Republicans have a huge financial advantage and that gives them the opportunity to actually get out there, get your message on the airwaves and tell your story as a Republican and prosecute the case against Democrats," Bednar told CBC News.
"The closer we get to these midterms, the closer the margins will be in some of these races."
U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to the press at the White House. The Republicans have a huge financial advantage, which could help them close the polling gap with the Democrats. (Alex Wroblewski/AFP/Getty Images)
Reliably 'red' states in play, polls suggest
These midterm elections will decide who controls the balance of power in Washington.
Despite state-level efforts by Republicans to gerrymander the maps in their favour, polls suggest the party is poised to lose the House of Representatives — the final result could be relatively lopsided even with the creative map-making — and possibly the Senate.
On the face of it, the electoral map this year looks unfavourable to the Democrats, with many contests in reliably Republican states. (Only one-third of Senate seats are up for election every two years.)
But the most recent New York Times-Siena poll, which politicos watch closely given its past accuracy, shows states long thought of as "red" ones are in play.
Kansas, for example, hasn't returned a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, but the Siena poll (and others) shows it could break that nearly century-old trend.
Farmers in particular have paid a dear price for Trump's trade war. Anyone who relies on a tractor or combine to get their products to market knows diesel prices have doubled on Trump's watch.
In the Republican crown jewel of Texas — where Trump beat Democratic nominee Kamala Harris in the last presidential election by nearly 14 percentage points — new Siena data shows Democrat James Talarico has a six-point lead over the embattled Republican Ken Paxton.
Polls reveal why there has been such a dramatic shift in that historically ruby-red state: Hispanic voters are turning away from the Republicans.
According to exit polls from the 2024 presidential election, 55 per cent of Hispanics in Texas voted for Trump. But just 34 per cent of Hispanics surveyed say they will back Paxton in this campaign, according to YouGov.
About 64 per cent of Hispanics disapprove of the job Trump's done to this point.
This Hispanic shift follows nearly two years of immigration raids that rooted out many undocumented migrants, including some violent criminals, but also tore apart communities by removing people long established in the U.S.
But white voters in Texas, too, say they are much more likely to vote for Talarico, a political moderate and Presbyterian seminarian with a savvy social media presence, than they were for Harris two years ago.
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico pictured in Dallas on Sept. 9. A new poll shows Talarico with a six-point lead over his Republican opponent in the race for the Senate. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)
The inflation-battered economy has scrambled the electoral equation elsewhere.
In Ohio, a "Rust Belt" state that voted for Trump by wide margins three times, Democrat Sherrod Brown is leading his Republican opponent by three percentage points in the Senate race. Brown's pitch: "Life is too expensive."
As part of his recent campaign blitz, Trump visited both Ohio and Texas, but also Alabama and Oklahoma. This was an unusual move so close to a vote, when parties usually focus their leader's time on must-win swing states.
It suggests the definition of a "swing state" is much different now than in the recent past.
"This could be a perfect storm, where it's not just a blue wave but a blue tidal wave or tsunami for the Democrats," McKercher said.

New Delhi, Oct 8: The Central Armed Police Forces (General Administration) Act, 2026, which provides a common framework for recruitment and conditions of service of Group-A general duty officers and other officers in the CAPFs, came into force on Thursday, according a government notification.
The notification came at a time when the Supreme Court is hearing a bunch of petitions filed by thousands of CAPF officers challenging the validity of the law that was passed by the Parliament in April.
"In exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (2) of section 1 of the Central Armed Police Forces (General Administration) Act, 2026, the Central Government hereby appoints the 08th day of October, 2026, as the date on which the provisions of the said Act shall come into force," said the notification issued by the Ministry of Home Affairs.
The CAPF Act provides for regulation of recruitment, promotion, deputation and other conditions of service of officers in the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), Border Security Force (BSF), Central Industrial Security Force (CISF), Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) and Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB).
The Centre recently told the apex court through an affidavit that the appointment of Group 'A' general duty officers in the respective CAPFs is now regulated by the CAPF (General Administration) Act.
It had said that the Act "expressly empowers" the Central government to prescribe the method, manner and mode of recruitment, including by deputation, and the conditions of service of officers in the five CAPFs-- CRPF, BSF, CISF, ITBP and SSB.
The cadre officers of these forces have petitioned the top court, including by filing a contempt petition, that the Act continues to restrict their career progression in comparison to the Indian Police Service (IPS) officers brought on deputation.
They have also asked the apex court to direct the Union government to implement its May 2025 judgement that said that the deputation of IPS officers up to the rank of inspector general in the CAPFs should be "progressively reduced" over a period of two years in order to give more opportunities to cadre officers whose delayed promotions can "adversely" impact the morale of these forces.
Under the new legislation, 50 per cent of the posts in the rank of inspector general are to be filled through deputation from the IPS, while a minimum of 67 per cent of posts at the additional director general level are to be filled through deputation.
The posts in the ranks of special director general and director general are to be filled through deputation only.
The Act comes against the backdrop of the Supreme Court's May 2025 judgment on the deputation of IPS officers in the CAPFs. In October last year, the apex court dismissed the Centre’s plea seeking a review of its 2025 verdict.
The court had said the number of posts earmarked for deputation in CAPF cadres up to the SAG level should be progressively reduced over a period of time, with an outer limit of two years, and had directed a cadre review.
The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the legislation said the expanding functional and operational requirements of the CAPFs had resulted in a distinct organisational structure for the forces.
"In recent years, due to the absence of an umbrella law, regulatory provisions have evolved in a fragmented manner, resulting in several litigation on service-related matters, leading to some functional and administrative difficulties," it said.
The law replaces the fragmented framework governing service matters with a common legislative framework for Group-A general duty officers and other officers in the five CAPFs.
A group of retired CAPF officers had also approached the Supreme Court with a contempt plea against then Home Secretary Govind Mohan over alleged non-implementation of the apex court's October 2025 order.
The group had said any legislative intervention affecting the command structure, service conditions and leadership opportunities within the CAPFs would have implications for institutional morale and the operational effectiveness of forces responsible for internal security and border security.

Thirty people have been killed after Russia struck two passenger buses in Kramatorsk, near the frontline in eastern Ukraine, according to local authorities.
“As of now, the death toll from this morning’s attack on buses has risen to 30. Eighteen people were wounded,” the Donetsk regional prosecutor’s office said. The governor’s office gave the same toll and said public transport had been suspended.
Images posted by police showed bodies strewn across a street littered with debris, as well as a charred shell of what appeared to be a bus.
“These are not ‘the consequences of war’, nor dry statistics. These are people killed by the Russian army,” regional governor Vadym Filashkin said on the Telegram app. “Russia comes to Ukrainian land with death.”
Moscow’s forces have stepped up drone and guided-bomb strikes on Kramatorsk and other cities in Ukraine’s so-called “fortress belt“, local officials say, the backbone of its defences in the Donetsk region.
Russia has demanded that Ukraine cede the rest of the region still under its control before it stops fighting, which Kyiv refuses to do.
Thursday’s attack came a day after dozens were killed in a Russian air strikes across Ukraine, primarily targeting the country’s power grid.
