The Indonesian government has been accused of “gross negligence” in a class action lawsuit over its handling of wildfires that have cloaked large parts of South-east Asia in a toxic haze, shuttered schools and caused a spike in respiratory illnesses.
The lawsuit, filed by indigenous and civil society groups in the Indonesian part of Borneo, named President Prabowo Subianto and the governor of West Kalimantan among 10 defendants. The case seeks comprehensive recovery and rehabilitation measures that would include covering the healthcare costs of residents.
None of those named in the lawsuit attended the opening day of court in West Kalimantan’s provincial capital Pontianak on Wednesday, leading judges to adjourn the hearing until 21 October.
“We feel sad and regretful about their absence … But on the other hand, we also understand that perhaps this haze condition caused them to be unable to land in Pontianak,” the plaintiffs’ lawyer, Glorio Sanen, told reporters.
Sanen said the case was “a step to address the problem” of wildfires that flare up annually in Indonesia, where they are often lit as a cheap way to clear land for oil palm planting.
Indonesia, the world’s largest producer of palm oil, has been accused of not doing enough to stop the so-called “slash and burn” land clearances, although the government has vowed a crackdown and deployed the military to fight the fires.
The blazes hit a crisis point this year due to an unusually intense El Niño weather phenomenon, which has created drier-than-usual conditions, sending a putrid smog to Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore, and even the Philippines.
The transboundary haze has angered Indonesia’s neighbours. Schools in the Malaysian state of Johor, just north of Singapore, were to be closed on Thursday and Friday due to deteriorating air quality, local authorities said.
The four plaintiffs in the West Kalimantan lawsuit, which was filed last month, include a chapter of Indigenous NGO AMAN and the local branch of Catholic Youth.
Yakobus Kumis, a plaintiff representing a Dayak ethnic group, indigenous to the island of Borneo, expressed disappointment that government representatives did not attend this week’s hearing, saying it was a “way of the central government teaching the people that violating the law is OK.”
He said the government ignored warning signs ahead of the fires breaking out, and called for the smoke crisis to be classified as a national disaster.
A similar lawsuit filed last year at a court in South Sumatra was dismissed.
The presidential office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this report

In its first live event in two years, Microsoft today announced its newest Surface laptop, outlined a host of changes coming to Windows 11, and shared a vision of how local-AI and agentic workflows could reshape personal computing for those in the dev community as well as home enthusiasts.
Surface Laptop Ultra
Originally teased in May 2026, the new Surface Laptop Ultra will be Microsoft’s first offering to take advantage of the new Nvidia RTX Spark SoC (system on a chip). The device has a starting price of $2,599, and comes in various SoC and memory configurations, with either a 5120-core or 6144-core Blackwell GPU and up to 128GB of LPDDR5x unified memory. It will begin shipping on October 16 and is available for pre-order now.
While the new Ultra is clearly focused on the developer crowd, graphical performance was highlighted during the presentation to show off just how capable the laptop can be. By leaning on unified memory allocation rather than the physical VRAM limits of a traditional GPU, the laptop can assign its resources to handle modern gaming tasks as well as local AI development and deployment. The new Gears of War: E-Day was shown running on the system, meaning that even without a traditional gaming GPU, AAA titles are on the table.
RTX Spark Dev Box
Joined on stage by Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, President of Windows and Devices Pavan Davuluri also unveiled the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box. This is a $5,999 anodized aluminum black box “designed to meet the needs of frontier developers.” The Spark Dev Box ships with a custom “developer-optimized” build of Windows 11 pre-configured for AI development and local AI use. With 128GB of unified memory and the onboard Nvidia RTX GPU, the box claims one petaflop (that’s 1,000 teraflops) of AI compute performance.

Ottawa to provide $2B in rebates for homeowners who install heat pumps
Rebate program targets homeowners with heating systems that have broken down or are nearing end of life
The federal government is launching a $2-billion rebate program that it says will help homeowners in Canada lower their annual heating costs while reducing emissions when they install heat pumps in their homes.
The funding will provide rebates for up to 820,000 homeowners over the next eight years, saving them an average of $1,400 a year on their heating bills when they replace existing heat pumps or heating systems, officials speaking on background said Thursday.
"Homeowners can apply quickly for the rebate when their existing heating system breaks down and they decide to replace it with a new heat pump system," a background document said.
"They can also apply as their existing heating system approaches end of life, and they want to make the transition before a breakdown occurs."
The federal government said it will also work with the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) to provide low-interest financing for apartment building owners to retrofit more than 280,000 homes over the next eight years.
"Today, we are helping one million more Canadian households make energy-efficient retrofits. We are lowering costs, reducing emissions and building a stronger and more sustainable economy for all,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement.

A Florida mailman has been arrested for allegedly driving under the influence while on the job, according to police.
Eliezer Valcourt, 32, is accused of being nearly three times over the legal limit when he was stopped in his U.S. Postal Service truck by Fort Lauderdale Police on Tuesday night, local outlet WSVN reported, citing an arrest report.
Fort Lauderdale Police told The Independent that they received a traffic complaint at around 8 p.m. “The caller reported a marked United States Postal Service vehicle stopped in the roadway with the driver inside,” police said.
Calls were coming in that the truck’s driver had been screaming while driving down the road, the arrest report said.
Police told The Independent that when they showed up, Valcourt “appeared to be intoxicated,” and a DUI officer was called to conduct an investigation. Before the cops stopped Valcourt’s truck, he nearly hit an officer, according to the arrest report.
Valcourt allegedly appeared unsteady on his feet with glassy, watery eyes and drooping eyelids, the report said. He was also allegedly slurring his speech, and the DUI officer reported a strong smell of alcohol on his breath.
Before starting a sobriety test, Valcourt stopped to pull a toothbrush out of his pocket and brush his teeth, according to the report. The DUI officer reported seeing seven of eight possible clues while Valcourt was completing a walk-and-turn exercise and said that he nearly fell at the end.
Valcourt told police he had been working since 9 a.m. and was almost done with his route. He reportedly denied drinking.
The mailman was arrested and booked into a local jail on two DUI-related charges. He later posted his bond and is expected to be released Wednesday night, WSVN reported.
The Independent has reached out to USPS for comment.

Trump said these words during an unscripted, tangential portion of a speech he gave at a Nebraska political rally. Many people, including high-level Democratic politicians and pundits, appeared to interpret him as saying the destruction of two large California cities would be a small price to pay for ending the war. White House spokesperson Steven Cheung replied on X that, on the contrary, Trump "was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped."
On Oct. 5, a rumor circulated online that, while speaking at a rally, U.S. President Donald Trump said Iran could "take out" Los Angeles or San Diego and that it would be a "very small price to pay" amid the war on Iran.
The joint U.S.-Israel military operation has killed thousands of Iranians, beginning with the assassination of Ali Khamenei, the supreme leader of Iran, on Feb. 28, 2026. According to an October poll by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research, only 28% of Americans approve of how Trump is handling Iran, as the cost of gas and groceries continued to soar.
"Trump on Iran: Let 'em take out Los Angeles and San Diego, it's a small price to pay," one X post showing a video of Trump speaking was captioned (archived). It had more than 15 million views.
The video was authentic, and the quote was correctly attributed to Trump. While speaking about economic sacrifices during the war at a Nebraska rally on Oct. 5, Trump said (at 1:47:01):
I want to see a tremendous victory. You want to see a tremendous victory 'cause it verifies all the things we did. And again, remember, with the war it's just artificial. It's a little bit high, it's a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe. They can take out a city. Let 'em take out Los Angeles, let 'em take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay and it's going to be over with very soon. It's essentially almost over with and they might keep going a little long. You know, they always say they have a big threshold for pain — they need it, let me tell you, they need it. But it's gonna end very soon and it'll end one way or the other and your gas and your gasoline and all of the things.

South Korea recalls Ukraine envoy over prisoner-of-war row
- Published
South Korea has said it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, the latest escalation in a diplomatic spat between both countries.
It started last month when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that his government had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul.
Seoul says Ukraine broke an agreement to keep the transfer a secret but Zelensky's office maintains that there was no non-disclosure agreement in place.
The two North Korean soldiers, who were among thousands from the country supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea.
South Korean Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo had in September lodged a formal complaint with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Vieshkin over the matter.
And earlier this week, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said he received an apology from his Ukrainian counterpart, but added that it fell short of Seoul's expectations, according to local reports.
But on Wednesday, Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi told reporters at a media briefing that its Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha had not apologised, according to Ukrainian news site Liga.
In a statement on Thursday, South Korea's Foreign Ministry said it would "continue consultations with the Ukrainian side", adding that it expected that "various outstanding issues...[would] be resolved smoothly".
- Ukraine says it captured two injured North Korean soldiers in Russia 
  - Published11 January 2025
Zelensky had revealed the transfer at a speech at the UN General Assembly in September, adding that the two North Koreans had not been "easy to capture alive".
It prompted a swift condemnation from South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who called it "greatly disappointing" and said the transfer was a "highly sensitive issue" impacting national security.
President Lee also faced heavy criticism at home in light of the revelation, with local opposition accusing him of wanting to cover up the transfer to appease Pyongyang.
But his office said that it had been kept confidential partly to protect the North Koreans' families and added that Kyiv also wanted the transfer kept secret to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war.
Lee's office explained Ukraine had indicated the soldiers would be mentioned in Zelensky's address, but not the fact of their transfer.
The spat escalated when Zelensky's office responded claiming that the two countries did not have a non-disclosure agreement.
Seoul later demanded Ukraine apologise for "announcing a falsehood" and said its actions had seriously damaged trust between the two nations.
Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has refused to break from its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war.
After North Korean troops were deployed to support Russia in 2024, Kyiv stepped up pressure on South Korea to supply cutting-edge anti-air missiles to help defend Ukraine's energy infrastructure from Russian drone and missile attacks.
This July, Seoul had announced a $100 million assistance package to Ukraine. Lee's office said it would be an expansion of earlier assistance which was comprised of non-lethal items including helmets, personal armour and medical equipment.
Meanwhile Russia's foreign ministry has warned it would have "no choice but to retaliate" if South Korea provided Ukraine with arms, without specifying action it might take.
South Korea has long pursued cordial ties with its neighbours who may be at odds with its ally, the US.
Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has worked to deepen trade and diplomatic relations with Russia, which borders North Korea, and views both Moscow and Beijing as key partners in efforts to influence Pyongyang.

Nana Patekar may have been best known for the intensity he brought to the screen, but away from the arc lights, that same intensity found an outlet in sport. Cricket was his abiding passion; shooting, for a brief period, became something more than a pastime.
For Anjali Bhagwat, the former World No. 1 and India’s first Olympic shooting finalist in 2000, Patekar’s sporting association was particularly personal. It began with a joke at the National Games in Pune in 1995.
The shooting events were held at a range in Worli, Mumbai, where Patekar had arrived as the chief guest for the prize distribution. Bhagwat had won all the gold medals on offer. As he handed them over, Patekar quipped: “Should I send over a truck for you to take all these gold medals home?”
The joke was followed by an act of generosity that Bhagwat has remembered for three decades.
After the ceremony, Patekar approached her mentor, Bheeshmaraj Bam, and asked: “We have such a talented bunch of shooters. How can I be of any help?”
He sponsored Bhagwat’s first professional shooting kit.
“He was also an excellent shooter. His focus and aggression as a shooter stood out,” Bhagwat recalled. “There are calm and quiet shooters and there are aggressive ones, but I always saw him as a focussed and aggressive shooter.”
Patekar’s own tryst with competitive shooting came when he was already in his 50s. Despite the demands of his acting career leaving him little time to practise, his natural ability and technical understanding were evident. He won a silver at the National Big Bore Shooting Championship in 2004 and added a bronze in 2007.
“He would get very less time to practise because of his busy schedule, but he was a natural. His technical knowledge was extremely impressive,” Bhagwat said.
Cricket, however, remained the sport closest to Patekar’s heart. Kiran More, India’s wicketkeeper during the 1980s and 1990s, remembers the actor’s calls during the 1989 tour of Pakistan, when a telephone communication from home was a prized commodity.
“We used to get a lot of calls from India back then, from celebrities and all. Nana Patekar used to regularly make those trunk calls,” More recalled. “At times he even tightened Sachin (Tendulkar) up to do well. He was so passionate that some of us would be cagey whenever he called. A genuine cricket fan indeed!”
Patekar followed not only India’s international matches but Mumbai’s domestic cricket scores, too. His friendships with several of the city’s cricketing stars from the 1980s and 1990s gave him an insider’s connection with the game. He was a regular at the annual party that Sunil Gavaskar organises for his close friends.
Whether standing behind a shooter at a range, offering a helping hand to a young talent or following Mumbai’s score from afar, Patekar did not appear content merely to watch sport. He wanted to feel it. Much like the characters he inhabited on stage and on screen, he did so with unmistakable intensity.

England to host 2031 Netball World Cup
- Published
England will host the Netball World Cup for the fourth time in 2031.
The quadrennial tournament will be held at Manchester's Co-op Live indoor arena, World Netball and England Netball announced on Thursday.
Liverpool staged the event when England last hosted in 2019.
World Netball president Liz Nicholl said: "After reviewing their strong bid, I am confident England Netball will host another thrilling international event, and I am excited to see what we can achieve together in 2031 and beyond."
Eastbourne put on the inaugural tournament in 1963, with Birmingham staging the 1995 edition.
England reached a World Cup final for the first time in 2023, but the Roses were denied a first title by 12-time winners Australia in Cape Town.
England also finished as runners-up in 1975, when the tournament was contested in a league format.
Baroness Sue Campbell, chair of England Netball, said: "To have the best netball players in the world coming to Manchester is a hugely exciting prospect, and I know the city will give them the welcome they deserve.
"This is a fantastic opportunity not only to showcase our sport on the biggest stage, but also to inspire the next generation of players and fans."
England Netball chief executive Fran Connolly said the tournament would provide "a powerful platform to grow the visibility, profile and impact of women's sport and netball across the UK".
The announcement comes in England Netball's centenary year.
The Co-op Live arena hosted this year's Netball Super League Grand Final between AO Thunder and London Pulse, which was played in front of more than 8,000 fans.

A payments business that operates across Africa and is ultimately controlled by an Indian billionaire has announced its intention to float on the struggling London Stock Exchange.
Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, is planning one of the biggest UK listings in years, in a boost for the shrinking London market that has faced a string of recent departures.
The company is understood to be hoping to raise about $800m (£601m) from the initial public offering (IPO) and is targeting a valuation of $8bn to $9bn, which would make it one of London’s largest listings in recent years.
Airtel Money has 53 million monthly active users across 13 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, including Uganda, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
It operates through a network of branches and kiosks, which enable customers to load money on to their phones, withdraw cash and access other money services, and the company generated revenues of just under $1.4bn in the last financial year.
Airtel Money’s parent company is Airtel Africa, a telecoms provider that is part of the Indian conglomerate Bharti Enterprises, which is ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal. Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but said it wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately.
“From a company perspective, [the listing] gives us flexibility for the future,” said Airtel Money’s chief executive, Ian Ferrao.
“We evaluated multiple [stock] exchanges, including the Middle East because we’ve got a headquarters in Dubai, along with European and North American exchanges. Ultimately, shareholders felt that London was the right choice. We still believe there is deep capital available … all the global institutional investors are here.”
Ferrao added: “Most importantly there’s a deep understanding of emerging markets in the London market and Africa specifically.”
Airtel Money said it would announce more details about the float in early October, including the indicative price range and number of shares to be offered, with final pricing to follow later in the month.
Airtel Africa had originally targeted a listing in the first six months of 2026 but delayed it to the second half of the year, blaming unfavourable market conditions as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Several other companies also pushed back planned IPOs amid the market volatility caused by the conflict.
Airtel Africa owns just under 78% of Airtel Money and will remain a long-term investor after the IPO. Minority stakes are held by TPG, Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding.
Revenue in Airtel Money’s most recent quarter to 30 June climbed 38% to £399m, according to Airtel Africa.
The decision to float Airtel Money in the UK could mark a turning point for the City, which has struggled to attract listings in recent times and has also been hit by departures, partly as a result of overseas takeovers of UK companies.
Airtel Money’s planned listing could be one of the biggest debuts since the international payments company Wise floated in 2021 with a valuation of £8.75bn. Wise has since moved its main listing from London to New York.

More fire, more ash, more crime, more death. And a globally important ecosystem driven ever more rapidly towards a point of no return. That is the prospect for the Amazon rainforest for at least the next four years if Flávio Bolsonaro holds on to the lead he established this week in the first round of Brazil’s presidential election.
This appears to be of far more concern to the outside world than to voters in Latin America’s biggest, richest and most biodiverse nation.
The far-right son of the former president and jailed coup-monger Jair Bolsonaro won 47% of the vote, putting him in pole position before the 25 October runoff with the incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who was backed by 44.2%.
The result is an unnerving jolt to climate and nature campaigners. Taken out of context, this appears to be a vote against the forest. The current administration of Lula (as the veteran Brazilian president is best known) has reduced deforestation in the Amazon by almost 50%. But that success secured little noticeable electoral traction for either Lula or pro-forest candidates in other polls held the same day. The former environment minister Marina Silva lost a bid for the Senate and Joenia Wapichana, a former head of Brazil’s Indigenous affairs agency, Funai, failed to win a seat in Congress. Out of 57 Indigenous candidates, only two won.
Flávio Bolsonaro is the heir to the political legacy of his father, Jair Bolsonaro, a former army captain whose four years in power resulted in a 59.5% increase in Amazon deforestation, roughly equivalent to destroying 2bn trees.
If he wins, Bolsonaro has promised to free his father, who was imprisoned for plotting a military coup and attempting to annihilate democracy in Brazil. He has said that his father could have any position he wants in his administration.
Flávio Bolsonaro has shown that he will be just as willing as his father to dismantle protections for climate and nature and allow illegal miners, loggers and land grabbers to invade Indigenous territories. As a lawmaker, he backed a 2019 bill to eliminate requirements for landowners in the Amazon to conserve a proportion of native vegetation. In his manifesto, he completely ignored the climate crisis. And he has courted support from some of the most predatory landowners in the rainforest.
He is also part of a movement – Bolsonarism – that is geared towards maximising profits for extractive industries regardless of the environmental cost. Take its victorious candidate for the Amazonian state of Pará, Daniel Santos, who was fined $275,000 (£208,000) for deforestating 280 hectares (692 acres) of his land without authorisation and is now promising to waive such penalties. As a result of Sunday’s election, Bolsonarists now control seven of the nine states in the Brazilian Amazon, and could win an eighth in the runoffs.
Bolsonarist influence in the legislature, which is dominated by agribusiness interests, is also growing. Jair’s brother, Eduardo, and mother-in-law, Michelle, were elected to the Senate, while an uncle and brother won seats in the lower house of deputies. Even before the election, Congress had been pushing hard to weaken environmental protections. Now it will be almost impossible to stop, particularly given the current chaos in the supreme court, which has been a partial check on untrammelled expansion by miners, ranchers and monoculturalists. Against these forces, Lula would struggle to govern even if he wins the runoff.
As a result, it is not just the Amazon that is in peril, but all of Brazil’s biomes, its traditional peoples and the stability of the global climate. The question now is why voters paid so little heed to these concerns.
That inquest is already under way. Many focus on the influence of social media, which has been used far more effectively by the far right. During the Bolsonaro administration, his sons were part of the “hate cabinet” that spread fear and disinformation via WhatsApp groups and other online channels – Bolsonaro’s second son, Carlos, was indicted by federal police for leading the group. Environmentalists were often the target.
Another factor is the expansion of US-style Pentecostalism, which is steadily supplanting Catholicism across Brazil, particularly in the Amazon. The political and environmental consequences of that religious shift can be seen by comparing the pro-nature treatise of the past two popes with the sermons of many evangelical preachers who encourage followers to seek wealth today as much as, if not more, than following moral creeds to ensure a good afterlife.
Lula, 80, has been slow to adapt. Although he is arguably the most iconic and successful Latin American politician of the 21st century, his messaging seems less attuned to the people than it was in his heyday. The Workers party has struggled in an era of weaker unions and in some ways been the victim of its own success – with education and social policies that raised millions out of poverty and created greater expectations for consumption and entrepreneurism; and huge subsidies to farmers, who now support the right wing because they chaff at environmental limits.
Tied into those explanations are the geopolitics of the climate and nature crisis, which is exacerbating great power rivalry between the US and China and amplifying extreme ideologies as much as extreme weather. In this light, the Brazil election is just the latest in a broader pattern of the far right taking control to expand extractivism despite growing evidence that the capitalist economy is breaking planetary boundaries. In the past two years, Donald Trump has ripped apart environmental regulations in the US and treated the rest of the Americas as his sphere of influence. Argentina was already onboard. Venezuela has been invaded for its resources, while in Colombia, Peru and Chile there has been a sharp shift to the right.
Will Brazil be the next domino to fall to Trumpism and its bonfire approach to nature? The Bolsonaro family certainly hope so. Jair went so far as to salute the US flag. His son Eduardo urged the US to apply tariffs on Brazilian people to “punish” the government for imprisoning his father. The Brazilian intelligence agency has warned that the US was trying to interfere in the election.
That election isn’t over yet. Lula stands a small chance if he can win over the many millions of voters who chose not to mark their ballots for either candidate. But the odds are stacked against him. Most of the eliminated candidates were on the right so their supporters are more likely to switch to Bolsonaro. No first round leader has ever failed to win the runoff of a Brazilian presidential election.
Voters, of course, are allowed to change their minds. Either on 25 October or, constitutionally, in four years’ time. But for how much longer will that be possible? If Bolsonaro wins, it won’t just be Lula that is finished, it could also be the Amazon and democracy itself.

Srinagar, Oct 7: Government Medical College (GMC) Anantnag has suspended seven MBBS students of the 2025 batch from academic activities and evicted them from the boys hostel following reports of alleged ragging on the intervening night of Sep 28 and 29.
The disciplinary action was ordered by the Principal, GMC Anantnag, on Oct 3 after the college’s Anti-Ragging Committee conducted an inquiry into the incident.
The Principal ordered that the students “shall stand suspended from all academic activities, including theory and practical classes, clinical postings and examinations, with immediate effect and till further orders.”
They “shall stand suspended from the Boys Hostel, GMC Anantnag” and “shall stand evicted from their hostel accommodation with immediate effect till further orders,” the order said.
The action was taken “in order to ensure a safe and secure environment for hostel residents,” it said.
The Anti-Ragging Committee “took cognisance of the matter” and conducted a “detailed, impartial and exhaustive enquiry,” affording the students “due opportunity” and acting “without prejudice to any party.”
The committee’s findings, submitted to the Principal GMC Anantnag, Dr Junaid Salam Wani established the involvement of the seven students, according to the order.
It does not detail the nature of the alleged ragging or the specific acts attributed to them.
Their parents or guardians have been directed to “accompany their wards” and appear before the Anti-Ragging Committee on Oct 12 at 2:30 p.m. for further proceedings.
Failure to comply “shall consequently result in initiation of further disciplinary action as envisaged under the extant National Medical Commission (NMC) Anti-Ragging Regulations and institutional statutes,” the order said.
A copy of the order was forwarded to members of the Anti-Ragging Committee, the Registrar Academics and the Chief Warden of GMC Anantnag. The Warden of the Boys Hostel was directed to ensure the eviction of the students from the hostel.
The finding is an internal disciplinary determination by the college and does not amount to a criminal conviction.
The action comes days after SKIMS Medical College Hospital, Bemina, suspended five MBBS students and interns for a week over a separate reported ragging case, imposing aRs 10,000 fine on each and summoning their parents before its Anti-Ragging Committee.
SKIMS Principal Prof. FazlQadir Parry had said the institution followed a “zero-tolerance policy towards ragging,” with the safety and well-being of students its priority.
Anti-Ragging Committees operate across professional and other higher-education institutions, and students are required to furnish anti-ragging undertakings as part of the admission process.
Under the Jammu and Kashmir Prohibition of Ragging Act, 2011, ragging is a punishable offence carrying up to two years’ imprisonment, a fine of up to Rs 10,000, or both.

The Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) held a protest at Shivaji Park Maidan in Mumbai on 02 October 2026, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation. The protesters raised concerns over the alleged exclusion of voters during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and demanded greater transparency in the election process. Although Mumbai Police had denied permission for the meeting, hundreds of people took part in the protest and raised slogans. Police later registered an FIR against the organisers and 400–500 unidentified participants for violating the restrictions.
Against this backdrop, a video circulating on social media (here, here) claims to show footage of the CJP protest at Shivaji Park in Mumbai. Let us verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Visuals of CJP’s protest demanding the resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar at Shivaji Park ground in Mumbai on 02 October 2026.
Fact: The viral video is unrelated to the CJP protest in Mumbai. It is an old video showing a public meeting organised by AIMIM leader Asaduddin Owaisi at the Central Library Ground in Bhopal on 15 September, opposing the Uniform Civil Code Bill passed by the Madhya Pradesh Assembly. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to the same footage (here and here) from 18 September 2026, nearly two weeks before the CJP protest in Mumbai.
We found that the video was uploaded on Facebook and Instagram by a Bhopal-based content creator, Amin Siddiqui, on 18 September 2026. We also found several other videos showing the same scenes on his Instagram page (here, here, and here). These videos indicate that the footage is from a public meeting addressed by AIMIM president Asaduddin Owaisi in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh.
News reports (here and here) also confirm that Owaisi addressed a public meeting at the Central Library Grounds in Bhopal on 15 September 2026, opposing the Uniform Civil Code Bill passed by the Madhya Pradesh Assembly.
When we compared the visuals from the viral video with the location on Google Street View, we found that the surroundings match the Central Library Grounds in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh, confirming that the video is related to the Bhopal meeting.
To sum up, an old Bhopal public meeting video is being falsely shared as a CJP protest video in Mumbai.

By the end, you should have a better idea of whether the Asus P3 G1 still makes sense or is worth going for the latest generations instead.

ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 Review
Design and Build: Practical Over Premium
Asus ExpertBook laptops are easy to spot from miles away. Most models across the lineup look the same and follow a very similar design language, with an understated gray finish and a clean, minimal look.
Asus ExpertBook P3 G1 also follows the same design. It may not impress you with flashy looks or an ultra-slim profile, which is something the ExpertBook P3 isn’t trying to do anyway. This is a practical, business-first laptop.
ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 comes in two chassis variants. The 1A variant has a plastic chassis, and the 2A variant has a metal chassis for those who want an even sturdier, more premium build.
My unit comes with a plastic body, but it doesn’t feel cheap by any means. In fact, it is a step up from some of the older ExpertBook laptops I have reviewed in the past.
Although the chassis is plastic, the matte, grainy finish hides it and gives it a much more premium feel. I love minimal laptop designs, and the ASUS ExpertBook takes that approach even further with nothing but the ASUS logo on the lid. The matte, grainy finish is also fingerprint-resistant; as a result, smudges don’t show up, and it stays clean.
The same treatment continues when you open the lid. The hinge is now slightly stronger. The display is stiffer than ideal to position, but it still wobbles a bit when you type and change its angle.
The lid opens up to 180 degrees, allowing the display to lie completely flat on the surface. It can come in handy if you want to share your screen with someone across the table. One limitation, though: since this variant doesn’t have a touchscreen, you cannot really use the display while it is lying flat.
Build quality is stronger than last generation, but it still has noticeable flex, especially in the center of the keyboard and between the touchpad and the keyboard. Thankfully, I didn’t notice it while typing. The deck doesn’t bend much under normal use unless you press harder.
The rounded corners also make the laptop more comfortable to hold during longer carrying periods.
One thing Asus continues to get right is port selection. In a world where fewer ports have become the norm for a premium experience, Asus ExpertBook P3 supports all major ports, including one Thunderbolt 4 USB-C, one USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-C, two USB 3.2 Gen 1 Type-A ports, a full-size RJ45 Gigabit Ethernet port, HDMI 2.1 TMDS, a 3.5mm audio jack, and a Kensington Nano lock. You get pretty much every port you expect from a business laptop. That also means you can connect most everyday accessories directly to the laptop without carrying a separate dongle.
The chassis is also MIL-STD 810H tested across 24 procedures. The laptop should handle everyday wear and tear. Note that the laptop is not water-resistant.
The keyboard supports backlighting. This makes it easy to see and type in low-light conditions. The backlight also doesn’t leak when you’re looking straight at the laptop. It also has durable keys, and ASUS claims the keyboard is tested for up to 10 million keystrokes to withstand wear and tear over time.
ASUS ExpertBook P3 is available in both 14-inch and 16-inch sizes. My review unit is the 14-inch variant with a WUXGA 16:10 display. The side bezels are fairly noticeable, and there is a rather large chin at the bottom that also houses the Asus ExpertBook logo. Above the display is a physical privacy shutter, which I truly appreciate for business-centric users who want better privacy.
Display: Good for Work, Not for Creative Use
The 14-inch display is a sweet spot if you want something compact without giving up too much screen space.
ASUS ExpertBook doesn’t get the kind of high-end OLED displays Asus offers on some of its high-end laptops or even more affordable VivoBook models. It is a 14-inch IPS-level display with WUXGA 1920 × 1200 resolution, a 16:10 aspect ratio, a 60Hz refresh rate, up to 300 nits of brightness, and 45% NTSC color coverage.
The display quality is decent and gets the job done, especially if you’re buying the ExpertBook primarily for office work. It is perfectly fine for browsing and using office apps like spreadsheets and documents, but if you work on photos or video editing, you will probably want something with better color coverage.
The display also has an anti-glare coating, which does a good job of cutting down reflections and makes it easier to use in bright environments. However, the trade-off is that a matte finish coating removes some of the visual punch you get from glossy panels. Colors aren’t as vibrant, although the text remains sharp.
Watching videos and content on this WUXGA IPS-level panel isn’t a pleasant experience, but as I said, for everyday tasks such as browsing, spreadsheets, and other office applications, it feels comfortable to use, and the text looks sharp enough to read clearly.
Performance: More Power Than Most Office Users Need
Performance is easily one of the ExpertBook P3’s strongest aspects. Asus offers it with either a Core Ultra 5 225H or Core Ultra 7 255H. My unit came with an Intel Core Ultra 7 255H, paired with 16GB DDR5 RAM and a 512GB M.2 NVMe PCIe 4.0 SSD.
At the heart of the configuration is the Intel Core Ultra 7 255H, a high-performance processor with 16 cores, 16 threads, a maximum clock speed of 5.1GHz, and integrated Intel Graphics. In everyday use, this combination handles almost any task without breaking a sweat. Whether you’re using multiple graphics-heavy applications, running dozens of browser tabs, or switching between office apps all day.
Another advantage is upgradability. Asus ExpertBook P3 comes with two DDR5 SO-DIMM slots, and the existing RAM isn’t soldered to the motherboard, so you can upgrade later if you want to, and it won’t cost you a bomb upfront, which is the case with most modern laptops.
It also has two storage slots: one M.2 2280 PCIe 4.0 slot and one M.2 2230 PCIe 4.0 slot, giving you more room to expand the storage later.
One thing I did notice is that the laptop gets quite warm at the bottom even during something as basic as browsing the web. You can definitely feel the heat when using it in your lap. It is not entirely surprising, though, considering the Core Ultra 7 255H is an H-series processor designed for higher performance.
Keyboard and Trackpad: The Keyboard Is the Star
The keyboard is easily one of my favorite things about the Asus ExpertBook P3. It offers one of the best typing experiences I have had on a laptop after Mac. A lot of that comes down to the 1.5mm key travel, which delivers a great typing experience. The keys are also large and well spaced, giving your fingers plenty of room to move around. It didn’t take me long to get comfortable with this keyboard.
The trackpad is also large enough for daily use. The large surface area makes it easy to move the cursor and also use gestures.
I have no issues with the keyboard and trackpad, though some users may find the fingerprint sensor placement inconvenient because it is integrated into the power button. To prevent accidental presses, ASUS made the power button slightly firmer.
Battery Life: The Biggest Compromise
This kind of performance is always welcome, especially if you regularly handle high-demand tasks. The trade-off, though, is battery life. My configuration comes with a 50Wh, 3-cell battery, and the ExpertBook P3 takes a noticeable hit here.
Even for basic use, I was getting only about 8-9 hours. On medium to heavy gaming, the battery life dropped to 4 to 5 hours, which isn’t the performance you want if you plan to use it on battery power all day.
ASUS bundles a 65W USB-C charger in the box, and it can take your laptop from 0 to 100 in less than 2 hours. That’s fairly quick, but I really wish Windows laptop makers offered more travel-friendly options instead of big, bulky charging bricks and three-pin plugs.
Sound: Decent, but Nothing Special
The speakers are decently loud, but they don’t get particularly loud. ASUS uses two built-in speakers with Dirac audio support. Thankfully, Asus includes a built-in 3.5mm headphone jack, so you can plug in wired headphones or earphones directly without relying on the built-in speakers.
Windows 11 Home: Still Too Cluttered
I have never been a fan of Windows’ cluttered experience. If you’ve used Windows for years, you probably won’t mind much, but if you are coming from a Mac or Linux, you’ll have to deal with Windows’ cluttered experience first.
It took me more than three hours to set up the device, including the unwanted Windows updates I had to install during setup. Plus, the Windows update prompts never stop. Even Microsoft has promised to improve the Windows laptop experience by eliminating these unwanted distractions.
Since this is an ExpertBook, ASUS includes business-centric features, including AI ExpertMeet for meetings. However, this configuration lacks some useful Copilot+ AI features for those who care about privacy and want to run AI features locally on the device. The Core Ultra 7 255H delivers up to 13 TOPS of NPU performance, well short of the 40+ TOPS required for a Copilot+ PC. You may need to rely on cloud processing for more demanding AI features.
Camera: Still Needs Work
ASUS has been pretty good at improving the little things in everyday use, but the camera is still one area that needs work. My configuration comes with a 1080p FHD IR camera with Windows Hello support and a physical privacy shutter. Even on the maxed-out ExpertBook Ultra, the camera quality is rather underwhelming, especially on business laptops like this, where it matters a lot.
Even in good lighting, the camera adds plenty of noise, and in low light, it gets worse. However, you can always connect an external camera if camera quality matters to you. But this is something Asus needs to improve.
ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 Review Verdict: Powerful and Practical, but Battery Holds It Back
Overall, if performance is high on your priority list, then the ASUS ExpertBook P3 might be a better choice. Everyday tasks feel quick and responsive, plus it also has plenty of power for more demanding tasks. The excellent keyboard, with 1.5mm key travel, makes typing sessions comfortable, and the full selection of ports lets you connect any peripherals without constantly reaching for or using a dongle. The biggest advantage of the Asus ExpertBook P3 is plenty of room to upgrade later. It offers dual SO-DIMM slots for memory and dual M.2 slots for additional PCIe storage.
Among the pros are also some compromises. Battery life takes a noticeable hit when you push the processor harder, and while the laptop can handle some AI workloads locally, it cannot run the full set of Copilot+ PC features.

- Great keyboard with 1.5mm key travel
- Plenty of ports
- RAM and SSD are upgradeable
- Fingerprint-resistant matte finish
- 180-degree hinge
- Good business and security features
- MIL-STD 810H tested
- Average battery life
- Poor color coverage
- Average webcam quality

ప్రధాన ఎన్నికల కమిషనర్ జ్ఞానేష్ కుమార్ రాజీనామా చేయాలని డిమాండ్ చేస్తూ కాక్రోచ్ జనతా పార్టీ (CJP) ముంబైలోని శివాజీ పార్క్ మైదానంలో 02 అక్టోబర్ 2026న నిరసన ప్రదర్శన నిర్వహించింది. ఓటర్ల జాబితా ప్రత్యేక సమగ్ర సవరణ (SIR)లో ఓటర్ల తొలగింపు ఆరోపణలు, ఎన్నికల ప్రక్రియలో పారదర్శకతపై నిరసనకారులు ఆందోళన వ్యక్తం చేశారు. ఈ సమావేశానికి ముంబై పోలీసులు అనుమతి నిరాకరించినప్పటికీ, వందలాది మంది నిరసనలో పాల్గొని నినాదాలు చేశారు. సమావేశంపై ఉన్న ఆంక్షలను ఉల్లంఘించారనే కారణంతో నిర్వాహకులతో పాటు, ఇందులో పాల్గొన్న 400-500 మంది గుర్తుతెలియని వ్యక్తులపై పోలీసులు FIR నమోదు చేశారు.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, ముంబైలో జరిగిన ఈ నిరసన సందర్భంగా సీజేపీ వ్యవస్థాపకుడు అభిజీత్ దీప్కేపై దాడి జరిగిందని పేర్కొంటూ ఒక వీడియో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. దీంట్లో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: 02 అక్టోబర్ 2026న ముంబైలోని శివాజీ పార్క్లో జరిగిన నిరసన ప్రదర్శనలో CJP వ్యవస్థాపకుడు అభిజీత్ దీప్కేపై దాడి జరిగినప్పటి దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియో 15 జూన్ 2026 నాటిది. రాజస్థాన్లోని జైపూర్లో పేపర్ లీక్లు, నిరుద్యోగానికి వ్యతిరేకంగా జరిగిన నిరసన సందర్భంగా అభిజీత్ దీప్కేపై గుర్తుతెలియని వ్యక్తులు దాడి చేయడాన్ని ఈ వీడియో చూపుతుంది. ముంబై నిరసనలో అభిజీత్ దీప్కేపై దాడి జరిగినట్లు ఎటువంటి నివేదికలు లేవు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
ముందుగా వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇదే వీడియో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) కనీసం 15 జూన్ 2026 నుండి ఆన్లైన్లో అందుబాటులో ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. ఈ వీడియోలో ఉన్నవి రాజస్థాన్లోని జైపూర్లో అభిజీత్ దీప్కేపై జరిగిన దాడి దృశ్యాలుగా పేర్కొన్నారు.
మీడియా కథనాల ప్రకారం (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ), 15 జూన్ 2026న రాజస్థాన్ జైపూర్లోని షహీద్ స్మారక్ వద్ద జరిగిన నిరసన ప్రదర్శనలో దీప్కేపై కొందరు వ్యక్తులు దాడి చేసి, ముఖంపై పలుమార్లు కొట్టారు. పేపర్ లీకేజీలు, నిరుద్యోగ సమస్యలపై నిరసన తెలుపుతూ, కేంద్ర విద్యాశాఖ మంత్రి ధర్మేంద్ర ప్రధాన్ రాజీనామా చేయాలని డిమాండ్ చేస్తూ ఆయన ఈ కార్యక్రమాన్ని నిర్వహించారు. మద్దతుదారులు దీప్కేను తమ భుజాలపై ఎక్కించుకుని వేదిక వైపు తీసుకువెళ్తుండగా, గుంపులోంచి కొందరు అతడిని కిందకు లాగి ముఖంపై కొట్టారు. దీంతో సీజేపీ మద్దతుదారులు వెంటనే ఎదురుదాడికి దిగగా, పోలీసులు రంగంలోకి దిగి అనుమానితులను అదుపులోకి తీసుకున్నారు.
అనంతరం దీప్కే ఈ దాడిని ఖండిస్తూ, ఈ ఘటన తన ప్రత్యర్థుల భయానికి నిదర్శనమని పేర్కొన్నారు. అంతేకాకుండా, ముంబై శివాజీ పార్క్ నిరసనలో దీప్కేపై దాడి జరిగినట్లు ఎలాంటి వార్తా కథనాలూ లేవు.
చివరిగా, అభిజీత్ దీప్కేపై జైపూర్లో జరిగిన దాడికి సంబంధించిన ఒక పాత వీడియోను, ముంబైలో ఆయనపై దాడి జరిగిందంటూ తప్పుడు ప్రచారం చేస్తూ షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు.

Police fire tear gas at a barricaded Paris school as protests show no sign of ending
Students in northeastern Paris gathered Thursday to protest outside a high school, with police responding using tear gas
PARIS -- Dozens of students dragged rubbish bins into position outside a high school in northeastern Paris early on Thursday, erecting fresh barricades before police moved in with tear gas as France’s nationwide protests show few signs of ending.
The Helene Boucher Lycee has been a flashpoint for clashes in the French capital, and is one of hundreds of schools disrupted by protesters Thursday.
At least a dozen demonstrations in support of the high school students' movement are planned around France later in the day.
Riot police gathered in side streets as students converged on the school. Many protesters wore surgical masks or hoodies, apparently afraid to be recognized.
Police have made more than 6,600 arrests since late September, when students, most of them under 18, started protesting to demand more education funding, according to the Interior Ministry. The Education Ministry said that 375 schools were either fully or partially closed on Thursday.
While the number of school closures was down compared to Tuesday, pressure is mounting on the government of outgoing President Emmanuel Macron.
The protests against the under-funding of schools — many of them struggling with dilapidated facilities and insufficient staff — have drawn troublemakers not concerned about the aims of the protest movement as well as unions and political groups.
In a TV address, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu lamented the “violence, students and staff being attacked, police officers and gendarmes injured, schools set on fire or vandalized, thousands of hours of classes lost, not to mention threats and insults.”
He took aim at “political leaders who use this anger to conduct their electoral battles." France goes to the polls for a presidential election in April. “We cannot play with the safety of France’s youth,” Lecornu said.
At the Lycee, 18-year-old university student Emma Khelil came to offer support to those at the barricades at her former high school. She told The Associated Press that she’s really concerned about police violence.
“We’re here to defend our rights, not to lose an eye or a hand,” Khelil said. She also said that she had noticed insulation problems and water leaks in the school building and had even seen rats on occasion. Other students confirmed that they’d seen rats too.
She was not convinced by Lecornu’s efforts to calm the situation.
“I don’t think the movement is going to lose momentum. As long as things don’t change, we’re going to see the movement grow stronger, and potentially a convergence of struggles, especially with the next presidential election coming up,” she said.
Not long after she spoke, police surrounded a nearby square. The crowd surged, and tear gas was fired.
The impact of France's protests is also being felt north of the border, in Belgium.
Liege Mayor Willy Demeyer issued a ban on public gatherings until midnight on Oct. 16, given what he described as the “real, serious and imminent risk” of repeated clashes and vandalism that authorities expected in coming days.
City police said they used water cannon and tear gas on Wednesday to keep several hundred protesters at bay. Authorities sent emergency mobile text messages warning shopkeepers to close their premises due to rioting.
Almost 90 people were arrested and several police were injured. Police reinforcements were sent from the capital Brussels and from Antwerp, and more are coming. Smaller protests have been held in Mons and Charleroi.
In a post on social media, Belgium’s Interior Minister Bernard Quintin said the “perpetrators will have to answer for their actions before the courts.”
The Belgian protests, organized through social media chat groups, include demands for more teachers and smaller classes as well as complaints about education reform in Belgium, but are also likely inspired by events in France.

Cook reported from Brussels. Masha Macpherson in Paris contributed to this report.

A landmark survey of the world’s largest free-roaming giant tortoise population has revealed the once endangered species is thriving.
A population of Aldabra giant tortoise lives on an island in Seychelles called Aldabra Atoll.
The most recent survey, led by Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter, revealed there were approximately 180,000 tortoises living on the island.
This is the highest figure ever recorded for the species and far exceeds the human population of Seychelles.
The new figure was obtained by a team who analysed five years of tortoise counts between 2018 and 2022.
It is the first update since a widely cited figure of 100,000 tortoises from the late 1990s.
Aldabra Atoll is one of only two places in the world where giant tortoises are found in the wild, with a much smaller population living in the Galápagos.
Dr Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, CEO of SIF, said: “More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve.
“This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra.”
The study, published in the scientific journal Ecology and Evolution, found that the population was relatively stable for this period, with a best estimate of almost 183,000 adult and sub-adult tortoises.
In the 19th century, exploitation of the animals meant there were fewer than 1,000 Aldabra tortoises left on the island.
But a recovery programme meant the island became a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a Unesco site in 1982.
Researchers are now saying it is one of the greatest conservation success stories of the Indian Ocean, with the new study confirming it.
“Aldabra’s giant tortoise monitoring programme is one of the longest running in the region, but the atoll’s dense vegetation makes counting tortoises genuinely difficult in places,” said Dr Nancy Bunbury, one of the study’s co-authors.
“By modelling what we didn’t see, as well as what we did, we’ve produced the most reliable baseline yet for this iconic Seychelles species, establishing a benchmark we can use to track the population for decades to come.”
Despite the good news, the study’s authors warn that vigilance is essential. Aldabra’s climate is changing, with longer and more frequent droughts predicted to reduce the shade and food available to tortoises, while rising sea levels threaten low-lying parts of the atoll.
The study authors say invasive mammals remain a key threat including feral cats and black rats that prey on tortoise eggs and hatchlings.
The planned eradication of these remaining invasive mammals, the authors say, could lift the last barriers to further growth of the population and help it withstand future climate pressures.
“These results are great news for the tortoises and testament to the fantastic work done in the field,” said Dr Dave Hudson, postdoctoral research associate at the University of Exeter’s Cornwall campus.
“But it’s important to remember that the numbers provide a baseline – not an endpoint.
“Hopefully we have provided the conservation managers the evidence they need to track future change and act early as the tortoises face increasing pressures from climate change, drought and invasive species.”

4 people on NASA's Crew-12 mission return to Earth after 8 months in space
Three astronauts and a cosmonaut of NASA's Crew-12 mission have safely returned to Earth after an almost eight-month trip to the International Space Station.
The crew, commanded by NASA's Jessica Meir and pilot Jack Hathaway with mission specialists Sophie Adenot of the European Space Agency and Andrey Fedyaev of Russia's Roscosmos, splashed down into the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Los Angeles, Calif., on Thursday, aboard a SpaceX Crew Dragon capsule.
Their trip home started about 45 minutes before, at an orbital speed of 17,500 mph.
The spacecraft lit its thrusters to nudge it out of orbit, causing the capsule to plunge into the atmosphere, its ablative heat shield battling extreme temperatures (up to 3,500 degrees Fahrenheit) during the fiery reentry. Over the course of about half an hour, the capsule slowed to a few hundred miles per hour, and then four orange-and-white parachutes took over, easing the spacecraft to just 16 mph above the cool, blue ocean and a gentle plop into the water.
The Crew-12 mission was the 20th time SpaceX had sent humans into orbit, lifting off in February on a Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral in Florida. It docked with the space station the next day. During the eight months in space, NASA said the crew completed dozens of science experiments and research, including studies of stem cells, how crystals grow in space and bone loss in microgravity.
Not all of their work happened inside the space station. Meir conducted four spacewalks totaling just over 27 hours to perform maintenance and upgrade the aging orbital outpost. Adenot performed three spacewalks.
Before departing, members of the Crew-12 mission were relieved by the three astronauts and cosmonaut of Crew-13, who arrived at the space station last week to start a six-month rotation.
During a pre-departure news conference on the station last month, Meir said she couldn't wait to be reunited with her 3 1/2-year-old daughter.
But there was something else she missed after all this time in orbit. "So looking forward to seeing nature again, feeling the breeze on my face, the wind rustling through the leaves. Experiencing all those things that we don't have up here," she said.
The two-time space veteran said there were two things she'd miss about space: weightlessness and the wonderful views of Earth.

With the Vivo V70 series, Vivo took a premium turn. You can check out our detailed Vivo V70 review. Previously, Vivo V series phones had flashy designs, tall displays, and curved screens, designed to attract people who like flashy looks. But the Vivo V70 changed that rather significantly. Vivo has gone for a more compact form factor and a sturdier build that appeals to anyone looking for flagship-level build quality in a Vivo V series phone.
Now the Vivo V80 continues the tradition. It keeps the same compact form factor and solid build, which feels more like a proper flagship than a typical Vivo design. Now has a bigger 7200 mAh battery, ships with OriginOS 7 out of the box, and is the first non-flagship phone with an excellent 144 AMOLED display and a Zeiss camera setup.
However, it also gets a huge price hike. The base variant now comes with 8GB + 128GB priced at Rs 62,999, 8GB + 256GB at Rs 69,999, and finally 8GB + 512GB at Rs 79,999. Vivo V80 sits next to flagship phones where the competition becomes much harder to ignore.
The Vivo V70 found a speed sweet spot for buyers who cared more about cameras than outright performance. So, with the Vivo V80, has Vivo found that sweet spot again, or has it pushed the Vivo V series a little too far this time? Let’s find out.
Table of Contents
Vivo V80 Review: Great Cameras, Premium Looks and a Price To Match
Compact Build, Flagship-Like Feel
The Vivo V80 looks strikingly similar to the V70 from the front. It keeps the same compact body design with rounded corners on all four sides. In fact, they have almost the same dimensions except the Vivo V80 is now slightly thicker: 157.52 × 74.33 × 7.69 mm (Vivo V70: 157.52 × 74.33 × 7.59 mm), and also slightly heavier at 203g compared to 194g on the Vivo V70 because of the larger battery.
The button placement is also very similar to the V70, with the power and volume buttons on the right being easy to access with one hand. They are clicky and tactile. On the left, it is clean, while on the bottom you will find the SIM ejector, speaker, and Type-C charging port.
You will notice the real difference when you turn the phone around. The camera module now stretches almost across the width of the phone, following the design trend we have been seeing in the phones lately.
Vivo also changed the camera placement to use that extra space better than on the V70, tucking it in with ZEISS branding neatly as well. It comes with a glass back, and the camera module blends neatly into the glass. It also doubles as a natural resting position for your finger while holding the phone. Design-wise, I would rate it 10/10 for its compact form factor and solid in-hand feel.
The device is also IP68 + IP69 rated, so it can protect against dust and water, and it comes in three color options this time. The Stellar Black for those who prefer black phones, Horizon Blue, the one I got, which honestly looks more like olive than blue, and the new Sunrise Anthem color that has a subtle orange, not a contrast look that we found on the iPhone 17 Pro. Here is how all colors look in person.
Sharp 144Hz AMOLED, but Performance Holds It Back
On the front, you get a 6.59-inch 1.5K Amoled edge-to-edge display with minimal bezels on all four sides. Vivo has gone with a flat AMOLED panel once again. The resolution remains the same. But Vivo has bumped the refresh rate to 144Hz from 120Hz.
The processor technically supports it, but pushing both resolution and refresh rate to the highest settings makes the phone noticeably choppier to use. By default, the screen resolution is set to HD, but you can set it to Ultra HD for a sharper display.
OriginOS also lets you choose different screen colors. By default, it is set to natural, but if you want a punchy, vibrant-looking display, you can switch to bright to make on-screen colors pop.
The display is very bright. You get almost all of the advantages of a good AMOLED panel. With its resolution and 459 pixels per inch, the display looks sharp, and the AMOLED panel ensures deep blacks and rich colors. It also has 5000 nits of local peak brightness for HDR content. The display can get very bright, so you can use it comfortably in direct sunlight without visibility issues.
My biggest issue is the same as what I have with the Vivo V70. The phone supports high resolution and the highest refresh rate, but the processor, because of its limitations, struggles to keep the experience smooth. The phone is also Widevine L1 certified, so you can watch Netflix, Amazon, or HD content on other streaming platforms.
Strong ZEISS Cameras, but the Ultrawide Needs an Upgrade
Cameras have long been Vivo phones’ biggest strength. Vivo V80 continues that tradition. Vivo has largely stuck with the same hardware on the V80 as on the V70. That is both a good and a bad thing.
The good thing is these cameras are capable and well-tuned for photography; the bad is Vivo still uses a lower-resolution ultra-wide-angle camera, which definitely needs an upgrade if it wants to compete with flagship phones at this price, especially when it still relies on the camera as its biggest strength.
For starters, it comes with a 50-megapixel ZEISS OIS Main Camera with OIS. It also has a 50-megapixel ZEISS Night Telephoto Camera and a 50MP 3x periscope telephoto zoom. The ultra-wide is the same 8MP ZEISS sensor, with an f/2.2 aperture and a 115-degree field of view.
Vivo V80 vs Vivo X200T: Which Has the Better Camera?
In the past, I compared Vivo V70 cameras with the Vivo X200T, but I also called it an unfair comparison because of the Rs 14,000 price difference between them. But fast-forward to now, after the price increase, the Vivo V70 now sells for the same price as the Vivo X200T, and the latest Vivo V80 is Rs 3,000 more expensive than the Vivo X200T.
I still have the Vivo X200T with me. Now it’s safe to compare both smartphones and decide which one to pick up if you care only about the camera.
Main camera in daylight
First, in daylight, Vivo X200T photos look closer to real life, while Vivo V80 photos look brighter and punchier. The Vivo X200T also handles shadows better than the Vivo V80.
As you can see in the first image, the Vivo V80 loses detail in the bushes, whereas the X200T handles shadows better. The Vivo V80 also has more detail.
Both photos look detailed normally; however, when you zoom in on the Vivo V80, the edges look rough, and the textures look crunchy because of the oversharpening. Both cameras do exceptionally well, but the Vivo V80 might appeal to most users because its contrasty photos work better on social media.
2x Zoom: Vivo X200T Pulls Ahead
Next, both smartphones have a telephoto lens. Side by side, Vivo V80 clearly falls behind in detail. As the images above show, when you zoom in, the Vivo X200T retains more detail than the Vivo V80. As you can see in the image above, the ground behind the cow on the Vivo V80 lacks detail, but on the X200T you can clearly see the grainy structure and other details.
3x Telephoto: Vivo V80 Comes Close
The Vivo V80 comes close to the Vivo X200T in the 3x telephoto shots. When you zoom out, both shots look really good to the eye; the Vivo V80 looks more contrasty and the colors pop, while the Vivo X200T keeps the colors closer to natural.
But again, the Vivo X200T has finer texture. For example, in the second image, when you zoom in, the bird feathers and stone details look better on the Vivo X200T than on the Vivo V80. But the Vivo V80 is also preferable here and retains plenty of detail, though it looks softer when compared side by side with the Vivo X200T. But still, most users prefer Vivo V80 photos simply because of their more vivid and punchy look.
Ultrawide: Vivo V80 Falls Behind
When it comes to the ultra-wide camera, even the specs show that the Vivo V80 falls far behind the Vivo X200T. Vivo still uses the lower 8-megapixel sensor, and it clearly struggles to capture the details. As you can see from the images below, the Vivo X200T shows clear leaves in the bark, whereas the Vivo V80 looks soft. Once again, Vivo oversharpens the image, making it look more contrasty than it does in real life. You can clearly see the difference in the image sample below.
Indoor Shots: The Gap Gets Smaller
Next, in the indoor and close-up shots, once again, Vivo X200T produces natural colors and also natural background blur with crisp and real details, whereas Vivo V80 also does a really good job, and when you look at both samples, the difference is quite small indoors.
Selfies: Both Are Good, X200T Is Slightly Better
Both the Vivo X200T and Vivo V80 produce sharp, detailed-looking selfies. The selfies on the Vivo V80 look cooler than the warmer tones on the Vivo X200T, as you can see in the images below. Both smartphones capture plenty of detail, with the Vivo X200T being slightly better, but not by much.
Shooting Into the Sun: Vivo V80 Struggles More
When shooting directly into the sun, both phones show lens flare. The Vivo V80 struggles more here with the white balance shifting, whereas the Vivo X200T keeps the colors natural and contrasty but still shows a visible ring of light across the frame.
Overall, in comparison, if camera quality is the top priority, and if you want natural-looking colors, a better all-rounder, and also a much better ultra-wide camera, the Vivo X200T takes the lead, while the Vivo V80 is still very capable and comes quite close in many situations. People may also prefer the more punchy look of the Vivo V80 that is ready to post on social media.
The same goes for low-light photos as well. The Vivo V80 is slightly behind the Vivo X200T in terms of retaining details, and some pictures look grainy in comparison.
You can also shoot portraits using the telephoto lens. The portraits look sharp, with strong blur and strong subject separation. You can also use the portrait mode with the telephoto lens to capture close-up portrait shots. Portrait mode also supports several Zeiss portrait styles, which are one of the highlight features of the Vivo V series phones.
And since the Vivo V80 is a camera-focused phone with a ZEISS partnership, you also get camera-focused features that are nice to play around with. It comes with various filters; Zeiss Natural mode is my favorite for getting more natural-looking photos. But still, the Vivo V80 tends to produce slightly punchier colors than expected.
In terms of video quality, the videos shot on the Vivo V80 are decent, bright, and colorful, same as the photos. Whereas the X200T leans toward more natural colors, the Vivo tends to make the overall quality brighter and the colors punchier, which, again, many people might like because of the contrasty colors that are good for social media posting.
Vivo V80 can record up to 4K 60fps from both the front and rear cameras. It also supports several video styles and modes. My favorite is 4K Cinematic Camera mode. Using it, you can produce cinematic-style, color-graded videos.
Fine for Everyday Use, Not for Performance Seekers
Vivo V80 comes with the same Snapdragon 7 Gen 4 used on the Vivo V70. It also comes with downgraded storage, UFS 3.1 compared to UFS 4.1 on the Vivo V70, and LPDDR4X compared to LPDDR5X. Also, the base variant now comes with 128GB instead of 256GB offered on the Vivo V70.
On paper, these are significant downgrades, especially when the Vivo V80 is priced close to flagship territory, where most phones are powered by Snapdragon 8 Elite-class processors.
I understand that most smartphones have recently gone through a price hike, and many smartphones are launching with even 4GB RAM in the budget segment, but those compromises are acceptable in the budget segment; for a phone with this experience, it is harder ot justiy, but considering the rise in memory and component costs, we do not have many choices.
In everyday use, I didn’t notice any big performance drop. Everyday tasks are decently faster. I didn’t have many expectations for the Snapdragon 7 Gen 4, but in gaming and when bumping up the refresh rate, I clearly noticed choppy performance. If performance is your highest priority, this phone clearly isn’t meant for that
Vivo V80 Benchmarks
Easy Two-Day Battery Life With Light Use
Battery life is not really a concern on the Vivo V80. Most smartphones today already come with fairly large batteries and support ultra-fast charging. Vivo also packed a dense 7200 mAh battery in the Vivo V80, and it also supports 90W super-fast charging. It can fully charge the device in under 1.5 hours.
Also, because of the less power-hungry Snapdragon 7 Gen 4, the battery can easily last up to two days with light usage and a full day with heavier use, which includes gaming and everyday tasks like browsing, watching videos, taking calls, and more.
Loud Stereo Speakers With Good Separation
Vivo V80 comes with stereo speakers. Both speakers are equally loud and offer very good stereo separation. There is no 3.5 mm headphone jack, which is pretty much the norm on most phones right now.
OriginOS 7 Is Good, but the V80 Misses Some Features
Vivo V80 is the first phone in India to ship with Origin OS 7 out of the box. OriginOS 7 has plenty of new customization features, including new themes, better lock screen customization options, a new liquid glass design, and a new workbench feature that lets you run five apps at once and switch between them easily. It also comes with useful AI features. Unfortunately, not all of those made it into the Vivo V80.
Vivo V80 lacks both the liquid glass design and the workbench feature because of RAM limitations (Workbench features require devices with 12GB RAM or more). OriginOS 7 still offers plenty of customization features on the Vivo V80. I already covered some of my favorite features in a different post. Adding custom stickers and the new pet pal wallpapers are a few of my favorites.
Vivo Origin OS 7 also brings plenty of AI features to the Vivo V80. After a very long time, I found very few of them useful beyond the AI image editing tools that we initially saw in many phones.
One of the favorite features is Snapshot. You can point the camera at a whiteboard, documents, or any text, and it can extract all the text. In the Notes app, it can arrange the text into tables, lists, and more.
The AI recorder is also useful. It allows you to create transcripts of your recordings, generate summaries, and pull useful insights. There are also plenty of AI camera features as well, letting you generate various AI-generated styles and effects.
Another feature I particularly liked is the Redirect Audio. It lets you play multiple audio tracks through different outputs without interfering with each other. For instance, if your phone is connected to Bluetooth and playing music, you can still watch a YouTube video at the same time using your phone’s speakers without affecting the music playing on your Bluetooth speaker.
Vivo also promised to roll out 4 years of major OS updates and six years of security updates for the Vivo V80, which is a very good software commitment
Vivo V80 Review Verdict: Great Cameras, but Vivo Has Pushed the V80 Too Far
For the asking price of Rs 62,999/-, Vivo has pushed the Vivo V80 a little too far this time. It now sits in the flagship territory, where you start getting phones with much stronger hardware.
It also competes with its own peers like the Vivo X200T, which at least for now feels like an overall better deal if value for your money is your highest priority. However, we are not sure whether the Vivo X200T will continue to exist as a competitor.
Vivo V80 is still a compelling device, especially for the cameras and also the new design. But if you’re open to other options or care about performance, Vivo V80 is harder to recommend. Of course,we all know that smartphone prices have gone up significantly over the past few months, and Vivo V80 is clearly another victim trying to justify its higher price.
