Medical debt is crushing hospital patients in LA. Health officials may have a fix
LOS ANGELES — Every Tuesday, Naman Shah sees tuberculosis patients at a small public clinic in Los Angeles' San Fernando Valley. Shah, a physician and epidemiologist at the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health, pores over images of battered lungs, listens to labored breathing and checks medications.
It's part of an initiative dating to the early 20th century to control infections so tuberculosis doesn't spread. "We like doing things upstream," Shah said, "meaning before they happen, not after the damage is done."
Today, Shah and his colleagues are applying the same principle to medical debt. A key part of that effort is a new system to allow every hospital in LA County to easily screen patients for financial aid. The goal: to stop low-income families from getting a bill that buries them in debt.
Shah estimates this system could prevent several hundred million dollars of medical debt every year.
Vicious cycle
In the U.S., an estimated 100 million adults have some form of healthcare debt. In LA County, the nation's most populous, public health officials calculate that about 800,000 residents have medical bills they can't pay.
"The impacts of medical debt were staggering," said Shah, who used to staff a rural health clinic in India and, since 2023, has led a county initiative in LA to tackle the debt problem.
"People end up with credit card debt and then a vicious cycle of high interest rates and poverty," he said. "People forgo their prescriptions. People forgo appointments. And then you get into worse health."
Hospitals typically offer financial aid to patients with low incomes. But information about assistance is often hard for patients to get. Applying can be cumbersome. And many eligible patients never seek aid, research shows.
"Most people walk into the hospital and walk out without any knowledge of financial assistance," said Jared Walker, founder of Dollar For, a nonprofit that helps patients nationwide apply for aid, often called charity care.
That's fueling debt. It's also driving costly collection efforts that even hospital officials acknowledge pointlessly target low-income patients who are unlikely to be able to pay.
"They're turning their wheels trying to collect on debt that isn't collectable," said Adena Tessler, regional vice president for the Hospital Association of Southern California.
Presumptive eligibility
One potential solution is a system that automatically screens and qualifies low-income patients for financial aid without requiring an application. This is called presumptive eligibility.
Some hospitals already use such systems, which rely on software that checks patient eligibility based on publicly available information such as credit history.
The strategy can be very effective. Shah said hospitals that have deployed presumptive eligibility systems have reported as much as a 50% increase in the amount of financial aid they give patients.
Under a state law passed last year, all California hospitals will have to start doing presumptive eligibility screening by next July.
But the systems can be expensive and difficult for smaller hospitals to implement. Only about 1 in 5 hospitals in LA County currently use them, Shah said.
Public health officials wondered whether they could help more hospitals set up the systems.
The county, which, like many local governments, faces major fiscal challenges, couldn't pay for this, Shah said. But the public health department could bring together healthcare and hospital officials in the county to figure out another solution.
"The beauty of government is not when it always has to do the work," Shah said. "We have the ability to make sure that people cooperate."
The Hospital Association of Southern California, initially wary of the county initiative, came to see improving hospital financial aid programs as beneficial to hospitals, many of which were wasting money on collections. "The billing process is cumbersome and costly," said Paul Young, a senior vice president with the association.
The association agreed to procure a digital presumptive eligibility system and make it available to its members. This bulk-purchasing approach, which Young compared to "a Costco model," would lower the cost for individual hospitals, he said.
At the same time, L.A. Care, a nonprofit health plan that administers Medicaid coverage for more than 2.5 million low-income county residents, committed $2 million to set up the system.
The investment reflected the safety net insurer's mission to make medical care accessible to more people, said Melanie Fontes Rainer, who leads strategic planning for L.A. Care. "It's going to make Los Angeles County better," she said.
Making it work
Getting the new system up and running by January, as the partners hope, faces challenges.
Hospital officials are figuring out how the system will be funded in the long term. And it's unclear how many of the county's 88 acute care hospitals will ultimately use it, even if it's cheaper and easier to access.
The partners are also working to improve the data that the system relies on to screen patients. One goal is to link the system to tax records maintained by the state of California. This would provide hospitals with more accurate information on patients' income than current systems, which often rely on estimated income.
Walker, the patient advocate at Dollar For, said he's heartened by the county's effort. "I'm optimistic that we can make a better charity care system," he said. "And the fact that hospitals in LA County are willing to be innovative and creative about ways we can do that is super encouraging."
For his part, Shah said county public health officials recognize that a better screening system at hospitals won't by itself eliminate medical debt. But he said the public health department couldn't ignore a problem that affects more county residents than asthma or tobacco use.
"Prevention is our bread and butter," he said.
This article is part of Hidden Help, an investigative series from Tradeoffs and KFF Health News about how hospitals can protect their patients from the life-altering harms of medical debt.

Italy overhauls electoral system after fiercely contested debate
- Published
Italy's parliament has approved fiercely contested changes to the country's electoral system championed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni ahead of elections due next year.
Lawmakers voted 227 to 164 in favour of moving to a fully proportional system, which Meloni has argued will boost the chance of clear winners and more stable government.
Opposition parties say her right-wing coalition has designed the proposals to improve its chance of retaining power and, in a heated debate on Thursday, accused it of flouting democracy.
Meloni had warned she could resign and trigger an early election if the plans were rejected, with the secret ballot seen as a test of her authority.
Meloni's coalition has overseen a rare period of political stability for Italy since her election in 2022, and last month her government became the country's longest-running since World War Two.
The voting reform will see the country move away from its current hybrid voting system, in which about a third of members are chosen through a first-past-the-post vote and the rest through proportional representation.
Parties proposing to form a coalition will be required to put forward their joint candidate for prime minister, and their political programme, before any general election.
A party or coalition which emerges with the largest share of the votes - provided this exceeds 42% - will be awarded 105 additional seats in parliament (70 in the lower house and 35 in the senate), which could turn a narrow victory into a more comfortable majority.
In a debate ahead of the vote, centre-left members accused the government of forcing through the new voting rules.
"Go ahead and change the electoral law, we will win in any case under any voting system," said Democratic Party (PD) leader Elly Schlein.
The proposals have also exposed tensions within the ranks of Meloni's coalition, too, with the Brothers of Italy (FdI) party and its allies, the far-right League and centre-right Forza Italia.
Analysts had predicted that Thursday's final vote was unlikely to fail - particularly given the number of lawmakers who would risk losing their eligibility for a parliamentary pension if their term was ended early as a result of the threatened snap election.
"To those who hoped to see the centre-right divided," Meloni wrote on social media after the vote, "today we respond with facts: we are united, cohesive, and determined to carry forward the commitments made to citizens."
She added: "We are introducing rules designed to promote the stability and parliamentary coherence of any government, regardless of its political colour."
Meloni's term officially comes to an end in October 2027, although she could bring elections forward to the spring.

Lhuan-dre Pretorius has broken Chris Gayle's record for the highest score in a men's T20 match with an unbeaten 188 in a domestic fixture in South Africa.
The 20-year-old South African's knock off 79 deliveries, including 13 sixes and 15 fours, helped Titans post 267-3 against Knights in the CSA T20 Challenge.

Pretorius, who has played 17 T20s, three one-dayers and two Tests for South Africa, finished with a strike rate of 237.97.
He made his half-century off 24 balls but only required 16 more balls to get to three figures and then got to 150 off just 58 deliveries.
Titans then bowled out Knights for 143 to wrap up an emphatic 124-run victory at the Mangaung Oval in Bloemfontein.

The most profitable move in artificial intelligence may no longer be selling intelligence. It is selling a model to a company, wiring it into that company's most valuable work, learning the business from the inside, and then shipping the product that competes with it. In a previous piece for Inc42, I argued that the black box was losing the boardroom, and that enterprise AI built on the customer's own terms was the opening worth chasing. The months since have made the argument more literal than expected. The frontier labs are now moving into their customers' markets, and they are doing it in plain sight. The Pattern Has Hardened Into A Playbook Read the moves of the past year together and a sequence emerges. Sell the model to the world's most valuable businesses. Help wire it into their most sensitive and highest-margin work. Map how the business runs from the inside. Then turn those learnings into a product and stand up as the customer's competitor. Each step, taken alone, reads as partnership. Assembled, they read as strategy. Of course, a lot still depends on execution. Just because a model company knows how a customer runs its business does not mean it can run that business better than the customer. However, the labs would say this is simply where the technology leads, and that is part of the truth. It is also the most dependable way to convert a supplier relationship into a market entrant position. Figma is the clearest illustration. It partnered with Anthropic on AI design tooling, the kind of collaboration that looks like validation for a newly public company. Then Mike Krieger, Anthropic's chief product officer, resigned from Figma's board, and three days later Anthropic launched Claude Design, a standalone tool aimed squarely at Figma. The stock fell around 7% on the day, and the activist fund Findell Capital has since pushed the board to review the entire Anthropic relationship. Asked about it at a closed event, Figma's Dylan Field reached for the exact phrase OpenAI's board once used to remove Sam Altman, saying the lab had not been "consistently candid." The partner had become the competitor inside a single news cycle. Harvey is a more practical example, because the evidence sits on Anthropic's own website, which still features the legal startup as a customer success story for contract analysis, due diligence and litigation. In May, Anthropic launched Claude for Legal and began selling those same workflows directly to law firms. Harvey carries an $11 Bn valuation, and the model that powered the challenger now stands beside it as a rival. The pattern repeats wherever a workflow is worth owning. Intercom built its support agents on OpenAI's models, and OpenAI now sells Presence, its own voice and chat support agent. Abridge and Ambience built clinical documentation on OpenAI's API, and OpenAI now sells ChatGPT for Healthcare to hospitals, with a free tier for individual clinicians and documentation built in. Benchling embedded Claude into biotech R&D across more than 1,300 companies, and Anthropic now sells its own research workbench, Claude Science. The same logic is reaching financial services, where Claude connects to market-data providers and runs credit memos and know-your-customer checks inside banks. In each case the supplier watched the customer prove the market, then walked into it. The strength of this incentive also shows up clearly in the earliest partnerships within the industry. Microsoft owns roughly 27% of OpenAI. It had bought GitHub in 2018 for $7.5 Bn. OpenAI is now building a jobs platform for professional hiring and, as per reporting in The Information, a code repository, moves that would sit against LinkedIn and GitHub, both Microsoft properties. This is not a claim that anyone has been denied. It is a measure of how far the pull toward the customer's market reaches, when it can tug even against an early strategic investor's own businesses. Pharma Is Where the Trap Is Sharpest Drug discovery is the case that should give every board pause. Novo Nordisk and Bristol Myers Squibb route revenue and workflow data into Claude, treating Anthropic as a supplier. In May, BMS placed Claude before more than 30,000 employees as what it called a shared intelligence platform across research, clinical development and manufacturing. On 30 June, Anthropic launched Claude Science and, in the same breath, announced it would run its own preclinical drug discovery programmes. The customers, through their unchecked reliance on the model, are funding what they treat as a vendor but is in fact a competitor lurking in the shadows, and are helping to sharpen the very capability that may one day contest their pipelines. The market read it at once. On the day, Schrödinger fell as much as 8.3%, Recursion 3.3% and IQVIA more than 2.3%. Anthropic frames the work around neglected diseases that large pharma overlooks, and that framing is fair as far as it goes. It does not change the structural fact that the vendor has walked onto the customer's field. The Economics Make Restraint Implausible Follow the money and the behaviour explains itself. Anthropic's revenue run rate reached about $65 Bn by the end of July, up from roughly $1 Bn in December 2024, at a $965 Bn valuation, with a filing already lodged for a listing that could come this autumn. OpenAI has roughly doubled to about $40 Bn in revenue. Eight of the Fortune 10 are already Claude customers, a sign of how much of the real economy now runs through a single supplier. Selling tokens is a commodity business with thin and contested margins. Selling the finished application into a market with real returns on capital is where the value pools. A company carrying a near-trillion-dollar valuation into public markets cannot credibly promise to leave the richest layer of the stack to its customers forever. None of this requires bad faith. The incentive is obvious, which is exactly what makes the move more likely. The AI Narrative Is Getting Harder To Reconcile This is where the public story and the operating record pull apart, and founders are reading one against the other. The labs speak the language of safety, abundance and responsible stewardship, and in the same year they have entered design, law, support, healthcare and drug discovery. The mood at the frontier can run further still. On the All-In podcast in August, investor Gavin Baker said he had been told by people he trusts that Dario Amodei has floated the idea that Anthropic "might be the only private company in the world" at some point, with only governments beside it. Anthropic rejected the account outright, with one of its researchers calling it false and Amodei rebutting it directly. Mark Zuckerberg has since published an essay making the opposite case, for open models and a distribution of power rather than its concentration. This episode matters not because it is settled, but because it is not. The claims are second-hand, disputed and changing week to week, and that instability is itself the point. Nobody, inside these companies or outside them, can tell you today how this resolves. Of course, this narrative is great support and justification for the enterprise value of an IPO this large. What is not in doubt is the direction of the incentive and the exposure it creates for everyone who builds on top. Alex Karp of Palantir has named the mechanism most plainly, arguing that enterprises are "paying for tokens that create no value" while surrendering their alpha, the proprietary edge that makes a business defensible. Michael Burry put it more bluntly, remarking that Anthropic was eating Palantir's lunch. The narratives will keep shifting. The opportunity arithmetic underneath them will not. Own Your Alpha For India the exposure is doubled. The country's software firms and its 1,900-plus global capability centres are among the heaviest consumers of frontier APIs, and its services industry wires client workflows through those same models, sending client alpha upstream with every integration. The lesson from the cases above is that being a large and loyal customer is no shield. It may simply be the reconnaissance. The opening is the same size as the risk, and it is the one I argued for last time, only more urgent now. Vertical AI built on domain depth the labs cannot see from the outside. Private and on-premise deployment of open models. Harnesses that keep proprietary data inside the building. Open-weight models isolated from the internet and run for a single enterprise. Intercom has already moved its agent partly onto its own in-house open-weights model rather than depend on a supplier that competes with it, and that is the direction of travel. India's sovereign-model efforts and its vertical software builders should read this moment as the start of a new market preference forming. Every Indian founder and CTO now faces the same reckoning before the next integration. It is to know precisely what alpha they are sending upstream, and whether they can protect it before it returns as somebody else's product. The labs may or may not become the last companies standing. The firms that decide early to own their alpha will not have to find out.

A woman who was allegedly choked and assaulted by the former Bachelor star Sam Wood told police she “thought she was going to die”, a Queensland court heard on Thursday.
The court also heard that police in Victoria had attended Wood’s home in relation to a similar incident about three years ago, but that the woman had not wanted to make a complaint at that time out of “fear of retribution”.
Wood, a 46-year-old wellness influencer from Melbourne, was denied bail in a Queensland court on Thursday and will be held in custody indefinitely awaiting trial, after police argued his behaviour was “escalating” and that he posed an unacceptable risk.
Wood appeared in court via video link from the Maroochydore police watch house cells, where he had been held for about four days. He was arrested at Noosa on the Sunshine Coast on Sunday and charged with two domestic violence offences: assault occasioning bodily harm and strangulation in a domestic setting.
In outlining the prosecution case, police prosecutor Jeanette Grigoris said the brief of evidence included a triple zero call made by a family member, photographs of the victim’s injuries, and a video-recorded statement by the complainant.
Grigoris said the complainant was supportive of the charges proceeding.
Wood’s lawyer has indicated the reality TV star will fight the charges.
The court heard that in the video statement, the woman alleges she was choked and that “there was a cessation of breath”.
“She articulates the banging of her head on the floor. She couldn’t breathe,” Grigoris said.
“She thought she was going to die.”
Grigoris said the video statement by the woman also refers to a previous matter in Victoria “being of a similar nature” and “involved choking”.
The court heard that in a police interview, recorded about midnight on Sunday morning.
Wood denied that any previous incident had taken place in Victoria.
Grigoris said there was body-worn camera footage of police attending his home and a police report in relation to that incident.
Grigoris said the woman “did not make any criminal complaints on that occasion, she was in fear of retribution of the defendant.”
Grigoris also raised concern that Wood, during his police interview, minimised his part in the alleged offending, and minimised the injuries suffered by the woman.
“He’s essentially victim blamed,” she said.
Wood’s lawyer, Matthew Cuskelly, sought bail and said his client denied the allegations. He cited a psychologist’s report that said Wood was suffering from “severe depression”.
“He ought to be given the opportunity to engage with mental health professionals,” Cuskelly said.
“And also try to salvage something of his professional reputation and career, which is taking a hell of a beating at the moment.
“Ultimately, as all families have, there was problems. And my client had been enduring the hardship of attempting to quarantine those problems from his family for some period of time. It was agonising.”
Cuskelly cited a psychologist’s report that describes ‘the difficulty that my client has been enduring in respect of the deterioration of his psychological state”.
“His depression is regarded as extremely severe.”
Cuskelly said Wood had no prior criminal history and if granted bail would reside in Victoria with his father, Andrew Wood, who attended the court in support of his son.
Acting magistrate Janelle Boegheim said she was not satisfied by the defence argument that the case against Wood was weak.
“The strength of the evidence against the defendant is … relatively strong at this juncture.”
Boegheim said it was likely the charges, if proven, would attract a term in prison.
Wood was stood down by his own fitness empire, 28 by Sam Wood, on Monday, a day after he was charged.
“We have all been shocked and saddened by the matters involving Sam Wood,” said Mark Watkin, the group’s acting chief executive.
“We have zero tolerance for domestic violence. While the matter is under investigation and before the court, Sam is on indefinite leave from his duties.
“Our thoughts are with the family and anyone in the community affected by domestic violence.”
He is due to face court again on November 23.

The State informed the Kerala High Court that in-principle approval had not been granted to Keralam for establishing an All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS).
The Division Bench of Chief Justice Soumen Sen and Justice V.M. Syam Kumar enquired into the reason why Keralam was not prioritised for building an AIIMS, even though the matter had been pending for almost 10 years. The Bench was considering a petition seeking establishment of an AIIMS under the Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY).
The court observed that the matter was presently at the stage of inter-ministerial consultation and any decision for setting up an AIIMS could be taken only after the continuation of the PMSSY scheme for the next five financial years, FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31, was approved.
In a previous order, the court noted that the idea of having an AIIMS in Keralam was raised in June 2016 and four locations were identified for this purpose. The court opined that Keralam should be considered on a priority basis considering the density of population, and asked the Union government to take a conscious decision concerning the proposal for the institute.
Prioritising other States
The Deputy Solicitor General of India, O.M. Shalina, informed the court that since Keralam had better health-care conditions than other States, the Union government was prioritising those States with a weaker health sector. At this point the court enquired whether the Union government’s stand was that Keralam did not require an AIIMS. The court orally asked whether the hospitals in the State were a disqualification or a ‘handicap’ to consider the establishment of the institute. The court orally remarked that Keralam had the highest density of population in the country, and that the existing hospitals would not be sufficient to provide medical facilities to the needy and poor.
The Union government responded that while considering all other States and Union Territories, Keralam’s status was much better, and that was the reason for the delay in approval. The court then enquired why there was an AIIMS in Delhi and two or three institutes in some other States, if the criteria was availability of medical facilities.

Prosecutors in the United States have accused Venezuela's former leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, of conspiracy to commit torture.
The fresh charges against the couple were made public on Thursday and are in addition to the drug-trafficking and weapons charges already brought against them, which they have denied.
Maduro, 63, and Flores, 69, have been in custody since January in a detention centre in Brooklyn, where they were taken after US forces seized them in a pre-dawn raid on their compound in the Venezuelan capital, Caracas.
Human rights groups in Venezuela and former prisoners have long denounced what they have described as "systematic torture" in Venezuelan jails.
The new accusations relate to the alleged torture of US citizens who were being held in Venezuela while Maduro was in power.
The trial for both Maduro and Flores is set to begin in June 2027.

In late September, two images circulated online purportedly showing ancient Egyptian sculptures depicting cats walking and resting on their owners.
One of the images shows a sculpture, possibly a wood carving, of a cat in a museum display as either standing or walking on a person at rest. The other image features a cat sitting right up against the chin of a person whose eyes appear to be open.
For example, on Sept. 29, a Facebook user posted a graphic (archived) featuring the two images, with text reading, "4,000-year-old statues prove cats have always ignored personal space." The post's caption adds, "Cats Have Been Sitting on Their Humans for 4,000 Years." The pair of images also spread on Threads and X (archived, archived).
(Nathanistic via Facebook)
Reverse image searches uncovered examples of the standing cat image on Facebook, Instagram and Threads, as well as the resting cat image on Instagram, Threads and X.
Cats prominently feature in ancient Egyptian artifacts, including in mummification. That may be one reason why some commenters under posts have posted remarks indicating they believe the images are authentic. Others mention artificial intelligence, saying they are skeptical about whether the images show actual artifacts that truly exist.
In sum, the images are fake and appear to be AI-generated — as do other images of Egyptian sculptures depicting cats interacting with people.
The aforementioned reverse image searches indicate that the earliest posts featuring the image of the cat standing or walking on top of the person first appeared on Soft Cat Memes (@softcatmemes) accounts on Facebook, Instagram and Threads on Sept. 25, as well as on the possibly-affiliated @hardcatmemes X account. The image contains overlaid text, reading, "Cats have been bothering their humans since the dawn of time."
(@softcatmemes via Facebook)
The image of the cat sitting on a person also first appeared on the same accounts on Sept. 26, receiving more engagement. That second image also features overlaid text, reading, "Evidence suggests cats have never understood personal space."
(@softcatmemes via Facebook)
Snopes contacted the manager of the accounts to confirm the user created the images with an AI tool. We also asked for the name of the tool and the exact text prompts submitted to create the content. We will update this article if we receive further information.
How we know images are fake
Reverse image searches failed to locate any posts or websites containing the same two images prior to late September. With the ongoing popularity of internet cat content, the idea that no one, until recently, would share supposedly real photos of ancient Egyptian sculptures depicting cats acting silly is unlikely.
As one Reddit user has noted, scans of the images with OpenAI's free tool, that verifies content generated using the company's chatbot, display the results, "This content was generated using OpenAI tools," and, "We found a SynthID watermark that originated from OpenAI." For example, a scan of the image of the cat sitting displays the information shown below.
(via OpenAI)
There is also an inconsistency with one of the shadows in that image. The faint shadow nearest where the photographer is meant to be standing (running from left to right along the long edge of the bed) indicates there is a light source on the other side of the display. However, only a shadow of the bed is cast. If the image were authentic, the angle of the shadow suggests the viewer would also be able to see a faint shadow of the human and cat sculptures. That is not the case in this image.
A scan of the other image of the cat standing or walking displays the same result using OpenAI's tool. The absence of a shadow of the cat's tail also further suggests this image is fake.
For further reading, we previously reported about another feline rumor that wild cheetahs have never killed humans.

Former Australian bishop jailed for sexually abusing young men
- Published
Former Australian bishop Christopher Saunders has been jailed for sexually abusing two young Aboriginal men during his time as a Catholic cleric.
Saunders - who resigned as Bishop of Broome when first accused of wrongdoing in 2020 - was found guilty of one charge of rape and 12 counts of indecent assault in August.
The 76-year-old was on Wednesday sentenced to six and a half years in prison, but will be eligible for release on parole in February 2031.
He is one of the most senior Catholic leaders in the world to face sex abuse charges.
His trial in the state of Western Australia heard Saunders systematically groomed the two young men, inviting them to "shirts-off" gatherings and plying them with alcohol, often using church funds and church-owned properties to do so.
He was convicted of kissing and molesting the men between 2010 and 2019, and in one instance forcing oral sex on one of them.
In a victim impact statement provided to the court, that young man said he still struggled to talk about what had happened.
"I was a toy that he was using," the victim wrote. "My head is pounding now, I'm in so much pain."
"I trusted him. I thought he wanted me to be a better person."
During the trial several child sex abuse charges were discarded, and Saunders was acquitted by the jury of alleged offences against a third young man.
First ordained in 1976, Saunders spent most of his career in the remote Kimberley region in the nation's north-west corner, and was appointed Bishop of Broome in 1996.
The diocese stretches about 770,000 sq km (297,000 sq miles) - an area roughly the size of Turkey - and encompasses some of the most remote parts of the country.
District Court Judge Martin Flynn said Saunders had professed to be an advocate for young Aboriginal men, but instead misused his authority and exploited their vulnerability.
He had "disregarded the dignity" of his victims and caused them lasting harm.
In a statement, Archbishop of Perth Timothy Costelloe said the men who had come forward had shown great courage and resilience in pursuing justice.
"We are sorry for the pain and suffering that was inflicted on you. We are sorry that your trust was so directly and profoundly betrayed by a leader of the church," he said.
"No court sentence can undo the suffering that has been caused or restore all that each person has lost."
The accusations were first aired in 2020, but the initial police investigation that followed was closed without charge.
However after a historic inquiry was ordered by the Pope, police began a new investigation.
Costelloe has previously said the church's investigation into Saunders - paused when police resumed theirs - will restart.
The church is under pressure to strip Saunders of his remaining title and ministry powers, a decision the Archbishop said would be determined by Rome.
Only a handful of "Vos Estis Lux Mundi" - meaning "You Are the Light of the World" in Latin - inquiries have been undertaken around the world.
The investigations are commissioned by the pontiff and were introduced in 2019 to combat sexual abuse and hold bishops and other high-ranking Catholic Church officials accountable for their actions.
Aside from the late Cardinal George Pell, who was jailed and then acquitted, Saunders is the most senior Catholic official in the country to be charged with sex offences.

NEW DELHI: Should Arvind Kejriwal’s AAP and MK Stalin’s DMK join INDIA bloc’s fight against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over SIR? Well, the answer would surely be “yes”, as far as the allies of the bloc are concerned.Now to the more difficult question: Will Arvind Kejriwal’s AAP and MK Stalin’s DMK join INDIA bloc’s fight against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over SIR? Well, there is no straight answer to this one.The AAP and the DMK have a common enemy in the Congress. Uddhav Thackeray’s Shiv Sena (UBT) has now urged the two parties to set aside their differences with the grand-old-party to fight against "dictatorship". In an editorial in the party mouthpiece 'Saamana', Shiv Sena (UBT) said, “The entire country has been witnessing protests against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), but the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) and the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) have stayed away from it."
-
The absence of both parties, who have officially withdrawn from the INDIA bloc, has highlighted the existing differences within the opposition camp on the strategy and format of the protest against irregularities in the SIR process.
'A very critical request'
Former Congress leader and senior political commentator Sanjay Jha feels Shiv Sena (UBT)'s suggestion to both the DMK and the Aam Aadmi Party to join the INDIA bloc is a very practical, very reasonable, and at the moment, a very critical request.
"This is not about, at the moment, anything other than the fact that Indian democracy is in peril. It is unlikely that the CEC is going to resign of his own volition. It is pretty apparent that the government of Mr. Modi is going to be stubborn, and they will stonewall any effort by the opposition to demand and get accountability. Public protests don't seem to make any difference to the government. So the more the merrier," Sanjay Jha says.While the AAP has openly announced it will not be a part of the INDIA bloc’s protest and said “we are fighting this battle in our own way, the DMK has spoken in different tones.DMK spokesperson Saravanan Annadurai accused Rahul of adopting inconsistent positions on the electoral roll revision exercise and questioned why developments in Tamil Nadu had not received the same attention as the broader campaign against the Election Commission.In a post on X, Annadurai called on Rahul Gandhi to clarify his stand on allegations concerning names allegedly removed from Tamil Nadu’s electoral rolls during the SIR process.The DMK spokesperson also referred to a statement attributed to Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge that governments elected after the SIR exercise should be dissolved and sought clarification on why Rahul Gandhi had not publicly endorsed that position and whether such a stand would also apply to Tamil Nadu.Interestingly, a day later, DMK senior leader TKS Elangovan backed Rahul Gandhi on protests against the Election Commission (EC), saying that citizens have a right to protest against the government.“It is the right of citizens to fight against the government’s wrongdoings. That is what Rahul Gandhi did yesterday. Still, this government does not want him to protest because Gyanesh Kumar is being very useful to the BJP. Because of him, the BJP captured power in many states. In all these states, re-elections should be held,” Elangovan said.
Will DMK, AAP join SIR protests?
The DMK and the Congress had a very unpleasant parting of their two-decade-old ties after the 2026 assembly elections in Tamil Nadu, which the alliance lost to actor-politician C Joseph Vijay’s Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam TVK. While the TVK emerged as the single largest party, it fell short of a majority. The Congress rushed in to help Vijay not just form the government but also eventually join it. Making Congress a part of the government was something the DMK had resisted all along. The Congress move offended the DMK to no end. Since then, MK Stalin’s party has been unrelenting in its attacks on the Congress at all forums from Chennai to Delhi. The Congress, on its part, maintains that it kept the DMK in the loop while shifting loyalties to the TVK.The DMK is missing no opportunity to drive a wedge between the new allies. On Thursday, it lashed out at Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay-led TVK for not explicitly naming the BJP government over the arrest of Congress leader Rahul Gandhi after a protest in the national capital demanding the resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar.Questioning the TVK's statement, Elangovan pointed out that it failed to identify the authorities responsible for the action against the leader of the opposition in Lok Sabha. "Who arrested Rahul Gandhi? They should condemn and explicitly mention the name of the BJP government," Elangovan told PTI videos.With the TVK establishing itself as the third pole of Tamil Nadu politics, at least for now, the Congress will have to choose one against the other, and to that extent its ties with the DMK will remain frosty for now. More so, after the TVK has officially joined the INDIA bloc. But the DMK’s measured criticism of the Congress-led INDIA bloc protests may offer a ray of hope to the opposition bloc allies of a future softening of stand by M K Stalin.Now, let’s turn to AAP. Here’s where untangling the strains in the ties may be very difficult, if not impossible. Relations between the Congress and the AAP have always been uneasy and tumultuous. AAP was initially a part of the INDIA bloc.However, ties between Kejriwal’s party and the Congress were never smooth given their competing political interests in several states. AAP attended the first three meetings of the INDIA bloc. The high point in their ties came in the run up to the 2024 Lok Sabha elections when the two parties agreed to a joint contest in Delhi, Haryana, Goa, Punjab and Gujarat.The alliance did not work and the ties ended for all practical purposes after the results were out. In July 2025, Kejriwal formally announced the end of ties.Uddhav Thackeray’s party has reminded Kejriwal of his bitter experiences with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Union home minister Amit Shah and the Election Commission.“While Kejriwal was the chief minister of Delhi, he was put behind bars in a "false" case. Kejriwal's defeat was engineered by deleting names of voters from his constituency, it alleged. So, it is not in the AAP's interest to stay away from the INDIA bloc,” the Shiv Sena (UBT) wrote in its editorial.
'All parties should look at larger picture'
Sanjay Jha is confident that these parties will eventually join the opposition protest. He argues it is extremely crucial that the opposition includes everyone.“Whether there are any small, petty differences, whether there is any degree of discomfort with one or the other partner, everyone has to look at the larger picture. And the larger picture is that today people are out on the streets because they're concerned about the future of their vote and the future of democracy,” Sanjay Jha says.
“And I believe it is very likely that the DMK and Arvind Kejriwal will join, because this is the time to put aside any petty squabbles and think of the larger goal of the country,” he adds.But this may be easier said than done. The Congress and the AAP are the main rivals in Punjab, where assembly elections are due early next year. The two parties are already engaged in a bitter war of words in Punjab, where AAP is defending its only government and the Congress is going all out to defeat Kejriwal’s party and reclaim its lost glory and government in the state.So, let’s see if this political compulsion decides the future course of ties between the two parties or the “larger goal of the country”?

Investors bullish on AI data centers may be fueling Nvidia’s multitrillion-dollar market capitalization, but the AI chipmaker has also bet billions of dollars on physical AI technologies such as robotics and self-driving cars. Part of that gambit has involved developing a full-stack safety system that companies can build upon to reduce the risk of their machines harming nearby people.
Nvidia’s Halos system launched in 2025 with hardware and software tools to help developers implement guardrails in self-driving cars and other autonomous vehicles. Then the company expanded its safety architecture to more physical AI technologies by announcing Nvidia Halos for Robotics in June 2026—with the goal of enabling safe deployments of autonomous mobile robots in warehouses, humanoid robots walking around inside a factory, or even surgical robots.
“Now the AI models are getting capable, the robot hardware is getting capable, and a thing we thought is going to be the next bottleneck is safety,” Amit Goel, head of robotics ecosystem and edge computing at Nvidia, told Ars. “So that’s why we launched our Halos for Robotics to unlock the capability of these systems.”
The expanded safety offering for robotics comes as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang described the physical AI business as already driving nearly $10 billion in annual revenue for the company during an appearance on the All-In Podcast in March 2026. Huang previously began highlighting physical AI as Nvidia’s second-most important growth category in 2025.
Expanding safety from AVs to robots
So what does Nvidia’s full-stack safety system involve? It starts with hardware, such as the Nvidia IGX Thor computing module for robotics and industrial applications that has an independent processor dedicated to safety-related workloads. “In the context of physical AI, you need to have your functional system and your safety system all running on the same silicon,” Goel said.

A purported screenshot circulated online in fall 2026 of a purported Truth Social post, dated Sept. 22, in which U.S. President Donald Trump wrote that he had "spoken to God" and that "tonight is Armageddon.".
The image spread on multiple platforms, including Instagram, Threads and Facebook. Many commenters appeared to believe Trump actually posted the remarks. The full text of the alleged post read as follows:
I have spoken to God and he has given me a vision of an ocean filled with blood a city of dust a golden throne for me to sit on, eternally!!!, Tonight is Armageddon, the final judgement of good and evil!!!! Lock your doors and do not directly at the flash!!!! God bless us all!!!
President Donald J. Trump
(X user @ZiemowitSzcze11.)
Despite the username matching Trump's real Truth Social username, there's no evidence Trump actually published the post. The earliest version of the image we found appeared on a Polish X account that captioned it (translation via X): "Well, fake, but would you be surprised?" (archived).
We searched Trump's Truth — an online archive of Trump's Truth Social posts — for the word "Armageddon," and none of the three results related to the quote above.
(Trump's Truth)
We also looked all posts Trump actually published on Sept. 22 and found he published four that day. None of the four posts matched the timestamp or content of that in the screenshot.
The fake quote appeared to echo whistleblower reports received by the Military Religious Freedom Foundation that U.S. military commanders told troops their action in Iran was "all part of God's divine plan," allegedly "referring to Armageddon and the imminent return of Jesus Christ."
Trump has echoed similarly apocalyptic language, posting in May 2026, for example, that "a whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again" — referring to U.S. attacks on Iran. He's also faced criticism for his posting an image depicting him in the likeness of Jesus Christ.

The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has proposed requiring international students to pay up to around ₹67.7 lakh ($70,000) for certain work-training programmes if they want to work in the US, as part of the Trump administration’s broader crackdown on foreign visa holders. The proposed rule would require non-immigrant students on F-1 visas to pay ₹67.7 lakh ($70,000) to a certified institution for on-the-job training under the Optional Practical Training (OPT) programme, as per a statement released by DHS. An additional work-training programme would attract a proposed fee of ₹29 lakh ($30,000). DHS said the proposed changes are aimed at “combating fraud, strengthening the integrity of the immigration system, and protecting US workers.” The proposal could have a significant impact on Indian students, who make up one of the largest international student communities in the US. Around 3.63 lakh Indian students enrolled at US institutions during the 2024-25 academic year, making India the largest source of international students in the country, according to Hindustan Times. The OPT programme is particularly important for Indian students seeking to transition from higher education into employment in the US. Participation in OPT among Indian students has risen to around 1.44 lakh, according to a report in The Times of India. However, Indian student enrolment reportedly fell by around 15% in the 2025-26 cycle, amid tighter US visa policies and proposed changes to the immigration system, The Hindu reported. Under the OPT system, F-1 students can undertake temporary work related to their field of study for up to 20 hours a week while their academic programme is in session and can also work for a limited period after graduation, according to Reuters. Students with degrees in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) can qualify for an extended period of work authorization. Students currently pay around ₹48,000 ($500) for OPT-related applications, making the proposed ₹67.7 lakh ($70,000) fee a dramatic increase, according to the report. DHS said the proposed fee is intended to ensure that “employers, students, and institutions are engaging in appropriate activities” consistent with F-1 nonimmigrant status. For many international students, OPT serves as a bridge between studying in the US and entering the country's skilled workforce. The H-1B visa programme has, for decades, allowed highly skilled workers, particularly engineers, scientists and technology professionals from countries such as India, to work for US companies after completing their studies. US technology companies have also relied heavily on H-1B workers to fill specialized positions and address skilled labour gaps. Doug Rand, Director of the Talent Mobility Fund, which works to attract foreign STEM professionals, criticized DHS's proposal on LinkedIn, arguing that it could face legal challenges. The proposal will first be subject to a 30-day public comment period before DHS can finalize it, as per Reuters. If finalized, DHS said it would wait another 60 days before implementing the rule, giving universities, students and employers time to prepare. New Delhi, Oct 8: The high-powered GST Council on Thursday approved removing the arrest power of tax officials and raising the threshold for prosecution fivefold to Rs 5 crore, while introducing faster and largely automated refunds for taxpayers.
Announcing the decisions taken at the 57th meeting of the GST Council, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said it also decided to bring down the general penalty from Rs 25,000 to Rs 10,000.
The changes approved by the GST Council will be implemented from April 1, 2027.
The Council also cleared a proposal that a taxpayer who files late, makes a mistake or falls behind on payment will face recovery, interest and a proportionate penalty, and nothing beyond that.
Another key recommendation was about extending refunds under the inverted rate structure to input services. The change will be available for credit availed on or after November 1, 2026, Sitharaman said.
The Finance Minister also said that the government intends to introduce faceless tax assessment for Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) taxpayers registered in multiple states.
Sitharaman said the power of arrest will be removed from GST and the threshold for prosecution will be raised from Rs 1 crore to Rs 5 crore.
Also, no notices will be issued in cases below a monetary threshold of Rs 10,000.
The Council, comprising Union and state finance ministers, also recommended removing the minimum punishment.
Also, the punishment, whether fine or imprisonment or both, will be left to judicial discretion in every case.
Sitharaman further said the general penalty, applicable where no specific penalty is provided, will also be reduced from Rs 25,000 to Rs 10,000.
She also said no GST rates have been changed at the meeting.
The recommendations of the Council will come into effect from April 1.
Replying to a query, Sitharaman said the GST Council had mostly addressed the aberrations because of ITC and addressed the duty inversion.
"So, I don't think there are many outstanding issues which are fundamental to ease of doing business or fundamental to anomalies and rates remain. So, yes, you can say GST next generation GST, 99 per cent issues have been addressed, rate or process," Sitharaman said.
The GST reform Process has been driven from the principle of trust, the Minister said.
"Business has to be trusted. Taxpayers have to be trusted. And businesses among themselves, with trust, if they do it, we shouldn't be too intrusive," she added.

A video showing a group of people marching on a road while waving Bangladesh’s national flags is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with claims that it shows illegal migrants raising Bangladeshi flags in Virar, Maharashtra. Some social media users have also linked the video to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, suggesting that the visuals highlight the need for the exercise. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows illegal migrants raising Bangladeshi flags in Virar, Maharashtra.
Fact: The viral video does not show illegal migrants raising Bangladeshi flags in Virar, Maharashtra. It shows participants carrying Bangladeshi flags during a Hero bike advertisement shoot in Virar on 03 October 2026. Prakash Kawale, Senior Police Inspector at Bolinj Police Station, confirmed to Factly that the video was from the shoot. Dinesh Jaiswal, owner of DJ Location, the production house involved, also confirmed this, adding that the shoot was cancelled after a ruckus and that all the participants were Indian. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
Upon closely reviewing the viral video, we noticed several details that raised questions about its authenticity. A mounted camera is visible at the beginning of the video and again around the 12-second mark. A cloth diffuser, typically used to control lighting during a shoot, is also visible. These details indicate that the footage was recorded during a shoot.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple media reports (here, here, and here) featuring similar visuals. According to these reports, a Bangladeshi flag was used during a commercial advertisement shoot in Virar, a suburb in Maharashtra’s Palghar district, which triggered protests from local groups. The reports noted that some locals complained to the police and later burned the Bangladeshi flags used by the production crew. One of the reports also captured the aftermath, showing several youths attempting to burn a Bangladeshi flag.
We contacted Mr Prakash Kawale, Senior Police Inspector at Bolinj Police Station in Virar, regarding the viral video. Speaking to Factly, he confirmed that the video was recorded during an advertisement shoot. According to him, “This was an ad shoot by a Hero Bike company on 03 October 2026.”
We also learnt from the inspector that the shoot was carried out by DJ Location. We also contacted Dinesh Jaiswal, the owner of the production house, who confirmed that the video was recorded during an advertisement shoot for a Hero bike. He said the shoot was cancelled after a ruckus broke out, following which the concept was dropped. He added that all the people involved in the shoot were Indian and clarified that the video was from an advertisement shoot, not a real incident involving illegal migrants.
To sum up, this viral video does not show illegal migrants raising Bangladeshi flags in Virar, Maharashtra; it is from an advertisement shoot.

GPT-6 is coming to all tiers of ChatGPT
It will come with a capability called Intelligent UI.
OpenAI is rolling out GPT-6 to ChatGPT, and it will come with a capability called Intelligent UI that the company says allows it to return responses quickly with fully interactive user interfaces. The company trained GPT-6 to be better at everyday conversations and to compose more visual responses within the chatbot itself. Based on what you're asking, it could include graphics, tappable buttons, forms, charts and other interactive experiences in its replies.
If you ask it to help you plan for a dinner you're hosting, for instance, ChatGPT's response could include an interactive table with the amount of ingredients you have to buy based on the number of people you say are coming. It could also include checklists and follow-up forms you can answer to get more detailed help. But if pure text makes more sense, the model can decide not add any visuals. To shorten wait times for complex tasks, OpenAI gave the model the capability to answer while it's still thinking unlike other reasoning models that decide its output first. The company trained the model to compose responses across multiple messages, with each one adding useful information so that the final output is cohesive.
OpenAI says the interactive responses could help you understand complex topics more easily with visual aids. And, you can use the feature to create specialized tools for your needs, such as a calculator to help you decide on investments or on how to split a bill. Plus, you can also use it to recreate retro games within ChatGPT, like Snake. "Instead of fitting every question into the same conversational format, ChatGPT can combine UI, data, and actions to create entirely new ways for people to explore, understand, and interact with information," the company explained.
GPT‑6 with Intelligent UI has already started rolling out to all ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise users around the world. It's powered by GPT-6 Sol if you're paying for those subscription tiers. If you have a Free or a low-cost Go account, you'll get access to the new model sometime today. It will be powered by GPT‑6 Luna, which isn't as capable as Sol, in those tiers.

Calm in real life but demons on court - Medvedev runs out of chances
- Published
Daniil Medvedev once said you would need to knock on his hotel door at 6am for seven days in a row to make him angry.
On court, though, he is a far more combustible character who finally ran out of chances when he was disqualified from Monday's China Open semi-final against Novak Djokovic.
Djokovic was serving for a place in the final when the ball ricocheted off the back of the court. Medvedev swiped it into the stands, where it hit a spectator in the face.
A few minutes later the Russian was defaulted, as he had to be, under rules that bar a player from "hitting a ball dangerously or recklessly, or with negligent disregard of the consequences."
Players have got away with worse. There is sometimes anger in their actions, but it is rarely of the bulging-neck-vein variety.
It is more often a sign of irritation and petulance, with frustrations taken out on the ball with little care for the safety of officials, ball kids and the spectators who line the court.
"I can only say I'm a really calm person in life - I actually have no idea why the demons go out when I play tennis," Medvedev said at the 2019 US Open, where he was fined for snatching a towel from a ball person and making an offensive gesture to fans inside the Arthur Ashe Stadium.
"Especially when I was a junior, I had a lot of problems with my attitude.
"I was not getting defaulted, but to have a game penalty was easy."
Returning to the theme at that year's end-of-season ATP Finals, Medvedev said any bad blood soon disappears after leaving the court.
"All my temper goes away after I leave the tennis court. If I'm not happy with my practice, I step out of the court and five minutes later, I'm OK," he said.
It is hard - and probably unwise - to take your eyes off Medvedev's matches, and he is very popular with the media for his engaging, reflective and humorous interviews once the dust has settled.
But he has gone too far on court on many occasions, with much of his aggression directed at umpires.
At Wimbledon in 2017, a 21-year-old Medvedev was so incensed about some of the decisions made by umpire Mariana Alves in his second-round match that he sprinkled coins at her feet as she climbed down from the chair.
He later apologised and denied he was accusing her of bias.
Two years ago, again at Wimbledon, it appeared officials were considering defaulting Medvedev for an outburst towards umpire Eva Asderaki-Moore.
Medvedev claimed he said something in Russian which was "not pleasant, but not over the line" - and, after a discussion between the umpire, supervisor and tournament referee, he escaped with a code violation for unsportsmanlike conduct.
He was fined more than £60,000 for his behaviour at the 2025 Australian Open, which included trying to destroy a net camera, and had an infamous meltdown later that year at the US Open.
On a rowdy New York night, Benjamin Bonzi had match point for a straight-set win against Medvedev in the first round when a photographer inexplicably walked on to court between his first and second serves.
Umpire Greg Allensworth awarded the Frenchman another first serve because of the delay, sparking fury from Medvedev.
Medvedev accused Allensworth of hoping to engineer a quick finish - as he gets paid by the match, rather than the hour - and there was a pause of over five minutes as he whipped up the crowd.
He did save the match point, but went on to lose in five sets before obliterating his racquet by smashing it repeatedly against the table next to his chair.
Medvedev will lose all the prize money and ranking points he earned from his run to the semi-finals in Beijing. He remains in the eighth and final qualifying spot for November's ATP Finals, but the loss of 200 points could yet prove crucial.
The 30-year-old has apologised for his actions and said he hopes to say sorry to the spectator in person.
In New York a month ago, Medvedev reflected on the role of genetics when explaining how his eldest daughter has "my personality on the court".
"She plays a bit. She enjoys it. Maybe it's a bit of a genetic somewhere there," Medvedev added.
"I took her to practice once. She's happy, so she throws the racquet through the whole court.
"The coach looks at me and says: 'I don't know where she got this from...'
"All the people that talk about that I should control myself more - she's three years old. It's not like we taught her to do the things she's doing on the court."

Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is among the most widespread of human viruses. More than 90% of adults are estimated to have been infected during their lifetime. Most people acquire the infection during childhood without developing symptoms. In some, particularly those infected during adolescence or adulthood, it can cause infectious mononucleosis. The virus then remains in the body for life.
A new analysis by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), the cancer agency of the World Health Organization (WHO), estimates that about 2.3 million new cancer cases worldwide in 2024 were attributable to infections. The analysis incorporates recent evidence linking EBV with gastric cancer and places EBV among the infectious agents responsible for a substantial cancer burden worldwide.
What is Epstein-Barr virus?
EBV, also known as human herpesvirus 4, belongs to the herpesvirus family. It spreads mainly through saliva, including through kissing or sharing drinks, food, eating utensils and toothbrushes.
According to WHO, many people infected with EBV have no symptoms. When illness occurs, symptoms can include fever, sore throat, swollen lymph nodes and marked fatigue. Infectious mononucleosis generally improves within a few weeks, although fatigue can last longer.
After the initial infection, EBV remains in the body in a dormant state. In most healthy people, the immune system keeps the infection under control.
EBV is classified by IARC as a Group 1 carcinogen. It has established causal links with several cancers, including nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Burkitt lymphoma and Hodgkin lymphoma. The latest IARC analysis also incorporates evidence linking EBV with gastric cancer.
Who is at risk?
Most people infected with EBV do not develop cancer. The infection is therefore not, by itself, an indication that a person will develop cancer.
People with weakened immune systems are at greater risk of serious EBV-related disease. This includes some people who have undergone organ or stem-cell transplantation and those receiving treatments that suppress the immune system.
The cancers associated with EBV also vary geographically. Nasopharyngeal cancer, for instance, is particularly prevalent in parts of eastern and southeastern Asia. The development of EBV-associated cancer is thought to involve factors beyond the infection itself.
How is it diagnosed?
A person does not normally need to be tested simply because EBV is common.
When infectious mononucleosis is suspected, doctors may make a diagnosis based on the symptoms and clinical examination. Blood tests can provide supporting evidence. These include tests for heterophile antibodies and EBV-specific antibodies, which can help determine whether an infection is recent or occurred in the past.
In suspected EBV-related cancers or serious disease in people with compromised immunity, more specialised tests may be needed. These can include testing for EBV genetic material in blood or other samples and examination of tumour tissue for the presence of the virus.
A positive EBV antibody test does not mean that a person has cancer. Since infection is so common, evidence of past infection is expected in most adults.
What are the treatment options?
There is no treatment that removes latent EBV from the body and there is currently no vaccine against the virus.
According to WHO, treatment for uncomplicated infectious mononucleosis is mainly supportive. Rest, adequate fluids and medicines to control fever and pain may be advised. Antibiotics do not treat EBV because it is a virus.
People with mononucleosis may also be advised to avoid strenuous activity and contact sports for a period, particularly if the spleen is enlarged, because of the risk of splenic injury.
When EBV is associated with cancer, treatment depends on the type and stage of cancer and may include chemotherapy, radiotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted treatment or a combination of these.
Can EBV be prevented?
There is currently no vaccine against EBV. Preventing transmission can also be difficult because infected people may spread the virus without knowing that they have it.
WHO advises avoiding the sharing of drinks, utensils, toothbrushes and other items that come into contact with saliva.
The development of an EBV vaccine is an important area of research. The latest IARC analysis adds to the evidence on the virus’s contribution to cancer and highlights the need for continued research into prevention.

What are emotions, really? And why do we have them?
Simply put, emotions are intangible responses to what we see happening around us. They arise spontaneously, without conscious thought.
Emotions allowed early humans to efficiently dodge dangers as they explored the world around them. While the world and our lives in it are very different today than the way they were for our ancestors, our emotions haven’t changed.
Despite being so fundamental to our survival as a species, however, scientists are still piecing together how emotions arise in our brains. In a study recently published in Science, in fact, scientists have just reported mapping the brain-wide activity patterns that trigger emotions.
The team found that once an emotion was set off, it outlasted the trigger that sparked it in the first place. If this sounds familiar, it’s because this is what you feel when you accidentally stub your toe, burn your hand, and even when you enjoy your favourite flavour of ice cream.
In all these examples, there is incoming sensory information that prompts an emotional response while the good or bad feeling lasts even after the body part has been reflexively pulled back or after the ice cream is finished.
Stories hidden in blinks
In the new study, scientists led by Karl Deisseroth at Stanford University examined how emotions emerged in response to unpleasant (but not painful) sensory stimuli.
The participants were subjected to an eye puff assay: a machine called a tonometer blew light puffs of air into their left eye in specific sequences. Each puff lasted about 60 ms, the gap between puffs was 3-8 s long, and the entire session lasted 5 minutes. The scientists varied the gap between puffs so that participants didn’t reflexively tense up for the next puff they knew was coming.
Also read: Making the brain transparent
During the entire duration, a high-speed camera recorded the way participants closed their eyes and their behavioral and subjective responses.
As expected, repeated puffs of air to the eye elicited reflexive blinking as participants instinctively pulled back from the tonometer. They also kept the eye closed for certain durations or squinted or blinked rapidly during the gaps. As part of their subjective reports, the participants said this experience was “unpleasant” and “annoying”.
The scientists recruited a separate group of participants who were, at the time of the study, inpatients at the Stanford university hospital and had electrodes planted in their brains to check for epileptic seizures. Members of this group who consented to participate underwent the same eyepuff assay. The scientists found that these participants’ behavioural responses were consistent with those of the previous group. They also blinked reflexively and kept their eyes closed for (relatively) long periods.
The real story emerged in the brain activity patterns.
Enter: ketamine
Each puff causes a signal to be broadcast throughout the brain, like a “breaking news” alert, followed by a slower, more persistent signal. In this second phase, based on data from the electrodes in the brains of participants, scientists found that specific circuits in the brain were activated, which were linked to the generation of an emotional response in the individual.
To confirm this possibility, the scientists administered ketamine to some of these participants and had them redo the eye puff assay. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved ketamine’s use as an anaesthetic and at lower doses as an antidepressant. Ketamine also induces short-term dissociation: i.e. for a brief period, it alters subjective perceptions. By injecting it, the team could separate a person’s reflexive response from the emotional one.
The scientists found that being subjected to air puffs in the eye when a person was on ketamine changed neither the initial reflexive behaviour nor the initial burst of neural activity in the brain. However, it caused the subsequent slower brain response to dissipate much faster, so much so that the volunteers no longer described the experience as annoying but as a “tickling of the eyeball”.
Consistent with this ‘weaker’ subjective experience from ketamine, the participants’ behaviour also changed. They didn’t blink or close their eyes between consecutive air puffs. Instead, they held their eyes open even though they knew more puffs were in the offing.
Ketamine is known to block a sensor in the brain whose job it is to integrate signals coming from different corners. This means in the participants injected with ketamine, the brain may not have integrated the various signals into a coherent emotional response.
Of mice and men
Even though vertebrates have brains of vastly different sizes and complexity, the overall ‘brain plan’ is highly conserved. (The brain plan is akin to the building plan of a house or apartment.) To zero in on those systems responsible for emotions and which have survived evolution, Deisseroth’s team repeated their experiments with lab mice. The mice went through the eyepuff assay, had their brain activity measured with surgically planted electrodes, and had ketamine injected.
The team noticed the same patterns in mice as they had in humans. Injecting ketamine substantially changed the spiking activity in some neurons but not others. Only those neurons (or brain regions) coordinating the second phase — the slower response after the burst — were affected by ketamine. The initial burst didn’t change in any way, just as with the human participants.
The scientists could also study the neural activity following a puff in greater detail in the mouse model. They found that the fast/reflexive responses corresponded with a sharp rise in activity in some of the midbrain regions. This included the thalamus, where incoming sensory signals converge before being relayed onward, and the periaqueductal grey, which is involved in emotional behaviours.
They also found that the second phase of neural activity corresponded with activity in the brain’s emotional centres (described by the umbrella term ‘limbic regions’) and the frontal cortex. Again, as expected.
Then they dissected the brain activity patterns by stages, focusing on how quickly activity in brain regions shot up after the eyepuff and how long it took to fade away. They noticed that activity patterns in most of the pertinent regions increased at an explosive pace right after the eyepuff — but the rate of decrease was more interesting.
A pattern appears
The patterns in different regions slowed at different rates, fading first in the midbrain regions and last in the frontal cortex. The thalamus was active both in the first and the second phase. Considering the thalamus is the brain’s coordinating centre for all sensory signals, it makes sense that it would be active in the first phase. Incoming sensory signals go on to higher brain regions from the cortex. So it also served the role of handing off the baton, so to speak, and thus essayed a sort of bridging role across timescales.
The new study is the first to report this sort of differential pattern across different parts of the brain vis-à-vis emotions. At this point, it is not possible to say with any certainty what the implications are for the brain’s cortical and mid-brain areas.
With computational models of neuron firing activity in the mouse and the mouse’s behaviour following the eye puff assay, the team found that the timescale of neural activity was an important factor that shaped the emotional response.
Indeed, if the sensory signals dissipate before the brain has a chance to integrate the information, the person won’t be able to learn the lesson: “protect yourself from that obnoxious thing”. On the other hand, if brain activity is more strongly coupled to the fast and slow phases that Deisseroth & co. observed, such activity also lasts longer than normal, causing its own problems. Over-stabilised brain states have been correlated with depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder, all of which cause people to experience uninterrupted or mistimed thoughts and emotions.
Beyond the binary of health and disease, the fast and slow phases of brain activity highlighted in the study could reveal the fundamentals of information processing in the brain. People differ in how their brains process information about their environment — in turn a product of their genetic makeup and their upbringing in their formative years.
First steps
Why do we have emotions? For now it may be more gainful to flip the question: what would happen if we didn’t have them?
In the absence of an instinctive reaction that our emotions afford us, the brain’s response would be based entirely on risk-benefit analyses, which can be very time consuming. Over time we’d struggle to make decisions both big and small. What should I wear today? What should I make for dinner tonight? What should I study? Whom should I marry? Purely rational thought would turn such questions into never-ending decision-making exercises with no final answer.
The new study has revealed what happens in the brain in the first seconds when an emotion takes root. One hopes future studies will reveal the specific information encoded by this primal circuitry, how they encode different emotions, and how they evolve with time.
Dr. Reeteka Sud is a neuroscientist by training and senior scientist at the Center for Brain and Mind, Department of Psychiatry, NIMHANS, Bengaluru.

The Nobel prize in literature has been awarded to the Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson, the Swedish Academy has announced.
The academy cited the author’s “bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature”.
Born in 1950 in Toronto, Carson is known for work that moves freely between poetry, prose and translation, drawing heavily on the literature and mythology of the ancient Greek world.
Carson’s first book, Eros the Bittersweet, was published in 1986, and combined literary criticism with an exploration of desire and the ancient Greek tradition.
Her best-known work is Autobiography of Red, a 1998 novel in verse inspired by the fragments of the ancient Greek poet Stesichorus. It reimagines the myth of Geryon, the red-winged monster killed by Herakles, as the story of a modern teenage boy navigating heartbreak and desire.
In 2001, she became the first woman to win the TS Eliot prize for her collection The Beauty of the Husband. She has also been awarded Guggenheim and MacArthur fellowships.
Her work has attracted praise from fellow writers, including Susan Sontag, who once said: “She is one of the few writers writing in English that I would read anything she wrote. If there’s a magazine that has something of hers in it, I buy it automatically.”
Carson’s books have ranged widely in form. Men in the Off Hours combined verse essays, poems, epitaphs and prose about artists and historical figures, and won the inaugural Griffin poetry prize in 2001. Decreation, another eclectic work, brought together poetry, essays and an opera. Nox, published in 2010, is particularly characteristic of Carson’s avante-garde approach to literature – the book takes the form of an accordion-fold box containing a reproduction of a notebook Carson made after the death of her brother. Her later works include Red Doc> and Float.
The Nobel prize in literature has been awarded on 118 previous occasions since 1901. Recent laureates include Annie Ernaux, Bob Dylan, Abdulrazak Gurnah, Louise Glück, Peter Handke and Olga Tokarczuk. Last year’s recipient was the Hungarian author László Krasznahorkai, known for his dystopic and avant-garde writing.
Carson, 76, will formally receive the medal and diploma in a ceremony in Stockholm in December.

'I've lost my peace' - Cape Verde hero Vozinha on newfound fame
- Published
Cape Verde's heroic World Cup goalkeeper Vozinha says he craves the "peace and tranquillity" of the life he led before he shot to fame.
The 40-year-old shot to global prominence in June when he almost single-handedly kept Spain at bay as Cape Verde drew 0-0 with the European champions on their World Cup debut.
Vozinha's follower count on social media sky-rocketed over the course of the game, from about 50,000 to more than one million.
But his fame shot up even further when Argentina needed extra time to beat Cape Verde in the round of 32.
Vozinha says his life was easier before his World Cup heroics.
"I've lost my peace and tranquillity," he told the Observer., external
"I no longer have any privacy, or at least much less than I used to.
"Now I go out, I go to a restaurant, and there's always someone who wants to take a photo with me or asks me for an autograph. Or, worse, someone is filming me.
"That's what has changed most in my life, and I don't think there's anything I can do about it."
Vozinha's mother became part of the fairytale too. After he revealed that she had could not afford a visa to watch his World Cup debut, US House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries announced that the visa fee had been waived.
Now Vozinha has revealed that his mother is visited on a daily basis by fans wanting to talk or to take photographs with him.
"A lot of people want to be famous and have a public profile, but they only see the positive side of that reality," said Vozinha.
"To be honest, if I were offered the life I have today or the life I had before, I'd choose the one I had before."
His World Cup performances for Cape Verde, a West African island nation with a population of 525,000, earned Vozinha a nomination for men's goalkeeper of the year at the Ballon d'Or awards.
"It's nice to feel like a kind of ambassador, but I want to make it clear that what we achieved was a collective effort," Vozinha said.
"We made history and the best news would be if we could harness that momentum to develop our country and improve the living conditions of our people."
