The European Union is bracing for a confrontation with China as a trade deficit exceeding $1 billion a day heightens anxiety over potential job losses and pushes the bloc’s political leaders to take a more aggressive approach toward its second-largest trading partner.
The European Commission’s top trade envoy, Maroš Šefčovič, will be in Beijing Thursday for a two-day meeting with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao. The goal is narrowing the EU’s 360 billion euro ($410 billion) trade deficit with China. Earlier this year, he gave Beijing a deadline of October to provide meaningful results in doing so.
Politicians and economists across the 27-nation bloc consider China’s massive subsidies and exports a major threat to core industrial sectors from steel foundries to car factories. China diverted many of its exports to the EU and other markets after the U.S. raised tariffs.
In a debate Tuesday in European Parliament in Strasbourg, lawmakers overwhelmingly expressed anxiety alongside defiance over trade with China. On Wednesday, they voted 454 to 86 on a resolution to toughen up on China that centered on a call for “economic reciprocity and a proportionate EU response if China does not open its markets.”
Ahead of the vote, Hilde Vautmans, the Belgian lawmaker who led the resolution, said that “Europe has economic power, it’s time we used it.”
EU options range from tariffs to a “trade bazooka”
Despite the seeming European unity this week, it remains unclear what the EU can or is willing to do. It has already rolled out trade measures against Chinese steel imports and e-commerce small parcels.
France’s High Commission for Strategy and Planning in February called for swift action, like 30% tariffs on many of China’s exports, and a devaluation of the euro against the Chinese currency. Sales of German autos are plummeting in China, but China is also poised to gobble up market share in Europe by undercutting European automakers on price thanks to heavy state subsidies. There have already been mass layoffs at major manufacturers like Volkswagen.
A letter by France and Germany, a copy of which was seen by The Associated Press, called for a sweeping rethink of the EU’s China policy. Among other actions, it proposed making it easier for the European Commission to use the bloc’s so-called “trade bazooka,” the Anti-Coercion Instrument. This is a never-used-before raft of measures for blocking or restricting trade and investment from countries found to be putting undue pressure on EU member nations or corporations.
Yet not all EU nations agree on such tough measures. Spain, the eurozone’s fourth-largest economy, has been less adversarial toward China in recent years. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has visited Beijing four times in three years.
The European Policy Centre in Brussels said in June that European battery producers, solar panels, steel, electric vehicles, chemicals and machinery are already hemorrhaging jobs and capacity and called for a trade investigative body modelled on Section 301 of the U.S. Trade Act.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the phenomenon another “ China shock ” for Europe, similar to what happened in the U.S. in the early 2000s when hundreds of thousands of factory jobs in the American heartland were wiped out.
The EU’s ailing economy requires both a domestic overhaul and a more aggressive foreign trade policy, especially with China, said Tim Rühlig, a China analyst at the European Union Institute for Security Studies, the bloc’s internal think tank.
Rühlig also said that European businesses and political leadership bear some blame.
“It’s clear that just protecting yourself from China is not the future,” Rühlig said. “But to have a chance of making yourself ready for future technologies and to remain competitive in the coming 15-20 years, you have to protect yourself.”
It is impossible to disengage completely with China as the EU did with Russia following its invasion of Ukraine, Rühlig said, but there is robust momentum now to reset trade relations with Beijing.
“Where do we make ourselves independent or at least more diverse? And where do we still work with the Chinese?” Rühlig asked.
China is ready for a long trade dispute
This week in Beijing, when asked about the letter penned by France and Germany, a spokesperson at China’s Ministry of Commerce said that the countries should refrain from encouraging the EU to resort to protectionist measures.
“Protectionism cannot enhance competitiveness, and decoupling or cutting off supply chains will only harm others without benefiting oneself,” the commerce ministry said in a statement.
China is the EU’s second-largest goods trading partner after the U.S., according to European Commission data. Chinese exports to the EU rose 15.3% in the first eight months of this year, according to China’s customs agency, while its imports from the EU rose 6.2%.
“The EU does not have the capacity to wage a trade war against China,” read an editorial last month in China’s state-run Global Times newspaper. “If it is truly determined to do so, then let it try.”
China’s exports to Europe, as well as Southeast Asia, Latin America and Africa, expanded after U.S. tariffs went into effect last year, but it still booked a $1.2 trillion trade surplus globally in 2025. So far, China’s export machine has remained remarkably resilient despite U.S. tariffs and other trade restrictions, said Max Zenglein, Asia Pacific senior economist at The Conference Board.
This past weekend, ahead of the meeting between Šefčovič and Wang, China launched an anti-dumping probe on EU exports of p-nitrotoluene, which is used in dyes and pharmaceuticals. The probe was initiated after Beijing warned last month that it would take retaliatory actions if the EU instituted tougher protectionist trade measures.
“China has been battle-tested by successive rounds of external pressure and, so far, has largely stared down attempts to force a change in course,” said Zenglein.
China’s economy has been largely driven by exports as domestic demand remains sluggish. The EU imports sizable amounts of Chinese lithium-ion batteries and hybrid electric vehicles, and Chinese carmakers are also expanding production capacity in Europe.
While China’s trade surplus has intensified concerns among its major trading partners, trade ties between the U.S. and China appear relatively stable following a summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump in Washington, wrote Bank of America economists, turning the attention to China-EU relations.
When it comes to negotiations with the EU, Chinese investment in Europe is likely to be among Beijing’s bargaining chips, Zenglein added, particularly as EU member states compete to attract capital, jobs, and new manufacturing projects.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

Our skin, hair and nails require adequate protein, energy, vitamins and minerals for growth, repair and normal functioning. When deficiencies are significant or prolonged, some may become visible. But many of these signs also overlap with hormonal disorders, chronic illnesses, dermatological conditions, stress, poor sleep and other factors. So when and how do you know if there is a nutritional deficit?
What the signs can indicate
Iron deficiency, particularly when it progresses to anaemia, can cause pallor of the skin and mucous membranes, and may be associated with diffuse hair shedding. Spoon-shaped nails can also occur with iron deficiency. Vitamin B12 deficiency may cause hyperpigmentation, particularly over the knuckles, as well as changes in the tongue and oral mucosa.
Zinc deficiency can affect skin integrity and hair growth, while inadequate protein intake can affect hair structure and growth and, in severe cases, cause marked changes in the skin and hair. Vitamin C deficiency can result in bleeding gums and poor wound healing. Dry or scaly skin may be associated with inadequate vitamin A, essential fatty acids or zinc.
Cracks at the corners of the mouth can occur with iron, vitamin B12, zinc or riboflavin deficiency. A smooth, red and sore tongue, or glossitis, can be associated with deficiencies of vitamin B12, iron, folate or niacin.
Ramya Subburaj, senior clinical dietitian and head of the department of dietetics, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, Vanagaram, Chennai, said these signs should be viewed as clues rather than proof of a deficiency. “There is considerable overlap between nutritional and non-nutritional causes,” she said, noting that a person with hair loss should not assume that poor nutrition is necessarily responsible.
What ‘ferritin face’ really means
Terms such as ‘iron-deficiency face’ and ‘ferritin face’ circulating on social media are not recognised medical diagnoses. Iron deficiency can cause anaemia and pallor, but there is no specific facial appearance through which low ferritin can be diagnosed.
Ferritin is a protein that stores iron and its level is used to assess the body’s iron stores. Low ferritin can occur before iron-deficiency anaemia develops. However, it does not produce a distinct facial appearance.
Pushpa Gnanaraj, senior consultant, dermatology, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, said pallor associated with anaemia may be visible in the skin, lips, gums or inner eyelids because of reduced haemoglobin. But dullness, dark circles or changes in facial appearance are not specific to low iron stores.
Vinitha Krishnan, chief clinical dietitian, nutrition and dietetics, SIMS Hospital, Chennai, said any changes associated with depleted iron stores are generally subtle and non-specific. Similar features can occur with inadequate sleep, stress, dehydration, allergies, ageing, thyroid disorders or other nutritional deficiencies.
A proper history and clinical examination are therefore important. Depending on the symptoms, investigations may include a complete blood count, ferritin and iron studies, vitamin B12 and vitamin D. Thyroid testing, zinc assessment or other investigations may be considered when clinically indicated. Dermatological conditions such as eczema, psoriasis, fungal infections, autoimmune disorders and pigmentary diseases may also need to be ruled out.
Correcting deficiencies
When a confirmed nutritional deficiency is responsible for a symptom, correcting it can lead to improvement. The timeline, however, depends on the nutrient involved and the severity and duration of the deficiency.
Pallor and some symptoms associated with iron deficiency may begin to improve within weeks of appropriate treatment, while mouth ulcers and glossitis can also improve after the underlying deficiency is corrected. Hair shedding and thinning generally take longer to recover because hair grows slowly; improvement may take several months. Nail changes can similarly take months to grow out.
Reshma Aleem, senior clinical dietician, Rela Hospital, Chennai, said the extent and speed of recovery depend on whether the deficiency is mild, moderate or severe and on how effectively it is corrected.
Fixing the basics
A varied diet remains the foundation. Adequate protein, pulses, whole grains, vegetables, fruits, nuts and seeds, along with eggs, dairy, fish, lean meat or fortified foods according to dietary preference, can provide a range of nutrients.
Experts caution against taking supplements based only on a social-media checklist. Excessive intake of some vitamins and minerals can itself cause adverse effects and may interfere with the absorption or metabolism of other nutrients. More importantly, treating an assumed deficiency can delay the diagnosis of the actual cause.
The appropriate approach is to investigate persistent changes, confirm a deficiency where indicated and then correct it with dietary measures or supplementation under clinical guidance.

Generic drugmaker Granules India has filed a Paragraph IV certification with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (U.S. FDA) in connection with its abbreviated new drug application (ANDA) for Ruxolitinib Extended-Release Tablets.
Based on the timing and status of its ANDA and Paragraph IV certification, and subject to the U.S. FDA’s review and determination, Granules said it believes it is eligible for first-to-file status for Ruxolitinib Extended-Release Tablets.
If confirmed by the FDA and subject to all applicable statutory and regulatory requirements, first-to-file status could make Granules eligible for 180 days of generic drug exclusivity under U.S. law, the company said on Wednesday (September 7, 2026).
The Paragraph IV certification sought is with respect to applicable patents listed in the U.S. FDA’s Orange Book. Granules said it has also issued the requisite notice to the relevant parties in accordance with U.S. regulatory requirements.
“First-to-file opportunities are an important part of our strategy to build a more differentiated and higher-value product portfolio in the U.S. This filing reflects our focus on identifying technically and commercially attractive opportunities where our development and manufacturing capabilities can create sustainable value,” Granules CMD Krishna Prasad Chigurupati said.
Ruxolitinib, a JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor, was approved by the U.S. FDA in 2011 and is used to treat certain cancers and related conditions. In the U.S., the drug is developed and marketed by Incyte Corporation under the brand name Jakafi. Jakafi and Jakafi XR are trademarks of Incyte.
In May, Nasdaq-listed Incyte announced that the U.S. FDA had approved Jakafi XR, the extended-release formulation of ruxolitinib.
The drug is marketed by Incyte in the U.S. and by Novartis outside the country under the brand name Jakavi.

Tottenham Sky Sports special podcast: Tim Sherwood and Michael Bridge assess Spurs' problems after winless start
In a special Sky Sports Spurs podcast, Tim Sherwood and Sky Sports News' Tottenham reporter Michael Bridge assess the club's winless start to the Premier League season, which has left them bottom; watch Man Utd vs Spurs on Saturday, live on Sky Sports; kick-off 5.30pm
Thursday 8 October 2026 11:21, UK
When Aston Villa went 1-0 up in north London, it felt inevitable that Tottenham would head into the international break winless in the Premier League.
That's because it has been nearly two years since Spurs have won a match after conceding the opening goal in any competition. Last month's 3-2 home loss to Villa was the 47th game in this dismal run (D11 L36).
"It is a worry, certainly at home because that's where you need the minerals," former Tottenham boss Tim Sherwood told a special Sky Sports Spurs podcast.

"That's where you need the characters and leaders to come forward, and at the moment, they're void of any leaders and characters.
"I'm not sure there's anyone really losing their head or galvanising the players to try and arrest [it], which is a poor trend, in not fighting back from losing positions.
"The manager is. He certainly looks like he doesn't lack in any passion. But you need that within the pitch and within the dressing room and within the training pitch every single day, and I'm not sure the characters are there."
With Spurs accumulating the fewest points (18) among ever-present Premier League sides in 2026, Sky Sports News' Tottenham reporter Michael Bridge aired his concerns over leadership too.
He said: "When Roberto De Zerbi chose his five captains [Micky van de Ven, Pedro Porro, Ben Davies, James Maddison and Archie Gray], and I asked him in the press conference, Andy Robertson wasn't one of the five.
"Archie Gray was, but Archie Gray's not going to be in the team much, so I am a little bit worried about leadership in that camp.
"How many of the players are really going to grab each other by the scruff of the neck?
"Cristian Romero maybe went too far in terms of aggression, but there were times when you did want him on your side, so I need to see a bit more aggression from some of these players as well."
Sherwood unimpressed by new signings
A winless start to the Premier League season has left Tottenham bottom of the table, and their worst start to a Premier League season after five games has already raised questions over Spurs' lavish summer spending.
So, have any of the 10 new players that cost over £330m impressed Sherwood?
"No, no one," he insisted. "I can't say anyone's really impressed me, and anyone would have done a better job than anyone who was there last season.
"They've underachieved, they really have. We always judge on results, so I don't look at any individual player and think, 'Well, you're coming out of some credit here', because the team's losing, and I'm not sure there's been any outstanding performers."
The lack of success from Spurs' signings before this summer worries Sherwood about the latest recruits.
"Probably the last four or five years, the track record of Tottenham signings has not been fantastic," he said.
"It's been a very long time since they've made a decent signing. Now, I'm not saying they're poor signings; I'm saying that they haven't done it yet, and there's still a lot of time to be able to get some confidence and show what they can really do.
"We've seen them in fits and starts and little cameos for other teams, but it's a different kettle of fish playing for Tottenham."
He added: "I've seen more nos than yeses at the moment over the last five years in the transfer market.
"I think the best signing they've made in recent history would have to be (Heung-Min) Son - and we're going way back there! We're talking about a real success.
"Maybe (Dejan) Kulusevski, but then he's picked up the injury. But other than that, I can't say there have been too many outstanding successes in the transfer market.
"But it's up to Roberto De Zerbi to develop them players, and hopefully some of these players we've seen in recent years can be unrecognisable."
'Spurs still need a striker'
With Spurs having scored just two league goals, the spotlight for Bridge is on Omar Marmoush to deliver.
The summer signing from Man City is yet to score in his first five Spurs appearances in all competitions, having missed one big chance and had two shots on target from his 10 attempts.
Bridge said: "I think the one for me is Omar Marmoush. How good is this guy?
"I really liked glimpses of him for City, but they were only glimpses; clearly a very talented player. He really showed it in the Bundesliga [with Eintracht Frankfurt].
"But can he do it consistently for Tottenham Hotspur, where he's going to be given a clear run of games.
"Were Tottenham right to spend as they did on Savio and Marmoush? So the jury's going to be out with these players."
With Dominic Solanke struggling for form and Richarlison frozen out against the backdrop of Spurs academy graduate Will Lankshear scoring freely in the Championship, Spurs' firepower is a problem.
Bridge said: "I think they need a striker - an actual number nine - but how many are there out there?
"It doesn't help that Will Lankshear is scoring every week for Middlesbrough because he looks like a proper old-fashioned centre-forward and he's young and English. That's my worry.
"I'm also not one hundred per cent sure if Antonin Kinsky is a Tottenham number one for years to come.
"If you've spent that amount of money and you still need, for me, a goalkeeper and a number nine, then there's still a way to go."
Is De Zerbi under pressure?
Tottenham aim for their first league win of the season at Manchester United on Saturday, live on Sky Sports.
But should their winless run continue, then Roberto De Zerbi would become just the second Spurs boss in Premier League history to fail to win any of the opening six games of a campaign.
Juande Ramos was the first, and he was sacked after Spurs had two points from eight games. But both Sherwood and Bridge are confident that De Zerbi will not follow the same fate as the Spaniard.
Ex-Spurs boss Sherwood said: "I'm not sure he's under pressure because they've given him everything he wanted, so they must have full trust in him.
"He's proven that he's a very good Premier League manager, albeit he's never been at a club the size of Tottenham Hotspur, with the scrutiny which is upon the club, but he looks like a character who can handle that scrutiny, and he just needs a win."
Bridge said: "I don't think Roberto De Zerbi is under much pressure at all.
"He was tracked by the club for some time. He's on a very good and long contract, and unless he's the one that initiates the departure, I don't see any change for the foreseeable."
But what has to change is Spurs' bouncebackability in games if De Zerbi is to ensure the pressure does not mount.

The Trump administration is facing growing questions over its decision to abandon a fraud and bribery case against the Indian billionaire Gautam Adani after he promised to invest $10bn in the US.
For the second time this year, two Democratic senators have demanded attorney general Todd Blanche answer questions about the US Department of Justice department’s handling of the case – and raised concerns over its judgment under Donald Trump.
In August, a federal judge in New York agreed to drop the fraud case against Adani, one of the richest people in the world, at the request of prosecutors, despite having concerns about “irregularities” in the “highly unusual” decision. It has become the latest example of judges raising eyebrows at Trump administration prosecutors for pushing to dismiss criminal cases.
Now, more than a month later, senators Elizabeth Warren and Richard Blumenthal are asking Blanche to clarify whether people close to Donald Trump were involved in that decision.
It comes aftera New York Times report revealed that Adani, represented by one of Trump’s personal lawyers, admitted to offering a $10bn investment in the US to resolve the criminal case. The federal judge overseeing the case determined the investment played no role in the DoJ’s decision to abandon the case.
“These fresh details continue to raise concerns about the judgment of the DoJ, and the extent to which the DoJ is willing and able to prosecute white-collar criminals under President Trump,” Warren and Blumenthal wrote in a letter sent on Wednesday, and seen by the Guardian.
Adani was indicted in 2024 in New York for allegedly participating in a bribery and fraud scheme in which he paid Indian officials to secure a contract for one of his companies. He denied the allegations.
Prosecutors suddenly moved to dismiss the case against Adani in May after he hired a new legal team, led by Robert Giuffra Jr, and offered to invest $10bn into the US.
Following the news, Warren and Blumenthal sent a letter to Blanche in June requesting information about the fraud case and raising concerns about whether the justice department dismissed the case in exchange for Adani’s investment.
However, the senators did not receive a response. Since then, new details about the case have emerged, including allegations that Boris Epshteyn, a member of Trump’s personal legal team who also served as an informal adviser, helped Adani.
Another report claimed Donald Trump Jr, the president’s son, met with Adani in November 2025, before the case was dropped. A spokesperson for Trump Jr said earlier this year that the conversation “had zero to do with DoJ’s actions in this case”.
A spokesperson for Epshteyn denied being involved in Adani’s “arguments, advocacy or efforts” to the Wall Street Journal in June. Epshteyn was never hired by Adani or his company, the Adani Group, nor did he maintain a relationship with Adani, the spokesperson added.
The Guardian has asked Epshteyn for comment.
The Democratic lawmakers are now asking the DoJ for more information about Adani’s alleged investment offer, including a list of employees who were present when the offer was made, the terms of the offer, when the offer was made and where.
They also want to know whether the DoJ employees knew Epshteyn was allegedly working on behalf of Adani, or if Epshteyn had any contact with DoJ employees regarding Adani, among other questions.
“We are also concerned about the involvement of two of President Trump’s personal lawyers in this case, and the extent to which they reveal potential political influence and special treatment for well-connected insiders at the DoJ,” Warren and Blumenthal wrote in their letter.
The Democrats also want to know if Trump Jr, or any person working on behalf of Trump Jr., had contact with a DoJ employee regarding Adani.
Warren and Blumenthal requested responses no later than 5 October. The Guardian has asked Blanche’s office for comment.

How NATO is prepping in the Baltic skies for a possible confrontation with Russia
While jets patrol overhead, Canada is tasked with holding the ground below
When Latvians cast their ballots in a national election this past weekend, many did so without realizing that three countries — Turkey, Spain and Italy — all had fighter jets patrolling the grey skies high above them for any overt Russian attempts to disrupt the vote.
"Nothing flies without authorization in the alliance airspace," said Capt. Antonio Moncebo, a Spanish F-18 pilot whose squadron was operating out of a base in Estonia next door.
So when NATO identifies a possible threat, "we trigger a scramble, and we seek them and shoot them down."
Spanish fighter pilot Antonio Moncebo spoke to CBC News at a NATO airbase in Lithuania. (Jason Ho/CBC)
NATO’s high-altitude vigilance with its "sky shield" is no longer just a routine drill.
While many NATO military planners believe Russia is unlikely to deliberately start a war with the Western alliance, if Russian President Vladimir Putin decides he wants to test NATO’s resolve with a lower-threshold provocation, the Baltic states could be vulnerable.
From suspected Russian arson attacks at high-tech defence facilities in Estonia to a foiled cargo plane bombing plot in Germany, Putin's intelligence services are increasingly pushing past traditional red lines in an effort to weaken Western resolve to aid Ukraine.
NATO jets from Italy, Spain and Turkey fly in a tight formation above Latvia, as part of a demonstration by the alliance's air command. (Adrian Di Virgilio/CBC News)
Justin Bronk, with the British military think-tank RUSI, says Putin may believe there's an opportunity to exploit U.S President Donald Trump’s often antagonistic relationship with Europe.
"Clearly at the moment, there's a lot of concern about the potential for Russian direct aggression against NATO members in order to presumably try … to demonstrate that the alliance won't come to the military aid of one of its member states," said Bronk.
Members of the media, including a CBC videographer, perch at the edge of the ramp in the back of a Lithuanian military aircraft to photograph NATO jets in the sky. The photographers were tethered with harnesses so they wouldn't fall out. (CBC)
Whether NATO is prepared to counter potential Russian aggression is an existential question.
Lieut.-Gen. Guillaume Thomas, who commands the air operations over the Baltic states, dismisses any talk that a Trump-led U.S. can’t be relied upon.
"I am completely confident in the support of U.S. forces in protecting the alliance. I have no doubt every day I can see the development of the U.S. force and I have no doubt about their support, their continuous support."
To prove its readiness, NATO, which is anchored by the principle of collective defence, recently invited a small group of media, including CBC News, to witness the air shield over the Baltic states first-hand.
High above Lithuania, aircrew lowered the back ramp of a military transport plane in mid-flight, allowing journalists a dizzying, close-up view of Italian Eurofighters, Spanish F-18s and Turkish fighter jets flying wing to wing.
Thomas says such tight formations are a visual manifestation of a deeper, more profound shift in how the alliance secures its eastern flank.
Spanish and Italian fighter jets fly in a tight formation next to a Lithuanian military plane carrying members of the media. (Adrian Di Virgilio/CBC)
"It was a shift in mindset to go from an air policing mission to an air defence mission," he said. "That enabled us to be more reactive, more flexible, more agile, to demonstrate our ability to protect our air spaces."
Building a 'drone wall'
But NATO’s air shield remains a work in progress.
Russia’s successful and repeated use of highly destructive jet-powered drones in Ukraine has forced Baltic nations to rapidly rethink their own domestic defences.
Latvia is now actively constructing what it calls a "drone wall" along its heavily forested eastern border.
"It consists of integrated radar, interceptors and command-and-control systems so that we're able to detect and intercept, if needed, a hostile drone," explained Airis Rikveilis, state secretary for the Latvian Ministry of Defence.
Police officers stand at the site of a Russian drone strike on the North Bridge in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 4. (Reuters)
NATO planners admit that building a flawless shield is mathematically impossible.
While heavy fighter jets can intercept larger threats, they represent a severe cost mismatch when deployed against tiny, low-flying surveillance drones.
On the tarmac in Lithuania, crews flew a new Latvian-designed anti-drone system called Blaze. It features a propeller-driven interceptor equipped with cameras and a high explosive warhead that can be used to crash into Russian drones as far as 10 kilometres away.
But Blaze is only just being introduced and its use at the moment isn't widespread.
Rikveilis, the Latvian defence official, acknowledges more work is needed to complete preparations but denies drone defence is a NATO weak spot.
The threat of Russian drones "is a new one, it's an evolving one, but at the same time it is being taken care of."
The Canadian connection
Holding the vulnerable ground underneath any of NATO's defensive gaps falls squarely on Canada.
Over the last decade, Ottawa’s commitment to the region has quietly scaled up from a localized battle group to full brigade leadership, placing up to 3,000 Canadian troops right on Russia’s doorstep.
As commander of Task Force Latvia (TFL), Canadian Brig.-Gen. Mason Stalker oversees Canada's military presence in the Baltic region. He is also deputy commander of Multinational Division-North (MND-N). (Adrian Di Virgilio/CBC)
For the newly appointed Canadian commander in this theatre, the immediate focus is keeping the multi-nation force integrated and lethal.
"My concern always is making sure that we have the combat power necessary to basically make sure our NATO commitments are adhered to," says Canadian Brig.-Gen. Mason Stalker.
"And we do. We can surge as required."
While military commanders and fighter pilots project absolute confidence in the skies, the reality for Latvians on the ground is more complex.
With its towering stone column, the historic Freedom Monument in Latvia's capital, Riga, is a reminder of a nation that fought hard to break free from foreign rule.
A large poster depicting Russian President Vladimir Putin with a skeletal, skull-like jaw is displayed across the road from the Russian Embassy in Riga, Latvia. (Chris Brown/CBC)
For many people walking past it on cobblestone streets, the memory of Soviet occupation is not ancient history but a lived experience.
With Russia’s brutal war against Ukraine now in its fourth year, this history creates a persistent, low-grade anxiety.
"We just have a history with Russia, so I'm thinking that something similar can happen again," said Leva Rosenberg, a 20-year-old music student in Riga who spoke to CBC News.
"I am scared about it every day, but I'm just living and hoping our government will save us."
That daily fear represents exactly the kind of psychological vulnerability Vladimir Putin’s hybrid campaign aims to exploit.
For others in Riga’s Old Town, the visible presence of NATO and Canadian troops on the ground and allied jets in the sky provides an ironclad sense of security that their grandparents never had.
"Latvia is part of NATO," said Lina Valaine. "So I think if something happens... then NATO will be involved, and I don't think Russia needs that at the moment. So, I don't think anything is going to happen."

One of Donald Trump’s biggest goals as president is to increase domestic manufacturing and reshore supply chains so that the most in-demand technologies in the world can be 100 percent made in the United States.
By executive order last December, he launched his “Genesis Mission,” an ambitious plan seeking to leverage US dominance in AI to maintain or seize an edge in advanced robotics, biotechnology, semiconductors, and nuclear technologies. According to Trump, that plan works best with self-sustaining supply chains. Not even neighboring countries or longtime allies should be relied upon to manufacture a single component of any US product in his ideal world.
The Consumer Technology Association (CTA) has long warned that Trump’s reshoring goals are not grounded in reality, but only recently has America’s largest technology trade association attempted to estimate what it would cost businesses and consumers to follow through on Trump’s plan.
“It is no longer enough to say that reshoring is difficult,” the CTA acknowledged. “The practical questions are what it would cost, product by product, what it would physically require, and who would pay for it.”
In new research shared with members this week, the CTA warned that reaching full US production of 10 categories of products most commonly found in US homes by 2031 “would require between $185 and $230 billion in capital expenditure, 555,000 to 668,000 additional full-time employees, and 19.1-19.5 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity per year.”
While the costs are eye-popping, the labor demand might be the bigger problem, requiring more than double the “existing US computer and electronics manufacturing workforce,” the CTA said. Additionally, the energy demand required to reshore all supply chains at once would clash with huge energy needs of AI data centers over the same time period.
Product categories included computer monitors, laptops, robotic vacuums, smart speakers, smartphones, smartwatches, televisions, video game consoles, wireless earbuds, and wireless headphones.
Smartphones are in a “league of their own,” the CTA said, emerging as the most expensive product to make in the US and the product that Americans consider least dispensable. Taking into account tariffs in place today, the cost of fully manufacturing a smartphone in the US would go up by 152 percent, CTA estimated, and some of those costs would inevitably have to be covered by consumers to maintain profit margins and keep investors happy.
The largest cost increases would be in products with processors, memory, and advanced displays, the CTA said. Building laptops would cost 93 percent more, and smartwatches 97 percent more. On the lower end of the spectrum, TVs would cost 41 percent more to build entirely in the US.
In this scenario, most tech companies wouldn’t immediately pass all extra costs on to their customers. But any big price jumps could hurt Americans already pinching pennies. CTA’s research indicated that companies could pass on between 25 and 50 percent of the cost increase.
On average, CTA estimated that “the 10 products in our report would see a weighted average price increase of 27 to 55 percent.” For the most cash-vulnerable and value-seeking US families, that could quickly add up as the devices they depend on wear down.
“A household replacing a phone, a laptop, and a television over a typical replacement cycle would face that increase on each purchase,” the CTA reported.
Households already facing budget strains—including rising costs of rent, groceries, and fuel—are already delaying technology purchases until prices come down in the US, the CTA reported. And while most people are unwilling to go without smartphones for very long, the fewer products that tech companies can sell over time, the worse their margins will get as they continue to absorb higher costs. As returns diminish, that could spook investors, the CTA suggested, making it even harder to reshore supply chains, despite Trump insisting that reshoring will ultimately attract more investment in the US. With each product category taking years to fully reshore, the jury is out on how many businesses could afford that, the CTA suggested.
Trump unlikely to embrace CTA’s alternative plan
Instead of rushing companies to invest in domestic manufacturing on expedited timelines that hardly anybody can afford, the CTA recommended a “first step” that could help tech firms manage costs while pursuing some reshoring.
If the US focused only on reshoring the assembly part of manufacturing—rather than reshoring the manufacturing of every component—firms’ costs would be substantially less, estimated between $16 billion and $19 billion.
In that scenario, the cost of manufacturing smartphones would still rise by 67 percent, CTA estimated, and laptops by 50 percent. But for businesses, that’s a comparably lower cost impact that allows them to perhaps avoid price increases while continuing working with “trusted trading partners, suppliers, and allies to secure component access,” until they can bring the full supply chain into the US.
To support that scenario, the CTA suggested that Trump pump the brakes on imposing tariffs on component parts—at the very least, considering eliminating tariffs on components from trusted trade partners and allies. That could further reduce costs for businesses without carrying the risk of the US overly relying on potentially less stable markets of foreign rivals like China.
“Component tariffs drive up US assembly costs relative to the current import mix,” the CTA reported. “They make it more expensive for companies to manufacture in the US and raise costs the most for products that matter most to consumers.”
Ideally, once assembly is brought into the US, businesses can then evaluate “on its merits” which products they can afford to fully manufacture in the US, components and all.
Trump seems unlikely to embrace an assembly-only plan for reshoring, as, for example, he has demanded that the US move quickly to reshore 50 percent of semiconductor manufacturing by the end of his term. On a press call, the CTA’s executive chair, Gary Shapiro, confirmed that “it is not realistic to think that roughly two years from now, we’re going to have over 50 percent of the semiconductor manufacturing in the US.
“I mean, that’s just physically impossible, labor-wise impossible,” Shapiro said. “And even if you threw full money at it today, you just can’t do it.”
Apple won’t blame Trump for price increases
The CTA didn’t forecast any specific product price increases. But Apple counts among the tech giants that the group represents, and it has faced the most pressure so far from Trump to commit to manufacturing its iPhone in the US—despite reports that this could dramatically increase the price of the world’s most popular smartphone.
But notably since then, the company has faced some backlash for announcing a $2,000 starting price tier for the foldable iPhone Duo. That pricing came after Apple rolled out a 2T storage tier for the iPhone 17 Pro Max, also set around $2,000. Apple has denied that these price increases are linked to Trump’s tariffs, but critics doubt that’s entirely true. They wonder if Apple is anticipating more challenging cost margins as it invests in reshoring supply chains for other products and is perhaps “testing how much customers will pay for the absolute best iPhone money can buy,” Yahoo Finance reported.
PC Mag defended the iPhone Duo price as fair, noting that “in the middle of an industry-wide memory crisis, almost every new piece of tech is painfully marked up” and claiming that “Apple could have slapped an astronomical price tag on a brand-new foldable form factor and still sold units day one.”
Although Apple’s silence about tariffs and US-made iPhones has made it clear that the company, like other Big Tech firms, can navigate whatever Trump throws at them, small businesses that represent 80 percent of the CTA’s membership are not in the same boat, the CTA said. Those businesses bring in billions to the US economy, and increasing their costs could “measurably affect overall US inflation at a time when inflation is already above target and rising,” the CTA said.
“Policy that treats consumer technology as a single undifferentiated reshoring target risks imposing the largest consumer costs precisely where the economics are least favorable,” the CTA said. “The categories consumers regard as most essential, led by smartphones and laptops, are exactly those where the modeled cost of full domestic production is highest.”
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

Mumbai: The Maharashtra Class Owners Association (MCOA) has urged the state government to reconsider 11 provisions in the proposed regulations for coaching classes, arguing that the rules should balance student safety and quality education with the practical and financial constraints faced by coaching centres.
In a representation addressed to School Education Minister Pankaj Bhoyar, the association called for a review of provisions concerning age restrictions, penalties, fire safety clearances, classroom space, fee refunds, sanitation facilities and teacher eligibility, among other issues.
Age restrictions and penalties questioned
The association has proposed replacing a blanket ban on students below 13 years of age with age-appropriate regulations, including limits on coaching hours, adequate breaks, parental consent and child safety guidelines. It said younger students often seek additional academic support, foundation courses and scholarship examination preparation, and that a complete prohibition could affect their learning needs.
Raising concerns over penalties, the association sought a graded system based on the size and turnover of a coaching centre, the nature of the violation and its impact on student safety. It recommended issuing notices and allowing time for rectification in cases involving minor, first-time violations instead of imposing hefty fines immediately.
Fire safety and regulatory representation
On fire safety, the association called for a practical compliance checklist covering fire extinguishers, electrical safety, emergency lighting, first-aid facilities and evacuation arrangements. It also sought transparent inspections, written reports, safeguards for students’ personal data and a formal appeals mechanism before penalties, suspension or closure.
The association further sought representation for two to three MCOA members on the committee framing the final regulations, arguing that coaching operators could provide inputs on ground-level challenges across urban, semi-urban and rural areas.
Classroom space and refund policies
Questioning the proposed requirement of one square metre of space per student, it said the norm could be difficult to implement in cities such as Mumbai, where commercial rents are high. It recommended assessing usable classroom space, seating arrangements, ventilation and emergency movement requirements collectively.
On fee refunds, the association opposed using a uniform pro-rata formula as the sole criterion, stating that coaching centres incur expenses on faculty, study material, test series and additional lectures before the completion of a course. It sought flexibility to frame transparent refund policies based on course structure and services already provided.
Sanitation and teacher eligibility norms
The representation also called for reconsidering mandatory separate male and female toilets at every centre, while insisting that clean and safe sanitation facilities must remain compulsory. It proposed a five-year registration validity period with a simplified renewal process.

On teacher recruitment, the association argued that an FIR alone should not automatically disqualify a person from employment, and called for decisions based on the nature of the offence, its relevance to student safety and the status of the legal proceedings. It also sought flexibility in making graduation compulsory for every teacher, proposing that subject knowledge, teaching experience and demonstrated competency be considered alongside formal qualifications.
The association said its suggestions were not intended to oppose regulation but to ensure that the final framework was transparent, proportionate and practical to implement, while protecting students and preserving employment in the coaching sector.

The Keralam government has constituted a high-level task force to develop an evidence-based road map for a phased prevention and early detection framework, along with appropriate treatment and rehabilitation plan, and an action plan for healthy ageing, with the broader objective of establishing a “Kerala Holistic Model for Health, Wellness and Longevity”.
According to the government order issued by the Health and Family Welfare department on Wednesday, the task force will be headed by the Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan, with Health Minister K. Muraleedharan as vice-chairman. Sharmila Mary Joseph, Principal Secretary (Health and Family Welfare and AYUSH), will be the member-coordinator.
The 16-member task force includes K.R. Jyothilal, Additional Chief Secretary (Finance); Ratan Kelkar, Secretary to the Chief Minister; Deepak Singhal, former Uttar Pradesh Chief Secretary; Shiv Kumar Sarin, Director of Institute of Liver and Biliary Sciences, New Delhi; Faizal E Kottikolon, chairman, KEF Holdings; C. Devidas Varier, managing director of AVP Coimbatore; Harsh Mahajan, chairman of Mahajan Imaging and Labs; Pratap Chauhan, chairman Jive Ayurva; Kancherioa Ravindranath, chairman, Global Hospital, Hyderabad; S.S. Lal, Director ReAct Asia Pacific; P.M. Varier, chief physician, Arya Vaidya Sala Kottakkal; M.V. Pillai, chairman International Cancer Care Network, USA, and Nisha Nigil, President-elect, Association of Kerala Medical Graduates in North America.
The task force has been asked first to assess Keralam’s disease burden, ageing trends, healthcare service capacity and gaps in access, and identify priority populations, diseases and districts.
Path forward
It will then design a phased prevention and early-detection framework covering risk assessment, screening protocols, referral pathways, follow-up and measurable coverage targets, aligned with existing State and national programmes.
A significant component of its mandate is to explore and identify evidence-based models for coordination among modern medicine, Ayurveda and other recognised systems of medicine. The order specifically calls for clearly defined scopes of practice, clinical governance, consent, contraindications, referral mechanisms and adverse-event reporting.
The task force will also examine the creation of a network of diagnostic, hospital, rehabilitation and wellness services, including criteria for pilot projects, accreditation, quality assurance and independent evaluation.
Another proposed component is the implementation of a Keralam Health Intelligence and Longevity Grid, with emphasis on interoperability with existing health systems, consent, privacy, cybersecurity and data stewardship.
Its mandate extends to workforce development in nursing, allied health, public health and relevant systems of medicine. It will also set uop research partnerships in health economics and financing.
The task force has been asked to examine possible investment and public-private partnership (PPP) models for diagnostics and wellness infrastructure, specifying fiscal exposure, procurement safeguards and public benefit.
It will also examine standards and opportunities for health and wellness tourism and identify the legal, regulatory and institutional changes required to implement its recommendations.
The order also recommends facilitation and support of the proposed World Holistic Health Forum, “a global NGO”, after assessing its purpose, financial commitment and expected outcomes so that Kerala’s positioning as a “cradle and destination” for holistic health, wellness and longevity can be explored.
Action-oriented report
The task force is required to submit an action-oriented report within two months of its first meeting.
The report is expected to contain a baseline assessment and priorities, two or three defined pilot projects with details; a three-year phased roadmap, indicative costs and funding sources and fiscal risks.
The task force is also expected to draft institutional and regulatory measures, and an implementation dashboard specifying milestones and accountable departments.
The Health and Family Welfare department will function as the nodal department, with support from AYUSH, Finance and other departments. Research, analytical, financial, technical and secretarial personnel will be deputed from the Health Department and its attached organisations.

Canada’s federal government said on Wednesday it would advance legislation to prevent people whose sole health condition is mental illness from accessing euthanasia, an effort by the ruling Liberal party to address a clash in the country over who has access to physician-assisted death.
Under the current rules, people whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness have been barred from accessing medical assistance in dying (Maid) to end their lives. But that ban – due to be lifted in March – has divided lawmakers over whether to permit this expansion of the Maid program.
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, the justice minister, Sean Fraser, said his government would indefinitely bar people whose sole condition is mental illness from accessing the program. He said that while there was no “perfect consensus” on this issue, upcoming legislation reflected the “correct” approach.
Earlier this year, a government committee concluded the government should expand access to Maid and should “indefinitely exclude persons whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness from eligibility for medical assistance in dying”. That report also flagged the need for “increased and more equitable access” to mental health services.
Canada’s Maid laws, drawn up after a 2015 supreme court decision, initially only permitted those who are terminally ill to be eligible for the procedure. But in 2019, a Quebec judge ruled that restricting access to those who had a “reasonably foreseeable death” was unconstitutional, forcing federal lawmakers to amend and expand the existing laws.
In 2021, the law was updated so adults could receive an assisted death if two doctors confirmed an irremediable physical condition causing immense suffering that cannot be relieved. Given the uncertainty surrounding mental illness, lawmakers in 2021 initially put a temporary exclusion in place for people who suffer solely from a mental illness. They renewed that pause in 2023 and 2024.
According to the latest government figures, the vast majority of Maid deaths – 95.6% – involved people whose natural death was considered “reasonably foreseeable”. Only 4.4% were cases in which death was not considered reasonably foreseeable. Those include people with conditions such as multiple sclerosis and incurable neurological disease that can causes profound disability and immense suffering.
The Liberal party’s legislation is also an effort to ward off a private member’s bill that would amend the section of the criminal code covering Maid so that “a mental disorder is not a grievous and irremediable medical condition”.
Advocates for expanding Maid to include mental illness alone say the current rules violate their constitutional rights and access to healthcare. Fraser acknowledged to reporters that a federal case – led by the advocacy group Dying With Dignity Canada – challenging the government’s previous decision to delay access to Maid for people with mental illness could affect the upcoming bill.
Fraser said lawmakers would also work to decriminalize what are known as advanced requests, effectively giving people suffering from some illnesses such as Alzheimer’s the chance to choose Maid before their illness deprives them of the capacity to consent.
At present, Quebec is the only jurisdiction that permits the use of these requests. Fraser gave no specifics on the timing of the legislation but said that provinces will decide whether to provide advance requests. While the province of Alberta has already said it will not permit advance requests, the justice minister said the bill attempts to ensure “the doctors who provide the services will not be treated as criminals for doing so”.

Update| October 8, 2026, 16:54 IST Shares of Paytm ended today's trading session 5.4% lower at ₹1,640 apiece on the BSE.Meanwhile, shares of Pine Labs fell 4.3% to ₹169.75, while Mobikwik declined 4.5% by the end of the session. Original| October 8, 2026, 14:05 IST Shares of fintech companies Paytm, Pine Labs and MobiKwik came under pressure today following reports that the proposed merchant discount rate (MDR) on select UPI transactions could be deferred. Paytm’s stock fell as much as 10% to an intraday low of ₹1,560.60 apiece on the BSE. As of 13:30 PM IST, the stock was trading 5.21% lower at ₹1,643 apiece, giving the company a market capitalisation of ₹1,05,416.1 Cr ($10.8 Bn). Pine Labs was trading 4.3% lower at ₹169.90 apiece, with a market capitalisation of ₹19,619.18 Cr ($2 Bn). MobiKwik, meanwhile, was trading 5.7% lower at ₹241.25 apiece, with a market capitalisation of ₹1,899.7 Cr ($196.3 Mn). The sell-off comes amid reports that the rollout of MDR on select UPI transactions may be deferred from October 15, to January 1, 2027. As per a report by Business Standard, a proposal to defer the MDR rollout is under consideration, with a final decision expected in the coming days. The delay, if approved, would keep eligible merchant UPI payments free of MDR through the festive season. The UPI and Services Steering Committee, headed by NPCI, met on Wednesday to discuss the proposed rollout among various other aspects of the framework. The committee is also considering increasing the exemption threshold to businesses with an annual turnover of up to ₹40 Lakh. Under the earlier proposal, merchants receiving up to ₹1 Lakh a month through UPI QR codes directly into their bank accounts would be exempt from the fee. Meanwhile, the RBI governor Sanjay Malhotra said on Wednesday that a “small fee” in the form of MDR is unlikely to have a major impact on UPI transaction volumes. “As of now, we do not see any drop in volumes. And I don't personally think that a small fee will have a major impact on the volumes,” Malhotra told reporters at the central bank headquarters. Meanwhile, UPI transactions continued to grow, with the platform processing 24.07 Bn transactions worth ₹29.37 Tn in September, up 22.6% YoY in volume and 18% YoY in value.

Eligible Amazon Prime customers do not need to do anything to receive their payment. The FTC is also warning people that some scammers are exploiting the legitimate class action lawsuit to steal people's personal information. The FTC said it will not call any eligible customers, nor will they demand money or promise a special prize.
Rumors are spreading online about supposed payouts from a class action lawsuit benefiting Amazon Prime subscribers.
Social media users on platforms like Reddit and Facebook shared screenshots of notifications about the lawsuit or receiving payment (screenshotted). Some online posters claimed they received payment, whereas others asked if the settlement was real.
Snopes readers also searched the website for information on the Amazon Prime lawsuit.
This is a legitimate settlement involving payouts to eligible Amazon Prime customers.
The Federal Trade Commission reached a $2.5 billion settlement with Amazon over allegations that the company "enrolled tens of millions of customers in Amazon Prime subscriptions without their knowledge or consent" and "made it difficult for customers to cancel their Amazon Prime subscriptions." As part of the settlement, Amazon did not admit fault.
An official notice on the Federal Trade Commission website states that Amazon began sending payments in November 2025 and "will continue to send automatic refunds to eligible Prime customers through April 2027."
Customers who received a previous payment of up to $51 may receive additional payments due to a revised settlement order. Eligible customers may receive up to $200 in total (so up to $149 if you received a $51 payment previously).
It is worth noting, however, that the FTC is also warning people that scammers are calling people and claiming to be part of the Amazon class action lawsuit payouts.
"The FTC will never demand money, make threats, tell you to transfer money, or promise you a prize. And no one from Amazon will ever ask you for money to get a refund," the FTC website said. "Only scammers say they can get you special access or a guaranteed refund."
Eligibility and payment process
According to the FTC, eligible claimants do not need to take any actions to receive a refund. Amazon will send automatic refund payments by mailed check, PayPal or Venmo, and all you need to do is accept the payment.
Here's how to know if you're eligible, per the FTC's news release (emphasis theirs):
Who is eligible for a refund?
Under the revised settlement order, you are eligible for a refund if you meet all three requirements:
- You are an Amazon Prime customer in the United States.
- You signed up for an Amazon Prime subscription through a "challenged enrollment flow" or tried to cancel through the online cancellation flow but were unable to do so between June 23, 2019 and June 23, 2025.
- You used no more than 20 Amazon Prime Benefits (including Prime Music or Prime Video products offered for free to Prime subscribers) in any 12-month period following Amazon Prime enrollment.
The "challenged enrollment flows" are universal Prime decision page, shipping selection page, single page checkout, or the Prime Video enrollment flow.
No action is needed to receive a refund. You do not have to file a claim, respond to a notice, or complete any forms. Amazon will send automatic payments to eligible customers.
Customers who have issues receiving payments or questions can reach out to admin@SubscriptionMembershipSettlement.com or call 1-888-999-8094. The official website for notifications about this class action lawsuit is at www.SubscriptionMembershipSettlement.com, per the FTC.
How to check if a class action lawsuit is legitimate
In the case of the Amazon settlement, the FTC's news release on the federal agency's official website — with a ".gov" domain — lends it legitimacy.
However, Snopes has previously verified class action lawsuits that are not brought by the government. In those cases, it's worth checking the lawsuit's case number in PACER, a public database for federal electronic court records, or CourtListener, a more user-friendly nonprofit repository that pulls information from PACER documents and other court records.
Even if the FTC did not make an announcement, for example, the screenshots of payments shared on social media include a case number for the Amazon settlement: 2:23-cv-01372.
Searching that case number in CourtListener returned two pages of results. On the second page, there's a case called "In re: Amazon Return Policy Litigation." That's proof that a real lawsuit has been filed. The case page includes links to all the documents in the court docket for that particular case. A document titled, "Exhibit A - Amazon Settlement Agreement" states that a settlement was reached.

Man charged in killing of British ex-politician tried to break into Farage's home
A prosecutor says a man accused of killing former British politician Ann Widdecombe allegedly tried to break into Nigel Farage's home about a year earlier
LONDON -- A man accused of killing former British politician Ann Widdecombe tried to break into the home of anti-immigration Reform UK party leader Nigel Farage about a year earlier and researched other prominent figures, a prosecutor said Wednesday.
Prosecutor Kashif Malik said Joshua Kerry left evidence on his digital devices indicating he had conducted “online reconnaissance” of well-known people and institutions between May 2024 and when Widdecombe was killed in July.
Kerry, 28, faces one count of preparation of terrorist acts, including against Farage. He did not enter a plea in Westminster Magistrates’ Court and remains in custody.
Farage’s partner returned home April 20, 2025, to find part of the door frame hanging off, a lighter fluid bottle and signs someone tried to get into the house, Malik said, adding that Kerry's DNA was detected on the flammable liquid container.
Tracking data showed Kerry’s journey from his home in northern England to London and his car being parked outside Farage’s home for several hours before his return trip.
The bearded defendant, wearing glasses and a gray sweatsuit, spoke briefly to ask Chief Magistrate Paul Goldspring to speak up and to state his name and birth date.
Goldspring sent the case to the Central Criminal Court for a hearing Friday.
The charge announced last week came a month after counterterrorism police reopened a probe into an alleged firebomb attempt at Farage's south London home.
Kerry was previously charged with murder in the July 8 beating death of Widdecombe, who was found dead in her house in an isolated southwest England village.
Widdecombe, 78, was a spokesperson for the Reform Party after a long career as a Conservative member of Parliament and government minister known for her blunt-spoken, socially conservative views opposing abortion and the expansion of LGBTQ+ rights.
She later found fame as a contestant on the reality television shows “Strictly Come Dancing” and “Celebrity Big Brother” and returned to politics.
Widdecombe's killing renewed concerns over the security for politicians, which had been tightened in the past decade after the murders of two prominent MPs.
Labour lawmaker Jo Cox was shot and stabbed in 2016 by a far-right extremist, and Conservative David Amess was stabbed in 2021 by an attacker inspired by the Islamic State group.

Two Latvian men arrested for trespass offences near RAF airbase
Meanwhile, we are getting a line from the UK that two Latvian nationals resident in the UK have been arrested on suspicion of trespass offences at an RAF airbase in Cambridgeshire.
The two men where found last night as security patrols near RAF Molesworth found an abandoned vehicle and a small breach in the perimeter fence. The two men were located and arrested at 2am.
In a statement, the police said the matter is being investigated by officers from Counter Terrorism Policing.
The incident comes just over a week after a widely reported security issue near RAF Fairford, and will raise concerns about security of UK airbases.
Head of Counter Terrorism Policing London team, Helen Flanagan, said:
“We’re very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites, but at this stage there is nothing to suggest this incident is connected to the events at RAF Fairford last week.
Our investigation into this incident is at its very early stages. A big part of this is looking at any potential motivation as to why the men were present at the site, but I must stress we are keeping an open mind at this stage and enquiries are very much ongoing.
As ever, I would ask the public to remain vigilant and if you see anything of concern, then to contact police.”
The police statement is also likely to prompt some questions about the response to the incident.
With the abandoned vehicle found at 10pm, and the two men only arrested at 2am, what happened in the meantime? And where were they found?
The statement points out that “a small breach of the perimeter fence was subsequently identified.”
The police said the vehicle was “recovered by police,” with further precautionary checks for a potential explosives – but “nothing of concern was found.”
On the two suspects – aged 32 and 36 – it said:
“They were initially arrested on suspicion of trespass on a prohibited site and criminal damage and taken to a Cambridgeshire police station.
The pair have since been further arrested on suspicion of an offence under section 4 of the National Security Act 2023 – namely entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK.
Both men currently remain in police custody at this time.”
There’s no point in speculating about the nature of this incident until we know more.
But it will undoubtedly raise further concerns about and scrutiny of the security of UK airbases after last week’s Fairford incident.
RAF Molesworth hosts some US troops and the Joint Intelligence Operations Center Europe Analytic Center (JAC), as well as Nato’s 24/7 intelligence fusion centre.

At a summit in Montreal later this month (29-30 October), the EU and Canada will pledge to launch “an alliance for the future”, with a host of agreements on digital trade and the economy, and plans to intensify ties on raw materials, the Arctic and people-to-people contacts.
The nine-page draft summit text seen by the Guardian does not mention the phrase “associate membership”, reflecting scepticism about the term European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen surprised EU diplomats with last month. Canada’s government also appeared to distance themselves from the term, which has no legal basis in EU treaties.
Semantics aside, the two sides will pledge to deepen ties on a long list of areas to build “a deeper and more integrated relationship”. The text, likely to be closely read by the UK and others, states:
“Our partnership may become a model for other countries seeking friendship in a challenging world.”
According to the draft, the EU and Canada will:
sign an agreement on the joint purchase of 50 waterbombers made by Canada’s DeHavilland to be ready by 2030 to fight wildfires in Canada and the EU.
negotiate Canada’s entry into flagship EU programmes, such as Horizon (research) and Erasmus+ (student exchanges and education) and the Galileo satellite programme.
assess options to export Canadian liquefied natural gas and critical minerals to the EU
deepen cooperation on AI safety and carry out feasibility studies on new subsea infrastructure to connect Europe, Canada and Asia
increase labour mobility to reduce barriers to young people and skilled professionals working on both jurisdictions
Ukraine war stalemate could 'quickly turn ... into a much broader ... regional conflict,' Rubio warns
Meanwhile, let’s bring you comments from the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, who was in Lisbon this afternoon and warned that the continuing stalemate between Russia and Ukraine was “very dangerous.”
Speaking alongside the Portuguese foreign minister Paulo Rangel, Rubio warned that any escalation “could quickly turn what is a war between two countries into a much broader and far more dangerous regional conflict.”
Rubio said there have been attempts to reach a negotiated settlement, and “we will keep trying”.
Here are a few more images showing the scale of the demonstration currently gathered at Place de la Bastille in Paris…
Left-wing presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon – whose party, France Unbowed (LFI), has long been supportive of the protests – is set to address the crowds shortly.
Main Paris protest gets under way amid anger at 'empty promises' on education
Today’s main student demonstration in Paris is just getting under way, and there are lots of people attending.
Protest leaders are criticising “empty promises” from the government, calling for “concrete measures” and saying their protest action will continue until their demands are met.
Number of school blockades gradually decreasing, French government data show
Back in France, there are initial signs that the student protests may be starting to subsidea bit – despite sometimes dramatic images continuing to emerge from across the country.
Thousands still turned out to support the movement – including a new march in Marseille this afternoon – but the education ministry’s figures showed the number of school blockades was gradually decreasing.
It said 224 were closed in the morning, down to 157 by lunchtime, meaning that 96% of schools were open, Reuters reported.
However, the student groups are calling for another day of mobilisation on Tuesday, 13 October, so we are likely to see the protests continue for some time, even if in a slightly different form.
AFP has a quick snap that the EU is confident it is capable of meeting demand for gas this winter but its reserves are at a “historically low” level.
The European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas association said “Europe is entering the winter with historically low storage levels while observing higher and more volatile global gas prices,” while adding “gas infrastructure remains sufficiently flexible to meet demand.”
While the British prime minister Andy Burnham has been in Berlin meeting chancellor Friedrich Merz, his foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has been in Ukraine, where he has announced further sanctions on Russia.
AFP reports that, visiting the site of a Russian missile strike which hit a residential area in Pryluky with Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Miliband said:
There can be no clearer sign of Putin’s evil, evil intent and strategy in this conflict. Putin once said that he was going to win on the battlefield. He is trying to win by terrorising civilians.
Miliband said the UK government was announcing fresh sanctions on Russia, which he said would apply “on the shadow fleet, on the oil companies, on the crypto, on the financing of the war”.
Strike on Kramatorsk buses 'will not go unanswered,' Zelenskyy says
In a post to social media, Ukraine’s president, who included graphic footage from the scene, has said that a Russian strike on public transport in Kramatorsk which has left at least 30 dead “will not go unanswered”.
Doctors are now fighting to save the lives of people injured in the Russian strike on Kramatorsk. As of now, 30 people have been confirmed killed, and sadly, that number may rise. My condolences to all their families and loved ones. Another 18 people were injured in the strike. Residential buildings and cars were also damaged.

French education minister to draft proposals on teachers' absences in response to protests
Back to France,education minister Édouard Geffray said his ministry would prepare a plan to address on of the key demands of the students’ movement on providing cover for absent teachers “in a few hours or a few days,” Le Figaro reported.
He is expected to meet with the three main student groups later today to discuss details (10:10).
In the meantime, protests continue across the country, and AFP notes that while they have been largely peaceful, some demonstrators resort to acts of violence or clash with police officers.
Burnham 'committed to securing deeper cooperation' with EU at looming summit
Burnham also talks about rebuilding the UK’s relationship with the EU after Brexit.
He says their meeting in Berlin comes ahead of the UK-EU summit later this year – expected in late November – as he says he is “very committed to securing deeper cooperation” with the EU at the summit.
He wants to see “if we can bring the UK closer to Europe, particularly in the interest of economic growth and collaboration on irregular migration,” he says.
In terms of more symbolic gestures, he says he will take part in talks with German business leaders later today, and hopes to host them in the UK next year – alongside the full German cabinet to show that “this treaty is not just words on a page, left on a shelf,” but a meaningful document.
He then turns to students standing somewhat awkwardly behind the pair throughout their exchange, and they briefly chat about their experiences with the UK, with someone mentioning their visited Scotland.
Merz welcomes new treaty as new opening after UK's 'regrettable' decision to leave EU
Merz is speaking now.
His remark focus exclusively on the bilateral British-German Kensington Treaty, as the pair exchange the documents and formally complete its implementation.
He says the treaty “opens up new opportunities” between the two countries, following Britain’s “regrettable” exit from the European Union.
He focuses on a particular element of the treaty that gives better access to both countries, with no visas required – even for extended stays by school pupils and university students – and for student exchanges between the two countries.
“That is precisely why we are doing this: so that the younger generation, within the context of bilateral relations between Germany and Great Britain, can simply see just how well we Europeans work together and how closely we belong together,” he says.

Son of Zambian bishop detained in post-election raid fears for his father's safety
The son of detained Zambian opposition politician Bishop Trevor Mwamba has told the BBC he is concerned for his father's safety after the former Bishop of Botswana was detained along with 10 other opposition figures by authorities.
Eno Mwamba said his father, who is leader of the United National Independence Party, has been charged with treason following President Hakainde Hichilema's disputed election victory.
The opposition politicians have been held since a raid by security forces on 14 August.
Opposition leader Brian Mundubile, head of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP), had gone into hiding after disputing the election result, but has since also been detained by the authorities.
The government accuses the opposition of planning an armed insurgency and have charged the detained politicians with treason. They have denied the charges.
