'We need to go. We need to help.' Israelis return to border to rebuild after Oct. 7
SDEROT, Israel — Shahar Goldenberg drives along a small road that circles Kibbutz Zikim, a cooperative farming community on Israel's southern border with Gaza.
He's lived here for nearly two decades, but he's never seen so many people clamoring to join their community of about 1,000 people.
"The demand is amazing — great, huge demand."
Zikim's waiting list is now two years long. 
New houses are going up fast: the community is currently building 25, with plans to add 100 additional homes over the next decade.
Sales of existing homes are soaring.
"This was not like this before Oct. 7, of course not. It is an internal joke — if you want to sell your house you can do it in less than a week."
Three years ago, much of this region was practically cleared out after thousands of Hamas-led militants poured across the border on Oct. 7, killing nearly 1,200 people and taking some 250 hostages.
Now, residents are returning — and new ones are joining them, driven by a sense of solidarity, but also by a growing sense of security as Israel maintains a heavy military presence across the border in Gaza.
Many people want to come and be part of southern Israel's rebirth, Goldenberg says. They feel safer now that Israel occupies more than 60% of Gaza.
Israeli troops have drawn what the military calls a border buffer zone — marked by a yellow line — extending deep into Gaza.
Before the war, hundreds of thousands of Gazans lived and farmed in that border area, according to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics.
On a hilltop in Zikim, Goldenberg shows off eight homes under construction, all with sweeping views of the Mediterranean.
"These new houses [have] a view of the beach and a view of northern Gaza. I hope that we will not see the north of Gaza in the next years."
There isn't much left of Gaza to see from here now. Just shells of blown-out buildings.
While there is mounting international pressure, including from the United States, for Israeli troops to ultimately leave Gaza, a large majority of Israelis support a permanent Israeli presence along the border in Gaza, according to a recent poll.
The Israeli government has repeatedly said it will not leave until Hamas is fully disarmed.
That's fine with Goldenberg.
"And this is the only plan, that we continue to live here. Without the yellow line it will be really difficult and challenging for us."
Subsidies and support for Israel's south
A new wave of arrivals is breathing life into this stretch of southern Israel known as the Gaza Envelope. For years, the region has been sparsely populated—a landscape of fertile farmland and close-knit kibbutz communities that stretched along Gaza's perimeter, reaching south toward the Egyptian border.
About half of the region's residents live in Sderot, the largest city on the border.
These days construction crews seem to be on every corner.
At one site, workers are putting the finishing touches on a brand-new kindergarten. It's one of several dozen schools and daycare centers included in the city's plans to double its population to more than 120,000 residents by 2040.
Robin Feldman is already part of that growth. She has just picked up her 6-month-old daughter, Nelli, from her first day at a childcare center. She then takes us to the family's new home, not far from the city center.
It's a small, three-room apartment, still largely empty. One bedroom has reinforced walls and a heavy security door.
"This is going to be Nelli's room — which is the bomb shelter. Hopefully we never have to use it."
The young family recently moved to Sderot from Paramus, New Jersey. Feldman's husband is a rabbi, and she teaches Jewish history. Her lessons include biblical prophecies that speak of the Jewish people's return to Israel — and of the prosperity that will follow.
"I teach these prophecies to my students, and I'm now living it, so it's very special."
Since Oct. 7 and amid rising antisemitism around the world, Feldman says she believes Israel is now the safest place for her family. Government incentives have helped with the move, too. The family receives 2,000 shekels a month toward its rent — about $650 — she says.
Sderot residents also receive substantial income and property tax breaks, according to the city spokesman, Yaron Sasson.
"We are working to convince people from all over Israel to come south," he says. "And from abroad too."
Returning to rebuild
For some residents, the decision to return south was made almost immediately after the Oct. 7 attack.
Galia Tzur says she and her husband made the decision to move back to Kibbutz Nir Oz "Oct. 7 on the dot." The kibbutz is about 30 miles south of Sderot, right next to the Gaza border.
The couple, now in their 50s, had lived in Nir Oz in the 1990s. The minute Tzur saw the news about the Hamas attack, she says they both knew they had to return.
"We were both were like — we need to go, we need to help, we can't stay here."
They had been living in New Zealand for more than a decade, but sold their house and moved back to Israel to help rebuild.
The kibbutz was hit hard in the Oct. 7 Hamas attack. One-quarter of residents — 117 people — were either killed or taken hostage on that day. All but six of the kibbutz's more than 200 buildings were damaged or set on fire.
But the community is already rebuilding. Reconstruction manager Ron Bahat is overseeing the work. As we drive through the community, we pass many burnt-out homes that have remained standing since the attack.
The kibbutz is debating what to do with the damaged buildings. Some residents want them to remain as a reminder of what happened.
"The question is how to remember how to keep the legacy," Bahat says. "Some see it in a different way."
Others prefer to demolish the charred homes and focus on the future. Bahat — who was born here 60 years ago — says that's what he's focused on.
Bahat takes us to a busy construction site, where a large backhoe is excavating the site for 76 new homes. Another 106 will be built in the next two years, he says.
"The mission is to make this place bigger, better, strong and nicer." Bahat is confident they will.

At the United Nations High Level Meeting (UN HLM), in New York in September 2026, India made official remarks on the Political Declaration on Pandemic Prevention Preparedness and Response (PPPR). The Declaration is part of the emerging global legal regime on pandemics led by the WHO-Pandemic agreement (PA).
Shaping the framework
The PA was adopted by 124 member-states in 2025, including India. No country voted against it, while 11 abstained, reflecting alignment across high-, middle- and low-income countries (HICs/LICs/LMICs). The negotiations hinged on how to balance national sovereignty with international cooperation and solidarity, exposing the fault lines between the Global North and the Global South. Key issues included whether a global treaty can set binding targets for measures such as ‘One Health’ without securing funding for countries with fragile health systems. Or whether national pandemic regulations can be harmonised through global frameworks. And whether private manufacturers can be required to share vaccines in real time at affordable prices.
The PA is not yet open for ratification because negotiations are still ongoing for an annex concerning the Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing (PABS) system. PABS could help ensure that, during a pandemic, LICs and LMICs receive a fair share of vaccines, medicines and other therapeutics.
Even without ratification, the PA has created a first-of-its-kind global legal regime for the PPPR. Operationalisation requires countries such as India to balance interests of the HICs, LICs and LMICs. This will determine whether the PA will further entrench the inequities of the COVID-19 pandemic or make global health governance truly inclusive.
Editorial | Landmark agreement: On the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement
At the UN HLM, India succeeded in enshrining the multilateral components of the PA within the principle of national sovereignty. India reiterated its commitment to strengthen global pandemic preparedness but stressed that effective pandemic management requires that international coordination is demonstrated. The first is equitable access to drugs, vaccines and therapeutics and the creation of global public goods, such as digital infrastructure (which admittedly align with its own national priorities).
The second is a respect for national sovereignty and the primacy of member-states in shaping global policy interventions according to national circumstance. As a contrast, the United States rejected the Declaration, calling the PABS and WHO’s role in declaring pandemics as a challenge to its national interests.
India’s line
In its remarks, India has acknowledged the concerns of the Global North and the South. Both sides have upheld national sovereignty as paramount in several provisions. The African countries did not give consent to commitments to monitor the human-animal-environment interface, a key source of pandemic outbreaks, without significant funding, which was not guaranteed by the Global North. Similarly, countries in the Global North did not want binding targets with regard to technology transfer (and other similar provisions).
But as India said at the UN HLM, ‘Global Solidarity must be demonstrated through action’; India must be an active player in the finalisation of the global PPPR regime. India is already actively engaged in the PABS negotiations and must lead the Global South in the post-PABS context. India can consider three options. First, developing partnerships on technical areas of the PA (One Health, surveillance, health workforce strengthening) to build trust with other countries in the Global South, and a ‘store’ of operational solutions to tricky national sovereignty problems.
Second, leveraging its leadership role within existing global political groupings. For example, the H20 summit (a health and development G-7 and G-20 partnership) will take place under the United Kingdom’s G-20 leadership at the end of 2027; pandemic preparedness is one of the core health agendas. During India’s G-20 presidency in 2023, India launched the Global Initiative for Digital Health and holds considerable influence within the platform’s health initiatives. Another is ‘Partners for Multilateralism’, which was launched in 2026 by the European Union (co-sponsors are Australia, Barbados, Brazil, Canada, India and Kenya).
Third, strengthening and aligning domestic policy and regulatory architecture around its own priorities for the PA. Global leadership always rests on domestic strengths. India must ensure that its national policies on PPPR such as regulation of access to biological material and distribution of the benefits uphold the highest standards of equity which India can then demand at the global level.
A South-South health role
An equitable global regime on PPPR is in India’s interests as much as a responsibility towards the Global South. India is the pharmacy of the world, manufacturing one of the largest shares of vaccines in the world in terms of volume. Yet, it needs an equitable global vaccine distribution regime. The patents for the vaccines that India manufactures are held by global pharmaceuticals. India is also import-dependent for Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs).
India needs access to the latest technology from the Global North to strengthen the manufacturing of high-grade personal protective equipment and medical devices. At the same time, India needs to lead South-South Cooperation and share its technological strength with other countries in the Global South.
India’s health system has a continental scale, and as India’s Health Secretary stated at the UN HLM, its interventions in digital health infrastructure, laboratories networks and One Health are valuable as global public goods. An effective PA needs an engaged India, and a strong PA will strengthen India’s own pandemic management.
Priyadarshini Singh is a Research Fellow at the Centre for Social and Economic Progress (CSEP). This article is based on a forthcoming CSEP working paper on the Pandemic Agreement.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

Wealthtech startup Zomint has raised ₹36 Cr (about $3.7 Mn) in a seed funding round from Lightspeed and Prime Venture Partners. The startup plans to use the fresh capital to strengthen its technology and investment capabilities, expand its team of wealth and investment experts, and grow its content-led distribution across new formats and regional languages. Founded in 2025 by Aman Mittal and Shavir Bansal, Zomint is a wealth management platform targeting working professionals and families building long-term wealth. It pairs customers with dedicated wealth experts, supported by investment research and AI tools. Mittal, the startup’s CEO, previously held product leadership roles at Flipkart and Pine Labs. Bansal, its COO, also founded personal finance content platform Bekifaayati, which claims to have more than 50 Lakh subscribers. Zomint allows customers to start with a monthly SIP of ₹25,000 or a lump sum investment of ₹5 Lakh, positioning its services beyond the high-net-worth individuals (HNIs) traditionally served by wealth managers. The platform provides a dashboard to track investments, while its experts review portfolios and recommend actions based on customers’ goals and fund performance. Its technology brings together portfolio information, financial goals, past conversations, and investment research to flag issues and track agreed actions. According to its website, Zomint operates as an AMFI-registered mutual fund distributor. Its listed offerings span equity, debt, hybrid, gold and silver, and global funds, including GIFT City funds. The startup said it plans to broaden its services beyond domestic mutual funds to address other investment and financial needs. Zomint claims to have acquired its entire customer base organically, led by Bekifaayati’s presence on YouTube and Instagram, without spending on paid customer acquisition. The startup said it has retained 97% of its clients since launch, while nearly one in three clients made additional investments through the platform within three months of their initial engagement. Each relationship manager currently serves more than 250 families, supported by investment specialists and AI tools, it added. The fundraise comes amid investor interest in startups offering wealth management, investment research, and portfolio tools. The broader segment includes platforms such as Centricity, Novelty Wealth, Tijori, and StockGro, although their offerings and target customers differ. Inc42 reported yesterday that IPO-bound StockGro has raised ₹110 Cr as part of its ongoing Series B round. This follows earlier tranches comprising ₹150 Cr from Param Capital founder Mukul Agarwal and $13 Mn from existing investor BITKRAFT Ventures.

Indian badminton’s solitary bronze medal at the Asian Games should be viewed as a disappointment rather than an aberration, according to former All England champion Prakash Padukone, who believes the country’s leading shuttlers have the wherewithal to be far more consistent.
“It was a little disappointing. We should have done much better,” Padukone said on Thursday.
“Considering the kind of talent we have, we should have done much better. Even I was expecting, if not better, at least equal to last time’s medal tally,” he added.
Padukone, however, stopped short of reading too much into the Asian Games result. Instead, he called for greater consistency from India’s established players, who have often followed big tournament victories with early exits.

“They play throughout the year, so it’s extremely difficult to be on top all the time for everybody,” he said, adding, “But I would definitely like the players to be more consistent. And it is possible. It is not due to lack of support — they have a lot of support. They need to put in a little more effort.”
Padukone was in Mumbai to announce a collaboration between the Padukone School of Badminton and the International Institute of Sports Management. Padukone suggested that Indian players should identify four or five important tournaments in a year and peak for them, while avoiding first-round exits at other events.
India’s singles pipeline, meanwhile, gives him reason for optimism. Ayush Shetty has emerged in the men’s section, while Unnati Hooda and Tanvi Sharma are among the promising women’s singles players.
“Singles has always been our strength and that will continue,” he said, while acknowledging that replacing established doubles combinations could be more difficult.
Padukone singled out P.V. Sindhu as an example of the hunger he would like others to emulate. Sindhu’s Japan Open triumph, he said, showed that she remained driven despite an enviable medal collection.
“She is 31 now; she has won so many medals; she can easily rest on her laurels and be happy. But she still wants to push. And I think she is an ideal example for others to follow,” Padukone said.

Meta Muse is a powerful AI agent that can handle emails, purchases, bookings, and more. But its need for deep access to personal data, combined with Meta’s privacy record and early reports of Muse ignoring user permissions, makes trust its biggest problem.
A few days ago, Meta hosted its annual hardware/software event, Meta Connect, at Menlo Park, California. The event was dominated by new hardware launches, such as the new Meta Ray-Ban glasses, new VR glasses, and camera-free Ray-Ban glasses (audio only), but swimming beneath the surface of all these was something that was actually introduced earlier. Meta had introduced Meta Muse in early September, but announced the rollout of the Muse AI agent on its Meta wearables and Meta Muse Charm at the event, and for us, that was easily the real highlight of Meta Connect.
After investing heavily in recruiting AI talent, Meta finally had something to show: an AI agent, which will basically make your dreams of having a robot butler come true. Not surprisingly, it has been making massive tech waves ever since. Since Meta Connect and its rollout, Muse has been topping app store charts, and its early numbers are being compared with ChatGPT, with many pointing out that it is far ahead of OpenAI’s chatbot’s numbers.
While this may paint a very rosy picture for Meta Muse, the reality may be a trifle thorny.
What those numbers do not tell – the “Threads” deception
These numbers, impressive as they are, do not necessarily mean Muse is a runaway success. There are a few reasons for this. Topping app store charts is more of a temporary phenomenon, often influenced by what is trending in a particular week, and does not represent real industry trends. Also, Meta has billions of users across different social media and messaging platforms, which makes it easy for the tech giant to get a few million users quickly without too much trouble. But the adoption rate might not match the number of downloads or sign-ups.
We have seen this happen with Meta’s X rival app, Threads, as well. It has more “active users” as per the numbers than X, which means it must be more used and popular than X, but that is mostly because of Threads’ integration with Instagram and Facebook, which gets the app most of its “active users.” However, the time spent on the app is not nearly the same as its other two sibling social media apps. Similarly, early ChatGPT comparisons with Meta Muse signups may not be fair, because ChatGPT was not launched or advertised as a tool for the masses when it was first launched. It did not have the sort of subscriber base and reach that Meta has, and back then, AI chatbots were not too common either.
Definitely a big deal
That does not mean Muse does not represent a big tech leap. So far, AI chatbots have generally been used for queries, information, help with work, and even personal advice, but that’s mostly about it. All of these chatbots are more about helping you with your queries, with no bar to the nature of the query. While useful in this regard, many are not able to perform actions that have an impact on your day-to-day life. That is where Meta Muse differs.
As we said earlier, Muse is actually the robot butler that the future always promised us. It can get tasks done and help you with managing your digital and even real life. Once you give it access, the AI agent can go through your mail, find messages, draft new messages, reply to emails, all without too much intervention. That might not sound too impressive, as most AI agents and virtual assistants can do the same with a simple command. But Muse goes a step further – it can even make purchases, make reservations, book appointments, and more, across different devices and platforms. In fact, if allowed, Muse can basically make deals on Facebook Marketplace or book you a table at your favorite restaurant or even call you a cab, all without needing any major intervention. Proper butling!
Muse has power and potential, but does Meta have our trust?
As impressive and life-altering as it may sound– some are calling it the biggest tech innovation since the iPhone – Meta still has a massive hurdle that it would have to cross to make Muse the AI butler it wants it to be. And that is the lack of trust in Meta.
For all its innovation and massive subscriber base, Meta has been in a number of controversial situations when it comes to security and privacy. Zuckerberg’s brand has been accused of and even found guilty in cases that range from rigging elections, pushing agendas and ads, to exposing young children to adult content and potential groomers, to monopolizing social media and personal messaging space and using unfair means and practices to kill competition. Its recent hardware “hit” the Meta glasses have also got into a privacy mess, and have been (in)famously christened pervert glasses, following reports of their being used to record people without their consent.
Now, Muse requires even more data and access to private information to actually deliver on its promises. For instance, to be able to draft emails, it needs access to your email account. To be allowed to send messages, it needs permission to read, understand, store, and reply to messages, and needs access to your contact list. To make a reservation, it needs to know your location; to order things online, it needs to have your bank details and also your address. Basically, it needs to have complete access to all your information to act like the magic help that Meta is claiming it can be.
Why I am not A-Muse-D
And that is where my beef with Muse really comes in. Had this been any other company– if Apple had managed to deliver on its intelligent Siri promises or Google had delivered Gemini with such prowess, I personally would have felt less apprehensive in handing over the keys to my digital life, but to give Meta even more access to my data than it already has just feels scary.
Even though I have come to terms with the fact that we are all under passive surveillance from brands at all times, it will take some time for me to give complete control of my data over to Meta without any struggle.
Some of the recent headlines Muse has made do not help its cause. Recently, the AI agent not only made a deal for its user on Facebook Marketplace but even shared his address with the buyer. All without consent. The user, a tech YouTuber, Matt Robb, mentioned how the AI agent accepted low offers and even pretended to be the user while chatting with the buyer, calling the buyer to his address when he was not home at all. Once Matt realized what was happening, he specifically instructed Muse to not share his address. He then asked his friends to send him messages on Facebook Marketplace to see if the agent shares the address. Rather disturbingly, it did: multiple times, and even accepted low offers, all without consent. In another report by Apple Insider, alleged that Muse accessed and uploaded past and present Apple Messages even though the user said he had not granted it permission to do so. All this despite Meta’s claims that Muse has strong privacy and security protections.
All of this does not take away from the fact that Meta has created something really powerful with Muse. It has managed to deliver a finished, capable AI agent which can manage your digital lives, if you let it. Unfortunately, it may also steal your data, force specific ads, and make conversations on your behalf by pretending to be you. And therein lies the problem. The AI Agent is not just about technology, but also about trust. Meta has delivered on the first front with Muse, but until it delivers on the second, I refuse to be A-Muse-D by it. Pun intended.

An under-the-radar procurement program led by the Department of Defense has been granting special statuses to would-be defense contractors that make it easier for the government to quickly purchase their AI offerings, based on product videos that must be no longer than five minutes.
It’s part of the Pentagon’s desperate bid to inject competition in a market the United States military itself destroyed.
The initiative, known as Tradewinds, is managed by DOD’s Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office (CDAO.) Companies can submit videos describing how their AI products address one of several different “strategic focus areas” that the government periodically updates. At least once a month, a panel of judges review submissions and decide whether to accept them into the Tradewinds Solutions Marketplace, where the videos can then be viewed by government officials.
If accepted, the pitched products are considered “post-competitive.” Many procurement regulations include competitive requirements. The status can let government buyers check off that box and potentially help shave months off of award timelines. A DOD official says that in several instances, the department has been able to make awards using Tradewinds in less than a week. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google are all listed as participants.
OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google declined to comment for this story.
Though the Tradewinds Solutions Marketplace has been around since late 2022, the Trump administration has been far more vocal than its predecessors about the military buying and operationalizing AI. It also hopes to have more money than ever to throw around: As part of its 2027 budget request to Congress, the White House asked for $1.5 trillion for the Department of Defense, citing “historic investments” in AI as a priority.
This year, the military is seeking video pitches for AI tech that can help “enhance force lethality” and those that can “unleash” AI-enabled agents that can assist in the joint targeting process, including so-called kill chain execution.
No longer as relevant? Pitches for products that promote “a culture of responsible AI” and provide guardrails for AI development and use—requests made during the final Tradewinds submissions cycle under the Biden administration. A DOD official says that the 2026 topics were selected to align with a January 2026 AI strategy memo.
“There has never been a better time to build for the Army,” wrote then-sitting US Army secretary Daniel Driscoll as part of a pitch for more defense tech startups included in Y Combinator’s Fall 2026 wishlist of companies to fund. (Driscoll has since resigned from his position and returned to the private sector. He did not respond to a request for comment.)
Opaque Transactions
Acceptance onto the Tradewinds marketplace—and the special “post-competitive” status that comes with it—lets government buyers more easily cut deals using special types of contracts such as “other transaction” agreements, or OTs, which aren’t subject to certain federal acquisition requirements. By law, the Pentagon can spend up to $500 million dollars on a single OT without having to notify Congress.
Procurement experts say that OTs are considered fast and flexible, which can be appealing to startups that don’t want to gamble on whether a months-long procurement process will result in a contract. However, not all agencies publicly report their OT spending, and even when they do, they’re difficult to find on government-run sites that track federal spending, like USASpending.gov and SAM.gov.
“While OTAs offer opportunities to attract new procurement partners and reduce red tape, numerous reviews have raised red flags,” US senator Joni Ernst of Iowa tells WIRED. “These include questionable costs, mishandling of restricted information, a lack of oversight, reduced accountability and transparency, and an inability to track and access OTA outcomes.”
Ernst recently worked to pass the Stop Secret Spending Act of 2025, which will require the Department of Defense and other agencies to report OTs to the public. They’ll have three years to get into compliance.
According to public records, Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI all have OTs with the Pentagon’s CDAO. According to a DOD official, Tradewinds was leveraged along with market analysis and research as part of the department’s AI acquisition strategy, but the three companies did not confirm whether Tradewinds was used for the specific agreements WIRED identified.
Armed Forces Meet Market Forces
One of the key goals of Tradewinds is to bring “nontraditional” players into the defense industry, says Will Roberts, a former acquisition lead for the Joint Artificial Intelligence Center, CDAO’s predecessor, who helped launch the effort. In some ways, it’s an effort to swing the pendulum back to where it was in the past.
Following the Cold War, the Pentagon encouraged defense companies to merge during a now-infamous meeting called the Last Supper, since Congress was preparing to slash defense budgets. Even though it may seem like only having to deal with a few large companies might make things easier, “it actually had a huge impact on market competition,” says Roberts.
Around the same time, explains Sharon Weinberger, a national security reporter and author of the book Valley of Death: How Big Tech Is Fueling the Future of War, the personal computer boom meant that Silicon Valley was able to make its own money and with that, set its own research priorities without being beholden to the funding and influence of the military.
Roberts and other defense professionals brought up the military’s historic role in funding—and shaping—technologies like the Internet and GPS. With those investments also came leverage, says Roberts. “We've sort of lost that leverage because there's billions of dollars in AI being invested by companies themselves.”
Weinberger says this has given Silicon Valley titans an immense amount of power over the Pentagon’s technological future. “The amount of money that the Pentagon can put into AI, compared to what venture capital can invest? It's like a drop in the bucket,” she says. “And that's really frightening for the Pentagon. What happens when they can't drive the direction of technology anymore?”
Publicly, this can play out in dramatic and confusing ways. Weinberger points out, for example, that the recent legal battle over Anthropic’s status as a supply chain risk could be seen as the government trying to figure out what legal mechanisms it has to flex its authority over AI companies.
Silicon Valley sensibilities have also been a roadblock in the past, albeit briefly. Roberts recalls how Google employees got “super paranoid” in 2018 about the company’s involvement with the Pentagon’s Project Maven, which eventually led to Google pulling out of the effort. Roberts says the Pentagon spent years trying to “appease” Google with less politically charged projects like those focused on humanitarian aid and veteran health.
Google declined to comment on whether that telling was accurate. One of the Google solutions listed as “awardable” on the Tradewinds site is called “Google for Military Health - Tradewinds,” and in July 2025, the company announced a $200 million deal with CDAO to utilize its frontier AI technology. In a press release, Jim Kelly, a vice president at Google Public Sector said that the company was “committed to advancing the deployment of innovative technology across the defense ecosystem.”

In 2025, India recorded 55 deaths by malaria, 131 deaths by dengue, and 27 deaths by kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis or black fever), according to Union Health Ministry data, whereas there is no single comparable and comprehensive national measure of its annual human rabies mortality, even as the country looks to eliminate dog-mediated human rabies by the year 2030.
While a community-based study led by researchers from the Indian Council of Medical Research-National Institute of Epidemiology (ICMR-NIE) and published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases recently estimated that 5,726 people die of rabies in India every year, the Health Ministry’s Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme-Integrated Health Information Platform (IDSP-IHIP) system reported 21 deaths by rabies in 2022, 50 in 2023, and 54 in 2024.
In contrast, the Registrar General of India’s Medical Certification of Cause of Death (MCCD) system recorded 66 medically certified rabies deaths in 2022, and 271 in 2023. The MCCD system, however, covers only medically certified deaths and does not capture all registered deaths.
These figures are not directly comparable — the IDSP-IHIP is a disease surveillance system, while the MCCD captures medically certified causes through civil registration. At the national level, the MCCD covered 22.3% of registered deaths in 2022, and 22.0% in 2023. Neither system, therefore, provides a complete national count — underscoring the gaps in India’s rabies mortality surveillance.
The government table, sourced to IDSP-IHIP, had recorded one death in January 2025 but did not provide a figure for all of 2025. The government’s published table, labelled ‘Human Rabies cases (Death)’, gives the source as IDSP-IHIP.
ICMR for its study surveyed 3,37,808 people in 78,807 households across 60 districts in 15 States and estimated that India sees about 9.1 million animal bites every year, including about 5.6 million dog bites.
The researchers used the community survey, laboratory data, and a probability decision-tree model to estimate the number of people who progress from an animal bite to rabies and die. The 5,726 figure is therefore a modelled estimate of annual deaths, and not a count of deaths recorded in hospitals or by government surveillance.
The difference between the two datasets is substantial. The 54 deaths reported through government surveillance in 2024 is less than 1% of the study’s estimated annual toll of 5,726.
“The two figures, however, are generated through different methods and should not be treated as directly equivalent. The figures therefore highlight a large gap between reported surveillance deaths and estimated mortality,” a senior Health Ministry official said.
“Lack of consolidated data is a challenge in rabies eradication. Very often cases and deaths occur in areas of the country where they are not measurable. Vaccination of stray dogs, stringent post-exposure vaccination for humans, and disruption of the rabies chain is essential to curb the problem,” Nirmal Kumar Ganguly, medical scientist, public health expert, and former ICMR chief, speaking exclusively to The Hindu, said.
The National Centre for Disease Control itself says efforts are continuing to make human rabies a notifiable disease across India, and that all States have been asked to notify the disease under the relevant State legislation.
The Health Ministry has also acknowledged the surveillance challenge, with deaths occurring outside the formal health system posing an additional difficulty in capturing the full burden of disease.
Meanwhile, the Lancet study found important gaps even after animal bites. About one in five dog-bite victims had not received the anti-rabies vaccine, while only 66.2% had received at least three doses. Among those who received only one dose, nearly half did not complete the vaccination course. Only about one in 10 eligible victims received passive immunisation.
Rabies is a vaccine-preventable viral disease that attacks the central nervous system and is almost invariably fatal once symptoms appear, with infected dog bites causing most human transmission.
The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that domestic dogs are responsible for up to 99% of human rabies transmission. Globally, rabies causes an estimated 59,000 human deaths every year, with more than 95% of deaths occurring in Africa and Asia.
The WHO estimates that India accounts for 35% of rabies deaths globally and 59.9% of rabies deaths in Asia, underlining the country’s significant contribution to the global burden. Children are particularly vulnerable. The WHO says 40% of people bitten by suspected rabid animals are children under 15 years. Rabies is entirely preventable through timely vaccination of dogs and prompt post-exposure care.
The ICMR-funded study states that although there has been a substantial decline in human rabies deaths over the past two decades, India needs to fast-track its actions to eliminate dog-mediated human rabies by 2030 by adopting a focused ‘One Health’ approach — integrating human and animal surveillance, ensuring timely administration of the full course of post-exposure prophylaxis, and accelerating dog vaccination across the country.

Sport is a kind of conquest. Rulers often get one significant, special coronation that cements their legacy before their followers. Sport, though, offers that sensational feeling of ‘taking over the horizon’ on a platter, again and again, patiently allowing those who persevere to have their fill.
The Indian women’s cricket team knows the feeling, with two such anointments in the span of a week, when it was undisputedly crowned the best in Asia — a record-extending eighth Women’s Asia Cup title in Dubai and a savoured gold medal at the Asian Games in Japan, both against the same opponent: Sri Lanka. Two summit clashes, two similar submissions to authority.
A marauding top order headlined India’s unopposed quest for glory, both in Dubai and Nagoya. The tempestuous youngster in Shafali Verma has well and truly given way to a wiser allrounder, hungry to contribute to a win in every way possible.
Smriti Mandhana rose to the zenith of international cricket, leaving behind names who had influenced her in the sport. Sree Charani’s incredible year kept getting better as she hacked down a number of records while reigning supreme in the T20I rankings.

Nothing came in the way: be it feeble attempts at a fightback from weaker opponents, an unforgiving travel itinerary that barely gave the team breathing space between the Asia Cup and the Asian Games, modest accommodation provisions or threats of a Japanese typhoon that ultimately steered clear of the Korogi Sports Park in Nisshin City.
Mismatch aplenty
Take away the passions of sporting merit from the consumption of these two tournaments, and the chronology and character pools are nearly identical. The traditional Asian top four — India, Sri Lanka, Pakistan and Bangladesh — are paired against starry-eyed gladiators emerging from the Qualifiers. Valiant campaigns and campaigners come up against the Full Members, akin to bringing a knife to a gunfight, and eventually get found out.
In the Asia Cup, Indonesia, Thailand, Hong Kong China and UAE asked the occasional tough question but were ushered out of contention without much mercy. One’s heart beats and breaks for the underdogs and keeps you invested long enough before you realise how every competition day across editions feels the same — lopsided contests, a glaring mismatch in resources and infrastructure, and a tape growing increasingly stale in an impatient consumer market where sport is primarily produced for broadcast.
The story was no different at the Asiad. While the big four — courtesy of some continuity gathered over their travels across the continent — found their rhythm, Thailand was the only constant among the rest, with Malaysia, China and Japan completing the pack. These are not random draws; qualifying tournaments guarded the gates to these stages. But as much as things change, teams improve or find their footing in the global game, the overall imbalance between the Associates and the Full Members stays the same.
ALSO READ | India wins first gold medal of Asian Games 2026 after women’s cricket team beats Sri Lanka in final
Asian teams are playing more fixtures, a welcome change from years of calendars filled with blots of emptiness. The focus now is on the quality of opponent one can afford to face.
Within the Asian fold itself, a tiered system operates where the likes of India, in particular, barely face Associates. So regardless of how futile a pampered cricket fan might think these tournaments are, they are, so far at least, the only avenues for teams to experience a top-class global opponent.
The knowledge transfer, by itself, becomes the biggest takeaway for so many of these teams. Images of Hong Kong players flocking around India’s senior players and Japan and China players lining up for photographs with women they had only watched in videos or heard about in lore passing over from the subcontinent made for heartening visuals. Hong Kong China’s Marina Lamplough’s videos through the Asia Cup, in which she showed glimpses of how the team took notes from the Indian openers’ style and strategy, are one such example.
But that’s as deep as the engagement goes. India’s ‘responsibility’ to democratise its presence in the Asian circuit now has the hurdle of a packed calendar standing before it.
In the Asian Games and Asia Cup, the eastern cricketing wave doesn’t realise what it has, Netherlands skipper Babette de Leede pointed out, highlighting Asia’s advantage over other continental groupings.
“You know how Asia has the Asian Games and the Asia Cup? We don’t have any of that in Europe. It would be great because you get more games. Look at the difference between the number of games we play and the number Australia or India play. We do have entities like the European Cricket Network... the T10 tournament they organise. Those numbers are developing. And now there’s the European T20 Premier League too. If there was something like that for us in Europe, it would be quite cool,” she told Sportstar on the sidelines of the T20 World Cup earlier this year.
ALSO READ | How Japanese women prepared for a moment of blossoming
The wish for integration isn’t random. With cricket making the Los Angeles Summer Games, the ecosystem hopes this is the start of a long stay in the Olympic roster. In 2028, six teams each will compete in the men’s and women’s events, with rankings deciding the majority of the slots and qualifiers filling the gaps. The Asian Games is no different: an eight-team tournament that begins at the quarterfinal stage in a continental showpiece involving 46 countries.
In Aichi-Nagoya, China didn’t even get to play, despite making the cut, after rain washed out its quarterfinal against Bangladesh, the latter advancing due to higher seeding. Cricket’s intense weather vulnerabilities leave teams on the bigger stage of amateur sport short-changed when months of preparation and dreams can drown in a downpour.
Work at the roots
The International Cricket Council, especially after the recent FIFA World Cup, has made its intention of expanding cricket to counter football, covertly and overtly, known. Development initiatives with Associates, infrastructure assistance and advocacy have spruced up since the turn of the decade.
The Indonesian ecosystem is a direct beneficiary, having landed Asian Cricket Council membership a few years ago. Cricket chief Abhiram Singh Yadav credits the role of former ACC president and incumbent ICC chair Jay Shah for making room for Indonesia at the high tables of Asian cricket.
“Mr. Shah thinks quite broadly about the game. He sees the potential of global markets. Indonesia is a country with a population of over 200 million. We are a G20 member. That recognition also came through in Mr. Sanjog Gupta’s (ICC CEO) visit. Both are working towards developing emerging markets and looking at non-traditional cricketing nations. With the sport now in the Olympics, this is the only way we can make cricket inclusive,” Yadav told Sportstar.
“Cricket wants to work towards becoming bigger than FIFA, and that requires looking deep into different international markets. As an Associate member, we want to support that vision. Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, Japan and Korea are promising markets, and we want to be a model for others to follow,” Yadav added. UAE, too, has a promising women’s side drawing heavily from the expat Indian population in the Gulf. While the national side benefits from their quality, the Emirates Cricket Board has been trying to foster an interest in the sport among natives too.
ALSO READ | Asian Games 2026: Shafali Verma scores her maiden T20I century during Bangladesh semifinal
“I won’t say that it’s a challenge,” Emirates Cricket Board COO Subhan Ahmed told Sportstar. “If you look at the overall demographics of this country, about 80 per cent of the population is expat. So it’s natural that the sports that they have played back home and that culture travels. The infrastructure here has grown because of it. We have 62 grounds across the seven states in the Emirates. There are some Full Members who do not have that kind of base. The local Emirati population is always a part of our plans. We don’t envisage a complete takeover by the local population, but we do anticipate greater participation given how much it can do for overall community unity here,” he added.
Indonesia, too, faced the same predicament of leaning entirely on the diaspora, but Yadav underlined that the setup is on a war footing to ensure cricket can become a 100 per cent localised sport.
Sports tourism has emerged as a way to galvanise smaller boards, as Yadav pointed out earlier, allowing them to tap newer markets within cricket. Sanjog Gupta has also identified China as a potential cash cow, hoping to convert at least some of its 1.4 billion people into cricket fanatics.
The ICC pumped USD 1.5 million into cricket in the nation, broadcast World Cup games in Mandarin to whet the appetite for the game, and has also seen the cricketing system build three top-level cricket venues, including a new 1,500-seat stadium in Taicang that is primed to host domestic and international matches and provide a training base for the national teams. The Marylebone Cricket Club has chimed in with support, saying it will send a women’s team there for an overseas tour next year.
The women’s national team, made almost entirely of homegrown players, has climbed 10 spots in the rankings over the last two years, which only underlines why that faith isn’t misplaced. That Asiad washout stings that much more now, right?
Dissonance at the top
The one-sided nature of this fairytale Asian romp was known to all before the curtains rose. But even for the world’s most successful team, backed by the world’s richest board and cricketing circulatory system, multi-sport events bring with them nostalgia and old-time achievement.
Indian skipper Harmanpreet Kaur, for instance, grew up in Punjab, where tales of legendary Olympians were often served alongside a child’s daily meals. The Games — of the Asian, Commonwealth and Olympic kind — hold a special place. It’s why her creaking knees want to carry on till she makes it to Los Angeles 2028, till that Olympic gold finds its way to her neck.
ALSO READ | Asian Games a teaser to 2028 Los Angeles Olympics: India Women’s head coach Amol Muzumdar
While parallels can be drawn between India’s comfort and dominance here and what might lie ahead at the Olympics, that would be an oversimplification. At the end of the day, Olympic cricket — as it stands — is still a T20 knockout tournament, the sport’s most fickle format. It cares not for past laurels. Fortune only favours the brave here, as India learned at the Birmingham CWG when it watched Australia don gold while it made do, grudgingly, with silver.
For all the expansion, the view from the top remains fairly myopic. Players being dragged into the political theatre of handshakes and trophy tug-of-war took the sheen off what is, in theory, one of the most promising learning opportunities for teams on the fringes of the power core. If one wants to be doggedly apolitical, two high-importance tournaments in 2026 without television referrals and held at a single venue are no vote of confidence in the efforts of the custodians of the sport. The ICC can’t wash its hands off either, as the inaugural Women’s Champions Trophy — taken away from Sri Lanka due to political interference in administration — is due to be held across just two Tier 2 Indian venues.
While the prosperous continue to prosper, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh face tumultuous transitions within and outside the team. Outside India, franchise cricket is not a reality or a liberating financial avenue for any other Asian nation. FairBreak Global, an ICC-based independent initiative that brought several Asian Associate nations much-needed game time with stars from SENA countries, is now defunct.
Indonesia, for all its ambition, still played the Asia Cup without a shirt sponsor, while a Full Member nation like Afghanistan is still being shielded from accountability for failing the cardinal principle of said membership — mandatorily fielding a women’s team.
Hierarchy masquerades as competition in Asian cricket, with one crown after another for those already on top, while the rest are left arguing over scraps of legitimacy. Showpieces without follow-ups, expansion without equity and Olympic ambition without Olympic-standard competitiveness will only widen the gap the game is desperate to bridge.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Republic of Korea have a long-standing partnership spanning over 75 years. As a result of their fruitful collaboration, there has been significant progress in health and development all around the world. The Republic of Korea has gone from being a donor-recipient country to a donor-country and is now a leader in global health and playing a critical role on the world stage.
Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General for External Relations and Governance (WHO) and Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination (Ministry of Health and Welfare, Republic of Korea), together with counterparts from WHO and the Government of the Republic of Korea. © WHO
To further strengthen this partnership and our commitment to working jointly to address global health challenges, WHO and the Republic of Korea convened their second Strategic Dialogue in Seoul from 28 to 29 August 2024. Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Directory-General for External Relations and Governance, led the WHO delegation and was accompanied by an in-person team and colleagues participating virtually from the three levels of the Organization (headquarters, regional, and country offices).
Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination, Ministry of Health, led the Republic of Korea delegation and was joined by senior officials including Dr Young-Mee Jee, Commissioner, Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency, as well as senior counterparts from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety.
In addition, in line with WHO's work to enhance collaboration with parliamentarians, the WHO delegation also met with various Members of the National Assembly that are championing the global health agenda.
The recently concluded two-day meeting resulted in an alignment of priorities and paved the way for enhanced collaboration between WHO and the Government of Korea.

Top executives at Prudential Financial’s Japan unit will take pay cuts after a panel of outside experts issued a report on widespread employee misconduct involving customers’ money.
President Hiromitsu Tokumaru and two others will take a 30% reduction in compensation for three months to take responsibility for the matter, the company said in a statement on Thursday. The investigative committee found that issues at the unit of the U.S. insurance group, Prudential Life, stemmed from structural problems in its governance framework and business model.
The case is the latest in a series of scandals to hit Japan’s insurance industry in recent years, undermining confidence at a time when households are looking to invest more of their savings. The country’s financial regulator is considering penalizing Prudential Life with measures including a temporary business suspension order, according to a person with knowledge of the matter.
Prudential Life established the committee after disclosing alleged misconduct by more than 100 current and former sales employees that caused more than ¥3.1 billion ($20 million) in customer losses. Cases ranged from staff pitching fictitious investments to borrowing money from clients.
Evaluation and compensation systems reinforced incentives to prioritize short-term results, the company said in the statement. The company will revise these to encourage behavior that emphasizes long-term customer relationships, compliance and sound sales practices, it said.
Prudential Life has voluntarily halted new life insurance sales since February to focus on overhauling its governance and sales practices. It extended the initial 90-day suspension until early November, saying it needed more time to complete the reforms.
Prudential Life, which began operations in Japan in 1988, has carved out a niche in a market long dominated by domestic players including Nippon Life Insurance and Daiichi Life Group. It relies on a relatively small sales force known as “life planners,” who target affluent customers including business owners and doctors and offer highly tailored products and financial planning services.
Traditional Japanese insurers, by contrast, employ much larger sales forces that have historically sold more standardized products through community-based, face-to-face networks.
Prudential’s sales representatives built a reputation for aggressive selling. At a news conference in January, company executives said a compensation structure heavily dependent on commissions had distorted incentives and contributed to breaches of internal rules.
In its annual policy priorities released in September, the Financial Services Agency said it would “take rigorous supervisory action” against misconduct by insurance companies.
Three years ago, authorities penalized the country’s largest property-and-casualty insurers for colluding on insurance premiums for corporate clients. More recently, employees of several major life insurers were found to have mishandled data.

The Center for Humane Technology, the online safety group cofounded by former Google product manager Tristan Harris and featured in the hit documentary The Social Dilemma, is laying off about half of its 16 non-founder employees, ex-staffers tell WIRED. The organization is ending its policy research and litigation work to focus instead on what it calls “founder-led” projects.
The nine departures, which include executive director Julie Guirado and senior director of strategy Camille Carlton, arrive shortly after the center scored a series of major courtroom victories against social media companies. The lawsuits drew on its research alleging that the platforms were deliberately designed to keep kids glued to their screens.
But amid that success, internal debates had been brewing for years over the organization’s direction, according to 16 former workers, most of whom spoke with WIRED earlier this year on the condition of anonymity because they feared professional repercussions.
CHT’s board ultimately determined that trying to operate both as an advocacy group fronted by Harris and a think tank producing policy papers had stretched it too thin. Moving forward, the organization will focus on initiatives with its founders at the forefront, including “public education, targeted briefings, and private coordination,” building upon their success “reaching broad audiences and engaging influential decisionmakers,” the board announced last week.
Functions such as assisting in litigation and evaluating AI tools would be eliminated, the board added, without specifying an exact number of layoffs.
“This moment of accelerated AI risk demands we focus on one strategy, and we have chosen to focus on what we have always done best so that we can meet the moment,” board chair Premal Shah said in a statement to WIRED.
In recent years, Harris has joined a growing chorus of voices sounding the alarm about the risks posed by advanced artificial intelligence, warning of a potential “AI takeover” if the software evades control. “We have to act right now before it’s too late,” he told NBC News last month.
The center encouraged people to sign a major petition to pause AI development and helped organize a hearing in Congress about the dangers of chatbots. It also advised on lawsuits and investigations probing AI labs for their design choices, including an ongoing case filed against OpenAI by parents of a teenager who died by suicide after interacting with ChatGPT. Harris also starred in a documentary released on Netflix last month, The AI Doc, which urges viewers to demand that Congress intervene to protect the public from the technology’s risks.
Founded in 2017, the Center for Humane Technology competes with well-established nonprofits and numerous newer entrants for funding and attention to shape AI policy. Cyberattacks by AI agents from OpenAI and other labs have renewed calls to hold tech developers liable for design and engineering failures.
With an annual budget of roughly $6 million and a similar amount in reserves, the center has been funded by wealthy families and foundations. But as it doubles down on Harris, former employees fear resources might be diverted away from addressing what they believe are more pressing concerns about AI’s impact on democracy and civil liberties.
Gail Barnes, who advised the center on social media strategy in its early days, says the board is dropping work that was supposed to convert Harris’ fame “into durable pressure” that could help facilitate real change inside companies.
“Whether that is wisdom or a retreat depends on whether you think the binding constraint on AI right now is still ‘people haven’t heard the argument’ or ‘the argument has no institutional teeth.’ CHT is picking the first,” Barnes says.
Big Star
Harris excels at producing compelling sound bites, and he has long been a fixture in the media, at conferences, and on Capitol Hill. “He’s brilliant. He’s articulate,” a former CHT colleague says. “He could have easily spent his entire career on the dark side. For whatever reason, he came to appreciate that this was messed up.”
Harris cofounded the center with Aza Raskin, the self-proclaimed inventor of the infinite scroll, and Randy Fernando, who once worked in developer education at Nvidia. The goal was to push tech companies to take more responsibility for the social consequences of their products, which in the early days meant examining issues like whether they were fomenting political radicalization or harming the mental health of teenagers. The language Harris used to describe these problems was quickly adopted across Silicon Valley.
Internal documents from Meta released in court this year show company researchers discussed reaching out to Harris as early as 2018, when his warnings that apps were intentionally designed to be addictive entered the mainstream. His national profile grew further with the release of The Social Dilemma on Netflix in 2020.
“It’s hard to understate how helpful The Social Dilemma was for launching tech accountability” as an advocacy field, says a leader at another nonprofit, who also sought anonymity to protect their relationship with CHT.
But inside the organization, Harris sometimes clashed with his team about whether to focus their efforts on consumers, tech companies, or lawmakers, former staffers say. Some colleagues grew frustrated with Harris’ frequently shifting whims, describing the organization’s culture as needlessly “frenetic” and “insanity-inducing.” Shah disputed the characterization, but acknowledged the center’s culture is fast-paced given the urgency of its mission.
The center developed an online course at one point for tech workers who wanted to learn how to build humane systems, and while it drew thousands of participants, CHT decided to retire it as Harris’ focus shifted to concerns about AI, according to people familiar with the project. Another initiative to create resources for educators to make sense of issues around screen time fell by the wayside, the people say. Harris kept coming back to the center being “a vehicle for him to speak to the world,” according to one ex-employee.
The center’s podcasts and videos featuring Harris and Raskin have attracted large audiences, former workers say. Harris also landed private meetings with US lawmakers and executives at top tech companies. Former employees describe the group’s strategy as putting more emphasis on “grasstops” activism over the more familiar “grassroots,” which some viewed as misguided.
Shah says CHT believes “mass communications creates grassroots pressure, which unlocks action from the grasstops” and that Harris “is one of the very few people in the world who is invited and can communicate effectively to mass media audiences across the political spectrum.”
Some former employees allege that CHT’s founders were eager to remain Silicon Valley insiders, and thus were more reluctant to criticize companies where they previously worked or where close personal contacts have worked. (Shah disputes the characterizations and says CHT “has always been tough on companies.”)
Some ex-employees described Harris’ management style as taxing, which they allege led to high turnover. In 2023, employees returned from a staff retreat feeling upset after being asked to participate in trust-building exercises they felt were overly personal, according to several former workers. CHT’s independent board members got involved, and Harris later stepped down as executive director to become the organization’s president, according to the former employees.
Shah says that employee turnover "stemmed from differences in problem analysis and approaches to achieving the organization’s core mission.” He also denied that Harris’ role change was related to what happened at the retreat.
Whatever turmoil may have been happening inside CHT, the broader strategy Harris used to go after tech companies was paying off. In 2021, state attorneys general across the US opened investigations into Meta and later sued the company for allegedly misleading teens and parents. This year, Meta agreed to settle some of the lawsuits for billions of dollars. Juries, including one that heard testimony from Raskin, put the company on the hook for additional penalties in separate cases. Other social media platforms agreed to settle similar litigation this year.
In an interview with WIRED earlier this year, the leader of the other tech nonprofit praised CHT’s less flashy work in statehouses and courtrooms. The shift away from it is “disappointing,” the person says now. “Change comes from movements and democracy, not celebrities and backrooms.”
Some former employees say they expect that CHT will increasingly resemble what they jokingly refer to as the “Center of Helping Tristan.” Shah says the organization’s sole goal is ensuring “today’s most consequential technologies serve humanity.”

On August 1, 2026, West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari claimed that of the 27 lakh people whose names were deleted from the voter list after adjudication due to ‘logical discrepancy’, only seven lakh had filed appeals before the court-appointed appellate tribunals seeking inclusion in the electoral rolls.
Speaking at the launch of the Census self-enumeration exercise in Kolkata, he said, “Out of the 27 lakh people who were given an opportunity to approach the SIR tribunal, around seven lakh had applied. The rest have not submitted any application or appeal so far.”
The figure was reported by multiple media outlets which quoted the chief minister (1, 2, 3). Adhikari went on to link the failure to appeal with questions of citizenship, and citizenship with access to welfare, saying, “Until the entire process was completed, it would not be possible to determine whether those who had not made any claim as voters would later seek recognition as Indian citizens.” He added, “If someone is not a citizen of the country, they will not get benefits of any social scheme.”
Five days later, The Telegraph published the same seven-lakh figure, this time attributing it to an unnamed senior official of the West Bengal government. According to the report, the official said, “It has been found that only about 7 lakh of the 27 lakh voters excluded by the adjudicators for ‘logical discrepancies’ have appealed before the tribunals.” The official said the figure had emerged from a compilation of reports from various districts, and that the state authorities had no idea why the remaining 20 lakh had not appealed before the tribunals.
The Figure was Unverifiable at that Time
In August, the seven-lakh claim could not be independently verified against any official source because the Election Commission’s own disclosure did not provide a separate breakdown of appeals filed against the exclusion of voters. An RTI reply that disclosed the total number of appeals carried a footnote clarifying that the figure included both appeals against the inclusion of names in the electoral roll and appeals against exclusions.
The RTI was obtained by Isha Khan Choudhury, Congress MP from Dakshin Malda in West Bengal, and placed before the Supreme Court on August 24, 2026, during the hearing of a petition filed by Prasenjit Bose of the Congress and Derek O’Brien of the Trinamool Congress against the Election Commission of India.
During the hearing, Justice Joymalya Bagchi observed that the break-up of the appeals mattered since “it was exclusion which was causing an immediate violation of a person’s rights.” The bench consequently directed the ECI to provide a separate account of the appeals, specifying how many were pending before the tribunals and segregating appeals relating to voters who had been excluded or included, as well as cross-appeals.
The ECI submitted this segregation on September 16.
ECI Numbers Refute Adhikari’s Claim
According to the latest affidavit filed by the ECI before the Supreme Court on September 16, 2026, of the more than 38.31 lakh appeals filed, over 22 lakh were filed against exclusion by voters whose names had been excluded or deleted, while more than 16 lakh were filed against inclusion.
Of the more than 38 lakh appeals filed, only 1.26 lakh had been decided by that date. Annexure R/1 to the ECI’s affidavit provides a district-wise break-up of the total appeals submitted to the appellate tribunals and is reproduced below.
It must be noted that the total number of appeals filed, as mentioned in the ECI’s affidavit (38,31,429), does not match the total number of appeals submitted in Annexure R/1 (38,29,926). The discrepancy is 1,503 appeals. Nevertheless, the outcome-wise data provided in the annexure shows that 8,649 appeals resulted in exclusion from the electoral roll, while 1,13,943 resulted in inclusion. In other words, nearly 93% of the appeals that had been decided resulted in the elector being included in the electoral roll.
Did the Claims Accumulate after the CM’s Statement? No
One may argue that the chief minister spoke on August 1, while the Commission filed its figure in the Supreme Court on September 16, leaving enough time for appeals to have accumulated in the intervening period. The available data, however, allows this possibility to be tested directly, because appeal totals are available for both dates. On August 7, 2026, six days after the chief minister’s statement and a day after The Telegraph report, the tribunals already had 38,10,620 appeals, according to an RTI response from the ECI to Isha Khan Choudhury, Congress MP for Dakshin Malda. By September 10, 2026, the figure stood at 38,29,926, according to the district-wise report annexed to the Commission’s affidavit. Thus, the total number of appeals increased by just 19,306 across the entire state during this period.
In the light of the latest revelations made by an Indian Express investigation, which have raised serious questions about the functioning of the Election Commission of India and chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, the seven-lakh claim takes on an even greater significance.
To sum up, Suvendu Adhikari’s claim on August 1 that out of some 27 lakh electors placed under adjudication and subsequently excluded from the electoral roll, only seven lakh had appealed against their exclusion is difficult to reconcile with the data that was already available at the time. The ECI has made it clear that the number is around 22 lakh. The discrepancy assumes greater significance given that Manoj Agarwal, the then chief electoral officer of West Bengal who oversaw the SIR process, is now the Bengal’s chief secretary.

Texas carries out first US execution since Christa Pike's botched lethal injections
- Published
A death row inmate was executed by lethal injection on Wednesday evening in Texas, the first execution in the US since the failed attempt to put Christa Pike to death last week.
Lawyers for 46-year-old Jamaal Howard had asked a judge to pause the execution in light of Pike's botched injections last week, according to the BBC's US partner, CBS News.
But courts denied their requests, and he received a fatal dose of pentobarbital at the state prison in Huntsville. He was pronounced dead at 20:03 local time.
Howard was convicted and sentenced to death for the 2000 murder of a convenience store clerk during a robbery he committed.
His lawyers had argued that because Texas planned to inject Howard with the same drug - pentobarbital - that was used on Pike, he faced the same risks. They also alleged that Texas' supply of the drug had become degraded, as Pike's lawyers have similarly argued.
A court twice denied their appeals and the US Supreme Court also turned down the appeal late Wednesday.
"Texas should not be eager to follow in Tennessee's footsteps; a stay would keep that from happening," Howard's attorneys had argued, CBS reported.
Howard's attorneys also asked Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a Republican, to delay the execution by 30 days so they could seek additional information about the drug used in the execution. The governor did not grant the delay.
Howard was 20 when he shot Vickie Swartout, 42, who was working at a convenience store in Texas. Howard stole a carton of cigarettes and $114 from the register.
Asked if he had a final statement before his execution, Howard apologized to Swartout's family, who watched from a witness room, US media report.
"I wish that you accept my apology, and I wish for your forgiveness," Howard said. "I'm sorry for what happened. I wish you can learn to forgive me one of these days."
