Jagtar Singh Johal, a British Sikh man who was arrested in India in 2017 in connection with alleged terrorism offences, has been granted bail by a Delhi court.
Johal, from Scotland, was arrested for his alleged role in funding the Khalistan Liberation Force, which had carried out targeted killings in India’s Punjab region.
His full trial has been repeatedly deferred by the authorities in the federal court but largely similar conspiracy charges were dismissed by a court in Punjab last year. Throughout his detention the prosecution has failed to produce verifiable evidence, leading to the deferred hearings.
Johal, now 39, travelled to India to marry his fiancee in late 2017. On 4 November, three weeks after the wedding, the couple were shopping with a relative in the Punjab city of Jalandhar when a group of men took Johal from his car, placed a black hood over his head and put him in an unmarked vehicle. He claims he was then denied access to a lawyer and tortured in an attempt to extract a confession. A question remains over whether he was arrested following a tip-off from British intelligence services.
Commenting on Friday’s ruling, Johal’s Scotland-based brother Gurpreet Singh Johal said: “The past two years has been an expensive rollercoaster, contesting bails at the supreme court and back to the high court. I had a long, sleepless night knowing that the decision would be made this morning. Now, all I can think about is Jagtar walking out of prison. We have waited so long and fought so hard for this moment.”
He added of previous hearings: “Whenever the evidence against Jagtar is tested in court, judges find what we’ve said all along, which is that there isn’t any.
“How long will this sick joke of a legal process be allowed to continue? We’re obviously delighted that Jagtar will soon be released, but he won’t be truly free until he is back in Dumbarton, with his wife and family.”
Gurpreet Johal, who also lives in Dumbarton, has lobbied a succession of UK foreign secretaries, who have repeatedly admitted the case has dragged on too long, but have been reluctant to call publicly for his release on the grounds that they should not interfere in the judiciary of another country.
The UK government recently appointed Alistair Burt as a special envoy for complex consular cases and he has met Gurpreet Johal in Scotland to discuss the case.
Dan Dolan, the deputy executive director of Reprieve, one of the organisation’s fighting for Johal’s release, said: “While this judgment is welcome as Jagtar should not be in prison a day longer, we must now watch closely to ensure this order is actually implemented and not obstructed in any way. The conditions attached are likely to be onerous. We must also remember that Jagtar will still be facing the death penalty in eight cases against him, despite these cases essentially duplicating trumped-up charges on which he has already been fully acquitted.”
Chris Esdaile, a senior legal adviser to Redress, another organisaiton representing Johal, said granting bail “can’t undo the intolerable suffering caused by nine years of arbitrary detention”.
He added: “The need for accountability for the allegations of torture and the deeply flawed proceedings against Jagtar remains urgent.”
Johal’s lawyers said they were still awaiting the details of what would happen next in relation to posting bail terms. While the judges’ order was that Jagtar should be released on bail, he remained in custody while judges confirmed his bail conditions, which may be stringent. The court must also confirm the sums of money that must be posted as a bond.

As part of its ongoing bid to more tightly regulate international students, the Trump administration on Wednesday announced a proposed $70,000 fee for a popular work authorization program meant to give students professional experience.
The Department of Homeland Security said the fee would help combat alleged fraud and abuse in the work program, known as Optional Practical Training, which allows students to get hands-on work experience related to their field of study while still on a student visa. The department also said the restrictions would help U.S. citizens compete against international applicants in the job market.
“Optional Practical Training was never meant to be a back door into the American workforce, a subsidy for cheap labor, or a prize for those who game the system,” said a department spokesperson in a press release. “American workers should not have to compete against a program that has been turned into a pipeline for cheap foreign labor.”
An additional $30,000 fee would apply to students looking to participate in Optional Practical Training beyond one year; many science students remain in the program for three years. Academic institutions would be expected to pay the fee for each student they recommend for the work authorization program, and DHS estimates that it would collect $12.4 billion annually if the fees are finalized. The department plans to publish the proposed rule to the Federal Register on Thursday, though an unpublished version is already accessible, and DHS has said it will accept public comments through November 9.
Experts are already raising concerns that the proposal is yet another attempt by the Trump administration to close its doors to international students and scholars, who make up about a quarter of life science Ph.D. graduates and 60% of postdoctoral researchers. The nonprofit NAFSA: Association of International Educators, which is currently suing DHS over a separate attempt to place time limits on the kinds of visas used by postdocs and graduate students, warned that the new proposed fee was misguided.
“Imposing this new fee structure on Optional Practical Training is the latest in a series of developments that creates deep uncertainty for international students. OPT enables international students to gain the same hands-on experience as their domestic peers while filling labor shortages in high-demand STEM fields and generating jobs for U.S. workers on U.S. soil,” said Fanta Aw, NAFSA’s CEO, in a statement. “The research is clear: international students don’t take opportunities from Americans, they create them.”
To participate in Optional Practical Training, often known as OPT, international students need an administrator at their school to recommend them for the program before they apply for authorization from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, a division of DHS. Students then have 90 days to find a job.
This program is often a bridge for students looking to work in the U.S. long term. OPT authorizations for STEM graduates have risen from nearly 27,500 in 2015 to more than 95,000 in 2024. But DHS argues that with these growing numbers have come increasing reports of students, employers, and school administrations “engaged in schemes to exploit the current OPT regulations for fraudulent purposes.”
In its unpublished version of the proposed rule, the department alleges that there has been “widespread” use of OPT as an unlimited employment benefit with little to no connection to a student’s area of study. DHS cited a 2020 incident in which federal agents arrested 15 foreign students charged with fraudulently using OPT to stay in the U.S. The department also cited a more recent investigation that it says identified more than 10,000 international students working for “highly suspect” employers, which in some cases included empty or non-existent worksites.
DHS estimates that the new policy could lead to $4 billion a year in opportunity costs due to students losing out on work experience, employers losing productivity if they’re unable to replace international workers, and academic institutions losing international student enrollment. But the agency also stated that the benefits of protecting U.S. workers and the integrity of the OPT program outweigh any potential costs.
The work authorization program, which was formally created in 1992, has been a major draw for foreign students. A NAFSA survey conducted last year found that 54% of current graduate students and postdocs would not have come to the U.S. if OPT did not exist, though the survey did not ask about the impact of program fees.
It’s not the first time the Trump administration has sought to use steep fees to cut off internationals from the U.S. workforce. Last year, Trump issued an executive order that would impose a $100,000 fee on H-1B visas, used by foreign workers in high-skill fields such as engineering and biotech. Federal courts have blocked the fee for now, though DHS has reintroduced it as a proposed rule.
The administration is also seeking to put four-year caps on how long students and postdocs can remain in the U.S., alleging that a longstanding policy allowing these scholars to stay in the U.S. for the length of their training has incentivized fraud. A federal judge has issued a preliminary injunction preventing the time limits from taking effect; the order notes that plaintiffs opposed to the policy are likely to ultimately succeed in an ongoing lawsuit.
Even though many of these new policies have yet to take effect, current students and immigration experts say the Trump administration’s efforts have created a climate of fear and uncertainty that will turn students away from the U.S. There’s some evidence that is already happening. A survey this summer by the Association of American Universities found that, while domestic student applications for U.S. Ph.D. programs went up by 3% this year, international applications dipped 21%.

The Keralam government’s announcement that it will make private health care more “affordable” through consultations with the private health sector, and that a Bill in this regard was in the offing, should be seen against the State’s seven-year legal battle before the Kerala High Court upheld the Kerala Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulations) Act 2018, throwing out all objections raised by private hospitals.
The KCE Act was the first ever attempt made in the State to bring the entire health sector, public and private, under a regulatory framework.
But the Act was systematically opposed and its implementation stalled at every turn by the private health sector in the State.
It was in November last year that the Kerala High Court threw out all objections raised by the Kerala Private Hospitals’ Association (KPHA) and the Indian Medical Association (IMA) and upheld the validity of the Act.
Contentious area
Unlike the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010 (Central Act 23 of 2010), which attempted to cap the treatment/procedure/diagnostic rates charged by the private health sector by fixing a price range, the KCE Act had not touched this contentious area at all.
The KCE Act just insisted on mandatory registration of all clinical establishments under all systems of medicines (including hospitals, clinics and laboratories) and that every establishment maintain certain minimum standards based on the category in which they fall. It also said that hospitals display their rates for various procedures openly so that there is transparency.
However, the private health sector argued that it violated rights under Article 14 and Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.
Appeal in SC
Even after the High Court specifically held that KCE Act’s Section 16 (mandatory registration of clinical establishments), Section 39 (display of fee rates and package rates for services) and Section 47 (obligations concerning life-saving treatment/emergency care and safe transfer of patients) were constitutionally valid and gave directives to the government to implement the Act without delay, KPHA went in appeal to the Supreme Court.
The Supreme Court has not stayed the KCE Act, but granted members of the petitioning associations interim protection against coercive action by the government.
Yet to register
Kerala Clinical Establishments Council, which is responsible for the implementation of the Act, maintains that the registration process is continuing and that even now, many clinical establishments are yet to register themselves under the council.
Small hospitals with up to 15 beds have been given some concessions by the council, trimming down the checklist for assessment to just basic and essential points, so that at least the basic registration brings these establishments too within the regulatory framework.
The government’s efforts to draft a new Bill to bring in a regulatory framework that “protects patients’ interests while taking into account the operating costs and practical difficulties of private hospitals” is well-intentioned, but the fact remains that the private health sector is still holding out against the KCE Act at the Supreme Court.
Questions are also being raised whether a new legislation is in order or if the costing regulations can be incorporated into the KCE Act itself.
‘Entirely welcome’
Meanwhile, public health activists like B. Ekbal have stated that any attempt by the government to regulate the treatment expenditure in the private sector and save people from catastrophic health expenditure is entirely welcome.
Dr. Ekbal said that though private hospitals are an essential component of the health system, health care cannot be left entirely to market logic. It is the government’s responsibility to regulate the sector adequately so that patients are not exploited.
In a statement here, Dr. Ekbal said that the Standard Treatment Guidelines (STGs) should be insisted on and that the government initiate a scientific cost evaluation of various medical and diagnostic procedures and treatments so that a rational and transparent rate list suited to the State can be evolved.

Indians, particularly IT sector professionals, hoping to work in the US, have a steep uphill climb. And, under the Donald Trump administration the fear is that the path may itself be lost! The repeated tightening of entry under the 
H-1B visa
 program is proof of the growing uncertainty.
Three H-1B related changes are stacking on top of each other: the multiple $100,000 fee proposals, the wage-weighted lottery favoring more senior workers, new layoff and compliance scrutiny, and now the OPT/STEM-OPT $70,000 fee proposal for students looking to work in the US.
And then there are statements from the Trump administration, hinting at doing away with the H-1B visa system itself. While admittedly, experts find that to be a far-fetched possibility, they do treat it as a symptom of the growing restrictions.
Indians are the biggest beneficiaries of the H-1B visa programme, making up around 70% of the total approved list. Hence, it’s obvious that they would absorb the maximum impact of the immigration restrictions.
H-1B visas: Indians biggest beneficiaries
The first consequence is the disruption to the traditional Indian pathway: Indian education gets you into an Indian IT company, which gets you an H-1B visa and US employment, and you get added to the green-card queue.
That pathway is set to become much narrower or worse may even disappear!
H-1B visas: What is happening?
Experts say H-1B visas are an indication of the larger crackdown to ensure Americans don’t lose out on jobs.
Rajiv Dabhadkar, Founder, National Organization For Software and Technology Professionals makes an important point: what is happening is not a visa system overhaul, it’s a deeper labour market problem from the US government perspective.
“The US government is increasingly looking not only at the worker but at the entire employment chain,” he tells TOI.
That means asking:
- Who sponsored the worker? 
- Who actually employs and controls the worker? 
- Where does the worker actually work?
-  What wage is being paid? 
- Was the worker recruited for a genuine job? 
- Is an intermediary taking a margin between the employer and the worker? 
- Was an American worker displaced? 
- Was a qualified American worker given a genuine opportunity to compete for the position?
“There is an older but highly relevant principle here. The 2010 Neufeld memorandum placed emphasis on the employer's “right to control” an H-1B beneficiary - essentially, who determines when, where and how the worker performs the job. That principle is particularly relevant when examining third-party staffing and intermediary arrangements,” Dabhadkar says.
“This matters because the H-1B worker can actually be a victim of the same system that potentially disadvantages the American worker. The DOL OIG's investigation specifically refers to foreign workers being exploited through wage kickbacks and coercive arrangements, while also referring to below-wage labour undercutting American workers,” he adds.
Indian IT professionals to be hit hardest
Indian-born professionals continued to dominate the H-1B programme in FY 2025. The US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) approved 406,348 H-1B petitions, of which 283,772, or approximately 70%, were for beneficiaries born in India.
Technology-related occupations were the largest category across the H-1B programme overall. Computer-related roles accounted for 252,088 approvals, or 62% of all beneficiaries. Systems analysis and programming was the largest detailed occupation, representing 50.4% of approvals.
H-1B visas by occupational Groups
According to Akhil Chandna, Partner and Global People Solutions Leader, Grant Thornton Bharat, these figures point to sustained demand for technology skills, although USCIS does not publish a combined breakdown showing occupations specifically for Indian-born beneficiaries.
As Xiao Wang, CEO, Boundless Immigration notes: A typical Indian H-1B holder is a computer and IT professional; the main beneficiaries are software developers, systems analysts, programmers, and IT consultants.
Indian nationals took about 70% of all approved H-1B petitions last year, and IT workers were over 65% of H-1Bs over the past 5 years!
The median annual compensation for all approved H-1B beneficiaries in FY 2025 was around $133,000, with median computer-specific roles at $140,000.
But, as Wang says: the range is large - $117,000 at the 25th percentile and $179,000 at the 75th.
According to the Boundless Immigration CEO, the impact for Indians is split across various job levels.
For example, senior and highly paid Indian engineers at US tech firms are relatively insulated, and the wage-weighting actually favors them.
But, early-career Indian workers and the IT-services staffing model are the ones squeezed hard, because that model runs on volume at lower wage levels, which is precisely what both the flat fee and the wage-weighting penalize.
As Akhil Chandna points out, the H-1B programme continues to be driven largely by demand for technology talent, and it’s a trend that is only expected to accelerate with the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence and emerging technologies.
“Against this backdrop, recent policy changes appear less focused on reducing H-1B numbers and more on reshaping the programme to attract highly skilled, higher-paid talent while strengthening safeguards for the US workforce,” he tells TOI.
H-1B visa selection rate by wage level
The bottom line is that litigation is now becoming a recurring feature of the immigration system.
The $100,000 H-1B fee has been blocked by two federal judges, with business groups and other organizations challenging the administration's authority and implementation.
In summary, the issue is not simply that one visa is becoming harder. The larger problem is systemic uncertainty across multiple legal pathways.
What Indian IT companies could do
According to a recent report, H-1B visa registrations by TCS, Infosys, HCLTech, Wipro, LTM and Tech Mahindra plunged 92% for FY27 to 1,763 from 21,919 a year earlier.
The fall is far steeper than at major US employers, pointing to a structural shift in how Indian technology companies deploy talent in America.
The shift is therefore already visible and further acceleration is likely.
The top seven Indian firms won a little under 5,000 initial H-1B approvals in the most recent cycle, down roughly 70% from FY2015 and 37% from FY2024.
Company-wise H-1B visa approval
“The main trend is that the body-shop model of flying Indian IT consultants to the client in the US model is gone, and it's being replaced by a mix of US local hiring for client-facing work and a much bigger offshore footprint in India for everything else. The crackdown speeds up a transition the economics were already driving,” Xiao Wang tells TOI.
According to Rajiv Dabhadkar, the traditional model was: India employee + H-1B + US client site + onsite delivery
The emerging model is increasingly: US local employee + India-based engineering/delivery team + global technology platforms
H-1B visas: What are the alternatives?
Xiao Wang does not see the H-1B visa programme being scrapped, despite the noise around it.
“No administration can unilaterally scrap H-1B. It's written into statute (the Immigration and Nationality Act), so abolishing it takes an act of Congress. What's actually happening is death by restriction, making it more expensive and harder to get,” he tells TOI.
Experts say alternative US visa options remain available for certain professionals, including the L-1 visa for intra-company transfers, the O-1 visa for individuals with extraordinary ability, and, in limited cases, employment-based green card pathways. These routes, however, typically have narrower eligibility requirements than the H-1B.
But, while alternatives exist, getting them is not straightforward or easy.
H-1B visa alternatives: In & Outside US
Rajiv Dabhadkar says L-1 and O-1 are not straightforward H-1B substitutes: L-1 is limited to qualifying intracompany transfers, while O-1 requires extraordinary ability and has a much higher evidence threshold.
EB-1 is similarly highly selective, while EB-2 and EB-3 face a major India-specific obstacle: long green-card backlogs, he notes. All available FY2026 EB-2 immigrant visas for India had also been exhausted before the fiscal year ended, he adds.
“It is tempting to say that if H-1B becomes unavailable, Indian professionals can simply move to another US visa category. That is not a realistic description of the current system. The alternatives exist legally, but for a large population of Indian professionals they are not scalable substitutes for H-1B,” says Rajiv Dabhadkar.
Akhil Chandna says that beyond the US, countries such as Canada, the UK, Australia, Germany, Singapore and the UAE continue to attract skilled Indian professionals through a range of work and residence programmes.
The unexpected advantage for India
Not all will be lost, though. In fact, India may stand to benefit.
There is the possibility of remote working, which in turn would create jobs in India.
“Work that can be performed remotely, such as software development, testing and support services, may increasingly be delivered from India and other global delivery centres,” says Akhil Chandna.
He also believes that a complete shift away from H-1B sponsorship is unlikely.
“US businesses will continue to need specialized talent on the ground for project leadership, client engagement and complex technology implementations. The more likely outcome is a balanced approach: stronger local hiring in the US, selective H-1B sponsorship for critical skills, and expanded offshore delivery for roles that do not require physical presence,” he tells TOI.
Rajiv Dabhadkar explains how this helps: it would mean more engineering in India; more Global Capability Centres; more AI and data science work in India; more product development in India; more cloud and cybersecurity engineering in India; more remote delivery; more US local hiring for customer-facing roles.
“This creates a potentially unexpected outcome. H-1B restrictions could simultaneously produce: more American hiring and more high-value employment in India. That is why I don't see the future simply as "Indian IT loses because of H-1B restrictions." The business model is being redesigned,” he concludes.

Spanish pensioner whose eviction sparked nationwide protests dies, union says
- Published
An elderly woman whose eviction sparked nationwide protests over Spain's housing crisis and a political row that triggered early elections has died, according to Madrid's tenants union.
Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was forcibly removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years on 23 September after she was unable to afford rent increases.
The company that owned the flat later offered to allow her to return at a lower rate - but she was unable to sign an agreement as she had been admitted to hospital.
"We regret to announce that Maricarmen passed away today," the Madrid Tenants' Union said in a statement, adding her situation marked "a turning point in the history of this country".
Union spokesperson Alicia del Río said: "Speculation costs lives, and today rentierism has finished killing our colleague Maricarmen" but "her memory lives on with us".
A cause of death was not announced.
Abascal's death was received in Puerta del Sol with a big collective gasp, then followed by a minute of silence.
It is in this square in the centre of Madrid where thousands have been camping since Abascal's eviction last month to demand more affordable housing.
On Wednesday, it became the place to pay tribute to her.
People lit dozens of candles around the square in a small improvised vigil that glowed with a warm light on a dry and warm autumn night.
Other candles formed an altar to Abascal in front of the headquarters of the Community of Madrid government.
Messages on cardboard banners next to the candles read "it's not a death, it's a killing", "the fight will continue" and "Mari Carmen, the grandmother of the whole country", among others.
A few hundred people then took to the streets that connect Puerta del Sol with the Spanish Congress, just 500m away, in an improvised protest.
During the march people chanted: "We will not tolerate a single eviction more" and "the fight will continue, Mari Carmen is still alive". There were other chants against fascism and against the police.
The police had set up barriers to block the march. There was not a big police presence, and there was the tension that protests sometimes have.
Many protesters seemed to feel the police have been complicit in the evictions, as under court orders they have to remove tenants who have been served eviction notices.
After a couple of hours, the chants near Congress gave way to another minute of silence. Then, a big collective shout of "murderers".
Wednesday night's march has finished, but the camping, already on its 12th night, will continue "as long as necessary" one of the protesters told the BBC.
Abascal became a symbol for Spain's housing crisis following her eviction.
Her father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent.
However, Urbagestión, which bought the property in 2018, increased the rent from €500 per month (£428; $572) to €2,650 (£2,280; $3,020).
The company later offered to reduce this to €1,650 - still €300 more than Abascal's monthly pension.
Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts and the case has received increasing media attention.
Anger over the situation grew, leading to protests and putting pressure on the coalition government to approve emergency housing legislation - but it was rejected in Congress last week.
That led to further protests, with tens of thousands of people taking to the streets in cities across the country over the weekend.
Referring to the rejected bills, the Madrid Tenants' Union said: "While a historic agreement was reached that would have allowed her to return to her home, this solution has come too late. An absolutely avoidable situation after a torturing process."
It said the events surrounding her eviction represented a turning point in the country's history, but added that the cost to get to this point had been "too high".
"Above all, we will fulfil what she always asked of us: 'fight, keep fighting for what is yours'," it said.
In a video recorded from her hospital bed following her eviction, Maricarmen said: "I haven't managed to defend my home, but I have fought so that others can learn to fight for what's theirs."
"All my love goes to Maricarmen's family and loved ones," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said. "A hug as well to everyone who today feels this loss as their own."
Opposition People's Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo also sent his condolences to Maricarmen's loved ones, as he said on X: "No campaign, no parties, no self-interested exploitation. No more stones in the wall.
"In the face of a person's death, only respect is in order," he added.
Earlier on Wednesday, unions had called a general strike to take place on 11 November, demanding housing reforms.
The public outcry over Abascal's situation has led to political turmoil in Spain.
On Monday Sánchez, who leads a leftist coalition that does not hold a majority in parliament, called an early election for 29 November. It followed his failure to get the emergency housing legislation through Congress.
The political right had argued that the government's attempt to intervene in the housing market would have led to fewer homes being rented and would have raised prices further.
Speaking on Monday, Sánchez said he needed "a broader progressive majority" that can "overcome the resistance of the elites" to push through reforms.
Other issues not relating to housing, such as numerous corruption scandals linked to his party, and pressures relating to the cost of living and immigration, have also caused him problems.
Most opinion polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next election. However, they would be expected to need the support of the hard-right Vox party to form a government.

A ‘Wall of Hope’, a youth-led initiative by the Schizophrenia Research Foundation (SCARF) and its Department of Youth Mental Health, was unveiled at the IIT-Madras Research Park in Taramani on Saturday, a press release said.
With young people facing increasing mental health challenges and suicide remaining concern, creating spaces for expression, connection, resilience, and help-seeking is vital.
The mental health campaign, which began on October 10, 2025, encourages young people aged 10-25 to express, share, and reflect upon their personal reasons for living, through brief messages of hope.
Adolescents and young adults across the country were invited to write the purpose of life on colourful post-it notes.
The activity is completely youth-led through peer leaders and trainer modules, where young people played a central role in leading and facilitating the campaign.
More than 20,000 responses from across six States have been collected.
Additionally, 400 volunteers have been trained to conduct this activity, which is voluntary and anonymous, to initiate and foster conversations around mental health.
Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, Madras High Court judge, and Lakshmi Vijayakumar, founder of suicide prevention organisation SNEHA, participated in the event, besides SCARF vice-chairperson R. Thara and director Sridhar Vaitheswaran.
(Assistance for overcoming suicidal thoughts is available on the State’s health helpline 104, Tele-MANAS 14416, and Sneha’s suicide prevention helpline 044-24640050)

Former world number one Jon Rahm is quitting LIV Golf, robbing the breakaway circuit of one of its biggest stars while it fights to emerge from Chapter 11 bankruptcy.
Rahm’s attorney John Beck told a bankruptcy hearing on Wednesday that the two-times major champion made his decision after looking over details of LIV Golf’s planned next phase.
“Mr. Rahm has independently reviewed the proposed terms of LIV 2.0, as the parties have been referring to it, and has determined that those terms are unacceptable as to him, and he will not be participating going forward in LIV 2.0,” Beck told the court.
Other golfers asked a US bankruptcy judge to help terminate their contracts and clarify their ability to negotiate with other tournament organizers and sponsors as their LIV contracts go unpaid.
LIV has already agreed to terminate Sergio Garcia’s contract after determining that the league would not honour its terms, and attorneys for Bryson DeChambeau, Cameron Smith, An Byeong-hun, Marc Leishman, Cameron Tringale and Matthew Wolff asked the judge to allow those players out of their old contracts.
Ending those contracts would not preclude those players from agreeing to participate in LIV 2.0.
According to sources with knowledge of league operations, conversations with players regarding their participation in LIV Golf 2.0 remain on track, and statements made in court today do not change the trajectory, timeline, or momentum of the transaction.
ALSO READ: Kapil Dev: Men and women pros could one day play under one golf umbrella
Rahm, one of the most high-profile players to join LIV Golf, has won three consecutive season-long individual titles on LIV since joining the circuit in late 2023, eight months after winning the Masters for his second major title.
When LIV Golf filed for Chapter 11 protection in New Jersey last month, its filing listed several star golfers as creditors still owed millions in unsecured claims. Among them, Rahm had the largest claim among players at $7.5 million.
Earlier this week LIV secured funding from BC Partners to help it emerge from restructuring and strengthen its financial footing ahead of the 2027 season. The financing, up to $300 million, remains subject to bankruptcy court approval and customary conditions.
BC Partners Credit, which provides financing to middle-market companies, said the funding would support what it described as the next phase of LIV Golf, under which players would become equity owners of both the league and its teams.

One Nation’s new AI-generated campaign video is a new low – even for them.
The video – reportedly played at the party’s Victorian campaign launch over the weekend – is an AI-generated collection of racist tropes, depicting a man who appears to be African brandishing a machete, an apparently Middle Eastern man with an explosive vest, a South Asian man in a turban talking about “mass migration” and an Indigenous elder talking about people receiving “money … on the basis of need, not identity”.
But the inflammatory clip says more about the wild west of online politicking created by cheap, unrestricted access to AI videos, and why governments need to empower watchdog bodies to do more about it.
The video was barely mentioned in most media reporting, which otherwise largely focused on the rousing reception Pauline Hanson received from her supporters, the music that was played over loudspeakers and the Trump-esque pledge from candidate Mark Nicholson – the producer of the “Please Explain” cartoon series – to jail Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan. Guardian Australia, previously barred from One Nation events, did not attempt to attend Saturday’s launch.
Coverage has focused on the first part of the video, an AI-generated scene of a young man “coming out” as a conservative to his leftwing family. As progressive campaign group GetUp observed, it’s a scene cribbing from a similar Israeli campaign video from Benjamin Netanyahu.
It could also be pointed out how tired the gags are. Blue-haired hipsters with nose rings, eating mung beans? Revolutionary. Were the jokes generated by ChatGPT as well?
There’s an argument for ignoring it entirely, so as to not give it the attention and free advertising the party obviously wants. It is rage bait, seeking to draw a response and then complain about the response as further proof that One Nation is being “picked on” or is “riling up the lefties”. The response of a Hobart cafe frequented by Hanson’s daughter Lee pledging to donate takings from One Nation customers to the Greens – and accompanied by predictable “genuine hurt” from the younger Hanson – was entirely on script.
But for all the bad taste, there’s little anyone can do about it right now.
The Australian Communications and Media Authority cannot take action, because its powers don’t extend to this kind of content, and the video thus far seems to only exist online – not promoted in broadcast forms. Electoral commissions only have powers to regulate misinformation about the electoral process – not lies or distasteful content.
The federal Labor government has so far shrugged off growing calls from inside and outside parliament to ban the use of AI-generated content in election periods. As the government works to legislate around a raft of AI-related harms this year, the time would be ripe to deal with this long-ignored issue.
News Corp reported a One Nation spokesperson saying they were preparing “another version for broadcast”. That could technically put it inside Acma’s remit, but the tone of the ad is unlikely to breach current broadcasting rules, one industry source said.
So, then, is there something to the idea of clamping down on AI-generated content more broadly? Senator David Pocock thinks so: he’s been pushing for two years for the government to address generative AI around election campaigns, with 35,000 people signing his online petition calling for Labor to “legislate a ban on the use of deepfakes in elections before the next federal election”.
This week, the parliament’s joint committee on AI heard from witnesses saying action was overdue. The AEC said in a submission to the inquiry that AI makes it “more difficult for people to distinguish between authentic and manipulated content, increase[s] confusion about authoritative sources of information, and create[s] challenges for [electoral agencies]”.
“Inauthentic content or deepfakes circulating during the voting period, for instance, may well compromise the actual or perceived integrity of an election.”
These are not new concerns. A parliamentary report from October 2024 warned of AI “being used to adversely influence or undermine electoral and democratic processes” and “to deceive the public, create or exacerbate bias or influence public opinion or sentiment corrosively”.
Of course, the One Nation video is a different beast. No voter is being tricked into thinking a leftwing family has really changed its allegiances. But it should open the door to a wider discussion about whether this kind of content is appropriate for an election campaign.
AI lowers the barrier for entry for making such inflammatory videos. Normally, it would be harder – and more expensive – to hire a film crew and actors willing to act out such rhetoric.
In 2024, the Macquarie Dictionary named “enshittification” as its word of the year, defining the term as: “The gradual deterioration of a service or product brought about by a reduction in the quality of service provided, especially of an online platform, and as a consequence of profit-seeking.” Even casual users of Facebook, X, email platforms, Google search and basically any online marketplace would be familiar with the term.
Australian politics, like many parts of the world economy, is enduring what I’m calling “ensloppification”: the permeation of AI-generated slop into every crevice of society – and politics is not immune.
This week we have seen conservative campaign group Advance’s own Victorian AI ad, picturing a Labor election win as Daniel Andrews pops champagne corks and leads a conga line. Liberal MP Jason Wood was factchecked by AAP for posting “a fake image of Anthony Albanese arriving at a deserted airport”, while AAP has also debunked numerous AI-generated political interview-style videos purportedly shot outside Parliament House.
Prof Terry Flew, of the Centre for AI Trust and Governance, told the inquiry on Wednesday that Australia had no single agency to address all misinformation risks, but recommended that government consider prohibiting AI-generated deepfakes during election periods.
“There are real risks that AI-generated misinformation, as well as what has come to be known as ‘AI slop’, will further erode public trust in institutions and degrade the wider information ecosystem,” Flew said.
“[AI-generated deepfakes go] beyond the legitimate bounds of public campaigning and prove to be genuinely threatening to the individuals and groups who are the targets of them.”
- Josh Butler is a Guardian Australia political reporter and chief of staff in Canberra

The new Stylophone Mini packs in iconic sounds and comes in three nifty colors
It's small enough to attach to a keychain and costs just $30.
The quirky Stylophone synthesizer has been around since the 1960s. You've probably heard it on tracks like David Bowie's "Space Oddity." As a matter of fact, he wrote much of the song on one. Now the company has refreshed its cute Stylophone Mini instrument for modern audiences.
The Mini was first introduced in 2010, but left production years ago. The new one is still extremely small, thus the name. A full-sized Stylophone can fit in a pants pocket, but the Mini is basically the size of a credit card. To that end, it includes a loop to connect it to a keychain or hang it from a car dashboard.
There doesn't look to be many changes here, but the refreshed Stylophone Mini is available in three colors. This includes pink, which is brand new.
However, I'm not sure what the company could've changed or added. This is an instrument that proudly wears its history on its sleeve, with little interest in modern accoutrements. The company's CEO said that "in the age of AI, we wanted to make something simple, fun and real." It looks like that mission has been accomplished.
Despite the diminutive size, this is still (more or less) a real-deal Stylophone. It has just as many keys as its larger sibling, comes with a stylus for playing and includes built-in speakers. It looks pretty nifty.
The best part? It's just $30. Stylophones have always been budget-friendly instruments and the technology here is about as simple as simple gets. The Mini is available right now.
Though Bowie was perhaps the most notable fan of the Stylophone, he wasn't the only big artist to find inspiration within its nickel-plated touch keyboard. Artists like The White Stripes, Kraftwerk, Blondie and Pulp have all used the device on records or during live performances. Even The Beatles fooled around with it while recording "Old Brown Shoe" during the Let it Be sessions, though it didn't make the final mix.

Boy driving luxury car on birthday runs over man in Delhi, rams other vehicles
The incident took place in Kishangarh area around 2am October 4, when the minor took out the car to celebrate his birthday.
A 17-year-old boy driving an Audi on his birthday allegedly ran over a 45-year-old man and rammed three vehicles in Delhi, police said.
The incident took place in Kishangarh area around 2am October 4, when the minor took out the car to celebrate his birthday. He was apprehended and produced before the Juvenile Justice Board.
“A road traffic accident was reported opposite CNG Pump, Red Light, Kishangarh, involving an Audi and three other vehicles. The Audi was allegedly being driven rashly and negligently by a 17-year-old boy. One pedestrian, an approximately 45-year-old man, sustained injuries in the accident and was shifted to JPN Apex Trauma Centre, where he was declared brought dead,” Deputy Commissioner of Police (Southwest) Amit Goel said.
The deceased was identified as Uma Shankar, a resident of Kishangarh area. The police said the Audi did not belong to the boy’s family and efforts are being made to ascertain if the luxury vehicle was rented or whether it belonged to a friend.
The drivers of the other vehicles did not sustain injuries in the crash, the police said.
The police added the boy was apprehended and booked on charges of rash driving and causing death due to negligence. He was also booked under provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act.
"The Audi driver was apprehended and was produced before the Hon’ble JJB through video conferencing. The vehicles involved in the accident were seized as per law,” the DCP said.

The World Health Organization (WHO) reports that there are approximately 19 million visually impaired children in the world, and 1.4 million are blind. In India, about 3 lakh children are said to be blind. Yet, nearly half of these cases are entirely preventable or treatable if caught in time.
This month, global campaigns will urge the world to protect child eye health. There will be calls for governments around the world to unlock funding and prioritise eye care so everyone, everywhere can access the care they need along with community screening camps, eye care in schools and global pledges. And while these are vital calls, as a clinician standing on the frontlines of an outpatient department (OPD), I am forced to confront a quiet, uncomfortable truth: threats to a child’s vision are not always due to a lack of access to healthcare; they are sometimes also due to a missed opportunity to identify visual problems within healthcare systems that the child has already accessed.
What happens in the system
Consider a recent encounter in my clinic. A couple walked in with their five-year-old daughter; I will call her Anu. I could immediately see that she was visually impaired. She was one of a twin. Her parents felt that her sibling was developing normally, while she seemed to have delays in reaching developmental milestones. Gradually they started to notice that Anu could not see clearly. On examination, I found that Anu had dense bilateral cataracts with nystagmus (involuntary movement of the eyes). The presence of nystagmus says that the visual impairment had been present since infancy. When I asked why they had waited five years to seek help, they explained that they were simply overwhelmed by the weight of raising twins and assumed it was best to wait until she was older so she could ‘cooperate’ during a standard eye examination. Now they had arrived, but a bit too late.
Childhood eye diseases that cause profound visual impairment need to be detected and treated early. A baby is born with an immature visual system, and the development of vision happens through the interaction between the eye and the developing brain. When clear images do not reach the brain during this critical period, amblyopia, or lazy eye, can develop. Once this period of visual development has passed, treatment cannot fully restore the lost visual potential. Anu had lost the chance of getting back her vision fully, even if she was operated upon now.
What doesn’t get seen
Anu had not been completely outside the health system; her vaccinations were perfectly up-to-date, and she had documented encounters with health personnel seven distinct times from birth to age five. Yet, across all these visits her profound visual impairment went entirely unnoticed. Why did this happen?
One of the reasons is the poor integration of vision screening with the vaccination schedule and general paediatric screening.
India has an extensive network of frontline health workers and child health programmes. The Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK), for example, is designed to identify and manage health conditions in children from birth to 18 years. Screening programmes, notably have demonstrated that large numbers of school-aged children with vision problems can be screened. The tools placed in the hands of mobile health teams to detect developmental delays are proven to be highly capable of detecting developmental delays at the community level. What then is going wrong?
Let’s take the example of Karnataka. There is no published standalone government data of the number of children screened, ocular morbidity detected and treated, for the 0–6 age category. However, according to the Karnataka Health & Family Welfare Department’s Annual Report 2023–24, the State screened 62,45,424 children (6 to 16 yrs) in government and government-aided schools. But only 1.2 lakh children received spectacles, representing a distribution rate of just 1.9%. This is in sharp contrast to localised epidemiological studies in Karnataka’s southern districts, which place the actual prevalence of paediatric refractive errors as high as 8%. This pronounced gap could be due to operational challenges such as drop-outs in the multi-tier referral system and supply chain delays. A study assessing the coverage gaps in child health screening under RBSK found that only 47.4% of children detected to have health problems received further care, indicating a significant treatment gap.
Even if the system successfully flags a child, the path from detection to actual restoration of sight remains riddled with problems. Independent field evaluations in Tumkur highlight that the system has some problems when dealing with younger children and follow-up care. The management process faces significant on-the-ground challenges, including parental non-cooperation for follow-up, logistical barriers, and potential training gaps among screening teams. In my own experience, when talking to the ASHAs in Tumkur district, they said they did not have the training required to detect eye diseases in children. If the parents or caregiver of the children specifically complained about any vision related issues, the ASHAs referred them to the paediatrician who visited the taluk hospital once a week. This exposes a significant gap in training frontline workers.
Bridging gaps
There is no need for an entirely new system. We need to make better use of the system that already exists.
The red reflex test: A simple red reflex examination using the direct ophthalmoscope is one example. The test takes less than 30 seconds, does not require a child to cooperate verbally, and can identify major, sight and life-threatening abnormalities such as cataract, retinoblastoma (eye cancer) and high refractive errors. RBSK mobile health teams, primary health centre nurses, and paediatric residents must be trained to perform this test. This simple check must become as routine as measuring a child’s weight and must get incorporated in the immunisation schedule, so it is never missed.
Improving frontline training for pre-verbal visual milestones: We also need to train ASHAs in simple ways of assessing visual behaviour in infants and young children who cannot read a chart or respond reliably to conventional visual-acuity testing. Can the infant fix and follow light and objects? Is there visual engagement? Is there an abnormal or asymmetric corneal light reflex suggesting a squint? These are not sophisticated examinations. They are observations that, with appropriate training and referral protocols, can help identify children who need an eye examination.
Strengthening referral pathways from the periphery to tertiary care centre: Detection, however, is only the first step. A child identified with a possible eye problem must reach the appropriate facility where treatment is available. Referral pathways need to be clear, practical and monitored. Where possible, digital systems could link frontline screening with appointments at district or tertiary eye-care facilities. Tele-ophthalmology could also help connect peripheral health workers with specialists and reduce some of the logistical barriers that cause families to drop out of care.
Anu’s story is not simply about a child who reached an eye hospital too late. It is about a child who was already within the health system, but whose eyes were never looked at. Young children cannot be expected to understand there is a problem; parents may not recognise signs or may believe problems will resolve with age. A child should not have to reach the age of five, with dense cataracts and established nystagmus, before a visual problem that could have been detected in infancy comes to attention.
India already has an extensive network of frontline health workers, immunisation services, RBSK teams, school health programmes and primary and tertiary healthcare facilities. The challenge now is to connect these pieces. The goal should, therefore, not be merely to increase the number of children screened. It should be to build a system in which every contact with a child is an opportunity to protect vision, every abnormal finding triggers a clear referral, and every referral is followed through to care.
As we mark World Sight Day, the question we should ask is not only how do we reach more children. It is also how many children are already within our health system whom we are failing to see. For children like Anu, finding the problem a few years earlier can mean the difference between having sight and living a life with visual disability, because preventing blindness in a child is not merely about saving sight. It is about protecting education, independence and the opportunity to reach their full potential.
(Dr. Vasudha Kemmanu is a paediatric ophthalmologist and a public eye health specialist at Narayana Nethralaya, Rajaji Nagar, Bengaluru. vasudhakemmanu@gmail.com)

Keralam Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan’s statement at a recent function about avoiding unnecessary angioplasty seems to have stirred a hornets’ nest with many doctors objecting to the “generalised statement,” while some lone voices pointed out that Mr. Satheesan was 100% right and that unnecessary procedures had become the norm.
In a Facebook post, Rajesh Gopalan Nair, Professor and Head of Cardiology at the Government Medical College Hospital, Kozhikode, had appreciated Mr. Satheesan “for pointing out a truth.” But it set off an avalanche of comments from the doctors and public, with the latter narrating their harrowing experiences in hospitals and appreciating Dr. Rajesh for calling a spade a spade, while many doctors expressed disappointment at Dr. Rajesh’s stand.
Dr. Rajesh, however, made it clear in his post that a person coming into the emergency with a suspected heart attack should in no way distrust the doctor, for the situation may call for an immediate angioplasty.
Second opinion
He also explained clearly the situations when one could afford to wait and seek a second opinion, if angioplasty was suggested to a patient. He also cautioned the public against looking at every doctor or hospital with suspicion. Angioplasty should definitely be done when it is clinically indicated and these situations are clearly documented, he said.
Even though much of the medical fraternity expressed their displeasure at the “unsubstantiated” statement of the Chief Minister and the support that unexpectedly seemed to have come from one of their own, Dr. Rajesh refused to be cowed down. He maintained that he stood by his position that some of the angioplasty procedures done in hospitals were indeed not warranted.
On Monday, the Interventional Cardiology Council of Kerala (ICCK) said in a statement here that public’s apprehension over “unnecessary” medical procedures should not delay life-saving treatment during a heart attack emergency.
Responding to the Chief Minister’s remarks on avoiding unnecessary investigations and angioplasty, the council said it supported evidence-based and ethical medical practice and the principle that every intervention must have a clear clinical indication.
ICCK president Rajesh T. said that public discussion on angioplasty should clearly differentiate between elective intervention in stable patients and primary angioplasty during an acute heart attack, where treatment is highly time-sensitive.
What the data show
According to Statewide ICCK registry data presented at the council’s last annual conference, more than 70% of angioplasties performed in Kerala involved acute and emergency clinical situations.
He said the council welcomed any discussion aimed at strengthening evidence-based care, transparency and public confidence in the health-care system. “In stable patients, there is usually greater scope for detailed evaluation and for deciding whether medicines, further assessment or intervention would offer the greatest benefit. In an acute heart attack, however, delay can have serious consequences,” ICCK said.
However, the council cautioned that a general atmosphere of mistrust surrounding cardiac procedures could have unintended consequences, particularly when a patient develops severe chest pain or other symptoms suggestive of a heart attack.

Inspiration from her favourite golfer. A crucial decision on the final hole. A little bit of well-earned luck. And just like that, Pranavi Urs clinched a historic first-ever gold in the women’s competition for India at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games.
Heading into the final round, the 23-year-old Pranavi had a three-shot lead over Singapore’s Shannon Xuan Yin Tan with China’s Ruoning Yin in third, trailing by one more shot.
But the Indian didn’t have the start she would have hoped for on the last day. A devastating triple bogey for her on the third hole after World No. 6 Yin had scored a birdie on the second meant her advantage had vanished. At that moment, she thought of what her idol Rory McIlroy did at last year’s Augusta Masters.
McIlory, the modern-day legend from Northern Ireland, was going after the elusive Green Jacket to finally complete the Career Grand Slam, having won the other three Majors at least once by 2014. But he did not have the best of opening rounds - an even par 72 - and was tied 27th. From there, he made a sensational comeback to eventually beat Justin Rose in a play-off and complete the set.
“After the third hole, he was one of the people I thought about. It was pretty random. But I thought if he can win the Masters after having a terrible start, so can I (win the gold). That’s one way that got me motivated towards the round as well,” Pranavi said in a virtual interaction facilitated by SAI (Sports Authority of India) Media on Thursday.
Another significant moment for Pranavi came on the 18th hole. “The thing that I did on the last hole, if you saw the video, I changed my club on my second shot after I hit the drive. I had a 6-iron but then, I said to my caddy that I’m feeling the adrenaline rush and I can’t be hitting 6-iron because it’s going to go over the green. I’m just going to hit a 7-iron,” she revealed.
As it turned out, the call was correct and the ball found the green, paving the way for two putts to finish with a par hole.
But she also needed a slice of fortune, which in some way, she had earned. To force a play-off for the gold, Yin had to score a birdie on the last hole. A dramatic lip out kept the Chinese golfer, a former World No. 1, from meeting her objective. It was, perhaps, also a consequence of the pressure Pranavi had put back on her with three birdies after that triple bogey early in the final round.
“I played with her for two days and I don’t think she made a single bogey in those two days and that’s why she’s world number six and former world number one. She’s a Major champion but sometimes, if it’s meant to be, it is, right? Nothing can stop you from winning. I think it’ll just be it.
“But at the same time, I feel like the way I handled my situation, coming down the stretch, I holed a few important putts, which she went on to miss after me. So, I had to put that pressure on her which I did,” reflected the 23-year-old Indian, who also clinched a team silver with Olympian Aditi Ashok and Diksha Dagar.
For someone who had just become the first Indian female golfer to win gold in the history of the continental showpiece, Pranavi’s celebration was pretty non-existent.
Simply because she didn’t know she had won.
“I was, perhaps, too zoned in and I had one of Shannon’s scores wrong on my scorecard because I was marking hers. I thought I needed to putt. Maybe there’s a playoff and I’ll still have a medal chance. I didn’t know and that’s why I didn’t celebrate after I won. I wish I had known,” admitted Pranavi.
In the coming days, the golfer from Karnataka will have a chance for a potential meeting with her idol as McIlroy is set to feature in the DP World India Championship in New Delhi starting from October 15. And if that dream turns into reality, she jokes it could be even more nerve-wracking than what she managed to achieve at the Asiad.
“My partner is also a golfer. So, he’s playing that event. I’m going to go watch him play anyway. I’ve asked my sources a little bit to get me to meet him (McIlroy). Hopefully that happens. And if that happens, I think I’m going to be more nervous meeting him than winning the gold,” said Pranavi.
