What can an economist teach us about misery?
There’s a silver lining to your unhappiness
Economist George Loewenstein’s new book is emphatically not self-help. It might still help you live a wiser life.
I had that question in mind while reading the new book The Opposite of Happiness: How Bad Feelings Make and Break Us, by eminent researcher George Loewenstein. The field is not exactly known for its facility with human emotions, but Loewenstein is a co-founder of behavioral economics, the subdiscipline that studies the many ways that people depart from the ideal of the perfectly rational actor. He’s spent a career investigating how psychology and emotion shape our judgments, and his latest book offers a sweeping account of how suffering structures human life.
That might sound very bleak, like the opposite of a fun read. But the book itself isn’t distressing — it’s a bracing, useful, and even comforting lens on what it means to be alive. It emerged from a period of profound suffering in his own life, one where, he writes, he “thought about suicide constantly.” Writing it, he told me in a recent interview, was “kind of a silver lining for my own misery.”
In Loewenstein’s own words, The Opposite of Happiness is not a self-help book. To him, understanding is its own reward. Though he adamantly refuses to dispense life advice, I still think the book offers much that can help us live more wisely, a little less at war with our emotions.
“Misery is inescapable,” Loewenstein writes. “It’s not some malfunction or a bug in the system. It is the system.” Negative emotions are “more powerful, persistent, and pervasive than positive ones.” That is because, he argues, unpleasant feelings — hunger, pain, anger, loneliness — are how evolution motivated us to do the things we need to survive and pass on our genes. They still heavily shape our conscious experience, however mismatched they may feel to our modern circumstances.
Some version of that insight, that dissatisfaction is woven into the human condition, has been known to humans for eons, of course, captured in philosophical teachings like Buddhism’s Four Noble Truths. The father of economics himself observed that people work hard to earn riches, only to discover the result offers no lasting contentment. “It is this deception which rouses and keeps in continual motion the industry of mankind,” Adam Smith wrote in The Theory of Moral Sentiments. “It is this which first prompted them to cultivate the ground, to build houses, to found cities and commonwealths, and to invent and improve all the sciences and arts.”
Loewenstein puts this understanding into the language of modern psychology, speaking to a current of anxiety and unhappiness running through American life today. It also points to enduring questions about what the purpose of human progress and prosperity is, anyway.
Many of us could particularly benefit from the concept of negative “meta-emotions,” or the judgmental feelings we have about our negative feelings. “At the heart of so many of our miseries is not the fact that we feel bad, but the belief that we should feel otherwise,” he writes. That line immediately rang true to me — merely acknowledging to myself that it’s not a big deal if I feel terrible from work stress, or my cat’s deteriorating health, or whatever else happens to be weighing on me, helps to lighten the load. What if we really tried to wryly embrace the reality that it’s extremely normal for life to suck sometimes? The reward might not be happiness, exactly (an elusive and poorly understood state anyway, Loewenstein points out), but a little less misery.
I recently spoke with Loewenstein about his book — he had a gentle, faintly melancholic air, and took a surprisingly generous interest in some of the choices I was weighing in my own life. Part of our conversation, condensed and edited for clarity, is below.
Americans seem pretty unhappy right now. There has been endless discourse about that. Do you think that your book adds something to that conversation?
I do — I was just an expert on the Meta case that recently settled. I was an expert on the side that was against Meta. I think one of the causes of declining mental health is, in fact, social media. It really exacerbates the types of social comparisons that lead to envy and loss of self-esteem. I would like to think that I provide some new insights into how these modern technologies help to exacerbate the mental health crisis.
One analysis of that, based on what I’ve learned from your book, might be: We as humans are so guided by negative emotions, and often those emotions are relational in nature and have to do with how we compare to other people. Social media is then quite naturally going to tap into and amplifying negative emotions that we’re easily manipulated by.
That’s right. I think of it in two ways. One is there’s kind of a mismatch between the circumstances in which we evolved and the modern environment. And the other is that in the capitalist economy, there are, especially in the internet age, all these entities that are trying to exploit our evolutionary programming for their own good and not for our good.
The premise of the book, as you write, is that “misery is inescapable. It’s not some malfunction or a bug in the system. It is the system” — it’s like our default state. Can you unpack what that means?
I agree with everything you said until “default.” Different people have different set points, and there are some happy people around. I happen to be a glass-half-empty person. My natural state is a little bit below zero. But there are very few people who don’t experience some form of misery frequently and intensely.
The evolutionary function of most negative emotions is pretty obvious, whereas the evolutionary function of happiness is sort of murky. And misery is so dominant that all it takes is a little bit of misery, a little bit of negative emotion, to wipe out any positive emotion. You go out to a really nice dinner at a fancy restaurant with your significant other, and you say something thoughtless and they get offended or they say something thoughtless and you get offended. All of a sudden you can’t even taste the food or appreciate the beautiful surroundings.
Paul Rozin at the University of Pennsylvania referred to this as the “roach effect”: If you drop a roach into a vat of fine French wine, you don’t want to drink the wine. But if you take a roach, you can add as much wine as you want to it and you’re not going to want to eat the roach.
One of the strongest positive emotions is relief — which is interesting and not a coincidence, because it’s relief from negative emotions. It’s telling that maybe the strongest positive emotion involves the elimination of negative emotions.
You can think of misery as a stick trying to get you to do things that evolution thought were good for you; the stick is very immediate, and you know exactly what it’s telling you. If you are hungry, it’s time to eat. If you’re in pain, you’re injured, you’ve got to do something about it. But the carrot is different. The carrot, which is positive emotions, you have to think ahead, Oh, if I did this, then I would experience this positive emotion. It requires a kind of second-order thinking, whereas misery is just immediate. Evolution figured out probably very rapidly, probably when we were single-cell protozoa or something, that sticks are a way better way to get an organism to do what it needs to do than carrots.
How confident are you that the evidence base we have about the psychology of negative emotions generalizes to humanity as a whole and that it’s not culturally biased?
“What I’d really like people to get out of the book is insight — into their own negative feelings, their own types of misery, and other people’s negative feelings.”
Emotion researchers have looked across cultures, and they tend to observe the same basic emotions in a very, very wide range of cultures. What does vary across cultures is what induces the emotions. For example, shame — something that we would be unashamed of, somebody in a different country might be very ashamed of, and vice versa. A lot of these emotions are self-conscious emotions. They have to do with how we interpret the world and whether we’re living up to some kind of standard. Often we get it from culture, from religion, things like that.
But I think the emotions themselves are not universal, but pretty close to universal. My guess is that all 12 negative emotions that I write about are manifested in pretty much all different cultures, from those that have very little connection to Western civilization to advanced economies.
Another timely thread that your book is in conversation with is this idea that American culture has become intolerant of ordinary negative emotions in a way that’s maladaptive. Suzanne O’Sullivan’s recent book The Age of Diagnosis, for example, covered our obsession with medical labels and how they might make us prone to thinking that feeling bad means that there’s something medically wrong with us. What do you think about that? Have we gotten bad at feeling bad?
It is striking to me how it seems like all the young people I meet talk about their therapist, and a lot of them talk about the drugs that they take. Young people also talk about anxiety and depression almost like one word, “anxiety-and-depression.” In my generation, anxiety and depression were two entirely different things.
I think it’s good that younger generations are more comfortable talking about these things and getting help. I do worry that it can be, to some degree, pathologizing. There’s an awful lot of self-focus there. And I kind of worry that if you are dealing with your mental health problems by taking drugs, that it reduces your motivation to figure out things like how to reorganize your life to feel better. But I don’t want to sound too much like a dinosaur.
There’s a contingent of people who might read your book and think, “Yes, isn’t it terrible that humans are built to be unhappy and our evolved instincts don’t serve us well anymore? And that’s why we should engineer humans in such a way that we don’t feel this way all the time.” Someone with a strong utilitarian philosophy might think that if your life sums up to more negative feelings than positive ones, then it’s not even worth living. But that’s not really the vibe that I get from you.
No, yeah. And one of the things I talk about in the book are what psychologists call meta-emotions. These are emotions that one experiences about emotions. I think the single best example is envy. If you envy your friend — almost everyone has friends that they envy, but they’re still your friends. But you might feel that you’re not supposed to envy your friend, and you feel guilty — the guilt is a meta-emotion. Or you can also have meta-emotions about a lack of emotion. So something bad happens to someone, or even somebody dies, and you don’t feel all that bad, and you feel guilty because you’re not grieving.
I think all the societal focus on happiness creates a kind of a meta-meta-emotion, which is that we think we’re supposed to be happy. And then we feel ashamed and guilty about the fact that we aren’t happy — we feel like we failed. That compounds and adds another level of depth to our misery. So I think it can be liberating at some level to understand that misery just is a constant in human existence.
I also think that my book is militantly anti-self-help. There’s no self-help in it whatsoever. But I don’t think it’s a depressing book to read, and it wasn’t particularly depressing to write, though some of the stories that I wrote about were a bit wrenching.
A goal for policy: Less misery
I asked Loewenstein whether all the social and economic progress humans have made over the last few centuries have made us better off psychology. He said: “I don’t think social progress makes us happier, but I do think that certain types of social progress can make us less miserable,” he said. He continued:
“A lot of people in this country are dealing with huge financial anxiety. They’re in debt, like credit card debt or student debt. Not only does that make people miserable day to day, but it destroys relationships and makes parenting much more difficult. And I think the societies that have the highest measures of happiness, which you can equally well interpret as the lowest levels of misery, are societies like the Scandinavian countries that have really robust safety nets.
“I think maybe the central focus of public policy should be to mitigate all sorts of different types of miseries. Living in one of the richest countries on earth, that should be in our power to do. … There are good ways to use your social wealth, and there are terrible ways. We tend to err on the terrible side.”
I like that — but what, then, ought people to do with the information that you’re presenting?
What I’d really like people to get out of the book is insight — into their own negative feelings, their own types of misery, and other people’s negative feelings. To me, insight is valuable in its own right.
The reason I read sad novels is not because they make me happy, but because I feel like I gained some kind of insight into people and into the world. Tess of the d’Urbervilles is the saddest book you could ever imagine, but it’s very meaningful to read, and it definitely feels like you’re a different person after you read it. I love novels, but I have no skill as a fiction writer. So this book was almost like a surrogate for me. Instead of writing a novel, I wrote this book.
I think the lack of self-help drives some people crazy. I did a podcast where the podcaster kept asking me questions about how reading the book would improve somebody’s life. And I kept saying it’s not a self-help book.
I’m just very skeptical of self-help talks and books and things like that. And I know that there’s certain things you are supposed to do to feel good, like you’re supposed to wake up and think of three things that you should be thankful for. And maybe if I did that, maybe I would get happier, but I’ve never been able to actually get myself to do that.
But you do have some insights that people could apply in their lives, like the idea that striving intentionally for happiness or meaning doesn’t really work, and that meaning often comes to us in unforeseeable spontaneous moments. On one hand, that implies a kind of randomness, and maybe there’s not a lot we can do about it. On the other hand, I can predict that I’m more likely to feel a deep sense of meaning in some scenarios than others, and I can put myself into those situations more, like choosing to be social on a weeknight.
A lot of the time the good things in life are just surprising, and sometimes you have to get dragged kicking and screaming into things that ultimately end up being the most fulfilling things in your life. So much of parenting is trying to get your kids to do things that they don’t want to do that you are absolutely convinced that if they started to do them, they would end up loving.
You argue, drawing from economist and philosopher Adam Smith, that human beings are constantly striving to achieve the next thing because we imagine it’ll satisfy us, though it never does. That helpful delusion is what leads us to build cities and cure diseases and all the rest.
Adam Smith is best known for the invisible hand, which is the idea that each person single-mindedly pursuing their own well-being inadvertently promotes the public good. But if you read Adam Smith’s other book, The Theory of Moral Sentiments, he didn’t believe at all that people pursue their own personal interest. He believed that people are driven by this illusion that the next raise, the next accomplishment, will bring happiness, and it never does. I love that contradiction between the conventional interpretation of the invisible hand and what Adam Smith really believed.
So civilization is powered by this dissatisfaction that never resolves itself. But I don’t think you would say the lesson we ought to take from the book is that we’ll always revert back to being miserable, so there’s no point in doing anything.
That’s absolutely not the point of the book. Misery evolved for good reasons, and the whole point of misery is that we’re supposed to take actions to lessen our miseries. That’s what we should be doing, because who wants to be miserable?

Torrential rain and potentially damaging flooding are forecast in eastern Spain over the coming days, as cold upper air moves over the warm, humid surface air of the Mediterranean Sea, fuelling violent, slow-moving thunderstorms near Spain’s east coast. The weather pattern, known as a Dana, occurs most often in autumn.
Models show more than 100mm of rain could fall across the region on Friday, with 200-300mm possible in some areas. Cities including Valencia and Castelló de la Plana, are most at risk. Valencia has experienced several damaging floods in recent years. Catalonia has now put three towns under lockdown and Valencia has shut schools for nearly half a million children.
Meanwhile, heavy rainfall in Nepal last week resulted in 542 disaster incidents and left 27 people dead between 24 and 27 September, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. Of the recorded incidents, 304 were related to landslides while 87 were linked to flooding.
During this extremely wet period, 186 meteorological sites recorded more than 100mm of rainfall, with Dedhgaun, in Lumbini province, recording 544.2mm. Nearly a million people received SMS flood warnings, and 2,000 people living in high-risk areas were relocated.
This heavy rainfall also affected the Gandak River in Bihar, north-east India, which reached a record water level of 91.25 metres on Tuesday, 0.35m metres above the previous record, set only in 2024, according to the water resources department. So far, 169 seepage points along the embankments have been repaired, with teams deployed across several sites along the river as the embankments continue to face heavy water pressure.
Strong winds, heavy rainfall and coastal flooding have hit the north-east US as a very deep area of low pressure developed into a nor’easter on Saturday. Such storms are named due to the north-easterly winds typically affecting coastal areas. This was the first nor’easter of the autumn and winter season, bringing gusts of up to 74mph (119km/h) and waves rising to 3 metres.
The storm left approximately 200,000 people without power, inundated the streets of New York City and killed one person when a tree fell in Brooklyn. However, the storm also uncovered a piece of history as the wreckage from the Warren Sawyer, a three-masted ship destroyed in 1884, washed ashore on Nantucket, off Cape Cod in Massachusetts.

NABVENTURES, the venture capital arm of the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD), has announced the first close of its second fund at ₹450 Cr. The firm, which invests in early to growth stage agritech startups, is targeting a corpus of ₹1,500 Cr for the fund. This also includes a greenshoe option. India's apex agriculture focused financial institution NABARD is the anchor investor in the fund The investment arm intends to double down on early and growth stage startups using tech to address challenges across the agricultural value chain and rural markets. The fund will invest across sectors including agritech, food and agribusiness, rural fintech, climate smart solutions, supply chain and logistics, among other businesses focused on rural transformation. The fund will also focus on businesses working on sustainability, climate resilience, financial inclusion and livelihood creation, NABARD chairman Dr Shaji Krishnan V said NABVENTURES was incorporated on April 23, 2018, as a wholly owned subsidiary of NABARD, to invest in businesses working across agriculture and rural development. Besides Fund II, it backs startups via NABVENTURES Fund I and AgriSURE. NABVENTURES' portfolio includes startups like Unnati, Eggoz, Beyond Snack, Jai Kisan, among 23 startups. The investor backed companies such as aquaculture-focused agritech startup Aquapulse, which raised ₹25 Cr in an ongoing Series A round led by NABVENTURES and KisaanSay through its AgriSURE Fund earlier this year. NABVENTURES' claimed that its earlier funds have collectively backed 23 enterprises, providing it with an existing portfolio and track record in India's agri and rural startup ecosystem The firm’s focus on agritech comes at a time when the sector has lost some allure that it had for investors. Agritech startups raised $202 Mn across 36 deals in 2025, down nearly 25% from $269 Mn in 2024 and sharply below the $728 Mn and $840 Mn raised in 2021 and 2022, respectively. The funding pullback has continued as investors have become wary of capital-heavy models, high customer acquisition costs and weak monetisation, particularly among marketplace and logistics-led agritech businesses. The shift also comes against a broader tepid funding environment in the Indian startup ecosystem. In Q3, overall startup funding rose 5% to $2.2 Bn, but deal count fell 13% and the active investor pool shrank 24%, signalling a sharper focus on high-conviction bets. Agritech, however, has seen some sizable bets in recent times. Balwaan Krishi raised $10.4 Mn in a Series B round in September, while Ninjacart raised $6 Mn in July.

A company called Steakholder Foods has launched a line of products under the brand name Perfecta. While the meat is 3D-printed, it is made from a formulation of plant material like other plant-based meats are. It is not made from cultured animal cells, which is often what people refer to when they mention "lab-grown meat." It is not clear which grocery stores or retailers are selling Perfecta-branded food, though the company has said its products have reached shelves in certain Northeastern U.S retail locations.
Between September and October, social media users claimed that 3D-printed, lab-grown meat had started being sold in U.S. stores from early September.
For example, one Facebook post (archived) claims the 3D-printed meat "has federal clearance" but will not have a "lab-grown meat" label on its packaging. The post reads, in part:
The first 3D printed 'meat' has federal clearance and is about to be sold in the United States.
Packaging will not say 'lab-grown meat' because there is not a law that requires the packaging to say it was printed.
3D-printed plant-based food is already on shelves in the U.S.
Federal labels for cell-grown chicken and pork fat must be pre-approved and have used the words "cell-cultivated."
The printed food was in stores on September 3 of this year.
The company Steakholder Foods put its Perfecta line into Northeast supermarkets.
The rumor has appeared elsewhere on Facebook (archived) and on Instagram (archived). Numerous Snopes readers also emailed us to ask if the story is true.
In short, on Sept. 3, Israeli company Steakholder Foods, which specializes in making 3D-printing technology for plant-based meats, announced the launch of its 3D-printed, plant-based meat products in Northeastern U.S. retailers under the brand name Perfecta. Therefore, the claim is true.
Steakholder Foods' news release says its "Premium Plant-Based Meat" products were launched at retail locations in the Northeastern United States on Sept. 3, "marking the brand's first commercial placement on U.S. store shelves."
According to the webpage, the launch "focuses on building awareness and consumer trial throughout the Northeast U.S. market while establishing a foundation for broader expansion across additional regions."
It is not clear which grocery stores or retailers have started selling or stocking the products.
Snopes reached out to the company via a contact form on its website for more information. We will update this article if we hear back.
According to Steakholder Foods, the company uses plant-based ingredients and cultivates cells to create what ultimately becomes the 3D-printed meat.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration and the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service do regulate "lab-grown" meat and require a label for such products. However, this regulation is specifically for food made with cultured animal cells, not for food made with other kinds of cells, which is what Perfecta products consist of.
Snopes reached out to both the FDA via contact form and the FSIS via email to confirm that there are not similar kinds of regulations for food made with other cultured cells, such as plant cells. Additionally, we asked both agencies to confirm if Perfecta products had received federal approval, as the above Facebook post states. We will update this story if we receive responses.
Based on how the product boxes appear on the website, there does not appear to be any text identifying the food as 3D-printed or made with cultured cells. The boxes do clearly identify the meat as "premium plant meat" and "plant-based."
Manufacturers of plant-based meat products usually have to process their ingredient mixes in a way that allows them to mimic the texture of conventional meat. According to the Good Food Institute's Asia-Pacific website, the most common processing method requires putting shear stress on the ingredients to align them into a meat-like texture. There are several other methods of processing plant-based meats, including 3D-printing.
For further reading, Snopes previously fact-checked a claim that a plant-based meat manufacturer was 3D-printing meat products in the Netherlands in 2024.

Inside Djibouti refugee camp for thousands fleeing Houthi advance in Yemen
Fighting on Yemen's west coast has prompted thousands of people to flee by boat across the Bab al-Mandab Strait to Djibouti over the last ten days.
The BBC's Frank Gardner visited a refugee camp in Obock, a small port town where officials are preparing for the arrival of up to 10,000 refugees.
The UN International Organisation for Migration said people were travelling on overcrowded boats and arriving with very limited food and water.
The crossings were sparked by an offensive by the Iran-backed Houthi movement to take control of a key island and seize the strategically important port of Mokha.

India’s youth-led Cockroach movement kicked off more nationwide protests on Friday as thousands of people gathered in Mumbai, amid mounting concerns that millions of citizens are being unfairly stripped of their vote.
The movement, which calls itself the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) and has massive support among the country’s gen Zs, returned to the streets to demand the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar.
Kumar has become a highly contentious figure after a report in the Indian Express newspaper alleged irregularities and internal concerns about a process to revise and “purify” India’s electoral register, called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
SIR, which was overseen by Kumar, has resulted in tens of millions of people being deleted from the electoral register. Large numbers are challenging their removal.
Opposition politicians and civil society groups have alleged SIR is part of a widespread manipulation of India’s electoral system to benefit the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
The CJP began as online satire but grew into a powerful manifestation of youth power and an unexpected challenge to the Narendra Modi government. There were protests for weeks in the heart of Delhi and the education minister was eventually pressured into resigning in July. In the aftermath, the group declared it would remain active as a “pressure group” to hold the government to account on issues of education and democracy.
Last week, after the revelations about the election commission, the CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, announced that if Kumar did not resign over the controversy, the “Cockroaches” would resume their agitation until he stepped down. Dipke said the Mumbai protest would kick off a nationwide movement, with more protests planned in Delhi, Goa, Kolkata and Bengaluru.
The authorities denied permission for the group to hold their protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji park but Dipke had vowed to go ahead regardless. “We are fighting against those in power,” he said, at a press conference. “We all remember Mahatma Gandhi, who fought against the Britishers. Did the British ever permit him to agitate?”
Hundreds of people assembled in Mumbai on Friday afternoon, amid a heavy police presence, including many young people who said they were there to fight for India’s democracy.
“Voting is the most basic right of any citizen, but because of the actions of Kumar and the election commission, that right is under attack,” said Deesha, 22, a student activist. “So many millions of people have lost their votes and aren’t even recognised as citizens of India any more. This attack on our democracy must stop. The first important step is to get Gyanesh Kumar to resign, and then SIR must be reversed.”
Janvi Upadhyay, 18, said that the Cockroach movement had awoken the young people of India “and if they think they can just come and take away votes and cheat the elections, we will show them just how wrong they are”.
“We already forced the education minister to resign. Gyanesh Kumar should be very worried right now because he is definitely next,” she said.
The election commission has denied wrongdoing in the SIR but in a move that appeared aimed at easing tensions, officials were directed to expedite the process to register newly eligible voters and those who claimed to have been wrongly omitted from electoral rolls.
Anger at Kumar and the election commission also erupted in Delhi on Friday, even as the police took draconian measures to try and stop people from protesting. Thousands of police were deployed to the Jantar Mantar protest site in Delhi – which was the epicentre of the last Cockroach agitation in July – a dozen metro stations in the surrounding area were closed and an internet shutdown was imposed.
Hundreds of those who turned out to Jantar Mantar were immediately forced into police buses. The mass detentions of at least 700 people, including civil society leaders and opposition politicians, prompted outrage, with protesters leaning out of the bus windows to accuse police officers of depriving them of their fundamental democratic rights.
Opposition parties said they would also start a nationwide protest movement to demand Kumar’s resignation. All opposition lawmakers plan to march to the election commission office in Delhi next week.

AI startup Inner Sky Labs, the maker of children’s companion robots under the Miko brand, has launched a suite of foundation models designed to help machines perceive their surroundings, plan and execute physical actions, and check those actions against safety rules. Alongside the launch, the startup is closing a ₹300 Cr (about $30.9 Mn) funding round involving existing backers YourNest Venture Capital and Keshav R Murugesh, as well as new global investors, cofounder and CEO Sneh Vaswani told Inc42. Once completed, the round would take the business’s total funding to $100 Mn. The startup plans to use the fresh capital for real-world data collection, computing infrastructure, and model training as it expands sales to enterprises, governments, and other machine makers. The expansion builds on technology developed for Miko, which has been the business’ public-facing consumer brand since its early years. Founded in 2015 by IIT Bombay alumni Vaswani, Prashant Iyengar, and Chintan Raikar, the startup focused on children’s companion robots while developing the underlying AI models. Vaswani said the broader physical AI initiative had been developed in stealth over the past decade. Inner Sky Labs is the newly unveiled umbrella brand for that business, operating under the same legal entity that owns Miko. “We built these AI models ourselves, with a strong focus on safety and sovereignty. Now, we are scaling these models beyond Miko, taking them into enterprises, government applications that require sovereign AI, and other areas,” Vaswani told Inc42. Taking Miko’s AI To Other Machines The CEO said that the expansion had been planned since inception. During investor pitches in 2017, the team was already discussing developing AI models, with Miko as their first application before expanding into enterprise, software, and government use cases. Limited demand for standalone AI models at the time led the team to focus on Miko. Its robots, designed to talk, play, and learn with children, provided an environment for deploying and testing the technology, particularly conversational safety. With Inner Sky Labs, the startup is opening those capabilities to businesses building robots, industrial machines, and other systems. Customers can adopt individual models or the full platform, which is available to qualified partners by invitation. Vaswani argued that developing foundation models is becoming too expensive for individual machine makers, particularly at modest production volumes. A common provider would allow multiple manufacturers to adopt the technology without each building their own models. The startup describes its platform as hardware agnostic, supporting industrial arms, humanoids, mobile and companion robots, quadrupeds, cars, and CCTV systems. AI For Sensing, Movement, And Safety The platform combines three functions needed to operate these systems — perception, action, and safety. Its perception models comprise Drishti for vision, Shruti for audio, and Sparsh for touch. Action models Kriya, Prana, and Karma use those inputs to help machines plan movements and anticipate their consequences. Kavach, the independent safety layer, checks proposed actions before execution and can block those that breach predefined rules. The startup says the system has more than 20 guardrails, including checks on the presence of people, movement speeds, and permitted operating areas. In a factory, for example, the models could help a robotic arm identify, grip, and move a component, while blocking movement if a person enters its operating area. Vaswani said the models draw on almost a decade of physical-world data collection from factories, Miko’s manufacturing ecosystem, and other environments. He said they were developed in-house: “This is not fine-tuned on an open source model. It is our own model.” The startup’s roadmap shows Kriya, Karma, and Prana scaling from 4 Bn, 4 Bn, and 9 Bn parameters to 12 Bn, 16 Bn, and 37 Bn, respectively. According to Inner Sky Labs, the first generation is already being used in industrial applications, combining vision, information about a robot’s position and movement, and force and torque readings. The next generation will focus on coordinating multiple robotic arms, handling more complex scenes, and processing richer touch signals from fingertips, fingers, and palms. Sovereign AI And Enterprise Deployments Beyond the models themselves, Inner Sky Labs is pitching control over deployment and operating rules as a selling point for enterprises and governments. The startup positions its offering as sovereign AI, saying customers can run the models within their own infrastructure and define the rules governing their behaviour. Deployment options include cloud APIs, on-premise installations, and on-device processing, including offline and air-gapped environments isolated from external networks. This allows sensitive operational data to be processed locally, with Vaswani citing drones and surveillance systems as potential applications. “If you have CCTV cameras in a city, those cameras need to monitor exactly what has happened. You would not rely on a vision model coming from another country for any purpose. So, you would use a vision model from us,” he said. Commercial deployments began two to three quarters before the public launch, Vaswani said. The startup has completed four to five large deployments across enterprises and governments, including outside India. However, he did not disclose customer names or specific government applications. The startup claims to serve enterprise markets in the US and Europe and is exploring opportunities in Africa. The launch comes amid growing activity in India’s physical AI ecosystem. While Addverb is developing humanoid robots for industrial applications, Mowito is building AI models that enable standard industrial robotic arms to learn tasks from human operators. The increased instances of indigenous and imported cases of malaria over the past five years have left the health authorities a worried lot.
Imported malaria is acquired outside Keralam, while indigenous malaria is acquired through local transmission, when a local mosquito picks up the parasite from an infected person and transmits it to another person.
Going by the Health department statistics, as of October 5, four confirmed indigenous cases were reported in 2026, and 974 imported cases.
One death due to indigenous malaria and six deaths due to imported cases have been reported this year. Last year, no deaths due to indigenous cases were reported, while two deaths occurred due to imported cases.
The number of cases began to rise after 2021, when 252 imported and one indigenous death case were reported. The highest number of indigenous cases was reported from Malappuram, Kozhikode, and Kannur. Kollam, which earlier showed a high incidence of these cases, is in a recovery phase.
Health officials attribute the abundance of mosquitoes and the frequent influx of travellers to the increase in the number of infections.
“Over the past several years, the number of imported malaria cases has increased substantially. We need to strengthen surveillance measures, screening of migrants for the disease and ensuring intensive screening and testing for the disease in asymptomatic fever cases,” said the official.
The Health department plans to introduce insecticide-treated bed nets, which will kill mosquitoes on contact, in houses in regions where indigenous cases are reported. Steps are being taken to intensify malaria prevention activities to prevent the development of malaria-endemic regions in the State,” said the official.
“The increasing number of malaria cases in the past few years is a concern,” said. T.S. Anish, associate professor, School of Public Health, Kerala University of Health Sciences, Thiruvananthapuram.
“The consistent efforts by the Health department back in the 1960s succeeded in freeing the State from malaria. However, with increased travel and the influx of the migrant population from disease-endemic regions, malaria cases are getting reported. The delay in timely detection and intervention measures will contribute to the rise of indigenous cases. The local conditions are ideal to facilitate the spread of the disease,” Dr. Anish warned.
Climate change
He further added that climate change can also emerge as a key concern.
He warned that malaria could spread to hitherto unreported regions due to climate change-induced developments. “The climate in Keralam and the frequent movement of domestic workers are favourable to the spread of the disease,” he said.

How October 7 changed everything
We still live in the long shadow of Hamas’s brutal 2023 attack — and Israel’s devastating response to it.
Jewish communities in Israel and around the world are currently marking the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks that killed 1,200 people and triggered the war in Gaza.
Memorials for the victims of the attacks have been held at homes, on highways, and at the site of the Nova music festival. In Tel Aviv, a massive art installation at the Trumpeldor beach commemorated both the victims and the 251 hostages taken by Hamas three years ago.
Of those hostages, 166 have since returned alive, and the remains of the last deceased captive were released to Israel in January. But there’s no undoing the national trauma of the October 7 attacks — the deadliest massacre of Jewish people since the Holocaust — or the brutal retaliatory campaign that Israel launched afterward.
Those events profoundly changed Israel, Gaza, the broader Middle East, and the United States, and they continue to shape global and domestic politics. So today, we’re taking a look at the very long shadow of the October 7 attacks and Israel’s response to them.
Go a little deeper
Writing about the first anniversary of October 7 two years ago, Vox’s Zack Beauchamp warned that the “horrors” first triggered by the attacks would continue to unfold in tragic and unforeseeable ways. “Events that might seem contained to the Middle East have come to hurt people around the world,” he wrote, “in ways that we may not yet fully understand or even be capable of predicting.”
That hurt has undeniably been most acute in the Gaza Strip, where three years of war have reduced entire cities to rubble. Israel’s military campaign has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians — most of them civilians — since October 2023. Most of Gaza’s 2 million residents have also been displaced from their homes, crowded into makeshift shelters and refugee camps riddled with hunger and disease.
But the consequences of October 7 extended beyond Gaza. Settler violence against Palestinians intensified in the occupied West Bank. And the ensuing conflicts also weakened Iran and changed the balance of power across the Middle East.
That’s because Iran had long relied on its allies, like Hamas in Gaza and Hezbollah in Lebanon, to project power and deter attacks by its longtime rival, Israel. After October 7, however, Israel significantly weakened both groups, leaving Iran vulnerable and setting the stage for the direct strikes on Iran that Israel and the US began last winter.
Both the war in Iran and the continued occupation of Gaza have badly hurt Israel’s international image. Across 36 countries surveyed by Pew last spring, a median of 67 percent of adults viewed Israel negatively. That disapproval has translated into diplomatic shifts, as well: 155 countries — including longtime allies of Israel, such as the United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia — now officially recognize Palestinian statehood, up from 136 before the war. That doesn’t change much on the ground, but it represents a real rebuke to Israel.
In the US, meanwhile, Israel has become a huge flashpoint in domestic politics. While more than half of Americans had a favorable view of the country before October 7, sentiment deteriorated sharply in 2025 and 2026, particularly on the left.
The issue could help determine some key midterm races, like the Michigan Senate election, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has called for ending US military aid to Israel. That’s a policy nearly half of House Democrats and many potential presidential candidates have also endorsed.
Cutting off US aid to Israel isn’t likely to change the country’s stance toward Palestinians, however. (Israel is a wealthy country in its own right, and American aid represents just a small piece of its budget.) Instead, changing Israeli policy on Gaza and the West Bank would likely require far more aggressive pressure — pressure that, even in the current political environment, the US is unlikely to apply.
A single day may have kicked off a cascade of hurt and horrors. But putting an end to them will take far more time.
One link for later
➨ Cultivate hope. It can feel difficult (not to mention: naive, pointless, and exhausting) to maintain optimism in the face of current events. So Jamil Zaki, a psychology professor and the director of the Stanford Social Neuroscience Lab, suggests another tact: Do away with blind optimism and lean into hope — that belief that the future could turn out well, but requires real care and attention.

The Charminar Zone police registered 27 cases against 51 persons for violating sound restrictions and creating public nuisance during the Ganesh festival celebrations in Hyderabad this year. The police also seized 68 sound boxes and 21 amplifiers used in violation of the prescribed guidelines.
According to the DCP Charminar zone, Kiran Khare, the violators were identified through CCTV footage and field-level monitoring conducted during the festival. The violations primarily involved the use of DJ sound systems, excessively loud music and activities causing inconvenience to the public.
All 51 persons were subsequently summoned to the office of the DCP, where they were counselled and warned against repeating such violations during religious festivals and public gatherings.
DCP Khare, along with the Additional DCP, directed police officers to ensure that public celebrations were conducted peacefully without causing inconvenience to residents.
The DCP also appealed to youngsters and festival organisers to refrain from using excessively loud sound systems and cooperate with the police in maintaining public safety and communal harmony.
“Celebration is everyone’s right, but public safety is everyone’s responsibility. Charminar Zone Police will stand with the public, but violations of law and safety norms will not be permitted. Let us celebrate with devotion, discipline and responsibility,” the officer said.

Bollywood veteran Amitabh Bachchan paid a heartfelt tribute to late actor Nana Patekar on the stage of Kaun Banega Crorepati 18. Dressed in a white ensemble, Amitabh began Thursday’s episode by remembering Nana’s immense influence not just on the film industry but also on everyone whose life he touched. “Aapko Nana vyaktigat roop se mera naman,” he said. The actor also recalled Nana’s appearance on the show and how he left a lasting impression on both him and the audience before donating his prize money to those in need.
Addressing the audience at the beginning of the episode, Amitabh Bachchan announced Nana Patekar’s demise and remembered him as an “adwitiya kalakar” (unparalleled artist), a friend, well-wisher and an exceptional social worker.
“Deviyo aur sajjano, Nana Patekar ji ka achanak aaj subah swargwas ho gaya. Ek adwitiya kalakar, mitra, shubhchintak, aur ek utkrisht samaj sevak aaj hamare beech nahi rahe,” Amitabh said. He further described Nana’s passing as a loss not only for the Indian film industry but also on a deeply personal level for everyone who had known and interacted with him.
“Ye na keval Bharatiya film udyog ke liye, balki ek vyaktigat taur par, jinka bhi unke saath sampark hua, usne hum sabko stabdh kar diya hai,” he said. Amitabh then highlighted the qualities that made Nana stand apart, particularly his fearlessness, simplicity and courage to speak the truth without hesitation.
Remembering the lasting impact Nana had on those around him, Amitabh said, “Kuch log hamare jeevan se chale jaate hain, lekin unki aawaz, unke paropkar, unki sikhai hui seekh hamare bhitar reh jaati hai. Nana unhi logon mein se ek the.” He emphasised that although Nana may no longer be present, his voice, acts of compassion and the lessons he imparted would continue to remain with people.
Amitabh concluded his tribute by offering his personal respects to the late actor and acknowledging his contribution to Indian cinema. “Aapko, Nana, vyaktigat roop se mera naman. Aur aapki us kala ko pranam, jise aapne puri imandari se jeeya aur hum sabko samarpit kiya,” he said, saluting the honesty and dedication with which Nana lived his art and shared it with audiences.
Nana Patekar’s mortal remains were brought from Goa to Pune on Thursday evening for his final rites. The veteran actor’s last rites are being performed at his farmhouse in Donje village, near Khadakwasla, on the outskirts of Pune. The Maharashtra government has accorded him a state funeral in recognition of his contribution to Marathi theatre, Hindi and Marathi cinema.

On the rickshaw ride to the hospital, Marian Haji Abdi Guled felt a mixture of joy and apprehension: the day they had been waiting for had finally arrived.
Almost a year earlier, her then seven-year-old son, Abdiqadir Salah, had been seriously injured, alongside his two siblings, in what a Guardian investigation found was a US drone strike on the village of Jamaame in Somalia that killed at least 12 civilians, including eight children.
Abdiqadir’s small body had been impaled by shrapnel in the attack, and several chunks remained embedded in his back.
Doctors feared that without an operation to remove them, the boy would lose his ability to walk, but Guled had no money for an operation. For 10 months, the family had languished in Mogadishu with growing expenses and no income – unable to afford surgery, but unwilling to let the boy return to the village without it.
After the investigation, which told the story of Guled and other civilians affected by the attack, a group of Guardian readers from across the globe fundraised for Abdiqadir’s surgery and recovery.
Within a few hours, enough money was raised to cover his treatment and rehabilitation, as well as any medical expenses and treatment for her other two children, who sustained less extensive injuries.
“I was so happy when I found out that Guardian readers raised the money needed for my son’s surgery. I didn’t know people like this existed,” Guled said.
“The people who contributed to the surgery – I really appreciate their support and how they stood by our family when we needed it the most.”
On a Saturday morning in September, Guled waited anxiously as Abdiqadir was finally taken for surgery at Kaafi hospital in Mogadishu.
“Other patients were taken into surgery after him and came out before him – so I worried maybe something went wrong,” she said. “I got to a point where I knocked on the operating room door asking if my son was still alive, then was held back by other patients.”
Finally, her son emerged. Doctors told Guled the surgery had been successful, but complex. While the first two pieces of shrapnel from the missile had been successfully removed, taking out the final piece was considered too risky, possibly resulting in paralysis, so they concluded that it was safer to leave it and monitor his condition.
When the Guardian visited Abdiqadir a few weeks later, he appeared bright, energised and visibly happy. “I have one piece of metal still in me, and if they touch it, I might become paralysed,” the seven-year-old said. “[But] I don’t have any problem with the last piece of metal in my body, because I’m no longer in pain.”
The Guardian investigation into the US airstrikes that injured Abduqadir raised myriad questions about US military intelligence, such as how the targets were selected and why children were hit while they were clearly visible and out in the open. The US has not responded to any questions about the Jamaame attack.
In the months since then, US attacks on the area have continued: from December 2025 to July 2026, it carried out at least three airstrikes around Jamaame, according to research by New America, a security thinktank that documents US military operations abroad. Residents say drones continue to fly above the town.
“We cannot return to Jamaame because what caused my children to be hurt is still there,” Guled said. “I fled Jamaame with my wounded children because of the drones, and the drones are still [flying].”
With the remaining financial support she received from Guardian readers, Guled plans to relocate with her children to the government-controlled port city of Kismayo, which has not been the target of drone strikes, and where Abdiqadir can receive further surgery if needed.
She still wants answers from the US government, nearly a year after they were bombed. “My son has been left scarred for life,” she said.
“I want the US government be held accountable for what they did to my family and for the US to stop bombing our community.”

A Reddit post by a person claiming to be a senior engineer at Uber has reignited a familiar debate in India over taxation, job security and the support available to employees during difficult periods.
The engineer claimed that he paid ₹92 lakh in income tax to the Indian government during the previous financial year after reaching what he called a “salary cliff” last year.
He now says he is struggling to find another job, even at a lower position offering a salary of ₹90 lakh a year.
“Being a senior engineer at Uber and hitting the salary cliff last year, I paid a crazy ₹92 lakhs tax to the Indian Government in last FY,” the user wrote.
According to the post, the engineer lost his job while he was away from work on paternity leave.
“Got laid off this year while I was on 4 months of Paternity leave," he wrote.
He also cited Uber's paternity leave policy, claiming that the company provides 18 weeks of official paternity leave. However, the Reddit post alone does not provide enough information to establish the circumstances surrounding his termination.
The engineer said the job loss has come at a particularly difficult time, with a newborn child at home and no family support available to him.
He claimed that these circumstances would make it difficult for him to immediately focus on searching for another job.
The Reddit user said his immediate priority was receiving his severance, which he needs while managing his family responsibilities and delaying his job search.
He also criticised the prospect of having to pay tax on the severance amount.
“The Government will again LOOT me through taxing on SEVERANCE as well," he wrote.
His statement, however, reflects his personal understanding of the situation and should not be treated as a definitive description of Indian tax law. The taxability of severance or compensation can vary depending on the nature, structure and terms of the payment and the applicable tax provisions.
Therefore, there is no blanket rule that every severance payment is taxed in the same manner.
The engineer also argued that workers in India do not receive sufficient protection and contrasted his situation with what he believed might have happened in other countries.
Those comparisons represent his personal views and cannot, based solely on the post, be treated as established conclusions about employment laws in India or elsewhere.
His account nevertheless highlights a concern that many employees in India's technology sector may recognise: even a highly paid job can disappear suddenly, while financial commitments and family expenses continue.
Towards the end of his post, the engineer said he had decided to move out of India.
“I am leaving India soon and would never want to come back.”
He concluded the post by urging others to reconsider their choices if they believe relocating could provide greater security for their families.
“Learn from my mistakes and leave if you want well for your family.”

A seven-storey residential tower block has collapsed in Istanbul, triggering a desperate search for residents trapped under the debris.
Authorities said the lower three floors of the building caved in at around 5.40am local time in the Maltepe district on the Asian side of the city.
Emergency crews rushed to Doğu Street in the Cevizli neighbourhood after receiving reports that multiple residents were buried beneath tons of concrete and twisted metal.
Top floors of the structure remained standing, allowing firefighters to safely evacuate residents stranded on the upper levels.
Rescue workers using heavy machinery, search dogs, and acoustic listening devices have now established contact with several victims buried inside the lower section.
The number of people believed to be trapped under the rubble remains uncertain.
So far, nine people – including two children – have been rescued from the rubble, according to regional outlets.
No fatalities have yet been confirmed.
Istanbul governor Davut Gül confirmed at the scene that rescue teams have made contact with a six-year-old child trapped beneath the debris, but crews are currently being forced to alter their approach due to the site’s instability.
“Our teams made contact with several individuals trapped beneath the rubble shortly after arriving,” he told reporters, adding that specialised units are working under extreme caution to prevent further collapse.
The cause of the structural failure remains under investigation.

New Zealand authorities have launched their own investigation into the flydubai co-pilot who allegedly tried to hijack an Israel-bound plane, after police confirmed he underwent flight training there about a year after he abandoned a degree in Australia.
Disaster was narrowly averted on 30 September when passengers and crew intervened to stop the alleged attempt of the co-pilot, Hamam al-Hammami, 29, to take control of a flight to Tel Aviv with 182 people onboard.
Hammami, an Omani national, had allegedly used a crash axe in the attempted “terrorist attack”, in which the pilot was stabbed mid-air, the United Arab Emirates’ prosecutor general said. Israeli and other officials in the region suspect he originally planned for such an attack in July, but postponed it.
The New Zealand police assistant commissioner, Michael Johnson, on Tuesday confirmed the man was in the country on a student visa for 175 days, from 30 November 2018 to 23 May 2019.
“Police can confirm the co-pilot was in New Zealand to complete a portion of his flight training for a UK-based company, no longer operating in New Zealand,” Johnson said in a statement
The police are now investigating his time in the country, Johnson said.
New Zealand joins multiple countries scrambling to piece together the background of Hammami and his intentions, as well as to establish if he acted alone.
Over the weekend, Australian security agencies launched an investigation after it emerged Hammami spent about two years in the country as a student until 2017. He left the country without completing his engineering degree, RMIT University in Melbourne confirmed.
On a now deleted social media profile believed to belong to Hammami, the then student appears in a selfie with other teenagers in a shopping centre food court in Melbourne’s CBD.
The UK’s Telegraph reported on a post on a now deleted X account that appears to be linked to Hammami that described his years studying overseas as “the golden years of my religious commitment”, and claimed he became less observant when he returned to Oman.
On Wednesday, Australia’s peak Jewish body, the Executive Council of Australian Jewry, called for a thorough investigation of Hammami’s associations in the country.
“We have seen over the years the availability of extremist literature in religious bookstores, the presence of preachers of hate and violence and the capacity for those living in Australia to fall under the sway of recruiters and nefarious street preachers,” the council’s co-chief executive, Alex Ryvchin, said in a statement.
“We have to understand who associated with this [alleged] terrorist, who influenced him and what vestiges of his murderous ideology remain.”
The flight’s captain, Smit Machchhar, who also trained in New Zealand for a time, said on Saturday that shortly after Hammami had left his seat to pray, he felt a “big blow” to the back of his head.
In a phone call on Saturday with Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, Machchhar said: “The blows kept coming … That’s when I realised that it’s not the aircraft, it’s the other guy who was in the cockpit with me.”
Despite his injuries Machchhar was able to unlock the cockpit’s security door to allow passengers to overpower Hammami. A reserve flydubai pilot travelling on the flight took control of the aircraft and landed it at a regional airport in north-western Saudi Arabia, where the co-pilot was detained by Saudi authorities.

- The claim that male students who were accused of raping a female student at Cornell University were fired from their jobs or expelled from Cornell is still under investigation.
- Snopes readers asked us to determine what happened to each of the seven accused, including whether the university penalized them or their employers fired them.
- A spokesperson for Cornell said via email that the university issued suspensions for some students and expelled others but did not specify which students received which penalties. Cornell did not respond to our specific questions about each student.
- Using the university database, social media posts, a lawyer's statements and college news reporting, Snopes was able to determine that at least one of the accused was still a student on campus. Three others were alumni at the time of the September 2026 lawsuit, while the remainder have an undetermined status at the university.
- Snopes has also reached out to most of the accused students using emails from the college database. We will update this report if we get more information.
In September 2026, a lawsuit brought against Cornell University and seven of its male students alleged the men drugged and raped a 20-year-old female student in October 2024. The story spread online along with claims that the accused students faced little or no consequences, though some allegedly lost their jobs or were expelled.
As Snopes previously reported, the lawsuit named seven male students as defendants: Matthew Ingalls, Johnathan Newell, Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris and Scott Kretzschmar. According to the lawsuit — filed on behalf of the plaintiff, identified only as Jane Doe, on Sept. 14 — the drugging and multiple assaults occurred the night of Oct. 19, 2024, into the early hours of Oct. 20 at the Xi chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity.
According to Doe's lawsuit, Cornell temporarily suspended the accused students on Nov. 8, 2024, (Page 29) but they were given the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by writing an essay to the university. Cornell has denied that the students only had to write essays as a disciplinary measure.
Posts on X, Facebook and Instagram claimed two of the accused students, Sarabia and Ingalls, lost their jobs at Wells Fargo and Data Annotation Tech, respectively. Jane Doe's attorney also reportedly claimed two of the students were expelled from the university, without naming them.
Snopes emailed a spokesperson for Cornell University to determine the enrollment status of each of the accused students. The university declined to respond to specific questions about the accused, directing us to its official statement. The statement says that students were expelled and/or suspended but would not identify which students:
Temporary suspensions and other restrictive measures were issued when the conduct was reported. Chi Phi, Xi Chapter was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus. Following the university's Title IX investigation, sanctions including expulsions and suspensions were issued by a hearing panel comprising trained faculty and staff. Federal privacy law prohibits Cornell from disclosing specific information regarding individual students, and the university is therefore unable to make a public statement regarding any other disciplinary response.
Below we break down everything we know about the education and employment status of each of the seven accused students. We will update this story as we learn more.
Diego Sarabia
Student newspaper The Cornell Daily Sun and Cornell's online directory say Sarabia is an alumnus from the class of 2025. 
Gossip outlet TMZ reported, citing anonymous sources, that Sarabia is no longer employed at a Wells Fargo bank branch in Charlotte, North Carolina. It was not possible to independently verify this ourselves. According to the report, Sarabia had worked at the branch since 2022. Wells Fargo has not publicly commented on the story as of this writing.
Snopes has contacted several Wells Fargo representatives to learn more about Sarabia's role, employment status and the circumstances around his alleged termination. The company has not responded to our queries.
An Oct. 3 New York Times investigation, that was updated on Oct. 5, says Sarabia received a persona non grata order from the university and was barred from campus for three years. Sarabia had graduated by the time Cornell's disciplinary panel issued a ruling. Given the Times reportedly obtained summaries of the punishments from an unknown source, it was not possible to independently verify the newspaper's findings.
Snopes has also reached out to Sarabia through an email address in the student directory.
Matthew Ingalls
On Sept. 30, Data Annotation Tech responded to the claim that it had employed one of the accused. The company, which hires independent contractors to train artificial intelligence models, said on Instagram (archived) that one of the accused was blocked from its platform in May 2024, long before the lawsuit.
According to its Instagram post, which does not name Ingalls, the claim that the company employed one of the accused is "incorrect." It continues, "He has had no access to our platform or our company at any point since then."
We contacted Data Annotation Tech to learn more about whether Ingalls, specifically, had ever been a contractor or employee there.
The Daily Sun reported that Ingalls was a member of the class of 2027. Cornell's online database initially listed Ingalls as a student but his college affiliation as "not applicable." When Snopes returned to the directory on Oct. 2, his name had been removed.
The New York Times investigation says Ingalls was expelled from Cornell.
Snopes has reached out to Ingalls through an email address in the student directory.
Gillio Lopes
The Daily Sun reported that Lopes was a member of the class of 2027 and was still listed in the directory as a student in the College of Arts and Sciences. Snopes was unable to confirm the directory listing.
Footage shared online purported to show a woman confronting Lopes on Cornell's campus in late September 2026. Lopes' lawyer confirmed the veracity of the footage to TMZ, saying:
What has emerged today only reinforces how dangerous it is to rush to judgment. The contemporaneous texts and other evidence now being reported show a far more complicated and evolving factual picture than the one initially presented to the public.
[…]
Due process exists for precisely this reason. Publicity is not evidence. Repetition is not proof. An accusation cannot be allowed to become its own proof. He is entitled to have the evidence tested through the legal process—not by headlines, social media, or people confronting him in public or threatening his family.
The New York Times investigation says Lopes received a three-semester suspension and two years of probation. He was reportedly ordered to not contact Doe, to study sexual harassment and to write a reflection paper.
Snopes has reached out to Lopes' lawyer, Andrew Miltenberg, to learn more.
Winston Lee
The Daily Sun reported that Lee was a member of the class of 2027 and was still listed in the directory as a student in the College of Arts and Sciences.
Some social media users claimed (archived) Lee was still on campus and had changed his name to Jay Lee. As of this writing, Snopes was unable to independently verify this claim.
The New York Times investigation says Lee received a two-year suspension, with several semesters of disciplinary probation upon his return. Like Lopes, he was reportedly ordered to not contact Doe, to study sexual harassment and to write a reflection paper.
Snopes was unable to determine Lee's status via the student directory or to find contact information for him.
Scott Kretzschmar
The Daily Sun reported that Kretzschmar is an alumnus from the class of 2026. When Snopes first looked at the student directory, it listed him as a student, but his college affiliation was "not applicable." When Snopes returned to the directory on Oct. 2, his name had been removed.
The New York Times investigation says Kretzschmar was ordered to not contact Doe, to write a reflection paper and to study sexual harassment, bystander intervention and social media use.
Snopes has reached out to Kretzschmar through an email address in the student directory.
Johnathan Newell
The Daily Sun reported that Newell was a member of the class of 2027. When Snopes first looked at the student directory, it listed a "Jonathan Newell" (with a different spelling) as a student, but his college affiliation was "not applicable." When Snopes went back to the directory on Oct. 2, there was no record of a Johnathan or Jonathan Newell.
The New York Times investigation says Newell was expelled from Cornell.
Snopes has reached out to Newell through an email address in the student directory.
Scott Norris
The Daily Sun reported that Norris is an alumnus from the class of 2026. Cornell's online database initially listed him as a student but his college affiliation as "not applicable." When Snopes returned to the directory on Oct. 2, his name had been removed.
The New York Times investigation says Norris was ordered to not contact Doe, to write a reflection paper and to study sexual harassment, bystander intervention and social media use.
Snopes has reached out to Norris through an email address in the student directory.

‘If a sibling uses a skin-lightening product, you may be more likely to use one too’. This was among the findings from behavioural research cited by the World Health Organisation (WHO) during a discussion on colourism in Hyderabad on Wednesday (October 7, 2026).
The discussion was part of ‘Complexion of Change: Challenging Colorism Through Policy, Art, and Science’, held at Goethe-Zentrum in Hyderabad. A documentary exploring global skin colour bias and the deep-rooted societal association of fair skin with higher status, beauty and success was also screened as part of the programme.
“Skin-lightening product use was not a single behaviour but was influenced by psychological, cultural and environmental factors,” said Ammaarah Martinus, Behavioural Insights consultant at the WHO.
The psychological dimension includes motivations such as wanting to appear fairer, younger or to fit into society. The cultural dimension includes the influence of families, communities and social networks. Mr. Martinus said research had found that people were more likely to use a skin-lightening product if a sibling used one. She also spoke about access to such products . In India, skin-lightening products could be easily purchased in local markets and supermarkets. “Interventions to address skin-lightening therefore need to work across all three levels rather than focus on only one aspect of the behaviour,” she added.
Psychologist and researcher Bharti Upparu said children begin receiving messages about skin colour at a very young age, often without anyone explicitly telling them that one skin tone is preferable to another. They observe who is complimented, who is bullied and who is teased, and gradually learn which physical characteristics society values. “A person perceived as fair and attractive may unconsciously be associated with other positive characteristics such as competence, goodness and trustworthiness. Such biases can compound into an overall perception of a person’s character and affect how others interact with them,” she said.
The discussion also highlighted that colourism is not restricted to women. Arpit Bhutani, co-founder of Circular Innovation Lab and moderator of the session, pointed to products marketed specifically towards men and noted that the pressure to conform to lighter-skin beauty standards also affects men.
Former Miss America Nina Davuluri recalled an incident involving a friend’s baby, when an older family member cautioned against taking the child into the sun because the child could become darker. “Such comments are not necessarily made with malicious intent but can come from a desire to see children succeed in a society where lighter skin is perceived to offer advantages,” she added.
Mercury in skin-lightening products
In remarks before the documentary screening, Monika Stankiewicz, executive secretary of the Minamata Convention on Mercury, said mercury was among the chemicals of highest public concern according to the WHO and that cosmetics were one pathway through which people could be exposed. “Mercury-containing skin-lightening products can damage the skin and may also contaminate households, potentially exposing other family members,” she added.
Ms. Stankiewicz stressed that the issue was not solely a chemical problem but also a social one linked to beauty standards and the pressure to conform to them. She said meaningful change could not come through regulations alone and that activism, art, culture and storytelling also had important roles to play.

Eradicating Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection early could become an important strategy for preventing gastric cancer, Nobel laureate and gastroenterologist Dr. Barry Marshall said, stressing the need for wider testing, appropriate treatment and confirmation that the infection has been cleared.
Dr. Marshall, who shared the 2005 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Robin Warren for their discovery of H. pylori and its role in gastritis and peptic ulcer disease, said the bacterium should no longer be regarded only as a cause of ulcers.
“H. pylori is much more than an ulcer organism. If the infection persists for many years, it can cause chronic inflammation in the stomach and increase the risk of gastric cancer. That gives us an opportunity because this is a potentially preventable cause of cancer," Dr. Marshall told PTI.
Dr. Marshall was in India to attend the World Congress of Gastroenterology (WCOG 2026) in the national capital.
Held in India for the first time, the four-day event, which concluded on October 3, brought together around 3,000 delegates from 61 countries to discuss the changing global burden of gastrointestinal and liver diseases, including H. pylori infection, gastric cancer prevention, early diagnosis and treatment.
His comments come amid renewed global focus on population-based H. pylori "screen-and-treat" programmes for gastric cancer prevention.
The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) working group has recommended such programmes in populations where the benefits are expected to outweigh potential harms.
Dr. Marshall said the priority should be to identify infected individuals and ensure they receive effective eradication therapy.
"If we can find the infection before there has been extensive damage to the stomach, we have a much better chance of preventing the chain of events that can eventually lead to cancer," he said.
However, rising antibiotic resistance is emerging as a major challenge to this approach, he highlighted.
A 2026 review in Gastroenterology noted that increasing antimicrobial resistance is threatening the success of established H. pylori treatment regimens, while concerns also remain about the effects of repeated antibiotic exposure on the microbiome.
"We cannot simply keep giving the same antibiotics and expect the same results. Resistance varies between countries and even between regions, so treatment needs to take local resistance patterns into account," Dr. Marshall said.
The IARC guidance similarly emphasises antibiotic stewardship, treatment based on local resistance patterns and follow-up testing to determine whether eradication has been successful.
Dr. Marshall said India, where H. pylori infection is common, has an important role to play in generating evidence on local bacterial strains and antibiotic resistance.
"India has a very large population with H. pylori, so it is an important setting for research. We need to understand which strains are circulating, what antibiotics are still effective and how we can make testing and treatment accessible," he said.
According to the IARC guidance, Indian recommendations have included bismuth-containing quadruple therapy in areas with high clarithromycin resistance, highlighting the importance of regional resistance patterns in treatment decisions.
Dr. Marshall also stressed that successful treatment should not be assumed simply because symptoms improve.
"Treating the patient is only half the job. We should confirm that the bacterium has actually been eradicated. Otherwise, the patient may continue to carry the infection and remain at risk," he said.
He said non-invasive testing could make detection easier and help expand screening.
Dr. Marshall has also invented PYtest, a C14 urea breath test that provides a 15-minute, non-invasive and quantitative method for detecting current H. pylori infection using a breath sample from the patient.
The patient-friendly test could help Indian doctors detect active H. pylori infection through a quick diagnostic procedure.
PYtest is available in India through Pylorium Diagnostics, part of Trimed Australia, founded by Dr. Marshall and headed by Bhanu Rahoni in India.
The need for prevention has gained urgency as gastric cancer remains a major global health burden, with the highest incidence concentrated in several Asian regions.

Just ahead of the collective protest called by Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and left groups on October 10, 2026, seeking the scrapping of the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls and the removal of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, Mumbai-based activist on Thursday (October 8, 2026) alleged that Mumbai Police detained and released them on the condition to stay in Mumbai.
Similar allegations have been made by All India Students’ Federation (AISF) members on police for attempting to arbitrarily detain a student delegation travelling aboard the 12779 Goa Express from Pune to New Delhi.
“Mumbai Police illegally detained activists Feroze Mithiborwala and Salim Saboowala around 11 a.m., after putting media pressure they were released on the condition to stay in Mumbai,” said Guddi. L, political activist and convenor of Hum Bharat Ke Log, a civil society group led by Tushar Gandhi, the great-grandson of Mahatma Gandhi.
Ms. Guddi suggested that the activists were picked up as they were seen in the October 2, 2026 protest in Mumbai.
Both the activists received a call from police in the morning and informed them of their visit on Thursday (October 8, 2026). “We had no plans to go to Delhi. Yet, such harassment is done at the hands of police. Besides, as a citizen we can move anywhere. How can police detain?” she added.
Hum Bharat Ke Log has referred the alleged state action a direct, calculated attempt to prevent civil society leaders from traveling to New Delhi to participate in the peaceful protest scheduled for October 10, 2026.
Attempt to detain students from Pune
The AISF condemned police attempt detains the students as “unconstitutional, and unlawful”.
“When the Goa Express reached Bhusawal, a police contingent comprising 8 to 10 personnel — led by Police Inspector Govind Pathak and Lady Police Officer Minal Tayade — barged into the train compartment and attempted to forcefully detain and deboard the AISF comrades without any legal basis,” said Shravani, AISF Pune District Convener in a statement.
She also alleged that police failed to produce valid warrants for detention adding that, they refused to go with the police.
The ASIF’s statement stated that the delegates remain on board the train, which is currently running over seven hours late and has been unexpectedly diverted through Uttar Pradesh, deviating from its standard route.
The CJP also highlighted that Instagram handles of three of their supporters — Gaurav bharti, Nisar, and Pranay Ahire — have been taken down.
Meanwhile, another delegation travelling from Pune to Delhi were detained by the Madhya Pradesh Police in the Itarsi region.
Mumbai Police is yet to respond to the queries from The Hindu.
