A mega free health and medical camp was organised at Government Polytechnic College in Anantapur on Wednesday. The camp extended essential healthcare services to nearly 600 students and youth with the message “Healthy Youth, Healthy Nation”.
The camp was organised by Nigama Foundation in coordination with NSS, JNTUA, Government Polytechnic College, Anantapur, Pragathi Padham Youth Association and MY Bharat of the Union Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports. The initiative was held as part of the foundation day celebrations of Nigama Foundation.
The programme was attended by G. Mamatha, NSS coordinator, JNTUA; Bisathi Bharath, MY Bharat Representative and national youth awardee; Jaya Chandra, principal, Government Polytechnic College; Vasundhara Penakalapati, Nigama Foundation, along with medical professionals, faculty members and volunteers.
In collaboration with KH Mind Care Hospital, Anantapur, Indian Red Cross Society, Anantapur, and Icon Eye Hospital, the camp provided free blood grouping, haemoglobin and diabetes screening, blood-pressure checks, general and orthopaedic consultations, and eye examinations to the students.
Speaking at the programme, G. Mamatha appreciated the Nigama Foundation for extending selfless healthcare services to students, particularly those from rural backgrounds. She highlighted the importance of such initiatives in promoting preventive healthcare, mental well-being and healthy lifestyles among young people.
She also appreciated Nigama Foundation’s continued youth-oriented initiatives, including mental health awareness, Nasha Mukt Yuva for Viksit Bharat, screen de-addiction and educational support for students and youth in rural and remote areas.

Mayor of Turkish opposition stronghold defects to Erdogan's party
A stronghold of Turkey’s opposition has fallen to President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s ruling party for the first time
ISTANBUL -- The mayor of Turkey’s third-largest city defected to President Recep Tayyip Erdogan ’s ruling party on Wednesday, giving it the mayoralty of the opposition stronghold for the first time.
Izmir had been led by the opposition Republican People’s Party, or CHP, for more than two decades until Mayor Cemil Tugay joined Erdogan’s Justice and Development Party, or AKP, at a ceremony at its headquarters in Ankara.
In a brief speech after Erdogan pinned a party badge on his lapel, Tugay described the AKP as the “voice of the voiceless” and pledged to revitalize and rebuild Izmir as the western port city’s first AKP mayor.
Tugay, who won the 2024 election with 49% of votes, resigned from the CHP in June after the party was hit by a legal case that removed its leadership.
The court’s decision in May saw droves of CHP members leave, with many joining the New Party established by deposed CHP leader Ozgur Ozel, which surpassed the CHP as the largest opposition party. Tugay, however, remained as an independent and denied plans to join the AKP.
Izmir’s municipal assembly remains under the control of a New Party majority.
Police set up barriers in Izmir’s main square Wednesday after the opposition called for people to protest Tugay’s defection.
Since 2024, when the CHP strengthened its grip on many major cities, including the capital Ankara and Istanbul, municipalities held by the party have been targeted by waves of criminal investigations that have seen hundreds of CHP members jailed.
The most prominent is Ekrem Imamoglu, the metropolitan mayor of Istanbul and the opposition’s favored challenger to Erdogan in the next presidential election. He has been behind bars since March last year.
Imamoglu faces several legal cases, with the main one alleging corruption within the Istanbul municipality. If convicted, he could be sentenced to more than 2,300 years in total.
While critics claim the court cases are politically motivated and aimed at weakening the opposition, the government insists the country’s judiciary is independent and free from political influence.

If there was a year the world began waking up to climate change, it might have been 1988. That June, the NASA climatologist James Hansen testified to Congress that the climate was warming and would continue to do so as long as humans pumped fossil fuel pollution into the atmosphere. Months later, the United Nations established the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.
And, just weeks before the UN vote, Frank Sprow of Exxon’s corporate research department warned his colleagues in an internal memo, “If a worldwide consensus emerges that action is needed to mitigate against Greenhouse gas effects, substantial negative impacts on Exxon could occur.”
Sprow’s memo is part of a batch of previously undisclosed documents released earlier this year without fanfare as part of an ongoing lawsuit Massachusetts filed against ExxonMobil in 2019. While the memo was quoted in a 2023 article by The Wall Street Journal, it has not been published in full. Several other documents included in the filings are being reported on here for the first time, including more recent statements from Exxon scientists challenging the company’s climate-solution claims about its work on biofuels and carbon capture and storage.
While the documents align with hundreds of confidential files that have previously come to light through reporting by Inside Climate News and other news organizations, as well as lawsuits and other sources, experts say they provide new details on internal deliberations at Exxon from the 1980s to the 2010s.
The release of the documents comes at a pivotal time for the oil industry and for efforts to hold it accountable for its role fueling climate change. This week, the US Supreme Court heard arguments from Exxon and oil producer Suncor Energy that a lawsuit filed by the city and county of Boulder, Colorado, should be halted. The outcome of that decision could decide whether more than two dozen other claims against oil companies proceed.
Aaron Regunberg, director of climate accountability at the advocacy group Public Citizen, said the documents from the Massachusetts case underscore why Exxon and other companies are fighting to block the lawsuits from even proceeding to the discovery phase.
“They are really scared of the public finding out about this reality,” Regunberg said of oil companies. The Massachusetts filings, he said, suggest “that we have seen just a sliver of the evidence that they actually have that they’ve spent decades knowingly deceiving the public about this crisis. How many more reports are they sitting on?”
Most of the lawsuits assert that oil companies should help pay the escalating costs being imposed on the public by climate-fueled extreme weather because they knew the risks their products posed but worked to publicly question climate science and stymie efforts to curb emissions. Those costs have surged, topping $100 billion in the US in four of the last five years. Exxon, meanwhile, reported nearly $19 billion in earnings over the first six months of this year alone.
Exxon did not respond to requests for comment, but it has denied misleading the public or investors about climate change. In its annual securities filing, the company said of the lawsuits, “We believe the legal and factual theories set forth in these proceedings are meritless and represent an inappropriate attempt to use the court system to usurp the proper role of policymakers in addressing the societal challenges of climate change.”
The case brought by the Massachusetts attorney general’s office in state court is slightly different from others, arguing that the company deceived the state’s consumers and investors into thinking it was taking action to limit warming when those efforts were more about public relations than real action. The state is seeking fines and an injunction blocking Exxon’s allegedly deceptive practices.
The new documents, filed as part of a dispute over whether Exxon should be forced to hand over more files and testimony, help lay out the state’s case.
Take biofuels. For years, Exxon ran a sustained public relations campaign touting its research into using algae to make fuel, which it said could be a sustainable alternative to petroleum.
In March, The Wall Street Journal reported on internal documents that showed Exxon’s scientists told executives the company’s targets were not feasible. The new disclosures in the Massachusetts case add to the evidence with excerpts from a deposition by an Exxon scientist who worked on the program.
Asked whether a 2018 press release, which said Exxon anticipated “10,000 barrels of algae biofuel per day could be produced by 2025,” was misleading, the scientist said “yes,” adding, “All the clauses in there are patently false.”
The scientist testified that the 10,000-barrel-per-day target was “completely impossible to achieve,” and that he told this to others at the company before the press release was issued.
In another instance, the scientist said a research development on algae that Exxon publicly claimed as a breakthrough was, in fact, “a dead end.”
Exxon later dropped its research into algae biofuels but has continued to promote carbon capture and storage as a climate solution. The documents include some statements which, according to the attorney general’s office, show Exxon knew that technology was also unlikely to present a scalable solution to cutting emissions.
A 2014 presentation on Exxon’s carbon capture portfolio included a slide listing challenges to reaching commercial scale. It noted widespread deployment would require a “massive investment” and an eventual storage rate “comparable to current oil and gas production.” It said costs were high and there were no market-based incentives.
Three years later, a different Exxon scientist was asked by a colleague to record an advertisement for the technology. He noted that the company was calling itself a leader in carbon capture but said he was “not a big fan” of the claim. At the time, Exxon’s carbon capture operations were largely restricted to gas processing plants that stripped the climate pollutant out of methane and injected it into oil or gas fields. That technology, he said, “has nothing to do” with the type of carbon capture that Exxon and others were promoting for power plants and industrial facilities.
That scientist later appeared in an ad promoting research he was conducting on carbon capture without any claim that Exxon was a leader in the technology.
Another presentation from 2017 appears to show the advertisements for algae and carbon capture were among the company’s highest performing, calling them “All-Around Winners.”
In 2021, Exxon was still promoting its work in carbon capture. An internal presentation about an advertising campaign targeting political and financial leaders said its objective was to get people to “believe ExxonMobil is committed to helping solve climate change” and to proving the company and carbon capture and storage “play an indispensable role in facilitating the transition to a lower carbon energy system.”
Under a header of “what we’re doing,” the presentation listed a proposed hub for carbon capture in Houston that Exxon no longer promotes.
While the Massachusetts case focuses on these more recent campaigns, the filings include earlier records that serve as concise roadmaps for what would become Exxon’s climate strategy in the following decades, said Geoffrey Supran, an associate professor of environmental science and policy at the University of Miami. He has published studies comparing Exxon’s public statements with its internal documents and is a consulting expert on some climate-related legal actions.
It was November 1988, five months after Hansen’s congressional testimony, when Sprow filed his draft memo.
With the threat of climate action looming, he wrote, the company’s research and development on “Greenhouse” should have two primary goals: “Protect the value of our resources (oil, gas, coal),” and “Preserve Exxon’s business options.”
Sprow then laid out an agenda for how to achieve those ends.
With modeling critical to climate science, he wrote, “it could be considered important to be at the forefront of this modeling effort.” Sprow proposed “supporting a person on staff at one of the leading modeling centers (e.g. Princeton) or by sending one of our people to work in such a center.”
Sprow also recommended monitoring alternative energy technologies, including nuclear, solar and biofuels, to understand their viability as alternatives to fossil fuels or, eventually, for possible business development. Finally, he added, Exxon could look for “a research breakthrough” in one of these areas that would align with the company’s business.
Sprow did not respond to requests for comment from Inside Climate News, but he told The Wall Street Journal that his memo was adopted as corporate policy.
By the late 1990s, Exxon and other oil companies were working assertively to convince the public and government officials that enacting policies to limit climate pollution would impose grave costs on society.
One newly published Exxon memo summarizing a 1997 meeting of a climate steering group at the American Petroleum Institute, a trade group, outlines many key elements of the strategy.
With governments poised to negotiate an international climate agreement in Kyoto, the steering group would recommend that API “continue to question the scientific basis and cite the high economic cost” of policies to address climate change and “avoid pressures to negotiate a compromise.”
The memo cited polling about which arguments would “resonate with the public.”
It also said Exxon was planning to fund a climate change project by Jonathan Adler of the free-market oriented Competitive Enterprise Institute, who had come to the meeting seeking support. Exxon asked Adler to “focus their project more narrowly” on the impacts of climate policy proposals on individuals and trade competitiveness. The memo outlined a grassroots campaign and efforts with labor unions, and said API continued to work with the American Enterprise Institute, another conservative think tank, to arrange a seminar about a letter written by economists. The goal was to “prevent its misuse by advocates or near-term action.”
“These are sophisticated strategies to use and weaponize experts in order to perpetuate their denial,” said Supran, who co-authored an amicus brief supporting Boulder in the case against Exxon and Suncor. “This is the playbook all in one place.”
In an interview, Adler rejected the argument that he was promoting climate denial. “I can’t speak to what API or Exxon’s motivations were,” said Adler, now a professor at William & Mary Law School. “What I can say is the work we did at CEI at the time was very much focused on what was accurate and correct and consistent with the principles the organization was founded on.”
He said it was natural for his organization to seek funding from companies and entities that also supported limited government regulation.
This year, Adler wrote a brief supporting Boulder in the case before the Supreme Court, arguing that its claims were not preempted by federal law and should be allowed to proceed in state court. He did not take a position on the merits of Boulder’s claims.
By 2005, when Exxon was facing public criticism for its support for groups that questioned climate science, a company spokesperson told Mother Jones magazine that Exxon believed “the scientific evidence on greenhouse gas emissions remains inconclusive and that studies must continue.” She also said Exxon had devoted large sums to university research programs, including a planned $100 million to Stanford University’s Global Climate and Energy Project.
The following year, documents from the Massachusetts case now show, a colleague arranged a meeting for the spokesperson with two self-identified global warming skeptics.
By the 2010s, Exxon’s public position on climate change had evolved. It was no longer questioning science, a position that became harder to maintain as scientists’ conclusions grew stronger and the United States joined the Paris Agreement in 2015. In fact, following Sprow’s advice, the company had one of its research scientists contributing to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.
Exxon was fending off concerns from shareholders that it was failing to prepare its business for the risks posed by climate change, so it began work on a “climate risk matrix,” the documents show. In 2016, the Exxon scientist who contributed to the UN climate panel warned colleagues of the risk of climate tipping points, the probability of which were “poorly understood but probability is expected to rise with temperature change.” He noted that failure to limit emissions would have a growing influence on temperatures beyond 2040 and cited concerns that the impacts of hitting tipping points “would be significantly larger” than the direct effects of heat.
And yet, the Massachusetts case shows, Exxon continued to promote solutions that its own scientists said were unlikely to reach commercial scale. The vast majority of its money instead went to oil and gas, the production of which Exxon plans to expand more than 15 percent by 2030.

Australia must become better at grinding out results in test cricket rather than relying on strong individual performances, captain Pat Cummins said on Thursday ahead of the series opener against South Africa.
The first test begins at Kingsmead on Friday and conditions are expected to fluctuate on what is often described as a tricky wicket, and Australia has to be ready to handle any ebb and flow, he told a press conference.
“For the batsmen and for the bowling group as well, getting into that grind is important. We haven’t played too many of those kinds of test matches in the last few years, particularly in Australia,” he said.
“They’ve been quite fast-paced. A lot of our success has come off big moments, be it a Travis Head century or Starcy (fast bowler Mitchell Starc) running through the top order, but I think we’ve got to get a little bit better, and we can get a bit better getting into the grind.
“It might not be the glamorous stuff, but it’s that grinding out of sessions, not these whirlwind innings at times. Whatever tempo gets thrown at us or what the game needs, we must make sure we match that,” he added.
Australia’s last test against Bangladesh in August was completed inside two days, as were two of the five tests in the Ashes series against England, played in Australia between last November and January.
Australia delayed announcing its team, in contrast to South Africa, whose captain Temba Bavuma had earlier revealed his side’s line-up.
“We don’t know our team at this stage; the selectors will come down here and we’ll just want to have one more look at the ground,” Cummins explained.
“We’re trying to work out what we think is the best batting line-up for these conditions. Obviously, Cam Green’s out and Josh Inglis isn’t here as well.
“So that’s a couple of changes that we’ve got to match up. What are the conditions going to throw at us? We’ve got a full squad. Everyone brings something a little bit different and it’s just trying to work out what we think the best combinations are,” he added.

Rising onion, edible oil, LPG prices push up cost of home thali: Crisil report
The cost of a vegetarian thali rose to ₹30.8 in September from ₹28.1 a year earlier, while the non-vegetarian thali increased to ₹59.5 from ₹56.
The cost of a home-cooked vegetarian thali rose 10% year-on-year in September, while a non-vegetarian thali became 6% more expensive, as higher onion, edible oil, rice and LPG prices pushed up costs of household food, according to Crisil Intelligence.
The cost of a vegetarian thali rose to ₹30.8 in September from ₹28.1 a year earlier, while the non-vegetarian thali increased to ₹59.5 from ₹56, the monthly Roti Rice Rate (RRR) indicator showed.
“The cost of home-cooked vegetarian (veg) and non-vegetarian (non-veg) thalis rose 10% and 6% on-year, respectively, in September, with food costs remaining elevated amid tightening supplies of key staples and higher input costs,” said Crisil Intelligence director Pushan Sharma.
Also read | Why edible oil prices could stay high long after the seasonal onion surge
On a monthly basis, the vegetarian thali became 4% costlier in September, while the non-vegetarian thali rose 3%. Onion was a major driver, with prices jumping 89% on-year to ₹53 a kg from ₹28 a year earlier.
Crisil attributed the onion price surge to tight rabi stocks and a 5-6% decline in production. June rainfall was 40% below the long-period average, delaying kharif transplanting and fresh arrivals. Seasonal festive demand is expected to add to the pressure in the first half of October.
“The near-term outlook remains firm, as seasonal supply constraints are likely to keep food costs under pressure. Onion prices could remain elevated in the first half of October owing to delayed kharif arrivals, before easing gradually towards the end of October as fresh kharif arrivals improve market availability,” Sharma said.
Also read | Home-cooked meals are getting costlier. Here's why your thali costs more now
Tomato prices could also firm up on delayed kharif arrivals and seasonal demand, while potato prices may come under upward pressure as higher-priced cold-storage stocks are increasingly liquidated, he said.
Pulses remain another key monitorable, particularly tur, amid weather-related production risks. Tur and Bengal gram are harvested from January, leaving the market relatively dependent on imports during the pre-harvest period. Tur imports attract zero duty, while Bengal gram imports face a 10% duty.
“Prices typically remain firm during October-November due to seasonal tightness,” Sharma said.
Rice and edible oil are also expected to keep food costs elevated. Prices of rice rose 8% on-year in September, with Crisil expecting paddy production to decline 5-6% because of lower acreage and weaker yields. Steady domestic consumption and export demand are likely to provide further support.
Also read | No relief on the chopping board yet: Why onion costs are over ₹50 per kg despite supply push
Vegetable oil prices rose 12% on-year despite a reduction in the basic customs duty on crude palm oil, while LPG prices remained 10% higher amid global supply disruptions.
“While the reduction in the basic customs duty on crude palm oil from 10% to 5% in late September is expected to lower landed costs by around 5%, robust festive-season demand is likely to keep prices elevated,” Sharma said.
Vegetable oil prices are consequently expected to rise around 10% on-year in October, although at a slower pace than currently, he added.
The non-vegetarian thali saw a relatively smaller increase because broiler prices, which account for about half its cost, rose only 2% on-year. Lower chick placements, monsoon-related supply disruptions and higher maize prices affected broiler supplies.
“Overall, while fresh crop arrivals should provide some relief later in the season, tight inventories, weather-related risks and firm global commodity prices are likely to keep thali costs elevated in the near term,” Sharma said.

Musk's comments come as a Starlink delegation is attending the India Mobile Congress organised in the national captial.
NEW DELHI: SpaceX CEO and the world's richest man Elon Musk on Thursday went on a rant explaining how the Starlink's satellite internet services will help the "least served" in India. Musk had just a day earlier alleged that his telecom firm was facing regulatory hurdles in India due to "oligarchs", a claim which was strongly rejected by the Indian government.Also read: Rahul Gandhi reacts to Musk's remarks; Starlink boss says 'thank you'The SpaceX chief then launched a tweet blitz posting about thrice in just a span of 10 minutes."Starlink will help the least-served in India," he said in a post at 6:18pm.He followed it up with another post at 6:25pm, writing, "Starlink provides Internet connectivity to the least-served, enabling self-education and prosperity by giving people access to sell their products worldwide!"Three minutes later, Elon posted again: "People who oppose @Starlink hurt only the least-served. The wealthy or those living in large cities already have good Internet, so they don’t understand."
Musk's comments come as a Starlink delegation is attending the India Mobile Congress organised in the national captial.Musk's claim about Starlink serving the "least-served" in India is somewhat ironic, as India already ranks among the countries with the lowest internet charges in the world."The last decade was about scalability, penetration, affordability.
We have discussed many times of how voice prices have crashed, data prices have lowered by almost 97%, which has led to greater penetration," information & technology minister Jyotiraditya Scindia said on Thursday.On the other hand, Starlink will reportedly cost Rs 8,600 per month, with an additional Rs 34,000 one-time hardware charge.
What Musk claimed & what the govt replied
"Unfortunately, we are being blocked by certain oligarchs in order to maintain their monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people. You can guess who they are … This is a crime against the people of India!" Musk said in a post on Wednesday.The telecom ministry rejected Musk's claim stating, "Security assessment as part of this process is currently under way in respect of all three licensees""The Department of Telecom has issued licences to all satcom companies as well as provisional spectrum. Now the issue is pending with MHA for security clearance. As soon as it is cleared, they will get it. It has nothing to do with one company," minister of state for communications Chandra Sekhar Pemmasani told reporters on the sidelines of the India Mobile Congress.
Why Starlink has sparked controversy
The logic behind Starlink is simple: Get internet to places where conventional networks are difficult or too expensive to reach. But Elon Musk’s satellite internet service has increasingly become much more than a tool for connectivity. Its growing use in war zones, conflict areas and during internet shutdowns has turned Starlink into a strategic technology and raised questions over who controls access to it.Critics have raised concerns about the company’s links with US intelligence and military agencies, arguing that a privately controlled satellite network could have implications for national security and sovereignty.
Starlink uses thousands of small satellites in low-Earth orbit, around 550km above the planet. Unlike traditional communications satellites positioned around 36,000km away, these satellites can transmit data with lower latency. Users connect through a small receiver with an electronically controlled antenna, which automatically links with satellites passing overhead. The satellites can also transfer data between themselves using laser links.
What are the major concerns
A 2024 report by the Kutniti Foundation, had described Starlink as “a wolf in sheep’s clothing”. The foundation argued that Starlink’s global satellite network gives it capabilities that go beyond conventional telecom services and could create strategic concerns for countries such as India.
US intelligence links: Kutniti has highlighted Starlink’s links with US intelligence and military agencies, including publicly known contracts involving Musk’s companies.
Dual-use technology:The foundation argues that Starlink can provide high-speed internet while also supporting capabilities such as high-definition imagery and live video transmission.
Control beyond borders: Unlike traditional telecom networks that rely on infrastructure within a country, Starlink’s satellites operate from outside national territory, raising questions over regulatory control.
Security requirements: Communications Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia has said Starlink has not yet fulfilled all required security conditions. India’s licence will be issued only after those requirements are met.
Furthermore, the satellites also raise security questions. Satellites travel at roughly 11,000 km/h to 28,000 km/h orbiting the earth and can also be used to monitor activity inside the territory of a country.

Ever since GTA 6 was announced, the excitement around Rockstar’s biggest game yet has been unlike anything I’ve seen in video games. For many gamers, GTA is where their love for video games began, whether that was Vice City, San Andreas, or GTA 5. That makes Grand Theft Auto 6 more than a big video game release. It’s one of the biggest entertainment releases of the decade that millions of players have waited years to experience.
I’m one of them. I’ve pre-ordered the game, saved the soundtrack on my Spotify, put the songs on loop in my playlist, and cleared my schedule for launch week.
The first set of leaks from Cyberleek got me intrigued like everyone else, but the endless stream that followed is what keeps getting in the way of that excitement. Some fans treat every new leaked clip as another piece of the puzzle, but not me. I see them as something that takes away the mystery that makes Rockstar’s video games so special and ruins the fun for me. And that’s why I choose to stay away from them.
GTA 6 Leakers Think They’re Doing Fan Service, but They’re Missing the Point
There’s one thing that we all can agree on: the internet has plenty of appetite for any piece of info related to GTA 6. Rockstar is returning to Vice City with an enormous new world, a story centered on a Bonnie-and-Clyde dynamic duo of Jason and Lucia, and a game that has been in development for over a decade. That level of anticipation is exactly what the leak culture feeds on.
Whether it’s an alleged trailer release date, gameplay footage, or even a previously unseen mechanic, there’s always another piece of GTA 6 info making its way across social media. I’ve run into plenty of the newer leaks myself while browsing for work, and most of the time I deliberately scroll past. Not because I’m not interested in the game; it’s actually the other way around. I’m excited about the game so much that I simply do not want to know.
You see, I approach video games the same way I approach a great book. If I’ve waited years to read something, I don’t want someone handing me the final chapter before I’ve opened the first page. I want to learn the controls myself, or stumble upon an unexpected mechanic, or even meet a strange character without being told they exist. I want to drive through Leonida and find a GTA 6 easter egg that makes me stop the car and wonder how long Rockstar has been hiding it there. That’s the magic of their games.
To be fair, the first set of leaks by Cyberleek did get me intrigued. There was no marketing back then, no extended look at the game, nothing, so it felt like seeing a pool of water in a desert and it not being a mirage. But the second round of leaks didn’t make me more excited. It had the opposite effect on me, like Lenz’s Law. The more info surfaced, the more I wanted to avoid social media altogether. Rather than being excited, I was frustrated, and I don’t think I’m alone in that.
There’s a strange assumption within the leak culture that more information automatically means more of what fans want. But sometimes the best fan service is letting people experience something for themselves rather than force-feeding them excitement.
RDR 2 is a perfect example of that exact experience. I went into Arthur Morgan’s journey wanting to discover that world on my own. I wasn’t following Rockstar’s tips or advice or exploring areas or missions that leakers had been hinting at for months, no. I experienced the journey by exploring, and that’s why the game’s biggest moments hit as hard as they did. GTA works in the same formula.
When you play its open world and dive inside, you realize that hours in that Rockstar quietly handed you another system to play with. However, social media has turned some of that mystery into a constant cycle of clips, screenshots, leaks, reports, and so on. Look, not to be a party pooper, but I understand the curiosity.
GTA 6 is arguably the most anticipated game of its generation. But curiosity doesn’t mean consumption. I’ll also be the devil’s advocate for the moment and say that Rockstar’s summer marketing hasn’t been everything that I hoped for. I would have loved more official gameplay or character-focused material, the way we got before Red Dead Redemption 2.
But I can understand the decision behind keeping things behind closed doors, and a gap in marketing doesn’t justify filling it with mindless leaks that were never meant to be public.
I Want to Be a Resident of Leonida in GTA 6, Not a Tourist Who Knows Everything
To be clear, when I pick up a GTA game, I don’t play it for its world-building or cool cars or blowing things up. I play them to live in them. When I played GTA 5 and GTA Online, Los Santos turned me into a resident where I learned the route to every street, found places I liked, indulged myself in some of the wackiest short films I’ve seen in-game, built my character, and successfully ran multi-million-dollar businesses, and slowly worked out how everything fit together.
The game actually rewarded me for spending time in its world. And that’s what I want from GTA 6. Whether I’m playing as Jason or Lucia, I want to explore every corner of the Grand Theft Auto 6 map for myself. I want to find out which businesses I should get involved with, who to meet to my benefit, stumble upon a heist because I was in the right place, or even find a cool feature to use again and again. But I want those discoveries to belong to me, and not to Cyberleek or any of the notorious leakers out there.
That’s why these GTA 6 leaks frustrate me so much. Even when you actively avoid leaks, they’re impossible to escape. But there’s an even bigger problem: first impressions. A lot of material circulating online is being viewed without the context of the finished game. People see an alleged feature or an unfinished sequence and immediately start judging it. Suddenly, there’s a preconceived notion formed among gamers that a mechanic looks bad or a feature isn’t impressive, or that GTA 6 won’t live up to expectations.
But how can anyone judge an unfinished game fairly until it’s officially in our hands? A leaked clip is not Rockstar’s final product until it’s shipped. A screenshot without context with a gimmicky watermark claiming it’s “real” doesn’t tell you how the mechanic works across an entire game. Still, a negative connotation is developed in people’s minds before they’ve played a single minute. That has me genuinely worried.
I don’t want to spend the next month watching people form opinions around the second round of Cyberleek’s leaks that aren’t the finished experience. The only version that matters to me is the one Rockstar officially releases on November 19, and that’s the version of GTA 6 I’ll judge as a player.
I know Rockstar is already taking all measures necessary to hunt down these leakers and take down all material as it’s released, but there’s one thing I truly do not want to see surface, and that’s the full game build appearing online a week or two before the November 19 release of GTA 6. That would genuinely break my heart as a fan.
There’s already so much material released online by Rockstar themselves to be excited about. I don’t need Cyberleek completely ruining the biggest video game launch for me or for any gamer. If you genuinely care about GTA 6, one of the best things you can do is stop buying into fake hype and leaks. The game is almost here.
Soon you’ll have a controller in your hands next to a console, and all of Leonida is going to be yours to explore. You’ll ride through Vice City, go skydiving, attend a party, find secrets, and live through all the moments Rockstar has crafted for you. When that happens, I want to be surprised, and even though Love is a Long Road, I want it all to lead to an adventure called Grand Theft Auto VI.

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): A 23-year-old woman, four months pregnant, died at a Tribal hostel near Depot Crossing under Kamla Nagar police station limits on Thursday morning. Police suspect suicide by hanging, but her kin have alleged foul play on the basis of injuries on her neck and back.
The deceased, Priyanka Ahirwar, was living at the hostel with her husband Vishnu Ahirwar, who works there as a caretaker. The incident reportedly took place around 4 am. Police reached the spot after receiving information and sent the body to the mortuary for postmortem. No suicide note was found at the spot.
Priyanka's father, Gajraj Singh, said they are residents of Vidisha district. His daughter had a love marriage with Vishnu around three years ago. He alleged that she had repeatedly complained that her husband assaulted her in an inebriated state.
Singh also alleged that the family was not informed about her death by her husband or in-laws, and that he learnt about it through an acquaintance living near the hostel.
Police officials said they are investigating all angles. Further action will be taken after receiving the postmortem report and statements of the family members.

American Airlines is bringing Starlink Wi-Fi to its entire mainline fleet in 2027
It’s more than double the number of aircraft the company quoted earlier this year.
American Airlines will equip its entire fleet of mainline aircraft with Starlink Wi-Fi starting next year, promising speeds of up to 1Gbps via the satellite network's Performance Aero Terminal.
SpaceX had previously signed a contract with American, but back in May the number was 500 aircraft. Today's announcement more than doubles that, with American's mainline fleet (including all narrowbody and widebody aircraft) totaling at more than 1,030.
The commitment means that American's more than 165 million annual customers should be able to expect fast and reliable satellite Wi-Fi during a flight, much more so than previous methods allowed. American appears to have pivoted from a Wi-Fi strategy that last year saw it agree a deal with AT&T to bring high-speed Wi-Fi to its AAdvantage loyalty program members.
Despite losing out to Amazon Leo in the battle for Delta's signature earlier this year, SpaceX and Starlink appear to be winning the broader in-flight satellite Wi-Fi race right now. The former's rollout won't begin until 2028, and Starlink's deal with American adds to the 724 United Airlines aircraft already running its service. That represents around 41 percent of its fleet. Globally, Starlink has now partnered with 48 airlines.

From Navy sailors to a DRDO scientist: Visakhapatnam case adds to string of ‘honey-trap’ spy cases
In Delhi, a serving IAF Wing Commander was arrested in May for allegedly sharing sensitive defence information and classified documents with a PIO.
A "honey-trap" espionage racket involving Indian Navy personnel in Visakhapatnam, which came to light recently, has put online entrapment of defence personnel back in the spotlight. Andhra Pradesh's Counter Intelligence Cell (CIC) has so far questioned 13 Navy personnel and identified 18 suspects in the case over the alleged sharing of maritime intelligence to Pakistani Intelligence Operatives (PIOs).
On Tuesday, the CIC announced the arrest of two people – an Indian Navy sailor Pradeep Mukherjee with the Eastern Naval Command in Visakhapatnam and Annam Sai Varaprasad, a contractual driver for the Navy. Investigators are examining whether sensitive details about naval assets and installations were passed on to the PIO.
Here is a look at similar cases from the past:
Operation Dolphin’s Nose
In December 2019, the Andhra Pradesh CIC busted a similar espionage racket in the Eastern Naval Command in Visakhapatnam, under “Operation Dolphin’s Nose”. Fifteen people, including seven Indian Navy sailors and a Mumbai-based hawala operator, were arrested on charges of having links with Pakistan’s Inter-Services Intelligence and spying for Pakistan after being lured by women into relationships online.
The sailors were recruited in early 2017 and a year later, contacted by “three to four women”, who lured them into online relationships, officials said. The women introduced them to a businessman, who happened to be a Pakistani handler. The sailors would receive money from a hawala operator for their services. The case is still under investigation and the accused are in prison, the officials said.
IAF officer arrested in 2026
In Delhi, a 44-year-old serving Indian Air Force (IAF) Wing Commander was arrested in May this year for allegedly sharing sensitive defence information and classified documents with a PIO after being “honey-trapped” through social media.
Police said the officer was allegedly contacted by a woman suspected to be working for Pakistani intelligence. The IAF officer was booked under the relevant sections of the Official Secrets Act (OSA) after a case was registered at the special cell police station and taken in judicial custody in June.
More such cases reported last year
In March last year, the Uttar Pradesh Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS) arrested two employees at ordnance factories in Firozabad and Kanpur, respectively, for allegedly sharing confidential information with Pakistan’s ISI, after being targeted through the same fake Facebook profile “Neha Sharma”. Investigators said the accused were contacted on Facebook and later WhatsApp, and were allegedly lured with money and blackmailed into sharing information.
In another case, the Maharashtra Anti-Terror Squad arrested Ravi Vermaa – a 27-year-old engineer working for a private defence technology company contracted by the Indian Navy – for allegedly passing restricted documents relating to the naval dockyard to a PIO. Investigators said a woman initially contacted him through a fake social media profile and later communicated with him over WhatsApp. The alleged sharing of documents took place between November 2024 and March 2025.
DRDO scientist case
In 2023, a high-profile "honey-trap" espionage case came to light when the Maharashtra ATS arrested Pradeep Kurulkar, a scientist with the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO). Kurulkar, then heading the DRDO's Research and Development Establishment (Engineers) laboratory in Pune, was allegedly contacted by a woman who called herself "Zara Dasgupta". Investigators said she was a Pakistani intelligence operative (PIO).
The ATS alleged Kurulkar exchanged WhatsApp messages, voice calls and video calls with the woman and shared sensitive defence-related information. Investigators also alleged he offered to show the woman a classified report relating to the BrahMos missile project. The ATS reportedly filed a chargesheet running into more than 1,000 pages.
Army soldier ‘honey-trapped’ in 2022
In July 2022, Rajasthan Police arrested army soldier Shantimoy Rana, accused of sharing classified information about his regiment and videos of military exercises with two PIOs. Police said the two women had contacted Rana through social media and WhatsApp, presenting themselves as being associated with the Military Engineering Service and Military Nursing Service. Investigators alleged Rana also received money for the information exchange.
Earlier that year, Delhi Police arrested IAF jawan Devendra Sharma – an administrative assistant at the Air Force Records Office in Subroto Park – over allegations that he was “honey-trapped” by a Pakistan-based woman and that he leaked sensitive information concerning defence installations and personnel. The Air Force had also initiated court-martial proceedings against him before handing him over to the police.
BrahMos engineer case
Another significant case dates back to 2018, when BrahMos Aerospace engineer Nishant Agarwal was arrested on allegations of spying for Pakistan. Investigators alleged he was “honey-trapped” through fake social media profiles and that sensitive BrahMos-related information was accessed through his computer. Agarwal was sentenced to life-imprisonment in 2024 by a Nagpur court.
In December 2025, the Bombay High Court set aside Agarwal’s life sentence, holding that the prosecution had failed to establish the transmission of sensitive data to Pakistani operatives. His conviction for negligence in handling classified material was retained, carrying a three-year sentence he already served.

The introduction of a merchant discount rate (MDR) on select UPI transactions may be deferred from October 15 to January 1, 2027, amid pushback from retail traders’ associations. A proposal to postpone the rollout is under consideration, with a final decision expected in the coming days, Business Standard reported. A deferment would keep eligible merchant payments free of MDR through the festive season. Members of the UPI and Services Steering Committee, headed by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), met yesterday to discuss the rollout and clarify aspects of the framework, the report said. The committee is also considering exempting businesses with annual turnover of up to ₹40 Lakh, the report added. This would significantly expand the proposed exemption from the earlier framework, under which small merchants receiving up to ₹1 Lakh a month through UPI QR codes directly into their bank accounts were to be spared the fee. Inc42 has reached out to NPCI for comment on the development. The story will be updated based on its response. MDR is a fee merchants pay for processing digital payments. Under the announced framework, a 0.40% charge would apply to eligible person-to-merchant (P2M) UPI transactions above ₹2,000, capped at ₹300 per transaction. Specified categories, including bill payments, utilities, education, and fuel, would attract a flat fee of ₹5 per transaction above ₹2,000. Consumers will not have to pay MDR. The ₹2,000 transaction threshold is expected to remain unchanged, according to the report. Separately, authorities are considering raising the daily UPI transaction limit for certain categories from ₹1 Lakh to ₹2 Lakh. Retailers Push Back Against MDR Retail traders’ associations have opposed the framework, arguing that the charges would increase payment costs for businesses operating on thin margins. The All India Mobile Retailers Association (AIMRA) and All India Consumer Products Distributors Federation (AICPDF) had called for a ‘No UPI Day’ on October 2. They withdrew the planned protest after meeting finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman on September 30. AIMRA has sought a fixed, nominal charge for digital transactions instead of the proposed 0.40% MDR. AICPDF, meanwhile, has estimated that the fee could add ₹7,000 Cr–₹9,000 Cr in annual costs across the FMCG distribution and retail ecosystem. The framework would mark a shift from the zero-MDR regime. Payments up to ₹2,000, person-to-person (P2P) transfers, and eligible small-merchant transactions would remain exempt. The Centre has told the Supreme Court that around 96% of merchant transactions would remain unaffected, putting the share covered by the framework at about 4%. The fee would create a revenue stream for banks, payment service providers, and third-party application providers (TPAPs). Under the standard 0.40% structure, the acquiring bank collects MDR from the merchant and pays 0.28% of the transaction value to the issuing bank as an interchange. The issuing bank then pays 0.12% to the payer-side payment service provider bank, which passes 0.08% to the UPI app provider. This comes as UPI transactions continue to grow in the country. UPI recorded 24.07 Bn transactions worth ₹29.37 Tn in September. Transaction volume rose 22.6% YoY, while transaction value increased 18% YoY.

In early October, a claim spread online that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the world needs to "accept some bad things happening" in exchange for the benefits of artificial intelligence technology.
For example, a post on the offical X account of Polymarket, a cryptocurrency-based prediction market, reads (archived), "JUST IN: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman declares the world needs to 'accept some bad things happening' in exchange for the benefits of AI."
In short, Altman did produce the above statement during an interview with Politico's The Decoded Podcast. As such, we rate the quote as correctly attributed to Altman.
The OpenAI CEO was speaking with Politico's Brendan Bordelon on Oct. 5. Altman was responding to a question about how he would enforce rules around AI compared to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodie, who is in favor of more regulations.
The transcript below begins at the 8:17 mark of the episode (emphasis ours):
BORDELON: Where do you specifically diverge from Anthropic and its pro-regulation CEO, Dario, when it comes to new AI rules? Where's the daylight?
ALTMAN: I think there's a lot of daylight. We have always been a big believer that this technology has to be democratized and put in people's hands. I think one of the biggest differences between us and some of the stricter, let's say, AI safety people is we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency.
So like, you know, I disagree but I understand the perspective of people who are like, "This technology is going to get so powerful and it's so dangerous that a single lab in San Francisco should have it and make sure nothing bad happens and kind of figure out how to dole out the benefits." I think that is a completely unacceptable trade-off from a perspective of liberty and human agency and people self-determining the future. But I understand where it comes from, and I do think the lighter touch regulatory stance that we advocate for comes with an accepting of the fact that some bad things are going to happen as society figures out the resilience.
So, I wouldn't take a trade of saying like, "We'll make sure there's no major hacks, there's no kind of, like, misuse of this technology, there's zero scams, there's zero all the other bad things that will happen," because I think people will do tremendously — orders of magnitude more — good stuff than bad stuff. But when it comes to the potential of, like, a serious loss of control to AI, and this is not a today worry, but it may not be in the distant future, this is where I would say to the accelerationists like, "Let's be a little thoughtful about lurching into this future."
So I would say, "Accept bounded risks, accept risks that we understand in exchange for the benefits and liberty, agency all those things I was just talking about, but don't accept, like, the really catastrophic risk."
The podcast episode is also available on YouTube.
In an article about the episode, Politico notes that Altman agreed with Amodei on the need to slow down AI development and that Altman's lobbyists have been backing new AI safety requirements from the government.
For further reading, Snopes has covered numerous claims about AI data centers and a rumor about Altman.

The era of Amazon's Fire tablets—cheap slate computers ranging from $60 to $280—is over.
All of the Fire tablets are being replaced by the all-aluminum Amazon Alexa Tablet. These tablets will, in a first for Amazon, run official Android and have full access to the Google Play Store. The lack of proper app support was always a sticking point for the Fire tablets, which ran a custom version of Android and had a much more limited app library.
The new Alexa Tablet series comes in three models: the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro ($500), Alexa Tablet 11 ($330), and Alexa Tablet 8 ($230), with the numbers corresponding to the display size. Amazon is also offering kids' editions of the latter two devices at the same prices. These include bumper cases for extra protection, a one-year, worry-free guarantee to replace the device if it breaks, and a year of Amazon Kids+ service to fill the tablet with age-appropriate content.
As for Fire tablets, Amazon says it will stop shipping the devices in the next month or two. It will support them for four years from the last ship date. Amazon is committing to at least four years of software updates for the new Alexa tablets, which will launch with Android 16 and will receive Android 17 early in 2027. Preorders for the new Alexa Tablets are open now, and they'll begin shipping on October 14.
Premium Tablets
The experience is largely the same on all three tablets, with aluminum builds designed to mimic the new aluminum Kindles. The MediaTek Dimensity 8189 chip powers the two smaller tablets, whereas the 12-inch device gets a little more power from the MediaTek Dimensity 8400.
The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is the outlier of the trio, as it's the only one with two display variants: a standard 12-inch LCD screen or a 12-inch Nanomatte display with anti-glare and anti-reflective properties. Upgrade to the Nanomatte—starting at $550—for a matte, paperlike look and feel. With a peak brightness of 500 nits, it should still be bright enough to view in sunlight.

Amazon says it developed this screen in partnership with Corning (the company that makes most of the glass that protects smartphone displays). It's similar to the matte displays found on devices like TCL's Nxtpaper series, though Amazon's vice president of devices, Kevin Keith, says the hexagon-shaped imprint on the Nanomatte display can push out vivid colors and crisp blacks while still retaining those matte properties.
The screen also offers a “really good” writing experience, according to Keith. He says the same engineers who worked on the Kindle Scribe worked with Corning to get that paperlike feel. The screen works with Amazon's new Alexa Tablet Pro Pen ($90), which has 4,096 levels of pressure sensitivity, plus tilt detection. The pen can magnetically dock to the top of the slate for charging and pairing. Amazon also sells a Pro Keyboard ($150) for the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, which attaches to the device via the pogo pins on the bottom edge—no Bluetooth needed.
Now that Android has recently gained multiwindowing features, attaching the keyboard turns the largest Alexa tablet into a productivity machine: split apps across the screen, resize them into various windows, and “save” several desktop arrangements so you can pick up where you left off.
For the kids’ versions of the Alexa Tablet 11 and Alexa Tablet 8, Amazon says the software is still Android with a heavily customized interface for kid-friendly content and built-in parental controls. Keith says one in five kids in the US has an Amazon tablet, so it'll be interesting to see how that changes now that these devices start at a higher price.
Alexa Front and Center
It may look and feel like Android, but Amazon has tweaked the interface to make these Alexa Tablets feel like Amazon hardware.
The top-left corner of the home screen features a persistent widget called the Dynamic Tab. This scrollable widget lets you dive into Amazon content you may have been consuming on another device—say, if you were reading on your Kindle, watching a movie on Prime Video on your iPhone, or snapped some photos and you want to view them on Amazon Photos.
Swipe right, and instead of Google's Discover feed, you're instead greeted with Amazon's For You experience. Amazon's Fire tablets were a vehicle to put Amazon content in front of your eyeballs, and that hasn't changed with the Alexa Tablets. Again, you can continue consuming content here, with tabs for movies and TV, games, and Kindle. There's also a news feed, and you can tap Alexa prompts for more information on a story.
Uniquely, opening the Kindle app triggers “Kindle mode,” which disables all notifications, turns on the blue light filter, and extends battery life to 20 hours (less on the smaller tablets). You can also choose one of three display treatments in this mode: subtle warmth with natural color, a softened paper tone, or monochrome. There's even a fun page-turn effect that mimics turning a page in a book. As soon as you exit the app, notifications turn back on, and the screen returns to normal. Annotations you make with the stylus will sync with Kindle apps on pen-supported devices, like the Kindle Scribe.
As the tablets’ names suggests, Alexa+ is front and center. So far, Amazon has restricted Alexa+ access to paid subscribers or Amazon Prime customers, but Keith says you don't need to subscribe to anything to use Alexa+ on these devices.
In the bottom-right corner, a persistent “Ask Alexa” chat box lets you call up the virtual assistant immediately. You can also trigger it by saying, “Alexa,” just like an Echo device. It can control your smart home devices, but the marquee addition is Alexa's On-Screen Intelligence. It's opt-in—with an on-screen indicator whenever it's active—allowing the assistant to see what you're looking at and answer contextual questions.
For example, if you're traveling to a new city and are looking at a guide filled with restaurant recommendations, you can ask Alexa, “Which of these is closest to my hotel?” and it can filter the list. Got a schedule for your kid's soccer games? Bring up Alexa and ask it to add all the events to your calendar.
Alexa+ also supports live sessions—much like Google's Gemini Live or ChatGPT's Voice Mode, you can have a real-time back-and-forth conversation with the assistant without speaking the wake word at every turn. Watching a TikTok and wondering whether a product in the video is available on Amazon? Naturally, you can ask Alexa, and the assistant can even add it to your shopping cart.
The hardware may finally have the look and feel of other premium Android tablets, but these slates are still built to keep you hooked on Amazon's retail empire.

Rivian R2 owners can now put a live pet cam on their phone's lockscreen
Keep an eye on your furry, feathered or scaly friends when you leave the car.
Rivian's latest software update is one many pet parents will be very pleased to see. EXCLUSIVE: Three years ago, following the last merger involving Warner Bros., Turner Classic Movies came under the spotlight after filmmakers Steven Spielberg, Martin Scorsese and Paul Thomas Anderson called an emergency meeting with David Zaslav about restructuring the network.
Now that Skydance has brought together Warner Bros Discovery and Paramount, the network has a new spot in the corporate structure.
Deadline understands that the channel, which airs classic films such as They Shoot Horses, Don’t They, The Blob and The Asphalt Jungle, will be housed within Skydance Motion Picture Group, which is now led by Co-Chairs Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein.
The move makes sense given that TCM was previously run by Warner Bros. Motion Picture Group bosses Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy, who left ahead of the Paramount-WBD deal, after Spielberg, Scorsese and Anderson’s involvement.
Watch on Deadline
At the time of the original move, De Luca and Abdy reported into then-U.S. Networks Chief Kathleen Finch on the channel, and some elements of the operational side of the business remained under the portfolio of Channing Dungey when she took over Finch’s network responsibilities in 2025.
Earlier this week, Goldberg and Greenstein said they they see themselves as “stewards of two of the most storied studios in Hollywood history,” which bodes well for TCM.
Dungey, who reports to George Cheeks, Co-Chair and Chief Content Officer, Skydance TV, and JB Perrette, Co-Chair & Chief Business Officer, Skydance TV and Skydance DTC, now oversees all of the company’s 50+ cable networks, taking on oversight of Paramount networks such as MTV, Comedy Central, BET and Nickelodeon.
There have also been other key hires in the cable distribution space in recent days; Ray Hopkins was just named President, Distribution, and he will be tasked with handling negotiations with pay-TV operators for the 50-plus cable networks at Skydance as well as CBS, with the resulting deals supplying much-needed revenue for the debt-laden company.

Saudi Arabia urged to spare man sentenced to death over Facebook post
- Published
"I plead for mercy for the wrongs committed by my son. Please forgive him and send him back to us."
Speaking through tears, Rasamanickam Yogalakshmi made a desperate plea for the life of her eldest son, Anojan Sivarasa. The 24-year-old migrant worker is facing the death penalty in Saudi Arabia after an appellate court found him guilty of blasphemy against Islam and the Prophet Muhammad over a comment he made on Facebook.
The case has sent shockwaves through Sri Lanka, sparking widespread concern and civil society petitions across the country. Multiple political parties and government bodies have co-ordinated diplomatic efforts seeking clemency.
However, the family has had no updates on his condition since 28 September. The Sri Lankan government has instructed the family to refrain from making further statements while diplomatic efforts take place.
Saudi authorities have not published an official execution timeline, and it remains unclear when the sentence will be carried out. Saudi Arabia has a history of carrying out executions without warning families or foreign embassies, only informing relatives after the sentence has been carried out.
Anojan was prosecuted after a dispute on social media following an incident that took place during a Hindu pilgrimage in Sri Lanka. In late June, footage of a young Muslim man kicking a dog following Hindu pilgrims circulated widely on social media, triggering religious arguments online.
During the exchange, a user posted derogatory remarks about a Hindu deity, leading Anojan to post a response in Tamil insulting the Prophet Muhammad.
Although Anojan promptly deleted his comment and posted an apology video, it was screenshotted and brought to the attention of his employer and Saudi officials, leading to his arrest in July.
His personal devices were subsequently seized, and his social media accounts were deleted by Saudi officials.
"People in Saudi Arabia knew nothing about this matter. It was individuals in Sri Lanka who sent emails to the company where my brother worked. I do not even wish to mention who those people are," Anojan's brother, Hamsidan Sivarasa, BBC Sinhala.
The company employing Anojan notified the authorities in Saudi Arabia who registered a case against him, according to Hamsidan.
Anojan was initially sentenced to five years in prison as well as a fine of 3m Saudi riyals (about $0.8m; £0.6m) by the Al-Ahsa Criminal Court. An appeal submitted on Anojan's behalf seeking to reduce his sentence was rejected, according to Sri Lankan Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath.
The case took a drastic turn on 17 September after Saudi prosecutors filed an appeal for Anojan to be prosecuted under Sharia law instead of the country's cybercrime legislation. The appellate court granted the prosecution's request, increasing his sentence to the death penalty.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Sri Lanka confirmed it is taking all available steps to assist Anojan.
His family met President Anura Kumara Dissanayake at the Presidential Secretariat on 21 September. The president assured them that the government would spare no effort to obtain a general pardon for him, instructing diplomatic channels to engage Saudi authorities.
The case has brought together cross-religious support. Senior Buddhist leaders, the Mahanayake Theros of the Ramanna Nikaya and the Amarapura Maha Nikaya, together with Hindu religious leaders, handed over a memorandum to the Presidential Secretariat calling for urgent state intervention.
In addition, a four-member Sri Lankan legal delegation is travelling to Saudi Arabia this week to meet Anojan's local defence lawyers.
"There are two law firms in Saudi Arabia handling Anojan's case. We are going there to meet the lawyers from these two firms, discuss the case and plan what can be done next," one of the team, Upul Kumarapperuma, MP, told BBC Sinhala.
Back home, communication between Anojan and his family has completely ceased.
"My brother hasn't called for two days." Hamsidan said on 28 September. "We informed the embassy and asked officials to look into the matter and update us. They said they would check. We are still waiting, as we have not yet received a response."
In Saudi prisons, inmates on death row typically lose access to personal mobile devices, with formal calls strictly facilitated through prison authorities.
Human rights organisations have repeatedly raised concerns regarding severe sentences for online speech in Saudi Arabia.
In July 2023, Mohammed Al Ghamdi, a retired Saudi school teacher, was sentenced to death over his comments on multiple social media platforms, according to the United Nations.
"The death sentence against Mohammad bin Nasser al-Ghamdi, who has a total of just 10 followers on both of his anonymous Twitter accounts and is accused of nothing other than expressing his opinions on social media, is ludicrous," Philip Luther, Amnesty International's Research and Advocacy Director for the Middle East and North Africa, said at the time.
Al Ghamdi's ruling was overturned, and he was sentenced to 30 years in prison, according to ALQST for human rights, an independent non-governmental organisation defending and promoting human rights in Saudi Arabia.
There are more than 10 million foreign workers in Saudi Arabia, according to the International Organisation for Migration (IOM). Rights groups emphasise that low-wage migrant workers face distinct vulnerabilities in the Saudi legal system due to language barriers and lack of proper legal representation.
Executions for blasphemy are relatively rare compared with those for drug offences or murder handed down by courts in Saudi Arabia.

The growth of women’s football worldwide needs careful collaboration to make sure players are not overloaded by increasing competitions, National Women’s Soccer League Commissioner Jessica Berman said on Wednesday.
FIFA’s inaugural Women’s Club World Cup is set to take place in January 2028, mid-season for Europe’s top domestic leagues but in the close season for the NWSL.
The new 19-team tournament is scheduled to take place six months after the Women’s World Cup in Brazil, and with anterior cruciate ligament injuries still blighting the women’s game, Berman stressed the need for mutual understanding among all parties involved to make sure players are not overworked.
“I think this next phase of growth really requires a ton of communication and collaboration between the different stakeholders, or tournament organisers, because we’re all leveraging the same players for these different tournaments,” Berman told reporters at the Leaders Week sports industry conference at Chelsea’s Stamford Bridge stadium.
“And we must communicate to make sure that we’re optimising for their performance in a way that allows for us all to have the longevity and sustainability that we’re looking to achieve.
“So, I think more details (are) to come from FIFA. We too are waiting for additional information about everything from the location to the format to the structure, and we will hope to continue to work with FIFA on making sure that it’s curated in a way that supports the growth of the game globally.”
The Women’s Club World Cup will have six teams in the play-in stage, with the three winners advancing to the group stage joining 13 other clubs. There will be four groups of four, with the top two teams from each progressing to the knockout stage.
The AFC, CAF, CONCACAF and CONMEBOL confederations will each have two direct slots, while UEFA will have five berths.
While FIFA has not announced a host, British media reports this month said the US was in advanced talks to stage the tournament. Should that be the case, the NWSL could get a boost from it, Berman said.
“I think there’s a lot of opportunity if it were to be hosted in America,” she said.
“I think I’d want to hear more about what the plans would be, but certainly (with) that exposure there could be benefits for our league and so we’ll continue to be available to discuss opportunities that might exist in our market.”
Defending NWSL champions Gotham, who will play in the Club World Cup, lead the 16-team league standings on 55 points, four ahead of San Diego, with three regular-season games remaining. The top eight teams contest the playoffs.
Berman, who became commissioner in 2022, did not put an upper limit on the number of teams the league could expand to but said 20 would be the “next touch point”.

The Bangiya Christiya Pariseba (BCP), an umbrella forum representing Christians from different denominations in West Bengal, on October 5 formally submitted complaints to the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), the West Bengal Human Rights Commission (WBHRC) and the National Commission for Minorities, alleging a pattern of targeted violence against the Christian community, including attacks, vandalism and desecration of small house churches and prayer gatherings across the state.
A public hearing was also held on the same day at Christ the King Hall on Syed Amir Ali Avenue in Park Circus, Kolkata, where pastors, victims and eyewitnesses recounted alleged incidents of attacks and intimidation before representatives of prominent human rights and civil rights organisations, including the Association for Protection of Democratic Rights (APDR) and Banglar Manabadhikar Suraksha Mancha (MASUM). Civil society figures, including retired IAS officer Jawhar Sircar, were also present to hear the testimonies.
The gathering was held amid a series of reported attacks on Christian communities, mostly in the hinterlands of Bengal. Alt News has previously documented at least 35 such incidents of violence and intimidation between July 1 and September 20, 2026.
Based on the testimonies of victims, the BCP, which is the eastern chapter of the All India Christian Council, formally submitted its complaints to the rights bodies alleging recurring patterns of targeted violence and intimidation, as well as institutional and governmental negligence in responding to the incidents.
The BCP identified four key concerns:
1. Systematic attacks on peaceful prayer gatherings – According to the BCP, small house churches and local Christian congregations conducting prayer services have repeatedly been targeted over the past three months. The organisation alleged that the intruders had assaulted worshippers, vandalised places of worship and desecrated religious symbols and objects. The BCP also criticised the efforts to downplay the attacks, saying, “Regrettably, some public figures and local leaders have characterised these lawless disruptions as “public protests” while remaining silent on vigilante groups taking the law into their own hands.”
2. Disinformation and manufactured narratives – The BCP alleged that several incidents followed similar “scripted patterns”, in which aggressors forcibly entered private prayer gatherings to disrupt services, “engineer chaos” and “record selective footage”, which was subsequently circulated on social media in edited form. According to the organisation, the videos were then used to make allegations of “forced conversion through inducement”, allegedly fuelling communal tension. BCP founder Herod Mullick said, “These edited videos are subsequently circulated online after false allegations of forced conversion to mislead local authorities and justify vigilante actions”. The organisation further alleged that such videos were presented to local district magistrates (DMs) and sub-divisional officers (SDOs) as evidence, and used to promote what it described as false narratives. The BCP rejected the allegations of forced conversion as “unfounded”, saying that “peaceful believers gathered for routine prayer are being falsely framed as perpetrators.”
3. Discriminatory police action and non-registration of complaints – The BCP further alleged that police responses to the incidents had been inconsistent. It said alleged aggressors were often allowed to leave the scene without immediate action, while injured believers and pastors who reported being victimised were taken to local police stations, “subjected to late-night questioning” and allegedly intimidated. Of the dozens of reported incidents, the BCP said FIRs have been registered in only 13 cases, and only “after extraordinary effort and legal intervention”. “In all other instances, local police authorities have displayed severe reluctance to accept formal written complaints from the victims,” the BCP added.
4. Institutional apathy and unaddressed concerns –The BCP also alleged that repeated appeals to local administrative authorities had failed, with officials “consistently declined to engage in dialogue with state church leaders or representatives of our organisation”, the organisation said. It further alleged that “no independent or impartial inquiries have been instituted to verify the authenticity of these viral video clips”. According to the BCP, “this persistent administrative apathy creates a climate of impunity for vigilante groups and deprives minority worshippers of equal protection under the law.”
Citing violations of Fundamental Rights guaranteed under Article 14 (Equality before Law), Article 19 (Freedom of Speech and Assembly), Article 21 (Protection of Life and Personal Liberty), and Article 25 (Freedom of Conscience and Free Profession, Practice, and Propagation of Religion) of the Constitution of India— the BCP urged the NHRC, WBHRC and NCM to direct the West Bengal Government and the director general of police (DGP) to conduct a high-level independent investigation of all the recent incidents of violence targeting the churches and prayer gatherings.
The organisation also sought an investigation into alleged cyber disinformation and circulation of edited videos allegedly intended to portray worshippers as perpetrators of violence. Additionally, the council pleaded for clear directions to the police and administration to immediately register FIRs in all pending cases and ensure prompt legal action against those responsible.
The BCP further requested the commissions to direct district administrations to provide police protection to vulnerable house churches and congregations during weekly prayer services, and to ensure that victims are not harassed, intimidated or pressured by law-enforcement authorities under alleged influence from vigilante or extremist groups.
After attending the public hearing, former Union culture secretary Jawhar Sircar shared a post on Facebook describing the recent attacks on Christian churches and communities in West Bengal as “tragic and unprecedented” and condemned the attacks as “dastardly”. Sircar expressed his support for the Christian community and their right to practice their faith peacefully.
