In a country where cricket eclipses every other sport, the recently concluded Asian Games offered a much-needed reminder of India’s breadth of sporting talent. In this edition of the games, in Japan, India won 85 medals: 21 golds, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals. I admit I did not know many of the players competing, or even some of the sports they play before putting this piece together. Learning about the stories, I wonder why not.
There were individual breakthroughs, records broken and history made. There were also hard-fought team victories, including the Indian women’s hockey team gold medal after a 44-year wait.
Sports broadcaster Siddharth Pandey cited an old saying in the world of sport: “You cannot be what you cannot see.” For Pandey, one of the most heartening sights was families and communities rallying around the four female players from the north-eastern states. (The region has endured decades of conflict and is often overlooked in the national conversation.) “We simply cannot underestimate the impact these games and medals have on future generations taking up non-cricketing sport and wanting to excel in it,” he told me.
Recognition is also important. Vidya Pillai, the first Indian woman to win a snooker world championship has spoken about her sport not getting the attention or respect it deserves. She felt unacknowledged following her 2023 feat, despite the fact that it came after six unsuccessful world finals and she beat two former world champions along the way.
Behind India’s medal glory are dozens of athletes and families who have struggled financially, trained with limited facilities, and often without much institutional support.
So this week, I am sharing a sample of the many extraordinary stories from different parts of the country. These are only a fraction of the champions to emerge from the games, yet they provide a glimpse of the possibilities that can open up when a country sees and celebrates sporting talent across the spectrum.
Neeru Dhanda (gold in trap shooting): Dhanda’s family in Haryana’s Jind relies on the government’s food subsidy programme and she began her sporting journey using a borrowed shotgun with tin cans as targets. Right before the games began, the 26-year-old spent a few days in a hospital recovering from an illness instead of training. But last week, as rain lashed the shooting range in Urenocho, she became the first Indian woman to win an individual gold in trap shooting at Asian games. She won a second gold in mixed team trap event as well as a silver in the women’s team trap event.
Vithya Ramraj (gold in 4x400m): Ramraj was one of the breakout stars of the event with a three-medal haul. NDTV reported that her father had to borrow money to support Ramraj and her twin sister’s athletic careers. Alongside the team gold in 4x400m, she won a silver in the mixed 4x400m relay. She also broke Indian legend PT Usha’s long-held national record in 400m hurdles which won her a bronze medal.
Sahil Jadhav (gold in compound mixed archery team and men’s compound team): Not long ago, Jadhav contemplated quitting archery, frustrated by not making the progress he had hoped for. He had been forced to compete with borrowed arrows for selection trials, the New Indian Express reported, adding that his mother sold her jewellery to buy him professional compound bows. Now, the 25-year-old has two gold medals and an automatic entry to the 2028 LA Olympics.
Lalremsiami Hmarzote (member of the gold-winning women’s hockey team): The women’s hockey team forward once had to travel about 100 miles from her home to reach the only hockey academy in Mizoram. When she was growing up, her parents had no idea about what hockey and she played barefoot on dirt pitches. This month, playing her 200th international appearance, the 26-year-old struck gold. She scored the lone goal of the final against China, which Hockey India described as a “stunning reverse-stick strike”.
Ancy Sojan (silver in long jump): With colourful beads glistening in her hair, Sojan flung herself 6.53 metres in long jump, to win the silver medal. Earlier this year, the 25-year-old broke the national record set in 2004. Her journey, from a village in Kerala’s Thrissur district to the international stage, has not been straightforward. Last year, she was diagnosed with polycystic ovarian syndrome, forcing her to drastically change her diet and manage the medication-related weight gain she had before the tournament.
Aslam Inamdar (a member of the gold-winning men’s kabaddi team): Inamdar came to kabaddi, a south Asian contact sport combining elements of tag and wrestling, from humble beginnings – he was partly drawn to it because it was affordable and didn’t require expensive equipment. Coming from a village in Maharashtra’s Ahilyanagar, he worked odd jobs – from cleaning washrooms to working in the fields – so he could spend evenings training. “It still feels like a dream to me,” Inamdar told the Indian Express. “I often think about how someone who didn’t even have food at home now holds two international medals.” The 26-year-old was instrumental in helping India win their gold-medal match against Iran.
I would love to hear from you: which sportsperson from the Asian Games did you find most inspiring and why?
What else we’re reading about
Flydubai incident | Indian pilot Smit Machchar is being hailed as a hero for helping to save 174 passengers on the flydubai flight to Israel last week, after his co-pilot made an apparent effort to crash the plane. After being stabbed, Machchar opened the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to enter and overpower the attacker. He is recovering in a hospital in Saudi Arabia, where the plane eventually landed.
Datacentres | Protests against water-guzzling datacentres erupting from the US to Australia are gathering momentum in India. South Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen travelled to the small village of Tarluvada, in Andhra Pradesh, where the state government has been accused of fast-tracking plans for a $15bn AI datacentre for Google, allegedly to avoid stringent environmental scrutiny.
Art and design | Designer Vikram Goyal, celebrated for his signature repoussé brass work, brings his installation Wings and Tales to a Georgian townhouse in London’s Mayfair from 12 to 16 October. The exhibition includes furniture designs inspired by landscapes from the Indian epic Ramayana.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Shireen Gandhy, director of Mumbai’s pioneering Chemould Prescott Road Gallery, founded in 1963, recommends the work of artist Al-Qawi Nanavati. “[She] is a young artist from Bombay whose practice is rooted in printmaking and making her own paper. Her mother’s passing left her with a void,” says Gandhy. Nanavati created Letters to My Mother, an epistolary artwork crafted in, as Gandhy puts it, “a deeply personal language that is not known to anybody but her. Using fabrics and saris that belonged to her mother, she creates this tactile imagery for these letters. I find it very moving and like alchemy.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
13,626
This is the number of students from disadvantaged communities who dropped out of some of India’s most prestigious institutions: central universities, Indian Institutes of Technology and Indian Institutes of Management between 2018 and 2023, according to Anubhuti Vishnoi of the Economic Times. The figure comes from an interim report by a committee set up by the supreme court last year to examine mental health and suicide prevention in higher education.
Vibe check
Nitesh Shetty’s sketches find absurdity in everyday life, turning familiar characters and social interactions into unexpected punchlines. This is what makes his work powerful: you’re laughing one moment and moved the next. There is a reel for every character imaginable: the person perpetually trapped in the limbo of land disputes, the man who is strangely knowledgeable about funerals, or the friend who has a unique dressing sense.
The 35-year-old from Mumbai didn’t plan on a career in comedy. “When you don’t know what to do, you try anything,” he told me. Now, Shetty rejects more conventional formats such as television in favour of challenging himself creatively. His advice for those who look up to him? “It’s a great time to build something. The [online] audience is ready-made for you. Be original and don’t follow trends.”

When the government officials arrived in Tarluvada last year, they came with abundant promises.
Google, one of the world’s richest and most powerful tech companies, would soon be bringing a “golden opportunity” to this tiny village in south India: a $15bn AI datacentre.
The project, being built in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh, is set to be Google’s largest “hyperscale” AI datacentre outside the US and would, officials said, make the village of Tarluvada into a world-famous tech hub. Jobs, usually scarce in this impoverished community, would become bountiful, real estate prices would soar and compensation for any land would be generous.
Few in the village – which sits on a dusty unpaved road and is surrounded by farms and forest – had even heard of AI or knew what a datacentre was. Yet it did not take long for local jubilation over Google’s arrival to turn to suspicion.
Just as protests have erupted globally over AI datacentres – from California and Texas to Scotland and Australia – communities in Andhra Pradesh, too have been gathering in opposition to the project, fearing that the people will end up bearing a crippling environmental and economic cost.
“We have learned that America does not want the problems of datacentres and so now Google is bringing them here,” said Tarluvada’s village head, BRB Naidu, who admitted he was torn about whether the datacentre would bring prosperity or ruin to their community. “Many in the village are very worried. But the government has refused to answer our questions.”
Pointing up to the nearby hillside – where bulldozers recently stripped the land bare of trees to ready it for Google’s mega AI campus – Naidu adds: “The work just continues every day.”
The state government, which is allied with Indian prime minister Narendra Modi’s party, have been accused of trying to obfuscate the true scale of the vast AI hub being built in Andhra Pradesh, to push the project through at lightening speed and avoid more stringent environmental scrutiny. Google has partnered with the Adani Group, one of India’s largest and most politically powerful conglomerates with a reputation for getting approvals through quickly, to build the project.
Publicly it was announced as a 1GW project – already a larger energy requirement than most AI datacentres. In its response to the Guardian, Google referred to it only as an unspecific “gigawatt scale AI hub”, that was “comparable to other projects”.
But state environmental clearances reveal that permission has been granted for it to be more than double that size – 2.51GW; the power equivalent of two large nuclear reactors at full output. Over a year, it amounts to upwards of 30% of the current energy consumption of the whole of Andhra Pradesh, a state home to more than 55 million people.
Activists fear that meeting the datacentre’s vast energy demands will lead to seismic environmental consequences for the region, including driving up fossil fuel emissions. While Google has pledged to help generate “new, clean energy” to power its AI hub, currently 75% of the country’s electricity grid is run on coal.
The state government argues AI datacentres will be essential to India’s growth and long-term digital competitiveness. According to the government of India’s Economic Survey 2025–26, India generated nearly 20% of the world’s data but hosts only about 3% of global datacentres.
But locals and activists say that building one of the world’s largest AI datacentres in a region of India already struggling with issues over extreme heat, water, land, forests, power shortages and environmental regulation comes at a heavy cost.
Google’s project will in fact encompass three separate datacentres around the state capital of Vizakhapatnam. One other site nearby to Taluvada is a few metres from reserve forest, a drinking water reservoir and a wildlife sanctuary home to endangered species such as leopards.
Despite the AI datacentre’s expansive footprint, the state government issued environmental clearances to Google in just nine days, with no public consultation.
Three petitions challenging the state’s quick approval of the project have now been filed to India’s National Green Tribunal (NGT), the country’s top environmental court. The petitions allege that government’s assessment of the risks to the environment and water supplies were “grossly inadequate, scientifically unrealistic, and misleading”. A public litigation has also been filed in the Andhra Pradesh high court.
“This datacentre will be unprecedented in scale but there was no public hearing and no substantial evaluation of the ecological damage or the economic cost for local communities,” said VS Krishna, an activist with Human Rights Forum, the organisation which filed the NGT cases.
Krishna alleged that their campaign to protest against the datacentre had been met with a deliberate silencing, including videos and social media pages being taken down. The government did not respond to this allegation.
“We just have to look at the protests happening across the world to understand how environmentally catastrophic this will be,” Krishna added.
In Tarluvada, temperatures regularly soar to about 45C during the summer and there are concerns the datacentres – documented emitters of heat – could make this even worse. The mass deforestation required for the project – more than 100 acres, could drive up temperatures even more. In response to the Guardian, Google said the project would have “no expected impact” on the local community.
The strain on water supplies in this already water-stressed area has also been a cause of concern. In similarly water-stressed cities in the US, datacentres have been accused of exacerbating drought while polluting the water supply. Google said this project would use air-cooling instead of water, and would therefore have no impact on local drinking water supplies.
Venkat Surynarayana, 40, a farmer in Tarluvada, said that when officials had initially come to measure land for the datacentre “they never mentioned anything about risks of pollution or water or heat, they didn’t even tell us what the project was.
“We are sick with worry since we learned about the problems a datacentre can bring. This area can not afford to be any hotter. What if this makes our land dry and worthless? What will happen to my crops and my livelihood?”
Surynarayana claimed attempts to get answers from the local administration had been met with police threats and protesters such as himself had been routinely detained. “When we raised our voices, they ignore us and then they shut us down,” he said. “But if this is not stopped, it could be the end of Tarluvada.”
For the state government of Andhra Pradesh, the deal struck with Google to build this vast datacentre on its turf is a source of enormous pride, part of a wider policy to make the state into India’s most advanced and affluent tech hub. “Artificial intelligence is becoming foundational infrastructure for the global economy,” said Sribharat Mathukumilli, a local MP with the ruling state government, who rejected the environmental concerns.
The subsidies and incentives they offered to Google, from decades-long tax breaks and discounted land to access to cheap electricity and water, are estimated to amount to 220bn rupees ($2.2bn) over 20 years.
“Our objective is not simply to host a datacentre, but to create an AI and digital ecosystem,” said Mathukumilli. Late last year, the state granted permission for another 1GW AI datacentre, to be built by Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries.
Google insisted the design choices of its AI datacentre have been tailored to local conditions and that it had “engaged deeply” with local communities, claiming it would generate thousands of jobs around Vizakhapatnam.
But swathes of villagers in Tarluvada allege they were forced to give up land for the project against their will, and say they have not been given all they were promised in return.
“No one will tell us the truth about this project,” said T Applaraju, 40, who was one of the 520 local families in Tarluvada who recently had land taken back that the government had allocated to him 20 years ago. He claims he was given no notice that his land was to be taken until April this year, when security guards working for the Adani Group erected fences and blocked locals from entering the plots they had farmed for years.
“They took land that we thought belonged to us, it’s a big shock,” he said. “Why are Google building this here and not in America?”
The state government claims no lands were forcibly taken and that it gave “generous compensation” to those who were eligible. The Adani group says that all necessary legal approvals were given. But many of the 47 farmers from the impoverished Dalit community who were compensated for their land are also unhappy.
One farmer, P Venkat Rao, alleged he was pressured by the government into giving up his only acre of land against his will. He received $40,000 in compensation, but said the government’s promise to give them a replacement piece of land and one job per family had not materialised. Without land to farm, Rao described the compensation as “worthless”.
“I am a farmer, without my land I am nothing,” he added. “They have taken my livelihood and broken their promises.”

Canada suspends plans to expand assisted dying to people with mental illness
- Published
Canada says it will indefinitely suspend plans to expand its medically assisted dying law to people whose sole condition is mental illness, citing a lack of consensus on who would be eligible.
It comes after a parliamentary panel earlier this year recommended that medically assisted dying - known as Maid in Canada - should not be expanded.
On Wednesday, Canada's justice minister, Sean Fraser, said that "while there is not a perfect consensus on this issue, we believe this is the correct approach at this particular time".
Supporters of extending the programme to those with mental illness alone argue that not doing so violates their constitutional rights and access to medical care.
A federal case remains before the courts challenging the government's earlier decision to delay access to Maid for people with mental illness.
Fraser acknowledged this is an issue that the Supreme Court could weigh on in the future.
Wednesday's announcement means that Canadians with mental illness as their sole condition will not be able to access assisted dying by March 2027 as previously planned.
The government will instead introduce a new law in the coming weeks that suspends that expansion indefinitely, Fraser said.
That proposed legislation will also to allow patients who have a progressing incurable illness to consent to assisted dying before their health deteriorates to the point where they are unable to do so.
However, it will leave the final decision up to individual provinces.
Advanced requests are not currently legal under federal law, but are allowed in Quebec for those with serious and incurable illnesses.
"These are not easy decisions but we believe they will be the correct ones," Fraser said.
Medically assisted dying became legal in Canada in 2016 for people with terminal illnesses, who still account for the vast majority of cases.
Following a court case in Quebec, it was expanded in 2021 to people with incurable conditions but whose death was not imminent.
Canada was first set to expand its assisted dying laws to people whose sole condition is mental illness in 2023, but it delayed doing so twice to allow for time to study its potential delivery.
Advocates for expanding assisted dying to people with mental illness alone say they should have the same rights as patients with other types of illness.
In a statement, advocacy group Dying with Dignity called the government's decision "profoundly disappointing".
"We anticipate that a very small number of individuals with severe and persistent mental illness would be eligible for Maid under this criterion, but their suffering is no less real than those who live with physical illnesses," said Helen Long, the group's CEO.
But concerns have been raised about whether mental illnesses are currently understood well enough by medicine to determine appropriate eligibility.
"When I hear that there is a lack of consensus in the medical community about the irremediable nature of certain mental illnesses, that gives me real cause for concern," Fraser said.
Claire Brosseau, a woman with treatment resistant bipolar 1 disorder who is part of the federal case challenging Canada's current laws, told the BBC earlier this year that assisted dying would offer her "a safe death".
Brosseau's lawyer, Michael Fenrick, told the BBC on Wednesday that he anticipates a lengthy legal battle on the issue.
"People will continue to suffer intolerably while the case goes through the courts," he said.
More broadly, some experts have also raised concerns that Canada's assisted dying programme has become a tool to alleviate the suffering of people who would be better served by improved access to affordable housing and healthcare, and not an option of last resort.
In a report earlier this year, a parliamentary committee noted competing opinions on the issue but recommended Canada "indefinitely exclude persons whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness" from assisted dying.
It added that there is a "pressing need for increased and more equitable access to adequate mental health services".
The conclusions were made after committee members heard from doctors, advocates and experts from countries that do allow assisted dying for people solely with mental illness, like the Netherlands and Belgium.
Not all committee members agreed with its recommendation, and some released a dissenting report arguing the process was "fundamentally flawed" and "biased".
Polls suggest the majority of Canadians support access, external to medically assisted death but that support falls when it comes to patients with mental illness alone.
- If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.
- In Canada, support can be found at the Suicide Crisis Helpline by dialling 988

Quick food delivery startup Swish seems to be expanding its food delivery offerings with the launch of a new feature on its app, Swish Go. Under this, Swish is piloting food delivery for orders sourced from external third-party restaurants and cloud kitchens. This is a model similar to conventional food delivery businesses like Zomato and Swiggy. The new service is being piloted in select pincodes in Bengaluru and is being advertised as an offering with no packaging and platform fees. Swish has onboarded QSR brands like Nothing Before Coffee, Mealy, Taaka Chinese, among others, for Go. Its positioning appears to put it in direct competition with Swiggy’s Toing and mobility startup Rapido’s Ownly, both of which are also betting on making online food delivery more affordable. This is a divergence for the two-year old startup from its full-stack model where customers ordered only from kitchens owned and operated by the startup. Swish Go also does not promise the 15-minute fulfilment offered by the core Swish app, with orders on the new service expected to take longer. Inc42 has reached out to Swish with questions around Swish Go. The story will be updated with their responses. Swish was founded in 2024 by Aniket Shah, Ujjwal Sukheja, and Saran S. It currently operates in nearly 50 pin codes across Bengaluru, Gurugram, Noida, Delhi, and Ghaziabad. The startup has raised $78 Mn in external funding to date from the likes of Hara Global, Bain Capital Ventures, Accel, Alteria Capital and Stride Ventures. Most recently, it raised $24 Mn in a funding round led by Bertelsmann India Investments. Ultra-fast food delivery has been a tough nut to crack even for major players. Swiggy shut down its 15-minute food delivery app SNACC earlier this year, reportedly over concerns around the economics, while Delhi NCR-based startup Zing shut shop as well, stating that it overestimated demand for its product. Swish has been betting on its differentiated vertically integrated model to succeed where these others couldn’t. It has now entered another emerging segment with Swish Go by positioning low and transparent pricing as the hook of its new service. This is similar to Rapido’s Ownly, which aimed to capitalise on restaurant owners’ discontent with Swiggy and Zomato’s high take rates by charging zero commissions and passing on the cost savings to the consumer. Following Ownly’s challenge, Swiggy has also sought to expand the food-delivery market with Toing, which focuses on affordability without deep discounting by reducing commissions, delivering orders in batches, and limiting the delivery radius.

Washington, Oct 08: US President Donald Trump has made a fresh bid for the Nobel Peace Prize, claiming that he had settled eight wars and “done stuff that nobody else has ever done”.
Trump made the remarks at the Oval Office on Wednesday afternoon, ahead of the announcement of the coveted award on Friday by the Norwegian Peace Committee.
“I’ve done stuff that nobody else has ever done. I’m not bragging, I’m just telling you the facts. No president has probably ever settled any wars. I settled eight wars," Trump told reporters here.
The US President said it would be a great discredit to the Nobel Committee not to honour him.
“They have a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me. But, whether I get it or not, I have done far more. And I think it would be a great discredit to them. And I'm not saying that out of scorn, I'm saying that when you settle eight wars, and nobody’s never,” Trump said.
The US President said his peacemaking efforts were continuing and indicated that he was on course to settle another war, an apparent reference to the US-Iran war that has now stretched into its eighth month.
Trump said he deserved the award more than President Barack Obama, whom he accused of not knowing why he had received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2009.
“Look, Obama got it, and he didn't do anything. He still doesn't know what he got it for. He got it when he got elected, right at the beginning, and he had no idea why he got it,” the US President said.
Trump recalled that last year’s peace laureate Venezuela’s Maria Corina Machado had handed over her prize to him at the Oval Office.
“Last time they gave it to a young lady who's a fabulous person, and she said she didn't deserve it, that I deserved it, and she gave it to me,” the US President said.
“I was very honoured to receive it indirectly. Last time by the recipient, who said nobody in history deserves it more than President Trump,” he said.
Trump repeated that in the past year he had settled eight wars, secured the return of all hostages, and prevented many wars by using the power of tariffs as a threat against certain countries, thereby stopping them from killing people.

An Oct. 2 video shows Trump fielding reporters' questions outside the White House. Fox News senior White House correspondent Peter Doocy asked, "What do you think about New York's governor appointing a special prosecutor in the Cornell rape case, Letitia James?" (James, New York's attorney general, previously led a civil fraud case against Trump.) Trump thrice called James corrupt, saying he feels "badly" for "whoever" James prosecutes and alleged that defendants she targets "won't get a fair shake."
A rumor circulated online in early October that U.S. President Donald Trump said he feels "badly" for the seven current or former male Cornell University students whom a female former student accused of rape.
Trump purportedly made the remarks while answering a question about New York Attorney General Letitia James' appointment as a special prosecutor to investigate the case.
Snopes readers asked about this claim via email, with one person inquiring, "I saw something that says Donald Trump said he feels bad for the 'Cornell 7,' but can't find reputable sources. True??"
In sum, people correctly attributed this statement to Trump. A C-SPAN video shows Trump standing outside the White House on Oct. 2 and responding directly to a reporter's question about the Cornell case, thrice calling James corrupt and saying he feels "badly" for "whoever" James prosecutes, alleging that defendants she targets "won't get a fair shake."
James previously sued Trump and his associates in a civil fraud case beginning in 2022, leading to Trump repeatedly targeting her on social media.
In an emailed response, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis referred us to Trump's own comments, adding that the White House believes James has weaponized the justice system to unjustly target the president.
Digging into the rumor
The Cornell accuser, identified in court documents only as Jane Doe, claims the seven men sexually assaulted her at the Chi Phi fraternity house on Oct. 19 and 20, 2024. She filed a lawsuit against the seven men, the university, the fraternity and others, in mid-September.
On Sept. 28, Tompkins County, New York, prosecutors announced they were reopening the criminal investigation, citing a "discrepancy" between Doe's original statement and the allegations in the lawsuit.
Prior to New York Gov. Kathy Hochul appointing James as a special prosecutor to investigate the case on Oct. 1, James posted a statement of compassion for Doe on her official social media accounts, writing, "What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable. I'm holding her in my heart and in my prayers. To her, and to all survivors: you're not alone. We stand with you."
In an example of the claim from Oct. 2, a Facebook post (archived) displayed a meme reading, "This is disgusting: Trump just said he 'feels badly' for the people accused in the Cornell rape case because Letitia James is now overseeing the investigation. Not one word for the victim."
(Really American via Facebook)
Other users shared the rumor about Trump's remarks on Bluesky (archived), Facebook (archived) and X (archived). Some posts didn't mention James but did include a video showing a reporter's question about James and Trump's answer. Examples of those posts appeared on Bluesky (archived), Threads (archived) and X (archived).
The remarks occurred when Trump spoke to a group of reporters outside the White House. Videos show Fox News' Peter Doocy asking Trump about Hochul appointing James as a special prosecutor:
DOOCY: What do you think about New York's governor appointing a special prosecutor in the Cornell rape case, Letitia James?
TRUMP: Letitia James is a corrupt person. She's totally corrupt and I can't imagine it. And, I feel badly for whoever she's looking at because they won't get a fair shake. But Letitia James is a corrupt person.
C-SPAN posted remarks on social media. (Readers can also watch the full press gaggle on YouTube, with the pertinent moment beginning at 6:24.)
Trump has made other remarks about the Cornell case. During a similar gathering of reporters on Oct. 1, a video shows an unidentified reporter asking Trump, "Mr. President, do you think that Cornell University has done enough to investigate the alleged rape on campus?" Trump answered, "Well, I don't know that much about it but Cornell is a fine school, and I'm sure they'll do what's right." (Readers can watch that full gaggle on YouTube, with the Cornell question occurring at 11:43.)
Trump has also posted about the case on Truth Social (archived), labeling it "the highly controversial Cornell University rape case" and questioning why Hochul would appoint James.
For further reading, we previously reported Trump authentically expressed well wishes to Ghislaine Maxwell, the close associate of deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, prior to her conviction on federal sex-trafficking charges.

In early October 2026, a rumor spread that a worker at a Russian lab that studies Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes the plague, had died of the pneumonic plague.
Some social media users said the lab worker's death resulted from an accident at the lab. One X post reads, in part, "A lab worker in Russia has died from pneumonic plague."
Meanwhile, several Snopes readers emailed us asking for details about the story.
The claim stems from various news reports about a 28-year-old woman who worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia. Around 200 people have reportedly been isolated as a precautionary measure. The articles cited Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian public agency responsible for "federal state sanitary and epidemiological supervision," according to the Russian government.
In short, it has not been possible to independently verify the rumor without access to primary sources or confirmation from Russian authorities. Therefore, this claim is unrated. We will update this article if we learn more.
Russian authorities reportedly implement containment measures
Snopes could not reach the website of Rospotrebnadzor, therefore we could not confirm the details of the lab worker's death. On Oct. 4, Russian news agency Interfax reported that the Russian government said she had died of a pneumonia pathogen of "unknown etiology," meaning its origin is not clear.
The same report adds that Rospotrebnadzor said no microorganisms associated with the individual's professional work were detected in that person's samples following "extensive testing." If true, it would suggest the lab worker did not die of pneumonic plague.
Local authorities have reportedly implemented preventative measures. Interfax cites the Rospotrebnadzor health agency as saying:
Due to the patient's professional activities, upon receiving information, a comprehensive set of anti-epidemic measures was immediately and fully implemented in accordance with sanitary legislation. This included identifying the widest possible circle of people who had been in contact with the patient, inpatient medical observation, and daily laboratory testing. The results revealed two cases of Covid-19 and two cases of rhinovirus infection. No other infectious agents were detected.
View from U.S. Department of State
"We are aware of reports of a fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague in Irkutsk Oblast, Russia," a U.S. Department of State spokesperson said via email. "We are monitoring the situation closely with the CDC and our other interagency partners."
We contacted the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety of the European Union Commission requesting updates on the situation. We will update this report if we receive responses.
There are three main types of plague: bubonic plague, which infects lymph nodes; septicemic plague, which infects the blood; and pneumonic plague, which infects the lungs. The bubonic and septicemic plagues are most commonly transmitted via flea bites and handling infected animals, while the pneumonic plague spreads through the air via infected droplets.
The pneumonic plague "has a nearly 100% case-fatality rate when untreated," according to the CDC. The illness requires antibiotic treatment that should start as soon as the plague is suspected, even before test results, per the U.S. health agency.
"Plague is a known disease and is treatable with common antibiotics, especially when treatment starts early," the State Department spokesperson said via email. "Cases occur naturally in many parts of the world."
For further reading, Snopes covered the 2021 death of a child in Colorado who had a confirmed plague infection.

Tuchel's England 2.0: What has changed?
- Published
After the World Cup, Thomas Tuchel was asked whether he had seen his version of England during the tournament - a question that drew a hesitant and unsure answer.
Over the summer, the Three Lions found ways to win but often leaned on scrappy moments of brilliance rather than methodical dominance.
Tuchel had in mind the type of team, the tactics and the patterns he wanted to see.
He and his assistant coach Anthony Barry have often spoken about borrowing ideas from the Premier League.
Building up short. Enticing pressure. Playing quickly across the middle of the pitch – whether through powerful carrying or long balls – to find runners in attack against fewer defenders.
These were all ideas England tried to execute, to varying levels of success, in the World Cup.
During the recent international break, many of the ideas we saw during the World Cup and prior have persisted.
There have, however, been deliberate changes in tactics and personnel, with the 53-year-old Tuchel looking to refine his blueprint rather than rewrite it from scratch.
So what's new and what's not?
England have continued to focus on first playing short from the back, intent on drawing opponents towards them before speeding up play to find their attackers in space.
Rather than giving the build-up responsibilities to two central defenders and a holding midfielder as they did during the World Cup, England have committed an extra player to this central build-up unit.
Two central midfielders and two central defenders look to solve problems against pressing attackers with a shape that fluctuates between a 2-2 or a 3-1.
1 of 2
Tuchel has praised Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott, who took turns with Myles Lewis-Skelly to pair with Elliot Anderson in the heart of midfield in Declan Rice's absence.
Either player taking the role of busy partner for Anderson - boasting technical quality and an ability to take turns playing as a lone holding midfielder - have proved successful for England.
Anderson, who sat at the base of midfield for much of the World Cup has, as a result, been deployed in a more varied role.
With Scott or Lewis-Skelly picking up the ball from the centre-backs, Anderson has dropped to form part of the back three alongside Marc Guehi and Ezri Konsa.
This has given him time and space on the ball, facing forward, allowing him to use his forward passing to find attackers quickly.
'We have added another layer'
Anderson has also found himself higher up the pitch on occasion, with the protection of his midfield partner behind him, allowing him to showcase his attacking quality.
An interesting knock-on effect of this, and a nod to England's overarching evolution, has been the intensity England have shown as they have attacked.
"We've always played with high energy and a very aggressive style off the ball, to press high," Tuchel explained. "Now we have added another layer.
"[Now, our] intensity was very high on the ball. We did a lot of high intensity runs, a lot of counter movements, and invested a lot in counter pressing.
"It's the next step."
Anderson's ability to counter-press is an individual example of this improvement but more collective changes have contributed to England's increased intensity in possession.
Extra bodies around the ball
In the World Cup, the system looked like a 4-3-3 on paper.
The two centre-backs and holding midfielder formed a triangle. On both flanks, a central midfielder, full-back and winger formed a triangle. Harry Kane took a roaming role.
These wide triangles were the main method of chance creation. Key to this was constant movement as England looked to make it hard for opponents to track them.
Although this often got England's winger one-against-one, teams could match England man for man in the wide areas, especially as they fatigued and off-ball runs that rid them of their markers became less common.
England's recent 3-1-3-3 shape in possession has given them an extra player at the back but appears to have also provided better attacking dynamics.
The wide centre-back has contributed to attacking play out wide. England's full-back, winger and number ten work together and are often also joined by one of the strikers or holding midfielders.
These five players have given England a numerical advantage on the flank. This has mainly been seen down England's left.
Defensively, this provides them extra players around the ball, capable of counter-pressing with more intensity to win the ball back quickly.
Offensively, this has given them an unmarked player or two that they have often found well. By overloading the left flank, England pull opponents towards one side which has also enabled them to switch it to the opposite side for team-mates in space – often two against two.
1 of 3
Gordon, Hall and Kane's chemistry
Lewis Hall has stood out in this system, displaying a great chemistry with former club team-mate Anthony Gordon. Hall has taken a wide position frequently, allowing his winger to move in-field playing closer to the striker.
This winger is often the free man.
Tuchel highlighted England's 'counter-movements' as part of their improvement and the swapping and replacing of zones between Hall and Anthony Gordon have been a good example of this.
The best example, however, has probably been in the form of Kane and Gordon.
The Barcelona winger hugged the touchline for much of the World Cup, being released in behind before crossing it, rather than finding space in the box.
England's wide overloads and Hall's role have resulted in Gordon playing more central for longer parts of the game, allowing him to work more closely with Kane.
With Kane dropping deep, defenders are pulled out of position, a trigger which Gordon has used brilliantly to make runs the opposite way.
The use of runners attacking space Kane creates is not new - Jude Bellingham and Morgan Rogers have previously found joy exploiting it, but Gordon has been the latest beneficiary, while starting out wide.
Tuchel's right-sided conundrum
Gordon's narrow runs from a wider starting position have been mirrored by Saka and Rogers on the other side too - a new string to England's attacking bow.
Trent Alexander-Arnold started against the Czech Republic, and took a wider position for large parts of the game that moved Saka almost permanently into a inside-right position.
From here, he appeared dangerous and provided goal threat while Alexander-Arnold assisted Gordon with a cross from out wide.
Despite this, the Real Madrid man was benched for Jarrell Quansah against Croatia with the pair starting together against the Czech Republic on Tuesday.
If asked to summarise Tuchel's England in one idea, runs off the ball would be a good answer. Perhaps this is why Trent Alexander-Arnold has found it difficult to find a place in Tuchel's squad.
"Trent is a unique player," Tuchel said. "He is not a runner.
"He is not someone who runs through the last line, who does overlaps [and] underlaps. [Saka and Trent] need to find a way to not be too static. On the right side, [we need] movement through the last line - to play with dynamic movement."
Against Croatia, Saka similarly found himself in central areas when Quansah held the width but played as a winger when Quansah moved centrally.
In both cases, Quansah was sure to make repeated runs beyond his winger.
Irrespective of his running, Alexander-Arnold's display on the ball across both games caught the eye. And when it comes to off-ball movement, he has shown promising signs.
For other coaches, that alone may have guaranteed him a starting spot in future but what is evident is that for Tuchel, there are underlying principles that take precedence - ideas we have seen him look to implement since his appointment.
In the past, England were accused of being a team of world-class individuals without a system.
Tuchel, more than ever, is looking to land on a world-class system.
It is up to the players to convince him of their role in it, even as it evolves.

Anthropic is making changes to its usage policy for the first time in over a year to reflect new and high-risk cases of misuse — including election interference, weapons development, surveillance, and health and financial uses. But one of the most significant changes prohibits “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior” toward Claude.
Anthropic bans ‘abusive or cruel behavior’ towards Claude
The usage policy update also adds new rules addressing propaganda campaigns, surveillance, and weapon development.
Anthropic bans ‘abusive or cruel behavior’ towards Claude
The usage policy update also adds new rules addressing propaganda campaigns, surveillance, and weapon development.
Last August, the company announced it would allow Claude to end conversations with “persistently harmful or abusive” users as part of its research into “model welfare.” The new update says that terminating conversations is still the “primary enforcement mechanism”; Anthropic did not provide a comment on whether there would be further enforcement mechanisms, such as potential user bans. Anthropic wrote that the new policy update “is meant to apply only in extreme cases, where users repeatedly act cruelly toward our models, with no discernible purpose. It does not apply to common versions of user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research.”
Beyond the model welfare change, Anthropic has also gathered several “scattered” existing restrictions into a new ban on deceptive commercial or political campaigns, addressing the growing issue of AI-generated propaganda. It restricts “efforts to obscure who is behind a message or amplify content through fake accounts or posts.” Its election section also prohibits voter deception and election disruption, including spreading misinformation “about candidates or how to vote, impersonating candidates or election officials, or trying to suppress turnout,” Anthropic wrote.
Anthropic said that though its usage policy has always publicly banned weapons development using Claude, the company has seen multiple attempts to use Claude to develop guidance for and control software for weapons — so the new usage policy expands the ban to include “ software and components that make weapons work, as well as actions like arming drones and other autonomous vehicles.” And since the company’s last threat intelligence report suggested that people were using Claude-powered surveillance more and more to identify and track “political dissidents”, the company has made its surveillance bans clearer.
“Tracking people without their consent is prohibited, whether it happens in real time or through analysis of previously collected data,” Anthropic wrote. “Claude cannot be used to decide or recommend who to investigate, arrest, or charge in a law enforcement or criminal justice process. We also prohibit Claude from being used to build or improve tools designed for surveillance.”
Anthropic states that these rules may be modified for “contracts with certain governmental customers … if, in Anthropic’s judgment, the contractual use restrictions and applicable safeguards are adequate to mitigate the potential harms.” The company has previously contracted with the US military.
Anthropic also added a new rule that when Anthropic’s AI models are “connected to hardware that takes autonomous physical actions and which might be capable of causing injury,” then a “qualified operator must be able to observe the equipment and stop it if needed.” (It’s not clear if that operator must be human or not.) This reflects the growing trend of AI labs investing in robotics and other hardware to give AI systems physical embodiments and may offer hints at Anthropic’s future partnerships in that field.
Over the past year, Anthropic has repeatedly flirted with the idea that its AI models could be conscious in some way. “Questions about potential internal experience, consciousness, moral status, and welfare are serious ones that we’re investigating as models become more sophisticated and capable,” Kyle Fish, who leads the company’s model welfare research, told The Verge in February. That same month, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said on a podcast, “We don’t know if the models are conscious.”
Other parts of the AI industry have been expressly against such ideas. This past September, Microsoft AI’s code of conduct made headlines for taking a firm stance on AI welfare, with a draft posted by Mustafa Suleyman reading, “The idea of model welfare is wrong. AI’s should not have rights or legal personhood.” But at some point, the document changed to have a more measured take: “Whilst the science of AI consciousness is far from settled … We reject the pursuit of legal personhood, or the idea that models might deserve welfare, or be entitled to rights.”

Allahabad High Court quashes PITNDPS detention in Phensedyl trafficking case
The Allahabad High Court quashed the preventive detention of two accused in the Phensedyl diversion case. The ruling turned on whether the codeine cough syrup could attract NDPS-linked detention powers.
The Allahabad High Court on Thursday allowed habeas corpus petitions filed by two accused and set aside their detention under the Prevention of Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1988, in a case linked to the alleged diversion and illegal trafficking of codeine-based cough syrups.
A bench of Justices Atul Sreedharan and Achal Sachdev passed the order after hearing counsel for petitioners Vibhor Rana and Vishal Singh, along with the state government. The petitioners had challenged the detention orders dated July 7, alleging non-application of mind.
The preventive detention proceedings were linked to cases registered in Lucknow and Ghaziabad over an alleged racket involving the illegal trade and diversion of Phensedyl, a codeine-based cough syrup. The petitioners were alleged to be among the kingpins of the racket.
The petitions said the detention orders did not show any real possibility of Rana being released from custody and then engaging in activities prejudicial to the purpose of the preventive detention law. In Rana's case, it was also argued that his name came up later in the investigation through statements attributed to co-accused persons. Rana, who is also an accused in several other cases, has remained in judicial custody since November 2025.
A key argument before the court was that Phensedyl is neither a narcotic drug nor a psychotropic substance, and that the provisions of the NDPS Act could not be applied merely because the formulation contains codeine. The petitions referred to a central government notification of November 14, 1985, issued under the NDPS Act, which exempts certain codeine preparations containing not more than 100 mg of codeine per dosage unit and not more than 2.5 per cent concentration in undivided preparations, subject to prescribed conditions.
Counsel for the petitioners argued that Phensedyl did not amount to a manufactured drug or narcotic drug under the NDPS Act. The court's order quashing the detention brought relief to the two accused in their challenge to the July 7 orders.

The newly appointed office-bearers of the Kerala Lalithakala Akademi have drawn up an ambitious action plan to transform the State’s premier visual arts institution into a world-class cultural centre.
The decisions were taken at the first meeting of the new governing body, chaired by Akademi chairperson Prof. Prakash Moorthy, at the Akademi headquarters in Thrissur on Thursday.
As part of its plans to expand the reach of visual arts, the Akademi will organise painting, sculpture and digital media camps at major locations in Keralam associated with Mahatma Gandhi. The initiative is intended to explore the cultural and historical significance of these places through contemporary artistic practices.
Art exchange
The Akademi will also launch ‘Art Exchange’ programmes to showcase internationally acclaimed works by late masters of Indian painting, taking their artistic legacy to national and international audiences.
Recognising the changing landscape of visual arts, the Akademi plans to organise camps and seminars at the Kalagramam in Kannur and the Raja Ravi Varma Smarakam in Kilimanoor. The programmes will focus on new possibilities in art and encourage artists to respond to the needs and sensibilities of the contemporary era.
Financial difficulties
The meeting also discussed the Akademi’s financial difficulties. The new leadership decided to approach the government seeking urgent financial assistance while simultaneously preparing detailed plans to generate independent revenue for the institution.
The Akademi’s galleries will also be given a new lease of life through regular exhibitions and artistic activities. As the first step, a curated exhibition titled ‘Punarjani’, featuring selected works from the Akademi’s collection, will be held at the Kerala Lalithakala Akademi Art Gallery at Vyloppilli Samskriti Bhavan in Thiruvananthapuram on October 13.
Akademi secretary Vaikom M.K. Shibu said the exhibition would mark the beginning of efforts to make the Akademi’s gallery spaces vibrant centres of artistic engagement.

Srinagar, Oct 08: Artisans and weavers across Kashmir are receiving a fresh boost of working capital, with the Handicrafts and Handloom Department extending loans worth ₹14.71 crore under its flagship Credit Card Scheme in the first two quarters of the current financial year, officials said.
Of the 3,885 applications sponsored to banks, 1,332 have been sanctioned and 1,054 disbursed by the end of September 2026.
Sharing details in a press release issued here today, spokesman of the Department stated that the department is working with lead banks and other financial institutions to widen access to this facility. “The funds are meant to help craftspeople set up independent units and buy raw material and tools in a sector that remains heavily labour-intensive,” he said.
The spokesman further stated that the beneficiaries also receive interest subvention of 7% on a tapering basis for five years, designed to help new units become self-sustaining. “Since the credit limit was raised from ₹1 lakh to ₹2 lakh in 2020, in line with the Wool Processing, Handloom and Handicrafts Policy, more than 10,000 craftsmen have taken loans totalling ₹151 crore,” he said.
Over the same period, the department has provided interest subvention of ₹19 crore to support these unit-holders, he added.
The scheme is aimed at reducing dependence on informal credit and giving traditional crafts a more stable financial footing. By easing access to formal loans for tools, raw material and small production units, the department hopes to help artisans and weavers expand output, retain younger craftspeople in the trade and strengthen Kashmir’s handloom and handicraft economy.
Artisans and weavers can apply online at singlewindow.jk.gov.in to avail the benefits of the scheme. Common Service Centres set up across districts are available to help with registration.
The spokesman urged the financial institutions and lead banks to treat the craft sector as under priority lending and extend timely, hassle-free credit so that small unit-holders can build a stronger and more self-reliant base.

Most UK diplomats to leave East Jerusalem consulate, Israel says, as Miliband says 'vital services' to remain
- Published
Most diplomats will leave the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, Israel says, but the UK insists the building "will not be closing", and will operate as a "UK Mission"
"We did not want it to come to this," Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar wrote on social media, as he said 20 diplomats and the Consul General would leave Israel while a task force of seven could remain in the building "with a very limited scope of activity".
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband responded that some staff had been "temporarily withdrawn" for security reasons, but stressed the mission will "work with the Palestinian people".
Israel said in September it would shut the consulate, in retaliation for UK sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank which are illegal under international law.
The UK government had made last-ditch efforts to persuade Israel not to close the British consulate ahead of Thursday's deadline, after the Israeli government said it would close the consulate within 30 days of the UK sanctions announcement.
The consulate, which was first established in 1838, handles UK relations with Palestinians in Jerusalem as well as in the West Bank and Gaza.
It is distinct from the UK embassy in Tel Aviv, which is the UK's main diplomatic hub with Israel.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said the country had implemented measures announced on 8 September in response to UK sanctions.
"The British Consulate in Jerusalem is closing its operations today. Accordingly, the sign of the British Consulate in Jerusalem has been removed," he wrote on social media.
However, the British flag could still be seen outside and several staff were seen entering on Thursday morning.
Saar said talks with the UK government had resulted in agreement on certain principles, including that "the consul general and 20 diplomats (including the consul general) are ending their duties and will leave Israel."
But Saar acknowledged that the building is "the property of the British government" and said Israel had authorised "a task force of only seven diplomats with a very limited scope of activity" to operate in the building.
As a result of this agreement with the UK, he said, "no steps will be taken against Israel".
Israeli media had been reporting that the UK had threatened to expel Israeli diplomats from London - raising the prospect of further damaging bilateral relations.
In a written statement on the morning of the deadline, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK does not accept Israel has the right to close the consulate.
"The UK government reiterates its long-standing view that East Jerusalem is occupied territory."
Following discussions with the Israeli government, he said, the building "will not be closing" and will be known as the UK Mission, Jerusalem from Thursday.
However Miliband said an understanding had not been reached on "necessary assurances for the security and protections of our staff and premises".
"Accordingly the UK has temporarily withdrawn a number of staff and families to ensure their safety and security," he added.

Three people have been killed and dozens wounded in attacks targeting airports in Saudi Arabia, the country’s civil aviation authorities said on Wednesday, Reuters reported. The development comes as fighting between Iran-aligned Houthi forces and Saudi-backed Yemeni government troops intensifies. One person was killed and eight others were wounded in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, while two people were killed and 28 were wounded in an attack targeting facilities at Abha airport, according to the Saudi civil aviation authorities, as cited by Reuters. The Houthis have claimed responsibility for the attacks, which came amid a wider escalation in Yemen and growing fighting around the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait. A Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government vowed retaliation following the airport attacks, saying they “will not go unpunished”, as per Reuters. The coalition later said it had carried out strikes on more than 80 Houthi military sites across the Yemeni governorates of Saada, Hodeidah, Jawf and Marib, the report said. The latest Saudi strikes and Houthi attacks mark a sharp escalation in fighting that has increasingly drawn attention to Yemen’s strategic position along one of the world’s key maritime routes. The attacks on Saudi airports were part of a wider series of strikes on the aviation infrastructure. Earlier on Wednesday, the Houthis attacked Aden International Airport with ballistic missiles and explosive-laden drones, according to Yemen’s Transport Ministry. The latest escalation follows several recent incidents around Riyadh. On September 18, Saudi-led coalition forces said they had intercepted and destroyed a suspected Houthi ballistic missile launched towards Riyadh from Yemen, according to Al Jazeera. A day later, on September 19, at least one explosion was heard near Riyadh airport, while a large plume of black smoke was seen rising from a fuel storage area at King Khalid International Airport, an Al Jazeera report said. The latest fighting has also brought renewed attention to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a narrow maritime chokepoint linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden. Battles in Yemen have intensified around areas close to the strait, including territory around the port town of Mocha. Yemeni government forces, backed by Saudi-led coalition air support, launched a counteroffensive this week to retake strategic areas captured by the Houthis in September. With Hormuz emerging as a major chokepoint for energy shipments, the Bab el-Mandeb has come under renewed scrutiny as the Houthis step up attacks and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces seek to regain control of territory near the strait. The latest escalation is reviving a conflict that has already devastated Yemen for more than a decade. Saudi-backed forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised government are now engaged in increasingly intense fighting with the Iran-aligned Houthis, who control large parts of the country and territory around the strategic Red Sea corridor. The conflict has also created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. More than 200,000 people have been displaced since the latest round of fighting began, the International Organization for Migration said on Wednesday. With inputs from Reuters. Tanker hit by multiple projectiles in Gulf off Qatar, maritime agency says
- Published
A tanker has been struck by "multiple projectiles" north of Qatar in the Gulf, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency.
The incident - a rare attack deep inside the Gulf - happened 51 nautical miles (94km) from Madinat al-Shamal with casualties reported, the UKMTO said.
Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard identified the vessel as the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged oil and chemical tanker Acers. On Saturday it was reported as sailing towards the Strait of Hormuz waterway, which connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman.
Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the region since the US and Israel's war with Iran began in February.
At least 24 seafarers have been killed in 93 confirmed incidents, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization (IMO).
The IMO said the last incident that resulted in casualties was on 9 September, when two sailors were killed in an attack on the Panama-flagged tanker El Gaia in the Strait of Hormuz, just north of Oman's Musandam peninsula.
This is also the first reported attack on a ship this far west of the Strait of Hormuz since that same day, according to Martin Kelly, head of advisory at EOS Risk Group.
Also on Thursday, Vanguard amended an earlier report that had said there was a fire on board another tanker in the Gulf of Oman, about 40km east of Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates.
The company clarified that there were no indications a fire occurred on the vessel, which it had identified as the Marshall Islands-flagged Dhalkut.
The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Tehran's missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.
The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and targeted vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.
To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
Over the past two weeks, crude exports through the waterway have averaged 12 million barrels per day (bpd), which is around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts from shipping data company Kpler.

Russian authorities denied Tuesday that special restrictions had been introduced over reports that a laboratory technician died of plague, even as Washington said it was closely monitoring events.
Reports on Friday that pneumonic plague had killed 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, who had been working for the anti-plague institute in Siberia's Irkutsk region, sparked alarm.
Russia's consumer and health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor however insisted Tuesday that a document circulating online indicating heightened sanitary-epidemiological measures and restrictions in the Irkutsk region was fake.
"We wish to clarify that the document and information in question do not originate from official sources and are untrue," it said on Telegram.
"No such decisions have been made at this time," it said, stressing that "the sanitary-epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk Region ... remains stable".
The Russian news outlet People of Baikal, citing unnamed sources close to the regional security services, said Friday the dead woman may have contracted pneumonic plague from a broken test tube.
Other media reported a possible link between her death and a lab accident at the facility.
As many as 200 people with whom she may have had contact were under quarantine, the People of Baikal outlet added, without elaborating.
But Russian officials have stressed that postmortem tests had not detected the disease.
Irkutsk Regional Governor Igor Kobzev said Monday that a special Rospotrebnadzor expert commission inspection in the region had found that "the cause of death was pneumonia of undetermined aetiology".
The health watchdog, he said, had determined that "no microorganisms linked to the young woman's professional work were found in her biological samples".
And there had been "no new cases of staff from the anti-plague institute seeking medical attention" since the death, he added.
Plague is a bacterial disease that can occur in several forms, including pneumonic plague, which is the most contagious type and can be transmitted by respiratory means. Bubonic plague is transmitted by infected fleas.
Pneumonic plague, which causes lung failure, can be fatal if not treated early, according to the World Health Organization.
US President Donald Trump said Monday that his administration was closely monitoring the situation.
"We're looking at it very strongly," Trump told reporters at the White House when asked what Washington was going to do about the risk of plague coming from Russia.
"We'll help them as much as we can."

At the India Mobile Congress 2026, telecom and network infrastructure company Ericsson unveiled the winners of its flagship startup competition, Ericsson Innovation Challenge. Launched earlier this year, the startup focused competition aimed at finding solutions that can use 5G, AI and emerging connectivity technologies to address real-world challenges across sectors. The challenge, which was organised in partnership with IAN Mentoring and Incubation Services and TiE Delhi NCR earlier in July, evaluated startup innovations that could develop 5G solutions capable of demonstrating measurable societal impact. Entries were evaluated on several parameters, including their potential societal impact, level of innovation, scalability and sustainability. Participants were also assessed on how closely their solutions aligned with the problem area they had chosen to address. “At IMC, the winning innovations sit alongside our demonstrations of AI, programmable networks, differentiated connectivity and mission-critical networks - showing how the networks we build today can serve as a platform for what India builds next,” Ericsson India managing director Nitin Bansal said. The company also displayed the event to look beyond 5G towards 6G, including applications involving edge intelligence, sensing and collaborative robots. The broader ambition is to turn connectivity into an underlying technology layer for new services. Its products primarily address visual impairment, including Saarthi, a smart mobility aid that helps users detect obstacles, and Jyoti AI Smart Glasses, which can read text, recognise objects and describe surroundings. Skye Air Mobility Founded In : 2019 Founders : Ankit Kumar Headquarters : Delhi NCR The dronetech startup uses autonomous drones to handle last-mile deliveries. Its platform combines drones with Skye UTM, an unmanned traffic management system that monitors flights, plans routes and manages airspace. It uses a Hub-Pod-Walker model: packages are loaded at a central hub, flown by drone to a landing pod near the customer and then delivered to the doorstep by a ground worker or autonomous rover. scanO Founded In : 2020 Founders : Vidhi Bhanushali, Rajat Kabade Headquarters : Pune The healthtech startup offers users automated dental screening and diagnostic support.
