New Delhi, Oct 8: Air India Express and Air India have cancelled flights to Riyadh till October 10 amid disruptions due to attacks at the airport.
Saudi Arabia's two airports in Riyadh and Abha came under attack, reportedly by Houthi militants.
Air India Express and Air India flights en route to Riyadh returned on Thursday, sources said.
"In view of the evolving situation in the region, we have cancelled flights to and from Riyadh until 10 October. Affected guests are being offered complimentary rescheduling or a full refund on cancellation. We continue to monitor the situation closely," Air India Express said in a statement on Thursday.
Air India Express operates 16 weekly flights to Riyadh from four Indian cities -- Bengaluru, Kochi, Kannur and Kozhikode.
Air India has also cancelled its services to and from Riyadh till October 10. The airline operates 7 weekly flights to Riyadh from Delhi and Mumbai.
"The affected guests are being offered a full refund on cancellation. We are closely monitoring the situation," the airline said in a statement.
On Thursday, Air India said AI2243 flight from Delhi to Riyadh returned to the national capital and the flight was subsequently cancelled.
Full refunds have been offered to passengers.
In a post on X, Akasa Air said that in view of the evolving security situation in Riyadh, it has cancelled QP 523 Kochi - Riyadh and QP 524 Riyadh - Kochi flights on Thursday.
"We continue to monitor and assess the situation on a real-time basis, and further changes will be notified accordingly," it said.
In recent days, there has been an escalation in the hostilities between the Iran-backed Houthi group and Saudi Arabia. There have been attacks with armed drones and missiles.

The US Department of Labor on Thursday (October 8) suspended several major technology companies, including Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe, from the Permanent Labour Certification Programme, in a move targeting the hiring of foreign workers.
US Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling announced the decision alongside Vice President JD Vance and the head of the US Anti-Fraud Task Force.
“I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labour Certification Programme some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini,” Sonderling said.
He added that the Department of Labor was also suspending Microsoft and Adobe from the programme.
No new or pending applications
Under the decision, the US Labour Department will not accept new applications or process pending permanent labour certification applications involving the companies.
“ We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies,” Sonderling said.
The Permanent Labour Certification Programme, commonly known as PERM, is a key route through which US employers seek labour certification for foreign workers who may subsequently qualify for employment-based permanent residency.
The latest move could have implications for technology companies that rely on overseas talent and seek to sponsor employees for permanent US residency.
US cites foreign-worker numbers
Sonderling said the companies had collectively sought millions of foreign workers over the past 17 years.
“Since 2009, just these companies alone have requested almost three million foreign workers. They've received over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 100,000 permanent labour certifications,” he said.
The labour secretary accused the companies of taking jobs away from American workers.
“That's hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers,” Sonderling said.
The announcement comes as the Trump administration has intensified scrutiny of US immigration programmes and the use of foreign workers by American companies.
The decision puts the companies' new and pending permanent labour certification applications on hold, although the announcement cited in the statement did not provide further details on the duration of the suspension or whether the companies could challenge the action.
The move is likely to be closely watched by Indian technology professionals in the US, particularly those navigating the H-1B and employment-based green-card process.

‘No boom is forever’: Singapore must seize AI opportunity before correction, says PM Wong
Speaking at the Forbes Global CEO Conference, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong also touched on how countries should deal with the risk of powerful and autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) systems going rogue.
SINGAPORE: The artificial intelligence (AI) boom that has benefitted Singapore economically will not last forever, and the country's approach is to make good use of this window of opportunity to build new capabilities and create better jobs for Singaporeans, said Prime Minister Lawrence Wong on Thursday (Oct 8).
"No boom is forever. At some point, there will be a correction. And we don't know when it will happen, or how it will happen, we don't know who the casualties will be when it happens,” said Mr Wong, who is also finance minister.
“So our approach is to make good use of this window of opportunity now, where there is external demand, capitalise on it, build new capabilities and create better jobs for Singaporeans.”
He was speaking during a dialogue with Forbes Media chairman and editor-in-chief Steve Forbes at the Forbes Global CEO Conference held at the Shangri-La Singapore.
Mr Wong said the current AI boom has benefited Singapore’s semiconductor industry and related industries, with positive spillovers in sectors such as logistics and professional services.
“We don't make the most advanced AI chips, but we have major firms here like GlobalFoundries, Micron, and they make memory chips and specialty chips, which are in demand now with the AI boom,” he said.
He added that Singapore has also built a semiconductor ecosystem that includes the precision engineering industry and equipment suppliers.
INTERNATIONAL AI SAFEGUARDS
Mr Wong said that no country can deal alone with the risk of powerful and autonomous AI systems going rogue, or by rogue actors misusing AI to cause harm.
While it is good that the United States has appointed a task force to oversee this space, the rules and standards for frontier AI development will eventually have to be international, he said.
“It cannot be just confined to a single country, so ideally international safeguards are put in place, perhaps under the auspices of the United Nations. But that will take time,” he said.
AI safety requirements will also depend on the needs and applications of various sectors, such as healthcare, finance and advanced manufacturing, said Mr Wong.
“I think that the requirements will vary from sector to sector, and the decisions every sector regulator will have to make will be what sort of decisions ought to remain within human control, where is the human in the loop, and what kind of safeguards do you have for your sector,” he said.
Such safeguards are already taking shape in areas such as finance and transport.
Mr Wong cited newly published guidelines by the Monetary Authority of Singapore on the use of AI in finance, and the testing of autonomous cars on Singapore roads – with a pilot by autonomous driving company Waymo letting the authorities test the technology and understand safety requirements before a broader rollout under some regulatory oversight.
Turning to AI’s impact on workers and the jobs market, Mr Wong said Singapore’s approach is “not to protect the job, but to protect every worker”. This is done through close cooperation between the government, employers, and unions over the decades, he said.
NAVIGATING GEOPOLITICS
During the dialogue, Mr Wong also highlighted the impact of tariffs on the economy and called for free trade and freedom of navigation globally.
“We are concerned that what's happening in Hormuz may set a precedent for elsewhere, because if a critical international waterway can be weaponised or arbitrary tolls imposed on shipping through something like Hormuz, then countries may be tempted to do the same elsewhere,” he said.
He drew comparisons with the Strait of Malacca and Strait of Singapore, which he called a “critical maritime chokepoint” in this part of the world.
Mr Wong said he has discussed this issue with his counterparts in the other littoral states – Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto – and they are fully aligned on the principle that “international waterways must remain open, freedom of navigation and the right of transit passage has to be respected”.
“Even if you may hear rhetoric to the contrary, the leaders are aligned. We will defend these principles strongly, and we will work with partners to uphold these principles,” he said.
Mr Wong said Singapore has “not been able to understand” the tariffs imposed by the US, but that it cannot do anything. “The right tariff should be zero,” he said.
He added that other countries are also putting up more trade barriers, amid increasing concern about competition.
“There's concern that exports from other countries will impact local industries, will impact jobs. So you can see the pendulum shifting,” he said.
While this does not mean trade will stop, the global economy will become more fragmented by regions, he added.
Noting the importance of trade to Singapore, Mr Wong said the country cannot afford to turn inwards, as it “will get poor very quickly” if it does so.
It therefore aims to accelerate the integration in ASEAN, adding that it will have initiatives to do more on that front when it takes the chair of the regional bloc next year, he said.
“We will step up our connections with existing partners, and I think there are also opportunities with new regions like Latin America, Africa and the Middle East, which we hope to do more,” he said, adding that Singapore hopes to be a connector across different regions.

Why pastors may not be seen - or heard - preaching on Ghana's buses for much longer
- Published
Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on vehicles taking travellers across the country.
Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana.
Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread.
On long-distance buses, pastors can often be seen - and heard - preaching the gospel.
Sometimes they stand in the stairwell next to the driver, at others they walk up and down the aisle reading from the Bible and calling on sinners to repent at the tops of their voices. They do not stop even if the trip lasts for several hours.
The faithful sometimes offer money to the preachers to support their endeavours.
But a new law means this familiar practice could be coming to an end.
Anyone found preaching in public service vehicles faces up to eight months in prison, a fine of up to $52 (£39) or both.
The new regulation, passed by parliament in May, and which has started to be enforced in recent weeks, targets preaching and hawking on vehicles while they are in motion, classifying both as a nuisance and citing the safety and comfort of passengers.
Boateng, a 61-year-old pastor at Gospel Light church, has been preaching on commercial vehicles leaving Neoplan station since 2023.
"I preach on commercial vehicles because not everyone is able to go to church on Sunday. There are a lot of passengers who need our message of salvation to repent from their sins. We even heal the sick on some buses," he told the BBC in Twi, a local language.
Wearing a clerical collared shirt, Boateng moves through rows of buses loading passengers before boarding one bound for Kumasi, Ghana's second-largest city.
We speak to him before the bus departs to avoid breaking the law.
Some travellers listen closely as he delivers his message. Others try to ignore him, browsing their phones, making calls or chatting among themselves.
"Some passengers are very happy with my message. Some even say they have never heard the message in church, but through my preaching they now know it is in the Bible," he says.
The new rules have divided opinion.
Critics say preaching on moving vehicles is a nuisance and a safety risk, as it could distract the driver, while supporters argue that evangelism is a Christian duty and should be protected under the freedom of religious worship.
One woman in her early 30s, who wishes to be identified as Chery Lokko, says she prefers to travel in peace.
''I don't like it because they are a nuisance. Some of them spit saliva on you unconsciously, especially if you are seated not far from them, and they are a nuisance in terms of noise and saliva. I like my peace whenever I'm on public transport.''
In one video widely shared on social media recently, a passenger on a minibus is seen angrily confronting a pastor attempting to board.
"Get down, I say get down," he shouts.
But in this devout country, ranked among the most religious in the world, external, others say evangelism on public transport is an important way of reaching people who may not attend church.
Bernice Nartey, a passenger travelling to Kumasi, says pastors should be allowed to preach, but only with passengers' consent.
"The preaching sometimes helps people to repent. For instance, if someone is going through a stressful situation, the message of the pastor can give the person renewed hope," she says.
Boateng says he was shaken by the regulation and wants religious preachers to be given an exemption.
"We are very worried, because most pastors here depend on preaching to take care of their families through the monetary gifts offered by passengers," he says.
"The government should allow us to preach on the buses and alight when it is exiting Accra," he adds.
For Boateng, preaching is not only a religious calling but also an important source of income.
"I have been able to take care of my children's education. My last-born just completed university, and half of the financial support came from money I got from preaching."
Ghana's constitution guarantees freedom of religion, although those rights are subject to considerations including public safety.
Preaching on commercial buses was first prohibited in Ghana in 2012, with offenders facing up to 30 days in prison.
But enforcement was weak and so the practice remained common, particularly on buses. The new law beefs up the penalties for those that flout the ban.
Preachers using megaphones can also often be seen and heard at Ghana's lorry parks and markets but they are not affected by the ban.
The Christian Council of Ghana did not respond to the BBC's request for a comment but Rev Enoch Paul Hayes, a senior pastor at one of the biggest churches in Ghana, the International Central Gospel Church, tells the BBC he does not think the new rules infringe on religious freedom.
He urges his fellow pastors not to break the law, saying they should find other ways of spreading their message.
"There is social media as an alternative outlet, where the same message can reach thousands of people," he says.
For Boateng and other bus preachers, the new rules create a difficult choice between adapting their ministry, giving up an important source of income, or risking falling foul of the law.

Indian embassy warns nationals in Saudi: 'Stay indoors, refrain from sharing videos'
The embassy has also strongly advised Indian nationals to refrain from circulating or reposting “any videos or news related to the ongoing events.”
The Embassy of India in Riyadh has issued an advisory for Indian nationals in Saudi Arabia, urging them to remain alert and vigilant and follow instructions issued by local authorities through official channels.
“In view of the current situation, all Indian nationals in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia are advised to remain alert and vigilant, stay indoors as necessary, and follow the instructions issued by local authorities through official channels,” the embassy said in its advisory.
The embassy has also strongly advised Indian nationals to refrain from circulating or reposting “any videos or news related to the ongoing events.”
Disruption at Riyadh airport
The advisory comes amid growing disruption at Riyadh airport after a fresh Houthi attack claim on Thursday. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group targeted King Khalid International Airport with a ballistic missile and that the strike had disrupted airport operations, AP reported.
Saudi authorities have reported deadly attacks on Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport over the past two days. Three people were killed and 36 injured in the attacks, according to Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation.
Two people were killed and 28 injured at Abha, while one person was killed and eight injured at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, as per Al Jazeera.
India condemns attacks on Saudi airports
India on Thursday strongly condemned the attacks on the two Saudi airports, calling the targeting of civilian infrastructure “completely unacceptable”.
The ministry of external affairs said, “India condemns the attacks over the past few days targeting Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, which have resulted in civilian deaths and injuries.”
“The targeting of civilian infrastructure is completely unacceptable. We express our deepest condolences to the families of those who have lost their loved ones. We wish speedy recovery for those injured,” the ministry said.
New Delhi also expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia, saying, “We express solidarity and stand with the people and government of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.”
Deep Dive
The Embassy of India in Riyadh, the Consulate in Jeddah and their outsourced services provider VFS will continue to function normally, according to the advisory. The embassy said it would issue further updates and advisories “as and when necessary”.

I found the trailer for Digger intriguing, starring a nearly unrecognizable Tom Cruise and giving off strong Dr. Strangelove vibes. Plus, it is four-time Oscar-winning director Alejandro G. Iñárritu’s (Birdman) first English-language film since 2015’s The Revenant. Those elements quickly moved it near the top of my “must-see” list even if details about the actual plot were lacking. Given Iñárritu’s pedigree, the film seemed poised to be prime Oscar bait.
(Major spoilers appear below the gallery. We’ll give you a heads-up when we get there.)
By now it’s clear that Digger is on track to be one of the biggest bombs of the year instead, racking up a mere $20 million globally its opening weekend, against a $125 million (possibly more) budget. It has sharply polarized critics and audiences alike, with some appreciating Iñárritu’s bold, creative swings and others finding the film practically unwatchable.
Count me among the film’s unabashed champions, even though Digger turned out to be nothing like what I expected. It’s closer to absurdist theater than satire or dark comedy, and it’s not the Dr. Strangelove of climate change. This is a film that doesn’t just challenge the viewer; it deliberately keeps the audience off-balance, its excesses pushing the boundaries of one’s patience at times—and then Iñárritu sticks the landing with a savagely moving third act in which the final pieces of his vision fall into place.
That said, it’s also the kind of film destined to irritate, if not outright alienate, a solid faction of the audience. I get why plenty of people dislike Digger so intensely, even if I came to the opposite conclusion.
Iñárritu had the idea for Digger the character shortly after wrapping The Revenant. “I knew who this character was,” he told Variety back in July. “I knew how he spoke, how he survived, how he seduced reality into agreeing with him.” Initially the project was being developed at Netflix with Leonardo DiCaprio as a possible star; Netflix opted to make Don’t Look Up with DiCaprio instead. (Some have compared Digger to Don’t Look Up; apart from a climate theme, they are very different films.) But the idea piqued Cruise’s interest; the actor was a longtime fan of the director. And thus Digger was born.

Can Bengal deport all who crossed Bangladesh border in 1970s? Calcutta HC asks state govt
Calcutta high court questioned whether West Bengal can deport to Bangladesh all those who crossed the international border in the 1970s while hearing a detention plea.
The Calcutta high court on Thursday questioned whether the West Bengal government could deport to Bangladesh all those who crossed the international border in the 1970s, while hearing a petition challenging the detention of a man held since August 10 for deportation.
“How many persons crossed the border in the 70s? Is it possible to send them back whole hog? Visit the bordering districts. Is it possible?” observed a bench of Justice Saugata Bhattacharyya.
The court was hearing a petition concerning a man, Sahidul Sheikh, who was detained by the police at Raninagar in Murshidabad on August 10 during a special drive. The police interrogated him and accused him of being a Bangladeshi.
The Foreigners Registration Officer (FRO) issued an order on September 28 to deport him.
The court observed that prior to deportation, the petitioner has to be given a chance to respond to the affidavit filed by the local police who detained and interrogated him. The deportation order was issued while the case was still being heard by the Calcutta high court.
“Else it will appear to the court that by filing the petition the petitioner has expedited the case. If he is deported then nothing remains. The petition will become infructuous,” the bench observed.
The additional advocate general said that if documents such as PAN or Aadhaar were obtained using forged documents, that itself could constitute a ground for deportation.
“In the writ petition a case of illegal detention has been made out. It is submitted that this court doesn’t have determination to hear the matter. For the ends of justice, the deportation order shall be kept in abeyance till the next date of hearing by the appropriate court,” the court said.
The bench, however, didn’t make any observation against the detention order of the person.
“The court has kept the deportation order passed by the FRO on September 26. The matter will be heard in another bench dealing with such cases,” a lawyer, aware of the development, said.
The court kept his deportation order in abeyance until the next hearing in October.

Voice AI startup Desible.ai has raised ₹32 Cr (around $3.7 Mn) in a seed funding round led by Prime Venture Partners, with participation from existing backer Invention Engine. The Bengaluru-based startup, which offers agentic AI workflows for companies in the BFSI sector, plans to use the fresh capital to deepen its agentic AI capabilities, strengthen compliance infrastructure, expand its go-to-market efforts and accelerate product development. Founded in 2025 by Uttam Tiwari and Omkar Raikar, Desible.ai currently orchestrates over 25 agentic AI workflows spanning revenue, risk and compliance, collections, underwriting, service and claims. The startup initially uses voice AI as an entry point into the BFSI ecosystem but is expanding its platform across WhatsApp, SMS and email. Beyond voice AI, the startup’s platform is designed to automate customer engagement, servicing, operations and compliance workflows for banks, NBFCs and insurance companies. Its use cases include persistence and renewal management, collections, lead qualification, welcome calling, TeleMER, claims intimation and cross-selling, among others. Desible.ai claimed that its platform currently handles more than 10 Mn customer engagements every month and is being used or evaluated by 40+ BFSI institutions. “Voice AI is our entry point, not our destination. We are building an outcome-driven agentic workflow orchestration platform for BFSI enterprises,” Tiwari said. The funding comes at a time when the rise of generative and agentic AI is pushing financial services companies to automate increasingly complex workflows. However, deploying AI in a regulated environment comes with additional challenges around compliance, auditability, customer consent and data security. This creates an opening for vertical AI platforms that can combine automation with industry-specific controls. The opportunity for AI in BFSI is also shifting from conversational applications towards agentic systems capable of executing multi-step workflows. Betting on this growing opportunity, voice AI startups like Navana.ai recently raised ₹40 Cr ($4.2 Mn) in a Series A funding round to scale its voice AI platform’s deployment across the BFSI sector, earlier in September. Additionally, voice AI startup Arrowhead raised $3 Mn (₹27 Cr) funding in its seed round earlier in January, for hiring and technology development.

She got Trump's $500 check for health insurance. To her, it's a 'political stunt'
Check out the NPR Politics Podcast for daily analysis of the biggest news on the midterms.
Ellen Allen has mixed feelings about the check from the U.S. Treasury and letter from President Trump that arrived at her house near Charleston, W.Va., on Monday.
"I just can't believe it; I mean, that's crazy," says Allen, who's the executive director of a small nonprofit called West Virginians for Affordable Health Care. She says, in her opinion, sending out these checks is a "political stunt."
NPR first spoke to Ellen Allen in the summer of 2025. She was 63 years old at the time and knew she needed coverage from Healthcare.gov even as generous federal subsidies for her premiums were ending. She has a serious eye condition and needs expensive drops to preserve her vision. She advocated for the Republican-controlled Congress to extend the subsidies. It didn't. She ended up using retirement savings to pay $1,967 every month for her premiums from January through August, 2026.
Then her birthday came; she turned 65 and was eligible for Medicare. "I was ready at midnight — the first day I could apply, I did," she laughs.
A second check on the way?
Allen chose traditional Medicare, which means she could soon be getting another check from the U.S. Treasury. Last week, President Trump announced that $90 checks will be sent to 20 million people enrolled in Medicare.
"The $90 is — I mean, that's just nothing," Allen says. In her work, she talks to people about healthcare costs all over West Virginia. "People aren't going to be fooled by this," she predicts. "People are hurting. People are feeling the cost of healthcare all year long."
"If they wanted to do something meaningful, they would work on affordable healthcare instead of just sending out checks every now and then," Allen says.
Both checks are directed to select groups. The $500 checks mailed by the Trump administration last week were only sent to people who live in one of the 30 states that use Healthcare.gov for their insurance marketplace. They also make more than $64,000 annually for an individual, which is too much money to qualify for subsidies. These are people, like Allen, who were likely to be hard hit when Congress failed to extend the extra financial help put in place under President Joe Biden.
The $90 checks that will be sent to Medicare beneficiaries are only going to certain people enrolled in Medicare Part B. People in Medicare Advantage plans, which are managed by insurance companies, will not get checks.
Can Trump do that?
The checks are hitting people's mailboxes just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The text of a letter sent along with the money touts the Trump administration's efforts on health policy and criticizes the Biden administration.
"This reads like electioneering," says Kathleen Clark, professor of legal and governmental ethics at Washington University law school in St. Louis, Mo. "This reads as though it's intended to influence votes. That is prohibited by law."
Specifically, it would violate the Hatch Act, "the statute that prohibits using federal power and money to influence partisan political elections," she explains. It may also be a use of funds that's unauthorized by Congress.
The money for Healthcare.gov enrollees is from fees insurance companies paid to participate in the marketplace, and the money for Medicare beneficiaries is from a general improvement fund. Neither of these funds has been used for direct payments to enrollees before.
"It looks like a pretty desperate effort to, in essence, bribe the recipients of this letter to vote in gratitude to Trump in the upcoming midterm elections," she adds.
An empowered executive branch
The checks and letters are arriving in people's mailboxes, whether they're legal or not. Clark notes the Supreme Court has enabled Trump's illegal actions many times in the past. "So, of course, he feels empowered to go ahead and do this," she says.
The White House did not respond directly to NPR's questions about electioneering, whether the action is a violation of the Hatch Act or if it is a "political stunt," as Allen put it.
"This is an out-of-touch criticism," Trump administration spokeswoman Allison Schuster wrote in an email. "Americans were overcharged for the operation of the Obamacare exchange, and President Trump returned their hard-earned money. This President will never stop enabling Americans to take control of their health by implementing policies that put money back in their pockets."
'Half a tank of gas'
Some Republicans in recent years have advocated for giving more money directly to people rather than to health insurance companies, although the party has yet to settle on a particular approach.
In any case, sending these checks is unrelated to that effort, says Joseph Antos, senior fellow emeritus at the conservative think tank American Enterprise Institute. There's nothing that requires people to use this money for their health.
"From the perspective of the average senior citizen, when they get a $90 check, it's money," he adds, referencing the forthcoming checks for Medicare beneficiaries. "You can go out to McDonald's and buy probably two hamburgers and a shake for $90 [and] maybe buy a half a tank of gas."
A widening trust gap, poll says
A few weeks from the midterm elections, voters say they are struggling with health costs and want candidates to address them, according to a poll released Tuesday by the nonprofit health research organization KFF.
"The cost of healthcare is what's going to be front of mind as they're casting their votes in November," says Ashley Kirzinger, director of survey methodology for KFF. "And what we are seeing is that the Democratic Party has the advantage overall among all voters on which party voters trust to handle healthcare, but they also have the advantage among independent voters, and that's a really important voting bloc for midterm elections."
She says there is "a widening gap" between the Democratic Party and Republicans when it comes to which party voters trust to handle health costs. "It was just a 10-point margin back in April, and now we're seeing it to be a 20-point margin," she says. The poll found 22% of voters trust Republicans on the issue, compared to 42% who trust Democrats.
Where's the credit for GOP candidates?
Antos, of AEI, calls the Trump administration's decision to send out these checks "inexplicable." He describes the move as politically strange, since a Republican administration that disparages Obamacare is investing more money into it, and "unreasonable from a fiscal standpoint," because of the growing national debt.
He also notes that most Americans won't be getting these checks. "How about the average, lower-income worker who has employer coverage?" he asks. "They're not getting anything. Why is that? Is that fair?"
He is doubtful the move will have a political benefit for Republican candidates. "For one thing, Trump is not saying that your local congressman did this for you, Trump is saying he did it for you," Antos says. "I don't get it, and I don't see any advantage to anybody, including Donald Trump."
Despite her mixed feelings, Ellen Allen of West Virginians for Affordable Health Care is planning to deposit the $500 check she just received. "I'm not going to send it back," she says. "I'm going to put it in my health savings account and keep working towards healthcare for all."

'I reduced my running because of urine leaks' – Commonwealth finalist Korir
- Published
Naomi Korir's career on the track reached a high point in August when she finished fifth in the final of the mile at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
But things could have been very different for the Kenyan middle-distance runner.
The 28-year-old was born with fistula, a medical condition in which abnormal openings develop between organs and can lead to uncontrolled leakage of urine or faeces.
While Korir loved athletics as a child, it initially forced her to rethink any plans to be a runner.
"I played most of the sports activities: football, netball, athletics, even rugby," she said.
"But it was difficult because [of] the training, and the urine is flowing continuously. It's bad.
"I reduced my running to shorter distances to reduce the leaking.
"I began doing 100m hurdles."
Despite the challenges, Korir's love of sport also offered a form of escape and belonging.
"I could do it because I loved it," she explained.
"Because most of the people could avoid me, I did a lot of activities just to pass time and not to feel that I'm excluded."
Three surgeries and a second chance
The charity Doctors Without Borders estimates that 500,000 women live with fistula globally.
Some develop a fistula after childbirth while for others, like Korir, it is congenital.
Access to good obstetrics, or to simple surgery, means that the condition has all but disappeared in some countries, but it remains a problem in sub-Saharan Africa, where high quality medical care can be hard to access.
Korir was born with genitourinary tract fistula - an opening between bladder and vagina which caused her urine leakage.
Surgery was required, but her first two operations failed to solve the problem.
In August 2013, a third operation finally brought relief for the then 13-year-old.
The procedure was carried out in her home town Eldoret by the Gynocare Hospital, which specialises in fistula, obstetrics and reproductive health.
"It's a difficult condition to live with every day," Gynocare director Caroline Mabeya told BBC Sport Africa when discussing the stigma and isolation women with the condition suffer.
"They are ostracised in the society. That's the psychological torture that they face with the fistula."
The hospital has treated patients from across East Africa since opening its doors in 2011. Its work extends beyond surgery, with a post-operation programme designed to help women rebuild their confidence.
"We offer free treatment for these women at Gynocare because most of them are very poor," Mabeya explained.
"When they come into the facility, they are crushed, they have low esteem. So, there's a huge amount of effort that is put in to make them at least be strong enough to be reintegrated and get back into the community."
'A champion in sport'
For Korir, successful surgery offered a second chance, both on the track and in the classroom.
As well as allowing her to run properly again, she continued her education through Gynocare's Beyond Fistula programme.
"I have a family in GynoCare, a fistula home," she said.
"That is where I schooled after my surgery until I finished my secondary level."
In 2019, Korir began competing professionally and two years later was part of the Kenyan duo which claimed a silver medal in the 2x2x400m mixed relay alongside her partner Ferguson Rotich at the World Relays in Poland.
A year later she went one better, bagging gold as part of Kenya's 4x400m relay team at the African Championships in Mauritius.
The mile at this year's Commonwealth Games was her first appearance in major global final.
"I'm giving hope to young women maybe who have lost hope," she said of her achievements.
"They need to come back again in living and enjoying life."
Mabeya says Korir's transformation makes her a powerful example to the women currently receiving support at Gynocare.
"She makes them realise that you can actually pull yourself out of these struggles and still make it in life and succeed.
"Naomi actually is one of those patients that inspires us to continue working very hard, because we struggle with this condition and these women. The work is not easy."
As a young girl, Korir sang in church and played the keyboard, convinced that music was a more likely career than athletics.
"But now I'm in different career and I'm so happy," she beamed.
And with the World Championships in Beijing next year and the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, Korir believes there is another chapter to write.
"I know I'm a champion in life, because conquering fistula alone is being a champion.
"Now I'm looking forward to be a champion in sport."

Kenya's Health Ministry on Tuesday (October 6, 2026) confirmed the country's first imported Ebola case from Congo.
Health Minister Aden Duale said a Kenyan citizen who arrived in the country on Saturday (October 3, 2026) from Congo, via Uganda, had been isolated and treated at Nairobi Hospital.
The patient tested positive for the Ebola virus after developing symptoms associated with haemorrhagic fever. The patient died late on Monday (October 5, 2026) while receiving treatment.
Health authorities have placed the country on high alert and are monitoring for possible additional cases. Mr. Duale said 28 contacts, including family members and health workers who had cared for the patient, had been identified. Another 23 passengers who had travelled on the same flight from Uganda were being traced.
The contacts will remain in isolation for 21 days, and will be released after testing negative for the virus, Patrick Amoth, the Ministry's Director, said. The patient will be buried within 24 hours, in accordance with recommended public safety protocols.
Kenya is the fourth country to record an Ebola case in the current outbreak, which was declared in eastern Congo in mid-May. Uganda recorded 20 cases, and France one. Before Kenya reported its case, there had been no active cases outside Congo since Uganda declared its outbreak over in late August.
This is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history. The World Health Organization (WHO) has warned it could become the deadliest, as it continues to outpace efforts to track and contain it.
The outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Vaccine and treatment trials are under way in Congo's Ituri province, the outbreak's epicentre.

RBI governor Sanjay Malhotra yesterday eased concerns over the new foreign exchange reporting framework, clarifying that individuals undertaking transactions of a personal nature would not have to report them. He also cited earnings from overseas tutoring and small software assignments among the transactions that would not require reporting. The clarification follows concerns among freelancers, creators, and small service exporters about additional paperwork under the Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2026. The rules, which took effect on October 1, bring goods and services trade under a unified framework. Malhotra said banks and authorised dealers would handle reporting to the RBI, while exporters could use self-declaration for bills of up to ₹10 Lakh — a threshold that applies per bill, not to annual earnings. For established SaaS startups already reporting software exports, industry participants expect mainly procedural changes. What Has The RBI Clarified? Malhotra said individuals’ transactions of a personal nature do not require reporting, irrespective of the amount. Examples include subscriptions to apps, television channels, journals, and newspapers. His clarification also covered individuals receiving payments for overseas tutoring and small software assignments, extending the reassurance beyond personal spending. Deputy governor Rohit Jain said the framework aims to simplify trade processes and give authorised dealers greater flexibility. Acknowledging confusion over reporting obligations, he said the RBI would issue FAQs to clarify the requirements. These FAQs are expected to explain how the clarification applies across different freelance and creator business arrangements. What Changes For SaaS Startups And Banks? Software exporters previously used SOFTEX, while goods exports followed a separate declaration process. Other service exports did not necessarily require equivalent declarations, although obligations to realise and repatriate overseas earnings still applied. The regulations prescribe an Export Declaration Form (EDF) for services, including software, and permit a single declaration covering a month’s service exports. According to CA Abhinarayan Mishra, a cross-border tax and FEMA expert, the broader use of “services” expands the reporting architecture. However, established SaaS companies already have reporting systems, so their changes could largely involve forms and procedures. Naganand Doraswamy, founder and managing partner at Ideaspring Capital, similarly expects limited changes for startups already filing SOFTEX forms. “From a founder's perspective, there's not a whole lot of change... what was being filed in SOFTEX, they'll go by and file it in EDF and the banks have to match,” Doraswamy said. He expects some transitional disruption but said processes should become smoother once the system settles. Banks would undertake more work matching invoices with remittances. Manav Garg, cofounder and managing partner at Together Fund, said consolidating export reporting through authorised banks could simplify compliance for software and AI startups. Mishra also expects banks to play a larger role in reconciliation and compliance, making their implementation of the revised processes important for startups. What Does The ₹10 Lakh Route Allow? The ₹10 Lakh threshold applies per export bill, not to total annual export earnings. Annual earnings exceeding ₹10 Lakh would therefore not, by themselves, rule out the simplified route for eligible individual bills. Banks may close export-monitoring entries for bills up to ₹10 Lakh based on an exporter’s declaration that payment has been realised in full or otherwise. Exporters can also submit these declarations quarterly to their authorised dealer for bulk closure of eligible entries in the export-monitoring system. This simplifies smaller transactions but does not remove every obligation to supply information to banks or constitute a blanket FEMA exemption. What Reconciliation Issues Could Arise? Mishra flagged reconciliation challenges where platform charges or deductions leave service providers receiving less than they invoiced, including through platforms such as PayPal. Similar questions arise for YouTube creators and influencers earning from overseas platforms. Larger creators may have agencies or accountants handling documentation, while smaller creators often maintain their own records. For service providers covered by the framework, these differences make it important to reconcile invoices, platform deductions, and actual receipts. What About The Nine-Month Deadline? Service export proceeds generally must be realised and repatriated within nine months of the invoice date. A 12-month period applies where exports are invoiced or settled in rupees, and authorised dealers may grant extensions on satisfactory grounds. It is pertinent to mention that nine months is not a fresh reduction introduced on October 1. The RBI restored this deadline in June after a temporary extension to 15 months. Through an amendment in September, the central bank aligned the incoming regulations with it. Mishra said larger companies may find it easier to structure contracts around deadlines, while smaller providers could struggle with delayed or disputed payments. A $1,000 invoice settled for $900, for example, leaves $100 requiring reconciliation. The regulations allow authorised dealers to approve reduced realisation on satisfactory grounds for bills up to ₹10 Lakh. This may be based on self-declaration. For cases where proceeds remain unrealised beyond one year after the applicable due date or extension, further exports require full advance payment or an irrevocable letter of credit. A disputed payment therefore does not automatically trigger an export ban when nine months expire. Why Is RBI Expanding Services Reporting? Malhotra said the framework would improve services trade data, bringing reporting closer to merchandise trade. Customers already provide information such as purpose codes, while the revised framework seeks additional details. Mishra said more comprehensive reporting could give policymakers a clearer picture of emerging service exports, including the creator economy, and more timely information on overseas service earnings.

Drones sank two cargo ships and damaged a third in the exclusive economic zones of NATO member countries for the first time, killing at least two sailors. The attacks represent a notable escalation as Black Sea commercial shipping has increasingly come under attack during the Russian invasion of Ukraine, with Russia also being accused of carrying out “hybrid warfare” incidents across Europe.
The Togo-flagged cargo ship Alfa Watan sank, and the Palau-flagged cargo ship Able was set ablaze after being attacked by multiple sea and aerial drones about 80 miles (128 kilometers) off the coast of Bulgaria on October 6, according to the Associated Press. In an interview, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev described the incidents as “an unacceptable attack in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone” and “a blatant violation of international law and maritime law.”
The fate of the Alfa Watan’s crew was not immediately known after the vessel sank. A Bulgarian ferry managed to evacuate the 18 crew members of the Able, with two severely injured mariners being flown to a hospital in the city of Varna.
This comes one day after drones struck the Turkish-owned cargo ship named Royad Mammadov within Romania’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea on October 5. That ship caught fire and eventually sank, with 11 crew members rescued by Romanian ships and helicopters while one crew member remains missing, according to Euronews. Two crew members were killed.
European Union president Ursula von der Leyen described the drone strikes on the three vessels in the Black Sea as “increasingly concerning” in a post on X. But she also cautioned that the circumstances of the attacks are “still being established” without naming a probable attacker.
“Attacks on civilian shipping are unacceptable,” Leyen wrote. “We stand in full solidarity with our Member States on the Eastern flank.”
By contrast, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described a joint investigation with Bulgaria’s navy as finding that the latest strikes represented a “Russian combined attack using both sea and aerial drones,” Reuters reported. Zelenskyy also said that Ukraine’s military was not conducting operations in that part of the Black Sea.

Tamil Nadu is recording around 200 cases of dengue a day. Fresh cases are being reported in places including Chennai and its neighbouring districts and cities such as Coimbatore and Madurai.
Officials of the Directorate of Public Health (DPH) and Preventive Medicine said the caseload remained steady and was not at outbreak proportions. A. Somasundaram, Director of Public Health and Preventive Medicine, said cases had not risen exponentially, with the numbers remaining broadly steady. “We are seeing nearly 200 cases a day. The numbers are not doubling or tripling, which usually happens in an outbreak. Right now, there is a static trend in the number of dengue cases, and we are expecting the cases to decline soon,” he said.
Cases are being reported across cities including the Chennai belt (Tiruvallur and Kancheepuram), Coimbatore, and Madurai. This could partly be due to a “natural bias” with these areas having more hospitals and testing facilities, Dr. Somasundaram said.
“We have specifically instructed staff to increase the number of tests for dengue for better surveillance and patient management. This is so we don’t miss a case, and when samples are tested, we can identify pockets of cases or clusters, which are likely to bring about an outbreak,” he said. There are over 4,500 government and private laboratories in the State, he added.
Surveillance measures to identify Aedes mosquito breeding pools are continuing, but the number of pools detected has started to decline as a result of source reduction measures. The mosquito density is slowly coming down, the official said. About 25,000 Domestic Breeding Checkers (DBC) have been engaged across the State, with 20 persons covering one block.
Dr. Somasundaram said while preventive measures had been intensified, they had been holding daily monitoring meetings with District Health Officers via video conferencing. “We are analysing the case trend, whether increase or decrease or static, and number of laboratory tests conducted. We are also monitoring fever triaging, patient management, and discharge policy. Patients are being categorised as having mild, moderate, or severe symptoms and treated appropriately. Right now, the severity of infections is less. Fogging operations and source reduction measures, along with work taken up by DBCs, are being supervised. We are also looking at creating awareness among the public,” he said.
With October and November being crucial months, he said, there could be intermittent or heavy rain and people should ensure that their household environment is clean. “Avoid storing water unnecessarily. If you have too, keep containers closed properly,” he added.

Ajay Devgn has joined several members of the film fraternity in mourning the demise of veteran actor Nana Patekar. On Thursday, October 8, the actor took to social media to remember his Apaharan co-star, sharing a picture from the Prakash Jha directorial along with a heartfelt note.

Former Bachelor Australia star Sam Wood denied bail over domestic violence charges
- Published
Former Bachelor Australia star and fitness coach Sam Wood will remain in jail after he was denied bail over alleged domestic violence offences.
Wood was arrested on Saturday at a beachfront property on Queensland's Sunshine Coast, and later charged with domestic violence assault and strangulation.
His lawyer told the court on Thursday Wood may defend himself by arguing he acted in self defence during a family fight, but stressed he denies the strangulation charge.
The 46-year-old rose to fame in the 2015 season of the reality TV show and later became the public face of a popular online home fitness and nutrition brand, 28 by Sam Wood - from which he was dumped after his arrest.
Wood - who lives in Melbourne but was on holiday in Noosa - appeared via videolink at Maroochydore Magistrates Court where he applied for bail after five nights in custody.
Police prosecutors told the court the alleged victim had provided a video statement in which she said she had been choked, couldn't breathe, and had her head banged against the floor.
"She thought she was going to die," Sergeant Jeanette Grigoris said.
They also tendered photos of the alleged victim's injuries, as well as a recording of a call to emergency services in which a witness says the woman was choked.
The complainant supports the criminal charges, Grigoris added.
Wood's lawyer Mathew Cuskelly had argued that there was a lack of evidence to support the strangulation charge, which "seems unusual" given the "nature" and "gravity" of the allegation.
He also said his client had been involved in an argument, in which the complainant had been "hostile" when he pushed her - circumstances which could entitle him to a self-defence claim.
Cuskelly said Wood suffers from severe depression, and argued he should be bailed so that he can access mental health support and salvage his professional reputation "which has taken a hell of a beating".
But Grigoris argued there was a risk Wood would interfere with witnesses or reoffend, or fail to return to Queensland to face court.
On Monday, a statement "from the Wood family" was released on both he and his wife's social media.
"This is a difficult time for all of us, we are working through this as a family and thoroughly co-operating with the authorities," the post said.
DBG Health, which bought Wood's fitness brand for millions of dollars in 2022, initially said Wood had been placed on "indefinite leave" but later announced it had cut its commercial arrangements with him "effective immediately".
"DGB Health does not tolerate domestic violence in any form, and our thoughts are with people impacted by it," the company said.
Since the charges, a number of fitness influencers and corporate sponsors have also cut ties with Wood including fitness trainer Tiffiny Hall and Married At First Sight star Jules Robinson.
Wood came to national prominence during the 2015 season of The Bachelor Australia where he met contestant Snezana Markoski.
They married in 2018 and have four daughters, including one from his wife's former relationship.
Wood is next due in court on 23 November.

South Korea to recall ambassador from Ukraine amid POW dispute
The two countries have been at loggerheads since Zelensky disclosed the transfer of the prisoners captured on the battlefield early last year
South Korea said on Thursday it would recall its ambassador to Ukraine in response to a deepening diplomatic row over the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war to Seoul.
The decision comes as the two countries have been at loggerheads since Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky sparked anger in Seoul by disclosing the transfer of the prisoners, who were captured on the battlefield early last year.

“The government has decided to recall its ambassador to Ukraine,” the foreign ministry said in a statement.

Amit Shah meets Manipur CM Khemchand in Delhi, says he will visit state later this month
Amit Shah met Manipur chief minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh in New Delhi, with the latter briefing him on the steps taken by the state government to restore peace
Union home minister Amit Shah on Thursday met Manipur chief minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh in New Delhi, with the latter briefing him on the steps taken by the state government to restore peace and normalcy amid ongoing ethnic tensions.
Shah also told Khemchand that he would visit Manipur later this month, according to the chief minister’s office.
HT had reported on Thursday that Khemchand and deputy CM Nemcha Kipgen, who had come to Delhi, were holding meetings with senior leaders and had other meetings scheduled.
“Manipur CM Yumnam Khemchand Singh today called on Union Home Minister Amit Shah at his official residence in New Delhi.During the meeting, the Chief Minister apprised the Union Home Minister of the measures taken up by the State Government for restoring peace and normalcy in the State. The CM informed the Union Home Minister that the State Government has succeeded in resuming the Imphal-Dimapur-Guwahati bus service, which has brought much-needed relief to the common people,” the statement said.
CM Khemchand also held separate meetings with Union ministers Nitin Gadkari and Mansukh Mandaviya.
The state has been roiled by Naga-Kuki clashes and the demand for the NRC exercise, because of which the census has also been postponed.
The ethnic clashes in Manipur first began between the Meitei and Kuki communities before involving almost every community. The state’s Meitei and Kuki-Zo communities have shut each other out from the areas they dominate since the ethnic clashes began in May 2023, leaving at least 260 people dead and displacing 60,000.
The fight is not restricted to just people on the ground. The state’s two deputy chief ministers, representing the Naga and Kuki communities, are not on speaking terms amid the ongoing Naga-Kuki clashes.
In fact, during the assembly session last month, Naga MLAs boycotted the proceedings, refusing to share space with Kipgen, who joined the session virtually as she is yet to visit Imphal amid the unresolved Kuki-Meitei conflict.
Dikho and eight other Naga MLAs on September 1 wrote to Shah seeking action against Kipgen and her husband, alleging they were colluding with Kuki militant groups and hampering the peace process. In an interview with HT last month, Kipgen denied the allegations and said she had worked to resolve the tension between the communities.
The Naga-Kuki tensions intensified following the twin ambushes on May 13 that left four people, including three church leaders, dead. In the aftermath of the ambushes, 48 people were taken hostage, triggering protests, shutdowns and a blockade along all three national highways in the state.
The Meiteis, mostly Hindu, live largely in the Imphal Valley. The Kukis, predominantly Christian, reside in the hills. The state government has maintained that there are no buffer zones dividing communities in the state, but it has identified certain sensitive areas.
A new government was formed in February, nearly a year after the imposition of President’s Rule. It includes representatives from all three major communities as part of an attempt to maintain ethnic balance.

Relative humidity is a simple concept as weather phenomena go – but it has significant, far-reaching consequences for how we must take care of ourselves on a hot or wet day.
Letting the wind flow freely is the secret to cooling our cities
Humidity is the amount of moisture in the air around us, and there are three ways to track it. The most common of them is absolute humidity: the mass of water vapour in a given volume of the air and water vapour mixture, expressed as kg/m3. The second is specific humidity, equal to the mass of the moisture divided by the mass of air. It is expressed as a dimensionless number (but sometimes also as grams per kilogram, among other similar units.)
The third way is relative humidity: it is important because it factors in the amount of vapour that air can hold at different temperatures. Determining its value is a bit more complicated: it is the vapour density of the air divided by the saturation vapour density at the dry-bulb temperature.
Why does relative humidity matter?
On a hot day, our body uses sweat to cool itself. Sweat is released via our skin to the surface. There, the liquid evaporates. When water changes phase from liquid to vapour, it absorbs heat from the surface on which it lies. So when sweat evaporates, it absorbs heat from the skin, cooling it.
The higher the relative humidity of air, the more it is filled with moisture. When air already contains a lot of moisture, it won’t easily accept more. This means that the sweat on your skin can’t evaporate. At the same time, the body keeps sweating because it is still expecting to cool itself.
As a result, if the relative humidity is high, you can sweat on a hot day even when you are sitting still – while your body also keeps accumulating heat. This can quickly become dangerous.
A relative humidity of 30-60% is generally considered to be comfortable. Environments that have lower levels than this typically use humidifiers to increase the humidity. When the level is higher, a fan will help move the air around you and help sweat evaporate better.
In both cases, drinking water is important.
What does relative humidity imply physically?
Warmer air can hold more moisture than cooler air. So at the same absolute humidity, the relative humidity of warmer air will be lower than that of cooler air. It is like saying two vessels can hold the same amount of water – just that the bigger vessel will be less full than the smaller vessel.
This is why, for example, while Chennai had an absolute humidity of 70% at 2.30 pm on April 23, its relative humidity was lower, around 60%, because it had an ambient temperature of 32 C.
The change in the capacity for moisture as the air warms is also non-linear, meaning it doesn’t increase by the same amount as the air warms. For example, the difference as it warms over 20º C from -20º C to 0º C is small, but there is an enormous improvement in its vapour-carrying capacity as it warms over 20º C from 30º C to 50º C.
How do you measure relative humidity?
There are a few ways to measure relative humidity. One is to conduct a simple experiment with household items; another is to use maths; a third is to use an app or device.
Experiment
For the experiment, you need two mercury thermometers, some cotton, rubber bands, and access to cold water.
First, make sure both thermometers show the same reading, say, under a fan. Next, soak some cotton in cold water and wrap it around the bulb of one of the thermometers with a rubber band. Hold this thermometer under the fan, such that water from the cotton evaporates, and record the thermometer reading after five minutes. Hold up the other thermometer in the air and record its reading after five minutes. You will thus have the wet-bulb and dry-bulb temperatures, respectively.
Next, subtract the wet-bulb temperature from the dry-bulb temperature to get the temperature difference. Finally, use the relative humidity chart (see below) to get the relative humidity value. For example, if the difference was 6 C and the dry-bulb temperature was 28 C, the relative humidity would have been 59%.
A psychrometer is a device that has two such thermometers plus a chart to get the final reading. Modern, electronic psychrometers can calculate the relative humidity directly.
For a rough sense, the lower the wet-bulb temperature, the drier the air is, and the less relatively humid it is.
Mathematics
There are two mathematical ways (among others) to estimate the relative humidity, one simpler and one a bit more involved.
The first way is to divide the actual vapour pressure by the saturated vapour pressure. The vapour pressure is the amount of moisture that air contains. The ‘saturated’ value is the maximum possible amount. The formula (below) requires the dew point (Td), which you can obtain from a weather website.
RH = (e/es)*100
e = 6.11 x 10((7.5 x Td)/(237.3 + Td))
For es, use the same formula but replace Td with T, the actual temperature.
The second way is to calculate relative humidity starting from the specific humidity, pressure and temperature, using the Clausius-Clapeyron equation.
App
If you prefer software: Search for “hygrometer” in your phone’s app store to locate some options. (A hygrometer is an instrument that measures humidity.) Note that the app will only work if your phone has a sensor that can sense humidity.
If you like hardware, psychrometers and devices called hygrometers are available in physical as well as online stores.
Why does the wet-bulb temperature matter?
This said, a more direct way to understand the implications of the relative humidity for your wellbeing is in the form of the wet-bulb temperature (a.k.a. the adiabatic saturation temperature). It is the lowest temperature a surface – like your skin – can reach when water evaporates from it. The wet-bulb temperature is equal to the dry-bulb temperature when the relative humidity is 100%.
A wet-bulb temperature in an environment of 32-35º C or higher can be quickly lethal, even if you are not doing any physical activity or are in the shade. (At least one study has shown that even a wet-bulb temperature of more than 29º C can be dangerous.)
The climate crisis is rendering heatwaves more common, more frequent, more spread out, and more potent over the Indian subcontinent. As a study published in May 2022 put it:
“Whether today’s most impactful heatwaves could have occurred in a pre-industrial climate, traditionally a central focus of attribution research, is fast becoming an obsolete question. The next frontier for attribution science is to inform adaptation decision-making in the face of unprecedented future heat.”
One way to adapt is to keep an eye on the relative humidity, drink lots of water, and cool yourself.
- Humidity is the amount of moisture in the air around us, and there are three ways to track it. The most common of them is absolute humidity: the mass of water vapour in a given volume of the air and water vapour mixture, expressed as kg/m3.
- The higher the relative humidity of air, the more it is filled with moisture. When air already contains a lot of moisture, it won’t easily accept more.
- A wet-bulb temperature in an environment of 32-35º C or higher can be quickly lethal, even if you are not doing any physical activity or are in the shade. (At least one study has shown that even a wet-bulb temperature of more than 29º C can be dangerous.)

Strike on Ukrainian public bus leaves 30 dead as blackouts worsen in Kyiv
KYIV, Ukraine — Thirty people were killed and at least 18 were injured by Russian strikes in eastern Ukraine that included an attack on a public bus, authorities said Thursday, as an intensive pre-winter wave of attacks continued and power outages worsened in the capital Kyiv.
Vadym Filashkin, head of the regional military administration, said public transport in Kramatorsk and the neighboring city of Sloviansk, in Ukraine's Donetsk region, was halted because of the sharp deterioration in security.
He accused Russia of deliberately targeting civilians, adding: "In such circumstances, we have no right to risk the lives of passengers and drivers. The safety of residents of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk is above all."
The attacks follow deadly missile strikes a day earlier in the northern Ukrainian town of Pryluky, where the death toll rose to 22, including five children. Rescuers searched through the rubble of a residential building hit by a Russian missile and at least 54 people were injured.
Heavy debris was removed from the cratered section of the building, while rescue dogs continued a search nearby for residents who have not yet been accounted for.
Several survivors of the attack were forced to sleep in heavily damaged apartments after they couldn't find anywhere else to sleep.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Russia will likely escalate daily missile and drone attacks as winter approaches. He appealed for additional defense support from NATO countries.
"It is important that support in words takes concrete form in new packages for Ukraine's defense," he wrote in an online post. "Supplies of anti-ballistic capabilities, ammunition for our combat aircraft, and investments in interceptors — all of this is directly helping save lives every day."
Ukraine's energy company DTEK said the national grid operator Ukrenergo had ordered emergency power outages in Kyiv. It explained that this is separate from regular, rolling outages scheduled across the country and would not be applied during those shutdowns.
A public awareness campaign, restarted this month, urged families to prepare emergency kits, store drinking water and maintain off-grid power sources ahead of expected prolonged winter blackouts, as Moscow keeps up the intensity of its attacks.
Kyiv police said bomb disposal specialists had defused two more unexploded ballistic missile warheads, each weighing about half a ton, after they landed near residential buildings. Late Wednesday, Russian drones struck Kyiv's Obolonskyi and Desnianskyi districts, killing four people and injuring 12, including four children, police said.
Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4 1/2 years since Moscow's full-scale invasion.
Russia's technology giant Yandex said one of its data centers in the western Ryazan region was damaged in a Ukrainian drone attack, taking the site offline and leading to potential online service disruption.
Separately, Ukraine said its forces struck a large oil refinery complex in the city of Salavat, some 1,200 kilometers (about 750 miles) east of Moscow. Ukraine's General Staff described the complex as one of Russia's largest oil refining and petrochemical facilities. The claim could not be independently verified.
