Amid increasing state-sanctioned censorship of digital content across platforms like Meta and X, activists, journalists, cartoonists, artists, opposition politicians and others critical of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government and its policies have faced sweeping content restrictions and takedowns in the last few months. The latest to face such censorship are those raising concerns over the establishment of large-scale data centres in Visakhapatnam.
The port city in Andhra Pradesh is witnessing a massive digital infrastructure push, with investments of up to ₹1.25 lakh crore planned over five years (2026–30) and more than 2,000 acres of land earmarked for data centre projects. In October last year, Google and Adani formally announced an AI hub project in Visakhapatnam. By December 2025, 308 acres at Tarluvada, 120 acres at Adavivaram and 160 acres at Rambilli had been identified for the project. In January this year, reports indicated a much larger expansion involving Google, Sify, Reliance and CtrlS.
In April, the state government and Google laid the foundation stone for the Google Cloud India AI Hub at Tarluvada village. The facility, spread across 266.6 acres, is expected to draw 1 GW of power and is reportedly Google’s largest data centre outside the United States.
The projects are expected to make Visakhapatnam a major eastern data and subsea-cable hub, providing direct routes for Indian data to the US, South Africa, Singapore and Australia. Officials say this could reduce reliance on existing routes through Chennai, Kochi and the Red Sea, while shifting high-value technology activity from expensive metros to other cities.
But local influencers and journalists have raised concerns about the environmental and ecological impact of this rapid expansion of data centre infrastructure in Visakhapatnam and beyond.
ALSO READ: Government orders trigger sweeping Instagram censorship days after CJP protest
Why the Data Centres are being Opposed
The Stop Dirty Data Centre campaign, led by over 60 individuals, formed to “oppose the setting up of 6.5 GW of AI data centres”, lists over 10 proposed data centres spanning across over 2,500 acres of land in Visakhapatnam. Besides the Tarluvada facility, the list mentions two other major Google-Adani Hyperscale data centers: At Rambilli village consuming 1 GW of power across 174.8 acres, and at Adavivaram-Mudasarlova consuming 512 MW of power across 165.40 acres of land. All three are currently under-construction.
It is important to note that Adavivaram-Mudasarlova is around 120 metres from the Mudasarlova reservoir — a critical drinking water source for the city; it also lies near the Kailasagiri-Kambalakonda forest landscape. The Tarluvada site is located 1.53 km from the Kambalakonda Wildlife Sanctuary and about 450 metres from its notified Eco-Sensitive Zone (ESZ) while the Rambilli site lies on the Anakapalli coast and is surrounded by forests.
As most of these sites lie on coastal regions, close to wildlife sanctuaries, forest areas and ESZs, opponents of this expansion project have flagged the disproportionate energy and land usage, large-scale hill cutting, deforestation, and further water depletion in an already water-scarce zone — Visakhapatnam’s water demand already exceeds supply by around 70 million litres per day. They also cite the massive impact on climate, biodiversity, wildlife sanctuaries, coastal ecosystems, and residential areas as serious detrimental effects.
“If fully built, the proposed AI data centers capacity could consume as much as the entire electricity currently used by the state of Andhra Pradesh,” states the campaign website. “Vizag is already severely water stressed and cooling these data centers could take up almost half of city’s supply based on estimates; the proposed land allocation is roughly equivalent to more than 700 cricket grounds, and is present in eco-sensitive regions; hyperscale AI facilities can significantly increase regional greenhouse gas emissions through backup Diesel Generator (DG) sets, solid waste, and more,” it adds.
Critics also highlighted the lack of transparency and public awareness around the setting up of these data centres, demanding that these projects be undertaken in consultation with locals and not unilaterally by the state and corporations. “In a brazen act of environmental lawlessness, forest land at the site [for the Adavivaram-Mudasarlova data centre] was cleared by the project proponent over several months even before environmental clearance was obtained,” alleges a petition initiated by the campaigners.
Citizen Movement Flagging Environmental Concerns Blocked
Against this backdrop, on September 19, the Instagram account of the Stop Vizag Data Centre campaign was banned in India under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology (IT) Act, 2000.
One of the founders, Deeksha Vanguru, told Alt News that they did not receive any prior notification. While the account was restored on September 27, nine of their posts critical of the data centre expansion, which were restricted over the last two months, remain unavailable in India.
“Our page was apparently blocked due to a local government request, we appealed to Meta and it was restored due to that request being either expired or reversed. However, our reach has been affected and posts are getting shadowbanned. We had to open a backup account in the meanwhile because we did not want to stop our fight. We are still fighting for the restoration of our nine posts,” Vanguru said.
“We started this as a citizen group in July this year. Most of us are born and brought up in Visakhapatnam and we couldn’t sit and watch the destruction of our home. We wanted to ensure that voices of the farmers, fishermen, villagers, and common citizens are heard. Initially, there was a small-scale mobilisation of citizens, but it needed more youth anger, therefore we turned the campaign into a social media project,” she added.
ALSO READ: Content creators decry Instagram censorship, call restrictions a ‘digital emergency’
“A big concern around AI data centres globally is the consumption of fresh water, and India is already going into a phase of water scarcity. The 10 data centres together are going to consume 200 MLD of water, which is 50% of the city’s daily water supply. The DGs will require constant air conditioning because they claim to be using advanced air cooling, thus the energy strain on the grid will be extremely high. Due to the constant running of generators and ACs, there could be overheating. The whole thing is going to be concrete, which will increase the land surface temperature and reduce night-time cooling. The average night-time temperature in Visakhapatnam has alreadt gone from 23-24 degrees to around 28 degrees,” she said.
Vanguru alleged there was no transparency while these data centres were being set up.
“The government hasn’t held any public consultation with either the farmers or the people of Vizag living close to these sites. In fact, environmental clearances for a 600-acre project, now broken up to escape scrutiny, was given within nine days. On April 9, the environmental clearance request was filed and it was received on April 18. There was no Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) because these projects haven’t been categorised as Category A projects (considered to have greater potential environmental impacts and are appraised by the Union environment ministry and require an EIA) but as Category B2 projects, which means buildings and construction. The way the government has gone about this is as if they’re building malls,” she said.
Further, Vanguru claimed that these data centres had nearly nothing to offer to the locals, even in terms of job creation, which she said was one of the upsides of an industrial construction. “When we checked the environmental clearances, the number of permanent jobs being created was only 1,725. The rest are all construction jobs and temporary jobs. These temporary and construction jobs are being positioned as skilled jobs, but in India, the government definition of skilled means blue-collar jobs. So it keeps people in the same worker or employee cycle and doesn’t really help uplift people from poverty,” she added.
Original Reportage on Dalit Displacement Blocked
After the Tarluvada data centre’s construction began, independent journalists Shamsheer Yousaf and Monica Jha began reporting the ground realities of the construction in early January, as part of the Dirty Data project undertaken by the Environmental Reporting Collective (ERC).
A 2-minute long Instagram reel posted by ERC in collaboration with Yousaf, which features interviews of Dalit farmers in the village who are faced with imminent displacement, was blocked in India on May 22 under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act with no prior notice. In the reel, which garnered 2.6 million views and 46,000 shares, several farmers say that they were granted the land over 50 years ago by the Congress government and have since cleared forests to build homes and farms, which is their only form of subsistence — all under threat as the same land has been allocated to the Google-Adani data centre.
View this post on Instagram
The reel formed part of a 5-minute-long video published on Dirty Data’s website alongside the report, ‘As data centers arrive, India’s poorest face displacement, health risks’ by Yousaf and Jha. Yousaf wrote to the Union ministry of electronics & information technology (MeitY), seeking the blocking order, reasons for the action, restoration of the reel and a personal hearing in order to appeal or respond. He also wrote to Meta’s grievance officer in India.
ALSO READ: Meta restricts posts by Indian Youth Congress, AAP, Opposition leader
Upon not receiving any response from either authorities, on June 30, Yousaf and Jha moved the Delhi high court with a writ petition. A month later on July 23, the petitioners were given access to the blocking order which revealed the authority behind the restriction as the director general of police (DGP), CID, Andhra Pradesh.
‘Procedural Lapses, Unconstitutional Takedown’
In a report, the Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF), whose lawyers are representing the petitioners, highlighted certain procedural lapses in the blocking order and claimed that the takedown was “unconstitutional”. The order names one Mr. Vemireddy Prabhakar Reddy, alleging that the video “spread misinformation” against him. However, this individual does not feature anywhere in the reel or any of the journalists’ reportage on the data centre issue; he is also not known to either of them.
IFF had then sent a legal notice to the principal secretary, home department and the DGP-CID, Andhra Pradesh, flagging this discrepancy and violation of the provision of the IT Rules, 2021. “…there have been several procedural lapses which violated Rule 14 of the IT Rules, 2021..the Petitioners were not served with any notice…never afforded an opportunity to submit a response/defend themselves…provided with a copy of the blocking order…[the takedown] directly affected [the petitioners] right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution,” the report read.
On September 10, the reel was restored. Yousaf found out through a notification this time, that the restriction was lifted as the “local legal requirement or government request that has now expired or been reversed” — similar to Vanguru’s case.
Local Influencers, HRF Silenced
In the same vein, several local influencers reported that their reels critical of the data centres were being arbitrarily taken down. Malla Gnanesh, who runs the page @vizag_blogger, told News Meter, that a reel he posted on May 28 titled ‘Vizag Welcoming Google Data Centre — At What Cost?’ was restricted in India on May 31. In the reel, Gnanesh spoke about the massive loss of green cover due to the construction of the data centre at the Adavivaram-Mudasarlova region.
Another account, @vizagmowa, also posted a reel on the negative environmental impact of the same data centre such as massive deforestation and water depletion due to its proximity to the Mudasarlova reservoir. This reel was withheld in India on May 30 with the same Section 79(3)(b) notification. Both reels remain restricted till date.
Human Rights Forum on June 1 published a statement condemning the rampant restrictions. Four of HRF’s own Instagram posts were blocked in India on May 31 and June 25, again under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act.
Speaking to Alt News, Vijayawada state coordinator of HRF, Rohith Gutta, stated: “We have moved the Andhra Pradesh high court with a writ petition against the unlawful restriction on September 28, demanding the blocking order, the reason for the action and the immediate restoration of our posts,” he said.

He mentioned that all four posts were critical of the date centre expansion. The two posts blocked on May 31 publicised an online petition seeking transparency and accountability regarding the proposed data centre projects; demanded an immediate stoppage of all ongoing site activities at the proposed sites in Adavivaram and Mudasarlova villages of Visakhapatnam Rural mandal.
The next two blocked on June 25 showed a protest in the city against the construction of all three data centres; questioned how the Adavivaram data centre received environmental clearance despite being located within an ESZ, close to the Mudasarlova reservoir. One of the these posts directly asked: “Should a Resource-Guzzling, Intensely Polluting Data Center be Located near a Reservoir? On its Catchment?”
“The restrictions imposed on HRF content by Instagram do not appear to be isolated incidents but form part of a broader pattern,” the Forum wrote while highlighting the restrictions imposed on Yousaf and Jha’s work with the ERC. The Forum also put out another statement condemning the restriction of the Stop Vizag Data Centers account.
Speaking about the ordeal, Rohith told Alt News, “The restrictions have not deterred us from speaking up against the data centres, however, it is a painful experience. We received no prior notification all four times and when we searched for the reason, it was only a vague message repeated word for word four times. It feels like you are legally violated because your work is banned without explanation. Now, blocking of posts is akin to being arrested digitally. We are living through times of ‘social media arrest’ and they [the authorities] have blocked all means to fight it.”
Alt News has reached out to Meta’s grievance officer in India and Kumar Vishwajeet, the principal secretary, home, Andhra Pradesh government. This article will be updated if and when we receive a response.
It is worth noting that the opposition to the projects has also spilled onto the streets, with residents, activists and environmental groups staging protests in Visakhapatnam over concerns around water consumption, deforestation, displacement and the environmental impact of the projects.

While the funding trends in the Indian startup ecosystem have been showing signs of stability over the past few months, investor appetite for startups operating across different sectors and stages is varying significantly. Although Indian startup funding in the July-September quarter increased 5% YoY to $2.2 Bn across 210 deals, the startup investment story is increasingly turning into one of growth stage capital rather than late stage backing. As per Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report Q3 2026, capital deployed at the growth stage jumped 46% YoY to $1.1 Bn during the quarter. Meanwhile, funding lapped by late stage startups remained flat at $994 Mn. Beyond the headline funding numbers, investors seemed to be more active in evaluating startups at the Series B and C stages as compared to late stage ones. During the quarter, growth stage deal count rose 38% to YoY 90, whereas late stage deals declined 10% to 27. The divergence is also visible in cheque sizes. The median growth stage ticket size rose 4% to $8.3 Mn, while the median late stage check dropped 18% to $18 Mn. The data points to a funding market where capital is flowing more readily into startups that still have substantial growth ahead, while investors are becoming more cautious about committing large sums to mature startups. Investors highlighted a combination of factors behind this shift, including a growing pool of early stage capital, more inflated valuations at the late stage, greater scrutiny of business fundamentals and exit visibility, and a changing sector thesis. Why More Capital Is Flowing Into Growth Stage Startups One explanation lies in the expansion of India’s startup ecosystem, which now comprises about 2.5 Lakh businesses. A growing pool of investors backing startups at their earliest stages is creating a larger pipeline of businesses seeking subsequent rounds. Vikram Gupta, founder and managing partner at IvyCap Ventures, said the number of early stage and micro VC funds in India has increased substantially, helping create this pipeline of capital as startups progress towards Series A and Series B rounds. “If the number of early stage funds has increased, very naturally you will see a growth in the early to growth stage investments,” Gupta said. The changing sector mix is also reinforcing this trend, with investor interest broadening beyond ecommerce, fintech and consumer internet startups towards frontier technologies such as AI, deeptech and cleantech. AI emerged as the top funded sector in Q3 with $438 Mn, up 265% YoY, followed by cleantech at $433 Mn, up 267%, and deeptech at $290 Mn, up 176%. In contrast, fintech funding declined 11% and ecommerce funding fell 31%. The quarter also saw some of the largest funding rounds concentrated in these newer categories. AI startup Emergent raised $130 Mn, EV startup River raised $120 Mn and spacetech startup Pixxel raised $100 Mn. Gupta said the newer sectors — AI, spacetech, EVs — have longer gestation periods, meaning investors often wait for technology validation, customer adoption and other milestones before committing larger sums. However, the growth of these newer segments doesn’t necessarily translate into investors shying away from more established segments like fintech, ecommerce or consumer companies, said Apoorva Ranjan Sharma, cofounder of Venture Catalysts. “Those are now more mature sectors and investors expect stronger numbers from them.” Why Late Stage Capital Pool Remains Thin Even as more startups reach the growth stage, the pool of investors capable of funding them at scale remains relatively small. IvyCap's Gupta believes that India has a limited number of investors capable of writing large late stage cheques. Prior to the funding winter, India's late stage ecosystem relied heavily on global investors such as SoftBank, Tiger Global, Insight Partners and Sequoia Capital, which were among the most active sources of large growth stage cheques. “The larger dollar capital comes from the US and other geographies,” Gupta said, adding that changes in US policies and market conditions have made overseas deployment more difficult. He said US government securities have also become more attractive as a lower-risk investment, making it harder for funds to raise and deploy capital in markets such as India. While family offices, high-net-worth individuals and government-backed funds have stepped in to bridge some of the gap, Gupta said India would need at least $100 Bn of capital to become globally competitive. This has created a funding asymmetry. India now has a growing base of early stage investors backing startups through initial rounds, but a much smaller pool of capital available when those companies need substantially larger cheques to scale further. Why Late Stage Investors Are Holding Back The availability of capital is only part of the problem. Investors active at the late stage are also becoming more selective. According to Venture Catalysts’ Sharma, Series A and B investors can assess a startup's product, revenues, customers and execution while the business still has significant room to grow. By Series C and beyond, valuations are substantially higher, leaving investors with less room for error and making the potential return harder to justify. Several startups that raised capital at high valuations in earlier rounds are still working to deliver the business performance needed to justify the premiums, Gupta said. This is particularly relevant for deeptech companies, where technology development and commercialisation may take longer. “If an investor is putting in $30-50 Mn, there has to be a clear plan for how that money will be used and what the company will achieve,” Sharma said. “Growth continues to be important, but growth alone is no longer enough.” The shift is also changing how late stage rounds are structured. Gupta said investors may commit less capital upfront and release additional funds only when startups meet specific milestones. An investor capable of writing a $25 Mn cheque, for instance, could invest $15 Mn initially and reserve the remaining $10 Mn for a later tranche. Similar structures of investment deals are also seen at early and growth stages as well. For instance, Fireside Ventures committed ₹100 Cr capital to Arovia Consumer, a new ecommerce rollup venture by ex-Soulfull MD Prashant Parameswaran, with investments flowing as and when the startup closes acquisitions. Founders, meanwhile, are becoming more cautious about dilution and raising only what they need, Sharma said. What Could Unlock The Next Funding Wave? The current funding mix could eventually help narrow the late stage gap. The startups attracting Series A and B capital today — particularly in AI, deeptech, climate and manufacturing — could become a larger pipeline of companies seeking Series C, D and pre-IPO funding as they prove their technology, build markets and demonstrate commercial traction. Gupta said AI-funded companies are now entering a phase where investors will be able to assess how much of the sector's promise translates into actual business performance. Some could emerge as major winners, while others may struggle to justify their valuations. Deeptech companies are also moving towards commercialisation, with recent public-market milestones providing investors with evidence that some of these businesses can scale beyond the venture stage. The bumper IPOs of SEDEMAC and ESDS Software Solution, along with Skyroot's progress towards its next funding round, point to a broader pipeline of deeptech companies moving towards larger capital requirements. The number of companies requiring late stage capital is also on the upward trajectory. Inc42's investor survey found that 72% of investors have late stage startups in their portfolios that are at some level of IPO readiness. But IPO readiness does not necessarily mean these companies will need another large private round. Sharma said mature startups can instead raise smaller amounts, facilitate secondary transactions or move towards public markets. Gupta said greater visibility on a public market exit can itself unlock late stage investor interest, as investors become more comfortable when a company has a clearer path to an IPO. Successful listings could therefore become an important catalyst for the next phase of late stage funding. Gupta expects more capital to return as investors see successful outcomes, while Sharma said stronger profitability, more realistic valuations and successful IPOs will be important for rebuilding confidence. The bigger question is whether the companies now raising Series A and B capital can build the scale, profitability and exit visibility needed to attract the much larger pools of capital required at Series C, pre-IPO and beyond. Xbox's new division will focus on TV and movie adaptations of its biggest franchises
Products and events will also be part of XP’s strategy.
A new division of Xbox called XP will focus on growing the fanbases of its various gaming properties through TV, film, products and events. Announced in a blog post written by Xbox's Chief Strategy Officer Matthew Ball, XP will seemingly play a significant role in the company's plan to become "the number one entertainment company in the world," and one that has set the lofty ambition of entertaining one billion people each and every day.
Microsoft hasn't paired this news with the announcement of any new movies or globetrotting concerts, but we do have a pretty good idea of how the new games-adjacent division will function. XP will be tasked with bringing Xbox's "worlds and characters to new audiences through film, television, and other forms of linear storytelling," as well as appealing to the existing Xbox community through "authentic" product launches, live events and attractions. The division will also seek to forge partnerships with creators and brands.
XP will be headed up by Kayleen Walters, who worked at Lucasfilm for 13 years before joining Microsoft and eventually becoming president of Minecraft studio Mojang. Walters also served as an executive producer on last year's box office-smashing (and notably not terrible) A Minecraft Movie, and is named as a producer on the upcoming sequel. A Minecraft theme park is set to open its doors in the UK next year, the promotion of which presumably now also falls within XP's remit.
Microsoft doubling down on its transmedia strategy isn't surprising when you consider its vast library of IP. The live-action Halo show may not have turned out as well as it would have liked, but Prime Video's Fallout has been a pretty big success, while an eventual Call of Duty movie was surely inevitable as soon as the ink was dry on the company's Activision acquisition.
According to The Hollywood Reporter, there are additional plans to adapt the likes of Gears of War, Candy Crush, Diablo, Forza and The Elder Scrolls in the future. Xbox also said it intends to collaborate with Kojima Productions on TV and film projects after swooping in to claim publishing rights for the Metal Gear Solid creator's upcoming action-espionage game, Physint, after Sony surprisingly let it go.

Is it better to buy or rent?
Try our calculator based on 2 decades of historical data
Buying a property is the largest purchase most Canadians will make in their lifetime. For many, it’s also their biggest investment. But strictly financially speaking, are you better off putting down a large down payment and facing higher monthly costs as an owner, or remaining a renter and investing your savings somewhere else? Who ends up with more money in their pocket at the end of the day?
Don't miss our simulator below. Keep reading to understand how to use it.
To answer this question, we analyzed over two decades of historical data on property prices, rents, inflation and interest rates across 22 Canadian metropolitan areas, alongside long-term stock market returns.
Using this data, we built an interactive simulator. Every time it runs, it calculates the monthly expenses and financial gains for three distinct paths: an owner with a fixed-rate mortgage, one with a variable-rate mortgage and a renter. Whenever the renter's monthly costs are lower than the homeowner's, those savings are automatically invested in stocks and bonds to compound over time.
The simulator projects these financial paths over a 25-year period across 1,000 unique scenarios. Some scenarios feature high rents and low interest rates; others simulate average inflation paired with weak stock market returns.
The calculations factor in mortgage payments, insurance, property taxes, maintenance costs, condo fees, rent and eventual selling fees. Every outcome represents a possible future based on historical patterns and the options you select.
Of course, no one can predict the future. This tool provides probabilities, not guarantees, and should not be used for major financial decisions. Below is a simplified version of our simulator. You can find a more comprehensive version with expanded options and a detailed methodology breakdown at the end of this article.
Home prices decline, while stocks surge
Our simulator is not perfect. The past is no guarantee of the future, and many macroeconomic factors are bound to change. Canada’s population is aging, the immigration outlook remains uncertain, an AI bubble could crash stock markets and countless variables continuously reshape the broader economy and housing markets.
Because comprehensive historical data is limited, our tool is based on the last 25 years, meaning it does not account for Canada's last major housing crash in the early 1990s. Several experts also pointed out that the cost of maintaining a property is often higher than estimated, especially when a roof starts to leak unexpectedly. Furthermore, realistically, few Canadians stay in the exact same home for a quarter-century.
A sandwich board is shown on a street on Quebec's unofficial moving day in Montreal on July 1. (Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press)
Still, home prices have been declining over the last few years, while interest rates, average property taxes and maintenance costs have increased.
Meanwhile, the stock market has been surging. An investment made in 2005 would be worth roughly seven times more today, compared to just three times more for a property bought at the same time.
Based on this, our calculations reveal a clear trend: If you rent an average studio or one-bedroom apartment and aggressively invest the cash you save by not owning a condo, you have a strong chance of pulling ahead.
But as soon as you step up to a two-bedroom apartment or larger, that math changes quickly. Rent prices swallow up the surplus, making it nearly impossible to save and invest meaningfully.
In fact, in many scenarios, the monthly cost of renting eventually eclipses the cost of owning. A homeowner's largest monthly expense is their mortgage, typically locked in for a five-year term. Adjusted for inflation, the real value of that payment actually decreases over time.
- Average asking rents fall 4.8% in August as trade war adds fresh uncertainty: report
- Why N.S. rents are still increasing far faster than we saw historically for decades
Rents, on the other hand, almost always rise, often outpacing general inflation. Eventually, the lines cross. The renter begins paying more per month than the owner, wiping out their monthly savings and halting any new investment contributions.
Location, of course, dictates everything. In some regions, owning a condo loses the least amount of money after all cumulative expenses, compared to renting a two bedroom or bigger. Buying and then selling a condo is not a guaranteed profit. Single-family houses or townhouses offer a higher probability of financial return, but they come with a much steeper upfront purchase price.
'2 housing crises in Canada'
Yet for millions of Canadians, this debate is purely theoretical, and renting is their only option. Half of all couples in the cities we analyzed do not earn enough to qualify for an average condo in the city they live in — a figure that jumps to two-thirds for a house.
The outlook is even starker for the growing demographic of single-income households. Most Canadians are forced to rent, even when doing so is the less financially advantageous path.
“I would argue there are two housing crises in Canada,” said Aled ab Iorwerth, deputy chief economist at the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC).
“One is the housing crisis for the middle class, affording a condo in places like Toronto, Vancouver and increasingly in Montreal, especially since the pandemic. But there's an affordability crisis as well for low-income Canadians, who really need help just finding a place to live.”
Affordability is one factor causing younger generations to live with their parents for longer, a May 2026 Statistics Canada study found. They also tend to settle on a career, form a family and buy property later in life, a phenomenon described as “life-stretching.” And when they do finally leave the family nest, they also typically live alone or with roommates more often than previous generations.
This purchasing delay observed among younger Canadian generations can have massive compounding consequences.
“Timing is everything,” said Jean-Philippe Deschamps-Laporte, assistant director of the Centre for Housing and Income Statistics at Statistics Canada, who was involved with the report. When younger generations buy their first property later in their life compared to their parents, this investment has less time to potentially bear fruit.
- Should you move back in with your parents? Does nothing beat a coupon?
- How Nova Scotia became one of Canada's most expensive rental markets
“Younger generations could face returns that are not what they would have had if they had been born earlier."
His own research has found that when people graduate during a recession, it carries consequences for the rest of their lives. The same logic applies to the housing and stock markets. If you are lucky, you buy when prices are low and sell when they are high. But more often than not, you do not really get to choose, he notes, as it depends entirely on your current life stage.
So, should you buy or should you rent?
“The calculations done here are very useful for a lot of Canadians, but the most important thing is to do some introspection on how much owning a home will actually improve your life,” said James Macek, assistant professor at the University of Alberta's School of Business.
Kiana Basiri, assistant professor at the Toronto Metropolitan University, had a similar sentiment.
“We are kind of pushing people toward ownership at the expense of them being tighter financially and less resilient, simply because they really want to own something," she said.
"We just assume ownership is the best way for people to accumulate wealth over time, but I feel we need more education for people on how they can invest their savings in different ways.”
Furthermore, when people move to the suburbs to find more affordable properties, they sometimes forget to factor in other costs, like maintaining two cars instead of paying for public transit.
As Jean-Pierre Lessard, an economist and partner at Aviseo Conseil, put it: “We are crazy about property ownership in Canada, but there is no link between a nation's economic growth and its homeownership rate.”
A key point he made during a talk in a May 2026 conference was that it’s possible for the average household in Quebec City and Montreal to build more wealth by remaining renters instead of becoming owners.
- Regina seniors, NDP call for rent control after increases at private retirement community
- Toronto board of trade urges province to reform housing regulations
“Originally, public policies to encourage buying were intended to stimulate construction. We've lost sight of that,” Lessard said. “We need to return to something more rational.”
In some nations, it is entirely normal to be a lifelong renter. Germany and Switzerland, for example, are famous for having populations where more than half of all residents rent, backed by robust regulations that cap rent increases and protect tenants' rights.
“Overall, we need to increase the supply of both homeownership and rental units quite significantly,” said ab Iorwerth. The challenge, he said, is to balance supply with measures that encourage homeownership, such as the first home savings account, which tend to push prices up, while simultaneously ensuring there is enough inventory to keep homes affordable.
In June 2025, the CMHC published a report projecting that around 250,000 new housing units would be started each year over the next decade, whereas twice as many are actually needed to restore affordability.
Methodology
The detailed data sets and calculations used can be found here. Our methodology was shared prior to publication with the experts quoted in the article above, and their suggestions helped inform the analysis.

25 years, many slogans: Modi's journey from 'Acche din' to 'We will do it'
The BJP’s spectacular win in the 2014 Lok Sabha elections was largely credited to Modi’s leadership, oratory and governance model in Gujarat.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi has coined a new slogan to give impetus to his ambitious plan for a developed India by 2047: "We will do it".
On Wednesday, he completed 25 years in public service and as head of government, first as the chief minister of Gujarat and since 2014, as the premier of India. To mark the occasion, he dwelt on the past, summarised the present, and came up with a catch phrase for the future.
The PM used the slogan to nudge people to take on the challenge of bringing about changes from the economy to the manufacturing sector. He also listed several sectors where India needs to be the leader – from artificial intelligence to the space sector, and from the environment to exports.
Deep Dive
After he was named as the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)’s prime ministerial candidate in 2013, his political journey from the state to the national capital was pivoted on the catchy “Abki baar Modi sarkar” (this time, a Modi government) and the hope-inducing “Acche din aane wale hain” (good days are coming) slogans.
The party’s spectacular win in the 2014 Lok Sabha elections was largely credited to Modi’s leadership, oratory and governance model in Gujarat. However, opponents also saw it as the victory of a Hindu nationalist sentiment fostered by the BJP and its ideological fount, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS).
Modi then came up with the slogan of “Sabka saath, sabka vikas” (together with all, development for all), which sought to instill a sense of confidence that the government would be egalitarian and non-discriminatory. He added “vishwas” (trust) to the slogan when he returned to power for his second term in office in 2019, winning with a bigger margin and number.
In its first tenure, the Modi government set itself the task of weeding out outdated laws, meeting deadlines for infrastructure development, and ushering in economic and social reforms. For this, it chose the slogan of “Minimum government, maximum governance”.
The underlying message was cutting the bureaucratic red tape.
He even relied on slogans and catchphrases to introduce and implement policy decisions. Take for instance, the "Swachh Bharat abhiyan", to drive home the need for cleanliness and sanitation or the "Make in India" tagline for giving impetus to indigenous manufacturing. To check the country’s gender imbalance and prevent female foeticide, the PM came up with the “Beti bachao, beti padhao” (Save the daughter, educate the daughter) campaign.
Key phrases and catchlines have now become central to his style.
The “Atmanirbhar Bharat” (Self-reliant India) and “Vocal for local” (to promote Indian made goods) taglines were used to deliver the message to cut down on imports and drive domestic manufacturing and consumption during challenges imposed by the global pandemic in 2020. These taglines were reinforced when the West Asia crisis caused havoc in supply chains and sent prices of crude, gas and other essentials skyrocketing.
Difficult political decisions that led to disagreements and disruptions in Parliament and sharpened the divisions between the political class were also padded with slogans. A case in point being the proposal to synchronise Lok Sabha and assembly elections, popularly known as “One Nation, One Election”.
As the third term nears completion, the PM who once referred to himself as the “chowkidar” (guard) and reassured the electorate with the “Modi hai toh mumkin hai” (Modi makes it possible) tagline, has now set the agenda for 2047.

Turning artificial intelligence research into real-world tools isn’t always straightforward, despite the remarkable progress in recent years ranging from self-driving cars to large language models. Systems that perform well in controlled lab settings often fall short when deployed in homes, in hospitals or on city streets.
Vision-based systems, for example, hold promise for improving safety, monitoring health and aiding rehabilitation. For example, a camera-based system could help a clinician assess a patient’s gait or rehabilitation progress.
In the future, an assistive robot in an older adult’s home might need to recognise when the person is struggling to stand or reaching for an object. But a major challenge is ensuring these robots perform reliably beyond the lab, particularly in messy, unpredictable or low-visibility conditions.
As a computer scientist who studies AI systems designed to understand human behavior – especially through visual cues like body movements and interactions with objects – I see three main challenges to taking AI from the lab to the real world: generalisation, human behavior and resources.
Challenge 1: The generalisation gap
Most AI vision systems are trained on well-lit, high-quality images, often from curated sources like motion capture studios or daytime recordings. But when these systems are deployed in real-world settings, such as in a dimly lit home, hospital room or nighttime street, they often struggle. This is not because the technology is flawed, but because the data used to train it cannot fully represent the enormous variability of the real world.
Take human pose estimation, for example. This task involves detecting key points on a person’s body, such as joints, to understand how they’re moving. The result resembles a digital skeleton that represents the positions of a person’s arms, legs and other body parts. Pose estimation has been studied for health and rehabilitation applications, including measuring a person’s gait, monitoring rehabilitation exercises and assessing movement patterns associated with the risk of falling. In well-lit environments, modern AI models do this with impressive accuracy. But in low or uneven lighting, performance can drop sharply. That’s because the model has learned from clean, consistent data and isn’t prepared to generalise to tougher conditions.
Would collecting more nighttime training data solve the problem? More labeled data would certainly help, but collecting it is especially difficult. When a person’s joints are hard to see in an image, they are also hard for a human annotator to label accurately. Low light can also obscure visual information rather than simply make an image darker, and nighttime conditions vary with cameras, shadows, glare and other sources of noise. Collecting and manually labeling examples that cover all these conditions is therefore difficult and expensive.
We’ve been working to close this gap by developing AI systems that perform better in low-light scenarios. One method we use is unsupervised domain adaptation, where a model trained on well-lit, labeled data is adapted to handle low-light settings, without needing manual body-joint labels for the low-light images. This helps bridge the “domain gap” between clean training data and the messier world where these systems are actually used.
In our 2026 study on low-light human pose estimation, we generated realistic low-light training images and designed the system to balance uncertain visual evidence with its learned knowledge of human body structure. The method substantially improved performance on two low-light benchmarks, although the broader challenge is far from solved.
Challenge 2: Human behavior
Another major hurdle is the sheer variety of human behaviors, especially when people interact with objects. In computer vision, this is known as human-object interaction detection. Teaching an AI system to recognise actions like cutting a tomato or passing a basketball requires not just object detection, but an understanding of context and intent.
The real challenge is scale. The number of objects is large, and the ways humans interact with them are even greater. You can sit on a chair, carry it, drag it or stack it. Each is a distinct interaction. A cup might be used for drinking, washing, pouring or handing something to another person. An assistive robot would need to distinguish among these actions to respond appropriately. It’s simply not feasible to collect and label data for every possible combination.
In my research, we study how an AI system can detect interactions it has never seen during training. Researchers call this a generalisation-to-unseen-classes problem, and it’s a key challenge for building models that don’t just memorise patterns, but can adapt to new situations. Our work has explored how foundation models can help recognise previously unseen interactions. In a more recent study, we used large vision-language models, models that combine computer vision and natural language processing, to identify the parts of an object that support particular actions, without training the system on labeled examples for that specific task. This matters in areas like assistive robotics and safety monitoring, where AI needs to respond intelligently to behaviors it wasn’t specifically trained on.
This challenge is different from the low-light problem. In low-light pose estimation, the system is trying to recognise a familiar type of movement under unfamiliar environmental conditions. In human-object interaction detection, the action-and-object combination itself may be new. Both are generalisation problems, but they require different solutions.
Challenge 3: The resource gap
Even when researchers know how to make models more robust, applying those improvements isn’t always easy, especially in academic or smaller research settings. Today’s most powerful AI systems depend on massive computational resources in the form of data centers that contain huge numbers of specialised computer chips.
These are often too expensive for university labs or public-sector researchers, and the computing power needed to train leading models has continued to rise. According to the 2026 AI Index Report, the technology industry produced more than 90% of the notable AI models introduced in 2025.
At the same time, a model developed using large computing clusters may ultimately need to operate in a clinic, school, robot or home device, which means running on much smaller hardware. Such systems may also need to respond quickly without continuously sending sensitive data to the cloud. This mismatch creates a widening gap between what’s possible in theory and what’s practical in deployment. Bridging that gap requires not just better models, but more efficient algorithms and open-source tools that broaden access to advanced AI.
Why it matters
These challenges aren’t just academic. They affect how and whether AI tools can be trusted in the real world. Imagine a fall-detection system that fails at night, a workplace safety monitor that misses a crucial action or a robot that misunderstands what a person is doing because it’s never seen that exact interaction before. These aren’t just minor bugs – they’re breakdowns in trust, usability and sometimes even safety.
AI systems are being deployed in homes, hospitals, factories, vehicles and other everyday environments. If they can’t adapt to different environments or recognise new human behaviors, their usefulness becomes limited and their risks amplified. That’s why researchers are increasingly focusing not just on accuracy in ideal conditions, but on robustness, generalisation and real-world readiness.
Looking ahead: Closing the gap
Closing the gap between lab-trained AI models and messy, unpredictable real-world environments won’t happen overnight, but it’s possible. In my research, we’ve explored techniques like using augmented data to simulate challenging conditions and help models adapt. We’ve also worked on enabling AI systems to better generalise to new, unseen situations by using knowledge from foundation models to distinguish unfamiliar interactions from similar ones encountered during training.
Ultimately, I believe that making AI systems more reliable in everyday settings is a challenge worth solving, not just to improve gadgets and apps, but because AI has the potential to support human well-being, whether that means safer streets, smarter healthcare or more secure homes.
Bo Wang, assistant professor of Computer and Information Science, University of Mississippi

Haaland tells embattled Man City fans to 'stick together'
MANCHESTER, England, Oct 8 : Manchester City striker Erling Haaland urged the embattled club's supporters to stick together in his first public comments since City were found guilty of more than 100 charges relating to breaches of Premier League financial rules.
City have appealed against the independent commission’s verdict, insisting the judgment contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact."
Asked what his message was to supporters ahead of what should be a combustible Premier League match at Liverpool on Sunday, Haaland called for unity and positivity amid the off-field turmoil.
"We have to stick together. We have to stay with each other, and we have to stay positive," the Norway striker told Sky Sports. "No matter what happens in life, we always have to have a smile.
"So we have to stay positive, look ahead, and try to win football games and try to enjoy the situation and win the game.
"We have to stick together; we have to spread the love to each other. So yeah: stick together, and enjoy the ride and smile."
The independent commission found that City arranged "sham" contracts with several commercial partners as part of what it described as a "disguised funding scheme" that artificially inflated the club's revenues and reduced its costs by more than 900 million pounds ($1.19 billion).
The charges spanned nearly a decade.
Haaland, whose father Alf-Inge also played for City, said his connection to the club and the UK in general extended beyond playing for Enzo Maresca's side.
"I care a lot about this place, and the UK generally, I care a lot about the fans because I'm a fan myself, and I feel with them as well," he said.
City take a three-point lead atop the table to Anfield on Sunday to face opponents with whom they developed a fierce rivalry during Pep Guardiola's battles with former Liverpool manager Juergen Klopp.
"It's always special to play against Liverpool," Haaland said. "Especially with Pep and Klopp. I remember sitting and watching the games (before signing with City), how much they pushed each other. It's always special games there.
"I won there, I drew there, I lost. So it's always special, and every Premier League game is different, and every game against Liverpool is always special."

A video of Israel’s opposition leader Yair Lapid is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows him criticising Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for allegedly using the 2026 Flydubai incident to build an election narrative, which he compares to Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s handling of the 2019 Pulwama attack.
In the video, Lapid can allegedly be heard saying, “Netanyahu is taking a page from Modi’s political playbook. In India, Modi used the 2019 Pulwama attack as an election campaign to frame a political narrative against Pakistan. Now in Israel, Netanyahu is using the Flydubai incident in the same way, turning a security crisis into an election narrative while diverting attention from the devastation in Gaza. Modi had his motherland election; Netanyahu has his fatherland election.” Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Yair Lapid accusing Netanyahu of using the 2026 Flydubai incident for political gains, comparing it to Modi’s use of the 2019 Pulwama attack.
Fact: The video is digitally manipulated. The original footage shows Yair Lapid criticising Benjamin Netanyahu over his handling of the Iran conflict and the US-Iran ceasefire. Lapid does not mention the Flydubai incident, Narendra Modi, or the 2019 Pulwama attack, nor does he accuse Netanyahu of using the incident for electoral gains. AI detection tools also indicated that the audio is likely manipulated. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to an extended version published on the Al Jazeera English YouTube channel on 09 April 2026, titled “Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid slams Netanyahu for ‘total failure’ in Iran.” In the video, Lapid criticises Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over his handling of Iran, accusing him of misleading the public and turning a potential military success into a political disaster. He also says that Iran’s government had not been defeated, the nuclear threat remained, and Israel had no influence over the ceasefire deal. However, Lapid does not mention Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi or the 2019 Pulwama attack anywhere in the original video, indicating that the audio in the viral clip has been added or altered.
We also found a transcript of Yair Lapid’s televised address from 08 April 2026, published by The Times of Israel, while Reuters also published video footage containing excerpts from the speech. Lapid said that although the Israeli military had performed exceptionally well, Netanyahu had turned the military achievement into a “diplomatic disaster” because of poor planning and a lack of diplomatic strategy. He said Israel had no influence over the US-Iran ceasefire agreement and argued that Iran’s nuclear and missile threats had not been eliminated. Lapid also accused Netanyahu of misleading the Israeli public and damaging relations with the United States, arguing that Israel had achieved a military success but suffered a diplomatic setback. Nowhere in the transcript did we find that he criticised Benjamin Netanyahu over the Flydubai incident, accused him of using it to build an election narrative, or compared the incident to Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s handling of the 2019 Pulwama attack.
We then analysed the viral video using multiple AI voice detection tools, including Hive and Hiya. The analysis indicated that the audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated. This suggests that the original footage was paired with fabricated audio to make it appear that Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid was accusing Netanyahu of using the Flydubai incident for political gains and comparing it to Modi’s handling of the Pulwama attack.
However, Yair Lapid accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of “fear-mongering” after warning that the country’s enemies may attack before the October 2026 general election, following the flydubai incident.
To sum up, this viral video of Yair Lapid allegedly saying PM Modi used the Pulwama attack to build an election narrative is AI-manipulated.

Punjab CBI probe: SC puts off state’s plea, declines interim order
The case has unfolded against a charged political backdrop in Punjab, with assembly polls due early next year and the Mann government alleging CBI and ED action is politically motivated targeting
The Supreme Court on Thursday deferred by a day the Punjab government’s challenge to a high court order directing the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) to register a criminal case into alleged corruption linked to chief minister Bhagwant Mann’s office, refusing to pass any interim order against the probe without first allowing both judges on the bench to examine the matter.
A bench of justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu agreed to hear the matter on Friday after senior counsel Vikas Singh, appearing for the Punjab government, pointed out the urgency and sought an interim direction that the CBI and Enforcement Directorate (ED) “may not precipitate the matter”.
Justice Datta, however, made it clear that such an order could not be passed without Justice Nagu having an opportunity to peruse the petition. “How can we pass this order when the file did not reach the other judge,” Justice Datta told Singh.
Deep Dive
The bench was told that the case file had not reached Justice Nagu, who was sitting as the puisne judge on the bench, in time. Singh agreed to the deferment to enable Justice Nagu to go through the state government’s challenge but pressed for the matter to be taken up at the earliest.
Justice Datta, who was heading the bench, then agreed to list the matter on Friday.

Singh also raised a possible issue concerning Justice Nagu’s participation in the case, pointing out that the judge, while serving as chief justice of the Punjab and Haryana high court, had dealt with some matters concerning the petitioners in the Supreme Court case -- Punjab director general of police Gaurav Yadav and the chief director. Singh clarified that those proceedings were unrelated to the present case.
Justice Nagu said he would need to examine the file before taking a call on whether he could hear the matter.
The case has unfolded against a charged political backdrop in Punjab, with assembly elections due early next year and the Mann government alleging that the CBI and ED action is politically motivated targeting by the BJP.
The development came a day after the CBI’s first steps under the high court’s October 5 order, including searches at eight locations across Punjab and the summoning of Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann’s officer on special duty (OSD), Rajbir Singh Ghuman, and five others in the corruption case.
Ghuman and the five co-accused did not appear before the CBI at its Chandigarh office on Wednesday. While the chief minister’s office said Ghuman had not been formally served the summons, sources indicated that the accused had also held off on appearing while awaiting the Supreme Court’s consideration of the Punjab government’s plea.
The CBI registered a 251-page FIR around midnight on October 5, naming Ghuman, alleged middleman Nitin Gohal, his brother Jitin Gohal alias Raja, Romi Raja Mahajan, Bir Devinder and RS Nagra. The agency has alleged that the accused operated an organised network to manipulate IAS and IPS postings, departmental proceedings, policy formulation, administrative approvals, tenders, licensing, arms licences and land-use conversions in return for bribes. The agency also alleged that unreleased government notifications and internal draft policies were leaked to private beneficiaries.
The case originated in three communications sent by the ED to Punjab DGP Gaurav Yadav between July 24 and August 12, raising allegations of corruption involving Ghuman and others. The ED had alleged that Gohal acted as an intermediary between people seeking favours from the state government and Ghuman, including for transfers and postings of officials, government approvals and arms licences.
The Punjab and Haryana high court, while directing the CBI to register an FIR and investigate the allegations, had said the material supplied by the ED prima facie indicated the involvement of senior public officials. It had also criticised the Punjab Police for failing to act on the ED inputs and directed the state authorities to extend full cooperation to the central agency.
The high court’s order followed a public interest litigation by advocate Nikhil Saraf, who alleged that the state authorities had failed to act on the ED’s communications despite the seriousness of the allegations. The court directed the CBI to submit an investigation report within two months.
The Punjab government approached the Supreme Court within hours of the high court order, arguing that the direction to register a CBI case was issued without sufficient material to establish a cognisable offence and raised serious questions concerning the federal structure.
When the matter was mentioned before Chief Justice of India Surya Kant on Tuesday, senior counsel Vikas Singh sought an immediate hearing and argued that the high court had ordered a CBI inquiry against state government officers without adequate material. The CJI declined to hear it the same day but said the matter would be accommodated on Wednesday or Thursday.
The CBI subsequently carried out searches at Ghuman’s official residence in Sector 2, Chandigarh, which was being used as a camp office, and his ancestral home at Gharachon in Sangrur district, besides six other locations. Electronic devices, including laptops and mobile phones, as well as financial and administrative documents were seized, according to officials.
The raids also triggered a political controversy after villagers and local opposition workers reportedly showered the CBI team with flower petals and distributed sweets during the search at Ghuman’s residence. The state government has alleged that central agencies were being used by the BJP to target the Mann government ahead of the Punjab assembly elections.
The CBI has clarified that its search was conducted at a residence used by the chief minister’s OSD and not at the Punjab chief minister’s Secretariat.

When The Social Network hit theaters in 2010, it was fair to wonder if the film had come too soon. Facebook had been launched from Mark Zuckerberg’s Harvard dorm room just six years earlier, and nobody really knew how it would reshape digital community in the decade to come.
But, with a breakneck screenplay by Aaron Sorkin, a menacingly propulsive soundtrack by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross, and a surgical performance from Jesse Eisenberg as Young Zuck, director David Fincher delivered a slick corporate thriller about the major drama to that point: intersecting lawsuits over who owned what percentage of the platform and who could lay claim as a founder. It was an electrifying film that seemed to only lightly fictionalize the newest and perhaps most cutthroat generation of Silicon Valley warlords.
Flash forward 16 years, and Facebook (now Meta) has accumulated more scandals than Hollywood could possibly hope to keep up with. Sorkin tells WIRED that he was approached many times over those years with pitches for a sequel, though he struggled to see an angle of approach. “Before a film can be anything else, before it can be relevant or thought-provoking, it has to be good,” he says. “It has to work as something that you watch while you're eating popcorn.”
Then, Sorkin says, he met Frances Haugen, the former Facebook data engineer who leaked damning internal memos to investigative reporter Jeff Horwitz. Horwitz wrote up what became known as the “Facebook Files” in a far-ranging 2021 series of articles for The Wall Street Journal, exposing much of what the company knew regarding harms to users—everything from hate speech and medical misinformation to body image issues and human trafficking—but had largely brushed aside in pursuit of growth.
Sorkin still wasn’t sure he had a film, but one day he asked Haugen why she finally decided to go to the media. “She just told me in kind of an offhand way, ‘Oh, I had this friend who was radicalized by Facebook after spending too many hours on the platform,’” he recalls. “And I began to get the idea for what is now the opening scene of the movie.”
The cold open of The Social Reckoning, written and directed by Sorkin, depicts an intoxicated woman pulled over on the side of the road in San Mateo, California, with an overheated car. Approached by police officers, she turns combative, pulling out her phone to record a video as she hurls racist abuse at the cops and is at last arrested for threatening to kill one of them. The video turns up on a Facebook page for far-right content, which is where Haugen (Mikey Madison) finds it in 2019, recognizing the woman as an acquaintance from her pilates class who used to hold progressive views. She also learns that this woman is a superuser, intensely active on Facebook for many hours each day.
Haugen first tries to get her colleagues at Facebook to recognize how their own algorithms are pushing many users, including her former friend, into extremist feeds. It’s only when she hits enough walls that she puts her tentative trust in Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White), a journalist whom Facebook staff have been explicitly warned not to speak to. As they develop the bickering rapport of two focused professionals with clashing ideals—Haugen wants to save the company from itself, while Horwitz suspects it’s too late for that—we see flash-forwards of Zuckerberg (Jeremy Strong) rehearsing for a congressional hearing on social media misinformation in 2021. In the room are a crisis PR adviser named Raya (Wunmi Mosaku) and Charlie (Bill Burr), a composite ex-employee (as in, not specifically based on any living individual). He’s been brought in as an agitator with the freedom to get under Zuck’s skin and dismantle his practiced talking points.
This plot structure is clunkier than the cross-cutting depositions of The Social Network, which neatly allowed for the characters to recount the early days of Facebook without narrative hand-holding. By comparison, The Social Reckoning is clogged with portentous intertitles (the first sequence is even labeled a “prologue”) and visual cues to remind us where we are in the timeline. From scene to scene, the sharp-edged performances and familiar crackle of Sorkinese dialog (which leaves room for the occasional and delightfully odd non sequitur) make for engaging fare. But the pieces fit together awkwardly—and you do wish Reznor and Ross were around to boost the momentum.
The movie arrives as part of a crowded slate of keenly anticipated tech films. There’s Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s satire about the firing and rehiring of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman in 2023; it picked up significant buzz as Amazon MGM dropped it this summer following a $50 billion deal between Amazon and OpenAI. Alex Gibney’s epic documentary Musk covers the exploits of the world’s richest man up through his disastrous reign as a “government efficiency” czar in the White House. And don’t forget You Can See Everything, for which directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim gained close access to Theranos founder and convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes shortly before she began serving a decade-long prison sentence.
Amid these timely offerings, The Social Reckoning is a just touch out of step. Its climax (spoiler alert) is the January 6 Capitol riot, the horrors of which are blamed in part on Facebook’s failure to either get a handle on election fraud conspiracy theories or remove Donald Trump’s account as he stoked such inflammatory falsehoods. Now, halfway into Trump’s second term, is it all that much of a revelation that he and his movement are emboldened by the complicity of tech oligarchs, who openly backed him in 2024?
Nevertheless, there are big issues at play here. The debate over ethics in tech continually boils over into agonizing questions of how truth is negotiated and who gets the last word on it.
Whether you find Reckoning to be a worthy interrogation of this stuff will probably depend on your appetite for what amounts to a mashup of The Newsroom and The West Wing. There are mic-drop moments that plainly invite the audience to “lib out,” such as when Haugen accuses Horwitz of bias against tech because it’s stealing journalists’ jobs and he fires back that it’s actually because “you are so bad at it.” Or when Zuckerberg taunts his traitorous former friend Charlie for cashing out his Facebook stake for $200 million instead of holding on until it was worth $1.3 billion, and he counters by torching the presumption that he’s “supposed to be embarrassed by that.”
“I love that line, because that is the disease,” Burr tells WIRED. “What you're seeing with these robber baron nerds that are out there right now is the way somebody is addicted to methamphetamine, they are addicted to money. They literally cannot have enough. They are insatiable. They behave like addicts. And an addict will do whatever they have to do, hurt whoever they have to, to get that next fix.”
There is a definite satisfaction to seeing Burr, a caustic stand-up comedian, stick this observation directly into Zuckerberg’s craw. On the other hand, it’s a little naive to imagine that it stings a guy expanding his massive top-secret Hawaii compound to include ancestral burial grounds. In so many ways, Reckoning attempts to shame a ruling class that has proved itself, well, shameless.
At its best, then, the film may serve to underscore Haugen’s bravery in turning whistleblower while capably illustrating the difficulty and dangers of mounting an exposé on a Silicon Valley behemoth. It reminds us that there is always something else these tech firms are concealing. Both Madison and White tell WIRED that Sorkin’s screenplay jolted their understanding of the forces at work in the industry.
“I had an inkling about certain things, but then to be confronted with the real statistics and facts—that really confirmed how I was already feeling about social media as a whole and some of the negative effects it can have on people,” Madison says. White adds that people shouldn’t give companies like Meta the benefit of the doubt when something goes wrong. “What you find out in watching this film is, there's a business model, there's a plan, there's engagement,” he says. “They're hyper-aware of exactly what's happening, and they still choose to put their foot on the gas.”
Though as to an actual “reckoning” with this reality, the title may have been an overpromise. The movie’s postscript notes that millions of Americans still get news from Facebook and that in 2025, Meta ended its fact-checking program, opting instead to solicit crowdsourced context notes from users. It’s a downbeat conclusion after Haugen and Horwitz have beaten the odds to drag countless dirty secrets into the light. You wish you could walk away from The Social Reckoning with a sense that this forever changed Facebook, or Zuckerberg, or the internet itself, yet it’s hard to avoid noticing that everyone got away with it.

Former senior Flipkart executives, including Flipkart’s former CEO Mukesh Bansal, former CFO Sanjay Baweja and former chief business officer Ankit Nagori, have reportedly urged Walmart to buyback their vested employee stock options (ESOPs) amid uncertainty over the ecommerce major’s public listing plans. Cadillac driver Valtteri Bottas says he was chased by a dog, saw snakes and leapt over a lizard as he cycled from Malaysia to Singapore for this weekend's Grand Prix.
The Finnish driver arrived in Singapore on Wednesday after choosing a 260-mile (419km) bike ride over a flight from last weekend's Formula 1 race in Sepang, outside the Malaysian capital of Kuala Lumpur.

WTO hikes 2026 trade growth forecast on AI boom
GENEVA: The WTO on Thursday (Oct 8) sharply raised its global trade growth forecast for 2026, with merchandise trade riding the AI boom and proving more resilient than expected amid the Middle East crisis.
Thanks to supply chain adaptations and the surge in artificial intelligence investments, the World Trade Organisation now projects 3.9 per cent growth in the volume of merchandise trade this year, up from 1.9 per cent predicted in March.
The WTO is forecasting 4.1 per cent trade growth next year, up from the 2.6 per cent predicted seven months ago.
Global GDP is expected to grow by 2.6 per cent this year and 2.9 per cent in 2027, it added.
"The numbers reflect trade resilience in action," said WTO chief Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala.
"When disruptions strike, an integrated world economy and a rules-based trading system provide economies flexibility to keep essential products flowing to businesses and households that need them," she said.
"Nevertheless, some have felt the shock more than others, and not everyone can access emerging opportunities like AI."
AI OFFSETS IRAN WAR
The WTO said that while disruptions of shipments through the Strait of Hormuz had reduced energy supplies and raised prices of key energy products and fertilisers, most economies outside of the region had remained resilient. 
It said supply chains had successfully adapted to disruptions in the energy, fertiliser and transport markets caused by the Iran war. 
Merchandise trade grew by 3.5 per cent in the first half of 2026, exceeding WTO expectations.
Global crude oil exports fell by only about six per cent, and liquefied natural gas exports dropped by one per cent.
Meanwhile global container traffic actually increased by 3.9 per cent during the first seven months of 2026.
And strong demand linked to AI investment "more than offset the negative effects" of the conflict.
Increased spending on semiconductors, data centres and digital infrastructure raised demand for imported AI-enabling goods, providing a significant boost to global goods trade.
Trade in semiconductors, servers and other equipment essential to AI surged by 67 per cent year-on-year in the first half of 2026.
That alone accounted for 47 per cent of global merchandise trade growth, accelerating an expansion trend that was already robust in 2024 and 2025, the WTO said.
WTO chief economist Robert Staiger told reporters the organisation was "surprised" that the Middle East conflict did not reduce trade as much as had been feared, and likewise "surprised in the strength of the AI investment boom".
"But any slowdown in AI investment could precipitate a slowdown in trade," he warned.
Global spending on AI infrastructure is expected to rise at least 30 per cent this year, and current market forecasts suggest AI capital expenditure will continue to rise by a further 10 to 20 per cent in 2027.
Trade in AI-enabling goods has evolved in two years from a component of merchandise trade to one of its main drivers, the WTO said.
"The expansion is rapid, sustained and very concentrated: a small number of East and Southeast Asian economies supply these goods, while North America is driving demand."
MIDDLE EAST EXPORTS HIT
However, the Geneva-based organisation said trade resilience was not uniform, with services trade and some regions more exposed to the effects of the conflict.
In 2026, Asia is expected to record the fastest merchandise export growth (9.9 per cent), followed by North America (5.7 per cent).
Export performance is projected to remain weak in Europe, down 0.1 per cent, and to contract sharply in the Middle East, down 17.2 per cent.
WTO economists have lowered their forecasts for trade in services, though growth is nonetheless expected to remain positive.
