Like "being shot out of a cannon" is the closest comparison that driver Susanne Callin can come up with for the extreme motorsport she competes in.
She is a two-time European champion in Top Fuel drag racing - often described as the fastest sport on the planet.
Races begin with a bone-shaking roar, as the world's fastest-accelerating cars leave the starting line, flames bursting out of their exhaust pipes.
The cars surge to more than 300mph (483km/h) in races that last just four seconds, with drivers experiencing more g-force than an astronaut launching into space.
It is the only elite class of motorsport where women frequently beat men to major titles.
Women have won seven out of the past nine European Championships, while, until recently, female US driver Brittany Force held the world speed record in the sport. In comparison, it is 50 years since a woman even competed in a Formula 1 Grand Prix race.
Women account for about 10% of participants across motorsport, and just 4% of elite drivers, according to campaign group More Than Equal. However, they made up 20% of the drivers competing in this year's US and European Top Fuel seasons.
So why is this high-velocity motorsport bucking the trend?
More Than Equal has described drag racing as "the most gender-equal motorsport in the world". Top Fuel is its most extreme form, named in reference to the powerful nitromethane fuel the cars run on.
Races take place on a straight track, just 1,000 feet (305 metres) long. Usually, two cars race each other. The intense g-force hits in the first second of the race, as the cars go from stationary to 100mph, with a second gut punch following as the clutch fully engages about half-way through.
It can look terrifying. The adrenalin rush is "extremely addictive", Swedish driver Callin, aged 43, tells BBC Global Women. Concern over the risks "is always there" she says, but "the safety really does work". Drivers are highly protected and safety precautions have been boosted further after fatal crashes in nitromethane-fuelled cars in 2004 and 2008, with races reduced in length.
Even just watching from the stands is a visceral experience, with vibrations shaking your body and the ground. Spectators are advised to wear ear defenders - the noise is comparable in decibels to standing next to a fighter jet taking off.
The highest official speed ever reached in a Top Fuel drag race is over 346mph, compared to 231mph in a Formula 1 Grand Prix. Brakes alone cannot slow the cars fast enough, so parachutes are deployed from the car's rear at the finish. The abrupt halt is "like someone kicking you in the chest", says Callin. "You lose your breath."
Top Fuel drivers need lightning-fast reactions and the physical endurance to withstand the intense forces. Precision driving skills are crucial as constant tiny adjustments are needed to keep the car on track.
"It has to be instant reactions with everything," says Callin. "By the time you've thought about it, it's too late… You really have to be one with the car."
And drivers need sheer guts. As Callin's rival and friend, 32-year-old Swiss driver Jndia Erbacher, jokingly tells the BBC - it takes "balls".
Callin clinched her second successive European Top Fuel title in September at the Santa Pod drag strip near Northampton. It is the fourth year in a row that a female driver has won the title. Meanwhile in the US, the record-setting Brittany Force won the US championship - run by the National Hot Rod Association (NHRA) - in both 2017 and 2022.
Drag racing is "highly unusual" among motorsports, says Fran Longstaff, chief innovation officer at More Than Equal, which supports and campaigns for women in motorsports.
Seeing women competing and winning in the sport has become "normalised rather than treated as exceptional", she says, including with "sustained success" in Top Fuel.
Research she co-led into why drag racing leads the way for equality in motorsport did not identify physical or biological factors, she says.
Instead, she points to a "continuous stream of visible female role models", as well as the sport's "accessible grassroots structure, junior programmes, open pits and family-oriented, collaborative culture".
In drag racing, points out Callin, women started winning major races "decades and decades ago".
The best known is Shirley Muldowney, dubbed the "first lady" of drag racing. The first woman to gain a Top Fuel licence, Muldowney won the NHRA championship in 1977 and went on to become the first driver to win three titles, with further wins in 1980 and 1982.
She had to battle to be allowed to compete at high levels, and faced hostility at times from other competitors and fans, but is now lauded for her perseverance.
When the BBC spent time with Callin in the pits between races at Santa Pod, surrounded by roaring engines and the smell of burning rubber, she signed autographs for fans - young and old, male and female - as her team prepared her car.
"I never feel I've been underestimated or treated badly for being a woman - never," Callin says.
This is in stark contrast to the experiences of women seeking to enter Formula 1. Young female drivers have spoken about being deliberately pushed off karting tracks by male competitors, and facing sexist comments in person or online.
More Than Equal's research also highlights a close-knit, family-oriented, collaborative culture in drag racing.
Like many top drag racers, Callin is from a racing family. She has been involved since childhood, following in the footsteps of her father and uncle, who both raced competitively.
Similarly, Erbacher's father Urs was a three-time European Top Fuel champion. And Brittany Force is the daughter of John Force, who holds 16 NHRA drag racing titles.
The 300mph motorsport where women keep winning
Watch the full documentary following Susanne Callin as she bids to retain her European Top Fuel title
Female drivers have also shown that success is possible in Top Fuel in the years after having children.
Callin took a break for more than a decade to raise her daughter and stepdaughters. It was when she returned, aged 35, that her career really began to flourish. Similarly, Finnish driver Anita Mäkelä has won the European championship four times – three of them after a six-year break focusing on her children and running her family's chicken farm.
For Callin, racing is ingrained in family life.
Her dad is still part of her team. Her husband, Keith Bartlett - sometimes referred to as the "godfather" of UK drag racing - runs Santa Pod Raceway. Two of their daughters were driving junior dragsters at 80mph before they were old enough to sit a standard driving test. The youngest, Jacqueline, is now 19 and racing in adult classes.
The culture is collaborative, despite fierce competition - evident at last year's championship, when Erbacher offered Callin spare parts after her car was damaged.
"We hate each other at the starting line, but we love each other at the finish line," Erbacher says.
Asked about safety, both Callin and Erbacher talk about having "respect" for the car and the risks.
Over the years, strict procedures and regulations in Top Fuel have evolved to improve safety.
Drivers wear fire-resistant suits and sit in highly protected cockpits. Even after dramatic accidents, drivers in many cases escape relatively unscathed. This includes Callin, who has had two major crashes, suffering a concussion and a bruised collar bone, but no lasting injuries.
She says serious accidents are a "very small percentage". Even so, she is still not sure she would be comfortable if her daughter wanted to race in Top Fuel, with its extreme speeds.
Erbacher says her father initially refused to let her race, but relented when she declared she would do it with or without his help. He now manages her team.
More Than Equal also points out that the financial barriers to participating in drag racing are lower than for some other motorsports.
It takes millions of pounds to reach Formula 1, requiring high levels of sponsorship. Elite drag racing is also expensive, but not on the same scale. At the lowest levels, accessible racing events called "track days" take place, where participants can turn up and drive their own ordinary cars.
In the biggest Top Fuel championships, drivers race for themselves and earn points based on how they perform against their competitors. The European championship consists of four events - two in the UK, and one each in Germany and Sweden - in which each driver takes part in six races. Prize funds are limited, mostly serving as a contribution towards costs.
The US championship is on a larger scale, with 20 events across the country. The NHRA has not published a breakdown of prize money, but according to drag racing website Competition Plus, there is $500,000 (£378,000) for the 2026 winner, and significant pots for winners of individual events throughout the season.
The US, Europe and Australia have all seen female drag racing champions, but in other parts of the world, the sport is less well established, Top Fuel is rare and the picture is more varied. Individual women are breaking barriers across a range of different motorsports, and in some countries female drivers are carving out space in drag racing.
Women have begun to make an impact in Brazil's popular drag racing scene, including Fabiola Dal Bo who has held a category record in recent years. A team in South Africa hosts all-female drag races, while the popular reality TV show The Fastest in Arabic has raised the profile of women racers in the Middle East.
In India, 35-year-old Uvashri Kannadasan Balajeyanthi has clinched victories over male rivals in India's major drag racing series, Valley Run, with wins across three different categories in events from 2022 to 2024.
Known as Octy Girl in reference to the modified Skoda Octavia she first raced in, she tells the BBC she has "mixed feelings" when her achievements are met with surprise: "Why do they have to get shocked? Anyone can drive, right?" But she adds "sometimes I feel proud… I'm breaking the barrier of being in a male-dominated sport".
Back in Europe, however, Callin says being a woman on the drag strip is "super-normal".
She describes winning the European championship two years running as a "massive achievement". And she is already looking towards her next goal: becoming the first person, male or female, to win the title three years in a row.
- This is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe

The Directorate of Enforcement (ED), which is probing the alleged manipulation of the recruitment examination for 400 Veterinary Officer posts, has said the alleged modus operandi included leaking question papers and candidate-specific answer keys, and misusing the confidential 1:3 merit list to demand money from candidates.
The ED said certain candidates were allegedly provided the correct answer keys a day before the Veterinary Officers’ examination, on January 8, 2026, in return for bribes ranging from ₹20 lakh to ₹40 lakh.
Investigators allege that Karnataka Public Service Commission (KPSC) member B.V. Geetha obtained the leaked answer keys from Gyanendra Kumar Gangwar, IAS, then Controller of Examinations (CoE), KPSC, who was responsible for confidential examination material. Gangwar allegedly accessed the jumbled question papers and answer keys and provided Geetha with the correct answers to the first 80 questions.
The ED alleged that Geetha collected ₹20 lakh in cash as an advance from one candidate against an agreed bribe of ₹40 lakh, while Sahukar allegedly collected ₹10 lakh as an advance against an agreed ₹20 lakh bribe from another candidate.
So far, six candidates who secured high scores in the final selection list have been identified, with the ED saying further investigation is underway to identify all beneficiaries.
10 candidates taken to resort before exam
The ED had earlier seized blank signed cheques worth ₹80 lakh and blank signed promissory notes from one successful candidate.
Investigators also found that 10 successful candidates were allegedly taken to a resort on the outskirts of Bengaluru a day before the examination, where they were given a question paper containing the correct answer options for 80 questions and allegedly made to memorise them.
The ED alleged that the marked question paper was leaked by Gangwar through his close associate Basavaraj Kannale. Kannale allegedly collected ₹40 lakh to ₹50 lakh from each candidate in return for facilitating their final selection.
Gangwar and Kannale were arrested by the ED on September 18 and September 17, respectively, and were earlier remanded to ED custody for 14 days. Gangwar was subsequently sent to judicial custody.
Confidential 1:3 merit list allegedly exploited
The investigation has also revealed an alleged second method of extracting money from candidates.
The ED said KPSC normally does not disclose individual marks when publishing the 1:3 eligibility list. However, certain KPSC members and officials allegedly accessed confidential merit positions from the CoE’s office and assessed which candidates were likely to make the final selection.
The accused allegedly used this confidential information to approach candidates and assure them of selection in exchange for bribes ranging from ₹10 lakh to ₹50 lakh, depending on the post.
The ED said the misuse of confidential merit information was part of the mechanism for generating and handling proceeds of crime.

The 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to Henri Kagan and Kensō Soai for discovering a solution to the enigma of nature’s chemical asymmetry, a finding that opened up new avenues for manipulating the reactions used in manufacturing pharmaceuticals and other materials.
Some molecules are chiral, meaning a molecule has two forms that are mirror images of each other but not identical, like your left and right hand. One of the most mysterious chemical phenomena in biology is that living organisms contain almost exclusively one of the two forms. This is known as homochirality.
Both versions of the molecules—each called an enantiomer—have similar physical properties but can behave differently. The Nobel Committee used a simple analogy to explain this: A locksmith can create two mirror-image keys, but “only one of them fits the lock—and the lock can be damaged if your customers try to unlock it with the other key.”
In the development of new drugs that use, for example, amino acids or sugar molecules as a basis, homochirality poses a problem: While one of the enantiomers of these chiral molecules produces the desired therapeutic effect, the other can cause unnecessary and, at times, harmful side effects. Scientists can’t always easily control which version of the molecule they get out of their synthesis.
The discovery of chiral molecules dates back to the time of Pasteur, who found two enantiomers that reacted very differently when exposed to bacteria. Since then, various researchers have attempted to replicate homochirality in the laboratory with the goal of understanding its spontaneous origin and applying this knowledge to the design of controlled reactions for various purposes. However, early experiments yielded equal amounts of the two variants, failing to reproduce the selectivity observed in nature.
At the beginning of the last century, the German chemist Willy Marckwald designed an asymmetric reaction capable of producing a slightly greater amount of one of the two versions. He achieved this using a chiral catalyst—a substance that facilitates a chemical reaction without being consumed and favors the formation of one of the enantiomers. The ratio between the two variants, however, only changed a little.
Later, in 1953, theoretical physicist Charles Frank proposed a mathematical model that outlined three conditions for reproducing homochirality. First, there must be an asymmetric reaction capable of favoring one of the two versions; that imbalance has to be amplified; and the reaction itself has to produce the catalyst that drives it. This last characteristic is called autocatalysis and generates a kind of positive feedback loop, in which a small initial advantage can cause one of the variants to assemble at an ever-faster rate until it dominates the reaction.
This framework formed the basis of Henri Kagan’s research. Beginning in the early 1980s, he focused on refining asymmetric reactions through a detailed study of the catalyst. At that time, scientists typically used catalysts consisting of a metal atom that acted as the reaction’s driving force and a chiral substance that ensured the process was asymmetric. They assumed that if they used a mixture containing equal amounts of the two versions of that chiral molecule, the result would also be a balanced mixture.
Kagan began to question that idea. He realized that the metal atom likely did not interact with just one enantiomer but with both at the same time. This meant that, by mixing versions A and B, three different combinations could form: A-A, B-B, and B-A. The first two would produce molecules that were mirror images of each other. But the A-B combination could behave differently during the reaction.
The A-B combination, the scientist discovered, could slow down the reaction, indirectly favoring the formation of one of the two versions of the final molecule. The phenomenon was called the “nonlinear effect” and represented a new way to manipulate chemical reactions.
“In addition to their practical interest, nonlinear effects are a very valuable tool for studying reaction mechanisms and the nature of catalytically active species,” explained José María Andrés García, a professor in the Department of Organic Chemistry at the University of Valladolid, in a statement reported by SMC Spain.
Inspired by Kagan’s findings, Kensō Soai sought to create a reaction in which the product itself would act as a catalyst and help produce more molecules identical to itself—one of those theoretical conditions for the homochirality. He conducted a test with a substance known as 5-pyrimidylalkanol. At the beginning of the experiment, one version was just 2 percent more abundant than the other version of the molecule. By the end of the reaction, that advantage had jumped to 87 percent.
In the years that followed, Soai worked toward achieving reactions that resulted in the near-absolute purity of one enantiomer, replicating the molecular state inside living organisms. Finally, in 2003, he engineered a reaction in which the starting substances had no defined orientation, but as they reacted, a slightly greater amount of one enantiomer appeared by chance. That tiny difference then produced many more molecules of the same variant. Gradually, that form came to dominate the reaction, accounting for up to 99.99 percent of the final product.
In other words, the reaction formed only one of the two possible enantiomers. As the Nobel Committee stated, “Other than life itself, no one had previously achieved this feat.”

TP-Link is facing more legal troubles in the US as Florida and three other states filed lawsuits alleging that it lied to consumers about its connections to China and the risks of its routers being exploited by Chinese state hackers.
The lawsuits were filed yesterday, about six months after the Federal Communications Commission announced a sweeping ban on consumer-grade routers produced wholly or partly outside of the US. Numerous router makers have obtained exemptions to the ban, but the Trump administration so far has not granted one to TP-Link.
Router makers that received exemptions include Netgear, Asus, Adtran, Amazon and its Eero subsidiary, Calix, Nokia, SpaceX’s Starlink division, and others. For now, TP-Link is unable to sell its latest Wi-Fi 8 routers in the US, though models approved before the ban can still be sold.
The state lawsuits claim that TP-Link misled US consumers by telling them its routers are safe. The suits allege that TP-Link committed unfair and deceptive trade acts in violation of the states’ consumer protection laws.
“Chinese state-sponsored hackers exploited TP-Link routers sitting in American living rooms,” Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier said while announcing his lawsuit filed in a Florida county court. Uthmeier said Florida “will not allow families to be misled into handing their personal data to the Chinese Communist Party. We are seeking an injunction, restitution for Florida consumers, and [financial] penalties under Florida law.”
TP-Link criticizes coordinated lawsuits
TP-Link was founded in China but moved its headquarters to California in October 2024 amid investigations into high-profile attacks linked to the Chinese government, including a botnet composed mostly of TP-Link routers. The Florida lawsuit accuses TP-Link of “lying about the safety of its routers and its ties to the CCP,” Uthmeier said.
Uthmeier was one of four Republican state attorneys general to sue TP-Link yesterday. Lawsuits were also filed against TP-Link by Montana, Iowa, and Nebraska.
“The coordinated lawsuits are built on false premises,” said Steve Kovsky, TP-Link’s corporate affairs officer. “They do nothing to advance national security while unfairly penalizing an industry-leading US company.” TP-Link said that for the past few months it has “provided state regulators with clear, verifiable documentation demonstrating two fundamental facts: TP-Link Systems devices sold in the US are manufactured in Vietnam and TP-Link Systems is an independent, US company that is not owned or controlled by any foreign government.”

Op Sindoor showed how fast IAF can move into combat: Air chief
In the early hours of May 7, 2025, the IAF struck two terror sites at Markaz Subhanallah in Bahawalpur and Markaz Taiba near Muridke, both in Pakistan’s Punjab province
Air Chief Marshal AP Singh on Thursday said that last year’s four-day military confrontation with Pakistan under Operation Sindoor showed the world how swiftly the Indian Air Force (IAF) can move into combat, even as he underscored the central role of air power in safeguarding national interests.
“Last year, the whole world witnessed the speed with which the IAF moved into combat operations. We saw first-hand the destructive power as well as the effective air defence operations of the IAF during Operation Sindoor,” the Chief of Air Staff said in his IAF Day address at the Hindan air force station.
In the early hours of May 7, 2025, the IAF struck two terror sites at Markaz Subhanallah in Bahawalpur and Markaz Taiba near Muridke, both in Pakistan’s Punjab province, while the army hit targets at seven places, including Mehmoona Joya in Sialkot, Sawai Nala and Syed Na Bilal in Muzaffarabad, Gulpur and Abbas in Kotli, Barnala in Bhimber, and Sarjal. On May 9-10, 2025, the IAF struck military targets in Rafiqui, Murid, Chaklala, Rahim Yar Khan, Sukkur, Chunian, Pasrur, Sialkot, Skardu, Sargodha, Jacobabad, Bholari and Malir Cantt in Karachi.

The men and women behind the machine matter most, he said.
“We believe that any air force can have the most advanced aircraft or systems in the world, but its true strength is measured by its operational preparedness...how quickly and confidently it can act whenever the call comes,” he said, drawing attention to the IAF’s tagline “Infallible, Impervious, and Precise.”

Marines are deploying with a new combat ration — that is, stuff to eat — built for the first days of war
After entering service last year, the Close Combat Assault Ration, or C-CAR, is now deploying with frontline Marine units.
The new ration condenses what would normally be three Meal, Ready-to-Eat packets into a single daily package, reducing the weight troops carry to free space for ammunition, batteries, and other mission-essential gear.
The Defense Logistics Agency, which manages and develops the rations, told Business Insider that the C-CAR is intended for use during the first 72 hours of a conflict, when troops need a lighter, less bulky alternative to traditional MREs.
Carrying less food gives Marines more room. It reduces the need for risky resupply missions during the first few days of a conflict, Capt. Matt Burdick, a logistics officer with the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit, told Business Insider.
The 13th MEU recently deployed to the Middle East with the new rations after they entered service last year. Business Insider spent three days on the USS Makin Island with the 13th MEU off the coast of California this summer as they prepared for their deployment.
Unlike traditional MREs, which are designed to be heated and eaten during longer pauses, C-CARs are built for troops on the move, Burdick said. Meals come in squeeze pouches that can be eaten without heating or utensils, eliminating the need for water to prepare them (though most service members rarely heat MREs).
There are just three menu options— spaghetti, chicken burrito bowl, and beef stew.
Troops have frequently stripped MREs ahead of training, throwing away unwanted extras or heavier food packets to pack more compactly and carry less weight. The C-CAR, Burdick said, arrives in a more bare-bones fashion.
Burdick said his unit first encountered the rations during an exercise last year— because each of the nearly 300 Marines he was responsible for feeding carried enough food from the outset, logisticians conducted fewer resupply missions, reducing both the supply burden and its signature in the field, he explained.
The new ration won't replace the MRE, which Burdick said is designed to be distributed at scale and for longer-term operations, though it does replace the older "First Strike Ration," which was also meant to provide troops more food in a smaller package.
The rations remain in the early stages of fielding, Burdick said, with Marines using them alongside traditional MREs as the Corps gathers feedback from units to guide future ration development.

The Trump administration is suspending some tech companies, including Microsoft, from an immigration program that lets an employer hire foreign workers that can reside permanently in the US, as reported by Reuters.
Trump administration says Microsoft ‘abused’ worker visa program and is cutting off access
Vice President JD Vance claims an immigration program used by tech companies has become ‘rife’ with fraud.
In a press conference, Vice President JD Vance claimed the permanent labor certification program — intended for use when there aren’t “sufficient” US workers available to do a job — has become “rife” with fraud over the “past several years,” and that no company has “abused” the system more than Microsoft. “Our message to Microsoft is: you’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers.”
The administration is also suspending companies including Adobe, Cognizant, and Infosys. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling claims Microsoft and Adobe “requested almost 3 million foreign workers,” received “over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals,” and “over 100,000 permanent labor certifications.” Vance also said Microsoft laid off 6,000 American workers last year and “benefited” from 6,300 H-1B visas and “almost 3,000 green cards.”
Microsoft, in a blog post responding to the suspension, said the following:
We look forward to providing the Administration with additional information. For example, of the approximately 6,000 H-1B visa applications we submitted in the last fiscal year, 80% percent were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees. These were not to hire new people. The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our U.S. workforce. They are not new arrivals to our country.
Microsoft only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category. We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings. We pay our H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work.
The suspensions are part of a broader crackdown on immigration from the Trump administration, including its recently-announced price hike on H-1B visas that are popular with Big Tech companies.

The FCC proposes new mid-band spectrum auction and unlocking 800MHz for drones
The agency is doubling down on direct-to-device service.
The US Federal Communications Commission laid out a trio of proposals for several rule changes around wireless connectivity. The plans will be put to a vote later this month and largely center on direct-to-device communications.
First, the agency suggested overhauling its rules for direct-to-device, or D2D, service. The stated goal is to "promote more flexible terrestrial, satellite, and hybrid business arrangements." Related, the second proposal is to auction 25 megahertz of mid-band spectrum. Bids would be targeting use cases such as "flexible-use terrestrial networks, innovative direct-to-device (D2D) operations, or a hybrid of both" according to the FCC. This could prove enticing to companies like Amazon, which are hoping to join the growing field of satellite-based cellular service.
One such company is SpaceX, which already has spectrum licenses it bought from EchoStar. Yesterday the FCC granted approval to SpaceX for a system of 15,000 satellites to operate at 330km. This push into D2D systems from SpaceX is a separate affair than the company's attempts to launch a network of orbital data centers aimed to provide compute power for artificial intelligence activity and would add to its existing network of more than 11,000 Starlink satellites. Suffice to say, SpaceX has a whole lot of gear overhead.
The final FCC proposal recommends allowing drones to operate on the 800MHz cellular band. Those devices are currently prohibited from using that frequency, and if passed, the change would open up about 50 megahertz for UAVs to use. Over the past year, the agency has been placing more restrictions on the drones that it deemed to be security risks, whether for containing foreign-made parts or for being equipped with tech such as LiDAR.

When the Vinoo Mankad Trophy gets underway on Thursday, young cricketers from Arunachal Pradesh will miss out on the national U-19 tournament.
The side is scheduled to face Sikkim in the Plate Group, at the KIIT Cricket Stadium in Bhubaneswar, but Sportstar understands that the Arunachal Pradesh Association (ACA) has not fielded a team this season due to an ongoing legal case.
Confirming the development, Devajit Saikia, the BCCI secretary, told Sportstar: “We have seen that Arunachal Pradesh is not fielding teams in some of the age-group tournaments. From what we have gathered, there is a court case going on in the Gauhati High Court-Itanagar Bench. There is also an interim stay on the functioning of the Arunachal Cricket Association,” Saikia said.
According to Arunachal News Live, six district associations in the State had alleged violations of rules and procedures in the conduct of the Arunachal Cricket Association (ACA) State executive elections and demanded a re-election.
The associations which disputed the election of president Nabam Vivek and other post holders are Lower Siang District Cricket Association, Upper Subansiri District Cricket Association, Kamle District Cricket Association, Tawang District Cricket Association, West Siang District Cricket Association, Papum Pare District Cricket Association.
The matter was heard in the first week of September. Till date, the judgment has not come and the interim order is in operation.
“Because of the internal bickerings between the two factions, there is litigation and a stay order regarding the functioning of the association. As a result, nobody could take up the matter of team selection or preparation, and ultimately the Arunachal team will not be playing in the age-group tournament,” Saikia said.
ALSO READ: The focus on developing red-ball skills, says India U-19 coach Yere Goud
This will lead to Arunachal forfeiting the match. As per BCCI’s playing conditions relating to the ‘BCCI Match Referee awarding a match’, section 16.2.1.2 states that, “A match shall be lost by a side which in the opinion of the BCCI Match Referee refuses to play and the BCCI Match Referee shall award the match to the other side.”
The situation could also have a bearing on Arunachal Pradesh’s participation in the Ranji Trophy, which begins on October 11. Arunachal features in the Plate Group, and is supposed to begin its campaign against Nagaland at Narendra Modi Stadium in Ahmedabad.
“I have an apprehension about what will happen to the Arunachal Pradesh team when the Ranji Trophy begins on October 11. I cannot say at this moment what will happen in the first match and whether they will be able to field a team or not,” Saikia said.
In Ranji Trophy, there are past instances of teams forfeiting their matches. Services forfeited its 2009-10 Ranji Trophy Plate Division match against Jammu & Kashmir in Srinagar, as it refused to travel to Srinagar, citing security concerns. The BCCI treated it as a forfeit and subsequently banned Services from the remainder of that Ranji season.
The BCCI has, in the past, appointed committees to oversee cricketing operations in state units such as Bihar, Rajasthan and Jammu and Kashmir following court directions. However, in the case of Arunachal, things are different.
“As far as the BCCI is concerned, it cannot step into the matter right now because the matter is sub judice and, till now, the court has not appointed any administrator. The BCCI on its own will not step into the matter when the litigation is going on in the court, and until the matter is resolved,” Saikia said.
This publication spoke to several cricketers from the State, who were clearly shattered with the way things have panned out. Speaking on the condition of anonymity, a senior player from the State said, “If we don’t get to play this season, we will have to seriously weigh our options and decide whether we would like to continue with the sport.”
In 2018, Arunachal Pradesh, along with the other states of Northeast, were drafted into the BCCI-affiliated tournaments after the then Committee of Administrators, appointed by the Supreme Court, granted them full membership. However, since its entry into mainstream cricket, Arunachal Pradesh has found itself marred in several controversies, including charges of corruption against office-bearers.

Do England already have their Kane replacement - or is he yet to emerge?
- Published
Where would England be without Harry Kane?
With every record he breaks and landmark he passes, the question becomes increasingly difficult to tackle. But, now aged 33, there is a growing need for an answer.
The Bayern Munich striker became his nation's joint-highest appearance-maker on Tuesday at Wembley, netting twice in the 3-0 win over Czechia, taking his tally to 91 goals in 125 caps.
He is arguably in the form of his life. He won a league and cup double with Bayern last term - scoring 61 goals in 51 games for the German giants in 2025-26 - and he's among the favourites for the Ballon d'Or.
However, when the next European Championship kicks off in the summer of 2028, Kane will be 35. Alternatives and eventual replacements will surely be on the mind of whoever is at the helm then.
Three Lions boss Thomas Tuchel said: "You will not get another Harry Kane, first of all. We look for different options and solutions."
So what are England's options in a world without him? Is the answer already in front of us - or could it be someone yet to even emerge?
- Kane's rise from childhood keeper to equalling England cap record 
  - Published1 day ago
- England's greatest international? Kane is now a serious contender 
  - Published1 day ago
'I like him as a nine' - new role for Bellingham?
Tuchel seems to think England may have an option within their ranks already in the guise of fellow superstar Jude Bellingham.
He shrugged off question marks over his place in the team ahead of the World Cup to quickly become a rival to Kane as England's most influential player.
"I like him as a nine," Tuchel admitted ahead of England's 7-0 win over Croatia. "He is a natural goalscorer and he has the hunger to be on the scoreboard.
"He wants to be there and have the decisive action, so it makes not a huge difference if he plays as a nine or a 10.
The German has certainly helped Bellingham add a productive edge to his game.
Since the start of the 2026 World Cup, the Real Madrid star has netted 10 times in 12 matches for England, having scored six times in the 48 games beforehand.
BBC Radio 5 Live's senior football reporter Ian Dennis said: "The person who is going to replace Kane has already emerged – and that's Jude Bellingham.
"We have seen it at times, when they play that false nine, Bellingham can go into that advanced role. He will also eclipse Kane in terms of appearances. This is a player who will continue to go from strength to strength."
At Real Madrid, Bellingham played frequently as a false nine in his first season for the club, with Vinicius Jr. and Rodrygo offering penetration from the wide positions.
It was Bellingham's most productive season for Real Madrid, with the numbers indicating just how much of an all-round package he's developed into now.
In a similar style, so much of Kane's good work for England comes from dropping deep, operating as a playmaker and then surging into the box to finish chances.
If England want another player who can straddle the No. 9 and No. 10 positions simultaneously, then Bellingham could be their best fit.
And, with the likes of Phil Foden, Cole Palmer, Morgan Gibbs-White and Eberechi Eze, there are no shortage of options to fill the Bellingham role.
However former England goalkeeper Paul Robinson said on 5 Live: "He is not a nine, Bellingham plays off others.
"I do think if England are going to play this system – and remember Kane has a long time left – I don't see Bellingham as the out and out number nine."
- Bellingham unlocks new level and potential to be 'one of the greatest' 
  - Published4 days ago
What about natural number nines?
In terms of natural centre-forward replacements for Kane, England do not have much depth.
Dominic Calvert-Lewin has made a case to be Kane's back-up. He has 17 goals in 40 Premier League appearances since moving to Leeds United last summer.
However, there is a sense that Calvert-Lewin is not a dependable finisher - he underperformed by 2.13 in terms of xG in the Premier League last season - while at 29 he is not a long-term solution to Kane.
Away from the Leeds striker, there are not many centre-forwards making a case.
The only other English strikers to score in the Premier League so far this season are Nottingham Forest's Liam Delap, rebuilding his career after a difficult spell at Chelsea, and Ipswich Town's Chuba Akpom, who both have one goal each.
Across the 2026-27 season, English left-backs, with six, have more goals than English centre-forwards, with five.
Danny Welbeck was pushing for a recall last season with 13 Premier League goals but at the age of 35, his time is likely to have passed and he is certainly no long-term solution.
Ivan Toney and Ollie Watkins, previously considered by Tuchel, are both playing their football in the Saudi Pro League and were both left out of the most recent squad. Both are also already into their thirties.
Do England even need a striker?
If England do have an issue at centre-forward due to a Kane injury or suspension - or his eventual retirement - they could always opt to play without one.
Tuchel has used the tactic before, with Kai Havertz often deployed at the point of the attack during his time as Chelsea boss. Havertz scored 10 goals in the 33 league games in which he was used as a centre-forward by Tuchel.
A more fluid system has also been used to great effect by world and European champions Spain, who have deployed converted wingers Mikel Oyarzabal and Ferran Torres as strikers.
Anthony Gordon, who scored three times during the international break, could fit that particular bill. The winger was used as a striker by Newcastle United late last season and had success in the Champions League, netting 10 times in 12 appearances overall.
Who could be the next striker to break through?
There are some intriguing centre-forward options coming through.
Aston Villa's 17-year-old striker Brian Madjo scored five goals in pre-season for Villa, including one in the UEFA Super Cup against European champions Paris Saint-Germain, bullying the elite centre-back duo of Marquinhos and Willian Pacho throughout.
Madjo has been sidelined for seven weeks since that game because of injury, but he is close to making a first-team return after appearing in a friendly against Sevilla during the international break.
In the Championship, 21-year-old Will Lankshear - a Tottenham academy graduate like Kane - has hit the ground running for Middlesbrough with eight goals in 11 appearances for his new club.
Man City's Divin Mubama, on loan at Southampton, has scored five goals in 10 European under-21 Championship qualifiers, while the likes of Bristol City's Dom Ballard and Millwall's Josh Coburn are seen as young strikers with huge potential.
And Kane could yet give them time to develop having been inspired by the longevity of the newly retired Lionel Messi.
"As you see on the other end with Leo there, he's still performing at the highest level," Kane said after England's semi-final loss to Argentina in the summer. "So I never want to put a limit on these things."
England supporters will hope so. So will Tuchel. That way, the Kane conundrum is likely to be passed on to one of his successors.
"There will be someone else, but it will not be Harry or a copy of Harry," Tuchel added. "We will find a solution when it comes to it but maybe not me. It might be another 10 years."

An alleged teenage victim of Alan Jones has denied his family tried to deceive the broadcaster and get as much money out of him as they could during a tense cross-examination in a Sydney court.
Asked whether he was intent on getting as much financial assistance as he could from the former 2GB host, the witness replied: “That is a lie.”
The youngest complainant in the trial has told the court he was 17 when Jones allegedly put his tongue inside his mouth and touched him on the bottom during a visit to the shock jock’s property in the Southern Highlands.
Known as complainant A, the witness said he visited the Fitzroy Falls farm several years after he started corresponding with Jones at the age of 13.
He posted a letter to Jones asking for help after his father left, a family member died and his single mother was struggling financially.
Complainant A is one of five men who allege Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched them between 2003 and 2020.
The host has pleaded not guilty to 21 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching.
Jones’s barrister, Gabrielle Bashir SC, has been cross-examining the young man for two days about the extent of his mother’s involvement in the hundreds of emails which were sent to Jones between 2013 and 2016.
The witness has accepted that his mother provided financial details and documents and made suggestions about what to write, but insisted the correspondence was largely his own work.
Bashir asked: “Were you trying to deceive Mr Jones about the author of the email when you sent emails just signed off from [A] that your mother had input into?”
Complainant A replied: “No.”
Bashir said: “I suggest that you were - what do you say to that?”
A replied: “That you’re wrong.”
Bashir took the witness to a particular email and asked the witness if he agreed that he wanted Jones’s assistance with his mother’s mortgage.
The complainant repeatedly refused to agree, saying “I am not going to be railroaded” and “I am not going to have my words twisted, Ms Bashir”.
Bashir asked: “You understood your mother had the intention of obtaining as much assistance from Mr Jones as she could?”
A replied: “That is a lie.”
The terse exchanges between Bashir and the witness elicited several objections from prosecutor Georgina Wright, who on Wednesday said: “I object to this, your Honour. This is annoying.”
After hours of detailed questions about whether the complainant wrote a specific email about a contract more than a decade ago, Judge Glenn Walsh intervened.
“He can’t approve a contract; he is 14 years of age,” Walsh said.
The court heard one email Jones sent to A when he was 16 years of age said he had provided in excess of $100,000, “the cost is out of hand” and needs to come to an end. “Enough is enough,” he said.
The teenager replied to Jones that he and his mother could start making repayments to reimburse him. Jones wrote he did not expect to be repaid.
The witness has given evidence that he did not consent to the kiss from Jones in 2017 and that he had pulled away, saying “Enough Alan. Good night.” He said Jones “had a grin on his face”.
The incident left him scared for the consequences of pushing Jones away, he said. “I needed to be grateful, and being defiant is not being grateful and making a scene is not being grateful.”
The trial continues under Judge Walsh.

Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray?
- Published
Fighting has erupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray between regional forces and the national army.
Tigray residents, who have been trying to recover from a brutal two-year war that ended in 2022, fear a return to full-scale conflict.
There are reports of panic buying - and now internet and call services have been disrupted.
This means people cannot get access to their money via digital apps in what has become a largely cashless society after ATMs stopped working several months ago.
Why has fighting broken out now?
It follows more than six months of worsening relations between the government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray.
The African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides, ending the war nearly four years ago - but several issues have remained unresolved that have inflamed tensions.
This year, both sides have been trading blame while troops have mobilised amid pockets of fighting.
This week, major clashes erupted in Tigray and quickly spread into the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions. The two sides disagree over who started the latest escalation.
The TPLF says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in Tigray.
Who are the TPLF?
For much of Tigray's modern political history, it has been governed by the TPLF, which first emerged as an armed movement in the 1970s fighting Ethiopia's military government.
It became a major force in the overthrow of the Marxist regime in 1991 and went on to become the most powerful component of the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), the coalition that governed the ethnically diverse country for nearly three decades.
At times this proved contentious as some felt the TPLF held too much sway as Tigrayans only make up around 6% of Ethiopia's population.
When Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in 2018, he replaced the EPRDF with the Prosperity Party, significantly watering down the TPLF's influence.
Relations between Addis Ababa and the TPLF rapidly deteriorated until war erupted in 2020 in what was one of the most deadly conflicts this century.
The AU mediator estimated some 600,000 people died during the war, which totally cut off Tigray from the outside world and drove the region to the precipice of famine.
An uneasy truce was agreed in November 2022.
Why has the peace deal faltered?
There are four key issues - and two concern the fertile area of western Tigray.
The TPLF lost control of this territory in the early days of the war to Amhara, a region which neighbours Tigray to the west and whose fighters had fought on the side of the Ethiopian army.
Many people in Amhara believe the territory of western Tigray should never have been incorporated into Tigray when regional boundaries were redrawn after the military regime was ousted in 1991.
When its fighters seized control during the recent civil war, hundreds of thousands of ethnic Tigrayan people fled and are now living in homeless camps in Tigray and in the capital, Addis Ababa.
The TPLF wants western Tigray back and for those displaced from the territory to return. The government says the future of the territory needs to be decided by a referendum.
For the government, a major matter of contention has been disarmament. It says the TPLF has only handed over old weaponry to the AU and has been hiding its arms.
The two sides have also been at loggerheads over how Tigray should be governed. Under the terms of the deal, an interim administration was appointed by Abiy.
But attempts by the prime minister to influence affairs caused disputes within the TPLF itself and just before the general election in May, which was not held in Tigray because of the security situation, it restored its pre-war administration, disbanding the one set up by Abiy.
This has meant that civil servants are longer being paid and other services have been seizing up, worsening economic conditions.
Who is backing the TPLF?
A major development has seen the TPLF, once politically isolated inside Ethiopia, gain several key allies.
Earlier in September, it joined six other armed movements in forming what is called the Alliance for Survival, which includes those actively fighting the government like Amhara's Fano militia and the Oromo Liberation Army.
Members of the new alliance have different grievances, but they do share one objective: they want to remove Abiy's government from power.
So while the TPLF and Fano forces were on opposite sides during the civil war - and still disagree over the fate of western Tigray - they have temporarily put some of their differences aside.
TPLF officials say they do not want to repeat the situation of 2020, when they felt surrounded and isolated.
Yet analysts caution the alliance may become difficult to maintain because its members ultimately have very different interests.
What is the government's position?
As well as blaming the TPLF for starting the recent fighting, it has criticised the new alliance, portraying it as an attempt to destabilise the country.
It has also accused Eritrea of supporting armed groups inside Ethiopia, something Asmara denies.
During the recent civil war, Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian troops but the two neighbours, which have long had a volatile relationship, have again fallen out.
Their disagreement centres on the Red Sea and its ports.
Ethiopia, the world's most populous landlocked nation, lost access to them when Eritrea seceded in 1993. Recently Prime Minister Abiy has been pushing for ownership of Eritrea's southern port of Assab - about 60km (37 miles) from the border - and hinted at taking it by force.
What do we know about the bombing in Tigray?
Reports indicate that federal forces have been using drones and other military operations against Tigrayan forces.
The government's stated justification is that it is responding to attacks and trying to defend federal positions and territory. However, the circumstances surrounding individual strikes are difficult to independently verify.
Residents in one recently targeted town told the BBC the drones had hit two schools, which local officials said had been used by Ethiopian troops as military bases during the war.
This suggests Addis Ababa may believe they are again being used for a military purpose - by Tigrayan forces.
The attacks have come amid reports that the TPLF has been forcibly recruiting young men to join its ranks.
What is being done to stop the fighting?
The main diplomatic effort is being led by the AU, which has called for an immediate cessation of hostilities and a return to direct talks.
It has asked former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, the AU's special Horn of Africa envoy, to engage the parties urgently.
The UN has made a similar appeal, warning against a wider and more devastating conflict.
The regional organisation Igad has also called for fighting to stop and dialogue to resume.
The difficulty is that trust between Addis Ababa and Tigray is extremely low, while the formation of the new armed alliance has made the situation more complicated.
Could the fighting spread?
Yes, there is a significant risk of wider conflict inside Ethiopia.
The fighting has already moved to areas over and along Tigray's borders, while the government is simultaneously dealing with armed conflicts in other regions, particularly Amhara and Oromia.
The new alliance potentially connects several of these conflicts politically and militarily.
There is also a fear that Eritrea could be drawn in again - this time against the government.
The two aggressors in Sudan's civil war are also on opposite sides when it comes to allegiances in Tigray, potentially complicating matters.
The AU has specifically urged all neighbouring countries not to take actions that could further escalate the crisis.

Pennsylvania’s explosive measles outbreak is now the largest the US has seen since the highly infectious virus was declared eliminated in 2000. With well over 1,000 cases, it’s the largest on record since 1991.
Pennsylvania’s health officials reported 1,078 measles cases in all of 2026 as of this afternoon. That includes 12 cases in January and March, with the remaining 1,066 cases since April, when the current outbreak began. The tally includes 145 cases recorded in the last seven days and 74 identified since the previous update on Monday. Health officials noted that 40 of the 74 cases added today were from more than two weeks ago and are just now being recorded.
Among the cases, there have been 207 hospitalizations and five deaths—a newborn, a 6-week-old, an 18-year-old, a 20-year-old, and a 40-year-old. All of the deaths occurred during the current outbreak in people who were unvaccinated; the two infants were too young to have been vaccinated.
With slipping vaccination rates nationwide, measles outbreaks and cases have come roaring back in the past few years. A large outbreak in Texas that spanned January–August 2025 ended with 762 cases, while an outbreak in South Carolina ended in April with 997 cases, the previous record holder. Pennsylvania exceeds that handily with its 1,066 outbreak-linked cases as of today. With 34 new infections reported since Monday, the outbreak does not appear to be close to ending.
Measles emergency
Measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000 after decades-long vaccination efforts. Elimination is earned and maintained with vaccination rates that prevent continuous transmission of the virus during a 12-month period. In November, experts at the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO)—which acts as a regional office for the World Health Organization—will review data on whether the US has lost its measles elimination status. Experts widely expect the US has lost the status. Canada lost its elimination status in 2025.

B-Pharma graduate held for AI-generated fake video of bomb blast at UP’s SSB camp: Police
A 22-year-old B-Pharma graduate held for allegedly creating, uploading an AI-generated fake video showing a bomb blast at a Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB) camp, police said
A 22-year-old B-Pharma graduate was arrested for allegedly creating and uploading an AI-generated fake video showing a bomb blast at a Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB) camp on the India-Nepal border in Uttar Pradesh’s Maharajganj district to gain views and followers on social media, police said on Thursday.
“The suspect was taken into preventive custody before being produced before the magistrate on Thursday,” Assistant Superintendent of Police (ASP) Siddharth said.
The suspect, Faiyaz Ahmad, a resident of Sevantari village in Maharajganj, allegedly created a nine-second video depicting the 22nd battalion SSB camp at Sevantari being blown up and uploaded it on Instagram. The post carried a provocative caption too.
“The police immediately traced the social-media account, which was found to be operated in the name of Faiyaz Ahmad, son of Abdul Kalam, a resident of Sevantari,” Maharajganj Additional SP Siddharth said in a statement issued on Wednesday night.
“The police subsequently got the objectionable post deleted through the person operating the account and took Faiyaz into custody. He was produced before a magistrate and sent to judicial custody,” the ASP added.
Police said that during questioning, Faiyaz admitted to creating and uploading the AI-generated video to make his social-media account go viral and increase his likes, views and followers.
Faiyaz’s Instagram account, a_faiyaz_001x, has around 11,600 followers and 327 posts, according to the police. His profile describes him as a chemist and pharmacy professional and contains several AI-generated videos, including clips depicting him driving luxury cars and visiting high-end destinations. His Facebook account has around 1,600 followers.
According to police, Faiyaz had completed his B-Pharma course but was unemployed and looking for work. He allegedly regularly created and uploaded reels and other videos for social media.
The incident has prompted police to intensify monitoring of social-media activity in the border district, particularly posts involving security forces, border installations and other sensitive locations.
Police have warned social-media users against creating or circulating provocative or misleading content involving security establishments merely to generate views, likes or followers, saying such activity can invite legal action.

Trump tells Texas crowd that wife Melania calls him ‘sir’
Bizarre rant kicks off rally for embattled GOP Senate candidate Ken Paxton

President Donald Trump on Wednesday told attendees at a rally in Texas that his wife of 21 years, Melania Trump, addresses him the same way as one of his employees rather than using his name or any other term of endearment.
The president was speaking in support of Texas Attorney General and GOP Senate candidate Ken Paxton when he began an extended rant alleging that Paxton’s opponent, Democratic state representative James Talarico, is a vegan, which Talarico denies.
But he quickly went off on a tangent about the pronunciation of “vegan” and recalled being corrected on it by his wife.
“You know, my wife told me ‘sir, you have to do me a favor — it’s not vay-gan, it’s vee-gan,” he said.
Talarico, the 37-year-old seminarian who is currently leading Paxton in most recent polls of the Texas Senate race, has repeatedly denied subscribing to a vegan or vegetarian diet — a lifestyle choice that would be politically perilous in a cattle-raising state such as Texas.
But Paxton’s campaign — and Trump — have repeatedly claimed the Democrat abstains from animal products.
The president continued repeating the scurrilous claim about Talarico’s diet, telling the partisan crowd that his claims to a carnivorous lifestyle are fabricated.
“Now he says he loves meat, but he's a vegan — see, Melania? I got that right,” he said.
“He's a vegan. He wants to eat a piece of lettuce, a little piece of lettuce, please.”
Trump then suggested that a recent absence from the campaign trail on Talarico’s part is because of gastrointestinal illness brought on by eating meat for political purposes.
“You know where he is? He's sick because he's been forced to eat meat for political reasons, and he's throwing up all over the place. He's sick,” he said.
He continued with the bizarre story, accusing Talarico of having “forced himself to go to barbecues” and “stuff some little ribs down his throat.”
“But he'd eat, and then what would happen? He'd go to the back of the tent, and he'd throw up all over the place because he doesn't want meat,” Trump claimed.
The GOP’s meat-based attack on the Texas Democrat stems from comments he’d made to the Texas Humane Legislation Network in which he said reducing meat consumption was "existential" for combating climate change.
At no point did Talarico claim to abstain from meat himself, but that hasn’t stopped Republicans from alleging without evidence that he does not partake.
For his part, Talarico has said he has "been eating barbecue since before Ken Paxton's first indictment,” a reference to the Republican’s long-running legal troubles.
Trump’s appearance in San Antonio on Wednesday was his fourth trip to the Lone Star State in the last six weeks and comes as Talarico has built a lead over Paxton that, if it holds, could make him the first Democrat to win a statewide election there since Ann Richards won the governorship 36 years ago, in 1990.
A recent Sienna College poll showed Talarico with a 51-45 percent lead over Paxton, while a separate Fox News poll also showed the Democrat leading Paxton by a margin of 51 percent to 49 percent.
The last Democrat to win a Senate race in Texas was Lloyd Bentsen, who won re-election to a fourth term in 1988 even as he lost at the top of the ticket as then-Massachusetts Gov. Michael Dukakis’ running-mate in that year’s presidential race.
Bentsen would resign four years later to become Treasury Secretary in the Clinton administration. His appointed Democratic replacement, Robert Krueger, served in the Senate for three months before losing a special election to Republican Kay Bailey Hutchison.

As tensions mount over who gets access to top-end artificial intelligence, French company Mistral has released a new freely available model that it claims can compete with the very best from the US and China.
The new 1 trillion-parameter model, Mistral Large 4—nicknamed Le Chonk—can be used and customized by anyone. It’s currently available in preview, with a final version to follow by the end of the month. Though Le Chonk is built to compete with leading general-purpose models, it’s optimized specifically for coding and cyberdefense, as well as tasks particular to manufacturing, finance, electrical engineering, and other niches.
“There are a lot of areas where the other labs will not focus that much,” Guillaume Lample, cofounder and chief scientist at Mistral, tells WIRED. “There are so many domains in which you can improve models.”
Mistral presents Le Chonk as by far the most capable open-weight model developed outside of China, and “very, very close” to some proprietary models. Whereas Chinese labs have been accused by the US government of abusing distillation—the training of a smaller model on the outputs of a larger one—to close the performance gap with OpenAI and Anthropic, Mistral claims to have trained its model from scratch.
It’s already considerably cheaper for businesses to run open-weight models, which cost only as much as the compute they consume. By reducing the performance gap on leading proprietary models and providing a competitive alternative to releases from China, Mistral says, Le Chonk will eliminate the few remaining reasons a business might hesitate to choose open source.
“Mistral is still in the race of getting the best model,” Lample says. “This is the main message.”
With less capital and fewer compute resources than OpenAI and Anthropic, Mistral has generally lagged behind on model performance, revenue, and the frequency of releases. While the US labs charge a premium for access to their proprietary, closed-weight models, Mistral generates revenue by charging pay-as-you-go fees for running models through its cloud and deploying engineers to help customers tune models to their specific needs. Recently, however, the French lab has been on a hot streak: In September, it raised a $3.3 billion funding round at a $24 billion valuation, the largest ever raise by a European tech company. Its earnings have reportedly increased 20-fold in the last year or so.

Twelve women have been killed in one part of South Africa since July. Here's what we know so far
- Published
Police in South Africa have confirmed the discovery of the bodies of three more women in an area east of Johannesburg, bringing the total number of bodies found there to 12 in just two months.
The latest bodies were found in Ekurhuleni between Saturday and Monday morning, according to local police.
Police have made arrests in three of the cases, which do not appear to be related to the others. Nevertheless, police have said they cannot rule out the possibility of a serial killer.
The discoveries have caused widespread alarm in Ekurhuleni, particularly around Kempton Park, and come against the backdrop of longstanding concerns about high levels of violence against women in South Africa.
Here's what we know.
Busisiwe Mahlangu
Case 1
Busisiwe Mahlangu's body was found in Kempton Park on 15 July 2026, the first of a string of bodies found in Ekurhuleni within a two-month period. The 37-year-old was found naked with her hands bound with cable ties.
Police arrested a suspect, believed to be her partner, two days after her murder. He has been in police custody since then and has not been linked to the other deaths that followed.
Itumeleng Kekana
Case 2
Itumeleng Kekana, 32, was the second woman whose body was found in the same area on 3 August 2026.
The young mother disappeared in July and her body was found badly bruised, partially clothed and dumped on a bridge in Kempton Park.
No arrests have been made so far.
Nomfesane Mjobo
Case 3
Nomfesane Mjobo's body was found on 26 August, also in Kempton Park.
Few details around her death have been released but like most of the victims, she was found partially or fully naked with bruises.
No arrests have been made.
Unknown woman
Case 4
Police confirmed the discovery of an unknown woman, in her 20s, on 7 September. The woman's body was found floating in a river in Olifantsfontain wearing only her underwear.
No further details have been shared about her death and no arrests have been made.
Gracious Nkomo
Case 5
Gracious Nkomo was the fifth woman whose body was discovered, again in the Kempton Park area.
Her partially clothed body was found on 10 September along a road close to South Africa's busiest airport. No arrests have been made in the 28-year-old's death.
Elizabeth "Tsontso" Moselakgomo
Case 6
Elizabeth Moselakgomo was the sixth woman to be found, after a highly publicised nationwide search for her. The 38-year-old went missing while out for a daily run near her home in Kempton Park.
Her body was found badly bruised and partially clothed on 12 September. It was the discovery of her body that really raised the alarm about the spate of killings. No arrests have been made in her case.
Unidentified woman
Case 7
Police confirmed the discovery of another body just two days after Moselakgomo was found. The body was found in Olifantsfontein on 14 September, but police have withheld her name as her family has not yet been informed.
No arrests have been made.
Dineo Motapane
Case 8
The body of Dineo Motapane, 38, was discovered on 15 September just two days after she was last seen alive.
Motapane's battered and partly burned body was found on the side of the road in Springs, another part of Ekurhuleni.
She leaves behind a young child. No arrests have been made in her case.
Jabulile Ntimba
Case 9
The body of Jabulile Ntimba, in her 30s, was discovered half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Boksburg on 17 September. This was the ninth body found in Ekurhuleni.
According to police, it appears Ntimba was killed because of a possible love triangle. Three people, two women and a man, were initially arrested for her grisly murder but the man was released due to insufficient evidence.
The two women have been charged with premeditated murder and defeating the ends of justice.
Ntombifuthi Nxumalo
Case 10
The body of Ntombifuthi Nxumalo, the 10th body found in Ekurhuleni, was discovered at a cemetery in the Tembisa neighbourhood north-east of central Johannesburg on 26 September. She was found naked with serious head injuries as well as stones near her body.
This has led to police believing she may have been stoned to death.
A 36-year-old man was arrested a day after Nxumalo's death after he had travelled to another province. He faces a murder charge.
Unidentified woman
Case 11
The body of a yet-to-be identified woman was found in Springs on Sunday - the 11th body found in Ekurhuleni.
The grim discovery was made by a security company patrolling the area.
The woman was found in an open field, but no further details have been shared.
No arrests have been made.
Boitumelo Gift Mashita
Case 12
Boitumelo Gift Mashita was shot and killed on Monday in Tembisa Ekurhuleni. The 23-year-old woman was on her way to work when she was gunned down and her belongings were taken.
Police say her estranged husband, who they suspected of being responsible for her murder, was later found dead inside his vehicle in Midrand.
Police have not found any link between this case and the discovery of the other bodies.
While most of the bodies were found in the same area, police confirmed the discovery of another body about 39 miles (63 km) away from Ekurhuleni on 20 September.
The body of a young woman, believed to be in her 20s, was found wrapped in a duvet in a dam in Soweto, south-west of Johannesburg.
It's unclear if her murder is linked to those in Ekurhuleni.
President Cyril Ramaphosa said the killing of these women and others was a "stain on our national conscience".
South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.
South African police statistics do not differentiate victims by gender but the South African Human Rights Commission said last week that 569 women were killed between April and June this year. This works out as an average of six women killed each day.
Police have set up a task team to investigate these murders and have offered a reward of 400,000 rand ($24,000; £18,000) for information that could lead to arrests.

The posters, just like the women holding them, were taking no prisoners.
“Girls don’t need curfews, rapists need consequences,” read one. “Lock your dicks rather than your women at home,” read another.
As hundreds of women walked from the gates of their university campus into the streets of Delhi – where sexual harassment, assault, catcalling and molestation are a constant, daily threat – they shouted together, in a chorus of rage and defiance: “We want justice.”
The fury that has erupted on India’s university campuses over the past week has been double-edged. The trigger was a series of brutal rapes that have taken place in Delhi in recent weeks, including the alleged gang rape of a 17-year-old in a public park close to Delhi university, by three men who posed as police officers.
Just a week earlier, another 17-year-old was gang raped and murdered in Delhi’s Swaroop Nagar neighbourhood, after she went to meet friends. The accused allegedly raped her, stabbed her to death and dumped her body in a field, where it was discovered days later half eaten by dogs.
Rapes of an 11-year-old and a six-year old were also reported in the same month. Last month, a 16-year-old was allegedly raped by the bus driver and conductor after she boarded a sleeper bus in Delhi.
Women who have taken part in protests on Delhi university campuses have condemned these alleged violent rapes on minors as disgusting and unforgivable – but they have also been at pains to emphasise that they are not out of the ordinary.
Fourteen years have passed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya rape case, when a woman was gang raped on a bus and died from her injuries. But while it provoked international outrage and a slew of legislation and government promises, women say that nothing has changed; for them, India’s streets, particularly in Delhi, remain as unsafe as ever. According to statistics, a women is raped in India every 20 minutes – though the real scale is believed to be far worse due to chronic underreporting.
This week, the supreme court said the five successive rape cases “starkly underlined a systematic failure” and they could not help but “draw painful parallels to the Nirbhaya incident of 2012”.
Vaishnavi Dhruw, 21, a history student at Delhi university, was among the female protesters at the “smash the patriarchy” protest march on Wednesday afternoon. “I don’t know a single woman who lives in this city and feels safe,” she said.
While some of the key demands of the protest have been better lighting and policing, Dhruw emphasised that for anything to change, the country requires a deep societal shift where men no longer feel they have ownership over women’s bodies.
“We are not marching for safety, we are here to protest for our freedom, for the most basic right to walk in our own streets,’ she said. “Again and again, women are told to stay indoors, to not go out at night, to cover ourselves, to protect ourselves. When will society tell men in our country not to rape?”
Much of the anger driving the protests has also been prompted by the response by the authorities to the rapes, which women say once again has only been to police their freedoms. Women in Delhi were told to stay out of parks at night, and classes were temporarily halted at one of Delhi’s most prestigious female colleges. Many hostels where female students stay impose strict curfews preventing them from going out at night.
“Instead of going after criminals, you’re going to tell women to sit at home,” said Aranya Rathore, 25, a student at Delhi University. “A demand for more surveillance is not a solution. In fact, it’s going to curtail our freedom more.”
Female students say a lot of their time is taken up by safety logistics – from wearing modest clothes to reorganising their days to ensure they do not travel alone or at night and always having a trackable live location on their phones. There is widespread awareness that should anything happen, the onus of blame – both within the family home and more widely in society – tends to fall on women; as one poster at Wednesday’s march pointed out, “no one ever asks what the rapist was wearing”.
Yet despite their best efforts, many women said it was almost impossible to avoid harassment. Ananya Wig, a 26-year-old a graduate of Delhi University and the founder of Her Huq, a gender-equality initiative, said she has experienced harassment both around university campuses and in public spaces.
She recounted an incident where a driver rolled down his car window and began masturbating as she and female friends got off a rickshaw and walked through the college gates. “This wasn’t at night, it was in the middle of the day,” she said. “I’ve always lived in Delhi and the city has not changed.”
The protests have brought into focus a dilemma faced by many Indian women, who are being educated in greater numbers than any time in the country’s history and have better job opportunities than ever before – but still have to navigate the constant debilitating threats to their safety and the conservative pressures from their families.
“I know so many girls, not just 10 years ago, but even today, who end up choosing educational institutions and jobs and other employment opportunities depending on how close they are from their home,” said Wig. “Not on the basis of their marks, not on the basis of their aspirations, but simply, ‘OK, the shorter the distance is, the more likely it is that I will be safe.’”
Many of the Delhi university students who took part in the marches said that sexual harassment had become prevalent on campus, and have demanded better accountability mechanisms for reporting assault. The university has not responded.
“Delhi University is one of the most prestigious universities in India right now but there are various cases of women being assaulted by professors, sometimes unfortunately also for grades,” said Devyani Sarkar, 24, who is studying for her masters in English at Delhi University. “It’s despicable, but it’s also a living truth.”
Many on the marches said that it was no coincidence the protests took place in the aftermath of India’s “cockroach” movement, which saw hundreds of thousands of young Gen Z Indians take to the streets over education reform.
“My generation is not afraid to stand up and protest. We know that society has to change,” said 17-year-old Subhani. “The days of women being silent is over.”

Serum Institute of India’s recombinant Quadrivalent Human Papillomavirus vaccine (qHPV) vaccine Cervavac has received World Health Organization (WHO) prequalification.
The vaccine targets HPV types 6, 11, 16, and 18. It is indicated for girls and boys aged 9 through 26 years. Inclusion on the WHO list of prequalified vaccines allows Cervavac to be procured by United Nations agencies, Serum Institute said.
The vaccine was developed in collaboration with the Department of Biotechnology (DBT) and the Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC), along with the WHO-IARC (International Agency for Research on Cancer) and the Gates Foundation. It is the 32nd WHO prequalification for products/biologicals received by Serum Institute, the vaccine maker said.
“WHO prequalification of Cervavac is an important step in strengthening the global response to HPV. We are pleased to see this indigenously developed vaccine reach this achievement,” CEO Adar Poonawalla said.
Approved for use in India by DCGI
Cervavac has been approved for use in India by the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI). The vaccine is administered for the prevention of diseases caused by the four HPV types — prevention of anal cancer in boys and young men, and cervical, vulvar, vaginal, and anal cancers in girls and young women. It is also indicated in preventing genital warts, as applicable to the indicated population.
The vaccine is administered intramuscularly and available in 1-dose vials of 0.5 ml and 2-dose vials of 1.0 ml presentations.
