Asian governments are rushing preparations for the most severe El Niño weather event on record, with hundreds of millions of people bracing for multiple crises at once as extreme heat, heavy rain and food shortages hit the region.
Fuelled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific – and developing alongside the human-driven climate crisis – El Niño is virtually guaranteed to grow to a very strong intensity towards the end of this year and into 2027.
The World Food Programme has warned that about 50 million people will probably be pushed into acute hunger due to the exceptionally intense weather system, while UN secretary-general António Guterres said this month that El Niño was “being supersized before our eyes”.
Here are the steps countries in Asia are taking to prepare for El Niño:
‘Climate risk maps’ in China
In Hong Kong, authorities have already been forced to revise workplace policies, after the city experienced its hottest day on record on 9 August. During times of extreme heat, companies are expected to reschedule work, provide cooling equipment and rest breaks for their employees.
Employers in the international financial hub could even face prosecution if they fail to provide staff with support at times of sweltering heat.
In mainland China a 100-day campaign has been launched to prepare for extreme weather and help safeguard harvests against the opposing extremes of drought and intense rainfall.
Beijing has plans to upgrade early warning monitoring systems, and in July, it launched a national plan encouraging cities to draw up ‘climate risk maps’ to help identify areas most vulnerable to flooding and severe heat.
Taiwan, meanwhile, is treating the predicted extreme weather as an emergency situation, and preparing using methods similar to what it would do to train for a terrorist attack or earthquake. In early September, the island nation held a mass exercise simulating three consecutive days of temperatures above 40C. Hundreds of people took part in the field exercises, which simulated power and water disruption, rail problems, air conditioner failure and mass heatstroke.
The government has also been testing its “Cool Map” online platform, which helps to direct vulnerable people to airconditioned and cool spaces.
Sri Lanka plans to process salterwater
El Niño is already wreaking havoc across south Asia; in parts of India there has been a shortfall of monsoon rainfall of almost 50% in September, with knock-on effects on key crops such as rice, pulses, cotton and maize. Concerns are mounting that there could be a diminished harvest in the coming months, likely driving up food prices – already crippling for poor and lower middle class families.
The Indian government has taken a hyper-vigilant approach to establish what the agriculture minister, Shivraj Singh Chouhan, described as a “protective shield for farmers”.
In more than 350 vulnerable districts authorities are boosting water conservation infrastructure and water harvesting, and are encouraging farmers to plant low-water, short duration crops – such as pulses and millets.
But the most intense impact of El Niño in the area is in Sri Lanka, where the absence of rainfall and high temperatures have become so severe that the country is experiencing its worst drought in a decade. More than 160,000 people are now facing a drinking water shortage as several key reservoirs run dry.
Officials have been forced to close the tourist areas of the Yala national park, home to leopards, elephants, crocodiles and spotted deer, and have been bringing in tankers of water to fill the ponds to make sure the animals do not die. In Mullaithivu lagoon, in the north-east of Sri Lanka, thousands of fish were found dead due to the lack of fresh water.
The country’s disaster management centre is preparing for a situation in which freshwater supplies could vanish. “If water sources dry up, there will be no alternative means of obtaining water,” an official said. Colombo would then be forced to process salt water from the sea, although relying on the country’s one desalination plant is not considered workable.
Tackling an agriculture crisis in south-east Asia
In south-east Asia, El Niño is compounded by a series of ongoing crises. The Iran war has already disrupted global energy and supply chains and inflated fertiliser costs, disproportionately hitting the region. At the same time, severe haze from seasonal fires across Malaysia and Indonesia has choked cities and is damaging plants and trees.
During the 2023–2024 El Niño, south-east Asian governments successfully cushioned agricultural impacts by adjusting planting calendars and managing water, but those strategies will be insufficient to deal with the scale of the crisis, experts warn. Regional rice yields are already projected to fall by 8 to 10%.
“We can’t just assume that this El Niño is going to be the same as the last because there are so many challenges that have been stacking on top of each other,” says Elyssa Kaur Ludher, a climate and food security expert based in Singapore.
The Philippines, Malaysia and Indonesia are particularly vulnerable to food price changes, says Kaur Ludher, a visiting fellow with the Climate Change for Southeast Asia Programme at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore.
“In Singapore, most of our income is not spent on food. It’s under 10%. But for Indonesians, it can be up to 50% or even more as a proportion of income spent on food. So any price rise affects them disproportionately.”
With the potential for price rises to leave people desperate and angry, Kaur Ludher has argued for food security to be reframed as a national security issue. In Indonesia and the Philippines in particular, she said, social stability depends a lot on food prices. “Rice is a lifeline to this region,” she says.
To prepare, south-east Asian governments and farmer cooperatives are promoting regenerative agriculture and shifting toward biofertilisers.
“We have come to a stage where climate change is putting so much pressure on us – on our existing, already crumbling or structurally unsound, systems,” say Kaur Ludher. “Nature will force us to have a reckoning.”
South Korea overhauls its heatwave alert system
South Korea saw the driest July on record in the country’s south-east. Weeks later came a freak reversal, as a weakening storm system dragged in a deluge that dumped some of the heaviest rainfall ever recorded at a Korean weather station. The heat was so intense that farmers described spoilt potatoes as being “boiled” in the ground.
The country’s weather agency has overhauled its heatwave alert system for the first time in 18 years, adding a top tier that triggers official guidance to stop non-emergency outdoor work once feels-like temperatures hit 38C. Nationwide, phones have buzzed for weeks with government alerts urging people to stay indoors during the hottest hours.
Officials are watching out for a rough autumn, with seas around the Korean peninsula remaining unusually warm for the season and forecasters expecting the north-west Pacific to produce far more powerful storms than usual this year, since a strengthening El Niño is weakening the high pressure that has so far kept them away.
Japan prepares for ‘cruelly’ hot days and typhoons
Japan is also bracing for the arrival of so-called super-typhoons, which experts attribute to a combination of El Niño and human-induced global heating.
El Niño was once associated with slightly cooler summers in Japan. But rising sea surface temperatures mean it is having the opposite effect, blanketing many parts of the country in record-breaking heat and humidity in 2023-4, the last time the weather pattern materialised.
Japan recorded its first official “cruelly hot day” – or kokushobi – in July, just after the start of the current El Niño event. The Japanese term, introduced in April to underscore the threat to health posed by rising temperatures, refers to days when the mercury exceeds 40C.
Now, as the summer heat dissipates, the country is bracing for the arrival of potentially destructive typhoons.
The public is encouraged to take measures to protect themselves and their homes, such as heeding official evacuation warnings and stocking up on food and water. People living in apartments are urged to secure or bring inside flower pots and furniture – anything that could become a dangerous flying object during a storm.
This month the infrastructure ministry said it had identified several high-risk underpasses on national highways that would be closed preemptively during heavy rain. Underpasses – which allow cars to travel beneath other roads or railway lines – became a focus of concern last month after two trapped motorists drowned during record-breaking rain in Chiba prefecture, east of Tokyo.

As scandals involving the use of artificial intelligence by professional authors pile up, a British startup has established a way for publishers to certify their books as “organic”—written by real people, no machines in sight.
On Wednesday, Books by People confirmed it had received approval from the UK’s Intellectual Property Office to begin distributing a mark that indicates a published book has been authored by a human. The stamp, which looks like a thumbprint, will be displayed on the cover.
“If people are going to be writing AI books or seeking it out for their own enjoyment, that’s their prerogative,” Esme Dennys, cofounder of Books by People, tells WIRED. “But if you want to read something that’s written by a person, you should be able to find that. We’re just trying to create that choice.”
Previous book-labeling schemes, like Human Authored, have operated under an honesty system, where an author promises they haven’t used AI in the development process. To try to add more weight to its certification, Books by People asks for an authorship declaration, runs each manuscript through proprietary software, and manually examines early drafts and research materials supplied by the writer and editor for “indicators of humanity.”
The organization is "looking at all the things that give us the best sense of whether a person wrote the work—whether the work was made during a natural process of drafting and redrafting,” says Dennys.
Books by People will charge publishers a flat membership fee, plus an additional sum for every book they put forward for certification. Five publishers have signed up so far. The startup expects the new mark to feature on its first book by the end of the year.
This year, the publishing industry has been caught up in a flurry of scandals involving the suspected use of AI by authors. A literary agent canceled a book deal reportedly worth $2 million; a publisher withdrew a novel from the shelves; readers alleged that a prize-winning short story had been generated with AI.
Writers and publishers are not necessarily worried about being replaced by AI, industry insiders tell WIRED. They believe that few people will ultimately want to read machine-generated books.
“You are essentially standing at the end of a conveyor belt, watching stuff fall off the edge. Once you know that, it prevents you from getting really emotionally invested in whatever falls into your hands from the belt,” says sci-fi author Ted Chiang, whose 1998 novella Story of Your Life was adapted into the Academy Award–winning film Arrival. “The knowledge of how something was created cannot be separated from your experience.”
However, repeated scandals could shake public confidence in the unspoken rule of publishing: That every book that reaches the shelf has been authored by a real person who has not indulged in plagiarism.
“Publishing has always relied on trust between the publisher, writer, and reading public. Cases where that trust is betrayed have been rare,” says Sam Jordison, codirector at independent publisher Galley Beggar Press, which intends to adopt the Books by People mark. “There’s almost a feeling of revulsion about the idea of reading an AI text that purports to be human. It feels like a con job.”
Against that backdrop, the idea of a certification for human-authored books has received backing from various writers and editors. In a statement praising Books by People, Markus Dohle, former CEO of Penguin Random House, described human storytelling as “the lifeblood of our industry.”
But while publishers might relish the chance to signal their commitment to “organic literature,” the routinization of AI detection is a double-edged sword for authors, who risk a false positive result spoiling their reputation.
“We need to be quite careful that this doesn’t end up becoming a witch hunt,” says Tom West, CEO of the Publishers’ Licensing Services, which helps publishers to collectively license works to third parties. “Obviously, the devil is going to be in the detail.”
New York–based startup Pangram, which has emerged as the leader in the field of AI detection, claims to be able to sniff out generated text with a 99.7 percent accuracy. But authors have questioned the reliability of its approach, which itself involves AI.
In September, Jerry Falade, the debut author whose agent reportedly pulled the $2 million book deal, alleged that detection software had misconstrued his Nigerian dialect as evidence he had used AI. Pangram’s software scored the book as 97 percent AI-generated. “It takes months, even years to write a book,” Falade wrote in a recent essay. “It takes AI-detection software two minutes to ruin your life’s work.” (Pangram did not respond to a request for comment.)
Others have warned against normalizing extreme scrutiny of authors. They claim the labeling schemes have it backward; the onus should be on platforms and publishers to declare when a piece of media is AI-generated, not when it’s written by a person. “Authors are being constantly quizzed about the origins of their ideas and their work. I think that’s something we need to resist,” says West. “The default should be that a book is human-authored.”
Approved by the Intellectual Property Office alongside the mark, Books by People’s verification process is different to Pangram’s technology-first approach, placing greater weight on interrogating documents and communication trails for signs of humanity. “I wouldn’t call it AI detection,” says Dennys. “We realized pretty early on that, as AI models get better, getting into that race is never going to be sustainable.”
In cases where Books by People is uncertain whether a piece of evidence indicates AI use, it claims to err on the side of the author. “When you have a public process that has been vetted, all we can do is make sure that a book has gone through the process,” says Dennys. “The bedrock of our organization is to avoid [writers] being unjustly accused.”
Some authors say the important thing is that publishers underscore their commitment to human-authored literature as a nonnegotiable standard for the industry, in whatever way they can. Even if methods for policing the rule are flawed.
“It’s just as important for publishers to have a ‘no cheating’ policy as it is for universities, even if there’s no perfect method for enforcement,” says Chiang. “It’s a statement of values.”

DIY fertilizer is a blessing as farmers face steep prices due to the Iran war
On 12 acres outside of Lusaka, Kanangwa Newlove has built a paradise.
Shady fruit trees dot her fields. During the growing season, long tomato vines drape over trellises. There are tidy rows of corn, pumpkins and a local leafy green called blackjack. Eleven varieties of lettuce.
"I started taking vegetables to my workmates, and before I knew it I was supplying the supermarket," Newlove says. "It went on and on."
For many farmers, 2026 has been a challenging year. The Iran war choked off the Strait of Hormuz and dramatically halted international trade shipments — including fertilizers. Prices spiked globally. The effects were quickly felt in African countries, where smallholder farmers are often vulnerable to rapid changes in fertilizer costs.''
Newlove, however, didn't feel the pinch. For years, she's fertilized her plants with a homemade, fermented compost known as bokashi.
A solution from ancient Asia
With roots in ancient Korean farming traditions and popularized in Japan, bokashi is relatively easy to make. According to Newlove, it's also highly effective.
"We could now have a potent fertilizer —– organic —– which is ready in [weeks]. For us that was amazing," Newlove says. "It was a game changer, to be honest."
Bokashi has become so popular in Zambia, she says, that farmers now sell homemade bokashi compost at markets and swap tips on social media. The Kasisi Agricultural Training Centre offers bokashi training and often sends students to her farm to see it in action.
"[Zambian farmers] have been looking for alternatives — how to grow food but reduce costs," says Rabecca Mwila of the Knowledge Platform for Organic Agriculture and Agroecology in Africa. "Inputs such as bokashi have come in to provide a cushion for them."
Here's the recipe
For home composters, bokashi is a method of fermenting food scraps in an anaerobic environment — no oxygen allowed! But many farmers make a version of bokashi outdoors. Ingredients are often easy to find on a farm: leaves or crop residues, animal dung, charcoal and ash from a fireplace. Then, they add yeast and a source of sugar (molasses or bananas, in a pinch) to jump start the fermentation process. The mixture heats up as microbes break it down.
After a couple of weeks of fermentation, the concoction is buried underground near Newlove's crops, so it can break down completely.
"There's a lot of excitement from farmers because they've been able to testify that it's cheaper for them, and their soil is rebuilding," Mwila says. "They're able to see earthworms."
As climate change makes rainfall less predictable and dry seasons longer, Mwila says farmers are increasingly interested in inexpensive, sustainable options.
Many voice concerns about the longer-term impact of commercial fertilizers. "Because of the overuse of synthetic fertilizers and pesticides and herbicides, the soil is completely depleted," says Mwila.
Zambia once imported nearly all of its fertilizer. After global prices tripled following the COVID-19 pandemic and the Russian invasion of Ukraine, finding alternatives became a matter of food security.
In addition to bokashi, the Zambian government has promoted the growth of its domestic fertilizer industry. Last week, a Chinese-Zambian conglomerate announced its intention to build a $1.5 billion fertilizer plant in the country.
Although global fertilizer prices largely dropped over the summer, including in Zambia, some fertilizers remain expensive in southern African countries, including Malawi, Tanzania and South Africa.
While the government subsidizes fertilizer, there isn't always enough to go around. Donald Zulu, a lecturer and researcher at Copperbelt University in northern Zambia, says that without subsidies — a farmer will pay about $400 USD to buy enough fertilizer to grow 2.5 acres of corn.
"It's quite expensive and out of reach for many smallholder farmers," Zulu says.
Do veggies like it?
Seeking an alternative, he started working with WeForest and local farmers to study how well bokashi worked on corn and cabbage in 2024.
"The results were very encouraging," Zulu says. "Bokashi echoed the yields of mineral fertilizer."
This suggested that small-scale farmers could use bokashi — which is cheaper — and grow a comparable amount of food. But to his surprise, the best-performing crops were planted with smaller amounts of both bokashi and mineral fertilizers.
"That's where bokashi becomes key in terms of helping farmers to be food secure," he said.
For farmers like Kanangwa Newlove, bokashi is less about the cost, and more about building a sustainable farming practice that preserves the land.
"Even when you're making it, you don't need to wear a mask because it's not toxic. There's no harmful chemicals," Newlove says. "So it's all just like a labor of love."

As the Union government continues to host the ‘Seva Sankalp Abhiyan’ — a month-long celebration of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s birthday and 25 years in public service, from September 17 to October 17 — one among the various events planned is the ‘Namo Seva: Untold Stories’.
Part of the larger celebrations aimed at promoting public participation towards the ‘Viksit Bharat’ vision, the theatrical performance has been carried out by students in functions across various schools and colleges. Several cultural forums, theatre groups, volunteers, and BJP workers themselves put up the play in events organised by state authorities to reportedly raise awareness about the welfare schemes launched by PM Modi as well as his life and work.
Also called ‘Namo Seva Gatha’, the play has been staged across several states, including Assam, Bihar, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Chattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, West Bengal, and many others. In the performances so far, despite its many forms — street play, cultural performance, panchayat event, school drama, puppetry show, and more — the script remained more or less the same, albeit in different languages.
Alt News read the script and instructions sent out by West Bengal school education department to primary, secondary, and higher secondary schools, as well as colleges and universities in the state. Further, a report by Ei Samay states that district school inspectors (DIs) had sent out instructions for the play to some schools.
Student participation in the play was reportedly voluntary. However, the performances have drawn criticism over the use of educational institutions to stage what a section of students and academics described as a politically charged celebration of the Prime Minister. Critics have questioned the appropriateness of asking students, especially young children, to enact a script that repeatedly praises Modi and his government, while also incorporating political and religious slogans such as “Modi hai toh mumkin hai” and “Jai Sri Ram”.
What’s There in the Script?
The script has “untold stories” about the Prime Minister were narrated in the form of a conversation between five school friends — Mohit, Raman, Kajal, Disha, and Sonali — who have reunited after many years at a cafe. They recall the days they have left behind and reflect on changing times, portraying Narendra Modi as the architect of ‘Viksit Bharat’ — a vision he has set for India to achieve by 2047.
Modi’s first appearance in the play comes in the aftermath of the 2001 Gujarat earthquake which killed over 20,000 people. He emerges through a screen of smoke amid the ruins of a collapsed structure, waving the Indian flag as a beacon of hope amid the devastation, before taking oath as Gujarat’s chief minister in his mother tongue.
The friends then turn to discussing range of topics from the advent of digital payments and UPI and the spread of modern technology into India’s hinterlands, to “Operation Ganga” during the Russia-Ukraine war, the abrogation of Article 370, the consecration of the Ram Mandir in Ayodhya — presenting them as beneficial and “grounbreaking” schemes and measures undertaken by Modi as the Prime Minister.
The script further represents the country as plagued by terrorism in the years preceding Modi coming to power. “Militants would carry out attacks whenever they felt like it. Bomb blasts, serial blasts, had become a daily affair,” a character reminisces. A scene that shows the Uri surgical strike of 2016 invokes the usage of “weeping, sounds of gunfire, and the notes of a bugle”. In one of the street plays staged in Varanasi, a character links the surgical strike to an alleged rise in the sale of diapers in Pakistan around that same time.

Modi’s role in curbing the spread of the COVID-19 pandemic is also emphasised through the dialogue: “When rumours were spreading across the country and ordinary people were afraid to get vaccinated, Modiji himself took the first vaccine shot and shared his photo, dousing all the rumours. In one segment of the script, a news reporter hails Modi by invoking the first half of the popular catchphrase “Modi hai toh…”, leaving the audience, presumably comprising students, to not only complete it, but also participate in it: “Modi hai toh mumkin hai” (Modi makes it possible). At another juncture, the script exalts the Prime Minister for bringing about unprecedented progress in the country, children are then made to chant religious slogans like “Jai Sri Ram”.

BJP Leaders As Audience Members
The play, following this uniform script, was enacted by performers, students and children across the nation, often with the presence of several Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leaders in audience. ‘We Were Coerced Into Participating’
The play stirred a controversy at Kolkata’s Scottish Church College. Some members of the college’s drama club spoke out against the college authorities, alleging that they were being coerced into participating in this play.
A student, requesting anonymity, informed Alt News that in an online meeting between faculty members and students organised on the evening of September 24, the matter came to a head, with students allegedly being reprimanding for not agreeing to take any part in the play. “As students of a college as prestigious as ours — one that counts Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose among its distinguished alumni — we cannot compromise on our individual convictions of what is right and what is wrong. Students should not have to face any undue pressure simply for exercising their fundamental right to act according to their own conscience and free will,” they said.
Posters stuck on walls around the college area on the evening of September 28, upholding the ideals of free expression by students, were allegedly removed within half an hour of them being put up, college sources who spoke to Alt News claimed.
Ultimately, the play which was scheduled to take place on September 29 at Scottish Church was cancelled after several students protested, The Telegraph reported. The report also quoted the mother of a student as alleging that college adminstration was pressuring students as well as the teachers to “act in a propaganda play”. She told the news outlet: “This resistance means a lot. It will also send a strong message to heads of other colleges that they cannot force their students to act in a play against their will.”
However, Madhumanjari Mandal, the principal of the college, squarely denied the allegations that there was any degree of pressure was involved. “Acting in the play was voluntary,” she told The Telegraph.
‘Propaganda’ Masked As Cultural Event?
Anwesha Sengupta, author and assistant professor of history at Institute of Development Studies, Kolkata (ISDK), believes that these plays represent a more effective form of propaganda.
Speaking to Alt News, she said, “When children come across the mention of Prime Minister Narendra Modi in their textbooks, they consume it dispassionately. This is not the case with performing a script, where it gets more internalised, as it is a group activity.”
“The play is a part of the same machinery which has been in the making for years now, and which tries to project the Prime Minister as a God-like figure. Since these directives come through teachers, and children usually grow up revering and trusting their teachers, the move comes across as more immediate, as compared to encountering Modi in a curriculum text, which seems to have mandated from a more distant, abstract authority,” she added.
Another student from Scottish Church College told Alt News, “It is unbelievable that an event so overtly political in nature was even allowed to be organised by the college.”

How Ceuta, football and Israel are shaping Morocco's election
- Published
Disillusioned young voters in Morocco were courted with viral football slogans, promises of one million jobs and anti-Israel rallying calls ahead of Wednesday's parliamentary elections.
Yet, for many young Moroccans, politics remains deeply disconnected from reality.
"I have no hope for this election. I'm ashamed of our political scene. It's a complete circus," Siham Azeroual, 32, an environmental activist who lives in the Atlas region, tells the BBC.
The outcome of the vote will decide the make-up of the next government, just weeks after 60,000 people risked their lives to cross from the North African country to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta - a sign of the lack of opportunities many young people feel they have at home.
Morocco operates as a constitutional monarchy where political parties compete for 395 seats in the House of Representatives, the legislative chamber.
Yet executive power remains closely tied to the crown. King Mohammed VI, the 63-year-old monarch, appoints the prime minister from the political party that comes first in the election, but also presides over the Council of Ministers - the country's most important policy-making body.
The current campaign also follows a wave of Gen Z protests that erupted in September 2025 over unemployment, healthcare and living costs.
Demonstrators chanted slogans like "freedom, dignity, and social justice" which escalated to "get out Akhannouch", a reference to current Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch.
More than 2,400 people faced prosecution following the unrest. Despite the crackdown, some young activists are choosing to enter the political arena.
Hamza El Kharroubi, 29, was briefly arrested during the protests. He is now running for parliament with the little-known Environment and Sustainable Development Party, which has a green agenda.
"As a young person, I don't have much hope. I joined this party because they wanted more Gen Z faces and they are allowing us to speak freely about our demands," El Kharroubi tells the BBC.
He comes from Tetouan, just 34km (21 miles) from Fnideq beach, where the migration wave to Ceuta started in late July.
Some 60,000 people crossed, both Moroccans and other nationalities. At least 100 people died in the largest migration surge to the enclave in recent history.
"We want justice for the families of those who died crossing to Ceuta. We want compensation for their families," El Kharroubi says.
He argues that the crossing was widely linked to economic hardship and unemployment.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates overall unemployment stood at 13% last year, while youth unemployment - between the ages of 15 and 24 - reached 37.3%.
El Kharroubi says his goal is not to compete with established heavyweights - but securing a voice in parliament to build toward 2031.
"As young people, we have to enter the parliament so by 2031 we have strong young politicians who can compete for a seat in the government."
Fouzi Lekjaa, head of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation and a senior politician who works in the finance ministry, has emerged as the kingdom's newest political sensation - and a definite heavyweight.
Credited with helping the Atlas Lions - as the national men's football team is known - become global contenders, Lekjaa joined the centrist Party of Authenticity and Modernity (Pam) in July.
Videos of his campaign rallies have gone viral in the football-mad nation that is jointly hosting the next World Cup along with Spain and Portugal.
The clips show crowds chanting "Sir" which means "Go" in Moroccan Arabic - the iconic catchphrase from Morocco's historic 2022 World Cup run, when it became the first Arab and African side to make it to the semi-finals.
Lekjaa has promised to make Morocco sixth in the world in education and healthcare, to match the Fifa ranking of the men's football team.
Pam is competing against 26 other parties, including Prime Minister Akhannouch's National Rally of Independents (RNI). In its bid for a second term, RNI has renewed a pledge to create one million job opportunities by 2031.
Political expert Rachid Aourraz, from the Moroccan Institute for Policy Analysis (MIPA), remains sceptical about this promise.
"The slogan 'one million jobs' has become an overused electoral slogan. There is also talk of raising the minimum wage, but what is proposed cannot withstand a structural inability to create stable net jobs," Aourraz tells the BBC.
He adds that major parties "do not compete over an alternative model", but rather over how to implement public policies set by a royal vision.
Also seeking a political comeback is the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD) - using anti-Israeli sentiments to woo voters.
Morocco normalised ties with Israel in December 2020 along with several other Arab countries, under the US-brokered Abraham Accords.
Led by populist former Prime Minister Abdelilah Benkirane, the PJD is campaigning heavily on a promise to end diplomatic ties with Israel. He says the normalisation was a "mistake" made by his party which led the government between 2016 and 2021.
Bilateral ties were hit during the Gaza war with weekly protests taking place in the capital, Rabat, against the Israeli diplomatic presence.
During the conflict the Israeli liaison office was closed and direct flights between the two countries were suspended.
Yet despite an outpouring of pro-Palestinian protests, with tens of thousands taking to the streets and setting ablaze the Israeli flag at the height of the war, it was announced earlier this month that Israel and Morocco had agreed to open full embassies in their respective countries.
This followed a meeting between their top diplomats and the US ambassador to the United Nations.
"We have to speak up," Benkirane told supporters at a campaign rally in Marrakesh.
"If we work hard, the king will close the Israeli embassy. The king does not like going against his own people," he added, warning of "the dangers of Israel and Zionism in Morocco".
I think young people should focus on the microscale: rather than running for office, helping build communities and connecting with people and then building up to the top"
More than half of Morocco's total population of roughly 38.8 million is under the age of 35 - though only 4% of the more than 15.8 million registered voters are aged between 18 and 24.
"I am not keeping up much with the campaigns - but I noticed the same faces as usual," says Hiba, a 27-year-old Moroccan living in Canada who preferred not to use her last name.
She lives in Montreal which has a large Moroccan diaspora of about 104,000 people, according to the 2016 census.
Many of last year's Gen Z protests were more vocal outside the country, where young Moroccans were able to express their anger without fear of repercussions.
Hiba, who co-organised several Gen Z protests in Montreal, says she would have considered voting had she been able to find a proxy in Morocco - which is how those in the diaspora can cast their ballot.
"Gen Z protests didn't go in vain. We achieved something. At least now we see more debates with young people on state TV," she says.
Azeroual, the environmental activist, agrees.
But having lived through both the 20 February movement in 2011 that changed the constitution and the recent Gen Z movement, she believes change must come from a multi-faceted approach.
"I think young people should focus on the microscale - rather than running for office, helping build communities and connecting with people and then building up to the top," she says.
Despite not being fully convinced by any political campaign, she says she will be heading to her local polling station to cast her ballot.

The Nobel Prize for Physiology for 2026 was awarded to scientists Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for “discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics,” the award-giving body said on Monday (October 5, 2026).
Karl Deisseroth, a 54-year-old American, Hegemann, a 71-year-old German, and Georg Nagel, a 73-year-old German, were selected by the Nobel Assembly of Sweden’s Karolinska Institute medical university and receive a prize sum amounting to 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million), which is shared if there are multiple winners.
Optogenetics “makes it possible to switch on, or off, the activity of individual nerve cells in a living brain,” the prize-givers said.
“This method is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain’s mysteries.”
Last year, US scientists Mary E. Brunkow and Fred Ramsdell, and Japanese scientist Shimon Sakaguchi won the prize for their discovery of regulatory T cells. Their discovery has helped blaze new paths into treating cancer as well as auto-immune disease – a condition by which the immune system ends up harming healthy cells they are meant to protect.
The announcement of medicine Nobel kicks off the Nobel announcement week with physics being announced on October 6, followed by chemistry, literature, and peace. The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences, popularly known as Economics Nobel will be announced on October 12.
The winners will get a cash award of 10 million Swedish kronor (nearly $900,000) and the award will be presented on December 10, the Nobel Prize day.
The Nobel Prize was created by Swedish inventor Alfred Nobel, who in his will dictated that his estate should be used to fund “prizes to those who, during the preceding year, have conferred the greatest benefit to humankind”. December 10 is Nobel’s death anniversary.

The deposed Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, have been indicted for alleged conspiracy to commit torture, according to Manhattan federal court papers unsealed on Thursday.
The superseding indictment was unsealed shortly before Flores appeared at court in her ongoing push for pre-trial release – which was denied by Judge Alvin Hellerstein. Maduro and Flores have been held in a New York City jail since early January.
They were captured in a US military operation and transported to New York to face “narcoterrorism” charges in a move that sparked widespread international outrage. Maduro and Flores have previously pleaded not guilty in the criminal case against them.
CNN on Wednesday first reported that a new indictment was expected.
The new charging document described how Maduro and his wife allegedly used horrific tactics to suppress opposition and maintain their control.
They presided “over a system of repression that relied on violence against political opposition, arbitrary detention, and the torture of detainees, including United States citizens”, the charging document said.
“That torture included electric shock, asphyxiation, rape, forced nudity, prolonged isolation, starvation, punishment cells, and psychological torture, such as threats to harm and kill victims’ families, including children,” it added.
Maduro and Flores, the new indictment alleged, “sat atop that violent power structure”.
Flores was integral to this effort, authorities claimed, saying she “helped develop this system of repression and ordered that individuals be tortured to protect her family members’ illegal activities”.
The victims of their torture included US citizens “who were believed to pose a threat” to Maduro’s power.
“One particular United States citizen was detained in Venezuela and subjected to, among other things, deprivation of food and water, simulated drowning, repeated beatings, electric shock to his testicles, and forced injections.”
Amid news of this new indictment, Flores’s attorneys argued for her release, pitching house arrest guarded by 24-hour private security. In doing so, they invoked chronic health issues, including cardiac infirmities.
Hellerstein pushed back on this claim, noting that Flores was refusing to have catheterization while detained in general population.
“I’ve undergone it, so I know what it is,” Hellerstein said, noting that it was generally an outpatient procedure. “There’s no pain. There’s no general anesthesia.”
Flores’s attorney then pointed to her high blood pressure. “It’s controllable by pills,” Hellerstein said.
Her team also said in court that Flores dropped more than 25lb and lost two teeth since her detention.
“For whatever it’s worth, her appearance today is no worse than, and perhaps a little better, than when I first met with her [at] her arraignment,” Hellerstein said. Flores’s lawyer said that during her arraignment she was “still bandaged up” from her rough arrest. 
The US attorney’s office for the southern district of New York opposed Flores’s now-failed bail request. They argued in court and legal filings that Flores presented an “extreme risk of flight and danger to the public”. Prosecutors also insisted that she had received adequate medical care.
Donald Trump has defended the controversial raid to Maduro, insisting it was a “surgical law enforcement operation”. At Maduro’s first US court appearance, he said: “I’m a kidnapped president – a prisoner of war!”
The Associated Press contributed reporting

As soon as I learned what business-class life was like, I never wanted to go back. Now, my husband and I use credit-card points to get the experience whenever we can, especially on long-haul overnight flights.
That's mainly because the lie-flat seat is an absolute game changer, and I was especially looking forward to it when my husband and I booked Virgin Atlantic upper class aboard a 787-9 Dreamliner from Los Angeles to London this summer.
It's a leg and an airline I'd flown before, so I knew all the perks of this airline's version of business class. I also knew one thing I probably wouldn't love as much as the other posh details of the flying experience: the seat.
Unlike most business-class seats I've experienced — I'm fortunate to have flown long-haul business class on about 10 different airlines — Virgin Atlantic's doesn't smoothly recline all the way from upright to lie-flat.
Instead, it's a seat or a bed. When you're ready to sleep, you get up, and a flight attendant flips the seat over and makes it up with bedding. It's pretty seamless, but I still find the setup a bit cumbersome. I'd rather just be able to gradually recline into a comfortable lounging position.
Nevertheless, I tried to head into this flight with an open mind.
For this overnight flight, I had a window seat
Our overnight flight from LAX to London Heathrow was scheduled to take 10 hours and 25 minutes.
I was traveling with my husband while our kids were in summer camp (a rare grown-ups-only escape!), and we'd booked an upper-class seat configuration that was both interesting and slightly awkward for a couple.
This part of the plane has a 1-1-1 configuration, and every seat has direct aisle access, which is a great perk. However, I was seated by the window, and my husband was across from me in the middle section of the partially herringbone-style cabin.
I liked that I could see him from my seat, but we were foot-to-foot across the aisle, so our heads weren't actually close enough to have a conversation without one of us standing up.
We could've been physically closer together, separated only by a short wall, if he'd been in a window seat behind or in front of me, but those seats weren't available when we booked.
My seat had another quirk: Because of the seat position relative to the window, I had to turn and look backward to see out of it, which felt a bit strange and awkward.
The seat was comfy, but I still wish it seamlessly flowed between upright and lie-flat positions
The seat itself was comfortable, with plenty of room (up to 22 inches wide, according to Virgin Atlantic). And once it was made up into a lie-flat bed, I found it plenty comfortable to sleep on.
My issue wasn't with the seat's comfort so much as how it functioned.
In most business-class seats I've flown, I can use the controls to find exactly the position I want: upright for eating or working, partially reclined for watching a movie, and fully flat when I'm ready to sleep.
This setup did not offer that same range with ease.
The seat does recline — it adjusts between 17 and 42 degrees, according to Virgin Atlantic — but beyond that, getting it fully flat required me to get up. In the slightly inconvenient manual process, the padded back flips toward the footrest area.
I appreciated that a flight attendant handled the seat conversion and added the bedding while I was in the bathroom, giving the whole process a hotel-like, service-oriented feel.
However, I like to lounge somewhere between sitting and sleeping throughout a long flight, so I missed being able to gradually recline all the way down whenever I wanted to rest.
I've encountered a similarly unconventional seat with only one other airline, and it's simply not my preference.
The food and service felt top-tier
As a vegetarian, I find that airline meals can sometimes feel like an afterthought, but I've found Virgin Atlantic's upper-class options to be flavorful and thoughtfully presented.
This time, I had a hearty tomato-based pasta for dinner. On past upper-class flights, I've had dishes like warm tofu rice bowls and vegetable gyozas, and the food has felt approachable and tasty rather than overly elaborate for the sake of seeming luxurious.
The service has similarly struck the right balance for me: attentive but relaxed, which fits the airline's personality.
Everything on board felt stylish and fun
The seat may not be my favorite, but Virgin Atlantic's overall vibe is what sets the airline apart.
Upper class felt polished without feeling stuffy at all. The cabin looked sleek, with distinctive purplish mood lighting and a playful personality overall.
Even tiny details have character. The meal service included airplane-shaped salt-and-pepper shakers, which have become favorites among Virgin Atlantic flyers.
The airline's upper class also has a social component that's unusual in commercial aviation. Rather than treating the cabin exclusively as a collection of individual seats, Virgin Atlantic incorporates spaces where passengers can get up, have a drink, or socialize.
Yes, there was an actual bar at the back end of the upper-class section on this flight — and, of course, drinks and snacks were all included, as they would be at my seat.
It was fun to see a cabin crew member pouring drinks at the bar on my way onto the plane, but I'm usually sleeping rather than chatting over drinks when I fly.
Passengers may not be able to enjoy these for much longer, though — the airline has announced plans to remove its in-flight bars in the next few years to make room for more premium seats.
All in all, I'd happily fly in Virgin Atlantic's upper class again
For me, the seat style is a bit of a drawback. However, a flight experience is about much more than only the seat.
Sure, business class is always a splurge — especially on long-haul flights — but this airline tends to offer good value for miles, in my experience.
I also appreciated that the experience didn't seem to take itself too seriously. Business class can sometimes feel formal, whereas Virgin Atlantic manages to make a premium cabin feel genuinely fun.
After more than 10 hours aboard, I came away with the same impression I've had of Virgin Atlantic before: It's stylish without being overly serious, the food is good, the service is warm, and the entire experience has personality that sets a fab vacation vibe right away.
I definitely expect to fly upper class with this airline again — and I look forward to it. Plus, Virgin Atlantic has announced plans to completely refurbish the cabins on its 787-9 fleet (including this plane) around early 2028, so I look forward to eventually trying the new version of this class, too.
Virgin Atlantic declined to comment.

D2C lifestyle startup DailyObjects has raised ₹332 Cr ($34.3 Mn) in a Series C funding round co-led by Xponentia Capital Partners, Anicut Capital and Axiom Asia Private Capital. The round, which included both primary and secondary transactions, valued the startup at ₹1,050 Cr ($108.4 Mn).
As part of the secondary deal, DailyObjects’ early investor Roots Ventures partially exited with a 18X return on its initial investment.
Roots Ventures first invested $2 Mn in DailyObjects in February 2022. Following which, the investor doubled down on the startup during its $10 Mn Series B funding round in 2024.
The fresh funds will allow DailyObjects, which is known for its lifestyle and tech accessories like phone cases, watchbands, bags, wallets and wireless chargers, to scale its offline network, deepen its product and R&D capabilities, strengthen brand building and evaluate opportunities in international markets.
As part of the expansion of DailyObjects’ physical retail network, it plans to build 150 exclusive brand outlets (EBOs) across India over the next five years.

The European Union on Wednesday called on Russia to "share timely and transparent reporting" about the death of a plague laboratory technician in Siberia.
"We think that it's necessary to have reliable epidemiological and microbiological findings," European Commission spokeswoman Eva Hrncirova said.
The EU is in contact with experts from the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control on the matter, she said, adding "we follow the situation very closely".
Russian news outlet People of Baikal reported Friday that a 28-year-old woman employed at a plague research institute in Siberia's Irkutsk region had died of the disease -- possibly after contracting it from a broken test tube.
Russian authorities have played down the reports, saying the cause of the woman's death was not confirmed and denying they are imposing anti-plague measures.

Satellite images show attack jets stationed at a new Chinese military facility in Laos, which opened last week and gives Beijing’s air force its first foothold in mainland south-east Asia.
Images provided by the commercial satellite provider Vantor show eight light attack aircraft positioned at Ban Keun airport alongside what appear to be more than a dozen military vehicles lined up in rows.
The planes’ shape matches that of the Chinese-made Hongdu JL-8 jet, a two-seat trainer that can be deployed in combat to carry bombs. Laos is reported to have four such aircraft, according to the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies.
In a rare example of Beijing’s overseas military expansion, China opened what it said was a joint “support and training centre” at Ban Keun on 29 September.
The airport, about 30 miles (50km) north of Vientiane, the capital of Laos, has been significantly expanded over the past year. Satellite images taken months ago show farmland and dirt paths where there are now new buildings and a paved runway.
Aside from its island bases in the South China Sea, Beijing does not have a significant network of military outposts in other countries, and the Laos airbase would be its first facility in another country capable of handling fighter jets.
The new satellite images, taken a day after the announcement and first reported by Reuters, show extensive construction work that appears to be focused on a future runway extension, which could make the airport capable of handling larger planes such as bombers.
In its announcement last week, China’s defence ministry said the new centre would “help Laos strengthen the training of its air force pilots” and was not “directed against any third party”.
Governments will be watching closely for signs of deployments or the installation of defence equipment that may serve wider military ambitions. After the announcement, the Singapore-based security analyst Collin Koh said it “may not be wrong to conclude this is the first full-fledged PLA [People’s Liberation Army] overseas base in south-east Asia”.
Over the past two decades, China has built up an extensive network of outposts on islands in the disputed South China Sea, including airbases with air defence installations. Otherwise, its navy’s sole overseas military base is a logistics base in Djibouti, on the coast of the Horn of Africa.
The Laos agreement follows a similar programme established in Cambodia, at the Ream naval base on the Gulf of Thailand, although that facility has no runway.
After years of speculation and denials, China announced in April last year that it had created the “joint logistics and training” facility in Cambodia. It said the centre would support the two militaries in “conducting regional counter-terrorism, disaster prevention and mitigation, humanitarian assistance, joint training and other operations”.
US forces are believed to have used Ban Keun airport in Laos during covert military operations at the height of the Vietnam war in the 1960s and 1970s. Its development will be monitored by Vietnam, which maintains disputes with China over the South China Sea, and Thailand, which shares a border with Laos.
After the announcement last week, Thailand’s defence ministry spokesperson said Bangkok considered itself a close partner of both Laos and China and saw it as Vientiane’s sovereign right to decide whether to grant permission for a Chinese base.
“Nevertheless, Thailand will continue to closely monitor developments and how the matter proceeds, particularly with regard to building mutual trust,” said R Adm Surasant Kongsiri.
China’s government did not mention sending aircraft to Laos in its initial announcement, while the government of Laos has not commented on the project.
The US-based Institute for the Study of War has described the Laos base as the “first PLA overseas military facility focused on air power”. In its assessment, the thinktank said the base was “not yet equipped to provide the PLA with the ability to execute major combat operations, unlike US military bases”.
It said the base would give the Chinese military alternate routes to access to the South China Sea and strategic air routes.
Reuters contributed to this report

Syrian general accused of atrocities is protected by U.S. and Lebanon, NPR and BBC find
NPR partnered with BBC Radio 4 to follow reporter Josh Baker and Sara Obeidat as they traveled through a changing country to attempt to uncover the truth about what happened to American journalist Austin Tice. Listen to the podcast in the NPR app.
A former Syrian general facing U.S. sanctions and wanted internationally for crimes against humanity is living quietly in Lebanon, bankrolled and protected by American and Lebanese authorities, a joint BBC and NPR investigation has found.
Bassam al-Hassan, who oversaw Syria's chemical weapons program and was a senior advisor to former President Bashar al-Assad, moved to Beirut after fleeing Syria following the Assad regime's collapse in 2024.
An investigation by the BBC and NPR has found that Hassan has been allowed to remain there under an arrangement involving the FBI and other U.S. and Lebanese authorities.
This is at least partly because of his willingness to provide information about the abduction of American journalist Austin Tice in Syria in 2012, as well as additional intelligence, according to four sources familiar with the arrangement who asked to remain anonymous because of threats to their livelihood and safety.
As part of a years-long investigation featured in the new NPR's Embedded and BBC series called Where is Austin Tice? the BBC has reviewed a detailed record of a meeting between Hassan, representatives of the FBI and CIA, and Lebanese security officials, where Tice's case is discussed.
In it, Hassan is offered "residency," "protection," and help securing his "living needs."
Sources with knowledge of the arrangement described how Hassan receives money through an intermediary, making it harder to trace.
Officials from two different branches of Syria's new government, who requested anonymity because they are unauthorized to speak to the press about this case, have told NPR and the BBC they want Hassan returned to Syria to face trial but that U.S. authorities want him kept in Beirut, and they say there is little Damascus can do about this.
When reporters for the BBC reached Hassan by phone last year to ask for an interview, he directed them to seek permission for him to speak from "the FBI and CIA officials at the [U.S.] embassy."
Asked for comment, officials with the CIA and Lebanon's security agency, the General Directorate of General Security, did not respond. The FBI declined to comment and instead pointed to a past statement that said its focus remained on establishing the facts around the Tice case and securing his return.
In response to our findings, Phil Elwood, spokesperson for the Tice family, said:
"If what you are saying is true, the fact that our tax dollars are being used to furnish a comfortable life for someone associated with the use of chemical weapons on Syrian civilians, who claims to have had Austin Tice executed, is offensive. This is nothing less than aiding and abetting the escape of a wanted war criminal. The Syrians deserve justice, and he should be returned to stand trial."
Hassan is under sanctions from the U.S. Treasury Department for his role in the Assad government, where, in addition to running the chemical weapons program, he served as a top adviser to the president.
Last month NPR and the BBC reported Tice's abduction had been a planned operation, with Hassan in the chain of command. Since his disappearance, Tice has been the subject of one of the American government's most high-profile missing persons cases, with presidents Biden and Trump both discussing it publicly and sending teams to the Middle East to negotiate with Syrian officials.
Hassan is not the only Syrian regime official connected to the Tice case who claims to receive financial payments or assistance for living abroad. Two others spoke on condition of anonymity, saying they feared for their safety if they spoke publicly.
One former regime member said he had received money from the FBI multiple times in exchange for his cooperation on Tice's case. It was "not in my interest to share all the information all at once," he told the BBC and NPR, "in order to be able to drag out how long I can continue to receive payments from them."
Another former regime member connected to Tice's case, who spoke by phone with the BBC, claimed he was living in Lebanon under the "patronage" of U.S. authorities, citing this as the reason he could not speak about Tice.
The BBC spoke to a former senior Lebanese intelligence official on condition of anonymity, because he is not authorized to speak publicly about intelligence matters of this nature and due to the sensitivity of the Tice case. He confirmed that Lebanese intelligence does have arrangements with the Americans and that payments have and do take place when both agencies have overlap in cases, but he said he had no knowledge of payments involving the Austin Tice case.
Following the fall of the Assad regime in early December 2024, Hassan initially escaped to Iran. A Syrian businessman, with strong connections to both the former regime and the Lebanese authorities, told the BBC that negotiations had then taken place to bring Hassan to Lebanon.
The businessman, who asked to remain anonymous to speak candidly, said Hassan was valuable, not only because of what he is believed to know about Austin Tice, but because of his knowledge of Syria's chemical weapons program and its military relationship with Iran.
Austin Tice's mother, Debra, told the BBC that an official with the FBI had informed her Hassan was in Beirut, and that they had spoken to him. In May 2025, she flew to Lebanon to attempt to meet Hassan but was unsuccessful.
At the time, she told NPR and the BBC: "I don't want to interrogate him. I don't want to berate him, I don't want to scold him. That's not my job. I want to know about my son."
Hassan told U.S. investigators last year that Tice had been executed on former President Assad's orders, the BBC reported, but several people with knowledge of the investigation have questioned the details of his account. Hassan has provided a potential location for Tice's remains. But according to multiple sources with knowledge of the case, who were granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak about it, the site was searched and nothing was found — casting doubt on the validity of some of Hassan's information.
There are questions, however, about how thoroughly the site was searched. Two sources who said they had intimate knowledge of the operation told the BBC that U.S. authorities stopped digging before the search had been completed, possibly because of security concerns.
Other Syrian officials connected to the Tice case have also apparently found refuge abroad.
Mohammad Makhlouf, a senior officer at the facility where Tice was detained and who took part in a staged abduction video of Tice, is residing in Lebanon. Sakr Rustom, who is connected to Austin Tice's abduction and is the nephew of Bassam al Hassan, was contacted by the BBC in the United Arab Emirates. When asked about Tice's case, Rustom said he "preferred to focus on matters of the future."
Ghassan Nassour, a former general in Syria's Republican Guard, is said by former members of the National Defense Forces to have presided over the jail Tice was held in, and is living in the United Arab Emirates with his family.

Ola Electric’s ₹1,000 Cr rights issue is set to open for subscription onOctober 22 and close on October 30, its board of directors finalised today. The last date for on-market renunciation of rights entitlements has been set at October 26. At an issue price of ₹27 per share, the company expects to raise ₹999.74 Cr, assuming full subscription and payment of call monies. To note, the issue price is set at a discount of over 5% to Ola Electric's closing price today (₹36.30). The rights issue will comprise 37.03 Cr partly paid-up equity shares with a face value of ₹10 each. Shareholders will be entitled to two rights shares for every 25 fully paid-up equity shares held as of the record date of October 13. The ₹27 issue price includes a ₹17 premium. Shareholders will have to pay ₹16.20 per share, or 60% of the issue price, on application. The remaining ₹10.80 per share will be payable through a first and final call. The company's board approved the rights issue on September 28. Following that, founder and CMD Bhavish Aggarwal pledged a 4.32% stake in the electric two-wheeler maker to fund his participation in the rights issue. Ola Electric plans to split the proceeds between debt reduction, business expansion and general corporate requirements. The company has earmarked ₹350 Cr for repaying or prepaying borrowings at Ola Electric and its material subsidiaries. The allocation will also cover accrued interest and any applicable prepayment penalties. A larger ₹400 Cr will be directed towards organic growth, with the company planning to invest across its electric mobility and energy storage businesses. The spending will include manufacturing, R&D, stores and dealerships, service infrastructure, as well as sales and marketing. The balance of the proceeds will be available for general corporate purposes. Ola Electric expects to utilise the funds during FY27 and FY28. This would be the second fundraise for Ola Electric within 2026. The company raised ₹780.24 Cr via a qualified institutional placement (QIP) earlier in June. Meanwhile, on the financial front, Ola Electric managed to trim its net loss for the June quarter (Q1 FY27) by 22% to ₹336 Cr from ₹428 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Operating revenue declined 45% to ₹455 Cr from ₹828 Cr in Q1 FY26.

Amid protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, the Centre has upgraded his existing Z+ security cover, Hindustan Times reported.
The move comes after protesters reached near Kumar’s residence in Delhi, while another demonstration was held outside his family home in Agra, according to NDTV.
Officials cited by HT said the security enhancement followed a fresh assessment of the threat perception.
More personnel have reportedly been deployed outside the CEC’s residence, at the Election Commission office and as part of his personal security detail.
A senior police officer told HT that protesters had managed to trace Kumar’s residence in Delhi, while another protest was held outside his family home in Agra.
“We had to assess all the threats and increase the security cover. We had also placed a few pickets near his house,” the officer said, as quoted by the publication.
The security upgrade comes as the Congress and Opposition INDIA bloc continue to demand Kumar’s resignation over alleged irregularities in the SIR exercise.
Congress leader Rahul Gandhi said the Opposition would continue its protests against the Election Commission’s actions.
“To save the Constitution and democracy, the Congress Party and the opposition are ready to take to the streets as many times as needed, face arrests, or endure legal cases,” Gandhi said in a post on X.
The development comes as the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) is also preparing to protest against Kumar. The CJP on Wednesday called for a united mobilization ahead of its 10 October protest, saying the “prolonged agitation” would continue until the electoral system is overhauled, The Hindu reported.
Earlier, the group also backed the 6 October protest march by INDIA bloc MPs towards the Election Commission office, describing the confrontation as part of a broader campaign to defend democracy and the Constitution.
The CJP has also called for the repeal of the 2023 law governing appointments to the Election Commission and demanded an independent selection process for election commissioners.
The Opposition’s criticism of Kumar has intensified following an Indian Express report that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had, on record, objected at least 14 times over the past 10 months to decisions and orders related to the SIR process, which they said were issued without their knowledge or recommendation.
Z+ is the highest category of general VIP security cover provided by the Government of India to individuals assessed to face a severe and credible threat to their lives.
The level of protection is not fixed permanently.
Security cover is reviewed periodically based on threat assessments, and the number of people receiving different categories of central security cover can change accordingly, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA).
The Centre determines security arrangements based on threat perception assessments prepared by central intelligence and security agencies, including the Intelligence Bureau, as per the MHA.
Z+ protection involves a large, round-the-clock security detail covering the protectee’s residence, workplace, movements and travel routes.
Such protection is generally provided by specialized units of the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) and other Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs), according to The Print.
The deployment can include armed personnel stationed at the protectee’s residence and workplace, escort teams during movement and personnel responsible for access control and route security.

The National Medical Commission (NMC) has brought the promotion of doctors and hospitals and how they attract patients online under the ambit of medical ethics, prohibiting paid rankings, fake reviews, referral fees, misleading claims and the use of artificial intelligence (AI) to create or manipulate patient testimonials.
The Ethics and Medical Registration Board’s Guidelines on Ethical Advertising and Public Communication by Hospitals/Medical Institutions and Registered Medical Practitioners, issued on October 6, apply to communication through websites, social media, messaging platforms, podcasts, sponsored content, influencers and online platforms. The guidelines have come into effect immediately.
The guidelines prohibit registered medical practitioners (RMPs) and hospitals from making claims such as “best”, “No. 1”, “leading”, “most trusted”, “top” or “unmatched”, unless these can be objectively verified through a transparent and independently ascertainable methodology. Any ranking or award used in advertising must also be independently verifiable, with relevant details disclosed where necessary to prevent the public from being misled.
Online promotion targeted
The NMC has specifically addressed online promotion. RMPs and hospitals cannot procure or manipulate fake followers, likes, reviews, ratings, testimonials, comments, views or other digital engagement. They cannot manipulate search rankings, visibility or algorithms to create a misleading impression of their professional standing.
The guidelines also target financial incentives for bringing in patients. An RMP cannot offer, pay, solicit or receive a commission, rebate, bonus, gift, gratuity, referral fee, lead-generation fee or other consideration connected with the referral, recommendation or procurement of patients, specimens or materials for diagnosis or treatment.
Advertising agencies, digital marketing agencies, influencers and online platforms cannot be engaged in a manner in which payment is linked to the procurement or referral of individual patients.
On patient testimonials
Patient testimonials have also come under specific restrictions. An RMP cannot use or permit a celebrity, influencer, patient, employee or other third party to promote professional services through prohibited testimonials, endorsements or recommendations. The guidelines also prohibit RMPs from requesting or sharing patient testimonials, recommendations, endorsements or reviews for professional promotion on social media.
The guidelines prohibit the use of AI to create or manipulate patient testimonials and other promotional material in a manner that misrepresents treatment, outcomes or professional standing. The provisions also cover manipulation of patient images or voices and synthetic endorsements presented as though they came from actual patients or professionals.
The NMC has also specified what doctors and hospitals can communicate. “Hospitals can provide factual information about their location, departments, facilities, equipment, emergency services, accreditation, services and fees. Doctors can provide factual professional information and participate in public-health and educational communication, provided it does not become prohibited promotion,” it said.
Discounts, limited-period offers, contests, coupons, gifts, cashbacks, referral benefits and free procedures are also prohibited where they are likely to encourage unnecessary consultation, diagnostic investigation or treatment. Lawful disclosure of fees and packages can be made if it is factual, transparent and not misleading.
The guidelines prescribe graded disciplinary action against RMPs. A first violation can attract a warning and mandatory ethics training; a second can result in censure and a monetary penalty; and a third can lead to suspension of registration for three to six months. Serious violations can attract suspension for six to 12 months, while repeated violations can result in removal from the medical register for one to three years.
For hospitals and medical institutions, the applicable penalty and appellate mechanism under the Clinical Establishments Act or the relevant State law will apply. Where an RMP has authorised, participated in or endorsed prohibited communication, the doctor’s professional conduct can separately be examined by the appropriate medical regulatory authority.
The guidelines have been issued in the context of a writ petition before the Supreme Court and the existing framework governing professional conduct.

Nobel Prize in chemistry set to be awarded in Stockholm
Scientists Henri B
STOCKHOLM -- Scientists Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai won the Nobel Prize in chemistry Wednesday for untangling mysterious mirror images in molecules, a discovery that has been used to develop countless drugs and transformed modern medicine.
Many molecules come in versions that look alike but are not exactly identical, like right and left hands. Kagan, who is from France, and Soai, from Japan, found ways to make chemistry pick a side, describing and designing reactions to produce the desired mirror image.
“The medicines we have today would not be possible without this chemistry,” said Rigoberto Hernandez, president of the American Chemical Society.
Soai was shopping at a neighborhood supermarket when he heard he had won.
“I’m very excited to receive the very nice news,” Soai told the Nobel committee and journalists by phone. “Of course, this is one of the most exciting days in my life.”
Mirror images of the same molecule can have different properties. For example, one version of the chemical carvone smells like mint, while the other has a whiff of caraway, a spice often used in rye bread.
The alternate versions can also behave differently when interacting with other chemicals. When designing drugs to treat diseases, scientists are choosy about which mirror image they use. They want the version of a molecule to treat a cold, not one that will make the sniffles worse.
In the 1980s, Kagan’s work showed there might be a way to design reactions to produce one form of a molecule over the other. Years later, Soai perfected the process. He created the first-ever chemical reaction to efficiently produce only one of a molecule’s mirror images, in what’s now known as the Soai reaction.
“This is probably the coolest experiment in organic chemistry,” said Peter Somfai, a member of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry.
Kagan, 95, is affiliated with the Université Paris-Sud in Orsay, France. Soai, 76, is affiliated with the Tokyo University of Science. The Nobel committee described their work as a feat never previously achieved by anyone “other than life itself.”
The French Academy of Sciences, where Kagan is a member, congratulated him, as did French President Emmanuel Macron, who called the prize “an immense source of pride for the country” and “a recognition befitting a lifetime of research.”
“It might be difficult to say that this drug, or that drug, was developed using this,” Somfai said. “I would say all of them, because we use this as a tool, we use this as an understanding, how to develop catalysts, how they function.”
Life, too, prefers one mirror image over the other. DNA twists to the right, and the proteins in human bodies are made of mostly left-handed building blocks.
In addition to developing better medicines or perfumes, deciphering the mirror images of molecules can help scientists understand the chemical architecture of life, said chemist Holden Thorp, editor-in-chief of the journal Science.
“There are still fascinating aspects that remain unknown and surely more yet to be discovered,” Soai said at a news conference hosted by his university in Tokyo. "I hope to do what I can, however modestly, to contribute to help advance research in this field."
Japan’s largest newspaper, Yomiuri, distributed an extra edition with a headline proclaiming “Nobel Prize Mr. Soai,” with a big photo of the scientist. The papers quickly disappeared as office workers picked them up on their way home.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winner in Stockholm.
Last year, three scientists won the chemistry Nobel for their development of new molecular structures that can trap vast quantities of gas inside, laying the groundwork to potentially suck greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere or harvest moisture from desert environments.
This year's prizes began with the Nobel for medicine, awarded Monday to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works. The physics award announced Tuesday recognized a scientist's efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos.
The literature prize is set to be awarded Thursday. After Friday’s peace prize is awarded, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, a small group of laureates or an organization.
___
This story has been corrected to correct that Kagan, not Soai, is 95.
___
Ramakrishnan reported from New York. Dazio reported from Berlin. Associated Press journalists Alexa St. John in Detroit, Catherine Gaschka in Paris and Mari Yamaguchi in Tokyo contributed to this report.
