Consumer electronics manufacturer Lumio raised $12 Mn (around ₹102.5 Cr) in a Series A funding round led by Blume Ventures, with participation from existing backers Stellaris Venture Partners and 3one4 Capital. “This funding gives us the opportunity to invest further in our products and software, explore new categories, and strengthen quality and after-sales support as we grow,” said cofounder Raghu Reddy in a social media post. The startup also plans to expand its retail presence, enabling customers to see and try its products offline before making a purchase. “India’s 3-3.5 Cr affluent households are reimagining their living rooms, and no longer default to legacy brands. Raghu and Kailash have leveraged their deep experience in home entertainment and customer insights to create a compelling home entertainment brand in Lumio,” said Sajith Pai, partner, Blume Ventures. Established in 2024 by ex-Xiaomi India CBO Reddy and ex-Flipkart exec Kailash Sankaranarayanan, Lumio launched its first smart TV lineup in early 2025 and has since expanded its hardware portfolio to include projectors and speakers. Aside from its catalogue, it has also created an AI-powered personalised content discovery engine called TLDR backed by multiple patent filings and available in nine Indian languages. The brand aims to leverage software as its differentiator from legacy electronics makers. To enhance speed and performance of their smart TVs, Lumio also compliments its products with high-performance SoC for rapid app launches, ample RAM to prevent slowdowns during multitasking, and a fine-tuned network chipset for stable connectivity in variable Indian internet conditions. Lumio currently claims to serve over 35,000 households across 5,000+ pin codes. It claims to have crossed ₹100 Cr in GMV within 13 months of commercial sales, more than tripling its GMV YoY for the April-August period in 2026.. Prior to this, it had raised a $4.3 Mn seed funding round in July 2024 from Stellaris Venture Partners, 3one4 Capital, Mamaearth’s Varun Alagh, and Tracxn’s Abhishek Goyal, as well as other angel investors. The startup competes with established players like Samsung, LG, Sony, and Xiaomi in India’s consumer electronics market, which is estimated to grow at 6.6% CAGR over the next eight years to reach $158.4 Bn by 2034.

The death of a laboratory worker in Siberia on October 2, 2026, and the subsequent quarantine of dozens of people have sparked concerns about a pneumonic plague epidemic, with Russia revealing little information publicly. The incident has revived memories of the COVID-19 pandemic and allegations that the coronavirus may have emerged at a Chinese lab.
What happened at the Siberia lab?
The 28-year-old woman, Darya Shipilova, employed at a research institute in Siberia, fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances, prompting authorities to quarantine dozens of people and dispatch the head of Russia’s health watchdog to the Irkutsk region.
The woman worked at the anti-plague research institute in the city of Irkutsk, where the plague occurs naturally in wild animals. She died at a hospital in nearby Shelekhov that the mayor said had been placed under quarantine. Following the incident, top Russian health officials have travelled to the region.
Russian authorities say the lab worker died of what initially presented as a “typical” acute respiratory viral infection.
Russia dismisses epidemic concerns
Meanwhile, Russia’s health regulator insists there were no risks of an epidemic breaking out in Siberia after the plague institute worker’s death.
Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s health watchdog, said on October 7 that it was winding down precautionary measures it had put in place after concluding there was no risk of an epidemic.
No cases of plague had been detected among anyone who had come into contact with the deceased worker, it said, while adding that 90% of those placed in quarantine had been released after nearly 5,000 lab tests had failed to detect any dangerous pathogens.
When asked about a second person in Siberia allegedly falling ill, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged caution against using media reports as a reference for what was happening.
‘Causative agent behind death not known’
A top official with the World Health Organisation (WHO) said it doesn’t know how the lab worker in Siberia died. Maria Van Kerkhove, WHO director of Epidemic and Pandemic Management, said the UN health agency doesn’t know what the “causative agent’ was behind the woman’s October 2 death.
She has urged Russia to provide more information about the incident that prompted global concerns about suspected pneumonic plague. The WHO initially said it estimated the risk of the Russia case to the public as low, but told a press conference on October 7 it could not make a fuller risk assessment due to insufficient information from the Russian authorities.
What is pneumonic plague, symptoms
Reports blamed the woman’s death on pneumonic plague — a less common but severe form of plague that can spread from person to person.
Pneumonic plague causes a severe form of pneumonia, but recovery rates are high if it is detected and treated in time. The severe disease is less common than the better-known bubonic plague linked to the Black Death in the Middle Ages.
Pneumonic plague and bubonic plague are caused by the same bacteria. The former is spread by respiratory particles while the latter is spread through bites from fleas that have jumped from infected rodents.
Symptoms of pneumonic plague include shortness of breath and coughing-up blood, and they can occur in as little as 24 hours after exposure, according to the WHO. If untreated, the illness can be fatal.
Not linked to a biological weapon
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Wednesday (October 8) that the death of the Russian plague laboratory worker did not appear to be linked to a biological weapon.
Mr. Trump said Russia insisted it had the situation under control, but added that not much information was coming out. He, however, said that the United States will help Russia over the incident.
The European Union has also called on Russia to “share timely and transparent reporting” about the death of the plague laboratory technician.

Every piece of AI content from Google’s Gemini models has a hidden SynthID label, which makes it very difficult to pass the content off as authentic. SynthID has also gotten buy-in from other major AI players, but actually checking for those invisible watermarks has been a convoluted process. It’s going to be a little easier going forward, though. Google has announced that its SynthID detector now supports watermarks from all its partners, and it’s available for anyone to use on a new dedicated website.
SynthID is an invisible signal encoded in the pixels of AI-generated images and videos, and in the waveform of AI audio. Google says Gemini alone has integrated SynthID with over 180 billion images and videos, plus 240,000 years of audio. Until now, the only way for those outside of Google’s trusted tester program to check for SynthID was to ask Gemini. This is rather clunky, and the model’s output could sometimes be confusing when you just wanted a simple “yes” or “no.”
Now you can cut Gemini out of the loop. Starting today, you can go to the new SynthID.com website to check a piece of content for an AI watermark. A major limitation of Google’s previous detector was that it only checked for Google’s version of SynthID. Even though ChatGPT images, for example, have SynthID, they wouldn’t be flagged in Google’s detector. That’s no longer a problem.
Google says that its expanded version of the detector will support the distinct watermarks from all its SynthID partners, including OpenAI, Nvidia, Kakao, and (soon) Apple. So you’ll be able to go there and check a file for the involvement of all those AI systems instead of accessing their detectors individually. The website won’t provide as much information as the internal tool, which highlighted regions of the image that showed SynthID pixels. Instead, you’ll just get a message telling you whether SynthID was used to produce or edit the media.

Yashasvi Jaiswal keeping wickets during Mumbai’s practice game has raised speculation over whether the India international is considering taking up wicketkeeping as a second role.
Mumbai captain Siddhesh Lad said Jaiswal is ‘trying hard’ to start keeping wickets. “That’s what I heard from him,” Lad told reporters on Thursday.
“And he wants to eventually, in future, keep wickets for maybe Mumbai or go on to keep wickets for the Indian team, is what he is aiming for. That is what I feel, but I haven’t got any clarity on that,” the Mumbai captain added.
Mumbai will start its campaign against Chandigarh at the Wankhede Stadium on Sunday, with Jaiswal available for selection. With seasoned campaigners like Shardul Thakur unavailable for the first game, Mumbai will be cautious.

Amid growing uncertainties over AI’s utilisation and its prospects, union IT minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said that the government is working on releasing a consultation paper on regulating the nascent tech. Speaking at the release of the World Bank’s latest World Development Report on the subject of ‘The Promise of Artificial Intelligence’, Vaishnaw said the timing is right for India to formalise AI regulation and the upcoming consultation paper will establish the foundational basis for future AI regulation. The regulatory blueprint is also likely to sharpen focus on AI safety and security, navigate the deepfakes risk as well as ensuring adequate skill development necessary to optimise the utilisation of AI. On the deepfake epidemic, Vaishnaw identified AI-morphed content as a “nuisance which can cause huge problems in society” while noting they establish dangerous precedents and narratives that mislead the public. He added that the quality of these is improving continuously. The minister further said that AI and emerging technologies cannot be effectively managed through legislation alone. Hence, the government intends to pursue a techno-legal solution with the active participation of industry stakeholders. “The industry has to take the primary responsibility,” said Vaishnaw, regarding issues such as cybersecurity, safety, user harm, psychological disorders, and deepfake proliferation. Notably, the IT minister had previously emphasised that the IT Act is becoming obsolete and India needs a new legal framework to regulate AI. Reports had also hinted that the Centre was looking at formulating a new framework for AI regulation. As frontier AI models’ capabilities are evolving, the government has increasingly focused on tightening rules to mitigate the harms caused by proliferation of AI-generated content. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) had proposed amending the IT Act to require online platforms to label all deepfakes and AI-generated content as “synthetically generated information.” The news also comes amid a storm over global tech giant Meta’s handling of child sexual abuse material (CSAM) on its platforms like Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. A BBC investigation earlier this year alleged that Instagram ads were directing users towards Telegram channels offering CSAM material for sale, resulting in the company facing summons from MeitY and an inquiry by the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR). Following the episode, Meta and Google both ultimately agreed to report content on child abuse to Indian law enforcement authorities.

NEW DELHI: The Trump administration has stepped up its crackdown on the US immigration system, suspending major technology companies including Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, Capgemini and HCL from the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme amid allegations of abuse of H-1B visas and the employment of foreign workers.
US Vice President JD Vance accused Microsoft of laying off thousands of American workers while simultaneously benefiting from thousands of H-1B visas and green cards. The administration has also put nine universities under investigation over alleged misuse of visa-related programmes, adding to growing uncertainty for foreign workers and international students in the US.
Announcing Microsoft's suspension from the PERM programme, Vance said the company had laid off 6,000 American workers while benefiting from 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards.
"There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft."
“If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” Vance said at a White House news conference.
Vance also accused companies of using foreign workers to undercut American employees, saying: "This is a fundamental INSULT to the American worker and to the American way of life. We CANNOT allow visa programs that were designed to ensure that American corporations had access to the best and the brightest, to use them to undercut the wages of American workers!"
What is the PERM programme
The Permanent Labour Certification programme, or PERM, is a Department of Labour process that allows US employers to seek certification to permanently employ foreign workers.
Under the process, employers generally have to demonstrate that there are not enough able, willing, qualified and available US workers for the job and that hiring a foreign worker will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed American workers.
Once the labour certification is approved by the Department of Labour, the employer can proceed with an immigrant petition to the US Citizenship and Immigration Services, generally through Form I-140.
For H-1B workers, PERM can therefore form an important step in the employment-based green card process. Suspending a company's access to the programme can make it harder for the company to sponsor eligible foreign workers for permanent residence.
How PERM was meant to protect US workers
The PERM programme is designed to ensure that American workers are not disadvantaged when employers seek to hire foreign workers for permanent jobs. Before sponsoring a foreign worker for a green card, an employer generally has to demonstrate that there are not enough qualified, willing and available US workers for the position and that hiring the foreign worker will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed Americans.
The concern for US authorities arises when employers manipulate or bypass this labour-market test. Fraudulent recruitment can make it appear that no suitable American worker is available when, in reality, qualified US workers may have been discouraged from applying or effectively excluded from consideration. The Department of Labor's inspector general has identified vulnerabilities in the PERM system, including concerns over fraudulent applications, inadequate supporting documentation and weaknesses in post-certification enforcement.
Wages are another concern. Employers are required to meet prevailing wage requirements, which are intended to prevent foreign-worker hiring from depressing wages for American workers in comparable jobs. If employers circumvent these requirements or use arrangements that effectively reduce the foreign worker's compensation, the government says the system can undermine the safeguards built into PERM.
The administration's latest moves have also extended beyond companies. The Department of Homeland Security has proposed a $70,000 fee for international students participating in the Optional Practical Training programme, which allows eligible foreign students to work in jobs related to their studies.

Two Indian cartoonists, Satish Acharya and Manjul, recently revealed that their Instagram accounts and posts were withheld in India, following orders from the government. While the former’s account was restored on October 6, the latter’s post remains unavailable in India.
On September 23, The Indian Express reported that election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised at least 14 formal objections over 10 months to decisions concerning electoral-roll management and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), including changes to Form 6, voter deletions and restorations, the centralisation of electoral-roll data, and appeals against decisions in West Bengal.
The investigation, based on internal notes and correspondence reviewed by the newspaper, showed that the two commissioners repeatedly said certain decisions had been taken without their knowledge or approval by chief election commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar, with Sandhu at one point describing an SIR-related change as “unauthorised and illegal.” Both Acharya and Manjul had posted cartoons satirising this case.
ALSO READ: Instagram takes down content critical of Vizag data centre projects, cites IT Act notices
On September 23, Acharya posted an illustration on Kumar and the SIR controversy. Five days later, on September 28, his account was restricted in India.
However, his profile was still available on Facebook and X, and the said toon was still visible on both platforms.
After his account was banned, on September 28, Acharya posted screenshots of notifications received by Meta, which said that several of his earlier satirical posts were also being banned in India under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology (IT) Act, 2000.
On the same day, he posted the screenshot of his account getting restricted in India, contrasting it with a screenshot of Modi’s comment that “cartoons have healing power and cartoonists are closer to God”.
Speaking to Alt News, Acharya said he found out about his account being restricted while checking news reports on the increasing banning of accounts critical of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government. “I thought of checking my own Instagram account status and found that a list of posts were restricted in India, some of them were posted in 2023-24. By the end of day, I found that my entire profile has been restricted in India,” he said.
“For the last one decade, I have regularly faced restrictions on my cartoons on different social media platforms. (Their) aim was to restrict the reach…mostly during elections or major protests like CAA protests & farmers’ protests. This is the first time that my entire profile was restricted in India. It’s quite shameful that they (the government) are scared that the narratives created by the regime over the last two decades will be demolished by cartoons, journalists, and comedians,” he added.
He said that his reach has been affected after the ban, adding that he written to Meta’s grievance cell.

On September 27, cartoonist Manjul made a post X claiming that Instagram has restricted one of his illustrations in India. He also posted the notice from Instagram, which claimed that this particular post’s access has been restricted in India “pursuant to a notice from the Government of India/Law enforcement”. (Archive)

The cartoon, posted on Manjul’s Instagram account on September 24, showed that an electronic voting machine (EVM) with three candidates — the three election commissioners. However, when a person was seen voting for Vivek Joshi, the VVPAT showed that the vote was cast for CEC Gyanesh Kumar.

A report by The Indian Express, published on August 18, revealed that between March and July, the government issued a blocking order for online content every 68 seconds on average, which amounted to 1,275 such cases daily and around 2 lakh cases over a period of five months.
According to that report, this government takedowns surged specifically after the Cockroach Janta Party-led students’ protest against the NEET exam irregularities in June and July. Although the government took down social media posts from Facebook, Instagram and YouTube as well, Instagram faced maximum content restrictions given that its user demographic is mostly the Gen-Z. According to the report, out of the total blocking orders, 1,00,000 such orders were for Instagram only while Facebook and YouTube accounted for 80,000 and 15,000 takedown orders, respectively.
ALSO READ: Government orders trigger sweeping Instagram censorship days after CJP protest
Alt News had earlier reported that in February, the government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021. The amendment reduced the time available to social media platforms to remove or disable access to unlawful content from 36 hours to three hours after receiving a valid court order or a “reasoned intimation” from the appropriate government or its authorised agency. This change was notified through a press brief on July 22.
Although the order focused predominantly on countering harms caused by AI generated content and information, critics believe that the amendments have served as a tool to curb anti-establishment content. In our reportage, we found that most of the blocking orders were issued through the Union Home Ministry’s Sahyog portal, a platform created to send such notices, under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, 2000. These orders were issued by various central and state government agencies. Meta has also integrated its Application Programming Interface (API) with the Sahyog portal, enabling content flagged through government directions to be automatically removed from its platforms without being reviewed by a human executive.

New York court hears arguments in ongoing 9/11 families' lawsuit against Saudi Arabia
- Published
The Court of Appeals in New York has heard arguments from both lawyers for families of 9/11 victims and the government of Saudi Arabia as it decides whether the families' long-running legal case against the Middle Eastern country can move to trial.
Almost 3,000 people were killed on 11 September 2001 after hijackers seized four US passenger jets and crashed them into the World Trade Center in New York, the Pentagon, and a Pennsylvania field, following resistance from passengers.
The families allege that a Saudi government employee, Omar al-Bayoumi, knowingly supported two of the hijackers and that he was working with a network of officials linked to the Saudi Ministry of Islamic Affairs.
Bayoumi, who is now retired from government work, has denied knowing the two men were hijackers or that he had any involvement in 9/11, while Saudi Arabia has said that any allegation that it or its officials are complicit in 9/11 is categorically false.
The Kingdom has argued that, as a foreign sovereign state, it has immunity from prosecution in US courts.
The families, who first filed the lawsuit in 2002, spent several years lobbying US Congress to pass an amendment to the foreign sovereign immunity law to allow the case to go ahead.
In 2016, Congress passed the Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act (JASTA), which allows civil claims against a foreign state or official for injuries, death, or damages from an act of international terrorism.
In August 2025, the Manhattan District Court ruled that the 9/11 families had presented enough evidence to meet the terms of the act and the case was allowed to proceed towards a trial.
Saudi Arabia on Wednesday asked the Court of Appeals to reverse that decision.
Counsel Gregory Rapawy argued core issues of fact – including the central question of the nature of Bayoumi's employment by the Saudi state – had not been decided and needed to be done so before the country could be stripped of immunity.
9/11 families' lawyer Gavin Simpson argued that the District Court had already found that Bayoumi's actions "were not just acts of a good Samaritan or an innocent participant".
"He was, in fact, following Saudi Arabia's instructions when assisting the hijackers," said Simpson, and that these were points that Saudi Arabia had "failed to rebut."
One option the judges seemed to wrestle with was whether to send the case back to the district court to make more concrete findings, which could involve taking testimony from live witnesses.
Asked by Judge Guido Calabresi which witnesses Saudi Arabia could call in that eventuality, Rapawy suggested that if the issue ultimately came down to Bayoumi's credibility, "we would have to see" if he could be called to testify.
As he drew the hearing to a close, Judge William Nardini said "it's a difficult case, and we will take it under advisement", meaning that the panel would issue a ruling at a future date.
Speaking outside the courthouse, Terry Strada, whose husband Tom was killed in the World Trade Center, told the BBC she felt positive about the hearing.
"25 years is an extraordinary time to go without accountability and justice for the murder of your loved one. What we hope is that the judges will uphold [District Court] Judge Daniels' decision and move to a trial."

The Sentinelese, living on North Sentinel Island in the Bay of Bengal, are one of the most isolated peoples on earth.
Part of an archipelago governed by India, it is prohibited by law to venture within 5km of their island. And when a missionary did manage to land on the beach in 2018, he was killed by bow and arrow.
Yet none of that was to deter influencer Mykhailo Polyakov, who last year filmed himself arriving on North Sentinel Island, and leaving a can of coke on the beach.
Features writer Elle Hunt documents the rise of a new breed of influencer, travelling around the world, and streaming to millions their attempts to contact the uncontacted – despite the warnings of indigenous rights groups that the consequences could be fatal, both for the social media stars and the communities they risk exposing to disease.
Helen Pidd also speaks to Ecuadorian indigenous rights activist María José Andrade Cerda about the rights and wrongs of this new world.

Eritrean troops who crossed into Ethiopia’s Tigray region have come under drone attack from government forces, raising the risk that renewed internal conflict in Ethiopia could trigger an all-out regional war between the neighbouring countries.
Military vehicles carrying soldiers drove across Eritrea’s southern border into Tigray on Wednesday, reaching the town of Adigrat 25 miles (40km) south, according to civilian witnesses, a militia commander and the conflict monitoring group Acled.
Eritrean troops were then targeted by Ethiopian government drones on Wednesday evening and Thursday morning, Acled said.
Eritrea has a historical enmity with the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which launched an offensive against the Ethiopian government on 23 September, but that previous hostility has been superseded by Eritrea’s desire to head off a perceived risk of Ethiopia invading it, in order to access the Red Sea.
In the last two weeks, the TPLF and six other armed groups in Ethiopia have fought the government in Tigray and the neighbouring regions Amhara and Afar. Ethiopia’s military pushed back and an allied militia, the Tigray Peace Force, took over Tigray’s regional capital, Mekelle, on 4 October after the TPLF withdrew from the city.
Eritrea’s information minister, Yemane Ghebremeskel, said in a statement: “We are not in the business of refuting wild allegations or narratives.” He did not explicitly confirm or deny the presence of Eritrean troops in Ethiopia.
Ethiopia’s foreign ministry said in a statement on Monday: “Ethiopia stands ready to defend its sovereignty, territorial integrity, and core national interests, while urging all regional actors to address shared challenges through constructive dialogue, partnership, and adherence to the principles of good neighbourliness rather than confrontation and zero-sum approaches.”
The TPLF and Ethiopia’s government fought a brutal civil war from 2020 to 2022. Between 300,000 and 800,000 civilians died, according to British government estimates. Both sides and their allies were accused of war crimes.
Eritrea intervened on the side of Ethiopia in that conflict, after a rapprochement between the two countries in 2018, which earned Ethiopia’s prime minister, Abiy Ahmed, the 2019 Nobel peace prize.
Eritrea, which gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, has a long enmity with the TPLF, which ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018. The two countries fought a war from 1998 to 2000.
Relations between the countries have deteriorated again in recent years. Abiy has said Ethiopia needs access to the Red Sea, and state media has claimed the country has historical rights to the Eritrean port of Assab. The US-Israeli war on Iran – leading Iran to limit shipping through the strait of Hormuz – has further raised the stakes of Red Sea access.
In its statement on Monday, Ethiopia’s foreign ministry said: “Any serious discussion of regional maritime affairs and security architecture must account for Ethiopia’s legitimate interests and its enduring connection to the Red Sea.”
Yemane said in a post on X on Wednesday that Ethiopia was “incessantly beating the drums of war and openly stating … that it will launch a war of aggression against Eritrea to acquire what it calls ‘sovereign access to the sea’ … In recent weeks, it has tried to repackage this war agenda in terms of ‘self-defence’ by fabricating various allegations against Eritrea.”
Magnus Taylor, Horn of Africa deputy director at the Crisis Group thinktank, said: “The big worry is that [Abiy] might try to solve all his problems at the same time, by invading Eritrea, possibly a regime change move and also a land grab for the Red Sea port, and also solving his problem with Tigray at the same time. It’s a very ambitious military agenda, though.”
While the full impact of the fighting on Tigrayan civilians is not clear, reports have emerged of the TPLF forcibly recruiting boys as young as 15 to fight.
“The civilians in these three regions [Tigray, Amhara and Afar] didn’t get healed from the first round of violence that was halted by the peace agreement [in 2022],” said Acled Ethiopia analyst Jalale Getachew Birru. “They just started healing recently.”
Associated Press contributed to this story

Dolly Parton's estate has filed a lawsuit against her nephew. Here's what's happened so far
Legal battle continues over estate worth estimated $450 million US
Bryan Seaver, Dolly Parton’s nephew and longtime head of security, is embroiled in a nasty and very public legal battle with the company managing her estate.
At its heart, the dispute appears to be about — what else? — money.
Forbes estimated that Parton, whose death from cancer was announced on Aug. 25, had a net worth of $450 million US.
While neither she nor her late husband Carl Dean had any children, Parton did have a large family — 11 siblings (six of whom are still alive), at least 12 nephews and nieces, according to People magazine, and even some great-nephews and -nieces.
She’s Alive, LLC is the name of the entity created to manage and protect Parton’s estate. It’s run by her longtime manager Danny Nozell.
The estate has also filed a lawsuit and restraining order against Seaver, the family member Parton had handpicked to announce her death.
Bryan Seaver was fired from his job providing security at Dolly Parton's properties, including Dollywood, last month, and ordered to immediately vacate the premises. (Melissa Sue Gerrits/Getty Images)
Want to know more? Here’s how the dispute has played out so far:
Aug. 25: Dolly Parton dies after a brief battle with cancer. Bryan Seaver announces her death to the public in a short video statement on her Instagram account.
Sept. 9: She’s Alive, LLC is created.
Sept. 21: TMZ reports Seaver has been fired from providing security services at Parton’s properties.
A copy of the termination letter obtained by the tabloid indicates Seaver and his staff were ordered to vacate the properties immediately. It says the decision was made "for the protection of the Trust and beneficiaries as a whole." It also states Seaver’s personal stake in the estate is not being terminated.
Sept. 22: She’s Alive files a lawsuit and temporary restraining order against Seaver.
TMZ publishes court documents filed by Parton’s former manager, Danny Nozell, alleging Seaver described himself as an international arms dealer, and raised his military experience to intimidate Nozell into giving him money.
Seaver denies he threatened Nozell, telling TMZ "a lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving."
Sept. 23: A Tennessee judge rules Seaver and his company show a "present and continuing disruption and threat" to She's Alive.
Parton’s sister Freida says there is no feud within her family on Facebook. "No one among the Parton/Owens family is fighting over Dolly’s estate," she says in the post. "We all love Bryan, just as we all love each other."
Oct. 2: Seaver asks a Tennessee court to delay a hearing scheduled for Oct. 9, saying he has been unable to find a lawyer to represent him. TMZ reports every attorney he approached had ties to Pinnacle Bank — which is involved with the trust at the centre of the estate battle — thus creating a conflict of interest.
Oct. 5: She’s Alive asks the court to deny Seaver’s motion and submits documents describing how he attempted to evade the person hired to serve him legal documents. They allege Seaver went so far as to put a no-trespassing sign in his front yard and drape barbed wire across the handrails leading to his front door.
Seaver’s next hearing is scheduled for Oct. 20. It’s still not clear if he has found a lawyer to represent him.

20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.

Thursday 8 October 2026 15:06, UK
Lewis Hamilton has revealed Ferrari held a "huge discussion" to reflect on a strategic error at the Bahrain Grand Prix that he says "wasn't good enough".
Ferrari fitted both Hamilton and his team-mate Charles Leclerc with slick dry tyres at last weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix, which was being hosted in Malaysia and started on a wet track that the Italian squad anticipated would quickly dry out once the race began.
The decision was proven wrong as Hamilton fell from his starting position of second to almost the back of the field in the opening stages, with the 14 of 22 drivers that started on the intermediate tyre gaining a huge advantage.

Hamilton ultimately produced a stunning fightback to finish on the podium in third, but having fallen 106 points behind championship leader Kimi Antonelli, reiterated his desire to see improvement from his team ahead of this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix.
"It wasn't good enough and we've had a huge discussion about it," Hamilton told Sky Sports F1.
"And we're going to try and work on how we can come to a better conclusion more consistently in the future."
Before revealing those talks, Hamilton had defended Ferrari from what he feels is disproportionate criticism the team receive compared to their F1 rivals.
McLaren also started the race in Sepang on dry tyres and suffered the same fate as Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri slid towards the back of the pack.
"We do for some reason as a team get far more flack than anybody else," the seven-time world champion said. "McLaren made the same decision and no one even said anything about it.
"You know, they made some excuse of some sort. McLaren made the same mistake and the same call."
'The call didn't come from the strategist'
Hamilton also offered a specific defence of Ferrari's strategists, insisting they alone were not responsible for the starting tyre choice.
He added: "It was ultimately a mistake but it's not the strategists. I think, unfortunately, my strategy team gets the brunt of the (criticism for the) call.
"But in actual fact, the call didn't come from the strategist. The call comes from collectively, us working together.
"(Team principal) Fred (Vasseur), (head of track engineering) Matteo (Togninalli), myself, my engineer, we make the decision together. And we discuss it and we put our input, we put all our ideas and information into the pot, whether that's good or not…
"I went into the pit lane, I'm like, 'it's wet'. I go to the pit wall, I'm like, 'it's wet'. Come back to the garage, I'm like, 'guys, we should be on the inters'.
"And then they all give a different perspective. And if you've got three people giving you a different perspective, you eventually get convinced by that. And you're like, 'OK, I'll go with what you suggest.' And that's how you work as a team.
"And you hope three are more right than one. But in some scenarios, it's the other way around. And you were right and your gut feeling was right. And then you're like, 'damn, I should have gone with my gut'. But everyone's generally trying to do the best they can."
'We're here to attack' - Hamilton hopeful of Singapore chances
Hamilton is hopeful Ferrari's car will be suited to the Marina Bay Street Circuit this weekend, with the track potentially providing the team with their best chance of victory over the final seven rounds of the season.
"I think with our car, it's generally good on street circuits, particularly when there's not particularly long straights," Hamilton said.
"If you look at the last races, we were quick through corners, not so quick on the straight line. This is a high-drag circuit, so I'm hoping the advantage others have on those long straights kind of comes down a little bit and we can start matching them through keeping up with them on the pace, through corners.
"I think for us, it's just making sure we've got a great, stable platform underneath us, particularly in the bumpy zones because it's bumpy here."
With Singapore hosting a Sprint weekend for the first time, meaning there is only one practice session before Sprint Qualifying on Friday, Hamilton believes quickly finding a strong setup will be crucial.
He added: "We've looked at Monaco, we've looked at Montreal, we've looked at Baku's setup. We're coming here and it is requesting something different.
"I've been pushing the car in a certain direction, and I think we are slowly making gains and improvements.
"We're here to attack. Qualifying is key, and it would be really great if we could start tomorrow on the right foot and then just be attacking in qualifying, but we have to wait and see."
Leclerc: Singapore layout seems good for us
Leclerc is also hopeful Singapore could present an opportunity for he or Hamilton to add to their sole victories this season, but is taking nothing for granted.
Ferrari failed to meet pre-weekend expectations when many considered them favourites for victory in Monaco and Budapest earlier this year, but claimed surprise victories when Hamilton won in Barcelona and Leclerc at Silverstone.
Asked whether Singapore represented Ferrari's best chance to add another victory this season, Leclerc replied: "Maybe. It definitely is one of those tracks where the layout seems to be pretty good for us.
"Whether this will pay off or not… Budapest and Monaco were strong layouts for us on paper and it didn't go well. Silverstone was a bad layout on paper and it went really well.
"I don't know if it tells the full story but we'll give our best. Historically we've been quite strong here but we cannot really rely on the past.
"We've got to do everything we can to be in the best possible situation. It's also true that the tendency lately has been that we've been losing a bit of performance compared to the guys in front, so to win will be very difficult."

Life is remarkably selective. Life relies on many molecules with what is termed “handedness”—they’re chemically identical but are mirror images of each other. Most chemical reactions will make a 50-50 mix of the left- and right-handed forms of a chemical, but life uses only one of them. In fact, because of the differences between left- and right-handed chemicals, most of the key enzymes used by organisms will fail to work if they’re presented with chemicals that have the wrong handedness.
That poses a bit of a challenge for origin-of-life research, as we’re forced to explain how a world that may have started with an even mix of left- and right-handed chemicals produced organisms that only used one of them.
Today’s Nobel Prize in Chemistry goes to two individuals, Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai, who discovered chemical reactions could be biased, producing large excesses of one of the two forms of a chemical.
Chirality and life
The technical term for molecular handedness is “chirality,” and scientists replace left and right with dextro (D) and levo (L). But the ideas are largely the same. Your hands have all the same components—fingers and thumbs—organized in the same way. Yet if you point your thumb upward, the fingers curl in opposite directions, making one the mirror image of the other. Depending on the arrangements of the chemical bonds, many molecules can form similar mirror-image forms, with all the same parts oriented slightly differently in space.
(For the geekier among the readership: carbon atoms have four potential sites that can form bonds, spread evenly across the surface of the atom’s sphere. If each of those sites is linked to a different chemical, then swapping the chemicals located in any two of them can potentially change the way it’s arranged in 3D space.)
Amino acids come in both D and L forms, but all of life relies on just one of those.
Amino acids come in both D and L forms, but all of life relies on just one of those.
Credit:
Nobel Prize Foundation
This can really matter when it comes to enzymes, which typically latch onto chemicals using binding sites that are sculpted by evolution to fit only that chemical and its close relatives. Try to feed the enzyme the mirror-image version of that same chemical, and it will often fail to fit the binding site. Since life uses nothing but the D form of sugars, all of its enzymes are optimized to latch onto those, and many cannot interact at all with the L form.
There are two ways this could have happened. The first life may not have been as picky about the reactions it catalyzed and only evolved chirality preferences slowly. Or life could have evolved in an environment where one chiral form dominated. Or there was some combination of the two. But either of the latter two cases simply pushes the question back a bit: How could chemistry create an environment where one chiral form dominates?
From theory to practice
Over the years, there have been a number of ideas about how this might occur. Several of those trace back to a physicist, Frederick Charles Frank, who addressed this issue in a data-free, theory-focused paper. (It’s clear from the Nobel Prize Committee’s writing that, were Frank still alive, he might have shared in this award.) One option is that a catalyst with only a slight preference for forming a D or L molecule could, over time, produce a large excess of that form. Another is that a chiral reaction product could itself serve as a catalyst for forming more of the same form. Or the chiral reaction product could inhibit the formation of its mirrored form.
Many chemical reactions reach an equilibrium, finding a point where forward and reverse reactions occur at similar rates. If the reverse reaction is indifferent to chirality, but the forward one is influenced by one of the factors above, then time would allow this to create a large excess of one chiral form.
All of these were hypotheticals, however, until the researchers being honored got to work. Henri Kagan of the University of Paris-Sud also approached his work very theoretically, describing the factors that would be needed to drive reactions that favored a single chirality. But in several cases, he was able to go out and find actual chemical reactions that demonstrated his ideas mattered in the real world.
Kagan worked with a catalyst that was itself chiral. He found that, in a mix of L and D versions of his catalyst, one of the forms was much more active than the other. While the forms might be present at the same level, most of the actual catalysis was performed by just one of them. And, if it was used to catalyze a reaction that produced a chiral product, this difference could lead to much higher levels of a single chirality.
By the mid-1960s, Kagan had found three different reactions that could produce an excess of a single chiral form. Other researchers who followed up on his ideas showed that chiral catalysts could also be selectively activated or inhibited by the addition of non-chiral chemicals, allowing a finer degree of control that found its way into the production of pharmaceuticals.
Self catalysis
About a decade later, Tokyo University’s Kenzo Soai was working on reactions where one of the products of the reaction acted as a catalyst to boost the same reaction. Eventually, he found one that selected for chirality; one form of the reaction product would catalyze the formation of more molecules of the same chirality. He started the reaction with a slight excess of one form of catalyst and found that, after a single round of reactions, the excess in the catalyst had risen to 55 percent. Using that as a catalyst for a new round of reactions would enhance the excess further; after several rounds, 90 percent of the products were a single chirality.
Eventually, Soai found conditions where one product would not only catalyze the formation of more of the same form, but inhibit the formation of the opposite chirality. This allowed him to start with a tiny excess of a single chiral form (0.00005 percent more) and, after a few rounds of reactions, bring the excess to over 99 percent.
Others later found conditions where a similar reaction that reached an equilibrium of forward and back reactions would gradually lead to a single chiral form dominating.
There are three different aspects of this work that are worth celebrating. One is that it’s simply great science; people reasoned through the ways that an excess of one chiral form could emerge, and then others found ways to demonstrate that the behavior took place in the real world. A second is that it has immense practical applications. Many of our drugs work because they interact with proteins, where chirality often matters. And there are many examples of drugs where the wrong chiral form can be inactive or positively harmful. So finding new ways to catalyze the production of specific chiral forms has a lot of utility.
But the final thing comes back to the origin of life. None of these reactions were demonstrated with anything closely related to a biomolecule, so it’s not obvious that this particular work is directly relevant to the origin of life. But it does show that small excesses of some chiral forms—smaller than the 90 percent seen in this work, but still significant—may be common in the natural world.
The current thinking is that those small differences weren’t decisive, but did help push the emergence of life along a pathway that ultimately led to the exclusive chemistry we see now.

Injured Assefa narrowly misses world record in Berlin
- Published
An injured Tigst Assefa hobbled over the line at the Berlin Marathon on Sunday after looking set to smash the women's world record.
The Ethiopian still won with the third-fastest time in history in two hours 11 minutes four seconds.
But the 29-year-old, a silver medallist at the Paris Olympics two years ago, had been cruising to a new record before fading in the final stages.
Kenyan athlete Ruth Chepngetich's time of 2:09:56, set at the 2024 Chicago Marathon, remains the world record time, though that result is overshadowed by the three-year doping ban she received in 2025.
Assefa, the 2026 London Marathon winner, started rapidly and led the field by a minute at the 15km mark. She was ahead of the record pace at 35km and is a renowned fast finisher - but began to suffer clear discomfort and her pace slowed.
However she still broke the Berlin course record of 2:11:53 that she set in 2023 - which was also her previous personal best.
In addition, she improved on her time of 2:15:41 at the London Marathon earlier this year.
"We have to bow our heads to this performance. She was on a world record course for most of the race but then something happened to her tendon," said race director Mark Milde.
"To finish like this, I've never seen something like this. The pain is hard to imagine.
"With a heavy heart, we saw her set a course record, but it could have been a lot more."

South Korea to recall its ambassador to Ukraine over North Korean POW dispute
SEOUL, South Korea — South Korea said Thursday it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, stepping up its protest against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's recent revelation of a supposedly secret transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.
The South Korean announcement came days after its President Lee Jae Myung threatened to take unspecified punitive steps if Ukraine refuses to apologize over the revelation.
South Korea's Foreign Ministry didn't say when the ambassador, Park Hee-chang, will be brought back home. A ministry statement said that South Korea will continue consultations with Ukraine, adding it hopes the dispute between the two countries would be resolved smoothly.
South Korea and Ukraine became embroiled in a diplomatic row after Zelenskyy spoke about the transfer of the North Korean soldiers during his U.N. speech on Sept. 23. South Korea has accused Ukraine of violating a nondisclosure agreement on their transfer in mid-September, but Kyiv has denied agreeing to such a deal.
The soldiers were among thousands of North Korean troops deployed to support Russia's war against Ukraine. Since their capture in early 2025, the soldiers had expressed their desires to resettle in South Korea, because they could face persecution if repatriated home. South Korea had said it would accept them, because it legally regards the North as part of its territory and has a policy of accepting and financially supporting North Korean defectors.
South Korean officials said the non-disclosure agreement was made because they were concerned about the safety of the North Korean soldiers and their relatives in the North. But many experts say South Korea's liberal government likely also worries the disclosure of their arrival may hurt its efforts to improve ties with North Korea.
North Korea's state media hasn't commented on the soldiers' transfer. But the North previously reacted with fury to major defections of its citizens, accusing South Korea of kidnapping them. North Korea has shunned any talks with South Korea and the U.S. and focused on bolstering its nuclear program since 2019.
It's unclear what other steps South Korea would take. Experts say maintaining good relations with Ukraine is in South Korean national interests because Kyiv could provide Seoul with intelligence about North Korea's expanding cooperation with Russia and its battlefield experiences. They say cooperation with Ukraine is important for South Korea's partnerships with many Western countries supporting Ukraine over the war.
Observers say Zelenskyy disclosed the transfer of the North Korean POWs to expose the danger of North Korea's military support to Russia as a way to win more international assistance.

Under regulatory scrutiny in India, social media giant Meta claims to have taken action against 5.3 Mn pieces of child sexual abuse material (CSAM) in the first half (H1) of 2026. The social media giant also noted that more than 98% of this content was identified and addressed proactively before being reported. This comes as Meta has come under fire over its lax policies around taking down child sexual abuse content. Globally, the social media company said that it took down 33.2 Mn pieces of such content during the same timeframe, with a proactive detection rate exceeding 97%. Meanwhile, Meta also said that it has rolled out new AI-powered systems and upgraded its ad review frameworks across Facebook and Instagram in India to detect and take down CSAM. The social media juggernaut also said that it has introduced LLM-driven systems to identify “signposting” within ads to counter predators who advertise illicit material in ways that can evade automated detection. For context, signposting acts as a roadmap to guide and enable users to anticipate what happens next. Meta’s new “signpost” safeguards evaluate where an advertisement leads rather than solely analysing its visible content. Furthermore, the social media company has also deployed AI-driven sweeps to uncover missed CSAM material. It has also integrated “red-teaming” AI agents to probe its own defenses and strengthen detection mechanisms against banned users creating new accounts. It is pertinent to note that red teaming AI agents intentionally probe autonomous AI systems or chatbots to find security flaws and safety gaps before malicious actors do. Meta’s clampdown on CSAM comes as the IT ministry (MeitY) recently pulled up the social media giant over alleged circulation and promotion of CSAM. A BBC investigation earlier this year alleged that Instagram ads were directing users towards Telegram channels offering CSAM material for sale. The controversy resulted in Meta ultimately agreeing to report child safety matters directly to Indian authorities. It also faced summons from MeitY and an inquiry by the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) over the matter. Previous reports also suggested that Meta could also lose its “safe harbour” protection under Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000. This would force the company to face greater legal liability in cases of CSAM or other illegal content being posted on Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.

Quick Answer
Turn rough screen recordings into polished demos with tools that auto-zoom on clicks, follow and smooth the cursor, add clean framing, and highlight key actions. Options include Screen Studio, FocuSee, Screen Awesome, and ScreenCursor.
When you record a two-minute walkthrough of your app, for instance, a setting buried five menus deep, or a spreadsheet trick you are proud of, there is something that can leave you frustrated. You press play, and the cursor is dancing all around without highlighting what you actually wanted to show. Either the text is too small to read on a phone or the whole thing looks like security-camera footage of your desktop. The old-school way is to use a video editor, add zooms by hand, pan the camera to follow your cursor, and nudge keyframes for an hour. Thankfully, there is a newer batch of screen recorders that automatically do that part for you.
In this guide, we have covered four of them. They not only differ in price, platform, and functionality, but each one also has one detail that surprised me.
|  | Screen Studio | FocuSee | Screen Awesome | ScreenCursor | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Works on | Mac only | Windows and Mac | Chrome (also Edge, Brave and similar) | Chrome (Mac, Windows, Linux) | 
| Price | $9/mo billed yearly, or $29/mo | Free trial, paid plans | Free | $49 one-time (early pricing) | 
| Best for | Maximum polish on a Mac | All-in-one AI extras | Privacy and zero cost | Pay-once simplicity | 
Table of Contents
Why do raw screen recordings look so rough?
When you use any standard screen recorder, like the one built into your OS, it captures pixels and nothing else. It has no idea what mattered. It doesn’t know if you clicked a tiny button that you want the viewers to look at. The result? You get a full-screen recording of everything, including your cursor wandering here and there. Viewers watch these videos on laptops and phones, and since the important part is not zoomed in or clearly shown, they will miss it. A better screen recording would be one where:
- Zoom is on the action so people can actually read what you click.
- A camera that follows your cursor instead of leaving viewers guessing.
- A cursor that glides rather than jitters.
- A clean frame, such as a gradient background and rounded corners.
With all of the above, your screen recording not only looks professional but also provides clear instructions for viewers.
Screen recorders with auto cursor follow and zoom
Here are some of the best screen recorders that you can use for automatic cursor follow and zoom.
Screen Studio: The one the others get compared to
If you are on Mac, then Screen Studio is one of the best options for screen recording with automatic cursor follow and zoom. When you’re recording using Screen Studio, it looks at what you did, like where you clicked, and zooms in on the moments that matter. Every zoom is balanced and animated automatically; you don’t have to worry about handling them. The best part is that you can choose between two styles: Classic zoom is the one you usually see in polished product videos. Then there is Loupe zoom, which is a magnifier-style alternative. If you want to zoom somewhere the app did not automatically add one, you can drop it onto the timeline and point it where you like. Notably, the cursor gets the same treatment. Shaky movement is smoothed out into a steady glide, and clicks get a soft ripple. Fast movements pick up motion blur so they look filmed rather than captured. You also have the option to change the cursor’s size and style later. Some of the notable features of Screen Studio are:
- Edit by transcript: Delete a sentence from the transcript, and it disappears from the video. Filler words and long pauses can be cleared in one pass.
- One recording, many shapes: Record once, then switch the aspect ratio between wide (16:9), square (1:1), and vertical (9:16). Zooms can be re-aimed, layouts rearranged, and captions moved to stay readable. You can also choose the “Reel mode” that shows where Instagram’s or TikTok’s interface would cover your video, so you’re in the grey area where your inputs get hidden.
- Hide the private stuff: If the recording shows an API key or email address, you can mask it after the recording is complete, and the mask blends into the interface around it.
- iPhone and iPad framing: Plug your iPhone or iPad into a USB cable, pick the device, and record. Screen Studio wraps the footage in a matching device frame.
FocuSee: The Windows-friendly all-rounder
FocuSee comes from the house of iMobie and is a screen recording tool that works on both Windows and Mac. This already makes it the practical choice for many people working on either OS. FocuSee’s auto zoom follows your clicks and even your typing. This tool adds a spotlight to highlight areas worth noticing, making it much easier for anyone following your instructions. You can also choose a “3D Motion” mode that adds tilt and perspective that follows your cursor, for a more cinematic look. The cursor can fade out when you are not actively using it or don’t need it and reappears when you do. Similar to other screen recording tools, you can swap the cursor style and click animations. There are a bunch of features that deserve to be highlighted.
- A built-in teleprompter: You can show your script on screen while recording with the option to adjust the font size, speed, and position. If you tend to forget the script midway, this alone might sell you.
- An annotation suite: You can add text, shapes, arrows, callouts, spotlights, and blur effects. Moreover, you can stack several layers to walk viewers through a tricky step, or blur out something sensitive.
- An AI avatar: This one is for those who are camera-shy or do not want their face in the video. FocuSee can create a digital presenter, or in simple words, an AI avatar. It is a niche feature, but a handy one for company tutorials.
- Smart cleanup: You can remove filler words and silence with just one click, and also enhance voice and reduce noise with just a button.
- Background fixes for your webcam: It can blur or replace a messy room behind you after recording without needing a green screen.
- Add Subtitles: FocuSee supports speech recognition in over 50 languages, with accuracy above 98%. You can add your own subtitles and make it easier for the follower to go through the steps.
Screen Awesome: Free, and it can’t upload your recordings
Screen Awesome is a different kind of tool. It’s actually a free Chrome extension built by a developer named Nitinbhai Viras. On one hand, most apps say “we respect your privacy” and simply ask you to take their word; Screen Awesome does things a bit differently. Screen Awesome points you at Chrome’s own permission screen and requests no access to any website. It is not allowed to contact any server. That means it cannot upload your recordings, even if it wanted to. The best part is that you can verify this yourself in about 30 seconds. Head over to chrome://extensions, find Screen Awesome, click Details, and look at the Site access line. According to the developer, it reads none. On the extension’s settings page, there is a button that jumps you straight there. On top of this security, you get this tool for absolutely free. Here are some features that set Screen Awesome apart:
- Auto-zoom to clicks: While recording a browser tab, Screen Awesome notes where you click. A virtual camera follows each click and pans between them. You have the option to preview it, turn it off, or export the file. This works for tab recording.
- Serious annotation tools: Arrows, pen, highlighter, shapes, text, speech bubbles, step counters, emoji stamps, and a blur that destroys the pixels rather than just smudging them. You can edit all of these marks.
- Product-shot framing: You can place a recording on a backdrop with rounded corners, a soft shadow, and an optional browser window around it, and also change its aspect ratio to 16:9, etc.
- Formats: You can export your recording in MP4, WebM, or an animated GIF.
- Webcam and voice: Screen Awesome lets you mix in your microphone and the tab’s audio, and even add a movable webcam bubble while recording if you want to show your face.
ScreenCursor: Pay once, and record in Chrome
ScreenCursor is another screen recording tool that works as a Chrome extension. However, its approach is the opposite of Screen Awesome’s. Notably, it does one thing and tries to do it well, which is turning clicks into camera moves with as little fuss as possible. When you hit the record button, ScreenCursor waits three seconds before it starts. That gap is deliberate, and it exists because Chrome shows its own “sharing your screen” bar while recording, and unfortunately it cannot be switched off. With this delay, you get the time to collapse the bar before the screen recording starts. Every click, drag, and keystroke gets zoomed in. Each zoom happens a beat before the action; this way, viewers are already looking at the right spot, then the camera holds steady and follows your cursor. ScreenCursor gives you the option to manually retime a zoom, push its depth in or out, switch the motion between snappy and gentle, or delete the zoom you don’t want. Here are some of the highlights of ScreenCursor:
- Zoom focus point: Right-click any zoom, drag a box over the part you want people to see, and the zoom shows exactly that. You can use this on recordings of desktop apps, since ScreenCursor can record your whole screen.
- Customization: You also get wallpapers, gradients, or use your own image as a backdrop. There is a browser frame that carries the real page title. Editing is also possible, as you can split the clip, delete boring stretches, and speed up slow ones.
- Price and limits: It costs $49 once, which is labeled “early pricing,” with $79 shown as the regular price. After one-time payment, you will continue to receive updates and can work on up to three of your own computers.

Fact Check
While it is unclear that whether the police are claiming that the entire video of the event is AI-generated, or the portion where the cops are seen watching and recording the performance, Alt News found that one of the dancers present in the viral clip posted several videos of the event on her Instagram page, @queen__juhi_002__.
In at least four videos that she had uploaded, the dancers are seen wearing the same attire as seen in Rai’s X post. These videos all show police personnel in the vicinity of the dancers, watching the performance and some filming it. However, at the time of writing this article, her Instagram page was taken down. Below is a screen recording of a video posted by the dancer herself, where the performers are seen wearing the same attire as in the video posted by Rai.
A closer look shows that police personnel are visible on the stage as well below the stage. Below are the highlighted portions of the phone recordings that clearly show the dancers. One of the keyframes also shows an audience member on a video call.
The setting and backdrop of the videos posted by the dancer and the one posted by Rai also match. Below are two screenshots comparing a keyframe from the video posted by Rai and keyframes posted by the dancer.
A video posted by another Instagram user, @aman_bhu_2427, showed a different angle of the same dancers in the same performance. The text on the video states that it was taken at the Lat Bhairav Mandir. Another Instagram user named Sushila Seth also posted a video of the dancers amidst several uniformed policemen.
View this post on Instagram
We found another video on Facebook where the structure of the stage can be clearly seen and a red temple can be seen behind it.
To sum up, the above videos posted by the dancers themselves and the attendees prove three things:
- The incident did take place during the Baba Lat Bhairav baarat procession. Several social media users posted videos of the same programme captured from different angles.
- The uniformed police personnel were standing on the stage as well as below the stage watching the dancers as the performance went on.

Thus, the Kashi DCP’s claim that the video is AI-generated does not hold up.

United Nations, Oct 08: Exposing Pakistan’s doublespeak on terrorism at the UN, India has called out Islamabad’s efforts to gloss over its state support for terror by announcing rewards for JeM chief Masood Azahar, underlining that the world has not forgotten 9/11, 26/11 and Pahalgam attacks.
India on Wednesday exercised its Right of Reply in response to the Pakistan representative’s statement in the Sixth Committee of the UN General Assembly on the Agenda Item: Measures to Eliminate International Terrorism.
“Pakistan speaks of combating terrorism while seeking to obscure the very question that this committee must confront: What happens when terrorists are financed, facilitated, trained, sheltered, or supported from the territory of a state?” First Secretary in the Permanent Mission of India to the UN Raghoo Puri said.
He said India has been consistent on this question, underscoring that terrorism cannot be defeated by declarations and instead requires action against its perpetrators, organisers, financiers, and sponsors.
“For years, Pakistan has presented itself as a frontline state in combating terrorism and as a victim while masking the fact that the Frankensteins the Pakistani state has created and lost control over have moved from wreaking havoc in neighbouring countries to doing the same in Pakistan,” Puri said.
Calling out Pakistan’s doublespeak on terrorism, Puri said the country “glosses over its state support for terrorism by announcing enhanced rewards for apprehending UN-listed head of Jaish-e-Mohammed terrorist and mastermind of several attacks against my country, Masood Azhar.”
He said the world is aware of Pakistan's financial support to terrorism.
“Yet, we also remember that just a few months ago, Pakistani representatives used this forum to call the Jaish-e-Mohammed a defunct organisation. The world has seen the script play earlier, and we are clear-eyed that this time also it is going to be no different,” he said.
Puri said that when the media can reach Azhar and get confirmation from him about the success of Operation Sindoor, "surely the Pakistani state knows his whereabouts”.
In May last year, India had launched Operation Sindoor targeting terror infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir in retaliation for the dastardly April 22 terror attack in Pahalgam in Jammu and Kashmir perpetrated by The Resistance Front, a proxy of Pakistan-based terror group Lashkar-e-Taiba, in which 26 civilians, mostly tourists were killed.
Earlier this month, India had dismissed as “gimmicks” Pakistan’s fresh announcement of a bounty of seven million rupees on Azhar, demanding that Islamabad take “concrete action” to combat terrorism.
India has for years accused Pakistan of sheltering Azhar, while Pakistan has maintained that he fled to Afghanistan – a claim rejected by Afghanistan’s Taliban government.
For the last few years, Islamabad has claimed that the JeM founder has been operating from Afghanistan.
However, the Taliban regime dismissed Pakistan’s repeated claims, with a senior Afghan Foreign Ministry official saying he is not in the country.
Islamabad’s fresh announcement on the reward for information on Azhar came as it faces pressure from the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) to crack down on terror groups and their leadership.
The Paris-based global watchdog is set to review Pakistan’s anti-terrorism efforts at its upcoming plenary.
Pakistan was placed under the FATF grey list between 2018 and 2022 for its systemic deficiencies in anti-money laundering and its failure to counter-terror financing.
Puri also recalled a recent statement by Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, daughter of former Pakistan prime minister Nawaz Sharif, who had said,“The unfortunate thing is that the threat [Punjab] faces comes less from my neighbouring countries and more from my neighbouring provinces.”
Exposing this “dark secret”, Puri said, “You cannot run with the hares and hunt with the hounds. Reality never works like that.”
“When terrorist groups are allowed to operate under state political power, international commitments become meaningless and when perpetrators are provided safe havens, the victims of terrorism are denied justice,” he said.
“The world has not forgotten 9/11 and where its perpetrators, including Osama bin Laden, were caught. The world has not forgotten 26/11. The world has not forgotten Pahalgam,” Puri said, adding that the list, “unfortunately”, is painfully long.
“The victims in Pahalgam were not asked about their political orientation, they were asked about their religion. It is therefore deeply ironic that Pakistan speaks of combating religious hatred while allowing the conditions that enable it to persist and thrive, especially by fomenting cross-border terrorism,” he said.
“Pakistan continues with its narrative building, misinformation, and disinformation. If bombed-out airfields and cratered runways look like victory to Pakistan, they are of course welcome to enjoy it," Puri said.
"Any regime against terrorism to be effective must do two things: assign responsibility and ensure accountability. India will defend its people, and continued terrorism against India will have consequences,” he added.
In another Right of Reply, Puri said India rejected Pakistan’s “circular economy” of words and narratives.
“If this much effort had actually been made in countering terrorism rather than narrative building, misinformation, and disinformation, the world would have been a better place. But nothing more can be expected from a Form 47 government,” he said, referring to a term used to describe allegations of rigging and manipulation in Pakistan’s 2024 general elections.

How an 'absolute fluke' exposed sandpapergate scandal
- Published
According to the man who helped catch them, it was blind luck.
Sandpapergate, the scandal that engulfed Australia eight years ago, was blatant cheating played out in real time on live television to a global audience.
As the Aussies prepare for their first Test series in South Africa since the ball-tampering controversy in Cape Town, the director of the TV coverage that day admits serendipity took down Steve Smith and co.
"The way the Australians were caught was an absolute fluke," Alvin Naicker, in charge of SuperSport's live broadcast from Newlands, tells BBC Sport.
Not just one fluke, but a series of them.
That the "leadership group" of the Australian team hatched their plan during the lunch break on that Saturday afternoon in March 2018; that an alert camera operator lingered on Cameron Bancroft when others would have turned their attention elsewhere; that the big-screen controller showed in the ground what was also being broadcast to millions around the world.
In understanding how Bancroft was rumbled, a little knowledge of how live cricket is shown on TV is helpful.
"Coverage of rugby and football is very coordinated. It's camera one and two, then when the ball is dead you tell the story with close-up shots," explains Naicker, a highly respected and popular figure in the TV industry with more than 30 years' experience.
"Because cricket has so much dead time, there is a lot more storytelling. There are between 80 and 100 people coming together and putting the story together in a matter of seconds, coordinated by the director."
Captain Smith, vice-captain David Warner and opener Bancroft later explained they cooked up the ball-tampering plot during lunch on the third day of the third Test.
Reverse-swing had been a key factor in the first two Tests of a bad-tempered series: Warner clashed with Quinton de Kock in the first Test in Durban, then Smith was involved in an altercation with Kagiso Rabada in the second.
Australia were exposed before the afternoon session was done, thanks to Naicker and his team. At the time, SuperSport were not on the lookout for cheating, despite the shenanigans of the first two Tests.
"No one mentioned anything to me," says Naicker. "The first Test in Durban spiralled out of control in terms of behaviour, then in Port Elizabeth for the second Test, there were still some fireworks going on. We still didn't understand."
Reports written live by ESPNCricinfo suggest the ball began reversing in the first hour after lunch, 35 overs into the South Africa second innings. In the 43rd over, Bancroft was caught in the act.
"The ball went to the wicketkeeper, then to Bancroft and he was shining the ball," says Naicker. "First it was on his pants, then the next ball, the cameraman happened to stay on Bancroft because he was not shining the ball on his pants, but he was rubbing the ball on his palm.
"When he threw the ball on, he put his hand in his pocket. The cameraman - and these are big, big lens cameras - he zoomed into his pocket. The slow-mo operator looked at it, spooled it back and forth, then zoomed in and could see the yellow spot."
