  - Published19 hours ago
Bancroft's work on the ball was not shown live, but as a replay later in the over. Inside Newlands, the operator of the big screen – working independently from Naicker – showed the same footage.
"They take a feed from broadcast but they also have to insert their own graphics and commercialisation," says Naicker.
"Between deliveries they tend to stay with live play, then at the end of the over they go to their commercials or whatever in the stadium. It was quite fortunate that when we showed it, it was in between deliveries, not at the end of the over."
Bancroft would later admit he "panicked" when he saw himself on the big screen. Comically, he hid the sandpaper inside his trousers. SuperSport caught that, too.
"When Bancroft looked up at the screen and saw it, he removed it and put it in his jocks," says Naicker. "The cameraman recorded it. It still wasn't live, we played a replay."
Bancroft, with Smith by his side, was challenged by on-field umpires Richard Illingworth and Nigel Llong.
The opener turned out his pockets, revealing only a black bag for his sunglasses. The ball was not changed and Australia were not given a run penalty. Play continued, yet SuperSport were on to what had happened.
"Australia coach Darren Lehmann was on the walkie-talkie to 12th man Peter Handscomb, who went on to the field, then the umpires get involved," says Naicker.
"An entire team of cameramen played their part. There was one following the ball, one on Handscomb, one on Lehmann, one on Warner. They all told a story that I happened to put together with this great team of replay operators."
As for Naicker, there was no hesitation in airing what his team had captured, even with the realisation of the magnitude of what was unfolding.
"A lot of people who watch cricket on SuperSport will know we are quite brave in terms of being quite creative and editorially sound," he says.
"It was a natural instinct. It wasn't something I previewed with 10 other people to say 'What do you think, should we show it?' I just went for it."
The footage was pored over by Naicker's team of commentators, while his phone was "WhatsApping off the hook" with messages from around the world, asking him to show it again and again. Replays drew the attention of the third umpire, Englishman Ian Gould.
"He's got comms with me while I'm directing," says Naicker. "There was a moment when he asked me 'I think that's enough now, do you mind not showing it?'
"My response to him was 'I'm quite comfortable in what I'm doing in my job and I think you should do yours'."
When the day's play finally ended, Naicker and his team went to a bar and heard Bancroft and Smith confess in their news conference. Both men and Warner were sent home from the tour and handed lengthy bans. When he returned to Australia, Smith broke down in a tearful address to the press in Sydney.
"It became disheartening for us," says Naicker. "It started becoming emotional to see how they were feeling.
"The most difficult thing for me was to see Steve Smith shedding tears. That was not nice and never the intention. You have to have some emotion for those guys."
1 of 3
There was still a fourth and final Test to complete. Feelings were raw, and SuperSport's access to interviews from Australia was heavily restricted.
Naicker and his team faced allegations of bias, that they were somehow part of an orchestrated plot to take down the Australians. Now, with the Aussies back in town, Naicker maintains he would have pounced on the same "fluke" had it been South Africa caught cheating.
He also highlights the power of television. Bancroft and Australia were exposed mere moments after their act of cheating. TV viewers knew before the on-field match officials.
Naicker points to a conversation he had with Stuart Broad, who also faced tampering accusations for treading on the ball on a tour of South Africa in 2010 and is now building a post-playing career as a pundit.
"When you played the Broad footage in ultra-motion, it looked worse than it was," says Naicker. "He said he never realised how much control and power the TV crew has until he worked in the commentary box.

New Delhi: The global order is increasingly characterised by power and bargaining rather than rules, requiring India to negotiate from a position of strength and build coalitions it can help influence, the government’s top economic adviser said, identifying five factors that would test the country’s ambition of becoming a developed economy by 2047. These five long-term shifts, including geopolitical realignment, strategic supply-chain chokepoints, China’s manufacturing scale, climate variability, and the interplay between demography and artificial intelligence (AI), will shape India's path to becoming a rich nation by the centenary of its independence, Chief Economic Adviser (CEA) V. Anantha Nageswaran said on Thursday. Speaking at the India Investment Seminar 2026 in Mumbai, Nageswaran said these shifts would make India’s climb harder than it was for earlier latecomers, but were “reasons to move faster, not to slow down.” On strategic chokepoints, Nageswaran's presentation identified energy, chips, rare earths, fertilisers and sea-lanes as potential sources of leverage, arguing that India needs buffers and redundancy because such redundancy should be viewed as insurance rather than waste, according to a press release issued by SBI Funds Management Ltd, one of the organisers of the seminar. He also highlighted the scale of China’s manufacturing sector, noting that the country accounts for close to a third of global manufacturing and that surplus capacity can be exported cheaply. The presentation said India would need to adapt domestically while contesting measures such as carbon border taxes abroad. The fifth shift concerns demography and AI. Hundreds of people in Siberia have been quarantined after a laboratory worker at a plague research institute died in undisclosed circumstances on Friday. A Russian news outlet reported the woman may have contracted pneumonic plague from a broken test tube, a narrative that Russian health authorities have denied.
As global health bodies and governments seek more information, Russia has said that the worker’s death does not risk an epidemic in Siberia. However, public health experts are vigilant, given the limited information available.
Mint explains the situation, how global authorities have responded, and whether there is cause for worry.
What happened in Russia?
Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old laboratory worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, fell sick on 29 September and died, reportedly on 2 October. The institute studies plague and other dangerous infectious diseases. Russian authorities said she died from pneumonia of ‘unknown’ origin, meaning the precise illness has not been established.
Some Russian media outlets reported that she may have been exposed to pneumonic plague after accidentally breaking a test tube containing the bacteria. However, Russian authorities have denied such an accident occurred. Other unverified accounts linked her illness to recent travel, but there is no publicly available evidence for these claims.
Her death, however, prompted rapid precautionary measures, with authorities placing about 200 people who’d had contact with Shipilova under medical observation. However, Russia’s health watchdog said on Tuesday that nearly 5,000 laboratory tests had been carried out, no plague had been detected among her contacts, and about 90% of those initially quarantined had been released.
What is the plague?
Plague is an infectious disease caused by bacteria that naturally circulate among rodents and other small mammals and their fleas. Humans can become infected through flea bites, contact with infected animals or, in the case of pneumonic plague, through respiratory droplets from an infected person.
There are three principal forms of plague. Bubonic plague, the most common form, affects the lymphatic system and causes characteristic painful swellings called buboes. Septicemic plague occurs when the bacteria infect the bloodstream. Pneumonic plague affects the lungs and is the form that has raised concern in Russia.
Pneumonic plague is particularly serious because it can spread between people through droplets produced when an infected person coughs or sneezes. While the nature of the transmission may lead to comparisons with covid-19, plague transmission requires close and prolonged contact to a person who is already showing symptoms. Also, unlike viral respiratory infections, plague is a bacterial disease and can thus be treated with antibiotics.
How has the world responded?
Neighbouring countries Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan have stepped up precautionary measures at their borders to guard against the possible spread of infectious diseases.
Meanwhile, global health authorities are seeking more information on the case. WHO director-general Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the organization requested information from Russia on Saturday, after reports of the death emerged, saying the agency does not have a “full picture” of the situation yet. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said it was “closely monitoring the situation” but stressed that the information available so far does not indicate wider transmission.
The US, which withdrew from the WHO in January, is also monitoring the situation. A US State Department spokesperson said Washington was “monitoring the situation closely” with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and other agencies, while urging Russia to “share accurate information quickly and openly”.
What have Russian authorities said?
Russian authorities have consistently rejected reports that Shipilova died from plague. Rospotrebnadzor, the country’s consumer rights watchdog, said she died of “pneumonia of unknown aetiology” and that tests had not found microorganisms associated with her professional activities.
Meanwhile, the health regulator said the epidemiological situation in the region was stable and that there was no basis for an epidemic in Siberia, adding that it was winding down precautionary measures. It also said Shipilova herself was vaccinated and therefore "immune to the dangerous infections with which she worked".
However, Russian authorities have not publicly established what caused Shipilova’s pneumonia. The lack of information, alongside conflicting early reports about lab exposure, fuelled by a regional governor’s initial comments suggesting this, have prompted global scrutiny.
Is there cause for worry?
There is no evidence at present of a wider plague outbreak or sustained human-to-human transmission. The ECDC said there were no reported secondary cases, while Russia has said none of Shipilova’s contacts tested positive for plague.
The WHO has so far assessed the available risk as “moderate to low” for Irkutsk, “low” for Russia as a whole, and “very low” for the WHO European region.
Public health experts say pneumonic plague has a short incubation period — around one to three days — and so far, none of the reported contacts have developed symptoms.
The immediate worry stems less from evidence of a spreading outbreak than from unresolved questions, recalling the uncertainty that marked the opening days of the covid-19 pandemic.

New U.S. indictment charges former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro with torture
NEW YORK — U.S. authorities charged former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro with conspiring to torture his fellow citizens in order to maintain his hold on power. The new indictment, unsealed Thursday, adds pressure on the ousted authoritarian leader already fighting drug trafficking offenses.
Maduro, who was previously charged with participating in a conspiracy to send cocaine into the U.S., is now also facing allegations of human rights abuses during his reign as president of the oil-rich South American nation.
"He authorized the use of torture against specific individuals and oversaw a system designed to use torture, arbitrary detention and violence as a means of repression against the political opposition," says the revised indictment, which newly charges Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, with torture conspiracy.
The allegations include electric shocks, beatings and asphyxiation at Maduro's behest.
Asserting that thousands of Venezuelans were "harassed, threatened, arrested, prosecuted, assaulted, tortured, or killed" by people acting at the behest of the government that Maduro controlled, the indictment alleges that the abuse included electric shocks, beatings and asphyxiation. Maduro, the indictment claims, signed off on methods of torture and personally threatened the killing of one prisoner's child "as a form of psychological torture."
A message seeking comment was sent to Maduro's lawyer; Flores was in court for a previously scheduled hearing, where her attorney said he hadn't yet had time to review the new allegations. Both Maduro and Flores have been behind bars in New York since early January when forces seized them from their Caracas home in a middle-of-the-night raid.
Both have pleaded not guilty in the U.S. drug case first brought years ago against them and numerous alleged co-conspirators. They had already been facing potential life prison sentences if convicted.
Maduro has been under investigation for years by the International Criminal Court over allegations of crimes against humanity, tied to his crackdown on opponents. He has always denied any wrongdoing.
Alleged torture victims included U.S. citizens
The revised indictment includes several mentions of the involvement of Venezuela's feared DGCIM military intelligence agency, which was headed for many years by one of Maduro's co-defendants, Gen. Hugo Carvajal. He broke with Maduro years ago, pleaded guilty last year to drug trafficking charges in New York, and has offered to testify against his former boss.
The indictment alleges that the torture victims included three U.S. citizens, who were not named in the court documents.
One of those Americans was punched, subjected to electric shocks and forced to eat his own vomit during eight months of imprisonment, the indictment says. Another was beaten badly enough to necessitate a long hospital stay and had a gun stuck in his mouth. A third was handcuffed, hooded and beaten for two days every half an hour, suffering a permanent eye injury, the indictment said.
Maduro has long ignored lawsuits brought in U.S. courts by Americans who alleged they were beaten while in custody in Venezuela.
Former first lady seeks release for medical treatment
Flores, meanwhile, was in court Thursday so her lawyers could urge a judge to free her from jail and put her under house arrest because she has heart problems.
Their attorneys have asked for the case to be dismissed on the grounds that they have immunity as the leader and first lady of a foreign country.
Lawyers for Flores, 69, have also argued that she has medical issues that cannot be treated effectively in jail, and that she could instead be allowed to live under 24-hour guard at a residence in New York.
They also said she suffered permanent scarring when she was "thrown against a wall or dresser" during the U.S. military action that led to her capture.
Her lawyers say she has lost 25 pounds (11 kilograms) while imprisoned at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn and has been told that she might need heart surgery. They said she has "lingering lightheadedness, dizziness and shortness of breath" and might have suffered a minor heart attack in July.
Prosecutors opposed the bail request. In a court filing, they wrote that Flores would pose an "extreme risk of flight and danger to the public" if released. They also said she has been taken from the jail to get treatment at a local hospital, when care was needed.
President Donald Trump's administration has defended the raid to capture Maduro as a "surgical law enforcement operation." Maduro has called himself a prisoner of war and his capture a kidnapping.
Flores is charged with participating in a cocaine importation conspiracy with her husband, Maduro, who served as Venezuela's president from 2013 until his capture by American forces in January.
Lawyers for Flores said she was no threat to flee because she is "intent on supporting her husband with her constant presence."

Ten people linked to Kenya's first-ever Ebola case quarantined as screening concerns grow
- Published
Ten people who came into contact with a man who died of Ebola in Kenya have been quarantined, health officials in the East African nation say.
They are also trying to trace 57 other contacts of the Kenyan patient after he travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo, dying in hospital in Nairobi on Monday.
This is the East African nation's first-ever Ebola case and there is now growing concern about the country's screening measures.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention chief has told the BBC that despite being sick for a month, the patient passed through multiple cities in DR Congo, driving to Uganda and eventually flying to Kenya without his sickness being detected.
"We know that he left Buta, a city in [northern] DR Congo, to drive to Kisangani. And from Kisangani, he took a flight to Beni. From Beni, he drove to Uganda. And from Uganda, he took a flight to Nairobi," Jean Kaseya told the BBC's Focus on Africa programme.
"What are symptoms he was presenting? Why was he not detected?" he asked.
The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The current outbreak in DR Congo, which began in May, has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
Kaseya said the Africa CDC was investigating the case, alongside the Congolese authorities. A team from the organisation was also due to meet the Kenyan health authorities.
- What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? 
  - Published15 September
Kenya's health ministry official Patrick Amoth said the patient might have passed screening after taking medications that masked his symptoms.
After arriving at the airport in Kenya's capital, he was transferred by a relative to a hospital in the city where he died, and was buried on Tuesday in line with health safety guidelines.
Kenyan authorities have urged people not to panic, with the health ministry assuring of heightened surveillance at airports and border crossings.
But Dr Dennis Miskellah, a representative from Kenya's main doctors' union, said the Ebola case did not come as a surprise to him and most health workers.
He told the BBC's Newsday programme that he had witnessed "lapses" at various border points, including with neighbouring Uganda and Tanzania, as well as at Kenyan's main airport.
"How could you have been sick for almost a month plus in DR Congo, come all the way to the country through not just any small border point, but the main entry point, the main gateway into the country and pass unnoticed?
"That's the question that most Kenyans are asking."
The health ministry says it has intensified measures to contain the spread, with a joint response involving county administrations, humanitarian partners and others.
President William Ruto has said that surveillance and rapid response teams are on the ground, building on the systems that the country adopted following the outbreak in DR Congo in May.
His spokesman said Kenya had the capacity to detect, isolate and manage suspected cases, adding that so far more than 650,000 travellers had been screened and 267 samples tested.
Facilities in four main hospitals have been designated for the management of Ebola patients, including at the Nairobi Hospital, where the first Ebola patient died.
In June, a US plan to establish an Ebola treatment facility at a military base in the central Kenyan town of Nanyuki sparked concern, with Kenyans reacting furiously about the risks of cross-border infection. The plan was halted by the courts.
On Wednesday, Health Minister Aden Duale told local television station NTV that pending the outcome of the court case, the government was considering turning the facility into the "first" infectious disease hospital in the region, to deal with outbreaks like Ebola.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak of the disease.
Shortly after DR Congo declared an outbreak of Ebola in May, it was also reported in Uganda, where two people died.
However, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared that county free of the disease in August.
On Tuesday, Uganda's health ministry emphasised that the country remained free of Ebola and was continuing to "maintain strong surveillance measures to protect public health".
It said the Kenyan Ebola patient had transited through the country for less than 24 hours and screening teams had "observed he had a normal temperature at the time of departure".
According to Africa CDC chief, his organisation was working with all the countries in the region to reinforce response mechanisms.
Kasiye said Kenya was "well prepared" and was therefore able to immediately receive the case, "but it is not the case for all other countries".
"It means the regional approach is more important today to stop this outbreak."
However, Kasiye said there was no quick testing available at border points and the taking of temperatures was unreliable as medication is able to stop a fever.
"I have to make it clear - we don't have diagnostics to test for Ebola. It's just about temperature," he said.
Dr Miskellah, from the Kenyan doctors' union, said he was concerned that governments were counting on the "honesty and full co-operation of the travellers to self-declare, to say the truth" about their health.
This was however undermined by a lack of proper health education to destigmatise the virus, meaning people often wanted to hide their symptoms, he said.

But the BBC investigation sparked a public outcry and led to calls from lawmakers for an investigation, after which the government announced a comprehensive review.
That review found "errors" resulting in Bechi's parole being revoked. He has now been returned to prison.
Immigration and Corrections Minister Agus Andrianto told the BBC that those responsible for approving Bechi's parole "will certainly face sanctions".
"We want to make sure that such mistakes or irregularities do not happen again," he said.
For Ira Puspitasari, one of several former students who accused Bechi of sexual abuse and testified at his trial, the decision is a vindication.
"I'm amazed, really. I didn't expect the government would pay such detailed attention to this case and really pay attention to us, the victims," she said.
Ira, who has waived her legal right to anonymity, told the BBC she was raped and sexually abused by Bechi for more than four years, from the age of 15.
"I was treated as his slave. I was held captive, raped, beaten," she said.
She said she tried to run away but Bechi's private security guards tracked her down, kidnapped her and took her to a secluded hut, where Bechi tortured and raped her.
She said she reported all of this to the police but was then intimidated into withdrawing her complaint. She also shared an audio recording of Bechi's mother telling her to say that "nothing had happened".

Watching BBC undercover footage of Bechi smiling and greeting supporters at an event in March, when he should still have been in prison, Ira became tearful.
"It's like nothing ever happened," she said.
Ira was invited to a parliamentary hearing this week into the state's handling of sexual abuse cases in religious and educational institutions, held in response to the BBC's investigation.
Lawyer Joko Jumadi, who has represented several victims of abuse in educational institutions, also addressed the hearing and said authorities were often reluctant to investigate allegations of abuse because they involved "influential religious figures who have large followings".
He told the hearing that he regularly faced threats and intimidation as a result of taking on such cases.
Bechi is the son of prominent Islamic cleric Muhammad Mukhtar Mu'thi, founder of the Shiddiqiyyah Islamic boarding school in Jombang, East Java.
He was arrested in 2022 after a 15-hour police siege at the school, where supporters had gathered to prevent his arrest.
Prosecutors had sought a longer sentence after Bechi was accused of rape by a number of students, but he was acquitted of the rape charges and convicted of the lesser sexual assault offence of one student.
The BBC sought comment from Bechi, his mother and the Shiddiqiyyah boarding school as part of its investigation but received no response.

It was, says Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport.
Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament.
At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren".
Plenty heard him.
Five days later, the team's semi-final against Uruguay was the most-watched thing of the evening on Israeli television, drawing a 23% viewing share.
Politicians clamoured to congratulate the team.
It was June 2023.
"That summer, everybody was watching under-20 football, everybody knew the players," says Rakovsky, who was covering the team for Israeli media outlet Haaretz.
"Everybody in Israel fell in love with these kids."
It wasn't just their deeds on the pitch that felt otherworldly, though.
After scoring a stoppage-time winner against Uzbekistan in the last 16, Anan Khalaili had given an interview to Israeli television.
In it Khalaili, an Israeli Arab, thanked the viewers back home for staying up late to watch his team win in Argentina.
To do so, he used the words 'Am Yisrael' - a Hebrew phrase that means 'People of Israel' and is bound up in Jewish religion, community, culture and history.
"That an Arab player used that figure of speech said something about the identity of that team," says Rakovsky.
"That team made real the claim that football can really bring people together - that Muslim players are part of the national team of the Jewish state, representing Israel and creating something better, both for the present and future."
But a little over four months after Khalaili's interview and the win over Brazil, Hamas attacked Israel.
The armed Palestinian group killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians., external
As the war goes on, can the potential of a golden generation of Israel's footballers, in sport and society, be realised?
Beaten 1-0 by eventual champions Uruguay, Israel finished third at that Under-20 World Cup in 2023.
Their run was no fluke.
The same set of players, with a few additions and omissions, had already impressed at continental level.
They were runners-up at 2022's Under-19 Euros, beaten by England in extra-time in the final, and would go on to make the semi-finals of 2023's Under-20 Euros.
Israel has produced outstanding players in the past. Eyal Berkovic and Yossi Benayoun were technical, gifted attackers with long Premier League careers.
But a depth of talent, emerging together, sets the current cohort apart.
Khalaili has been one of the most sought-after young prospects in Europe this summer.
After his £21.5m move to Inter Milan fell through, Crystal Palace saw off competition from Nottingham Forest to pick him up for a similar fee from Belgian side Union Saint-Gilloise.
Playmaker Oscar Gloukh, 22, wears Ajax's number 10 shirt after his form earned a move from Red Bull Salzburg.
Left-back Roy Revivo signed for Spanish club Elche on transfer deadline day this month from Maccabi Tel Aviv, while Twente defender Stav Lemkin, also 23, is also highly rated.
Dor Turgeman, Ilay Feingold and Idan Toklomati are impressing in Major League Soccer in the United States.
All have now won full caps, but were moulded into a collective, cohesive unit - something that has often been beyond the senior side - by Israel's age-grade coach Ofir Haim.
"It isn't an issue at all here," Haim said, external of the different backgrounds in his squad during the 2023 Under-20 World Cup.
"We don't have any problem with religion. Not at all. We have players here who put on tefillin [Jewish ceremonial wear, containing verses from the Torah] - and Anan [Khalaili], Hamza [Shibli] and Ahmed [Salman] perform the Muslim prayers.
"We don't even talk about this. We unite everybody, and I wish the country were as united as this team."
Football has long been the part of Israeli society where communities mix together who may not otherwise meet.
"The majority of the Jewish people who arrived in the mandate period [a spell between 1923 and 1948 where the region was run by Britain] emigrated from Europe," says Dr Omer Einav, a historian and author of Defending the Goal, a book on Israel's football history.
"They were Europeans and when you think about cinema, music, theatre, dance, they had nothing in common with Middle Eastern culture. Nothing, except football. That was the only common language, the only thing they both love in the same way."
Encouraged by the British administrators who ran the region, teams from different communities, and some made up of elements of each, would play against each other.
When the modern state of Israel was formed in 1948, much of the Arab population that remained inside its borders continued to identify as or with Palestinians. Most still do.
They are also an intrinsic part of Israeli football.
While they make up 20% of Israel's population, they represent about 35% of those involved in the sport at elite level nationally.
The first Arab player to represent Israel's national team was Rifaat Turk in 1976. In 2018, Bibars Natcho became the first Muslim to captain the team.
Neither was without controversy.
Turk was roundly abused. Natcho's decision not to sing Israel's national anthem, the lyrics of which relate to the Jewish search for a homeland, was condemned by some., external
For a short time in the summer of 2023, it seemed as if Haim's under-20 side might offer a watershed moment of unity and co-existence.
But football, like everything in Israel, changed on 7 October.
Matan Segal directed Kick It Out Israel, an anti-discrimination initiative with similar aims but no link to the English organisation of the same name, for almost four years before stepping down a few months ago.
Racism has long been present in Israeli club football. Beitar Jerusalem's fans are among the most notorious.
In 2013, ultras burned down their own club's offices in protest at the signing of two Chechen Muslims.
The most extreme Beitar fans have long taunted Israeli Arabs with chants of "may your village burn", while declaring themselves "forever pure".
However during his time at Kick It Out Israel, Segal saw racism against Arab players become more virulent and widespread.
Covid, during which fans radicalised online during lockdown, was one cause.
The election of Israel's far-right government at the end of 2022, legitimising views towards Palestinians that were previously seen as extreme, was a second.
The war was undoubtedly another.
"Before 7 October, people generally respected the Arab players," Segal said.
"Even though they had difficulties with them not singing the Israeli anthem, they respected them and they could talk about it.
"After 7 October though, we saw an increase in racist remarks.
"It was happening at small clubs where we hadn't seen it before. There were terrible songs - 'Let's kill all Arabs', 'There are no schools in Gaza because there are no children left'."
Football, inevitably, has become a focal point for emotion generated by the conflict.
Clubs which are usually bitter rivals came together to remember those killed by Hamas. Scarves were part of the commemoration at the site of the Nova music festival, where hundreds were killed.
Hapoel Jerusalem's club badge now features a silhouette of Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was abducted and killed in captivity and whose parents have campaigned for peace through their grief.
Meanwhile, Israeli Defence Force (IDF) soldiers have posed with club flags and banners while on operation in Gaza, dedicating their actions to the clubs and ultras back home., external
In such a heightened atmosphere, young footballers – closely connected to the conflict through Israel's programme of national service and a barrage of online commentary and images – are under constant scrutiny and pressure.
Gloukh's lifelong friend Afik Tery was killed by a Hamas explosive while serving in the IDF.
After his death, Gloukh posted a poignant set of pictures, external of the pair arm-in-arm over time - as young boys at birthday parties, as young men at a wedding - with the final slide showing Tery's funeral.
Among the online replies were the taunts of pro-Palestinians.
For Israel players with Palestinian heritage, the stakes are especially and dangerously high.
Dia Saba plays in a similar playmaking role to Gloukh. The 33-year-old has scored three goals in 13 appearances for Israel.
He is unlikely ever to add to that tally.
Saba was one of Maccabi Haifa's most high-profile stars when, at the start of the conflict, his wife Narmin posted a message to Instagram.
"There are children in Gaza, too," she wrote.
Saba apologised for the outrage caused, but could not save his career in Israel. He left Maccabi Haifa in 2025 and now plays for Turkish side Amedspor.
"My dream was to play for Maccabi Haifa, the club that I support, the team that I grew up with," Saba said at the time.
"I wanted to continue. But sometimes there are reasons that are stronger than us that don't allow it."
Saba and others are used to having their loyalty questioned. From all sides.
Many in the Arab world would like more Palestinian prospects within Israel to follow the example of Ataa Jaber.
Jaber captained Israel's Under-21 side but switched nationalities, external to represent Palestine in June 2023, saying he could no longer separate sport and politics after seeing police evict Palestinian families from their homes in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem.
Switching away from a high level of international football damaged his prospects of a move to Europe. At home, there were calls for his Israeli citizenship to be revoked. But, for Jaber, it was preferable to representing a country whose actions he deplored.
Those footballers who voice an opinion on the conflict choose their words carefully.
Beram Kayal, the former Brighton, Celtic and Israel player, knows the dilemmas and reality well.
"To be Arabic in Israel, it's sometimes hard," he says. "Sometimes it is tough.
"Opportunities-wise, sometimes we are not on the same level."
However, he believes in a pluralistic future for Israel and football as a tool to achieve it.
His friendship with Tomer Hemed - whom he first met as a young teenager at Maccabi Haifa's academy and later played alongside at Brighton and Charlton, as well as international level - sums up his approach.
"When I played with Tomer, he prayed like this," he says, touching his hand to his back of his head to indicate a kippah, the small skullcap worn as a sign of Jewish faith.
"And I was praying for Allah," he adds, raising his arms above his shoulders in worship.
"He was my team-mate and he is my brother.
"In football, on the pitch, you never look at colour, culture or religion. You just want the best people around you to win the game."
The 38-year-old is now employed by Israel's Football Association to work with young talents from Palestinian areas.
In doing so he works alongside former Israel goalkeeper Boni Ginzburg, who played across Glasgow at Rangers and is now the IFA's technical director.
After Arabic was relegated behind Hebrew as Israel's official language by a controversial 2018 law promoted by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the IFA put on Hebrew language lessons for Arabic-speaking coaches to ensure they could still obtain their qualifications.
"Not in our building," says Kayal when asked about the precedence given to Hebrew.
"I'm in this place [the IFA] to bring the culture of the Arabic people to the table.
"I say to the Arabic players when they come into the national team: Speak in your language, don't be afraid, don't be shy to speak, don't just afraid to show yourself.
"Israel is a young country. We need to learn from our DNA, to see the different between the Jewish, the Circassians, the Arabic, the Muslim, the Christian, the Druze – all the colours – put that together and learn what we could do better."
Israel's aim is to go better than their national team has managed in more than 50 years.
Ran Ben-Shimon was appointed as the senior side's head coach in 2024. He was given the goal of converting youthful promise into qualification for Euro 2028, which will be staged in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.
Success would place more stress on Israel's players and, potentially, squad unity.
Large-scale protests are planned for Republic of Ireland's forthcoming Nations League matches with Israel. Dublin will host seven games at the tournament.
Villa Park in Birmingham, from which Maccabi Tel Aviv fans were banned from attending a Europa League match in November, will stage four matches.
Hampden Park, two miles across Glasgow from where Celtic fans have held vociferous pro-Palestine protests, has six.
Wherever Israel play, players will be confronted with criticism of their country's treatment of Palestinians, both at home and in Gaza, that is rarely voiced at home.
"Israelis are very sensitive to anyone showing any kind of sympathy for what happened on 7 October," says Dr Sophia Solomon, part of Ben-Gurion University's Center for Sports Diplomacy.
"It is like denying the Holocaust, that is the proportion of it. A war is a special situation, it wasn't like this before, but to express your agony became more encouraged as we saw the European arena become more anti-Israeli.
"One reaction ignited another and there is more obligation to identify yourself with the victims of 7 October."
She believes that it will take time for Israeli society, footballers included, to understand the past three years and speak openly about the conflict.
"Until the ongoing war ends, no-one can say what he thinks," she said. "Even after the Middle East returns to its 'normal' craziness, maybe it will take a decade to pass before people can start talking about their experiences and expectations.
"Time has to pass until you can touch certain areas, and at the moment you can see a lot of avoidance about talking about it, even mentioning it."
The time for this stellar generation to fulfil their potential may come before that.
It may not. Translating youth-level promise to senior-level product is never simple.
But, whatever the future holds, for a few months, in the summer of 2023, Haim and his team gave Israel something special.
"We saw Anan Khalaili and Hamza Shibli scoring against Brazil and that was our hope, that was the future. That was our future," says Einav.
"I'm not so optimistic, but people thought maybe it's really a magical thing that can help Israeli society in general.
"There was something there, something new, something where people said 'OK, if we co-operate, if we work together, we can also succeed in sport.'
"That's what we all care about, right? We want to be good at sports. We are sick of watching the World Cup from our living room.
"I think football is in some isolated, sterilised dimension - some kind of bubble - inside Israeli society. It is not hermetic. A lot of dirt comes in - racism, violence - but I do believe that football can reflect good things that can happen. The equality of chances, the tolerance and solidarity of all people living here.
"It can't heal anything but it can help us see one another in a more human way.
"So, yeah there was definitely a moment, but it was before our world changed and collapsed."
Only time will tell what remains of that moment and whether it can be revived.

WASHINGTON — The brand drug industry’s main trade group is suing the Trump administration over a pilot program tying Medicare drug prices to those in peer countries.
The Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America said Wednesday that it had filed a complaint in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia asserting that the so-called “most-favored nation” pilot in Medicare Part B exceeds Medicare’s statutory authority.
The pilot, called GLOBE, is not expected to have much impact because the administration exempted all but a handful of companies in return for their agreement to voluntary deals to charge Medicaid MFN prices.

On the Nobel Prize, healthcare inequities, mental health, new research, and more
(In the weekly Health Matters newsletter, Zubeda Hamid writes about getting to good health, and staying there. You can subscribe here to get the newsletter in your inbox.)
This week began with a bang: the Nobel Prizes are being announced, and first in the line-up was the prize for medicine or physiology. Additionally this week, we’ve looked at access to, and affordability of healthcare in India, mental health and research developments.
The Nobel Prize
Nobel week is always exciting: guessing games are played as to who will win the prize; there’s surprise (or not) once the winner is announced and the work behind the prize is delved into and decoded. This week was no different. The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, announced on Monday (October 5, 2026) went jointly to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegeman and Georg Nagel “for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.” What is optogenetics you ask? Ramya Kannanexplains that it is a method that makes it possible to show how nerve cells shape memories, feelings and behaviour in the brain. Sounds exciting, doesn’t it, especially as it concerns an organ that has long remained mysterious. What was also interesting was that it upended what was touted to be a favourite for this year’s prize: the GLP-1 class of drugs. Do also watch our video on the prize.
Access and affordability in India
For all of the progress the country has made in medicine, for all of the breakthroughs, scientific advances and use of AI, it’s disheartening -- but also important -- to remember that access to quality healthcare is still not something everyone can take for granted. A video that circulated widely on social media a few days ago showed a Dalit woman who was allegedly denied admission to a government hospital in Bhadohi district, Uttar Pradesh, while in labour and was forced to deliver outside the hospital in public. The victim’s family alleged untouchability, reportsMayank Kumar. Around the same time, an ill child died in his mother’s arms in Meghalaya’s West Khasi Hills district during his parents’ three-hour trek to reach the nearest hospital. The village headman said the boy’s parents tried to arrange for a vehicle after his health deteriorated at night on October 1. No driver wanted to come to the village because of the poor road conditions.
Stories like these force us to stop and ask ourselves what our definition of ‘progress’ really is, and if we’ve progressed at all, if we can’t ensure basic access to care for all our citizens.
Even when care is available though, the question of affordability remains -- a question we delved into last week, amid the Supreme Court’s scrutiny of drug prices that Aaratrika Bhaumik is tracking. This week, Bindu Shajan Perappadanreports that the Jan Swasthya Abhiyan and the Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatment have called for regulation of charges levied by private hospitals and ceilings on trade margins for medicines, medical devices and medical consumables. C. Maya, meanwhile asks, if the Keralam government’s promise to make private health care more affordable is possible, given that it is still in a legal battle with the private sector over the Kerala Clinical Establishments Act, 2018.
Spotlighting mental health
Ahead of World Mental Health Day, which falls on October 10, Afshan Yasmeen reported on a study from NIMHANS that revealed temperamental traits and adverse experiences during childhood may together offer clues to vulnerability to major psychiatric disorders. Such studies could help determine whether particular temperamental characteristics precede the onset of psychiatric illness or are partly consequences of illness and its treatment.
Another story this week looks at a subject that doesn’t often make it to mainstream news headlines: Dr. Sachin Barbde, Dr. Christianez Ratna Kiruba and Dr. Debasmita Saren write on rethinking suicide prevention in Adivasi communities, calling for better representation of Adivasi communities across the spectrum, the fostering of community spaces that offer familiar language, relationships, cultural understanding and for policies to do things with Adivasis, not for them.
Chennai-based organisation, SCARF, meanwhile, unveiled a ‘Wall of Hope’, an initiative that encourages young people to express, share, and reflect upon their personal reasons for living, through brief messages of hope, and thereby, foster conversations around mental health and encourage help-seeking.
Research developments
The Nobel Prize has made it to all the headlines this week, but there’s been some other interesting research too! Dr. C. Aravinda and Dr. Veera Rajagopal look at an experiment by Stanford University researchers called ‘xenocortication’ that lets human brain tissue develop inside a living mouse, offering a novel way to study the developing human brain and, potentially, how disease develops.
Another study, this published in The Lancet Global Health journal, found that India is among the top countries with 90% of the world’s chewing tobacco-related health burden -- highlighting the urgent need for action.
A recent report on E.coli contamination in Kerala in flood-affected areas along the Meenachil river detected the bacteria in 67% of the samples -- what this means, is explained in this story.
Bo Wang, in The Conversation, explains why turning artificial intelligence research into real-world tools isn’t always straightforward: systems that perform well in controlled lab settings often fall short when deployed in homes, in hospitals or on city streets.
And finally, shining a light on the people behind all of the research work, Dinesh C. Sharma profiles Gursaran Prasad Talwar, scientist, institution builder, lifelong researcher who is now 100.
And some more:
Dr. Subramanian Swaminathan tells you what you need to know about seasonal infections
Athira Elssa Johnson talks to doctors about brain fog and when it should be evaluated, and also writes on the social media trend ‘ferritin face’
Geetha Srimathi, in our all you need to know series writes on Swyer syndrome

P.S. Niranjana writes on vitiligo and speaks to people affected by the condition

Nobel laureate Barry Marshall stresses that eradicating H. pylori can prevent gastric cancer

US-based AI cloud infrastructure provider CoreWeave has announced its entry into India, with plans to deploy 240 MW (megawatts) of data centre capacity in Navi Mumbai in partnership with AdaniConneX. The planned campus will comprise three 80 MW buildings at AdaniConneX’s Taloja facility. The first phase is expected to be operational by mid-2028, with additional capacity coming online in phases. CoreWeave will be the sole tenant across the three buildings and will have the option to add another 240 MW at the campus, taking the potential total capacity to 480 MW. AdaniConneX is a 50:50 joint venture between Adani Enterprises and US-based data centre operator EdgeConneX. CoreWeave plans to deploy NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin platform at the campus through its AI cloud platform to support AI training, inference, reasoning, and agentic workloads. The company also plans to establish an India office and hire locally to work with customers and partners in the country’s AI ecosystem. “We are investing in the infrastructure, technology, and local presence needed to support that growth, bringing 240 megawatts of capacity, NVIDIA Vera Rubin, and CoreWeave’s expertise to customers building and scaling AI in India,” said CoreWeave COO Sachin Jain. The Taloja facilities are being designed for high-density AI infrastructure and will feature direct liquid cooling for GPU data halls and a non-evaporative chilled water system. The expansion comes amid growing investment in India’s AI and data centre infrastructure, with Adani Group pursuing projects with global technology companies. In February, Adani Group announced plans to invest $100 Bn in renewable energy-powered AI data centres by 2035 as part of its sovereign AI infrastructure push. In March, the conglomerate was reported to be in talks with Google and Meta to set up data centres in India. These discussions followed AdaniConneX’s partnership with Google, announced in October 2025, for an AI data centre campus in Visakhapatnam as part of Google’s $15 Bn investment. Uber also announced in May that it was setting up its first data centre in India with Adani Group to test and deploy its technology. At the time, Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said the facility was expected to be operational later in 2026. In June, Adani Group also partnered with US-based manufacturer Jabil to manufacture liquid-cooled AI racks, servers, storage units, and networking systems in India for global hyperscalers and enterprise data centres.

WHO welcomed Mr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Spain’s Secretary of State for Health and his delegation on 23 and 24 April 2024 to discuss joint global health priorities. Amongst others, Spain's focus is on universal health coverage and health systems strengthening; pandemic response and emergency medical teams; organ and tissue transplantation; malaria and other tropical diseases; and polio.
During the visit, participants focused on plans and on-going work across a number of areas, including WHO’s Transplantation Program to increase availability; ethical access and oversight of transplantation of human cells; tissues and organs. They also discussed social determinants of health; tobacco and alcohol control; primary health care; access to medicines; universal health coverage; ensuring healthy lives at all ages; nutrition and food safety; health workforce; and emergencies.
Mr Javier Padilla was accompanied by Ms Paola Cannata Molero, Director of the Cabinet of the Secretary of State for Health, Mr Jacobo Fernández Álvarez, Technical Secretary General, Mr Héctor Tejero Franco, Advisor in the Cabinet of the Minister of Health and Responsible for Health and Climate Change, and Mr Roberto Carro Vázquez, Senior Technician of the Office of the Secretary of State for Health. The delegation also had representatives of Spain’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office and Other International Organizations in Geneva, including H.E. Ambassador Ms A. Díaz-Rato Revuelta, H.E. Ambassador Ms Clara Cabrera Brasero, and Counsellor Ms María del Carmen Martínez de la Peña.
The Spanish delegation met with Dr Ailan Li, Assistant Director General (ADG) for Universal Health Coverage, Healthier Populations, Dr Catharina Boehme, ADG for External Relations and Governance, Dr Yukiko Nakatani, ADG for Access to Medicines and Health products and ADG for Antimicrobial Resistance ad interim, Dr Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director for WHO Health Health Emergencies Programme.
Left to right: Dr Maria Neira, Director, Environment, Climate Change and Health, H.E. Ambassador Aurora Díaz-Rato Revuelta, Dr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Secretary of State for Health, Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director, WHO Health Emergencies Programme. Credit: WHO/Chris Black
WHO’s Management and their teams thanked Spain for their financial and technical support over the years. Spain’s support was instrumental in the last biennium in improving access to quality essential health services and medicines; addressing climate change and healthier environments; and strengthening country capacity in both data and innovation. Spain continues to be a champion of the Global Polio Eradication Initiative.
Spain also contributes to WHO’s work in tackling malaria and neglected and other tropical diseases, and has helped the Organization strengthen countries’ preparedness, readiness, prevention and response for health emergencies, epidemics and pandemics. Spain’s contribution to WHO’s Health Emergency Appeal has helped to protect health in humanitarian emergencies to break the cycles of poverty.
As a world leader in the field of organ and tissue transplantation, Spain plays a key role in WHO’s efforts through its Ministry of Health to improve the safety, quality, efficacy and access to transplants. WHO appreciates and acknowledges Spain as a partner who is not only leading and sharing expertise in support of countries’ development of sustainable, self-sufficient organ transplant systems, but also more generally, a key partner to WHO in health for all.

In Summary
- Sennheiser has updated its Momentum Wireless series and has launched the Momentum 5 Wireless headphones.
- The Momentum range has been famous mainly for its sound quality, but brings more to the table with the Momentum 5 Wireless, including elements like spatial audio and head tracking, and a sleeker carrying case.
- However, along with these upgrades, comes an upgraded price tag as well, which puts the Momentum 5 Wireless in the same price league as the Sony WH-1000XM6. It is still the master of sound, but can it also challenge others in areas like ANC and calling?
Whenever someone asks us to recommend ANC headphones with great audio quality, Sennheiser’s Momentum Wireless series is among the first to come to our minds. Yes, they are very good in other departments too – they are premium flagship headphones after all – but their real strength has been their sound. If someone prioritizes top-notch ANC and calling or even slightly more bass-y mainstream sound, the momentum (pun intended) shifts towards the likes of the Sony WH-1000 XM series, Bose’s QuietComfort and JBL’s Tour series. The Momentum 5 Wireless could change that. With it, Sennheiser has upped its ANC and calling game considerably, while adding a few new dimensions to its already strong audio performance. The result: perhaps the most mainstream Momentum Wireless ever, and one that can compete in many departments, and not just audio.
Table of Contents
Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless Design and Appearance: Flatter, and a little flash
In terms of design, the Momentum 5 are a refined version of the Momentum. The outer parts of the cups are flatter, and the finish is cleaner. We got the Denim variant, which has a dark blue exterior with mauve-colored cushioning on the earpads and headbands, giving the headphones a very distinct dual-tone look. While most of the headphones are made of plastic, the headband also has a cloth-like, textured finish, which is a classy touch. Rather unusually, there are a lot of shiny elements on the Momentum 5 – there are metallic colored circles with the Sennheiser logo at each of the ends of the headband, as well as microphones in metallic enclosures on the earcups, two of which have Sennheiser branding.
The right ear cup contains all the ports and buttons: a single control button, a 2.5 mm audio jack and a USB Type-C port. There is also a line of LEDs next to the button to show connectivity and battery status. There are no volume control buttons or a 3.5 mm jack (Sennheiser has opted for a 2.5 mm one, although there is a cable that allows you to connect the headphones to a device with a 3.5 mm jack), but the outer part of the right earcup has a touch panel.
The right and left earcups are clearly marked on the inner part of the earcups. The earcups fold 180 degrees but not inwards, which means that they cannot fold up completely, which means that one cannot just bunch them up and put them in a bag. The hinges around which the earcups move are well built, and although the headphones are mainly made of plastic, they have a very solid feel to them.
At around 290 grams, the Momentum 5 Wireless are on the heavier side (the Sony WH-1000 XM6 are about 255 grams), but thanks to all the cushioning, are comfortable to wear. The clamping force is also just right, keeping the headphones in place without making us feel that our head was being squeezed. While they will stay in place during a brisk walk or even a jogging session, we would advise against using them while working out as they do not have any IP rating.
The Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless have been released in an assortment of colors, although they are currently available in black and blue. The black ones are understated and elegant, but the blue ones will turn heads with their dual tone and metal accents. They come in a smart, flat hard case, with a slightly recessed section that makes them easy to carry. It is a tough case and is slim enough not to take up too much space in your backpack or bag. There are two cables in the package: a Type-C to Type-C and a 2.5 mm to 3.5 mm.
Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless Specs and Features: Hello, spatial audio, head tracking, more mics and much more…
The Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless are a big step forward from the Momentum 4 Wireless, although they come with a similar-sounding 42 mm Dynamic Driver. Whereas Sennheiser had in the past avoided features like head tracking and spatial audio, these are very much present in the Momentum 5 Wireless, which come with 3D Spatial Audio, head tracking and support for Dolby Atmos. They also come with 8 microphones for hybrid active noise cancellation, which is double the number on the Momentum 4 (and claim to deliver three times superior ANC), although still less than the 12 on the Sony WH-1000 XM6.
There are considerable improvements on the audio front too – the headphones now come with aptX Lossless as well as adaptive, and users now have access to an 8-band equalizer (the Momentum 4 had a 5-band EQ), which they can completely customize as well. Like the Momentum 4, the Momentum 5 also supports hi-res audio wirelessly as well as through the Type-C port.
Apart from this, the Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless come with Bluetooth 5.4, active noise cancellation (ANC), an anti-wind mode, multiple device connectivity, on-head detection, own voice detection, and, if you have a compatible dongle, also a gaming mode. And in a very notable move, the Momentum 5 Wireless come with a removable and replaceable battery (Sennheiser says even a user can do so using a Philips screwdriver) which can deliver up to 57 hours of audio with ANC on. In spec and feature terms, the Momentum 5 Wireless are a big step up from the Momentum 4 Wireless.
Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless Interface and App: Business as usual
In terms of interface, the Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless are very similar to the Momentum 4 Wireless. All the controls are on the right earcup and are a blend of touch, taps, and swipes. The single button is used to switch the headphones on and off, and long-pressing puts the headphones in pairing mode.
Gestures are a little complicated. Sliding your finger up and down regulates the volume, which is fine and works smoothly. A single tap pauses and resumes audio; sliding your finger horizontally from back to front takes you to the next track, while sliding it from front to back takes you to the previous track. Sliding forward and holding triggers fast forward, while sliding backward and holding results in a rewind. Two taps let you switch between ANC and transparency mode, while two taps with two fingers turn Dolby Atmos on and off. One can accept a call by sliding a finger forward and end a call by sliding it backward. It is not a super intuitive set of instructions and takes a bit of getting used to, especially the gestures that involve finger sliding.
However, pinching and expanding your fingers, which should decrease and increase transparency levels, take a bit of getting used to. One cannot customize these gestures or the button, and while there are tone and voice prompts, there is no way to invoke a virtual assistant from the headphones, which is a bit odd these days.
Detailed controls and settings of the headphones are available on the Sennheiser Smart Control + app, which works smoothly with both iOS and Android. One can tweak the levels of ANC one needs (our tip: leave it at Adaptive, where it works best), turn Immersive Audio (or spatial audio) and head tracking on and off, find your headphones, check features, get updates, and also turn touch controls on and off. The app also gives you access to the 8-band equalizer, which has 8 presets (Speech Clarity, Rock, Pop, Dance, Hip-Hop, Classical, Movie, and Jazz), as well as options to let the software create your own Sound Personalization profiles. You can even set different presets and noise cancellation levels for different places – for instance, I set the headphones to switch to transparency mode when I am home, and to a high ANC mode when I am at my favorite cafe. It actually works very smoothly. The app is simple and easy to use. It does not offer the kind of options one gets on JBL’s companion app, but is classically Sennheiser – focusing on strong basics.
Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless Sound Quality: Upping the bass, adding soundstage, without sacrificing detail
Sennheiser’s Momentum range has always been known for its detailed yet well-balanced sound. And the Momentum 5 Wireless deliver the same level of detail that we are used to in the series, but there is one subtle change – these have a slightly higher accent on bass. The result is a sound that is warm and pleasant. Sennheiser’s handling of the mids (generally the vocals) is masterly as usual – voices sound clear and are never overwhelmed by other frequencies.
There is a slight reduction in the level of treble, though, giving these a slightly softer sound. This might annoy some of the purists, who love tinkling treble, but will please most listeners. There is a bit more “punch” to the Momentum 5 Wireless than any of their predecessors, but it is important to note that this does not come at the cost of clarity. If anything, the slight stress on bass gives the Momentum 5 Wireless a slightly richer sound and a distinct audio flavor, different from the Momentum 4 Wireless, which now seem a little plain in comparison. There is a “Bass Boost” option in the app, but even switching it on does not make the bass overwhelming or rumbly. In many ways, the Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless’ handling of bass is similar to what we used to get from Bose in 2016 – warm without ever getting fuzzy.
Whether it is watching films, playing games, listening to podcasts or a wide variety of music, the Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless deliver detailed, clear and pleasant sound. Of course, one can change the frequency levels using the excellent equalizer options in the companion app, but it is a fair chance that you will love how the Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless sound right out of the box.
Spatial audio or Immersive audio with Dolby Atmos helps in creating a wider soundstage, and enabling head tracking allows you to get the feeling of being actually in a room in which audio is playing, as every time you move your head, the source of the sound changes subtly, just as it would in a real room. Do keep in mind, though, that using immersive audio will reduce the volume levels a bit. Speaking of volume levels, the Momentum 5 Wireless are classic Sennheiser – you will get a sense of loudness at maxed-out volumes but are unlikely to ever feel in danger of being deafened (as can happen with some other brands).
There are a few minor irritants. The Head Detection system is a little too sensitive at times, so even moving the headphones slightly sometimes led to the audio pausing. Even sudden movements of the head sometimes triggered it. Perhaps this could be addressed in a software update. Similarly, it would be great if one could control ANC levels through a pinch or an expand gesture, just as one can change transparency levels. Finally, we do wish Sennheiser would put volume control buttons back on the Momentums – the swipe up and down are not as convenient.
Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless ANC, Calls and Battery Life: Finally, a contender in all categories
Perhaps the most dramatic change in the Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless as compared to the Momentum 4 has been the improvement in both ANC and call quality. While the Momentum 4 Wireless is supposed to be the boss in terms of audio quality, its ANC and call handling abilities were decent, rather than exceptional. The Momentum 5 Wireless changes that. The ANC on the headphones was streets ahead of what we got on the Momentum 4 Wireless or even the more recent HDB-630. The headphones were able to drown out a fair degree of the hum of the Metro and the traffic, and made it easy to work even in relatively loud cafes. No, they do not deliver the sort of Sounds of Silence that the Sony WH-1000XM6 serve up, but they are not too far behind, and can easily match them in most general circumstances. We also feel they are comfortably ahead of the Bose QuietComfort series in this regard. Transparency mode, however, needs a bit of work as external sounds can sometimes be a little muffled, although it is very usable.
Call quality has also improved significantly and is on par with other flagships. You cannot tweak your own voice or that of the speakers as you can on JBL’s headphones, but call clarity is excellent, and most of the people we spoke with did not even realize we were using headphones, which is the litmus test for calling.
Battery life on the Momentum 5 Wireless is similar to that of the Momentum 4. Sennheiser claims 57 hours with ANC, and we got through close to ten days of regular use on a single charge, which involved 5-6 hours of daily usage. Sennheiser also claims that ten minutes of charging can give one up to seven hours of audio, and this is once again close to our experience – we generally got between 5-6 hours. We have been told that the battery will easily last 4-5 years, so the need to change it manually is unlikely to arise soon, but having the option is reassuring. Switching between devices was smooth – once paired with two devices, the Momentum 5 Wireless moved to whichever one produced sound.
Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless Review Verdict: Should you buy?
The Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless are available for Rs 39,990 (USD 399.95). That is significantly more expensive than the Momentum 4 Wireless, which were launched at Rs 34,990 (USD 349.95), but had been available for about Rs 26,990 (USD 199.95) for the past year or so. But with that higher price come very significant improvements, especially in ANC and call quality, as well as a slightly warmer, richer sound. Purists and hardcore loyalists might not like this, but they can always set matters right with the equalizer or go for the Sennheiser HDB 630, which are arguably the best audiophile-level Bluetooth headphones around and cost about Rs 4,000 more.
The Momentum 5 Wireless face stiff competition from the Sony WH-1000XM6, which come with a similar price tag, and are pretty much the bosses in the ANC segment. A detailed comparison of these two is coming up soon, but we can safely say that the Momentum’s improved ANC means that the days of “if you want great audio, get the Momentum, and if you want great ANC, get the Sony” are over. The Momentum 5 Wireless are the most mainstream-sounding Momentum headphones we have used, and deliver great sound without compromises on ANC and call quality. They are easily the best-sounding ANC headphones you can get for under Rs 40,000 (USD 400), and this time the ANC rocks as much as the sound does!
